If the EC2 SG has a restrictive outbound that only allows specific destinations, the Interface Endpoint ENI IP or SG must be added.<br> *Common misconfiguration: Interface Endpoint created, private DNS enabled, but EC2 SG has outbound rule only to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443. Since traffic goes to the ENI private IP (not 0.0.0.0/0), if the outbound rule is only for specific IPs, it may need updating. Generally 0.0.0.0/0 outbound on 443 from EC2 allows both NAT and endpoint traffic.<br>

790. [ VPC-Endpoints ] In a Well-Architected review for a company using only NAT Gateways for all AWS service traffic, what is the highest-priority recommendation? ; Immediately create Gateway Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (free, no risk). These are the highest-volume, highest-cost AWS service API calls in most workloads. Eliminating NAT Gateway processing ($0.045/GB) for S3/DynamoDB traffic provides immediate cost reduction. Then audit Interface Endpoint opportunities for other high-volume services (SQS, SNS, Secrets Manager, KMS). <br><br> *NAT Gateway cost structure: $0.045/hr + $0.045/GB. For a workload processing 1 TB/day to S3: $0.045 × 1,000 GB/day = $45/day = $1,350/month for NAT data processing alone. Gateway Endpoint eliminates this entirely. At $0 cost for Gateway Endpoint, the ROI is immediate.<br> *Well-Architected Cost Optimization pillar: specifically recommends using VPC Endpoints to avoid NAT Gateway charges for AWS service traffic. AWS Trusted Advisor and Cost Optimization Hub both surface "Enable VPC Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB" as a high-priority finding.<br> *Security improvement as bonus: moving traffic off the internet path (even via NAT) to AWS backbone reduces attack surface. A Well-Architected Security pillar recommendation as well. Two pillar improvements from a single free action.<br>


791. [ S3 ] What is the maximum size of a single object that can be stored in Amazon S3? ; 5 TB. A single S3 object can be up to 5 TB in size. Objects larger than 5 GB must use multipart upload, objects up to 5 GB can use a single PUT. <br><br> *Multipart upload is required for objects exceeding 5 GB in a single PUT request. AWS recommends multipart upload for objects larger than 100 MB to benefit from parallelism and retry efficiency.<br> *The 5 TB limit is a hard limit — no workaround exists. For datasets exceeding 5 TB per file, the data must be split into multiple objects or a different storage service (e.g., EFS or FSx) must be used.<br> *For exam questions about "maximum object size in S3" the answer is always 5 TB. For "maximum single PUT size" the answer is 5 GB.<br>

792. [ S3 ] What are the three versioning states of an S3 bucket, and can a bucket return to the unversioned state? ; The three states are: Unversioned (default), Versioning-Enabled, and Versioning-Suspended. Once versioning is enabled on a bucket, it can only be suspended — it cannot return to the unversioned state. <br><br> *In the Unversioned state, objects have no version IDs. Overwriting an object replaces it permanently. Deleting removes the object with no recovery option.<br> *In Versioning-Suspended state, new uploads receive a `null` version ID, but all previously stored versions are preserved. This is useful when you want to stop incurring version storage costs for new uploads while protecting existing versions.<br> *This behavior is a common exam trap: "Disable versioning on a bucket" is not a valid option. The answer is always Suspend, not Disable.<br>

793. [ S3 ] What is the difference between a delete marker and permanently deleting an object version in a versioned S3 bucket? ; A delete marker is created when you DELETE an object without specifying a version ID — it hides the object from standard GET requests but does not remove any versions. Permanently deleting a specific version requires specifying the version ID in the DELETE request, which irreversibly removes that version. <br><br> *Delete markers have their own version ID and are themselves objects in the bucket. To restore a deleted object: delete the delete marker. The previous version then becomes visible again.<br> *With MFA Delete enabled, permanently deleting a version requires both the MFA token and the security credentials. This prevents accidental or malicious permanent deletion.<br> *Exam scenario: "A user deleted objects in a versioned bucket and needs to recover them" — the answer is to list and delete the delete markers. The object versions were never destroyed.<br>

794. [ S3 ] What are the four Block Public Access settings in S3, and at what levels can they be applied? ; The four settings are: BlockPublicAcls (reject PUTs that grant public ACLs), IgnorePublicAcls (ignore existing public ACLs), BlockPublicPolicy (reject bucket policies granting public access), RestrictPublicBuckets (restrict access to AWS services and authorized users when a public policy exists). They can be applied at the AWS account level or individual bucket level. <br><br> *Account-level settings override bucket-level settings. If BlockPublicAcls is enabled at the account level, individual buckets cannot allow public ACLs even if their bucket-level setting is disabled. This is the strongest control.<br> *AWS enables all four settings by default for new accounts since April 2023. Organizations should enforce these via SCPs and AWS Config rules to ensure no bucket can be made public unintentionally.<br> *RestrictPublicBuckets is the most subtle: even if a bucket has a public policy, only AWS services and authorized IAM principals can access it — anonymous internet access is blocked. This does not remove the public policy, it just overrides its effect.<br>

795. [ S3 ] What is SSE-KMS S3 Bucket Keys and why would you enable it? ; S3 Bucket Keys generate a short-lived data key at the bucket level using the KMS CMK. This data key is then used to encrypt individual objects instead of calling KMS for every object. This reduces KMS API calls by up to 99%, dramatically reducing KMS costs and avoiding KMS request rate throttling for high-throughput S3 workloads. <br><br> *Without Bucket Keys, every S3 object PutObject/GetObject with SSE-KMS generates a KMS GenerateDataKey or Decrypt API call. KMS has request rate limits (5,500–30,000 req/sec per region). High-volume S3 workloads can easily throttle KMS.<br> *With Bucket Keys enabled, the short-lived bucket-level key is cached in S3, and only periodically refreshed via KMS. This means millions of objects can be encrypted/decrypted with far fewer KMS API calls.<br> *Trade-off: with Bucket Keys, CloudTrail audit granularity changes — you see the bucket-level KMS event rather than per-object KMS events. For compliance environments requiring per-object KMS audit: disable Bucket Keys or accept the audit granularity change.<br>

796. [ S3 ] What are the requirements for enabling S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR)? ; Requirements: (1) Versioning must be enabled on BOTH the source and destination bucket. (2) An IAM role with permissions to read from source and write to destination must be created. (3) The source and destination buckets must be in different AWS regions. (4) For cross-account replication, the destination bucket must have a bucket policy allowing the source account's replication role to replicate objects. <br><br> *Versioning is the most commonly missed requirement. If versioning is not enabled on the destination before configuring replication, the replication job will fail. Both buckets need versioning — not just the source.<br> *The IAM role permissions needed: s3:GetObject, s3:GetObjectVersion, s3:GetObjectVersionAcl on source, s3:ReplicateObject, s3:ReplicateDelete, s3:ReplicateTags on destination.<br> *Objects that existed before CRR was configured are NOT automatically replicated. To replicate pre-existing objects: use S3 Batch Replication to create a job targeting existing objects with the same replication configuration.<br>

797. [ S3 ] What is S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) and when is it required? ; RTC is an add-on to S3 replication that guarantees 99.99% of objects are replicated within 15 minutes. It also provides replication metrics (pending bytes, pending operations) in CloudWatch. RTC is required for workloads with strict RPO (Recovery Point Objective) requirements — typically financial, healthcare, or compliance-mandated systems where data loss must not exceed 15 minutes. <br><br> *Without RTC, standard replication is best-effort — most objects replicate within seconds to minutes, but there are no SLA guarantees. For most DR scenarios, this is acceptable. Only use RTC when a specific RPO ≤15 minutes is contractually or regulatorily required.<br> *RTC has additional cost on top of standard CRR pricing (data transfer + storage). Calculate whether the RPC SLA justifies the cost. For truly critical systems: RTC + same-region standby (SRR to same-region replica) provides the strongest data protection.<br> *Replication metrics with RTC: CloudWatch metrics show `ReplicationLatency` (maximum seconds for pending operations), `BytesPendingReplication`, and `OperationsPendingReplication`. Alarm on these to detect replication backlog.<br>

798. [ S3 ] Which S3 storage classes store data in only a single Availability Zone, and what are the implications? ; S3 One Zone-IA and S3 Express One Zone both store data in a single AZ. If that AZ suffers a failure, data stored in these classes may be permanently lost. They should only be used for data that can be regenerated (e.g., thumbnails, derived datasets, cached files) or data that is already replicated elsewhere. <br><br> *S3 Standard, Standard-IA, Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Glacier Deep Archive, and Intelligent-Tiering all store data redundantly across minimum 3 AZs. They provide 11 nines durability even if an AZ fails.<br> *One Zone-IA costs ~20% less than Standard-IA. The cost savings come from single-AZ storage. Never use One Zone-IA for primary copies of data that cannot be regenerated or is not replicated to another class/region.<br> *Express One Zone is designed for millisecond-latency performance (ML training, HPC, real-time analytics) where durability is traded for extreme performance. Data should always have a durable copy in S3 Standard or another class.<br>

799. [ S3 ] What is the minimum storage duration charge for S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and what are the retrieval time options? ; Minimum storage duration is 180 days. If an object is deleted before 180 days, you are charged for the full 180-day minimum. Retrieval times: Standard retrieval = 12 hours, Bulk retrieval = up to 48 hours. There is no Expedited retrieval option for Glacier Deep Archive (unlike Glacier Flexible Retrieval). <br><br> *Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 storage class ($0.00099/GB/month in us-east-1) — approximately 23× cheaper than S3 Standard. It is designed for data that is rarely or never accessed — regulatory archives, compliance data retained for 7+ years.<br> *The 12–48 hour retrieval time means objects are not immediately available. Unlike Glacier Instant Retrieval (milliseconds) or Glacier Flexible Retrieval (minutes with Expedited). For compliance-only archives where retrieval is rare: Deep Archive is correct. For archives needing occasional fast retrieval: use Glacier Instant Retrieval.<br> *40 KB minimum billable size for Glacier Deep Archive: objects smaller than 40 KB are billed as 40 KB. This makes Deep Archive cost-inefficient for large numbers of small objects. Combine small files into archives (tar/zip) before uploading to optimize costs.<br>

800. [ S3 ] How does S3 Intelligent-Tiering work, and when is it NOT a good choice? ; Intelligent-Tiering monitors access patterns and automatically moves objects between access tiers (Frequent Access → Infrequent Access after 30 days without access → Archive Instant Access after 90 days → optionally Archive Access and Deep Archive Access). A per-object monitoring fee of $0.0025/1,000 objects/month applies. It is NOT cost-effective for small objects (< ~128 KB) where monitoring fee exceeds storage savings, or for objects with known, predictable access patterns. <br><br> *No retrieval fee for moves between Frequent and Infrequent Access tiers (unlike Standard-IA which charges per GB retrieval). This is the key advantage over Standard-IA for data with uncertain access patterns — if the object is accessed, it moves back to Frequent Access automatically with no retrieval penalty.<br> *Break-even analysis: monitoring fee = $0.0025/1,000 objects. For 1 million objects: $2.50/month monitoring. If those objects are in Standard-IA and occasionally accessed (paying retrieval fees), Intelligent-Tiering becomes cheaper. For very small objects (<128 KB), monitoring fee exceeds storage savings.<br> *For data that is ALWAYS accessed frequently: Standard is cheaper (no monitoring fee). For data NEVER accessed after initial write: Glacier lifecycle rule is cheaper and more predictable than Intelligent-Tiering's deepest tiers.<br>


801. [ S3 ] What is the difference between SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS encryption in terms of audit capability? ; SSE-S3 uses AWS-managed keys and provides no per-request audit trail. SSE-KMS uses KMS CMKs and logs every GenerateDataKey and Decrypt API call to AWS CloudTrail, providing a complete audit trail of who accessed which data and when. SSE-KMS is required when an audit trail for encryption key usage is needed. <br><br> *CloudTrail KMS data events show: which IAM principal called KMS, which CMK was used, what operation (GenerateDataKey for writes, Decrypt for reads), the S3 object's S3 bucket ARN. This enables forensic investigation of data access patterns.<br> *SSE-KMS also allows key rotation (annual automatic rotation for AWS-managed keys, configurable for CMKs) and key revocation — if the CMK is disabled or deleted, objects encrypted with it become inaccessible. This is a strong data access revocation mechanism.<br> *For regulatory compliance requiring proof of encryption key management (SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP): SSE-KMS with CMK is the required encryption method. SSE-S3 meets encryption requirements but not key management audit requirements.<br>

802. [ S3 ] What is S3 Object Lock Compliance mode vs Governance mode — which can be overridden and by whom? ; Compliance mode: retention period cannot be shortened or removed by ANY user — not root, not AWS Support, nobody. Objects are fully immutable until the retention period expires. Governance mode: users with the `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` IAM permission can override the retention setting. Both modes prevent deletion without the appropriate permission. <br><br> *Compliance mode maps to regulatory requirements like SEC 17a-4(f), FINRA 4511, and CFTC 1.31 which require WORM storage that cannot be modified even by administrators. This is the mode required for these compliance frameworks.<br> *Governance mode is useful for testing WORM workflows, protecting data from accidental deletion while allowing administrators to fix mistakes, or meeting internal data retention policies that don't require strict regulatory compliance.<br> *Object Lock requires bucket-level enablement at creation time. It cannot be added to an existing bucket. Once Compliance mode is set with a retention date, no AWS API, SDK, or console operation can delete or modify the object before that date.<br>

803. [ S3 ] What is a presigned URL and what determines its maximum validity period? ; A presigned URL is a time-limited URL granting access to a private S3 object. It is signed with the creator's AWS credentials and embeds the expiry time. Maximum validity: 7 days when signed with permanent IAM user credentials, 12 hours when signed with a temporary STS token (IAM role, Cognito, federated identity). <br><br> *The presigned URL inherits the permissions of the signing entity. If the signing IAM role is deleted or its permissions are revoked after the URL is generated, the URL becomes invalid immediately — the URL does not independently carry permissions.<br> *Presigned URLs work for both GET (download) and PUT (upload). A presigned PUT URL allows the URL recipient to upload exactly one object to the specified key without having AWS credentials. Commonly used for direct browser-to-S3 uploads in web applications.<br> *Bucket policies with Deny conditions still apply to presigned URL requests. A bucket policy denying public access (even via presigned URLs) will override the presigned URL mechanism. Ensure the bucket policy does not have conditions that block presigned URL access patterns.<br>

804. [ S3 ] What is the minimum part size for S3 multipart upload, and what happens to failed/abandoned multipart uploads? ; Minimum part size is 5 MB (except the last part which can be any size). Maximum 10,000 parts per upload. Abandoned multipart uploads accumulate incomplete parts in S3 and incur storage charges. Use a lifecycle rule with `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` (e.g., after 7 days) to automatically clean up incomplete uploads. <br><br> *Each part is uploaded independently — if one part fails, only that part needs to be re-uploaded. This improves reliability for large object uploads over unreliable networks. Parts can also be uploaded in parallel, improving throughput.<br> *Incomplete multipart uploads are a common hidden cost in S3. The parts exist in the bucket but are not visible as complete objects. Tools like S3 Storage Lens and the S3 console storage class analysis can reveal orphaned multipart data.<br> *AWS CLI automatically uses multipart upload for objects over a configurable threshold (default 8 MB). The `aws s3 cp` command handles multipart automatically. For SDK users: must explicitly call `create_multipart_upload`, `upload_part`, `complete_multipart_upload`.<br>

805. [ S3 ] What is S3 Transfer Acceleration and how does it work? ; Transfer Acceleration routes upload/download traffic through the nearest CloudFront edge location, then over the AWS private backbone to the S3 bucket. This reduces internet latency for geographically distant uploads. It uses a special endpoint: `bucket.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com`. It must be enabled per bucket and costs $0.04–$0.08/GB additional on top of standard transfer fees. <br><br> *AWS provides a speed comparison tool to test whether Transfer Acceleration is faster than direct upload for your location. If it's not faster, AWS does not charge the acceleration fee. The feature automatically falls back to direct transfer if it would be slower.<br> *Transfer Acceleration is most beneficial for: global users uploading to a single S3 bucket, cross-continental transfers, upload-heavy workloads with variable internet quality. It is not beneficial for uploads within the same region as the bucket.<br> *Transfer Acceleration does NOT use Direct Connect. DX can be used to upload directly to S3 via a Public VIF or via a VPC with Gateway Endpoint — this is completely separate from Transfer Acceleration which only uses CloudFront edge infrastructure.<br>

806. [ S3 ] What is S3 Select and what formats and compression types does it support? ; S3 Select allows running SQL queries on the contents of individual S3 objects server-side, returning only matching data instead of the full object. Supported formats: CSV, JSON, Apache Parquet. Supported compression: GZIP and BZIP2 (for CSV and JSON). Parquet supports its own built-in columnar compression. <br><br> *S3 Select can reduce data transfer by up to 80% and query time by up to 400% for structured data queries. Billing is per GB scanned and per GB returned — minimizing returned data reduces both costs.<br> *Limitations: no JOINs between objects, no GROUP BY aggregations, one object per query. For complex multi-object queries, use Athena. S3 Select is for simple column/row filtering on a single object.<br> *Glacier Select extends this capability to objects archived in Glacier Flexible Retrieval. It is not available for Glacier Deep Archive. Glacier Select initiates a retrieval job that runs SQL and returns only matching data — useful for compliance audits of archived logs without full restore.<br>

807. [ S3 ] How does S3 handle concurrent writes (PUT) to the same object key? ; S3 uses a last-writer-wins model for concurrent PUTs to the same key. S3 processes writes atomically — each PUT either fully succeeds or fails. With versioning enabled, each concurrent PUT creates a new version with its own version ID, the most recently written version becomes the "current" version. Without versioning, the last successful PUT overwrites previous data. <br><br> *Strong consistency (since Dec 2020) means the reader always gets the latest version. There is no window where a read might return stale data after a PUT completes. This eliminates the need for read-after-write retry patterns that existed before the consistency change.<br> *For distributed systems writing to the same key: S3 provides no locking mechanism. If two processes must not overwrite each other's data, use a separate locking mechanism (DynamoDB conditional writes) or ensure only one writer per key via application design.<br> *Versioning as write protection: with versioning, concurrent writes create multiple versions — no data is lost. The application can detect and handle concurrent version conflicts by examining version IDs. Without versioning, concurrent writes race and only one wins.<br>

808. [ S3 ] What is the S3 strong consistency model as of December 2020, and what changed? ; Since December 2020, S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations: PUTs of new objects, overwrites, DELETEs, and LISTs. Immediately after a successful PUT, any GET returns the latest version. Immediately after a DELETE, GET returns 404. LIST immediately includes newly created objects. This replaced the previous eventual consistency model for overwrite PUTs and DELETEs. <br><br> *Before December 2020: overwrite PUTs and DELETEs were eventually consistent — a GET immediately after a PUT might return the old version, LIST might not include newly created objects. Applications needed retry logic to handle stale reads.<br> *The consistency change applies globally — no additional configuration needed. All existing applications automatically benefit from strong consistency. Code that implemented read-after-write retry loops or consistency workarounds can be simplified.<br> *Important caveat: S3 consistency is per-object, not transactional. Two separate PUTs to two different objects are not atomic — you cannot guarantee that a reader sees both writes or neither. For transactional multi-object operations: use DynamoDB.<br>

809. [ S3 ] What is an S3 Access Point and why would you use one instead of a bucket policy? ; An S3 Access Point is a named endpoint attached to a bucket with its own IAM-like policy and optional VPC restriction. Instead of one complex bucket policy managing access for 50 different applications, each application gets its own Access Point with a focused policy. Access Points simplify access management at scale and allow per-application network origin control. <br><br> *Bucket policy size limit is 20 KB. For large organizations with many teams accessing a single data lake bucket, this limit is quickly reached. Access Points each have their own policy, and the combined policies can be much larger. Each Access Point policy can be owned/managed by the team that uses it.<br> *VPC restriction on Access Points: an Access Point can be configured to only accept requests from a specific VPC. Even if an IAM principal has permission on the Access Point, requests from outside the VPC are denied. This provides network-level isolation without complex bucket policy conditions.<br> *Access Point ARN: `arn:aws:s3:region:account:accesspoint/name`. SDK and CLI requests use the Access Point ARN instead of the bucket ARN as the target. The bucket policy must allow the Access Point to access the bucket (or delegate all access to Access Points).<br>

810. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 server access logging and AWS CloudTrail S3 data events? ; Server access logging captures HTTP request details (IP, user agent, response code, request time, bytes sent) but does NOT capture the requester's IAM identity. It is best-effort delivery (not guaranteed, may be hours delayed) and is free. CloudTrail data events capture the exact S3 API call with the full IAM identity (user ARN, role ARN, account ID), near real-time, and cost $0.10 per 100,000 events. <br><br> *For security investigations requiring "who accessed which object and when with full identity": CloudTrail data events are required. Server access logs cannot answer this question — they only have the source IP address.<br> *CloudTrail data events for S3 must be explicitly enabled. They are disabled by default because S3 generates extremely high volumes of API calls. Enable selectively for sensitive buckets (PII data, financial records, compliance-required buckets).<br> *Both mechanisms can be used together: server access logs for operational debugging (request patterns, errors, performance), CloudTrail data events for security audit (unauthorized access attempts, specific user activity).<br>

811. [ S3 ] What is S3 Object Lambda and what problem does it solve? ; S3 Object Lambda allows Lambda functions to transform S3 objects on retrieval, returning the transformed data to the caller without storing a modified copy. It solves the problem of needing to serve different versions of the same data to different consumers without storing N copies (e.g., redacted PII for some users, full data for others, resized images vs originals). <br><br> *Architecture: caller → S3 Object Lambda Access Point → Lambda (transforms) → returns modified data. The original S3 object is never modified. The Lambda reads from a supporting S3 Access Point and calls `write_get_object_response` with the transformed data.<br> *Use cases: PII redaction (mask SSNs, credit card numbers for lower-privilege users), format conversion (CSV to JSON, XML to JSON), image resizing/watermarking, row-level filtering (return only rows the caller is authorized to see), metadata enrichment.<br> *Cost: Lambda invocation cost + Lambda execution time + S3 GET cost + Object Lambda Access Point data return cost. For high-frequency access of the same transformed output: consider storing the transformed version separately. Object Lambda is ideal for infrequent or user-specific transformations.<br>

812. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Requester Pays feature and what restriction does it impose? ; With Requester Pays, the requester (downloader) pays for data transfer and request costs instead of the bucket owner. This requires the requester to include `x-amz-request-payer: requester` in their request headers. As a consequence, anonymous (unauthenticated) access is not allowed — all requesters must be authenticated AWS users. <br><br> *Use case: data distribution at scale. AWS Public Datasets (e.g., 1000 Genomes, OpenStreetMap, NOAA weather) use Requester Pays so AWS hosts the data but researchers pay their own download costs. The data provider doesn't bear the egress cost of millions of downloads.<br> *Presigned URLs do not work with Requester Pays buckets for the requester — the URL generator's account is charged, not the URL user. For Requester Pays to work with presigned URLs, the presigned URL must be generated with `RequestPayer: requester` in the SDK call.<br> *Cross-account access with Requester Pays: the requester's AWS account pays. If an EC2 instance in Account B downloads from a Requester Pays bucket in Account A, Account B is charged for the data transfer and request costs.<br>

813. [ S3 ] What is S3 Storage Lens and how does it differ from S3 server access logging? ; S3 Storage Lens is an analytics service providing organization-wide visibility into S3 usage — storage size, object counts, request rates, cost savings opportunities, encryption coverage, replication status. It aggregates across all accounts in AWS Organizations. Server access logging captures per-request HTTP details for a single bucket. Storage Lens is for strategic analytics, access logging is for per-request operational debugging. <br><br> *Storage Lens default metrics are free (28 usage metrics, 14-day retention). Advanced metrics ($0.20/million objects/month) add 35+ additional metrics including prefix-level analysis, detailed request metrics, and CloudWatch publishing.<br> *Storage Lens recommendations: identifies Intelligent-Tiering candidates (infrequently accessed objects in Standard class), lifecycle optimization opportunities, unencrypted objects, incomplete multipart uploads, versioning-enabled buckets with high non-current storage.<br> *Organization-wide scope: with AWS Organizations, Storage Lens can cover all accounts and all regions in a single dashboard. This is impossible with server access logging, which is per-bucket and requires log aggregation separately.<br>

814. [ S3 ] How does S3 event notification differ when using EventBridge vs direct SNS/SQS/Lambda notifications? ; Direct notifications (SNS/SQS/Lambda): only specific event types are supported, configuration is per-bucket with limited filtering (prefix/suffix only). EventBridge: receives ALL S3 events (including types not available via direct notifications), supports rich filtering by event metadata, can fan-out to 20+ target types, supports event replay and archiving, and enables cross-account event delivery. <br><br> *EventBridge is the recommended destination for new architectures. It requires explicit enabling on the S3 bucket (`EventBridgeConfiguration`). Once enabled, all events flow to EventBridge, you create rules in EventBridge to filter and route to targets.<br> *Direct notification limitation: S3 can only send to one SNS topic, one SQS queue, or one Lambda function per event type without complex fan-out. EventBridge rules can send to multiple targets with different filters from one event stream.<br> *EventBridge features unavailable with direct notifications: event archiving and replay (reprocess historical events), schema registry, cross-account event bus targets, dead-letter queue for failed deliveries, input transformation.<br>

815. [ S3 ] What is the minimum number of days before an object in S3 Standard can be transitioned to S3 Standard-IA via a lifecycle policy? ; 30 days from the object creation date. S3 enforces a minimum 30-day duration in S3 Standard before any lifecycle transition to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA. This is because Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum storage duration charge — transitioning objects before 30 days would waste the minimum duration cost. <br><br> *Minimum storage duration for Standard-IA: 30 days. If an object is deleted from Standard-IA before 30 days, you're charged for the full 30 days. The lifecycle rule minimum of 30 days before transition exists to align with this minimum storage duration.<br> *For Glacier classes, the minimum transition is 0 days (technically) from Standard, but Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive all have their own minimum storage durations (90/90/180 days) which will still incur minimum charges if deleted early.<br> *Lifecycle rules cannot transition objects backward (from Glacier to Standard) — transitions only go to cheaper/deeper classes. To restore an object to Standard from Glacier: use the Restore Object operation (temporary copy in Standard), then copy to a new Standard object if needed permanently.<br>

816. [ S3 ] What is MFA Delete and who can enable it on an S3 bucket? ; MFA Delete adds an additional layer of protection requiring a valid MFA token for two operations: permanently deleting a specific object version, and changing the versioning state of a bucket. It can only be enabled by the root account (not IAM users or roles, even those with admin permissions). <br><br> *MFA Delete is separate from IAM MFA conditions in IAM policies. IAM MFA conditions require MFA for specific API actions. MFA Delete is an S3-level feature that requires the MFA code in the API request itself (using `x-amz-mfa` header).<br> *CLI command to enable MFA Delete: `aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket BUCKET --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled,MFADelete=Enabled --mfa "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:mfa/DEVICE CODE"`. Must be run as root or with root credentials.<br> *This is critical for compliance scenarios where buckets contain regulated data (financial records, healthcare) and preventing any deletion — even by compromised admin accounts — is required. The requirement for physical MFA device makes automated deletion impossible.<br>

817. [ S3 ] What S3 storage class should be used for data that is accessed once a quarter with immediate retrieval needs and must minimize cost? ; S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. It provides millisecond retrieval (same as Standard and Standard-IA), minimum 90-day storage duration, and is significantly cheaper than Standard or Standard-IA for infrequently accessed data. It is designed exactly for archives that need occasional rapid access. <br><br> *Glacier Instant Retrieval vs Standard-IA cost: Standard-IA ~$0.0125/GB/month. Glacier Instant Retrieval ~$0.004/GB/month — approximately 68% cheaper for storage. Retrieval fee is higher for Glacier IR vs Standard-IA, but for quarterly access the storage savings far outweigh the per-retrieval cost.<br> *The 90-day minimum storage duration must be considered. If the quarterly access pattern means deleting some objects before 90 days, minimum charge applies. For truly archival data retained 90+ days: Glacier Instant Retrieval is optimal.<br> *Glacier Flexible Retrieval would NOT meet the immediate retrieval requirement (hours retrieval time). Deep Archive would NOT meet it either. Only Glacier Instant Retrieval and above (Standard, Standard-IA) provide millisecond retrieval. The question specifies immediate retrieval → Glacier Instant Retrieval is the cost-optimized answer.<br>

818. [ S3 ] How does S3 Batch Operations work and what is the maximum scale it supports? ; S3 Batch Operations runs a specified operation on a list of S3 objects (manifest). It supports billions of objects per job, handles retries automatically, tracks progress, and delivers a completion report. Operations include Copy, Lambda invocation, tag replacement, ACL replacement, Glacier restore, and Object Lock settings. Manifests can be S3 Inventory output or custom CSV files. <br><br> *Job flow: (1) Generate manifest (S3 Inventory CSV or custom), (2) Create Batch Operations job specifying operation and manifest, (3) Review estimated cost and confirm, (4) Job runs managed by AWS, (5) Completion report written to specified S3 location with per-object success/failure.<br> *Common use case: retroactively apply encryption to existing unencrypted objects (use Batch Operations Copy with SSE-KMS as destination encryption), apply Object Lock retention to existing objects, bulk re-tag objects after taxonomy change.<br> *IAM role: the Batch Operations job assumes an IAM role. This role must have permissions for the source bucket (read, get-tagging, etc.) and destination bucket (write, replicate, etc.). Also needs `lambda:InvokeFunction` for Lambda jobs. The role must trust the `batchoperations.s3.amazonaws.com` service.<br>

819. [ S3 ] What is the S3 static website endpoint format and does it support HTTPS natively? ; The static website endpoint format is `http://bucket-name.s3-website-region.amazonaws.com` (HTTP only). S3 static website hosting does NOT natively support HTTPS. To serve over HTTPS: put a CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 static website endpoint (or use the S3 REST endpoint as CloudFront origin with OAC). <br><br> *CloudFront + S3 + ACM pattern: create CloudFront distribution with S3 as origin, request ACM certificate for custom domain, attach to CloudFront. CloudFront handles HTTPS termination. Set S3 static website endpoint as origin (for redirect and index document support) OR use S3 REST endpoint with Origin Access Control (OAC).<br> *Route 53 for custom domain: the bucket name must exactly match the custom domain name (e.g., bucket = `www.example.com` for domain `www.example.com`). Create Route 53 Alias record pointing to the S3 website endpoint (not CNAME, which doesn't work for zone apex).<br> *S3 website endpoint vs S3 REST endpoint: website endpoint supports index document (default.html) and custom error pages, REST endpoint does not. When CloudFront origin is S3 REST endpoint with OAC, CloudFront must handle default root object and error pages itself.<br>

820. [ S3 ] What is CORS in the context of S3 and when is a CORS configuration required? ; CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) configuration on an S3 bucket is required when browser-based JavaScript code from one domain makes HTTP requests to an S3 bucket on a different domain. The browser enforces CORS policy and will block the request if the S3 bucket does not return the correct CORS headers in the response. <br><br> *CORS only applies to browser-initiated requests. Server-to-server API calls (Lambda → S3, EC2 → S3) are not browser requests and do not require CORS. If a web application's backend calls S3, no CORS needed on S3. Only needed when the browser JavaScript itself calls S3 directly (presigned URL uploads, direct GET requests).<br> *CORS preflight: for non-simple requests (PUT, DELETE, custom headers), the browser first sends an HTTP OPTIONS request. S3 must respond with the CORS headers allowing the origin and method, or the browser will block the actual request. CORS configuration must include the OPTIONS method handling.<br> *Common misconfiguration: `AllowedOrigins: ["*"]` (allow all origins) is insecure for production. Specify exact origins: `["https://www.example.com"]`. For development: `["http://localhost:3000"]` is fine. Never use wildcard in production for write-capable endpoints.<br>


821. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Inventory feature and what are its output formats? ; S3 Inventory generates scheduled reports listing all objects in a bucket (or a subset by prefix) with their metadata. Output formats: CSV, ORC (Optimized Row Columnar), Apache Parquet. Reports delivered to a destination S3 bucket on daily or weekly schedules. Used for auditing, compliance reporting, Batch Operations manifests, and cost analysis. <br><br> *Fields available in inventory reports: object key, size, last modified date, ETag, storage class, encryption status (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, SSE-C), replication status, multi-part upload status, Object Lock retention mode and date, legal hold status, intelligent-tiering tier.<br> *Destination bucket: must be in the same region as the source. Must have a bucket policy allowing S3 to write inventory data. Can be a different account's bucket (cross-account inventory delivery) for centralized audit repositories.<br> *Athena integration: create an external table in Glue Data Catalog pointing to the inventory output. Query with Athena SQL across billions of objects. Example: `SELECT key, storage_class, encryption_status FROM inventory_table WHERE encryption_status != 'SSE-KMS'` — identify all non-KMS objects.<br>

822. [ S3 ] What is MountPoint for Amazon S3 and what workloads is it NOT suitable for? ; MountPoint for S3 is a FUSE-based filesystem client that mounts an S3 bucket as a local directory on Linux EC2 instances. It supports sequential reads, random reads, and sequential writes. It is NOT suitable for: random writes (overwrite of specific byte ranges), file locking, POSIX-full compliance workloads, applications requiring rename, or workloads needing strong consistency of concurrent multi-writer access. <br><br> *MountPoint translates filesystem calls to S3 API calls. Sequential reads are efficient (parallel multipart GET). New file writes work (PUT object). Appending to or overwriting part of an existing file is not supported — S3 objects are immutable.<br> *EFS vs MountPoint: EFS is a true NFS filesystem with full POSIX semantics, file locking, random read/write. MountPoint is appropriate for ML training data (sequential read of large files), data lake processing, media workflows. EFS is for general-purpose shared filesystem needs.<br> *MountPoint performance: optimized for S3 throughput, not random I/O latency. Reads up to the full S3 throughput. Writes are full object uploads — no incremental writes. Ideal for reading training datasets in PyTorch/TensorFlow, processing large video files, or genomics workflows reading large reference files.<br>

823. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Multi-Region Access Point (MRAP) and how does it handle regional failover? ; MRAP provides a single global endpoint that routes requests to the nearest S3 bucket replica. It uses AWS Global Accelerator's anycast network to direct traffic. Failover between regions can be configured as active-active (route to closest) or active-passive (failover to secondary when primary is unavailable). Supports bidirectional and unidirectional replication between buckets. <br><br> *ARN format: `arn:aws:s3::account:accesspoint/mrap-name.mrap.ra-prefix.s3.amazonaws.com`. Unlike single-region Access Points, MRAPs have no region in the ARN. AWS resolves the nearest replica at request time using anycast IP routing.<br> *Failover routing control: administrators configure routing status per region (Active, Passive). To test DR: set primary region to Passive — all traffic automatically routes to the secondary. To fail back: set primary back to Active. This enables tested, controlled DR failover without DNS TTL delays.<br> *Use case: globally distributed applications (CDN origin, globally accessed static content, global data lake) where users in multiple continents need low-latency S3 access. Without MRAP: applications must implement their own region selection logic. MRAP handles it transparently.<br>

824. [ S3 ] What happens when you try to access an object in S3 Glacier Deep Archive? ; Objects in Glacier Deep Archive are not immediately accessible. You must initiate a Restore Object request, specifying the number of days for the temporary restored copy to be available. Retrieval takes 12 hours (Standard) or up to 48 hours (Bulk). The restored copy appears in S3 Standard class temporarily, after the specified days expire, it is removed. The original Glacier Deep Archive copy remains. <br><br> *The restore operation copies the object from Glacier Deep Archive to a temporary S3 Standard location (billed at Standard rates for the restore duration). The original archive copy continues incurring Deep Archive storage costs. After restoration period expires, the temporary Standard copy is deleted but the archive copy remains.<br> *For one-time retrieval: initiate restore, wait 12–48 hours, access temporary copy, let it expire. For ongoing access after restore: copy the temporary restored object to S3 Standard permanently (using CopyObject or Batch Operations). Then update storage class — object is no longer in Glacier.<br> *Expedited retrieval for Glacier Deep Archive: does not exist. If a compliance scenario requires within 12 hours: use Glacier Deep Archive Standard retrieval (12 hrs). If within minutes is required: data should not be in Glacier Deep Archive — use Glacier Instant Retrieval instead.<br>

825. [ S3 ] How do you enforce that all objects uploaded to an S3 bucket use SSE-KMS encryption? ; Use a bucket policy with a Deny effect for PutObject requests that do not include `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms` or include `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256`. The bucket default encryption can be set to SSE-KMS, but a bucket policy Deny is the only way to ENFORCE it and prevent non-KMS encrypted uploads. <br><br> *Bucket default encryption: sets the default for uploads that don't specify encryption. If an upload explicitly specifies `AES256` (SSE-S3), the default is overridden. Bucket default encryption alone does NOT prevent SSE-S3 or unencrypted uploads.<br> *Combined policy for full enforcement: (1) Deny any PutObject that doesn't have `x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms`, AND (2) Deny any PutObject over HTTP (`aws:SecureTransport: false`). This ensures: all objects are KMS-encrypted AND the encryption header is transmitted over HTTPS only.<br> *Specific CMK enforcement: add condition `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id: arn:aws:kms:...` to require a specific CMK, not just any KMS key. This prevents use of AWS-managed keys (aws/s3) when a customer-managed key is required for compliance.<br>

826. [ S3 ] What is S3 Object Tagging and how does it differ from S3 metadata? ; Tags are key-value pairs attached to S3 objects, modifiable without copying the object (unlike user metadata). Up to 10 tags per object. Tags can be changed after creation. Used for: lifecycle filtering, access control (tag-based IAM conditions), cost allocation, replication filtering, S3 Batch Operations filtering. Metadata is set at upload time, immutable (requires copy to change), and includes system metadata (Content-Type, ETag) and user metadata (x-amz-meta-* headers). <br><br> *Lifecycle policies can filter by tags: transition or expire objects with a specific tag. Example: add `archive: yes` tag to objects ready for Glacier, lifecycle rule targets objects with this tag only. Without tag-based lifecycle, all objects in the prefix are affected uniformly.<br> *IAM policies can use tag conditions: `s3:ExistingObjectTag/department = finance` allows access only if the object has the tag `department=finance`. This enables attribute-based access control (ABAC) on S3 objects without managing hundreds of individual bucket policies.<br> *Cost allocation tags: S3 charges can be broken down by tag in AWS Cost Explorer. Tag objects with team name, project, or environment to allocate S3 costs to specific cost centers. Tags must be activated as cost allocation tags in the Billing console.<br>

827. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Glacier Vault Lock policy and how does it differ from S3 Object Lock? ; Glacier Vault Lock applies a WORM policy (Vault Lock policy) to an entire Glacier Vault. Once locked (after 24-hour confirmation window), the policy cannot be changed or deleted even by the root account. It operates at the vault level rather than per-object. S3 Object Lock operates at the object level (per-object retention periods and legal holds) and works with S3 buckets (including Glacier storage class objects in S3). <br><br> *Vault Lock vs Object Lock: Vault Lock = Glacier-native feature for vaults (not S3 buckets with Glacier storage class). Object Lock = S3 feature working on versioned S3 buckets, with per-object Compliance and Governance modes.<br> *For SAP-C02 exam: S3 Object Lock (Compliance mode) is the primary answer for WORM requirements. Vault Lock is relevant when question mentions Glacier Vaults specifically. Most modern architectures use S3 with Glacier storage classes (Object Lock), not standalone Glacier Vaults.<br> *Both support regulatory compliance (SEC 17a-4). The Vault Lock policy is a JSON resource policy that denies DeleteArchive operations — analogous to Object Lock Compliance mode. The 24-hour initiation window allows testing the policy before it's permanently locked.<br>

828. [ S3 ] How does S3 cross-account access work using bucket policies? ; Grant access in the destination bucket's bucket policy: add a Statement allowing `s3:GetObject` (or other needed actions) with the `Principal` being the other account's root ARN (`arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT-B:root`) or a specific role/user ARN. The IAM principal in Account B also needs an IAM policy allowing the S3 action. Both the bucket policy (resource-side) and IAM policy (identity-side) must allow the action. <br><br> *Cross-account pattern: Account A owns the bucket. Account B's users need access. (1) Account A bucket policy: Allow s3:GetObject for `arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT-B:role/data-reader`. (2) Account B IAM role `data-reader` policy: Allow s3:GetObject on `arn:aws:s3:::account-a-bucket/*`. Without both, access is denied.<br> *Simplification: if Account A's bucket policy grants `arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT-B:root`, Account B's administrator can grant access to individual users/roles within their account via IAM policies. Account B manages its own access, Account A only manages which accounts are trusted.<br> *Object ownership cross-account: by default, objects uploaded by Account B to Account A's bucket are owned by Account B — Account A cannot access its own bucket's objects. Solution: use `BucketOwnerEnforced` Object Ownership setting — all objects become owned by the bucket owner regardless of who uploaded them.<br>

829. [ S3 ] What are the naming rules for S3 buckets and why must names be globally unique? ; S3 bucket names must be 3–63 characters, use only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, start/end with a letter or number, and cannot be formatted as IP addresses. Names are globally unique across ALL AWS accounts and regions because S3 uses virtual-hosted-style URLs (`bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com`) — a globally unique name ensures the subdomain is unambiguous on the internet. <br><br> *The global uniqueness constraint means: if another AWS customer already has a bucket named `my-bucket`, you cannot create one with the same name even in a different account or region. Bucket names are a first-come, first-served global namespace.<br> *Path-style URLs (deprecated): `https://s3.region.amazonaws.com/bucket-name/key` — does not require global uniqueness at the DNS level. AWS deprecated path-style access in September 2020 (existing path-style access still works but is not recommended for new applications).<br> *Naming tip for enterprises: use account-ID or environment prefix to avoid conflicts: `companyname-prod-us-east-1-data-lake`. This namespace convention also prevents bucket name guessing/enumeration attacks where attackers try to access predictably named buckets.<br>

830. [ S3 ] What is the S3 data consistency model for LIST operations after multiple PUT operations? ; Since December 2020, S3 LIST operations are strongly consistent. If you PUT an object and then immediately call LIST on the bucket or prefix, the new object will appear in the listing. This was previously eventually consistent — LIST might not include a recently created object. All S3 consistency (GET, PUT, DELETE, LIST) is now strongly consistent. <br><br> *The consistency change applies to S3 API list operations (ListObjectsV2, ListObjectVersions, etc.). There is no configuration needed — it is the default behavior for all S3 buckets globally.<br> *This also means after a DELETE, LIST immediately omits the deleted object. Before December 2020, a deleted object might still appear in LIST results for a brief period. Applications that implemented LIST retry loops or checked for stale list results can simplify their code.<br> *Pagination consistency: LIST returns paginated results. If objects are added/deleted between pages of a paginated LIST call, the behavior follows eventual consistency within a single paginated traversal. Strong consistency guarantees the snapshot at the time of each individual LIST call, not the consistency of the full paginated dataset across multiple calls over time.<br>

831. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Express One Zone storage class and how does it differ from S3 Standard? ; S3 Express One Zone provides single-digit millisecond latency (vs tens of milliseconds for Standard), up to 10× higher throughput, and stores data in a single AZ. It uses a different bucket type called a Directory Bucket (not a general-purpose bucket). It does not support versioning, replication, Object Lock, or most S3 features. It is priced higher per GB than Standard but with lower request costs. <br><br> *Directory Bucket vs General Purpose Bucket: Express One Zone uses Directory Buckets with a different naming convention (`bucket-name--az-id--x-s3`). API requests use a CreateSession call for short-lived credentials before accessing objects. The API is a subset of S3 standard API.<br> *Use cases: ML/AI model training data access (highest bottleneck is data loading, Express One Zone eliminates this), real-time analytics where sub-millisecond data access matters, financial services tick data processing, HPC workloads.<br> *Single AZ risk: all data in one AZ — if the AZ fails, data is inaccessible (and potentially lost). Always maintain a durable copy in S3 Standard or another resilient storage class. Express One Zone is a performance cache, not a primary durable store.<br>

832. [ S3 ] What is the S3 lifecycle rule for aborting incomplete multipart uploads and why is it important? ; The `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle action specifies the number of days after a multipart upload is initiated before S3 aborts it and deletes the incomplete parts. Without this rule, abandoned multipart uploads accumulate and incur storage charges indefinitely (parts are stored at Standard pricing but never visible as complete objects). <br><br> *Incomplete multipart parts are charged at the storage class rate of the in-progress upload. For large objects (100 GB), an incomplete upload's parts can cost as much as the complete object. With many concurrent large uploads, abandoned parts can be a significant hidden cost.<br> *AWS recommendation: always add an `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle rule to every bucket with a threshold of 7 days. This cleans up parts from failed or abandoned uploads automatically without requiring manual intervention.<br> *Storage Lens metric: "IncompleteMultipartUploadSizeBytes" in S3 Storage Lens identifies the volume of incomplete multipart data. Use this to detect and quantify the cost impact before and after applying the lifecycle rule.<br>

833. [ S3 ] How does S3 replication handle objects encrypted with SSE-C? ; Objects encrypted with SSE-C (customer-provided keys) are NOT replicated by S3 replication. S3 replication cannot access SSE-C encrypted objects because it requires the customer-provided encryption key to decrypt the object during replication, and S3 does not store SSE-C keys. Only SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS encrypted objects can be replicated. <br><br> *For SSE-KMS encrypted objects: replication requires the IAM role to have KMS permissions to decrypt with the source CMK and encrypt with the destination CMK. The destination can use a different CMK than the source. This is important for cross-account replication where CMK policies must allow the replication role from the other account.<br> *SSE-C limitation is fundamental: since AWS never stores the SSE-C key, S3 cannot decrypt the object during the server-side replication process. If SSE-C is required AND replication is required: reconsider the key management model (switch to SSE-KMS which supports both).<br> *Exam pattern: "Company uses SSE-C for all S3 objects. They enable CRR. Why doesn't replication work?" — Answer: SSE-C encrypted objects cannot be replicated. Solution: switch to SSE-KMS for objects that need replication.<br>

834. [ S3 ] What is the cost model for S3 data transfer and what transfers are free? ; Free transfers: data uploaded to S3 from the internet (ingress), transfers between S3 and EC2/Lambda in the same region, transfers to CloudFront, transfers between S3 and same-region AWS services. Charged transfers: data downloaded from S3 to the internet (egress, $0.09/GB), cross-region replication data transfer, Transfer Acceleration ($0.04–$0.08/GB). <br><br> *Same-region free: EC2 → S3, Lambda → S3, Glue → S3, Athena → S3, EMR → S3 are all free when in the same region. This is why the AWS data lake pattern (compute + S3 in same region) is cost-efficient compared to on-premises alternatives.<br> *Cross-region data transfer: downloading from S3 in eu-west-1 to an EC2 in us-east-1 incurs inter-region transfer costs ($0.02/GB between US regions, more for APAC). Cross-region replication incurs the same inter-region data transfer rate on replicated data.<br> *Direct Connect pricing: downloading S3 data via Direct Connect uses DX data transfer rates (typically $0.02/GB outbound) instead of internet egress rates ($0.09/GB). For large data volumes from on-premises: DX significantly reduces data transfer costs vs internet downloads.<br>

835. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 CRR (Cross-Region Replication) and S3 SRR (Same-Region Replication)? ; CRR replicates objects to a bucket in a different AWS region. SRR replicates to a bucket in the same region. Key differences: CRR incurs inter-region data transfer costs, SRR has no data transfer cost (same region). CRR is used for DR, compliance data residency, latency optimization across regions. SRR is used for log aggregation across accounts in the same region, live replication between production and test environments, and data sovereignty (keeping data within a region while distributing access). <br><br> *Both require versioning on source and destination. Both replicate new objects only (not existing objects). Both require an IAM role. Both support replication of delete markers (optional). Both support RTC (Replication Time Control).<br> *SRR for multi-account log aggregation: each account's S3 bucket replicates logs to a central security account's bucket in the same region. No inter-region transfer cost. Central security team has read-only access without needing access to individual account buckets.<br> *CRR for compliance: some financial and healthcare regulations require that backup copies exist in a geographically separate location. CRR to a different AWS region (even across continents) satisfies geographic separation requirements. SRR to a same-region bucket does not satisfy geographic separation.<br>

836. [ S3 ] What are S3 Access Grants and how do they differ from S3 Access Points? ; S3 Access Grants (launched 2023) provide a way to grant access to S3 data at scale by mapping corporate directory identities (Active Directory users, groups, SSO users) to S3 data locations. Access Grants automatically vend temporary credentials via STS. Access Points are fixed endpoints with static IAM policies. Access Grants are for dynamic, identity-directory-driven access at scale where the corporate identity system is the source of truth. <br><br> *Access Grants use case: a company has 10,000 employees in Active Directory. Different teams own different S3 prefixes. Instead of managing IAM roles for every team, Access Grants maps AD group "finance-team" to `s3://bucket/finance/*`. When a finance employee requests access, Grants vends STS credentials scoped to `/finance/*`.<br> *Access Points vs Grants: Access Points require creating a named endpoint per application/team and managing its policy. Access Grants work from your existing identity store (Okta, AD, IAM Identity Center) without creating individual Access Points. For large organizations with existing identity management: Access Grants is more scalable.<br> *Both Access Points and Access Grants work with the bucket policy. The bucket can delegate all access decisions to Access Points or Grants by allowing the access point/grants service as a principal.<br>

837. [ S3 ] What types of objects can S3 Batch Operations process, and what is the maximum number of objects per job? ; S3 Batch Operations can process objects in the billions per job (up to 2 billion objects per job manifest). Operations available: CopyObject, InvokeLambda, RestoreObject, PutObjectTagging, DeleteObjectTagging, PutObjectAcl, PutObjectRetention, PutObjectLegalHold, ReplicateObject, DeleteObject. The job is limited by the size of the manifest file rather than a hard object count limit. <br><br> *Manifest formats: S3 Inventory output (CSV, ORC, Parquet format) or customer-generated CSV (with bucket name and key per row). S3 Inventory is the recommended manifest source for large-scale jobs as it's already formatted and can be generated automatically.<br> *Progress tracking: Batch Operations provides a real-time progress report in the console and via CloudWatch metrics showing completed, failed, and total objects. A completion report (CSV) is written to a specified S3 destination with per-object success/failure status and error codes for failures.<br> *Retry behavior: failed operations are automatically retried (configurable number of retries). If an object consistently fails (permissions, missing object), it is recorded in the completion report as failed. The job continues processing other objects — a failure on one object does not halt the job.<br>

838. [ S3 ] What is the S3 default encryption setting and what effect does it have on existing objects? ; Default encryption sets the server-side encryption method applied to all new objects uploaded to the bucket that don't specify their own encryption. It does NOT retroactively encrypt existing unencrypted objects. Existing objects remain in their original encryption state. To encrypt existing unencrypted objects: use S3 Batch Operations with a CopyObject operation specifying SSE-KMS as destination encryption. <br><br> *Since January 2023, AWS automatically enables SSE-S3 as the default encryption for all buckets, including existing ones. This means all new uploads are encrypted with SSE-S3 by default even if you never explicitly set default encryption.<br> *Overriding default encryption: if default is SSE-KMS and an upload specifies `x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256`, the upload uses SSE-S3 overriding the default. To prevent this: add a bucket policy Deny for non-KMS encryption (as described in Q825).<br> *Performance note: SSE-S3 (AES-256) is performed in S3 infrastructure with no measurable latency overhead. SSE-KMS has a slight latency overhead for the KMS API call (typically <5ms). For extreme throughput scenarios, enable S3 Bucket Keys to minimize KMS call frequency.<br>

839. [ S3 ] What S3 feature enables you to query object metadata across billions of objects without downloading them? ; S3 Inventory generates flat-file reports of object metadata (size, storage class, encryption status, replication status, tags, Object Lock status) on a daily/weekly schedule. These reports can be queried with Amazon Athena for SQL-based analysis. For real-time metadata queries: S3 Storage Lens provides aggregated analytics dashboards. <br><br> *Athena on S3 Inventory: create a Glue Data Catalog table pointing to S3 Inventory output. Use Athena SQL to find all unencrypted objects, all objects in Standard class not accessed in 90 days, all objects larger than 1 GB, etc. This analysis would be impossible via standard S3 API calls (which are per-object).<br> *Storage Lens dashboard: automatically aggregates metrics across all accounts/buckets. No querying needed — dashboards show trends, anomalies, and recommendations. Cannot drill down to individual object level (unlike Inventory + Athena).<br> *For real-time per-object metadata lookup: use S3 Object Tagging and query via ListObjectsV2 with tag filters, but this is limited to per-prefix scanning. For true object catalog at scale: integrate with AWS Glue Data Catalog or a custom metadata database backed by Lambda/DynamoDB.<br>

840. [ S3 ] How can you ensure that a specific S3 bucket can only be accessed from within a specific VPC? ; Use a bucket policy with a Deny for requests that don't have `aws:sourceVpce` matching the specific VPC Endpoint ID, or `aws:sourceVpc` matching the VPC ID. Also create a VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3 in the VPC. This ensures: (1) VPC traffic uses the endpoint, (2) bucket policy blocks all non-VPC traffic. <br><br> *Policy condition: `"Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:sourceVpce": "vpce-xxxx"}}`. This Deny blocks any request not coming from the specified VPC Endpoint. Requests from the internet, other VPCs, or even the AWS console are denied.<br> *Important: this pattern blocks the AWS console, AWS CLI from your laptop, and all non-VPC access. Ensure an emergency access method exists (a secondary bucket policy statement with an explicit Allow for admin roles, or access from a bastion in the VPC).<br> *Cross-account consideration: if Account B's EC2 (in the approved VPC) accesses Account A's bucket, the request traverses Account B's VPC Endpoint. The `aws:sourceVpce` condition checks the VPC Endpoint ID, which belongs to Account B. Account A's bucket policy must allow Account B's VPC Endpoint ID.<br>


841. [ S3 ] What is the S3 presigned URL expiry limit and what determines it? ; The maximum expiry for a presigned URL depends on the credential type used to sign it. IAM user (long-term credentials): up to 7 days (604,800 seconds). IAM role / STS temporary credentials (including Lambda, EC2 instance profile, Cognito): up to 12 hours (the STS session duration). The presigned URL cannot be valid longer than the credential it was signed with. <br><br> *If a Lambda function generates a presigned URL using its execution role (which has a 1-hour session token), the presigned URL cannot be valid beyond 1 hour even if you specify `--expires-in 86400`. The URL will expire when the underlying STS token expires.<br> *For long-lived presigned URLs (e.g., download links valid 7 days): generate using IAM user credentials or a role with a long session duration. IAM user long-term credentials allow the full 7-day expiry. STS tokens capped at 12 hours are too short for multi-day URLs.<br> *Security consideration: long-lived presigned URLs are a security risk if the URL leaks. Prefer shorter expiry and regenerate on demand. For sensitive data: generate presigned URLs with very short expiry (minutes) and require re-authentication to get new ones.<br>

842. [ S3 ] What are the two types of S3 metadata and what are their key differences? ; System metadata: set and managed by S3 or AWS (e.g., Content-Length, Content-Type, Last-Modified, ETag, x-amz-version-id, x-amz-storage-class). Cannot be set arbitrarily by users (some can be overridden like Content-Type). User metadata: custom key-value pairs with the `x-amz-meta-` prefix, set at upload time, max 2 KB total. BOTH types are immutable after object creation — to change them, you must copy the object to itself with the new metadata. <br><br> *The immutability of user metadata is a key exam point. Unlike object tags which can be updated at any time without copying, user metadata requires a CopyObject operation. This makes tags more suitable for frequently changing attributes (status, processing state).<br> *User metadata is returned in the HTTP response headers on GET requests. Applications can use user metadata to store application-specific information without maintaining a separate database. Example: `x-amz-meta-owner: john.doe`, `x-amz-meta-department: finance`.<br> *Maximum 2 KB for all user metadata combined (not per key). For applications needing more metadata per object: use S3 Tags (10 tags, up to 128+256 chars each) or maintain a separate metadata store (DynamoDB) keyed by S3 object URL.<br>

843. [ S3 ] What are the implications of enabling CRR (Cross-Region Replication) on a bucket that already has existing objects? ; Existing objects are NOT automatically replicated when CRR is enabled. Only new objects created after CRR is enabled are replicated. To replicate existing objects: use S3 Batch Replication (create a Batch Operations job using the replication configuration). Without Batch Replication, an organization may believe their DR bucket is fully populated when it only contains newer objects. <br><br> *This is the most common operational mistake with S3 replication: enabling CRR on a bucket with 100 TB of data and assuming the DR bucket receives all 100 TB. After enabling CRR, only new PUT operations are replicated. The DR bucket starts empty (or with whatever objects existed if Batch Replication was run).<br> *S3 Batch Replication: specify the source bucket and use the existing replication configuration as the operation. Batch Replication scans all existing objects (via a manifest or the full bucket) and replicates them to the destination. This may take significant time for large buckets.<br> *Bidirectional replication: CRR can be configured in both directions between two buckets (A replicates to B, B replicates to A). S3 prevents replication loops (objects that were replicated are not replicated back). Useful for active-active multi-region deployments.<br>

844. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Expedited tier, and is there a risk of retrieval failure? ; Expedited retrieval in Glacier Flexible Retrieval typically completes in 1–5 minutes for objects up to 250 MB. It is the fastest Glacier Flexible Retrieval option. However, Expedited retrievals may fail during periods of peak demand — AWS provides no throughput guarantee for on-demand Expedited retrievals. For guaranteed capacity: purchase Provisioned Capacity Units (PCUs), which provide reliable Expedited retrieval capacity. <br><br> *Provisioned Capacity Units: purchased in advance ($100/month per unit), each unit guarantees 3 Expedited retrievals/5 minutes and up to 150 MB/s of retrieval throughput. Required for compliance scenarios where guaranteed fast Glacier retrieval is contractually mandated.<br> *Cost comparison: Expedited retrieval ($0.03/GB + $0.01/request) vs Standard ($0.01/GB + $0.05/1,000 requests) vs Bulk ($0.0025/GB + $0.025/1,000 requests). Expedited is ~12× more expensive per GB than Bulk. Only use Expedited when the 1–5 minute retrieval time is actually needed.<br> *Exam scenario: "Company needs to retrieve Glacier data within 5 minutes and cannot afford failure" → Provisioned Capacity Units + Expedited retrieval. Without PCU, Expedited retrieval may fail at peak times. "Within a few hours" → Standard retrieval (no PCU needed).<br>

845. [ S3 ] What is the maximum number of lifecycle rules per S3 bucket? ; 1,000 lifecycle rules per bucket. Each rule can have filters (by prefix, tag, or object size), transition actions, and expiration actions. If more than 1,000 rules are needed (unusual), consider restructuring with tag-based rules (one rule per tag value covers multiple object patterns) or separating data into multiple buckets. <br><br> *Lifecycle rule filtering: rules can filter by prefix (path), tag, minimum object size, maximum object size, or combinations. A rule without a filter applies to ALL objects in the bucket. Multiple filters in one rule are ANDed together.<br> *Common lifecycle architecture: one rule for each major data category — raw logs (transition to IA after 30 days, Glacier after 90 days, delete after 365), processed data (IA after 60 days, delete after 2 years), compliance records (Glacier after 30 days, Object Lock + no expiration).<br> *Overlapping rules: if multiple rules match the same object, S3 applies the most favorable action. For transitions: the earliest transition date wins. For expirations: the earliest expiration date wins. Review lifecycle configurations carefully to avoid unintended early expirations.<br>

846. [ S3 ] How does S3 Intelligent-Tiering handle objects smaller than 128 KB? ; Objects smaller than 128 KB are stored in Intelligent-Tiering but are never automatically moved to Infrequent Access or Archive tiers — they always stay in the Frequent Access tier. The per-object monitoring fee ($0.0025/1,000 objects/month) is still charged. For small objects: Intelligent-Tiering provides no tiering benefit but still costs the monitoring fee, making it less cost-effective than simply using S3 Standard. <br><br> *Cost calculation for small objects: a bucket with 10 million objects all 128 KB or smaller in Intelligent-Tiering. Monitoring cost: 10M/1,000 × $0.0025 = $25/month. These objects never tier to IA (no savings). Total cost = Standard storage rate + $25/month monitoring = more expensive than S3 Standard alone.<br> *When to use Intelligent-Tiering with mixed object sizes: if the bucket has a mix of small and large objects, IT still optimizes the large objects (which dominate storage cost). The monitoring fee for small objects is negligible relative to savings on large objects.<br> *Optimization for buckets with many small files: avoid Intelligent-Tiering, use Standard + lifecycle transition to Standard-IA based on access patterns, or combine small files before upload (tar/zip). S3 Batch Operations can help combine small files by invoking Lambda for each to append to a larger archive.<br>

847. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Object Lambda access point architecture? ; S3 Object Lambda requires three components: (1) A standard S3 Access Point (the supporting Access Point that Lambda reads from), (2) A Lambda function that transforms the object, (3) An S3 Object Lambda Access Point (the endpoint that callers use). When a client calls GetObject via the Object Lambda Access Point, S3 invokes the Lambda function with a presigned URL to the original object. Lambda fetches the original, transforms it, and returns the result via `write_get_object_response` API. <br><br> *The Lambda function is responsible for fetching the original object (using the provided presigned URL), performing transformation, and calling `s3.write_get_object_response()` to return the transformed data to the caller. The Lambda has 60 seconds to return the response.<br> *Multiple Object Lambda Access Points can share the same Lambda function (different transformations for different access patterns). Example: one Access Point for redacted data (Lambda redacts PII), one for full data (Lambda passes through). Different IAM policies on each Access Point control which callers use which transformation.<br> *Cost: Lambda invocation per GET request, Lambda duration (transformation time), S3 GET to fetch original via supporting Access Point, S3 Object Lambda data return ($0.005/GB). For high-volume read paths: cache transformed results in another S3 prefix to avoid repeated Lambda transformations of the same object.<br>

848. [ S3 ] What is the S3 bucket policy size limit and what alternative handles very large access control requirements? ; S3 bucket policy size limit is 20 KB. For complex access requirements exceeding 20 KB: use S3 Access Points (each has its own policy, up to 20 KB per Access Point, unlimited Access Points per bucket), S3 Access Grants (for large-scale identity-based access), or Lake Formation for data lake governance. <br><br> *S3 Access Points don't increase the bucket policy limit per se — the bucket policy can delegate all access to Access Points with one line, then each Access Point has its own 20 KB policy. Effectively unlimited total policy space.<br> *Bucket policy delegation pattern: `"Principal": {"AWS": "*"}, "Condition": {"ArnLike": {"aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:s3:region:account:accesspoint/*"}}` — allows any Access Point to access the bucket, delegating all fine-grained access control to individual Access Point policies.<br> *Lake Formation: for data lake scenarios, Lake Formation provides column-level and row-level security on S3 data accessed through Glue/Athena/Redshift Spectrum. Policies defined in Lake Formation, not in S3 bucket policies. Better for data governance at scale than S3 Access Points.<br>

849. [ S3 ] What are the S3 server-side encryption options and which does NOT store the key in AWS? ; Four server-side encryption options: SSE-S3 (key managed by AWS, stored in AWS), SSE-KMS (key stored in AWS KMS, customer controls key policy), DSSE-KMS (dual-layer, both keys in KMS), SSE-C (customer-provided key per request — AWS uses it to encrypt/decrypt but never stores it). SSE-C is the only option where the encryption key is never stored in AWS infrastructure. <br><br> *SSE-C requirement: must use HTTPS for every request (key transmitted in header — never over HTTP). The customer must store the key and provide the exact same key for every subsequent GET request. If the key is lost, the object is permanently inaccessible.<br> *AWS CLI limitation with SSE-C: `aws s3 cp` does not support SSE-C for upload. Must use `aws s3api put-object --sse-customer-algorithm AES256 --sse-customer-key file://key.bin`. For SSE-C downloads: `aws s3api get-object` with the same key parameter.<br> *Client-side encryption: different from SSE-C. Client-side means the client encrypts before upload — S3 stores encrypted bytes and knows nothing about the encryption. SSE-C means S3 performs the encryption/decryption using the customer-provided key (server-side). With client-side: S3 never sees plaintext. With SSE-C: S3 sees plaintext during the encryption operation.<br>

850. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Batch Replication operation and when is it needed? ; S3 Batch Replication replicates existing objects that were in a bucket before replication was configured, or objects that failed replication. It creates an S3 Batch Operations job using the bucket's existing replication configuration as the operation. Needed when: enabling CRR/SRR on a bucket with existing objects, replication failed for some objects and needs retry, or initial sync of data to a new replica bucket. <br><br> *Normal replication only applies to new PUT operations. Objects that existed before replication was enabled, and objects in Glacier (which are not replicated by default), require Batch Replication for explicit replication.<br> *Job manifest for Batch Replication: generate via S3 Inventory (run inventory first, wait for completion, use inventory output as manifest). For large buckets (billions of objects), this can take significant time. Alternatively, create a custom CSV manifest with specific objects to replicate.<br> *Charges: Batch Replication charges both the standard S3 Batch Operations request cost and the standard CRR data transfer cost for replicated objects. For large existing datasets (TB or PB range): estimate the cost before running Batch Replication and confirm with finance/management.<br>


851. [ S3 ] What S3 feature provides a global endpoint that automatically routes to the nearest S3 bucket? ; S3 Multi-Region Access Points (MRAP). A MRAP provides a single global ARN/endpoint that resolves via AWS Global Accelerator to the nearest configured bucket replica. Supports active-active (route to lowest-latency) or active-passive (failover) configurations. Supports failover routing control for DR testing and execution. <br><br> *Without MRAP: application must implement regional routing logic (detect user location, select nearest region, use region-specific S3 endpoint). With MRAP: application uses one endpoint, AWS handles regional selection transparently.<br> *MRAP does not replicate data — you must configure S3 Replication separately between the member buckets. MRAP only routes requests, the data must exist in the target bucket for reads to succeed. Configure CRR between all MRAP member buckets in both directions for active-active.<br> *Cost: MRAP charges $0.0033/GB for data accessed through it (in addition to standard S3 request/storage costs). For very high-volume global workloads: calculate whether MRAP cost is justified vs application-level regional routing.<br>

852. [ S3 ] What is the S3 requestor pays header and what happens if it is missing from a request to a Requester Pays bucket? ; The header is `x-amz-request-payer: requester`. If a request to a Requester Pays bucket omits this header, S3 returns HTTP 403 (Forbidden).
