Anonymous (unauthenticated) requests are also rejected — all requests must be authenticated and include the requester pays header for the requester's account to be billed. <br><br> *This design ensures: bucket owner cannot be charged for anonymous downloads (only authenticated users can pay), requesters explicitly acknowledge they will be charged (by including the header), unauthenticated access is impossible (protecting bucket owner from DDoS cost attacks).<br> *SDK support: most AWS SDKs automatically add the header when configured: `s3.get_object(Bucket=b, Key=k, RequestPayer='requester')`. The CLI: `aws s3api get-object --request-payer requester`. Higher-level `aws s3 cp` may need the `--request-payer requester` flag.<br> *Requester pays is per-bucket, not per-object. Once enabled, all access to the bucket requires the header. Cannot selectively apply Requester Pays to specific objects within a bucket.<br>

853. [ S3 ] How do you configure S3 to send notifications to both an SQS queue AND a Lambda function for the same event type? ; Use Amazon EventBridge as the notification destination. EventBridge receives all S3 events and can fan-out to multiple targets using rules. Alternatively: use S3 → SNS topic as the notification destination, then subscribe both the SQS queue and Lambda function to the SNS topic (SNS fan-out pattern). Direct S3 notification can only have one destination per event type per notification configuration entry. <br><br> *SNS fan-out: S3 → SNS → (SQS queue 1, SQS queue 2, Lambda function, HTTP endpoint). One S3 notification sends to SNS, SNS delivers to all subscribers. Clean pattern for multiple consumers of the same S3 event.<br> *EventBridge fan-out: S3 → EventBridge → rule 1 (SQS target) + rule 2 (Lambda target) + rule 3 (Step Functions). More flexible filtering per target. EventBridge is the modern recommended approach. Multiple rules can match the same event and send to different targets simultaneously.<br> *Direct S3 to multiple targets limitation: S3 event notification can have multiple notification configurations, but each `EventBridgeConfiguration`, `LambdaFunctionConfiguration`, `QueueConfiguration`, `TopicConfiguration` can only point to one target. Multiple configurations for the same event type are allowed but the order of delivery is not guaranteed.<br>

854. [ S3 ] What is the maximum key length for an S3 object and what characters are allowed? ; Maximum key length: 1,024 bytes (UTF-8 encoded). All Unicode characters are allowed. Keys can include forward slashes to simulate directory hierarchy. Special characters (spaces, +, &, %, etc.) should be URL-encoded when used in URLs but are valid in object keys themselves. <br><br> *The forward slash in keys creates the appearance of directories in the S3 console and AWS SDKs. For example, `photos/2024/january/IMG001.jpg` appears as nested folders but is a flat key. S3 has no true directory structure — just object keys with arbitrary characters.<br> *Key design for performance: keys in S3 are lexicographically sorted by prefix. Sequential keys (timestamps, sequential numbers) historically led to hotspots (all requests to the same S3 server partition). Modern S3 auto-scales per prefix, but for extreme throughput: use randomized prefixes or hash-based prefixes.<br> *URL encoding in keys: keys with spaces or special characters must be URL-encoded in REST API requests and presigned URLs. AWS SDKs handle URL encoding automatically. Issues arise when keys with special characters are manually constructed in URLs or scripts.<br>

855. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 path-style and virtual-hosted-style URL formats? ; Virtual-hosted-style (current, recommended): `https://bucket-name.s3.region.amazonaws.com/key`. Bucket name is a subdomain. Path-style (deprecated): `https://s3.region.amazonaws.com/bucket-name/key`. Bucket name is in the URL path. AWS deprecated path-style access in September 2020 for new buckets. Existing path-style access still works but new applications should use virtual-hosted-style. <br><br> *Why virtual-hosted-style: supports custom domains and CloudFront CNAME. Bucket name is in the hostname — DNS resolution can route to the correct region. Path-style puts bucket in path — DNS always resolves to a global S3 endpoint first.<br> *S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoint: only works with virtual-hosted-style: `bucket-name.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com`. Path-style is not supported with Transfer Acceleration.<br> *HTTPS certificate: virtual-hosted-style with `bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com` uses a wildcard certificate covering all bucket names. Custom domains (e.g., via CloudFront) require a specific ACM certificate for the custom domain. Path-style URLs do not work well with custom SSL certificates.<br>

856. [ S3 ] What is S3 Object Ownership set to BucketOwnerEnforced and what does it disable? ; `BucketOwnerEnforced` sets the bucket owner as the owner of all objects regardless of who uploaded them. It completely disables S3 ACLs (both bucket ACLs and object ACLs are ignored). Access is controlled entirely by bucket policies and IAM policies. This is AWS's recommended setting for all new buckets as it simplifies access management. <br><br> *Problem solved: with the default Object Writer setting, objects uploaded by Account B to Account A's bucket are owned by Account B. Account A's bucket owner cannot control these objects — Account A is at the mercy of Account B's ACLs. BucketOwnerEnforced removes this: bucket owner always controls all objects.<br> *ACL disabled implications: all existing ACLs on the bucket and objects become ineffective. Any application that previously relied on object ACLs (e.g., setting `public-read` ACL on individual objects) will break. Migrate these use cases to bucket policies before enabling BucketOwnerEnforced.<br> *Migration: AWS provides a migration tool to audit ACL usage before enabling BucketOwnerEnforced. S3 Storage Lens "ACL" metrics can identify buckets with non-default ACLs. For new buckets: always enable BucketOwnerEnforced from the start.<br>

857. [ S3 ] What is S3 Lifecycle expiration and what is the difference between Current version expiration and Noncurrent version expiration? ; Current version expiration: deletes the current (latest) version of an object. Without versioning: permanently deletes the object. With versioning: creates a delete marker, making the object appear deleted (the version still exists). Noncurrent version expiration: permanently deletes versions that are no longer current (have been replaced by newer versions). This is the primary mechanism to control versioning storage costs. <br><br> *Without lifecycle noncurrent version expiration on a versioned bucket: every overwrite keeps the old version permanently. A bucket with 1 million objects each overwritten daily accumulates 365 million versions per year — costs grow unbounded. Noncurrent version expiration is essential for cost control in versioned buckets.<br> *Configuration: `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` with `NoncurrentDays: 30` deletes versions that have been noncurrent for 30+ days. `NewerNoncurrentVersions: 3` keeps the 3 most recent noncurrent versions regardless of age — useful to maintain a rollback history while still deleting old versions.<br> *Delete marker cleanup: after all versions of an object are deleted, an orphaned delete marker remains. Use `ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker: true` in the lifecycle rule to automatically clean up these orphaned delete markers. Without this, empty objects with delete markers persist indefinitely.<br>

858. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Inventory report delivery process and how long does it take to appear after configuration? ; After enabling S3 Inventory, the first report is delivered within 48 hours of configuration. Subsequent reports are delivered daily or weekly at a consistent time. Reports are delivered as CSV/ORC/Parquet files to the destination bucket with a manifest.json indicating the latest inventory files. The report reflects the bucket state at a specific time (not real-time). <br><br> *48-hour initial delay: S3 Inventory runs a full scan of the source bucket. For very large buckets (billions of objects), the initial inventory can take up to 48 hours. After the initial delivery, subsequent reports are incremental (faster to generate).<br> *Manifest file: `s3-inventory/source-bucket/config-id/hive/dt=YYYY-MM-DD-HH-MM/manifest.json`. Contains the S3 paths to all inventory data files. Athena, Glue, and other services use the manifest to locate the current inventory snapshot.<br> *Completeness: inventory reports do not guarantee 100% completeness for very active buckets (objects created or deleted during the inventory scan may be missed). For compliance scenarios requiring exact counts: use S3 API ListObjectsV2 (exact but slower for large buckets).<br>

859. [ S3 ] How does S3 handle bucket policy evaluation when both allow and deny statements exist? ; S3 evaluates policies using the standard IAM policy evaluation logic: explicit Deny always overrides any Allow. The evaluation order: (1) Check if any policy statement explicitly Denies the request — if yes, deny. (2) Check if any policy statement explicitly Allows the request — if yes, allow. (3) If no explicit Allow, implicitly deny. The Deny always wins regardless of where in the policy it appears. <br><br> *Cross-policy evaluation: when both IAM policy (identity-based) and bucket policy (resource-based) exist, access is granted only if BOTH allow it (or if one allows and the other doesn't mention it — implicit allow). Exception: for same-account access, either the IAM policy or bucket policy can grant access, both don't need to. For cross-account access: BOTH the bucket policy and the IAM policy in the requester's account must allow it.<br> *Block Public Access as an override: Block Public Access settings act as super-denys. They override bucket policies that grant public access. Even with an Allow in the bucket policy for `Principal: *`, if `RestrictPublicBuckets` is enabled, anonymous access is blocked.<br> *SCPs: AWS Organizations Service Control Policies also apply. An SCP Deny from the Organization level applies regardless of bucket policy or IAM policy. The full evaluation order: SCP → permission boundary → identity policy → bucket policy → ACL → endpoint policy.<br>

860. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Accelerate test endpoint and how can you verify if Transfer Acceleration is faster for your use case? ; AWS provides a comparison tool at `s3-accelerate-speedtest.s3.amazonaws.com` that measures upload/download speeds from your location to S3 both with and without Transfer Acceleration. AWS also provides a flag: if a Transfer Acceleration upload would not be faster, AWS does not charge the acceleration fee (it falls back to standard transfer automatically). <br><br> *Use the speed comparison tool before committing to Transfer Acceleration for a workload. For uploads from the US to a US S3 bucket: acceleration provides minimal benefit (already close to the AWS backbone). For uploads from Southeast Asia or Europe to a US S3 bucket: acceleration can provide 50–500% improvement.<br> *Transfer Acceleration endpoint: `bucket-name.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com` (always, regardless of region). Dual-stack: `bucket-name.s3-accelerate.dualstack.amazonaws.com` (for IPv6 + IPv4). Must enable acceleration per bucket before using the endpoint.<br> *Transfer Acceleration vs Direct Connect: both provide private path uploads. Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge for public internet clients. DX with VPC Endpoint is for on-premises clients with dedicated fiber. They serve different use cases and cannot substitute for each other.<br>

861. [ S3 ] What is S3 Object Lock Legal Hold and how does it differ from retention period? ; Legal Hold is an Object Lock feature that prevents object deletion/modification until the legal hold is explicitly removed. It has no expiry date (unlike retention periods which expire at a specific date). Legal Hold can be toggled on/off by users with `s3:PutObjectLegalHold` IAM permission. It is independent of retention period — an object can have both a retention period and a legal hold simultaneously. <br><br> *Use case: litigation hold. When a legal case is filed, place legal holds on all relevant documents. The documents are immutable until the legal hold is removed (after litigation resolves). Unlike retention periods, legal holds don't expire automatically — they require explicit action to remove.<br> *Legal hold vs retention period interaction: if an object has both a retention period (Compliance mode) and a legal hold, BOTH must be cleared for the object to be deletable. Retention period expiry alone does not remove the legal hold. Legal hold removal alone does not override the retention period (if still active).<br> *Who can remove legal holds: any user with `s3:PutObjectLegalHold` IAM permission, including admins. This is less restrictive than Compliance mode retention (which cannot be shortened by anyone). Legal holds are suitable for enterprise/legal team use where holds must be managed by legal personnel.<br>

862. [ S3 ] How does S3 pricing work for storage, and what are the key cost components? ; S3 pricing components: (1) Storage: per GB/month by storage class, (2) Requests: per 1,000 GET/PUT/COPY/LIST requests, (3) Data retrieval: per GB for IA/Glacier classes, (4) Data transfer OUT: per GB to internet or cross-region, (5) Management features: Inventory, Storage Lens advanced metrics, Object Lock, Replication Time Control, Intelligent-Tiering monitoring. Data transfer IN and same-region transfers to AWS services are free. <br><br> *Storage class pricing order (cheapest to most expensive per GB/month): Deep Archive < Glacier Flexible Retrieval < One Zone-IA ≈ Glacier Instant Retrieval < Standard-IA < Standard. Intelligent-Tiering dynamically adjusts (Standard pricing + monitoring fee).<br> *Request pricing matters for small objects: if you store millions of tiny objects in Glacier and retrieve them individually, the per-request retrieval cost may exceed the storage savings. Combine small objects (zip/tar) before archiving to reduce request counts.<br> *Data transfer out to internet: $0.09/GB for first 10 TB/month (us-east-1). Significant for large public datasets. Use CloudFront to cache content — CloudFront DTO to internet is $0.085/GB and CloudFront → S3 is free. For very high traffic: CloudFront dramatically reduces S3 DTO costs.<br>

863. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 server access logs and S3 object-level CloudTrail events in terms of delivery guarantees? ; Server access logs: best-effort delivery only. Logs may be delayed by hours and are not guaranteed to capture every request. CloudTrail S3 data events: near real-time delivery to CloudTrail's S3 bucket, highly reliable, and captures essentially every API call. Server access logs are appropriate for access pattern analysis where some loss is acceptable. CloudTrail data events are required for security audit where completeness is essential. <br><br> *Server access log format: each line contains request details (timestamp, bucket, key, operation, requester IP, HTTP status, bytes sent, response time). Useful for identifying hot objects, error patterns, traffic sources. No IAM identity information.<br> *CloudTrail data event format: structured JSON with: eventName (GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject), userIdentity (full IAM ARN including assumed role), requestParameters (bucket and key), responseElements (ETag for PUTs), sourceIPAddress, eventTime. Full forensic trail.<br> *Cost consideration: for a bucket receiving 1 million requests per day: CloudTrail data events cost $0.10/100K = $1/day = $30/month. For a bucket receiving 1 billion requests/day: $1,000/day. Enable CloudTrail data events selectively for high-value buckets, use server access logs for high-volume operational buckets.<br>

864. [ S3 ] What is S3 Select performance and how is it billed? ; S3 Select performs server-side SQL filtering and returns only matching rows/columns, reducing the amount of data transferred. Performance: up to 400% faster and 80% less data transfer compared to downloading the full object. Billing: per GB of data scanned + per GB of data returned. Minimizing both (use WHERE clauses to filter rows, SELECT specific columns) reduces cost. <br><br> *When to use S3 Select vs Athena: S3 Select queries one object at a time. Athena can query multiple objects across prefixes, supports joins, aggregations, and uses Glue catalog for schema management. For simple per-object filtering (get specific rows from a log file), S3 Select is simpler and cheaper. For complex multi-object analytics: use Athena.<br> *Format support: CSV (with or without header), JSON (lines or documents), Parquet. Compression: GZIP and BZIP2 for CSV/JSON (transparent decompression before SQL). Parquet uses its own internal compression which S3 Select handles automatically.<br> *SDK usage: `s3.select_object_content(Bucket=b, Key=k, Expression="SELECT * FROM S3Object s WHERE s.age > 30", ExpressionType="SQL", InputSerialization={"CSV": {"FileHeaderInfo": "USE"}}, OutputSerialization={"CSV": {}})`. Returns a streaming response of matching records.<br>

865. [ S3 ] What is the S3 bucket policy for enforcing HTTPS-only access? ; Use a Deny effect for requests where `aws:SecureTransport` is `false`. This denies all HTTP (plaintext) requests. Combined with TLS, all data in transit is encrypted. The policy applies to all actions on the bucket and objects. <br><br> *Policy: `{"Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*"], "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "false"}}}`. The Resource must include both the bucket ARN (for bucket-level actions like list) and the object ARN (for object-level actions).<br> *Why both resources: `s3:ListBucket` operates on the bucket (`arn:aws:s3:::bucket`). `s3:GetObject`, `s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteObject` operate on objects (`arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*`). Without both, HTTPS enforcement has gaps.<br> *This policy is required for PCI DSS compliance (encryption in transit). Combined with SSE-KMS enforcement (Q825): all data is encrypted at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS). These two bucket policies together cover most encryption compliance requirements.<br>

866. [ S3 ] What happens if you PUT an object to S3 without specifying a Content-Type? ; S3 defaults to `application/octet-stream` (binary stream) as the Content-Type if none is specified. This can cause issues when browsers try to render the file inline — they will download instead of render it. For web assets (images, HTML, CSS, JS), always specify the correct Content-Type. Content-Type is stored as system metadata and can only be changed by copying the object. <br><br> *Impact: an image uploaded without `Content-Type: image/jpeg` will be served as `application/octet-stream`. Browsers prompt download instead of displaying inline. For S3 static websites and S3-backed CDN (CloudFront): always set correct Content-Type on upload.<br> *Bulk Content-Type fix: use S3 Batch Operations with an InvokeLambda operation — Lambda function copies each object to itself with the correct Content-Type based on file extension. This is the only way to update metadata (Content-Type is metadata, requires copy).<br> *SDK auto-detection: some SDKs (boto3, AWS SDK for JavaScript) auto-detect Content-Type from file extension during upload. AWS CLI `aws s3 cp` also guesses Content-Type. Verify with `aws s3api head-object` after upload to confirm correct Content-Type was applied.<br>

867. [ S3 ] What is the relationship between S3 and Amazon Athena for data lake analytics? ; Athena is a serverless SQL query engine that reads data directly from S3. It uses AWS Glue Data Catalog for schema (table definitions, column types, partition layout). Pay per TB of data scanned ($5/TB in us-east-1). Use Parquet or ORC format with partitioning to minimize data scanned. Athena + S3 + Glue = the foundational serverless data lake stack. <br><br> *Cost optimization: `SELECT * FROM large_table` on a 10 TB CSV = $50 per query. Same query on Parquet with 10:1 compression and year/month/day partitioning: scans only the relevant partition (e.g., 1 GB) = $0.005 per query. Format conversion and partitioning are critical for Athena cost control.<br> *Glue catalog: Glue Crawlers auto-discover S3 data schema and create/update table definitions. Alternatively: define tables manually with CREATE TABLE in Athena. Partitioned tables reference `s3://bucket/prefix/year=2024/month=01/` style paths — each partition is a separate S3 prefix.<br> *Athena Federated Query: query across S3 AND relational databases (RDS, DynamoDB, Redshift) in one SQL query using Athena Data Source Connectors (Lambda-based). S3 remains the central data lake, federated queries allow joins between S3 data and operational database data.<br>

868. [ S3 ] What is S3 Replication and what is Replica Modification Sync? ; S3 replication copies new objects from source bucket to destination bucket. Replica Modification Sync extends this to replicate metadata changes made to replica objects back to the source. Without it, if you modify object tags or ACLs on the replica, those changes do not propagate back. With Replica Modification Sync: changes made to replicas are synced back to source (bidirectional metadata sync). <br><br> *Replica Modification Sync use case: active-active replication scenarios where both source and destination are written to. Tag updates, storage class changes on the replica need to be reflected in the source. Without sync, the two buckets diverge over time in metadata.<br> *Only metadata changes are synced: object data changes are not synced by Replica Modification Sync (that would be bidirectional data replication, requiring separate CRR in both directions). Replica Modification Sync specifically covers: tags, ACLs, and Object Lock settings modifications on existing replica objects.<br> *Not the same as bidirectional replication: bidirectional replication = configure CRR A→B AND CRR B→A (new objects replicate both ways). Replica Modification Sync = changes to replica object metadata sync back to source. Both can be enabled simultaneously.<br>

869. [ S3 ] How can you implement data lake access control with fine-grained column-level security on S3 data? ; Use AWS Lake Formation. Lake Formation provides column-level security (allow/deny specific columns per IAM principal), row-level security (filter rows based on user attributes), cell-level security (mask specific cell values), and table-level security — all on data stored in S3 and cataloged in Glue. Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR Spark can query S3 through Lake Formation permissions. <br><br> *Without Lake Formation: access control on S3 data is at the S3 object level (bucket policies). Every file is accessible or not — no column-level filtering. To implement column filtering without Lake Formation: create separate S3 prefixes per user type (expensive, duplicates data), or use S3 Object Lambda (transforms data per requester). Lake Formation is the purpose-built solution.<br> *Lake Formation data filters: define a filter as `"column1, column2, column3" WHERE status = 'public'`. Grant this filter to an IAM role. When that role queries the table via Athena, only columns 1, 2, 3 and rows where status='public' are returned — even though the S3 data file contains all columns and rows.<br> *Integration: Lake Formation manages permissions via its own grant/revoke model on top of Glue Data Catalog. Athena checks Lake Formation permissions before executing queries. Data stays in S3 — Lake Formation does not copy data, it applies access policies at query time.<br>

870. [ S3 ] What is the maximum number of object tags per S3 object, and what constraints exist on tag keys and values? ; Maximum 10 tags per object. Tag key: maximum 128 Unicode characters. Tag value: maximum 256 Unicode characters. Tag keys must be unique per object (no duplicate keys). Tags are case-sensitive. Tags can be used for lifecycle filtering, replication filtering, IAM ABAC conditions, cost allocation, and S3 Batch Operations filtering. <br><br> *Tags vs user metadata: tags can be updated after object creation without copying. User metadata is immutable after creation (requires CopyObject to change). For dynamic attributes (processing status, owner, environment): use tags. For static attributes set at upload time: metadata or tags both work.<br> *Replication tag filtering: configure replication rules to replicate only objects with a specific tag (e.g., `replicate: yes`). Objects without the tag are not replicated. This allows fine-grained control over what gets replicated without managing separate prefixes for replication inclusion/exclusion.<br> *Cost allocation tags: S3 object tags can be used for cost allocation if enabled in the Billing console as cost allocation tags. AWS Cost Explorer can then show S3 costs broken down by tag value (e.g., by department or project). Tags on objects (not bucket tags) are required for per-object cost allocation.<br>


871. [ S3 ] What is S3 bucket versioning and how does it protect against accidental deletion? ; Versioning preserves every version of every object ever uploaded to a bucket. When an object is deleted (without specifying version ID), S3 creates a delete marker — the object appears deleted but all previous versions are still stored. To recover: delete the delete marker. Even after overwriting an object (PUT same key), the old version is preserved with its version ID. <br><br> *Protection mechanism: versioning protects against user error (accidental delete/overwrite), application bugs that overwrite data, malware that deletes or corrupts files. Even a ransomware attack that overwrites all objects leaves original versions intact (attacker cannot delete versions without version ID + MFA Delete).<br> *Cost consideration: versioning multiplies storage costs. A 100 GB bucket with objects overwritten 10 times holds 1 TB of version data. Combined with lifecycle `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` rules to control version history depth. Best practice: keep last 3-5 noncurrent versions for normal buckets.<br> *MFA Delete adds another layer: even if an attacker gains admin access, permanently deleting versions requires physical MFA. Enables "defense in depth" for critical compliance buckets where data must never be permanently deleted.<br>

872. [ S3 ] How does S3 event notification work for large-scale event processing, and what is the recommended pattern? ; S3 generates events for object operations (created, deleted, restored, replicated). For large-scale, reliable processing: use S3 → EventBridge → SQS (for buffering and backpressure) → Lambda/Fargate consumers. EventBridge provides rich filtering and fan-out. SQS provides buffering for spiky workloads. Lambda polls SQS for processing. <br><br> *Why SQS buffer: S3 can generate thousands of events/second (burst uploads). Direct S3 → Lambda invocation at this rate may hit Lambda concurrency limits or overwhelm downstream systems. SQS absorbs the burst and delivers events at the consumer's processing rate.<br> *DLQ (Dead Letter Queue): attach a DLQ to the SQS queue or Lambda for failed event processing. Failed events (Lambda errors, timeouts) go to the DLQ for investigation and retry. Without DLQ: failed events are silently dropped or retried indefinitely depending on configuration.<br> *EventBridge filtering reduces noise: if only large object creation events matter (objects > 1 GB), add an EventBridge rule filter: `"detail.object.size": [{"numeric": [">", 1073741824]}]`. Only matching events reach the SQS queue — Lambda is not invoked for irrelevant events.<br>

873. [ S3 ] What is S3 Inventory and how does it differ from S3 Storage Lens? ; S3 Inventory provides object-level metadata reports (each row = one object) for a specific bucket, delivered daily or weekly to S3. S3 Storage Lens provides aggregated analytics metrics (storage totals, request counts, recommendations) across all buckets and accounts. Inventory = granular per-object data for specific bucket audit. Storage Lens = organization-wide high-level analytics dashboard. <br><br> *Use Inventory when: you need to know the exact list of objects, their storage class, encryption status, Object Lock settings, or replication status for audit/compliance. You process the report with Athena for SQL queries over all objects.<br> *Use Storage Lens when: you want to understand trends (storage growth over time, request patterns), get cost optimization recommendations, monitor replication health, or see encryption coverage percentage — across the entire organization without per-bucket processing.<br> *Combined use: Storage Lens identifies a bucket with high unencrypted object percentage (recommendation). Run S3 Inventory on that bucket to get the exact list of unencrypted objects (object key, ETag). Use S3 Batch Operations (with Inventory as manifest) to re-encrypt all unencrypted objects. Three services working together for operational remediation.<br>

874. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage class and when should it be preferred over Standard-IA? ; Glacier Instant Retrieval provides millisecond retrieval (same as Standard-IA) at ~68% lower storage cost, but with a 90-day minimum storage duration (vs 30 days for Standard-IA) and higher retrieval fee per GB. Prefer Glacier Instant Retrieval when: access frequency is quarterly or less, objects are retained for 90+ days, and retrieval cost per access is acceptable given lower storage cost. <br><br> *Break-even: compare storage savings vs retrieval costs. For an object accessed quarterly: Glacier IR saves ~$0.0085/GB/month vs Standard-IA. Over 3 months = $0.0255/GB saved. Glacier IR retrieval fee: ~$0.03/GB per retrieval. Break-even: retrieval cost ($0.03) vs quarterly storage savings (~$0.025). For large objects or very infrequent access: Glacier IR wins.<br> *Standard-IA preferred when: objects may be deleted within 30–89 days (to avoid 90-day minimum charge), access frequency is monthly rather than quarterly, or retrieval fees are a concern for large-volume occasional access.<br> *Intelligent-Tiering Archive Instant Access tier: equivalent to Glacier Instant Retrieval pricing, automatically moved to after 90+ days without access, with NO retrieval fee. For objects with uncertain access patterns: Intelligent-Tiering with Archive Instant Access enabled is better than manually managing Glacier IR + Standard-IA transitions.<br>

875. [ S3 ] What are the S3 request rate limits per prefix, and how do you design for high-throughput workloads? ; S3 supports 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE requests per second and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix. For high-throughput workloads: distribute objects across multiple prefixes (e.g., hash-based prefixes, date-based prefixes, user-ID-based prefixes) to multiply effective throughput. With 10 prefixes: 35,000 PUT/sec, 55,000 GET/sec. <br><br> *Prefix strategy: previously (pre-2018) recommended random hash prefix (first 4 chars of MD5 hash). Now S3 auto-scales per prefix — but for extreme throughput, explicit prefix distribution still helps. Design prefix structure based on access patterns: date-based (yyyy/mm/dd/) for time-series data, hash-based for random access, user-ID-based for user-specific data.<br> *S3 Express One Zone as alternative: for extreme latency-sensitive high-throughput workloads, Express One Zone provides 10× higher request rates without the prefix management complexity. Trade-off: single-AZ (durability risk), limited feature set, higher per-request cost.<br> *Multipart upload for throughput: large objects should use multipart upload with parallel part uploads. Each part is an independent PUT request to different internal S3 shards, effectively multiplying write throughput without needing explicit prefix management.<br>

876. [ S3 ] What are the implications of disabling versioning (suspending) on a bucket that has existing versions? ; Suspending versioning preserves all existing object versions — they are not deleted. New PUT requests to existing keys create a `null` version ID overwrite (no new version created). The `null` version may overwrite an existing `null` version. Existing versioned objects (with non-null version IDs) remain and are still accessible via their version IDs. <br><br> *Critical implication: suspending versioning does NOT clean up existing versions. A 10 TB bucket with 50 TB of version history continues charging for 50 TB of version storage after suspension. Versioning suspension only stops creating new versions — does not delete old ones.<br> *To clean up after suspension: create a lifecycle rule with `NoncurrentVersionExpiration: 0 days` to immediately delete all noncurrent versions. Or use S3 Batch Operations to explicitly delete old versions. Then suspend versioning to prevent new version accumulation.<br> *Versioning suspended + new PUT: the new object gets `null` version ID. If a `null` version already exists (from a previous upload before versioning was enabled or from a previous suspension PUT), the old `null` version is replaced. Non-null versions are unaffected by new PUTs to the same key.<br>

877. [ S3 ] What is S3 Glacier and how does it relate to S3 storage classes? ; "Amazon S3 Glacier" historically referred to a separate service (now called Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes). Modern S3 Glacier means the storage classes within S3: Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and Glacier Deep Archive. The legacy standalone Glacier service (with Vaults) still exists but is different. For SAP-C02: Glacier storage classes in S3 (accessed via S3 API) are the primary exam topic. <br><br> *Legacy Glacier Vaults vs S3 Glacier classes: Legacy Vaults use a completely different API (Vault operations, Vault Lock, TreeHash checksums). S3 Glacier classes use the standard S3 API (PutObject, GetObject, RestoreObject). Modern architectures use S3 Glacier classes, not legacy Vaults.<br> *Object in S3 Glacier class: stored with S3 metadata (key, version ID, etc.) but the object data is moved to Glacier infrastructure. To access: call `RestoreObject` first (specify number of days for temporary copy), wait for restoration, then GET. Unlike S3 Standard where GET works immediately.<br> *Direct upload to Glacier: use `x-amz-storage-class: GLACIER` in the PutObject request header. Or configure lifecycle to transition after N days. Glacier Deep Archive: `x-amz-storage-class: DEEP_ARCHIVE`. Objects land directly in Glacier — no initial Standard copy required.<br>

878. [ S3 ] What is the S3 CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) and why is it preferred over Origin Access Identity (OAI)? ; OAC (newer) and OAI (legacy) both restrict S3 bucket access to only the specific CloudFront distribution — preventing users from accessing S3 directly bypassing CloudFront. OAC is preferred because it supports: all S3 regions (OAI doesn't work with new regions), SSE-KMS encrypted objects (OAI cannot sign requests for KMS), S3 bucket policies with OAC principal (instead of OAI magic user). <br><br> *OAI limitation: uses a legacy CloudFront special principal (`cloudfront.amazonaws.com` was not the OAI principal — OAI used the OAI S3 canonical user ID). OAI cannot send AWS Signature Version 4 requests required for SSE-KMS encrypted S3 objects. If your S3 bucket uses SSE-KMS: must use OAC, not OAI.<br> *OAC bucket policy: `"Principal": {"Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com"}, "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::account:distribution/DIST_ID"}}`. Precisely scoped to one CloudFront distribution. Multiple distributions serving different S3 buckets need separate OAC configurations.<br> *Combined with Block Public Access: S3 bucket with Block Public Access enabled + OAC on CloudFront = objects are private in S3, only accessible via the specific CloudFront distribution. This is the standard pattern for S3-backed static websites and media delivery.<br>

879. [ S3 ] What is the S3 byte-range fetch technique and how does it improve download performance? ; Byte-range fetch uses the HTTP `Range` header to request a specific byte range of an S3 object (`Range: bytes=0-1048576`). Multiple parallel GET requests for different ranges can be issued simultaneously, downloading different parts of a large object in parallel and reconstructing it client-side. This significantly improves download throughput for large objects. <br><br> *Example: download a 10 GB file in 10 parallel ranges (1 GB each). Each range request runs simultaneously to different S3 shard servers. Total download time ~1/10 of sequential download. AWS CLI uses this automatically when `--range` is not specified for large files (via `aws s3 cp`).<br> *Partial file access: byte-range fetch also enables accessing specific parts of large files without downloading the whole object. For CSV files: fetch just the first N bytes for header detection. For video files: fetch specific frame ranges. For archive files: fetch table of contents bytes.<br> *Resilience: if one range request fails, only that range needs to be retried — not the entire file. This makes large file downloads more reliable over intermittent connections. Combined with parallel requests and checksum verification per range, it provides robust large file transfer.<br>

880. [ S3 ] What is AWS S3 Access Grants and what identity providers does it integrate with? ; S3 Access Grants maps corporate identity directory entries (users, groups, applications) to S3 data locations with permissions. It integrates with: AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO), corporate SAML 2.0 identity providers (via IAM Identity Center), AWS IAM roles/users, and third-party IdPs (Okta, Azure AD via SAML federation). When a principal requests access, Grants vend scoped STS temporary credentials for the specific S3 prefix. <br><br> *Flow: user authenticates via IAM Identity Center → calls Grants GetDataAccess API → Grants maps the user's group to an S3 location grant → Grants vends STS credentials scoped to that S3 location → user uses STS credentials to access S3. All credential management is automated.<br> *Scale advantage: managing S3 access for 10,000 employees via IAM roles requires maintaining hundreds of roles and policies. With Access Grants: define grants based on directory groups. Adding/removing employees from the directory group automatically grants/revokes S3 access. No IAM changes needed.<br> *Audit: all Access Grants credential issuance is logged in CloudTrail. CloudTrail shows which directory user received credentials for which S3 path. Combined with S3 CloudTrail data events: complete audit trail from "who logged in" to "what S3 data they accessed".<br>


881. [ S3 ] What are the S3 event notification sources that can be filtered by object key prefix and suffix? ; All S3 direct notification destinations (SNS, SQS, Lambda) support filtering by key prefix and suffix. EventBridge also supports prefix/suffix filtering via rule event patterns (`"detail.object.key": [{"prefix": "images/"}, {"suffix": ".jpg"}]`). Filtering reduces notification volume by only sending events for objects matching the pattern. <br><br> *Prefix filter: `images/` sends notifications only for objects whose key starts with `images/`. Useful for partitioned buckets where different prefixes represent different data types/teams.<br> *Suffix filter: `.jpg` sends notifications only for JPEG files. Combined with prefix: `images/` prefix AND `.jpg` suffix = only JPEG files in the images/ prefix. Multiple filter rules cannot overlap in S3 direct notifications (AWS rejects conflicting configurations).<br> *EventBridge advanced filtering: beyond prefix/suffix, EventBridge supports regex patterns, numeric comparisons (object size), array membership, and "anything but" patterns. Allows sophisticated routing — e.g., "new files > 100 MB in the raw/ prefix ending in .parquet" trigger a specific workflow.<br>

882. [ S3 ] How can you replicate S3 data between two accounts without giving the destination account direct access to the source bucket? ; Configure CRR with an IAM role in the source account that has permission to read source bucket and write to destination bucket. The destination bucket policy grants the source account's replication IAM role permission to replicate objects into it. The destination account only manages its own bucket — it does not have access to the source bucket. Replication happens account-to-account via the IAM role assuming permissions on both sides. <br><br> *Source account: creates IAM role `S3ReplicationRole` with s3:GetObject/GetObjectVersion on source bucket. The role trust policy: `s3.amazonaws.com`. Bucket replication configuration references this role ARN.<br> *Destination account: bucket policy grants `S3ReplicationRole` from source account: s3:ReplicateObject, s3:ReplicateDelete, s3:ReplicateTags on the destination bucket. The destination account admin controls exactly what the source account's role can do in their bucket — never grants general source account access.<br> *Object Ownership cross-account: by default, replicated objects are owned by the source account's S3 role — destination account cannot manage them. Enable `BucketOwnerEnforced` on the destination bucket: all replicated objects become owned by the destination account. Required for destination to have full control over replicated data.<br>

883. [ S3 ] What is S3 Replication and how does it handle objects that fail to replicate? ; Failed replication attempts are retried. If an object consistently fails (e.g., destination bucket policy denies, KMS key access denied), the failure is tracked in replication metrics (CloudWatch: `OperationsPendingReplication`, `ReplicationLatency`). With Replication Time Control (RTC): failed objects generate CloudWatch alarms. Without RTC: no automatic alerting for failures. Use S3 Batch Replication to retry failed objects after fixing the root cause. <br><br> *Common replication failure causes: destination bucket Block Public Access conflicts, destination bucket policy missing allow for replication role, KMS key policy not granting replication role permissions, destination bucket versioning disabled, CIDR/network-based access control blocking S3 service.<br> *Replication failure detection: with RTC, CloudWatch metric `BytesPendingReplication` growing over time indicates replication lag. Alarm on this metric. Without RTC: S3 Inventory shows replication status per object (`COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `REPLICA`, `NOT_IN_PROGRESS`). Query with Athena to find FAILED objects.<br> *Replication of delete markers (optional config): if delete marker replication is disabled (default), deleting an object in source creates a delete marker in source but object in destination remains visible. Enable delete marker replication for full DR parity: deletions in source propagate to destination.<br>

884. [ S3 ] What is the S3 static website hosting difference between using the S3 website endpoint as CloudFront origin vs the S3 REST API endpoint? ; S3 website endpoint as CloudFront origin: supports index documents (e.g., `index.html` for directory requests) and custom error pages. S3 REST API endpoint as CloudFront origin with OAC: requires CloudFront to set default root object, does NOT support S3 index document behavior for subdirectory paths. Use S3 website endpoint when index.html behavior for subdirectory paths is required. Use S3 REST endpoint + OAC for private bucket access with SSE-KMS. <br><br> *Practical difference: request for `https://example.com/docs/` with website endpoint origin → S3 returns `docs/index.html`. With REST API endpoint: S3 returns 403/404 for directory paths (no index document support). CloudFront's "Default Root Object" only handles the root path (`/`).<br> *OAC limitation with website endpoint: S3 website endpoint is HTTP only and does not support OAC (requires HTTPS and Signature V4). To use OAC (for private bucket): must use S3 REST API endpoint. Trade-off: lose subdirectory index.html behavior.<br> *Workaround: CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge can rewrite directory requests (append `/index.html`) when using S3 REST API endpoint with OAC. This restores the index document behavior while keeping the security benefits of OAC and private S3 bucket.<br>

885. [ S3 ] What is SSE-C and what are its operational requirements? ; SSE-C (Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys): customer provides a 256-bit AES key in the request headers for each API call. S3 uses the key to encrypt (PUT) or decrypt (GET) the object, then discards the key — it's never stored. HTTPS is mandatory (key is in the HTTP header). Customer must securely store and manage keys. AWS CLI does not support SSE-C via high-level commands, must use `s3api` subcommands. <br><br> *Required headers: `x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-algorithm: AES256`, `x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-key: base64-encoded-256-bit-key`, `x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-key-MD5: base64-encoded-MD5-of-key`. AWS verifies the MD5 to ensure the key was not corrupted in transit.<br> *Key management responsibility: customer must maintain a key-to-object mapping. If the key for an object is lost, the object is permanently inaccessible — AWS cannot recover it (key is never stored). This is the highest customer responsibility for encryption key management.<br> *Use case: organizations that cannot allow AWS to access their encryption keys under any circumstances (regulatory mandate). S3 processes data but the key control remains entirely external. For less strict requirements: SSE-KMS with CMK provides key audit trail and control without the operational burden of SSE-C.<br>

886. [ S3 ] What is the S3 checksum feature and how does it ensure data integrity? ; S3 supports additional checksums beyond ETag for data integrity verification: SHA-256, SHA-1, CRC32, CRC32C. Specify the checksum algorithm at upload time (`x-amz-checksum-*` header). S3 verifies the checksum on receipt and returns an error if it doesn't match. For multipart uploads, S3 can compute a full-object checksum from part checksums (trailing checksums). <br><br> *ETag vs checksum: ETag is an MD5 hash but for multipart uploads, ETag is a hash of hashes (not a direct content checksum). For CRC/SHA checksums: they reflect the actual content. CRC32C is recommended for performance (hardware-accelerated on most processors).<br> *Trailing checksum: the checksum can be included at the end of the object payload (trailing checksum). This enables streaming uploads where the checksum is computed during the stream and verified by S3 without pre-computing before upload starts. Reduces latency for large streaming uploads.<br> *Cross-replication checksum: when S3 replicates objects, the checksum is replicated with the object. The destination bucket verifies the checksum on receipt. This ensures bit-perfect replication. Enabling checksums provides end-to-end integrity verification from source to replica.<br>

887. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access tier and how does it differ from Glacier Instant Retrieval? ; Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access tier (optional, requires enabling): automatically moves objects that haven't been accessed for 90–180 days to this tier. Same storage cost as Glacier Instant Retrieval. Difference: Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access has a retrieval fee of ~$0.01/GB when accessed (tier is automatically, moves back to Frequent Access). Glacier Instant Retrieval also has a retrieval fee. Key advantage of IT Archive Access: objects automatically moved back to Frequent Access when accessed — no manual restore operation needed. <br><br> *Comparison: Glacier Instant Retrieval (direct class) — retrieval in milliseconds, retrieval fee applies, object stays in Glacier IR until lifecycle moves it. IT Archive Access — retrieval in milliseconds, retrieval fee applies, object automatically promoted back to Frequent Access after retrieval. IT is more convenient for unpredictable access patterns.<br> *IT Archive Access vs IT Deep Archive Access: Archive Access (90-day threshold, instant retrieval), Deep Archive Access (180-day threshold, 12-hour retrieval). Both are optional IT tiers. Deep Archive Access is the cheapest IT tier but with 12-hour retrieval — same as Glacier Deep Archive standalone.<br> *IT monitoring fee still applies: $0.0025/1,000 objects/month for all objects in Intelligent-Tiering, regardless of which tier they're in. This fee is the trade-off for automatic tier management. For very infrequent access with known patterns: manual Glacier lifecycle is cheaper (no monitoring fee).<br>

888. [ S3 ] What happens to S3 objects when a KMS key used for SSE-KMS is disabled or deleted? ; If the KMS CMK is disabled: existing encrypted objects cannot be read (S3 cannot call KMS Decrypt → access denied for all GET requests). New objects cannot be encrypted with the disabled key. If the CMK is scheduled for deletion (7–30 day waiting period): during the waiting period, behavior same as disabled. After deletion: objects encrypted with the deleted CMK are permanently inaccessible — no recovery possible. <br><br> *This is both a security feature and an operational risk. Intentional: disabling a CMK provides immediate data access revocation for all objects encrypted with it — useful for compliance scenarios requiring "right to erasure" without physically deleting 1 billion objects. Accidental CMK deletion: catastrophic and irreversible.<br> *Key deletion protection: enable AWS KMS key deletion protection best practices. Use resource-based key policies that deny `kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion` except for specific authorized roles. Never delete a KMS key unless all objects encrypted with it are either migrated to a new key or no longer needed.<br> *Key rotation: AWS-managed keys auto-rotate annually. Customer-managed keys: enable automatic annual rotation or manually rotate. Key rotation changes the backing material but keeps the same key ID — existing objects encrypted with old material are still accessible (KMS manages the version). Rotation does NOT re-encrypt existing objects, it only applies the new material to new encryptions.<br>

889. [ S3 ] What is an S3 directory bucket and how does it differ from a general-purpose bucket? ; Directory buckets (used with S3 Express One Zone) differ from general-purpose buckets in: naming (includes AZ ID suffix: `bucket-name--az-id--x-s3`), scope (single AZ vs multi-AZ), supported features (no versioning, replication, Object Lock, lifecycle transitions), authentication (CreateSession API for short-term credentials), and performance (10× faster, single-digit millisecond latency). General-purpose buckets support all S3 features. <br><br> *CreateSession authentication: instead of every request independently authenticating via SigV4, Express One Zone uses `CreateSession` to get short-lived credentials (~5 minutes) and then uses those for multiple requests. Reduces authentication overhead for high-frequency request patterns.<br> *Not for general use: directory buckets are for specific high-performance use cases. Missing features (versioning, lifecycle, replication) make them unsuitable as primary data stores. Use directory buckets for: ML training data scratch space, real-time analytics input, HPC simulation data — always with durable backup in general-purpose buckets.<br> *Feature gap implications: no versioning = no accidental deletion protection. No replication = no geographic DR. No Object Lock = no WORM compliance. For any compliance or DR requirement: only general-purpose buckets are appropriate. Express One Zone is purely a performance optimization tier.<br>

890. [ S3 ] What is S3 Object Lock and when must the bucket be Object Lock-enabled? ; Object Lock must be enabled at bucket creation time — it cannot be added to an existing bucket. Once enabled, it automatically enables versioning (Object Lock requires versioning). Object Lock can then be configured per-object (Retention mode + period, or Legal Hold) or as a bucket default (default retention mode and period applied to all new objects). <br><br> *Cannot enable post-creation: this is the critical constraint. Organizations must plan for Object Lock at bucket design time. If a bucket was created without Object Lock and WORM compliance is later required: create a new Object Lock-enabled bucket, use S3 Batch Replication to copy existing objects, then configure Object Lock on the new objects.<br> *Bucket default Object Lock: set a default retention mode (Compliance or Governance) and retention period (days or years) at the bucket level. All new objects uploaded without specifying Object Lock settings receive the default. Objects can override the default by specifying a longer retention period (never shorter — can't reduce below default).<br> *Compliance use case: for SEC 17a-4, all records must be immutable from day one. Create Object Lock bucket with Compliance mode default retention (7 years). Every uploaded record is automatically protected. No application changes needed — Object Lock is enforced transparently by S3.<br>


891. [ S3 ] What is the S3 CopyObject operation and what are its use cases? ; CopyObject copies an object within S3 (same bucket or different bucket, same region or cross-region) server-side without downloading and re-uploading. Use cases: (1) Rename objects (copy then delete), (2) Change storage class without re-upload, (3) Change metadata or tags (copy to same key with new metadata), (4) Change encryption (copy with different encryption settings), (5) Copy across accounts or regions. <br><br> *Metadata update: the only way to change object user metadata or system metadata (Content-Type, Cache-Control) after upload is CopyObject to the same key with the `REPLACE` metadata directive and new metadata values. The object is copied in place — same key, updated metadata.<br> *Storage class change via CopyObject: `aws s3api copy-object --copy-source bucket/key --bucket bucket --key key --storage-class INTELLIGENT_TIERING`. For bulk class changes: S3 Batch Operations with CopyObject is more efficient (manages thousands of copies in parallel).<br> *Cross-region CopyObject: copies the object from source to destination region server-side. Source is read by S3 infrastructure and written to destination — no bandwidth on the caller's side. Charged at inter-region data transfer rates. Cannot copy objects in Glacier classes directly (must restore first).<br>

892. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) CloudWatch metric for monitoring replication health? ; Key RTC CloudWatch metrics: `BytesPendingReplication` (bytes waiting to be replicated — should trend to 0), `OperationsPendingReplication` (object count pending — should trend to 0), `ReplicationLatency` (max time in seconds for any pending operation — should stay well below 900 seconds). Alarm thresholds: `BytesPendingReplication > 0 for 15 minutes` indicates replication is falling behind. <br><br> *Without RTC: these metrics are not available. Only RTC provides replication metrics in CloudWatch. Standard replication has no visibility into pending operations or latency. For any workload with RPO requirements: enable RTC to get metrics and alerting capability.<br> *Replication failure metric: `ReplicationFailedOperations` counts objects that failed replication (not retried successfully). Alarm on `ReplicationFailedOperations > 0` for immediate notification of any replication failure. Investigate the failed object's metadata to identify the root cause.<br> *Metric granularity: metrics are per replication rule (if multiple rules configured). Combine CloudWatch alarms per rule or use CloudWatch metric math to aggregate across rules. For critical data: alert on any rule's pending bytes exceeding a threshold for the defined RPO window.<br>

893. [ S3 ] What is the S3 request pricing difference between GET and LIST operations? ; GET requests: $0.0004 per 1,000 requests (us-east-1). LIST requests (ListObjectsV2): $0.005 per 1,000 requests — 12.5× more expensive than GET. DELETE requests: free. PUT/COPY/POST: $0.005 per 1,000 requests. SELECT requests (S3 Select): $0.002 per 1,000 requests. For applications that frequently list bucket contents: high LIST costs can accumulate. Use S3 Inventory for bulk object discovery instead of repeated LIST API calls. <br><br> *LIST at scale: listing 1 billion objects via ListObjectsV2 (1,000 objects per page = 1 million LIST API calls): $0.005 × 1,000 = $5.00. S3 Inventory: fixed schedule delivery to S3 at minimal cost. For periodic full-bucket audits: Inventory is dramatically cheaper than repeated LIST calls.<br> *Lifecycle rules with tag filters: lifecycle evaluation requires S3 to read object tags. Lifecycle rules that filter by tags incur a storage request cost per object per lifecycle evaluation. For very large buckets with tag-filtered lifecycle: the lifecycle evaluation cost itself can be significant (not billed directly but adds to S3 operational overhead).<br> *Application design: avoid polling patterns (LIST bucket every minute to detect new files). Use S3 event notifications instead — zero LIST cost for change detection. Event-driven architecture is both more responsive and cheaper than polling at scale.<br>

894. [ S3 ] What is the S3 dual-stack endpoint and when should it be used? ; Dual-stack S3 endpoints support both IPv4 and IPv6 connections. Format: `bucket-name.s3.dualstack.region.amazonaws.com`. Use when clients may connect via IPv6 (mobile networks, modern ISPs, AWS networking internally that prefers IPv6). Transfer Acceleration dual-stack: `bucket-name.s3-accelerate.dualstack.amazonaws.com`. <br><br> *IPv6 adoption: AWS recommends using dual-stack endpoints for new applications. IPv4 addresses are scarce and increasingly costly (AWS charges for IPv4 addresses). IPv6 eliminates this. Applications running in IPv6-enabled VPCs should use dual-stack S3 endpoints.<br> *VPC with IPv6 enabled: if your VPC uses an IPv6 CIDR block and your EC2 instances prefer IPv6, using the dual-stack endpoint ensures S3 connections use IPv6 within the AWS network (free) rather than IPv4.<br> *Bucket policy IP conditions: if using `aws:SourceIp` conditions in bucket policies with specific IP ranges, ensure the IPv6 address range is included. Policies that only list IPv4 CIDRs will deny IPv6 connections. For `VPC-only` access policies: use `aws:sourceVpc` or `aws:sourceVpce` instead of IP-based conditions to avoid IPv4/IPv6 complications.<br>

895. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 Replication and S3 Cross-Region Transfer? ; S3 Replication is an automated, ongoing process that copies new objects (and optionally delete markers) from source to destination bucket asynchronously. S3 Cross-Region Transfer (using CopyObject, CLI copy, or SDK) is a manual, one-time operation to copy specific objects. Replication is for continuous sync. Manual transfer is for one-time migration or specific object movement. <br><br> *Replication for ongoing DR: once configured, replication runs automatically for all new objects matching the replication rules. No manual intervention needed per object. Ideal for DR, compliance copies, global distribution scenarios.<br> *S3 Sync for bulk transfer: `aws s3 sync s3://source s3://dest --source-region us-east-1 --region eu-west-1` copies all objects not present in destination. Good for one-time migration or periodic manual sync. Not a replacement for CRR (no automatic new object sync).<br> *AWS DataSync for managed transfer: for large-scale, managed, automated transfers between S3 buckets (or on-premises to S3), AWS DataSync provides bandwidth throttling, scheduling, delta sync, and CloudWatch metrics. More operational control than raw S3 CopyObject or sync commands.<br>

896. [ S3 ] What is S3 analytics storage class analysis and how does it help with lifecycle policy design? ; S3 Storage Class Analysis monitors access patterns and recommends when to transition objects to Standard-IA. After 30 days of observing, it generates daily CSV reports showing access frequency distribution. Use this data to configure appropriate lifecycle policies (transition after N days of no access). Available per bucket, prefix, or tag filter. <br><br> *Analysis takes 30 days: you must wait at least 30 days after enabling analysis before useful recommendations appear. Plan ahead — enable analysis before planning lifecycle policies. The analysis identifies the access frequency percentile distribution over the observation period.<br> *Report output: CSV exported to a destination S3 bucket showing object age at access, access frequency by object age group. Insight: "80% of objects in this prefix not accessed after 45 days" → set lifecycle transition at 45 days. Without this data, lifecycle configuration is guesswork.<br> *Not for Glacier class recommendations: Storage Class Analysis only recommends Standard → Standard-IA transitions. For Glacier class recommendations: use S3 Storage Lens (shows objects not accessed in 90+ days in Standard-IA) or Intelligent-Tiering (automatic class management, no manual analysis needed).<br>

897. [ S3 ] What are S3 Access Points and how do they work with bucket policies for access delegation? ; S3 Access Points are named endpoints on a bucket with their own policies. The bucket can delegate access control to Access Points using a bucket policy that allows any request via an Access Point. The Access Point policies then manage per-application access. This pattern allows the bucket owner to delegate policy management to application teams while maintaining centralized bucket-level governance. <br><br> *Delegation pattern bucket policy: `{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*"], "Condition": {"ArnLike": {"aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:account:accesspoint/*"}}}`. This says "any access via an Access Point in this account is allowed at the bucket level." Individual Access Point policies control specific permissions.<br> *Network origin restriction per Access Point: Access Point can restrict to VPC only. `aws s3control create-access-point --name team-access --account-id ID --bucket bucket --vpc-configuration VpcId=vpc-xxx`. Requests from outside the VPC to this Access Point are rejected — even with valid IAM credentials.<br> *Alias hostname: each Access Point has an alias bucket hostname (`access-point-name-account-id.s3-accesspoint.region.amazonaws.com`) that can be used in place of the bucket name in SDK/CLI operations. Applications use the Access Point alias — they don't need to know the underlying bucket name.<br>

898. [ S3 ] What is the S3 account-level Block Public Access and how does it differ from bucket-level? ; Account-level Block Public Access applies the four Block Public Access settings to ALL buckets in the account, current and future. Bucket-level Block Public Access applies to a specific bucket. Account-level overrides bucket-level — a bucket cannot be more permissive than the account-level settings. If account-level `BlockPublicAcls` is enabled, no bucket in the account can have public ACLs regardless of bucket-level settings. <br><br> *AWS default for new accounts: all four Block Public Access settings enabled at the account level since April 2023. This means no new bucket can be made publicly accessible without first disabling account-level Block Public Access. Intentional public buckets require explicit opt-out at both account and bucket level.<br> *SCP enforcement: for AWS Organizations, use a Service Control Policy to deny `s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock` with `Allow` effect unless the principal is a specific security admin role. This prevents teams from disabling account-level Block Public Access and accidentally exposing data publicly.<br> *AWS Config rule: `s3-account-level-public-access-blocks-periodic` checks that all four account-level Block Public Access settings are enabled. Enable this rule in all accounts via AWS Config conformance packs. Auto-remediation via SSM Automation re-enables disabled settings.<br>

899. [ S3 ] What is S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and what are the three retrieval tiers? ; Glacier Flexible Retrieval (formerly Glacier) is an archive storage class with 90-day minimum storage duration at ~$0.004/GB/month. Three retrieval tiers: Expedited (1–5 minutes, ~$0.03/GB + $0.01/request — may fail without PCUs), Standard (3–5 hours, ~$0.01/GB + $0.05/1,000 requests), Bulk (5–12 hours, ~$0.0025/GB + $0.025/1,000 requests). Objects are not directly accessible — must initiate a Restore Object request first. <br><br> *Restore vs access: `RestoreObject` API call initiates retrieval. After retrieval time, a temporary copy appears in S3 Standard (accessible via GetObject). After the restore days expire, the Standard copy is deleted. The Glacier original remains. To keep permanently: CopyObject the restored Standard copy to a new Standard object.<br> *Bulk retrieval for compliance restore: if a regulator demands all records from 2018–2020 (Glacier archived), use Bulk retrieval to minimize cost. Create an S3 Batch Operations job to RestoreObject on all qualifying objects. After 5–12 hours, all objects available. Bulk is the cheapest — appropriate for planned, non-urgent large-scale restores.<br> *vs Glacier Instant Retrieval: GIR provides the same price point (~$0.004/GB/month) but with instant (millisecond) access. GIR replaced the use case of "quarterly-accessed archives needing fast access." Glacier Flexible Retrieval is for archives where hours of wait time is acceptable — the key differentiator is retrieval time vs cost.<br>

900. [ S3 ] How does S3 handle eventual consistency for bucket creation and how long does it take for a new bucket to be accessible? ; S3 bucket creation is strongly consistent and immediately available. Once `CreateBucket` returns 200 OK, the bucket is accessible in the creating region. Global DNS propagation for the bucket's virtual-hosted-style URL may take a few seconds but the bucket is immediately accessible via path-style or the API. <br><br> *Strong consistency applies to bucket creation, just as it applies to object creation. As of December 2020, all S3 operations (including bucket creation and listing) are strongly consistent. No waiting period after bucket creation before starting to use it.<br> *Cross-region bucket creation: `CreateBucket` must specify the region (except us-east-1 which has no LocationConstraint). The bucket is created and accessible in the specified region. Accessing the bucket from a different region works immediately via virtual-hosted-style URLs.<br> *Exam note: before December 2020, there were questions about S3 eventual consistency. After December 2020 all S3 consistency questions have the same answer: strong consistency. Watch out for outdated study materials that still reference eventual consistency for overwrites or deletes — this no longer applies.<br>


901. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Lifecycle transition ordering rule? ; Lifecycle transitions must follow the order from more expensive to less expensive storage classes. The sequence is: Standard → Standard-IA / One Zone-IA → Glacier Instant Retrieval → Glacier Flexible Retrieval → Glacier Deep Archive. You cannot configure a lifecycle rule that goes in reverse order (e.g., from Glacier to Standard-IA). Each transition must be to a class that is the same or "cheaper" in the hierarchy. <br><br> *Multiple transition actions in one rule: you can have multiple `Transition` actions at different days. E.g., transition to Standard-IA at 30 days, Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days, Deep Archive at 365 days. Each action must be in the correct order with increasing days.<br> *Minimum days constraint: Standard to Standard-IA requires minimum 30 days. Standard-IA to Glacier requires minimum 30 additional days (so minimum 60 days from upload). These minimums exist because minimum storage duration fees make early transitions economically undesirable.<br> *Transition from One Zone-IA: One Zone-IA can transition to Glacier classes but not back to Standard or Standard-IA. Transitions are unidirectional. If you need an object back in Standard class from Glacier: use Restore Object to create a temporary Standard copy, then CopyObject to a permanent Standard location.<br>

902. [ S3 ] What is S3 access logging and what is the format of the log destination bucket configuration? ; S3 server access logging is enabled per bucket. Logs are delivered to a target bucket (which can be the same bucket — though not recommended). The target bucket must be in the same region. Best practice: use a dedicated logging bucket. Set the log prefix to distinguish between different source buckets. Access: `s3:GetBucketLogging`, `s3:PutBucketLogging` permissions required to configure. <br><br> *Logging bucket best practice: use a separate logging bucket in the same region. Grant S3 log delivery group write access to the logging bucket. If logging to the same bucket: log delivery for the logs generates more logs (recursive, fills bucket). Use a separate bucket to avoid this.<br> *Log format: space-separated text records. Fields: bucket owner, bucket, time, remote IP, requester, request ID, operation, key, request URI, HTTP status, error code, bytes sent, object size, total time, turnaround time, referrer, user agent, version ID, host ID, signature version, cipher suite, authentication type, host header, TLS version.<br> *Log delivery latency: best-effort, typically within a few hours. Not guaranteed. For time-sensitive security monitoring (detect access within seconds): CloudTrail data events provide near real-time delivery. Server access logs are for historical trend analysis, not real-time alerting.<br>

903. [ S3 ] What is S3 Intelligent-Tiering Deep Archive Access tier and how does it compare to Glacier Deep Archive standalone? ; Both have the same storage cost (~$0.00099/GB/month) and 12-hour retrieval time. Differences: IT Deep Archive Access has no retrieval fee (but monitoring fee applies). Standalone Glacier Deep Archive has a retrieval fee ($0.02/GB). IT Deep Archive Access: object automatically moves back to Frequent Access when accessed. Standalone Glacier DA: requires RestoreObject, object stays in Deep Archive after restore (original archive remains). <br><br> *When IT Deep Archive Access wins: objects that are occasionally accessed (even if rarely) and need to move back to active tier automatically. The monitoring fee ($0.0025/1,000 objects/month) is negligible for large objects but significant for millions of small objects.<br> *When standalone Glacier Deep Archive wins: objects that are never expected to be accessed again (pure regulatory archive). No monitoring fee. Pay-per-retrieval when needed. For 10 million small files: IT monitoring = $25/month, standalone Glacier DA monitoring = $0. The retrieval fee (rare) is cheaper than ongoing IT monitoring.<br> *Both provide 180-day minimum storage duration. IT moves objects to Deep Archive Access tier only after 180 days in the Archive Access tier (or after 180 days without access if Deep Archive is enabled directly). Objects under 128 KB: never moved to any IT archive tier.<br>

904. [ S3 ] How does AWS DataSync differ from S3 CRR (Cross-Region Replication) for data movement? ; S3 CRR: automatic ongoing replication of new S3 objects to another S3 bucket. Continuous, asynchronous, managed by S3 service. Best for real-time DR, compliance copies of all new data. AWS DataSync: managed data transfer service for scheduled or one-time transfers between S3 (or EFS, FSx, on-premises NFS/SMB) and other storage. Supports bandwidth throttling, scheduling, encryption, delta sync, and CloudWatch metrics. Best for migration, batch transfer, or on-premises-to-cloud sync. <br><br> *DataSync for S3: transfers objects between S3 buckets (including cross-region, cross-account) with more operational control than raw S3 Sync. Filters by include/exclude patterns, timestamps, file attributes. Provides per-task metrics and logs. Can be scheduled.<br> *CRR for ongoing replication: once configured, runs automatically. No scheduling needed. Cannot be throttled (runs at S3-determined speed). No support for on-premises sources. Only S3-to-S3 replication.<br> *Use DataSync when: migrating data from on-premises NAS to S3, scheduled periodic sync between S3 and on-premises, or needing bandwidth throttling/scheduling for cross-region S3 transfers. Use CRR when: automatic continuous replication of all new objects is required with no operational management overhead.<br>

905. [ S3 ] What is the S3 `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key and how is it used in bucket policies? ; `aws:PrincipalOrgID` allows bucket policies to grant or restrict access based on whether the requester's AWS account is a member of a specific AWS Organizations organization. Use it to grant access to all accounts in your organization without listing individual account IDs. Example: `"Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-xxxxxxxxxx"}}`. <br><br> *Use case: a shared S3 data lake bucket accessible to all accounts in the organization. Instead of listing 200 account IDs in the bucket policy, one condition `aws:PrincipalOrgID = org-id` allows all current and future accounts in the org. Adding a new account to the org automatically grants access — no bucket policy update needed.<br> *Security implication: `aws:PrincipalOrgID` allows any IAM principal in the org. Combined with `aws:PrincipalTag` conditions: restrict further to only principals with specific IAM tags (e.g., `aws:PrincipalTag/data-access = approved`). Layered conditions provide both organizational scope and role-level restrictions.<br> *Cross-org access: if a partner organization needs access, `aws:PrincipalOrgID` won't work (their account is in a different org). Use explicit account IDs or role ARNs in the bucket policy for cross-organization access. `PrincipalOrgID` is intra-organization only.<br>

906. [ S3 ] What is the S3 consistency model for list operations when objects are being added concurrently by multiple writers? ; S3 provides strong consistency for LIST operations — any object PUT that returns 200 OK will be included in subsequent LIST responses. However, S3 LIST pagination: when paginating through a large bucket while new objects are being added, objects added between pages may appear in the current page set OR on a subsequent page, or potentially both (very rare race condition at page boundaries). For a complete inventory of a changing bucket: use S3 Inventory. <br><br> *Practical implication: for a single LIST call, all objects existing at the time of the call are returned (strongly consistent). For multi-page pagination of a live bucket: the pagination token creates a snapshot-like view but the bucket continues changing. New objects added after the first LIST call may appear on later pages.<br> *Use case for Inventory over LIST: compliance audit requiring complete object count. Running ListObjectsV2 on a 1 billion-object bucket takes hours — during which objects are added and deleted. The final count may be inaccurate. S3 Inventory takes a point-in-time snapshot and provides a definitive inventory file.<br> *List performance: ListObjectsV2 is the recommended API (not the deprecated ListObjects). Returns up to 1,000 objects per request. For 1 billion objects: 1 million API calls needed. At $0.005/1,000 = $5,000 for a full listing via API. S3 Inventory provides the same data for a fraction of the cost.<br>

907. [ S3 ] What S3 security control prevents accidental public access via an existing bucket policy that was misconfigured to allow `"Principal": "*"` ? ; The `RestrictPublicBuckets` Block Public Access setting (part of the four Block Public Access settings). When enabled, even if the bucket policy has `"Principal": "*"` granting public access, S3 treats the bucket as if it only allows access to AWS services and authenticated users (from any account) — anonymous public access is blocked. This acts as a safety net for bucket policy misconfiguration. <br><br> *RestrictPublicBuckets doesn't remove the misconfigured policy — it just ignores the public-access grant effect. The policy still exists but its grant of public access is overridden. To fix properly: update the bucket policy to remove the public grant AND ensure RestrictPublicBuckets is enabled as defense-in-depth.<br> *AWS Config rule: `s3-bucket-policy-not-more-permissive` checks for bucket policies that grant access to all principals (*) without conditions. Alert and remediate. Combined with RestrictPublicBuckets, provides both prevention and detection.<br> *Account-level Block Public Access: if all four settings are enabled at the account level, no bucket can be made public regardless of bucket policy. This is the recommended configuration for all accounts where public S3 buckets are not needed. Use as default, explicitly disable for specific buckets that genuinely need public access (e.g., static website hosting).<br>

908. [ S3 ] What is S3 Batch Operations pricing model? ; S3 Batch Operations pricing: $0.00 per job (no charge for job creation), $1.00 per million objects processed, $0.00 per job completion. Additionally, the operation-specific charges apply (e.g., standard S3 PUT/COPY/GET requests for the operation performed, KMS charges for encryption). For InvokeLambda: Lambda invocation and duration charges apply. <br><br> *Cost calculation example: process 1 billion objects with CopyObject. Batch Operations charge: $1 × 1,000 = $1,000. CopyObject request charges: $5/1,000 requests × 1,000,000 requests = $5,000. Data transfer (if cross-region): $0.02/GB × total GB. Total for 1B objects at 1 MB each = 1 PB: significant cost.<br> *Completion report: delivered to S3 — additional S3 PUT cost for the report file. For a job with 1 billion objects: the completion report can be very large. Specify a prefix for report delivery and ensure sufficient storage in the destination bucket.<br> *Free job creation with cost preview: before confirming a Batch Operations job, AWS shows an estimated cost. Review this before confirming large jobs. This "confirm before run" step prevents accidental expensive operations on billions of objects.<br>

909. [ S3 ] What is the S3 event notification for S3 Replication failure? ; S3 generates replication-related events accessible via EventBridge: `OperationMissedThreshold` (RTC: object not replicated within 15 min SLA), `OperationReplicatedAfterThreshold` (RTC: object replicated after SLA), `OperationNotTracked` (object not tracked by replication — e.g., SSE-C, Glacier class, already a replica), `OperationFailedReplication` (replication attempt failed). Route to SNS/SQS for alerting. <br><br> *OperationFailedReplication: indicates a specific object failed all replication attempts. This is actionable — investigate the object, check destination bucket policy, KMS permissions, and run S3 Batch Replication to retry. Automated alert → PagerDuty → on-call engineer.<br> *OperationMissedThreshold: only available with RTC enabled. Indicates object not replicated within 15 minutes. Triggers before OperationFailedReplication (failure).
