Allows proactive investigation before declaring a replication failure. <br> *Monitoring pattern: EventBridge rule for `s3:Replication:*` events → SQS → Lambda for analysis → DynamoDB to track failed objects → Batch Replication job creation for bulk retry → CloudWatch alarm on DynamoDB failed object count.<br>

910. [ S3 ] What is the maximum number of S3 buckets per AWS account and can this limit be increased? ; Default limit: 100 buckets per account. This is a soft limit — can be increased via AWS Support request. Hard limit: 1,000 buckets per account. This cannot be increased beyond 1,000. If more than 1,000 buckets are needed: use multiple AWS accounts (each with up to 1,000 buckets) or redesign to use prefixes within fewer buckets (infinite objects per bucket). <br><br> *100-bucket default rationale: encourages using prefixes within buckets rather than creating a new bucket for every use case. S3 bucket creation has overhead (global namespace registration, DNS propagation, IAM policy updates). Prefixes within buckets are free and instant.<br> *1,000-bucket hard limit constraint: organizations sometimes hit this for per-customer isolation patterns (one bucket per customer). At scale (thousands of customers), this model requires multiple accounts. Alternative: one bucket with customer ID as prefix, with S3 Access Points per customer for isolation.<br> *AWS Organizations + Control Tower: each account gets 100-bucket default limit. Large organizations with 50+ accounts each with 100-1,000 buckets can have 5,000–50,000 total buckets. Manage at scale with AWS Organizations for account management and RAM for shared resources.<br>


911. [ S3 ] What is S3 Intelligent-Tiering and what are the different activation tiers? ; S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects through access tiers based on activity: Frequent Access (always active, standard pricing), Infrequent Access (auto after 30 days no access, ~45% cheaper), Archive Instant Access (optional, auto after 90 days, ~68% cheaper, instant retrieval), Archive Access (optional, 90–180 days config, ~71% cheaper, hours retrieval), Deep Archive Access (optional, 180+ days, ~95% cheaper, 12-hour retrieval). Monitoring fee: $0.0025/1,000 objects/month. <br><br> *Archive and Deep Archive tiers are optional and must be explicitly enabled per Intelligent-Tiering configuration. Enabling them allows objects to be moved to these cheaper tiers automatically — but retrieval time increases (hours to 12 hours). Only enable Archive tiers if retrieval time requirements allow.<br> *The key innovation: no retrieval fee for FA and IA tiers (unlike Standard-IA which charges per retrieval). Objects move back to Frequent Access automatically when accessed — no manual intervention, no restore operation for FA/IA. Archive Instant Access also requires no restore (millisecond retrieval despite lower price).<br> *Monitoring fee vs savings: for objects under ~128 KB, monitoring fee may exceed tier savings. For objects ≥ 128 KB with uncertain access patterns: Intelligent-Tiering almost always saves money vs Standard class with manual lifecycle management.<br>

912. [ S3 ] What are the S3 Bucket Policy key elements and how does evaluation work? ; A bucket policy is JSON with Statement array. Each Statement has: Sid (optional label), Effect (Allow/Deny), Principal (who), Action (s3:* actions), Resource (bucket/object ARNs), Condition (optional constraints). Evaluation: explicit Deny > explicit Allow > implicit Deny. Cross-account: requester's IAM policy AND bucket policy must both allow. Same-account: either IAM policy or bucket policy alone can grant access. <br><br> *NotPrincipal with Deny: advanced pattern. `"Effect": "Deny", "NotPrincipal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::account:role/admin"}` denies everyone EXCEPT the admin role. Useful for lock-down scenarios. Warning: if admin role ARN changes, you're locked out. Always test NotPrincipal carefully.<br> *Condition keys for S3: `s3:prefix` (filter by key prefix in list operations), `s3:delimiter`, `s3:max-keys`, `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption`, `s3:x-amz-storage-class`, `s3:x-amz-acl`, `aws:sourceVpce`, `aws:sourceVpc`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:SecureTransport`, `aws:SourceAccount`.<br> *Policy size limit: 20 KB for bucket policies. JSON whitespace counts. Minimize whitespace in production policies. For policies approaching the limit: switch to Access Points (each has its own 20 KB) or use IAM resource tags with ABAC conditions instead of enumerating individual ARNs.<br>

913. [ S3 ] What happens to objects in S3 when an AWS account is closed? ; When an AWS account is closed: all resources, including S3 buckets and objects, are retained for 90 days during the account closure period. After 90 days, all data is permanently deleted. During the 90-day window, the account can be reopened and data recovered. Post-90-days: data is irrecoverable. This affects cross-account data access too — the source account's buckets become inaccessible if the account closes. <br><br> *Data recovery during closure: to recover data before account deletion, reopen the account within 90 days, then use DataSync, S3 replication, or CLI to move data to another account/region. Time is critical.<br> *Design implication: for data that must persist beyond account lifecycle (compliance archives, long-term data lake), replicate to a separate, long-lived account with strict account lifecycle controls. Never store sole copies in accounts that might close.<br> *CRR as account closure protection: configure CRR to a second account's bucket. If the source account closes, the replica in the second account is unaffected (data was already replicated). This is a governance best practice for Organizations with accounts that may be decommissioned.<br>

914. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Select output format options and how do they affect billing? ; S3 Select output formats: CSV (comma-separated) or JSON (record-delimited or lines). Input format determines supported output: CSV input → CSV or JSON output. JSON input → CSV or JSON output. Parquet input → CSV or JSON output. Billing: charged per GB of data scanned from S3 (input) and per GB of data returned (output). Smaller output formats (CSV with only requested columns) reduce the "data returned" billing component. <br><br> *Column selection optimization: `SELECT s.name, s.email FROM S3Object s` scans the full CSV but returns only two columns. The scanned bytes are charged (full CSV), but returned bytes are charged only for the selected columns. For wide CSV with many columns: column selection dramatically reduces return charges.<br> *Compression savings: compressed input (GZIP CSV) reduces scanned bytes proportionally. A 10 GB CSV compressed to 1 GB is billed at 1 GB scanned. S3 Select decompresses transparently before SQL processing. Compression + S3 Select = lowest data scanning cost combination.<br> *vs Athena for repeated queries: S3 Select queries one object. If the same filter is applied to thousands of objects: consider converting to Parquet + Athena (partition pruning + columnar scan). S3 Select on 1,000 GZIP CSV files = 1,000 separate S3 Select calls. Athena on 1,000 Parquet files = one query with columnar pruning. At scale, Athena with Parquet is more cost-efficient.<br>

915. [ S3 ] What is the S3 presigned POST and how does it differ from presigned PUT? ; A presigned POST allows uploading directly to S3 from a browser form without exposing AWS credentials. It includes policy conditions (max file size, allowed content types, key prefix) enforced by S3. Presigned PUT: direct HTTP PUT to S3 with a signed URL — simpler but no server-enforced conditions on file size/content type. Presigned POST: more complex to generate (policy document + signature) but allows per-field validation. <br><br> *Presigned POST use case: web form file upload. Server generates a presigned POST policy with conditions (key prefix, max content-length, allowed content-type). Browser submits multipart/form-data directly to S3. S3 validates the policy conditions and rejects non-compliant uploads.<br> *Presigned PUT limitations: the file size must be exact (Content-Length header). Conditions cannot be enforced (S3 accepts any file at the PUT URL). A malicious user could upload a huge file (if they can guess/intercept the URL) or a different file type than expected.<br> *Presigned POST conditions: `["content-length-range", 100, 10485760]` allows 100 bytes to 10 MB uploads. `["starts-with", "$Content-Type", "image/"]` allows only image types. `["starts-with", "$key", "uploads/user123/"]` restricts uploads to a specific prefix. Server-side enforced without application code in the upload path.<br>

916. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 Server-Side Encryption and Client-Side Encryption? ; Server-Side Encryption (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, SSE-C, DSSE-KMS): encryption performed by S3 servers after receiving data. Data travels to S3 unencrypted (but over HTTPS TLS for transport security). S3 handles key management. Client-Side Encryption: data encrypted by the client before upload. S3 receives already-encrypted bytes and stores them — S3 never sees plaintext. Client fully controls key management. <br><br> *Security model difference: SSE = S3 encrypts at rest. If S3 infrastructure is compromised, the attacker needs the KMS key too. Client-Side = S3 never sees plaintext, even if S3 infrastructure AND KMS are compromised, data is safe (client holds the encryption key separately). Client-side is the highest security level but highest operational complexity.<br> *AWS SDK support for client-side: AWS Encryption SDK for Java, Python, .NET supports client-side encryption with KMS CMK as master key (envelope encryption). Encrypt object, upload to S3. Download, decrypt with SDK. S3 sees encrypted bytes only.<br> *When required: regulated environments where AWS employees must never have access to data in plaintext. Government classified systems, financial sector with strict confidentiality requirements. For most enterprises: SSE-KMS provides sufficient security with less operational burden than client-side encryption.<br>

917. [ S3 ] What are S3 Lifecycle rules and can they be applied to specific object versions? ; Lifecycle rules can target both current object versions and noncurrent (previous) versions separately. For current versions: use `Transition` (move to cheaper class) or `Expiration` (delete/create delete marker). For noncurrent versions: use `NoncurrentVersionTransition` (move to cheaper class) and `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` (permanently delete old versions after N days). Both current and noncurrent version rules can be in the same lifecycle rule or separate rules. <br><br> *NoncurrentVersionExpiration best practice: `NoncurrentDays: 30, NewerNoncurrentVersions: 5` — keep the 5 most recent noncurrent versions, delete anything older than 30 days. This provides a 30-day rollback window while bounding version storage growth.<br> *Lifecycle interaction with delete markers: after all versions of an object are deleted by `NoncurrentVersionExpiration`, an orphaned delete marker remains. Add `ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker: true` to clean up these orphaned markers automatically. Without this, the bucket accumulates thousands of orphaned delete markers over time (visible in metrics but not objects).<br> *Transition ordering for noncurrent versions: same constraints apply as current version transitions. Noncurrent versions can be transitioned through Standard-IA → Glacier → Deep Archive. Use this to achieve cost optimization: recent versions in Standard (fast recovery), old versions in Glacier (cheap long-term storage).<br>

918. [ S3 ] What is S3 WORM and which specific bucket/object settings implement it? ; WORM (Write Once, Read Many) in S3 is implemented via S3 Object Lock. Enable Object Lock at bucket creation (requires versioning). Set Retention Mode: Compliance (no deletion/modification by anyone including root until period expires) or Governance (admins with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` can override). Legal Hold: toggle WORM with no expiry date. All three together implement the full WORM compliance capability. <br><br> *AWS WORM vs Vault Lock: S3 Object Lock (Compliance mode) and Glacier Vault Lock are both WORM implementations meeting SEC 17a-4(f) requirements. Object Lock works with S3 API (modern). Vault Lock works with legacy Glacier Vault API. For new implementations: S3 Object Lock is preferred.<br> *Compliance mode characteristics: retention period cannot be shortened by anyone. If set for 7 years, the object version remains for exactly 7 years. No root override. No AWS Support override. This is a legally binding commitment — AWS guarantees immutability for the retention period.<br> *WORM in multi-account: create an Object Lock bucket in a dedicated compliance account. Data is written to this account via cross-account bucket policy allowing writes but not deletes. The compliance account has strict access controls. Even the source account's admin cannot delete objects after writing (Object Lock Compliance prevents it).<br>

919. [ S3 ] What are the S3 data transfer pricing tiers (outbound to internet) and when does it start being free? ; Data transfer OUT from S3 to the internet pricing (us-east-1): first 100 GB/month FREE, 100 GB – 10 TB/month: $0.09/GB, 10 TB – 50 TB/month: $0.085/GB, 50 TB – 150 TB/month: $0.07/GB, 150 TB+/month: $0.05/GB. Data transfer IN to S3 from internet: always FREE. S3 to EC2/Lambda in same region: FREE. S3 to CloudFront: FREE. S3 cross-region (to EC2 or another S3 bucket): varies by region pair. <br><br> *High-volume workloads: at 150 TB+/month outbound, tiered pricing ($0.05/GB) significantly reduces cost vs flat $0.09/GB. For large public dataset providers: negotiate AWS custom pricing at petabyte-scale volumes (Enterprise Discount Programs).<br> *CloudFront as cost reducer: S3 → CloudFront is free. CloudFront → internet: $0.085/GB (first 10 TB). For frequently accessed content: CloudFront caches at edge — each subsequent hit is served from CloudFront cache (no additional S3 DTO). Only cache misses hit S3. At high cache hit ratios (>80%): CloudFront dramatically reduces S3 DTO costs.<br> *AWS PrivateLink for S3 (Interface Endpoint): allows on-premises access to S3 via DX without public internet egress. DX data transfer rates ($0.02/GB) are typically lower than internet egress rates ($0.09/GB) for high-volume scenarios. Route 53 Resolver required for DNS resolution.<br>

920. [ S3 ] What is S3 Object Ownership and which setting is recommended for new buckets? ; S3 Object Ownership has three settings: ObjectWriter (legacy default — uploader owns objects), BucketOwnerPreferred (bucket owner takes ownership if uploader includes bucket-owner-full-control ACL), BucketOwnerEnforced (recommended — ACLs disabled, bucket owner owns all objects regardless of uploader). AWS recommends BucketOwnerEnforced for all new buckets as it disables ACLs and simplifies access management. <br><br> *BucketOwnerEnforced implications: completely disables ACLs. All access control via bucket policies and IAM. Objects uploaded by any account are immediately owned by the bucket account — the bucket owner can delete, tag, replicate, and access any object in the bucket.<br> *BucketOwnerPreferred migration: for buckets with existing ACL-based access, migrate by: (1) audit ACL usage (S3 Storage Lens), (2) convert ACL grants to bucket policies, (3) enable BucketOwnerPreferred, (4) update uploaders to include bucket-owner-full-control ACL, (5) enable BucketOwnerEnforced after all ACLs migrated.<br> *Cross-account uploader scenario: Account B uploads to Account A's bucket. With BucketOwnerEnforced: object is immediately owned by Account A. Account B has no special ownership rights. Account A's lifecycle rules, replication, and access control apply to all objects uniformly — simplifying multi-account data lake management.<br>


921. [ S3 ] What is S3 Object Lock Governance mode bypass and what permission is required? ; Users with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` IAM permission can: shorten or remove a Governance mode retention period, delete an object version before its retention period expires. They must include `x-amz-bypass-governance-retention: true` in the API request header. Root account also can bypass Governance mode. Neither root nor any IAM principal can bypass Compliance mode. <br><br> *Governance mode use case: protect data from accidental deletion while allowing authorized admins to correct mistakes. Example: uploaded wrong file version to a compliance bucket — admin with bypass permission can delete it and upload correct version. Compliance mode would prevent this correction.<br> *Governance bypass audit: CloudTrail logs the `x-amz-bypass-governance-retention` header usage. Any governance mode bypass is visible in CloudTrail data events. Create a CloudWatch alarm triggered by CloudTrail events containing this header to alert on any governance bypass — potential security signal.<br> *IAM policy for bypass: `{"Action": "s3:BypassGovernanceRetention", "Effect": "Allow"}` in the IAM policy. This should be granted sparingly — only to specific admin roles. Combined with a Deny in the SCP preventing most roles from having this permission: organizational control over who can override data protection.<br>

922. [ S3 ] What is the S3 data lake architecture with three zones (raw, processed, curated)? ; Raw zone: landing area for source data as-is (JSON logs, CSV exports, Parquet from Kinesis Firehose). Processed zone: cleaned, normalized, deduplicated data (Glue ETL output, Parquet/ORC format). Curated zone: business-ready aggregated data (Redshift Spectrum tables, Athena views, direct QuickSight source). Each zone: separate S3 prefix or bucket, separate IAM roles (write-to-raw, read-from-raw/write-to-processed, read-from-curated), separate lifecycle policies. <br><br> *Glue ETL: reads raw zone, transforms (type casting, deduplication, normalization), writes Parquet to processed zone. Glue crawler updates Data Catalog with processed zone schema. Athena queries processed zone via Data Catalog. This is the standard serverless ETL pipeline.<br> *Lake Formation: provides column-level and row-level security across all three zones. Analytics users get access to curated zone only. Data engineers get access to processed zone. Data ingestion services write to raw zone. Lake Formation governs who sees what without per-bucket IAM policy management.<br> *S3 Intelligent-Tiering for raw zone: raw data may not be accessed again after processing. Set IT on raw zone to automatically move old raw data to cheaper tiers. Processed zone: Standard or Standard-IA depending on query frequency. Curated zone: Standard for frequently queried business data.<br>

923. [ S3 ] What are the four S3 Block Public Access settings and what is the effect of each? ; 1. BlockPublicAcls: rejects any PUT (bucket or object) that would grant public access via ACL. 2. IgnorePublicAcls: disregards existing public ACLs — they have no effect. 3. BlockPublicPolicy: rejects bucket policies that grant public access. 4. RestrictPublicBuckets: if a bucket has a public policy (even if blocked at creation), restricts it to only AWS services and authorized users — no anonymous internet access. Each can be independently enabled or disabled. <br><br> *All four enabled at account level: complete protection against public access. No bucket in the account can be made publicly accessible regardless of bucket policy, ACLs, or any object-level setting. Maximum protection.<br> *Selective disable: some use cases require specific buckets to be public (S3 static website, CloudFront public content). Disable all four at the bucket level for specific public buckets while keeping account-level settings enabled does NOT work — account level overrides bucket level. Must disable at account level and rely on bucket-level settings only for that account.<br> *For accounts hosting public websites: cannot use account-level Block Public Access for all settings. Use SCP to prevent disabling Block Public Access on non-website buckets (tag-based: `s3:RequestObjectTagKeys/public-website: true` allowed to disable). Defense-in-depth for the few intentionally public buckets.<br>

924. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 Gateway Endpoint policy and S3 bucket policy when controlling VPC-restricted access? ; Gateway Endpoint policy: resource-based policy on the VPC Endpoint — controls what actions through the endpoint are allowed (acts as a filter for all S3 traffic via the endpoint). Bucket policy: resource-based policy on the S3 bucket — controls who can access the bucket. To restrict bucket access to VPC only: use bucket policy condition `aws:sourceVpce` (not endpoint policy). To restrict what resources the VPC can access via endpoint: use endpoint policy. <br><br> *Endpoint policy for data exfiltration prevention: `{"Effect": "Deny", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:ResourceAccount": "123456789012"}}}`. This blocks all S3 traffic from the VPC to ANY external S3 bucket (only allows access to company-owned buckets). Prevents exfiltration via attacker-controlled S3 buckets.<br> *Both policies work together: bucket policy says "only allow from this VPC endpoint." Endpoint policy says "only allow access to this account's buckets." Together: VPC can only access company buckets, and company buckets only accept VPC traffic. Defense-in-depth for data exfiltration.<br> *Endpoint policy evaluation: the endpoint policy is in addition to, not instead of, IAM/bucket policies. Access is granted only if: IAM policy allows + bucket policy allows + endpoint policy allows. Any one of these denying = access denied.<br>

925. [ S3 ] What S3 feature allows you to automatically move objects back from Glacier to Standard after restore? ; Standard S3 restore (RestoreObject) creates a temporary copy in Standard class that expires after the specified number of days. This is NOT permanent. To permanently move from Glacier to Standard: (1) RestoreObject, (2) wait for restore, (3) CopyObject from restored object to new Standard key (or overwrite same key with new storage class specification). S3 Lifecycle rules cannot transition backward (from Glacier to Standard). <br><br> *Automating permanent restore: S3 event notification on `s3:ObjectRestore:Completed` → Lambda → Lambda calls CopyObject to copy restored object to Standard class → optionally delete the Glacier version if it should no longer be archived.<br> *S3 Batch Operations for bulk restore: create a job with `RestoreObject` operation targeting many Glacier objects. After job completes, create another Batch Operations job with `CopyObject` targeting the restored objects to copy them to Standard class. Two-phase bulk restore at scale.<br> *Cost: RestoreObject request fee + restore retrieval fee + Standard storage for temporary copy + CopyObject request fee + Standard storage for permanent copy. For large-scale restore: estimate cost before proceeding. For deep archives: restore cost can be significant relative to the storage savings accumulated.<br>

926. [ S3 ] What is the S3 key design best practice for time-series data and how does it affect performance and lifecycle? ; Use date-based hierarchical prefixes: `logs/year=2024/month=10/day=15/hour=12/file.gz`. Benefits: (1) Athena partition pruning — queries filtered by date scan only relevant prefixes. (2) Lifecycle rules target specific date ranges by prefix (`logs/year=2022/` → transition to Glacier after 1 year in Standard). (3) CloudWatch Events based on new daily prefix creation for automated processing. (4) Human-readable data organization. <br><br> *Hive-style partitioning: `year=2024/month=10/day=15/` is the Hive partition format. Glue Crawlers automatically detect Hive-style partitions and create partition metadata in the Data Catalog. Athena uses partition metadata for query optimization without scanning all files.<br> *Performance: time-series prefixes distribute objects across multiple S3 storage shards (different prefixes route to different backend shards). High-volume time-series data benefits from the natural prefix distribution. Avoids the prefix hotspot problem where all objects go to the same shard.<br> *Lifecycle targeting by time prefix: `logs/year=2020/` matches all 2020 data regardless of month/day depth. Lifecycle rule with prefix `logs/year=2020` transitions all 2020 objects together. This enables precise year-based data archiving policies without object-level lifecycle configuration.<br>

927. [ S3 ] What is S3 Delete Object vs DELETE with version ID? ; `DELETE` on a key without specifying a version ID (versioned bucket): creates a delete marker — object appears deleted but all versions preserved. Soft delete. `DELETE` with a specific version ID: permanently removes that specific version. Hard delete. On a non-versioned bucket: `DELETE` on a key permanently removes the object. MFA Delete (if enabled) is required for hard deletes (DELETE with version ID) but not for creating delete markers. <br><br> *Application implications: application that calls `DELETE` on versioned bucket: creates delete marker, object "disappears" from standard GET but versions persist. Application must explicitly request version ID deletion for permanent removal. This prevents application bugs from permanently destroying data.<br> *Compliance implication: in a Compliance mode Object Lock bucket, DELETE with version ID is rejected until retention period expires. DELETE without version ID creates a delete marker (the current version is hidden but not removed). The versioned object with Object Lock retention remains intact under the delete marker.<br> *Cost implication: delete markers have no storage cost (< 1 KB each). But millions of orphaned delete markers (objects where all versions are deleted but marker remains) can accumulate. Use lifecycle `ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker: true` to clean them up. Without cleanup, LIST operations return markers, increasing list request counts.<br>

928. [ S3 ] What is the S3 minimum object size for Standard-IA and what happens if smaller objects are uploaded? ; Standard-IA has a 128 KB minimum billable object size. Objects smaller than 128 KB are stored successfully but billed as if they were 128 KB. For 1 million 1-byte objects: storage cost = 1M × 128 KB = 128 GB billing (not 1 MB of actual data). This makes Standard-IA cost-prohibitive for small objects. Use Standard class for small objects. <br><br> *Same applies to: One Zone-IA (128 KB minimum), Glacier Instant Retrieval (128 KB minimum), Glacier Flexible Retrieval (40 KB minimum), Glacier Deep Archive (40 KB minimum). Only Standard and Intelligent-Tiering have no minimum billable size.<br> *Impact on lifecycle policies: if a lifecycle rule transitions many small files to Standard-IA, the billing may be HIGHER than Standard. Always analyze the average object size in a prefix before applying lifecycle rules. `aws s3api list-objects-v2 --query "Contents[?Size<131072]" --output text | wc -l` to count objects smaller than 128 KB.<br> *Workaround for small file archives: combine small files into larger archives (ZIP, TAR, or custom format) before archiving to Glacier. Each archive object contains thousands of small files. A 1 GB archive object in Glacier Deep Archive costs pennies per month vs thousands of small files each billed at 40 KB minimum.<br>

929. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 Public Access and S3 Authenticated Access? ; Public access: accessible to any internet user without authentication (Principal: "*" in bucket policy, or public-read ACL). No AWS credentials needed. Authenticated access: accessible to any authenticated AWS user (IAM principal from any account). A bucket policy with `"Principal": {"AWS": "*"}` (without conditions) grants authenticated access — still publicly readable but only by AWS account holders. Block Public Access restricts both unauthenticated and some authenticated open access patterns. <br><br> *AWS Principal "*" (all authenticated) vs anonymous "": `"Principal": "*"` in a bucket policy allows any AWS principal (authenticated). `"Principal": ""` in an S3 ACL allows anonymous (unauthenticated) access. These are different access levels.<br> *Block Public Access effect: `RestrictPublicBuckets` restricts buckets with ANY public policy (including `Principal: "*"` policies) to only AWS services and authorized users. This effectively blocks the "any authenticated AWS user" access too — it must be from an authenticated user in a specific authorized context.<br> *Exam scenario: "Make bucket accessible to all AWS accounts but not to anonymous internet" → bucket policy with `"Principal": "*"` (no conditions). All AWS account holders can access (authenticated). Enable all Block Public Access settings to prevent anonymous access while still allowing authenticated access.<br>

930. [ S3 ] What S3 features support cross-account access? ; Cross-account access to S3 is supported via: (1) Bucket policy with destination account's principal as `Principal` (resource-based access), (2) S3 Access Points with cross-account access (both bucket policy delegate and Access Point policy allow cross-account), (3) S3 Multi-Region Access Points (MRAPs with cross-account routing), (4) VPC Endpoint policies allowing cross-account endpoints, (5) S3 Replication IAM role in source account with cross-account bucket policy in destination. <br><br> *Cross-account IAM evaluation: requester in Account B needs IAM policy in Account B AND bucket policy in Account A both allowing the action. Unlike same-account (where either IAM or bucket policy alone is sufficient), cross-account requires both sides to explicitly allow.<br> *S3 Object Ownership cross-account: default ObjectWriter = Account B owns objects it uploads to Account A's bucket. Account A cannot control those objects. Fix: BucketOwnerEnforced on Account A's bucket → all uploads immediately owned by Account A.<br> *Access Point cross-account: Account A creates Access Point on its bucket. Grants Account B's role as principal in the Access Point policy. Account B's role can access S3 via the Access Point. The bucket policy must also allow the Access Point (or Account B directly). Both bucket policy and Access Point policy must allow for cross-account access via Access Points.<br>


931. [ S3 ] What is S3 Versioning and what happens to the bucket's storage costs when enabled? ; Versioning stores every version of every object. Storage costs increase because each overwrite/delete preserves the old version. A 1 GB file overwritten daily accumulates 30 GB of version storage in one month. Without lifecycle `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` rules: storage costs grow unbounded. Versioning is worth the cost for protection against accidental deletion/corruption, but requires lifecycle management. <br><br> *Cost management: enable both current version and noncurrent version lifecycle policies. Transition noncurrent versions to Standard-IA after 30 days, Glacier after 90 days. Expire noncurrent versions after 365 days (or appropriate retention period). This bounds version storage at a predictable cost.<br> *Versioning + replication: both source and destination require versioning for CRR/SRR. The destination bucket stores all replicated versions — same cost implications. For DR buckets that are write-only: optimize destination lifecycle policies to transition replicated objects faster (they're for recovery, not active access).<br> *Version ID uniqueness: each version has a globally unique version ID (string). Version IDs are not sequential — they are opaque unique identifiers. Applications that need to reference specific versions must store version IDs alongside the object key in a metadata store (DynamoDB).<br>

932. [ S3 ] What is the S3 lifecycle rule for expiring incomplete multipart uploads? ; The `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle action with `DaysAfterInitiation: N` automatically aborts and deletes incomplete multipart uploads older than N days. This prevents orphaned parts from accumulating and incurring storage costs. AWS recommends setting this to 7 days on all buckets. Incomplete multipart parts are billed at the Standard storage rate regardless of the intended final storage class. <br><br> *How to detect existing incomplete uploads: `aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket bucket-name`. Each result shows the upload ID, key, initiated date, and initiator. Large numbers of incomplete uploads indicate either application failures or missing lifecycle cleanup rules.<br> *S3 Storage Lens: advanced metrics include `IncompleteMultipartUploadSizeBytes` showing the volume of incomplete multipart data per bucket. Use this to quantify the hidden storage cost before and after adding the lifecycle rule.<br> *Application-side mitigation: applications should call `AbortMultipartUpload` in error handlers when multipart uploads fail. Combined with lifecycle cleanup: belt-and-suspenders protection. Lifecycle handles cases where the application crashed before it could abort the upload.<br>

933. [ S3 ] What is the S3 replication requirement for encrypted objects with SSE-KMS? ; For CRR/SRR with SSE-KMS encrypted source objects: the replication IAM role must have KMS permissions: `kms:GenerateDataKey` on the destination CMK (to encrypt replica) and `kms:Decrypt` on the source CMK (to decrypt source during replication). If source and destination are in different accounts: both CMK key policies must grant the replication role the required permissions. The destination can use a different CMK than the source. <br><br> *Cross-account KMS: source CMK key policy must allow the replication role ARN from the source account to call `kms:Decrypt`. Destination CMK (in destination account) key policy must allow the same replication role ARN to call `kms:GenerateDataKey`. Cross-account KMS access requires explicit key policy grants — CMK is not accessible by other accounts by default.<br> *Bucket Key with replication: S3 Bucket Keys work with replication. The destination bucket can use its own Bucket Key with the destination CMK. The source's Bucket Key material is not replicated — destination generates new data keys from the destination CMK.<br> *Common failure scenario: CRR configured but objects not replicating. Root cause: missing KMS permissions on the replication role or destination CMK key policy. Check CloudTrail for KMS `AccessDeniedException` events from the S3 service principal — this indicates KMS permission gap.<br>

934. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Object Lambda supported payload limit? ; S3 Object Lambda Lambda functions must return the transformed object within 60 seconds. The transformed response must fit within 6 MB for synchronous Lambda responses. For objects larger than 6 MB: use Lambda with streaming response (presigned URL → Lambda ranges + streams). The Lambda function calls `write_get_object_response()` with the transformed data or with chunks for streaming. <br><br> *Lambda timeout: if the Lambda function takes >60 seconds to process and return `write_get_object_response`, S3 returns a timeout error to the caller. For large objects requiring intensive processing: optimize Lambda (use /tmp for intermediate storage, parallelize processing) or reconsider whether Object Lambda is the right approach.<br> *Streaming pattern: Lambda can call `write_get_object_response` multiple times (chunk streaming) to return large objects. This avoids the 6 MB in-memory limit. For video transcoding, image resizing of large images: use chunk-based streaming responses.<br> *When to use vs pre-processed copy: if the same transformation is applied to every access of an object, and the object is accessed frequently: store the transformed copy once (Batch Operations → Lambda → S3). Only use Object Lambda for per-request dynamic transformations (user-specific redaction, caller-specific filtering).<br>

935. [ S3 ] What is the Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval minimum storage duration and what happens to cost if object is deleted early? ; Glacier Instant Retrieval has a 90-day minimum storage duration. If an object is deleted (or transitioned to another class) before 90 days, you are charged for the full 90 days of storage at the Glacier Instant Retrieval rate. This is the "early deletion fee." For objects that may be deleted before 90 days: Standard or Standard-IA are better choices depending on access frequency. <br><br> *Calculation: Glacier IR rate ≈ $0.004/GB/month. 90-day minimum = 3 months. Early delete on day 1: pay 89 days of unused storage. For large objects deleted early: substantial cost. For objects with uncertain retention (may be deleted in 60 days): Standard-IA (30-day minimum, higher price but lower minimum duration cost) may be cheaper.<br> *Lifecycle rule timing: if a lifecycle rule transitions objects to Glacier IR at 30 days and then expires them at 60 days: objects pay 30 days in Standard + 60-day early delete in Glacier IR (30 days actual + 60 days minimum remaining = 90 days billed). Lifecycle transitions must account for minimum storage durations.<br> *S3 Storage Class Analysis helps: after 30 days of analysis, it shows the access pattern. Objects frequently accessed in the 0-90 day window should stay in Standard or Standard-IA. Objects consistently not accessed after 90 days are candidates for Glacier IR.<br>

936. [ S3 ] What is the difference between S3 replication and S3 sync for moving large datasets? ; S3 Replication: automatic, ongoing, server-side. New objects replicate asynchronously. No bandwidth on the requester's side. Continues indefinitely as new objects are added. S3 sync (`aws s3 sync`): manual, on-demand, CLI-based command. Compares source and destination (by ETag or size/modification time), uploads missing/changed objects. Requires network bandwidth on the machine running the command. One-time or scheduled manually. <br><br> *AWS DataSync: managed version of sync with scheduling, bandwidth throttling, CloudWatch metrics, and support for on-premises NFS/SMB sources. For automated, scheduled, managed sync: DataSync > aws s3 sync. DataSync can handle petabytes with parallel transfers and retry logic.<br> *Migration scenario: migrating 100 TB from old AWS account to new account. S3 sync or DataSync (one-time migration). CRR (ongoing continuous replication for new data). Combined approach: DataSync/sync for historical data, CRR enabled for new data going forward.<br> *Cost: S3 sync: standard S3 request costs + inter-region transfer if cross-region. DataSync: $0.0125/GB transferred. CRR: inter-region data transfer costs + replicated request costs. For one-time migration: DataSync (managed, faster, parallel). For ongoing: CRR (zero-management, automatic).<br>

937. [ S3 ] What are the S3 CloudFront integration patterns and when is each appropriate? ; Pattern 1: CloudFront with S3 REST endpoint + OAC (Origin Access Control): private S3 bucket, only CloudFront can access. Best for: static website with HTTPS, private content CDN. Pattern 2: CloudFront with S3 website endpoint: enables S3 index document behavior for subdirectory paths. Best for: SPA (Single Page Application) static websites needing directory index. Pattern 3: CloudFront with MRAP: global S3 distribution with CloudFront as the CDN layer. <br><br> *OAC vs OAI: OAC is the modern replacement for OAI. OAC supports SSE-KMS encrypted buckets (OAI doesn't), all S3 regions, and uses SigV4 signed requests. For new CloudFront + S3 integrations: always use OAC. Migrate existing OAI to OAC when convenient.<br> *CloudFront cache behavior for S3: configure CloudFront cache behavior to cache S3 responses (Cache-Control headers from S3 objects control TTL). Objects with long TTL (365 days) are cached aggressively. Use Cache-Control: no-cache for dynamic objects. Versioned file names (bundle.1234.js) allow aggressive caching with immediate cache invalidation by changing the filename.<br> *S3 Transfer Acceleration vs CloudFront: Transfer Acceleration is for uploads TO S3 from distributed clients. CloudFront is for downloads FROM S3 to distributed users. They serve opposite directions. Both use AWS edge infrastructure. Not interchangeable — use both for a globally distributed read/write S3-backed application.<br>

938. [ S3 ] What is S3 StorageLens free tier vs advanced tier? ; Free tier (default): 28 usage metrics, 14-day data retention, account and bucket level metrics. Available for all accounts, no cost. Advanced tier ($0.20 per million objects/month): 35+ additional metrics, 15-month retention, prefix-level analysis, CloudWatch publishing, advanced activity metrics (request counts, data transfer metrics per bucket). Advanced tier unlocks prefix-level analysis for identifying storage hotspots. <br><br> *Prefix-level metrics (Advanced only): identify which prefix in a bucket contains the most unencrypted objects, which prefix has highest GET request rate, which prefix has most objects in Standard that should be in IA. This granularity is essential for large data lakes where per-prefix optimization drives cost savings.<br> *CloudWatch publishing (Advanced only): Storage Lens metrics published to CloudWatch every day. Create CloudWatch alarms: "if total Standard storage increases by >10% day-over-day" → alert. Or: "if unencrypted object count > 0" → alert for compliance. Storage Lens becomes part of the operational monitoring stack.<br> *ROI calculation: 1 million objects × $0.20/million = $0.20/month for Advanced metrics. If Advanced metrics identify 5 TB of objects in Standard that can be moved to Glacier IR ($0.004/GB vs $0.023/GB) → savings $19/TB/month = $95/month for the 5 TB. $0.20 cost → $95 monthly savings. Always cost-positive for large buckets.<br>

939. [ S3 ] What is the S3 Transfer Acceleration pricing model? ; Transfer Acceleration charges in addition to standard S3 data transfer costs: $0.04/GB for transfers accelerated between the client and the edge location (for most regions), $0.08/GB for transfers between some edge locations and S3 regions (higher cost edge locations). If acceleration is not faster than standard transfer, AWS does not charge the acceleration fee. Standard S3 upload costs still apply. <br><br> *When not charged: AWS provides a comparison tool and automatically falls back if acceleration is not beneficial. The "free fallback" means there's no financial risk in enabling Transfer Acceleration — you only pay when it's actually faster.<br> *Annual cost model: for a company uploading 10 TB/month from Tokyo to S3 us-east-1 bucket. Without acceleration: $0.00 (ingress is free from internet). Wait, uploads (ingress) to S3 are free — the $0.04/GB applies to... Wait: Transfer Acceleration charges apply to data RECEIVED BY S3 via the accelerated path, not just egress. Uploads via accelerated endpoint cost $0.04/GB. Check current pricing carefully.<br> *For uploads from multiple global locations: run the speed comparison per location. Enable Transfer Acceleration globally (bucket setting). Applications automatically use the accelerated endpoint — those in close regions skip it (no charge), those far away use it (charged when faster). One setting covers all upload locations.<br>

940. [ S3 ] What does it mean that S3 is "eventually consistent" for list operations when using parallel S3 delete-and-replace patterns? ; Since December 2020, S3 is strongly consistent for all operations including DELETE and LIST. There is no more eventual consistency in standard S3 operations. A DELETE returning 200 means the object is immediately gone from subsequent LIST and GET calls. Old study materials referencing eventual consistency are outdated. For the SAP-C02 exam: all S3 consistency is strong consistency. <br><br> *Historical context: before December 2020, overwrite PUTs and DELETEs to existing keys had eventual consistency — a GET immediately after DELETE might return the old data. This required retry logic in applications. Now: immediate consistency on all operations.<br> *The one nuance: pagination across a very large, actively-changing bucket. A paginated ListObjectsV2 call spans multiple API requests. Between pages, objects may be added or deleted. Strong consistency applies to each individual API call, not the full paginated traversal. For a complete point-in-time listing of a live bucket: use S3 Inventory (atomic snapshot) rather than paginated API calls.<br> *Exam trap watchout: if a question mentions "eventual consistency in S3," the answer is that S3 is strongly consistent as of December 2020. Any scenario suggesting waiting for consistency propagation after S3 operations is describing outdated behavior — the correct answer is immediate strong consistency.<br>


941. [ S3 ] A financial services company must retain trade records for 7 years and no employee (including the CEO) must be able to delete or modify any record during that period. SEC 17a-4(f) compliance is required. What S3 configuration achieves this? ; Create an S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled at creation time. Configure bucket default retention: Compliance mode, 7-year period (2,555 days). Enable versioning (Object Lock requires it). Enforce SSE-KMS encryption with a CMK. Restrict S3 access via bucket policy to write-only for the ingestion application and read-only for authorized auditors. <br><br> *Object Lock Compliance mode: no user, including root or AWS Support, can delete or modify object versions before the 7-year retention period expires. SEC 17a-4(f) requires WORM storage that cannot be modified even by the service provider. Compliance mode satisfies this requirement.<br> *Bucket default retention: rather than requiring applications to set retention on each upload, the bucket default applies Compliance + 7 years automatically to every PUT. Applications don't need to be modified — protection is infrastructure-level.<br> *Audit trail: enable CloudTrail data events on the compliance bucket. Every GetObject, PutObject, and any Object Lock bypass attempt is logged. Required for SEC 17a-4(f) audit trail demonstrating all access to regulated records.<br>

942. [ S3 ] A media company stores 500 TB of video in S3 Standard. 80% of videos have not been accessed in the last 90 days. What is the most cost-effective immediate action? ; Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket (or migrate to IT via S3 Batch Operations CopyObject job). Objects not accessed for 30 days auto-move to IA tier (~45% cost reduction), those not accessed for 90 days move to Archive Instant Access tier (~68% cost reduction). No manual lifecycle analysis needed — IT adapts to actual access patterns automatically. <br><br> *Alternative: S3 Storage Class Analysis + Lifecycle. Run Storage Class Analysis for 30 days, then configure lifecycle policy based on results. This is more manual but may achieve better cost optimization with known patterns. For "immediate action" + "uncertain access patterns": Intelligent-Tiering is faster to implement.<br> *Cost estimate: 500 TB in Standard ≈ $11,500/month. 80% (400 TB) in Archive Instant Access tier ≈ $1,600/month. Total with IT: 100 TB Standard + 400 TB Archive IA ≈ $2,300 + $1,600 = $3,900/month. Savings: ~$7,600/month (~66% reduction). IT monitoring fee: $25/month for 10M objects — negligible.<br> *With S3 Batch Operations: create a CopyObject job targeting all existing objects (S3 Inventory manifest) to copy them to IT storage class. This is the "immediate action" to move existing objects — IT alone doesn't retroactively change existing objects' storage class.<br>

943. [ S3 ] A company's developers accidentally deleted all objects in a production S3 bucket. The bucket had no versioning. How can data be recovered? ; Without versioning, S3 deletion is permanent — there is no native S3 recovery mechanism. Recovery options: (1) Check AWS Backup if S3 backup was configured. (2) Check if CRR/SRR was configured — recover from replica bucket. (3) Check any event-driven copies (Lambda archiving objects to another bucket on write). (4) Re-ingest from source systems. (5) S3 support cannot recover permanently deleted unversioned objects. <br><br> *Prevention (the real answer): enable versioning on all production buckets immediately. With versioning: deletions create delete markers, all versions preserved. Recovery = delete the delete markers. MFA Delete on critical buckets: prevents even accidental root-level permanent deletes.<br> *AWS Backup for S3: if AWS Backup was configured for the S3 bucket before deletion, backup snapshots (S3 Inventory-based backups) may be available for restore. AWS Backup for S3 supports recovery of buckets, prefixes, or specific objects from a backup point. This requires pre-existing backup configuration.<br> *Lesson for exam: the answer to "deleted unversioned S3 objects" is always "cannot recover" + "prevention = enable versioning." Never suggest S3 native recovery for unversioned buckets — it does not exist.<br>

944. [ S3 ] A company needs to provide 500 different partner companies read access to specific prefixes in a data lake bucket. Each partner accesses only their own prefix. How do you manage this at scale without a massive bucket policy? ; Create an S3 Access Point per partner (500 Access Points). Each Access Point policy restricts to the partner's specific prefix and their IAM principal. The bucket policy delegates all access to Access Points (`aws:PrincipalArn` matches any Access Point). Partners use their Access Point alias/ARN — they cannot access the bucket directly or other partners' prefixes. <br><br> *Access Point scaling: 500 Access Points vs one 20 KB bucket policy. Each AP has its own focused policy. Adding partner 501 = create one new Access Point with one policy. Removing partner 200 = delete the Access Point. No bucket policy changes needed. This is the exact use case Access Points were designed for.<br> *VPC restriction per partner: if partners access via their own VPC (via DX or VPN to a shared service VPC), configure each Access Point with a VPC origin restriction. Partner's Access Point only accepts requests from their VPC endpoint. Network isolation without complex bucket policy conditions.<br> *S3 Access Grants alternative: if partners authenticate via IAM Identity Center (SSO) or SAML federation, Access Grants can map their identity directly to their prefix. Even more scalable than Access Points — no per-partner resource to create. Grant = directory group → S3 prefix permission.<br>

945. [ S3 ] A company runs global operations and uploads large media files from offices in Tokyo, London, and New York to an S3 bucket in us-east-1. Tokyo and London uploads are slow and unreliable. What is the solution? ; Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the us-east-1 bucket. Offices in Tokyo and London use the accelerated endpoint (`bucket.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com`). Traffic enters the nearest CloudFront edge location (Tokyo and London have major PoPs), then travels AWS backbone to us-east-1 S3. Significantly faster and more reliable than internet routing across the Pacific/Atlantic. <br><br> *Verification: run the Transfer Acceleration speed comparison tool from Tokyo and London offices before committing. For Tokyo → us-east-1: typical improvement is 40–80% faster. For London → us-east-1: typical improvement is 20–50% faster depending on internet path quality.<br> *New York (same continent as us-east-1): may not benefit significantly from acceleration. The fallback behavior means New York uploads use standard transfer (no extra cost). Only Tokyo and London pay the acceleration fee when faster.<br> *Alternative: create regional S3 buckets in ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo) and eu-west-1 (London). Configure CRR to us-east-1. Local offices upload to their regional bucket (fast local upload). CRR consolidates to us-east-1 over AWS backbone. This eliminates the need for Transfer Acceleration and may be cheaper for very high-volume uploads.<br>

946. [ S3 ] A healthcare company stores patient records in S3 and must comply with HIPAA. Auditors require proof of who accessed which patient file and when. What S3 configuration is required? ; Enable CloudTrail data events on the patient records S3 bucket. CloudTrail captures every GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject with the IAM identity (user ARN or assumed role ARN), timestamp, source IP, and object key. Store CloudTrail logs in a separate S3 bucket with Object Lock (Compliance mode) in a dedicated security account. Enable CloudTrail log validation (SHA-256 hash chain) to prove logs were not tampered with. <br><br> *HIPAA audit trail requirements: must be able to answer "who accessed PHI file X at time T." Server access logs cannot answer this (no IAM identity). CloudTrail data events + IAM identity = complete audit trail. CloudTrail log file integrity validation provides tamper-evidence required for compliance.<br> *Server access logs as supplement: use server access logs for operational analysis (error rates, response times, traffic patterns). CloudTrail for identity-level audit. Both can run simultaneously with no performance impact on S3 operations.<br> *CloudTrail cost: CloudTrail data events for S3 = $0.10/100K events. A healthcare application with 10M object accesses/day = 100K × $0.10 = $1,000/day. For high-volume production systems: filter CloudTrail data events to specific S3 prefixes containing PHI only (not all S3 traffic). Or aggregate with CloudTrail Lake for cost-efficient long-term querying.<br>

947. [ S3 ] A startup wants to build a user-generated content platform where users upload photos directly from the browser to S3 without proxying through application servers. How do you implement this securely? ; Generate presigned POST URLs on the application server. Include policy conditions: max file size (e.g., 10 MB), allowed Content-Type (`image/*`), and key prefix (`uploads/user-id/`). Return the presigned POST data to the browser. Browser submits multipart/form-data directly to S3 using the presigned POST. Configure CORS on S3 bucket allowing the application domain for PUT/POST. Never expose AWS credentials to the browser. <br><br> *Security: presigned POST policy is validated by S3 server-side. Even if a user modifies the form data, S3 rejects uploads that violate the policy (wrong content type, exceeds size limit, wrong key prefix). This server-side enforcement is the advantage over presigned PUT (which has no conditions).<br> *User isolation: key prefix `uploads/user-id/` ensures users can only upload to their own prefix. Application generates the presigned POST with the user's specific key prefix. A user cannot upload to another user's prefix (the presigned POST is for a specific key pattern).<br> *Post-upload processing: configure S3 event notification → Lambda on new objects in `uploads/` prefix → Lambda scans for malware (Amazon Macie or custom), validates file format (not just Content-Type header), moves validated files to `public/` prefix. Quarantine infected files. All done server-side after S3 upload.<br>

948. [ S3 ] A company has 10 billion small files (average 10 KB) in S3 Standard that have never been accessed after initial write. What is the optimal storage strategy? ; (1) Combine small files into larger archives before storing in Glacier. Use S3 Batch Operations with InvokeLambda to combine small files into 1 GB archives (Lambda reads, packages, writes archive, records manifest). Then transition archives to Glacier Deep Archive. (2) For files that MUST remain individually accessible: use Standard-IA is NOT recommended (128 KB minimum billable, making 10 KB files cost 12× more). Direct Glacier Flexible Retrieval (40 KB minimum, less overhead than Standard-IA for small files). <br><br> *Small file cost trap: 10 billion × 10 KB in Standard = 100 TB = $2,300/month. 10 billion × 10 KB in Standard-IA (billed at 128 KB each) = 10B × 128 KB = 1.28 PB billing = ~$16,000/month — MORE expensive than Standard due to minimum billable size. Standard-IA is wrong for small files.<br> *Glacier Deep Archive for small files: 10 billion × 40 KB minimum (actual 10 KB) = 400 TB billing = $396/month. Savings: $2,300 → $396 = 83% cheaper. But requires 180-day minimum storage — suitable for files that are truly never accessed again.<br> *Archive combination strategy: combine 1,000 × 10 KB files into one 10 MB archive. 10 billion files → 10 million archives. Each archive in Glacier Deep Archive at actual 10 MB (not 40 KB minimum). 10M × 10 MB = 100 TB = $99/month. 97% cheaper than Standard. The archive manifest (which small files are in which archive) stored in DynamoDB for lookup.<br>

949. [ S3 ] A company's legal department needs to immediately freeze all documents related to an ongoing litigation for an indefinite period. What S3 feature handles this? ; Apply S3 Object Lock Legal Hold to all litigation-relevant documents. Legal Hold has no expiry date — the documents are immutable until the Legal Hold is explicitly removed by a user with `s3:PutObjectLegalHold` permission. This is separate from and in addition to any existing retention periods. Documents remain frozen indefinitely until the legal team removes the hold after litigation resolves. <br><br> *Legal Hold vs retention period: retention period has a defined end date. Legal Hold has no end date — it's removed by explicit action. For litigation: the end date is unknown (case may settle tomorrow or in 5 years). Legal Hold is the correct mechanism, retention period with a guessed end date is incorrect.<br> *Implementation: S3 Batch Operations with PutObjectLegalHold operation. Manifest = S3 Inventory output filtered by prefix (e.g., `documents/2024/` related to the case). Batch Operations applies Legal Hold to all objects in the manifest in one managed job. Much faster than individual API calls for millions of documents.<br> *Legal Hold removal: when litigation ends, create another Batch Operations job with PutObjectLegalHold (OFF) to remove all holds. Requires the `s3:PutObjectLegalHold` permission — typically held only by the legal team admin role. Audit this action via CloudTrail.<br>

950. [ S3 ] A company processes IoT sensor data: 1 million readings/minute uploaded to S3. Each reading is a 1 KB JSON file. After 30 days, readings are aggregated and individual files are never accessed again. Design the optimal S3 architecture. ; Upload 1KB JSON files to S3 Standard (no minimum size, no minimum duration). After daily aggregation (Glue ETL → Parquet), expire individual JSON files via lifecycle rule (transition to... actually delete: `Expiration: 1 day after object creation` — or after 30 days with: `Expiration: 30 days`). Store the Parquet aggregates in Standard-IA (larger files, infrequent access) or Glacier IR. S3 event notifications → Kinesis Data Streams → Lambda for real-time processing pipeline. <br><br> *Volume: 1M readings/minute × 1 KB = 1 GB/min = 60 GB/hour = 1.44 TB/day. In Standard: $0.023/GB × 1,440 GB/day × 30 days = $993/month if kept for 30 days. Lifecycle expiration at 30 days caps storage at 30 days × 1.44 TB = 43.2 TB = ~$994/month. Actually deleting after 1 day (post-aggregation): only 1.44 TB stored at any time = $33/month.<br> *Key design: `sensors/year=2024/month=10/day=15/hour=12/sensor-id/timestamp.json`. Date-based prefix enables lifecycle targeting by date. Athena can query specific days. Glue can crawl daily partitions for aggregation jobs.<br> *Parquet aggregates: 1.44 TB/day compressed Parquet ≈ 200-400 MB/day (typical 4-8× compression). 1 year of aggregates = 73-146 GB. In Standard-IA: <$2/month. The architecture converts costly 1.44 TB/day of small files to <2 GB/day of Parquet aggregates, driving 99.8% storage cost reduction.<br>


951. [ S3 ] A data lake stores PII (Personally Identifiable Information). Different teams need different views: data scientists see anonymized data, data stewards see full data. Storing two copies is too expensive. What S3 feature provides per-consumer data transformation? ; S3 Object Lambda. Create two S3 Object Lambda Access Points: one for data scientists (Lambda function redacts PII fields), one for data stewards (Lambda passes through full data). The original data is stored once in S3 Standard. Each team uses their respective Object Lambda Access Point endpoint. S3 invokes the appropriate Lambda for each access. <br><br> *Implementation: Lambda for data scientist AP reads object via supporting Access Point, parses JSON, replaces PII fields (SSN, phone, email) with masked values (***-**-1234), returns modified response. Lambda for data steward AP: reads object, returns unchanged. Both Lambda functions read from the same underlying S3 object.<br> *IAM control: data scientist IAM role can only access the anonymized Object Lambda Access Point (not the direct S3 bucket or the data steward Access Point). Data steward IAM role accesses the data steward Object Lambda Access Point. IAM policies enforce the separation.<br> *Cost: Lambda invocation per read request. For high-frequency reads: consider caching anonymized versions in a separate S3 prefix (refresh on original update via event notification). Object Lambda transforms on every read — for very high-volume read workloads, pre-computed copies may be more cost-efficient.<br>

952. [ S3 ] A company migrated 500 TB from on-premises NAS to S3. After migration, they realized none of the objects have SSE-KMS encryption (they were uploaded without encryption). How do you encrypt all 500 TB without re-uploading from on-premises? ; Use S3 Batch Operations with CopyObject operation: copy all 500 TB objects to themselves (same bucket, same key) specifying SSE-KMS encryption in the destination. S3 CopyObject is server-side — no data downloads to the internet. The operation reads each object from S3, re-encrypts with KMS, and writes the new encrypted version back to S3. <br><br> *Batch Operations job: (1) Generate S3 Inventory on the bucket (daily schedule → wait 48 hours for first report), or use custom CSV manifest of all object keys. (2) Create Batch Operations job: CopyObject, source = same bucket/key, destination = same bucket/key, SSE-KMS with target CMK. (3) Confirm job (review estimated cost). (4) Monitor progress. Job runs all copies in parallel managed by AWS.<br> *KMS cost: each CopyObject with SSE-KMS incurs one KMS GenerateDataKey call per object. For 500 TB with millions of objects: significant KMS API call cost. Enable S3 Bucket Keys on the destination to reduce KMS API calls during the copy operation (batch encryption with one CMK call per S3 partition).<br> *After encryption: set bucket default encryption to SSE-KMS. Add bucket policy denying non-KMS PutObject (Q825). This ensures future uploads are also encrypted and prevents re-occurrence of the unencrypted upload issue.<br>

953. [ S3 ] A company's S3 bucket is receiving 50,000 GET requests per second to objects in a single prefix. Some requests are failing. How do you solve this? ; Distribute objects across multiple prefixes (hash-based prefix strategy). Move objects from `/logs/` to `/logs/a/`, `/logs/b/`, ... `/logs/z/` (26 prefixes × 5,500 GET/sec = 143,000 GET/sec). Update application to write/read with hash-based prefix selection. Alternatively: enable CloudFront in front of S3 to cache hot objects at edge — cache hit rate reduces origin requests dramatically. <br><br> *Prefix distribution: S3 scales 5,500 GET requests/second per prefix. With 50,000 GET/sec on one prefix: 9× over the limit. Need at least 10 prefixes (50,000 / 5,500 ≈ 9.1). Use 16+ prefixes (first hex character of MD5 hash of the key) for comfortable headroom.<br> *CloudFront as faster fix: if the 50,000 GET/sec are for the same popular objects (not unique objects per request), CloudFront caching at edge eliminates most origin requests. Cache hit rate of 90% → only 5,000 requests/sec reach S3 (within one prefix limit). CloudFront is the easiest short-term fix for hot object access.<br> *S3 Express One Zone: for extreme throughput on latency-sensitive single-AZ workloads, Express One Zone's Directory Bucket provides 10× higher request rates without prefix management. Trade-off: single AZ, limited features. For the given scenario: CloudFront + prefix distribution + standard S3 is more resilient and feature-complete.<br>

954. [ S3 ] A company wants to store application logs in S3. The operations team in a separate AWS account needs read-only access to all logs. Development teams should only read their own service's logs (e.g., service-A team reads only `/service-a/` prefix). Design the access control. ; Bucket policy: allow operations-account IAM roles read access to entire bucket. Use S3 Access Points: create one Access Point per service team with VPC origin restriction (dev teams access via their VPC) and prefix-scoped policy. Operations team uses bucket directly (full read, separate IAM role in ops account). <br><br> *Operations access: bucket policy `"Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ops-account:role/log-reader"}, "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::log-bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::log-bucket/*"]`. Simple cross-account read-only grant.<br> *Dev team isolation via Access Points: Service-A Access Point: policy allows `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:region:account:accesspoint/service-a-ap` with `s3:prefix` condition `service-a/*`. Service-A dev team's IAM role can only use the Service-A Access Point. Even if they guessed the bucket name, direct bucket access is blocked (bucket policy only allows ops-account role + Access Point ARNs).<br> *Log aggregation with SRR: if ops account needs the logs in their own account for analysis, configure SRR with destination bucket in ops account. Ops team then reads from their own account's bucket. No cross-account bucket policy needed for log analysis — only for the initial replication setup.<br>

955. [ S3 ] A company needs to serve static content globally to millions of users with <50ms latency. Content changes monthly. How do you architect this? ; CloudFront + S3: S3 bucket in us-east-1 stores static content. CloudFront distribution with S3 REST endpoint + OAC as origin. 400+ CloudFront edge locations serve cached content globally (<50ms to most users). Cache TTL: 30 days (monthly update cycle). For content updates: use versioned filenames (bundle.v2.js replaces bundle.v1.js) — no cache invalidation needed. Or trigger CloudFront invalidation for the specific files after each monthly update. <br><br> *Cache TTL strategy: `Cache-Control: max-age=2592000` (30 days) on all objects. CloudFront caches globally for 30 days. Users always get cached content — sub-millisecond edge serve. Monthly update: upload new files with new version suffix (no cache collision) OR upload over same names + create CloudFront invalidation (first 1,000 invalidation paths/month free, then $0.005 per path).<br> *Multi-region S3 not needed: CloudFront edge handles global distribution. S3 Standard in one region + CloudFront = effectively global CDN. S3 MRAP would add complexity without benefit for read-only CDN workload (CloudFront already handles the global routing).<br> *S3 + CloudFront cost: S3 storage: minimal. S3 → CloudFront transfer: free. CloudFront DTO: $0.085/GB (first 10 TB/month). For millions of users downloading 100 KB each: 1M × 100 KB = 100 GB/month = $8.50 CloudFront DTO. Very cost-effective vs serving directly from S3 (would be $9.00 DTO + much higher latency).<br>

956. [ S3 ] A compliance team discovered that several S3 buckets have public-read ACLs set on individual objects from several years ago. The team needs to identify ALL such objects and remove the public ACLs. There are 10 billion objects across 50 buckets. What is the approach? ; Enable S3 Inventory on all 50 buckets with the `Encryption Status` and `Replication Status` fields. Wait for first inventory (48 hours). Query inventory output with Athena: find all objects with ACL = public. Use the inventory CSV as manifest for S3 Batch Operations with PutObjectAcl operation (set all to private) or enable BucketOwnerEnforced (disables all ACLs). <br><br> *Fastest fix: enable `BucketOwnerEnforced` Object Ownership on all 50 buckets. This immediately disables ALL ACLs (public and private) on all objects. No per-object scanning needed. All public ACLs become ineffective instantly. Verify no applications rely on ACLs first (Storage Lens ACL metrics show ACL usage).<br> *S3 Batch Operations for targeted fix: if BucketOwnerEnforced cannot be enabled yet (ACL-dependent applications exist), run Batch Operations. Inventory (CSV with object key + ACL) → Athena query finds public ACL objects → export to CSV → Batch Operations manifest → PutObjectAcl to set private.<br> *Also enable Block Public Access: `IgnorePublicAcls: true` immediately makes all existing public ACLs ineffective (objects not publicly accessible) before Batch Operations completes. Immediate protection + batch cleanup = defense-in-depth remediation.<br>

957. [ S3 ] A company's ML team trains models on a 100 TB dataset in S3. Training jobs read the entire dataset sequentially (each file once). Jobs run daily. Dataset is updated monthly (20% of files change). What is the optimal S3 configuration? ; S3 Standard for the active training dataset. Enable Intelligent-Tiering for files older than 3 months (auto-archive rarely accessed files). Use S3 Express One Zone for hot training checkpoints (fastest reads). Configure CRR to a second region for DR of the training dataset. Use multipart upload (parallel) and byte-range fetches (parallel download) in the training framework for maximum throughput. <br><br> *Daily sequential read: 100 TB read once per day = $0.0004/GB × 100,000 GB × 1 request/1,000 = ~$40/day in GET requests. Storage: 100 TB Standard = $2,300/month. Optimize by using S3 Express One Zone for the 10 TB most-read hot files (millisecond access, 10× faster I/O → faster training) + Standard for the rest.<br> *Monthly updates (20% churn): 20 TB of new/updated files per month. CRR replicates updates to DR bucket automatically. S3 Replication + Batch Replication for initial sync. RTC optional for monthly updates (no strict RPO needed unless model training is mission-critical).<br> *MountPoint for ML: deploy MountPoint on EC2 training instances. Mount the S3 bucket as a local filesystem. Training frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow DataLoader) read files via standard POSIX calls without S3 SDK changes. Sequential read performance is optimized by MountPoint's parallel prefetch.<br>

958. [ S3 ] A company wants to perform daily SQL analytics on JSON log files stored in S3. Logs are 10 GB per day. Analytics look for error patterns across the last 7 days. How do you minimize query cost? ; Convert JSON logs to Parquet (10× compression, columnar). Partition by date (`year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/`). Use Glue ETL daily job (JSON → Parquet + partition registration in Glue Data Catalog). Query with Athena using `WHERE year='2024' AND month='10' AND day BETWEEN '09' AND '15'` — only 7 partitions scanned instead of full dataset. Cost: 7 × 1 GB (Parquet from 10 GB JSON) = 7 GB scanned × $0.005/GB = $0.035 per query vs 70 GB JSON = $0.35 per query. <br><br> *Compression impact: 10 GB JSON → ~1 GB Parquet (typical 10× for logs). Athena scans 1 GB Parquet (compressed) = $0.005. Same query on 10 GB JSON = $0.05. 10× cost reduction from format alone. Plus partition pruning: instead of scanning 70 days × 10 GB = 700 GB, scan 7 days × 1 GB = 7 GB. 100× cost reduction from partitioning.<br> *Glue ETL daily: triggered by CloudWatch Events at midnight. Reads previous day's JSON from `logs/raw/year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/`, converts to Parquet, writes to `logs/processed/year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/`. Registers partition in Data Catalog. Analytics team always queries `logs/processed/`.<br> *S3 lifecycle for raw logs: expire raw JSON after 7 days (once processed into Parquet). Keep processed Parquet in Standard-IA for 90 days, Glacier for 7 years. Processed Parquet is the archiveable format — smaller and queryable via Glacier Select.<br>

959. [ S3 ] An audit reveals that S3 data is being downloaded to the public internet from several EC2 instances. All traffic should go through private AWS connections. What changes are needed? ; Remove internet routes from private subnet route tables. Create VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3 (free). Add prefix list route to all private subnet route tables. Update S3 bucket policy to deny requests not from the VPC Endpoint (`aws:sourceVpce` condition). Verify no NAT Gateway routes for S3 traffic remain. Test S3 connectivity from EC2 via VPC Endpoint. <br><br> *Gateway Endpoint route: `Destination: pl-xxxxxxxx (S3 prefix list) → Target: vpce-xxxx`. This ensures all S3 traffic from the private subnets routes via the endpoint (AWS backbone) instead of NAT Gateway → internet.<br> *Bucket policy enforcement: `"Effect": "Deny", "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:sourceVpce": "vpce-xxxx"}}` blocks all S3 access not via the specific endpoint. Even if an EC2 instance had a public IP, S3 rejects the request. Belt-and-suspenders: endpoint routes prevent internet path, bucket policy blocks non-VPC requests.<br> *Verify with VPC Flow Logs: after configuration, check VPC Flow Logs for S3 traffic. Traffic to S3 prefix list IPs via the Gateway Endpoint appears as internal VPC traffic (not internet egress). Previously visible internet egress to S3 IPs should disappear. CloudWatch metrics on NAT Gateway: BytesOut should drop significantly.<br>

960. [ S3 ] A company stores customer data in S3 with SSE-KMS. The security team wants to immediately revoke access for a specific former customer (data must become inaccessible). There are 50 million objects belonging to this customer. What is the fastest and most permanent solution without deleting data? ; Disable or schedule deletion of the KMS CMK used exclusively for that customer's objects. Once the CMK is disabled: all 50 million objects encrypted with it become immediately inaccessible (S3 cannot call KMS Decrypt → 403 Access Denied on all GetObject). Data still exists in S3 but is cryptographically locked. To restore access: re-enable the CMK. <br><br> *CMK per-customer model: use separate CMK per customer (or per customer data partition). This enables per-customer key revocation without affecting other customers. If all customers share one CMK: disabling it locks ALL customer data, not just the target customer.<br> *Alternative (slower but permanent): S3 Batch Operations with DeleteObject targeting the customer's prefix. For 50 million objects: Batch Operations handles this efficiently. But deletion is more permanent than key revocation — cannot recover deleted objects (without versioning). Key revocation allows future re-enabling if legal requirements demand it.<br> *GDPR "Right to Erasure": cryptographic erasure via CMK deletion satisfies GDPR erasure requirements for encrypted data. Once the CMK is permanently deleted (after the 7–30 day waiting period), the 50 million encrypted objects are permanently inaccessible without needing to delete each object. This is more efficient than deleting 50M objects and is legally defensible as "erasure."<br>

961. [ S3 ] A company has compliance requirements to keep all customer communications for 10 years in an immutable state. They also need to search across communications for specific terms for eDiscovery. What S3 architecture supports both requirements? ; S3 Object Lock bucket (Compliance mode, 10-year retention). Enable versioning. Store communications as JSON/text objects with metadata tags (customer ID, date, communication type). Use Athena + Glue Data Catalog for full-text search across objects. CloudTrail data events for access audit. For eDiscovery: Athena SQL on S3 JSON data with `LIKE '%search-term%'` queries. <br><br> *Object Lock ensures immutability: 10-year Compliance mode. Athena provides searchability without requiring a separate database. S3 Inventory + Athena partition metadata = efficient search. For full-text search at scale: integrate AWS OpenSearch Service with Lambda function that indexes communications on write (S3 event → Lambda → OpenSearch index → eDiscovery search via OpenSearch).<br> *OpenSearch as eDiscovery layer: OpenSearch indexes text content. When compliance team issues eDiscovery request for all communications mentioning "contract dispute," OpenSearch returns object keys. Objects fetched from S3 (immutable originals). This provides both retention compliance (S3 Object Lock) and search capability (OpenSearch).<br> *Cost consideration: 10 years × communications volume. Transition to cheaper storage classes as objects age: Standard-IA after 1 year, Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 3 years (still searchable via Glacier Select or restore → Athena). Object Lock prevents transitions that would undermine immutability. Note: lifecycle transitions don't override Object Lock retention — objects remain WORM regardless of storage class transitions.<br>

962. [ S3 ] A company's data engineering team noticed S3 costs jumped 3× month-over-month. How would you investigate and identify the cause? ; Use S3 Storage Lens (organization-wide or per-bucket) to identify storage growth, request count changes, and data transfer increases. Check AWS Cost Explorer with S3 breakdown by operation type (storage, requests, data transfer) and by bucket. Identify buckets with highest cost delta. For top offending bucket: check S3 Inventory for unexpected versioning storage (NoncurrentVersions accumulation), incomplete multipart uploads, unexpected large objects. <br><br> *Storage Lens diagnostics: Storage Lens shows month-over-month comparison for storage size, object count, and request metrics. Jump in NoncurrentVersionSizeBytes → versioning without NoncurrentVersionExpiration lifecycle rule. Jump in IncompleteMultipartUploadSizeBytes → missing AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule. Jump in BytesDownloaded → unexpected data access or egress.<br> *AWS Cost Explorer: group by Usage Type (DataTransfer-Out-Bytes, Requests-Tier1, TimedStorage-ByteHrs). Significant jump in DataTransfer-Out = unexpected egress (data leak? New high-traffic use case?). Jump in Requests = new high-volume S3 access pattern. Jump in TimedStorage = versioning accumulation or large new data uploads.<br> *Resolution actions based on root cause: versioning accumulation → add NoncurrentVersionExpiration lifecycle rule. Multipart debris → add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload rule. Unexpected egress → CloudTrail data events to identify who/what is downloading data. Unexpected storage growth → review recent PUT patterns in server access logs.<br>

963. [ S3 ] A startup needs to store user profile images. Images are uploaded by users and read on every page load (high read frequency). Design the optimal S3 + CloudFront architecture. ; S3 Standard for images (high read frequency, S3 Standard no minimum duration).
