Presigned POST for direct browser-to-S3 upload (no application server bandwidth cost). S3 event notification → Lambda for image resizing (create thumbnails on upload). <br><br> *CloudFront edge caching: user profile images are accessed on every page load by everyone viewing profiles. CloudFront cache hit rate approaches 99% for popular profiles. S3 origin requests drop dramatically. CDN serves millions of users with sub-50ms latency from global edge locations.<br> *Cost calculation: 1 million user profiles, average 200 KB image. Total storage: 200 GB × $0.023/GB = $4.60/month. CloudFront: 10 million page loads/day × 200 KB = 2 TB/day = 60 TB/month DTO. At $0.085/GB: $5,100/month CloudFront. Direct S3 DTO would be $5,400/month + high latency. CloudFront is marginally cheaper AND provides better performance.<br> *Image variants: Lambda creates 3 thumbnail sizes on upload (100×100, 300×300, 800×800). 964. [ S3 ] A company needs to detect and alert when any S3 object containing PHI (Personal Health Information) is publicly exposed. How would you implement continuous monitoring? ; Enable Amazon Macie on all S3 buckets containing PHI. Macie automatically classifies objects (detects PHI patterns: SSNs, names, medical record numbers) and reports public accessibility. Enable S3 Block Public Access at account level + EventBridge rule on Macie findings → SNS → security team alerts. Also: AWS Config rule `s3-bucket-public-access-prohibited` for bucket-level access monitoring. <br><br> *Amazon Macie: uses ML to classify S3 object content and detect sensitive data. Continuously monitors for bucket policy changes that expose data. Generates findings for: unencrypted sensitive objects, publicly accessible buckets with sensitive data, shared access to sensitive data with external accounts.<br> *EventBridge + Macie findings: EventBridge rule matching `{"source": ["aws.macie"], "detail-type": ["Macie Finding"]}` routes findings to SNS topic → PagerDuty or email alert. Add filter for `"detail.severity.description": ["High", "Critical"]` to avoid alert fatigue from low-severity findings.<br> *Preventive + detective: Block Public Access (preventive — prevents public exposure) + Macie (detective — finds if something slips through + identifies PHI in existing objects). AWS GuardDuty S3 protection: detects anomalous S3 access patterns (unusual download volume, access from TOR exit nodes, credential anomalies). Three layers: Macie (data classification), GuardDuty (access anomalies), Config (configuration compliance).<br>

965. [ S3 ] A company's CTO asked: "We have 500 TB in S3 Standard. Some of it is accessed daily, some monthly, some never. We don't know which is which. What single change reduces our S3 bill most?" ; Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on all 500 TB via S3 Batch Operations (CopyObject to IT storage class). IT automatically classifies objects: never-accessed objects move to IA tier (45% cheaper) after 30 days, archived objects move to Archive Instant Access tier (68% cheaper) after 90 days. No analysis required. No access disruption. Monitoring fee: $0.0025/1,000 objects. <br><br> *Expected savings: if 20% accessed frequently (100 TB Standard cost: $2,300/month), 30% accessed monthly (150 TB → IT IA: ~$1,725/month saved from $3,450), 50% never accessed (250 TB → IT Archive Instant: ~$5,475/month saved from $5,750). Rough total: ~$7,200/month savings on $11,500/month bill = 63% reduction.<br> *Why not manual lifecycle: manual lifecycle requires knowing access patterns upfront. "We don't know which is which" = Intelligent-Tiering is the correct answer. If they knew 50% is never accessed: Glacier lifecycle would be cheaper (no monitoring fee). Unknown patterns → IT.<br> *Implementation: S3 Batch Operations CopyObject job with `--storage-class INTELLIGENT_TIERING` targeting all 500 TB. Use S3 Inventory as manifest. Job copies each object to itself with IT storage class. AWS handles the copy server-side. Duration: hours to days for 500 TB. After job: IT monitoring starts and auto-tiering begins within 30 days.<br>

966. [ S3 ] A company's S3 bucket is used as a CloudTrail log destination. They discovered the CloudTrail logs themselves are being tampered with (some logs are missing). How do you prevent future tampering? ; Move CloudTrail logs to a separate account (security/audit account). Enable CloudTrail log file integrity validation (SHA-256 hash chain). Store logs in an S3 bucket with Object Lock (Governance or Compliance mode, 1-year retention). Restrict write permissions: only the CloudTrail service principal can put objects. No delete permission for any human. Audit account is separate from production to prevent compromised prod account from accessing/modifying logs. <br><br> *CloudTrail log integrity validation: when enabled, CloudTrail creates a digest file every hour containing the SHA-256 hash of each log file + the previous digest's hash (chain). To verify: `aws cloudtrail validate-logs`. Any tampered or deleted log file breaks the hash chain. Provides cryptographic proof of log completeness and integrity.<br> *Object Lock for CloudTrail logs: Governance mode (admins can investigate incidents by reading logs, but cannot delete). Compliance mode (no deletion at all — maximum protection). For SOC 2 / PCI DSS: Compliance mode is preferred to prove logs cannot be deleted even by compromise of admin credentials.<br> *Separate account: even if production account is fully compromised (root access obtained by attacker), the security account's S3 bucket is in a different account. Cross-account CWL delivery to the security account bucket. Attacker in prod account cannot access security account resources. This is the foundation of AWS security architecture: separate accounts for audit/security.<br>

967. [ S3 ] A data lake has 10,000 Parquet files totaling 100 TB. A new data governance requirement says all files older than 2 years must be re-encrypted with a new KMS CMK (the old CMK is being retired). How do you accomplish this at scale? ; S3 Batch Operations CopyObject job: (1) Generate S3 Inventory with LastModifiedDate filter (select only objects older than 2 years). (2) Create Batch Operations CopyObject job specifying new KMS CMK ARN as destination encryption. (3) Copy copies each object to itself with the new CMK. (4) After job completion: disable old CMK. <br><br> *Inventory for manifest: S3 Inventory with `LastModifiedDate` field. Export to Athena: `SELECT key FROM inventory WHERE last_modified < date_sub(current_date, INTERVAL 2 YEAR)`. Export query results as CSV manifest for Batch Operations.<br> *CopyObject re-encryption: `CopyObject` with `ServerSideEncryption: aws:kms, SSEKMSKeyId: arn:aws:kms:...:key/new-key-id`. S3 decrypts the source (using old CMK in KMS), re-encrypts with new CMK, writes the object. Source and destination are same key — in-place re-encryption. Version ID changes (new version created if versioning is enabled).<br> *Old CMK retirement: after Batch Operations job completes (verify completion report shows all objects succeeded), disable the old CMK. Test that old CMK-encrypted objects (if any remain) are inaccessible. Delete CMK after the minimum 7-day waiting period. Update key policies, CMK rotation schedules for the new CMK going forward.<br>

968. [ S3 ] A company has a multi-tenant SaaS product. Each customer's data is stored in S3 under their own prefix. They need to prevent one customer from accessing another customer's data, even if they share the same IAM role for the application. How do you implement tenant isolation? ; Use IAM session tags (attribute-based access control / ABAC). When a customer's session is created via STS AssumeRole, tag the session with `tenant-id: customer-123`. S3 bucket policy condition: `s3:prefix must start with "${aws:PrincipalTag/tenant-id}/"`. Each session can only access its own prefix. <br><br> *STS session tagging: `assume_role(RoleArn=..., RoleSessionName="customer-123-session", Tags=[{"Key": "tenant-id", "Value": "customer-123"}])`. The assumed role session inherits the tag. The tag is available as `${aws:PrincipalTag/tenant-id}` in IAM/bucket policy conditions.<br> *Bucket policy: `"Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": "${aws:PrincipalTag/tenant-id}/*"}}`. Only allows the session to list/get objects in their own prefix. Customer-123's session can only access `customer-123/` prefix. Same IAM role, same bucket, tenant isolation via session tags — no per-tenant IAM policy needed.<br> *Advantages: one IAM role for all tenants, one bucket policy, no per-tenant resource management. Adding a new tenant = create their prefix, onboard their session tagging. No IAM policy changes, no Access Point creation. At 10,000 tenants: ABAC scales where per-tenant IAM policies do not.<br>

969. [ S3 ] A company processes 1 million financial transactions per day. Each transaction is ~5 KB. After the trading day, all transactions must be archived to immutable storage for 7 years for SEC compliance. Transactions may need to be retrieved within hours for audit queries. What S3 design achieves this? ; Stream transactions to S3 Standard during trading day (event-driven via Kinesis Firehose → S3). At end of day: S3 Batch Operations copies day's transactions to an S3 Object Lock bucket (Compliance mode, 7-year retention). Daily batch converts individual transaction files to Parquet + Athena queryable format. Glacier Flexible Retrieval (Standard tier, 3–5 hours) for queries older than 90 days. <br><br> *Volume: 1M transactions × 5 KB = 5 GB/day. 7 years = 5 GB × 2,555 days = 12.75 TB total. In Glacier Flexible Retrieval: 12.75 TB × $0.004/GB = $52/month at steady state. Excellent cost for 7-year compliance archive.<br> *Query retrieval: for audit requests on last 90 days: objects in Standard-IA with Athena query (millisecond metadata, quick retrieval). For older audits: RestoreObject (Standard tier, 3–5 hours) then Athena query on restored objects. 3-5 hours fits "hours for audit queries."<br> *Object Lock Compliance mode: ensures no user (including executive) can delete transactions during the 7-year period. SEC Rule 17a-4(f) requires this exact capability. CloudTrail data events on the compliance bucket: complete audit trail of who accessed which transaction record.<br>

970. [ S3 ] A global e-commerce company has S3 buckets in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. US users access the US bucket, EU users access the EU bucket. Product catalog data is managed from a central US team but must be available in both regions. What design ensures both regions have consistent, low-latency catalog access? ; Configure S3 Multi-Region Access Point (MRAP) across both buckets with active-active routing. Central US team writes product catalog updates to MRAP (routes to nearest bucket = us-east-1). Configure bidirectional CRR between the two buckets. MRAP routes reads from US users to us-east-1 (low latency), EU users to eu-west-1 (low latency). Both regions have identical up-to-date catalog data. <br><br> *Bidirectional replication: CRR us-east-1 → eu-west-1 AND eu-west-1 → us-east-1. Updates in either bucket replicate to the other. S3 prevents replication loops (replicated objects not re-replicated). With RTC: 15-minute SLA for updates to appear in both regions.<br> *Write path: US team writes to us-east-1 (via MRAP). CRR replicates to eu-west-1. EU users read from eu-west-1 via MRAP (low latency). Read path: MRAP routes each request to nearest bucket. No user latency impact from the centralized write path.<br> *DR benefit: MRAP failover routing control. If us-east-1 has an issue: set us-east-1 route status to Passive. MRAP routes ALL traffic to eu-west-1. US users experience slightly higher latency but remain operational. When us-east-1 recovers: set back to Active. Tested, controlled failover without DNS changes.<br>


971. [ S3 ] A company stores video files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. An executive urgently needs a specific video within 5 minutes. The request comes at 3 PM on a Monday (peak business hours). What is the best approach and what risk exists? ; Use Glacier Flexible Retrieval Expedited retrieval (1–5 minutes) if Provisioned Capacity Units (PCUs) are available. Without PCUs: Expedited retrieval may be throttled and fail at peak hours. If PCUs are not provisioned: escalate to AWS Support for emergency capacity, or accept Standard retrieval (3–5 hours). For future prevention: maintain PCUs for time-sensitive retrieval needs. <br><br> *Provisioned Capacity Units: $100/month per PCU. Each PCU guarantees 3 Expedited retrievals every 5 minutes + up to 150 MB/s throughput. For organizations with occasional urgent archive retrieval needs: one PCU provides sufficient capacity. The $100/month is insurance against urgent retrieval failures.<br> *Alternative storage class: if this type of urgent access happens regularly, Glacier Flexible Retrieval is wrong. Use Glacier Instant Retrieval instead (same storage cost ~$0.004/GB, but millisecond retrieval). The executive's access pattern (occasional urgent retrieval) is exactly Glacier Instant Retrieval's use case.<br> *Without PCU and peak throttle: `aws glacier initiate-job --account-id - --vault-name VAULT --job-parameters '{"Type": "archive-retrieval", "Tier": "Expedited", ...}'` returns `InsufficientCapacityException`. No guarantee, no SLA without PCU. If the executive's request has business urgency: always have PCU provisioned for any Glacier Flexible Retrieval workload with potential urgent access needs.<br>

972. [ S3 ] A startup has a mobile app. Users can upload and download files. After 6 months of growth, S3 costs are 40% of total AWS spend. Files average 50 MB. Users upload once and rarely download (< 1 download/year on average). How do you reduce costs? ; Transition files to S3 Intelligent-Tiering or directly to Glacier Instant Retrieval via lifecycle policy (90 days after upload → Glacier IR). 50 MB files are well above minimum billable size. For files rarely downloaded: Glacier IR provides 68% cost reduction vs Standard. Enable multipart upload for 50 MB files to improve upload reliability. Use CloudFront for downloads (cache popular files, reduce S3 DTO). <br><br> *Storage cost reduction: files in Standard at $0.023/GB. After 90-day lifecycle to Glacier IR: $0.004/GB. 82% storage cost reduction. For 100 TB of files: $2,300/month → $400/month. That's 83% of the "40% of total spend" problem addressed in storage alone.<br> *Download optimization: CloudFront caches popular files. For files downloaded <1/year on average: CloudFront cache miss rate is near 100% (every download is a cache miss for low-frequency access). CloudFront doesn't help here unless some files are popular. Direct S3 DTO: $0.09/GB. DX if large enterprise. Accept S3 DTO cost for rare downloads.<br> *Multipart upload for 50 MB: recommended (not required at 50 MB, but good practice). Parallel parts improve reliability over mobile networks. SDK `aws s3 cp` auto-uses multipart at 8 MB threshold. Enable with parallel transfers for faster mobile uploads (better UX).<br>

973. [ S3 ] A security audit found that developers have been downloading production data to their local machines via the AWS CLI. All data should remain within AWS infrastructure. How do you prevent this? ; Remove IAM permissions for S3 GetObject/ListBucket from developer IAM roles (deny direct S3 access). Provide data access only through managed tools: Athena (query but not download files), S3 Object Lambda (transform and return subset), or a dedicated data access application. Use S3 VPC Endpoint + bucket policy restricting access to specific VPCs. Developers' laptops (outside VPC) cannot access S3 directly. <br><br> *VPC restriction bucket policy: `"Effect": "Deny", "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:SourceVpc": "vpc-prod-xxx"}}`. Developers' laptops have no IAM role and are not in the VPC. Even if credentials were accidentally shared: laptop requests are denied by bucket policy VPC check.<br> *IAM approach: use resource-based access control. Developer IAM role gets `athena:StartQueryExecution` (query data), `athena:GetQueryResults` (see results in console/app) but NOT `s3:GetObject` directly. Athena reads from S3 on behalf of the developer (Athena service role has S3 access, not the developer's personal role).<br> *Lake Formation + Athena: grant developers column-level SELECT permission on specific tables via Lake Formation. Lake Formation checks on every Athena query. Developers see data in Athena console but cannot download the underlying S3 files (no s3:GetObject permission). CloudTrail captures all Athena queries for audit.<br>

974. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 as a backup destination for on-premises databases. They currently upload via internet. Some backup jobs fail due to network timeouts on large backups (100 GB+ files). How do you improve reliability and speed? ; Use AWS Direct Connect (Private VIF or Public VIF) for dedicated bandwidth. Implement multipart upload for large files (split 100 GB into 10,000 × 10 MB parts). Use S3 Transfer Acceleration as an alternative for locations without DX. Configure retry logic with exponential backoff in backup software. <br><br> *Multipart upload for 100 GB: split into 10,000 parts × 10 MB. Each part uploaded independently. If internet drops mid-backup: only the in-progress parts need retry (not the entire 100 GB). AWS CLI and most backup software support multipart automatically.<br> *Direct Connect for reliability: DX provides dedicated, private bandwidth with no internet dependency. 1 Gbps DX connection can upload 100 GB in ~14 minutes (vs hours on a shared internet connection). DX eliminates internet-caused timeout failures.<br> *Backup software + S3: most enterprise backup solutions (Veeam, NetBackup, Commvault) have native S3 connectors. Configure with AWS credentials and S3 bucket endpoint. Enable multipart upload in the backup connector settings. Set appropriate timeout values (DX is reliable but network issues can still occur).<br>

975. [ S3 ] A regulated industry company needs to provide third-party auditors with read-only access to specific S3 objects for a 3-month engagement. Auditors use their own AWS accounts. Access should automatically expire after 3 months. How do you implement this with minimum ongoing management? ; Create a dedicated S3 Access Point with the auditor's account ARN as principal. Grant GetObject and ListBucket for the specific audit prefix. The Access Point policy includes a `aws:CurrentTime` condition expiring in 3 months (`"DateLessThan": {"aws:CurrentTime": "2025-01-15T00:00:00Z"}`). After the expiry date, Access Point policy denies all requests automatically. <br><br> *Time-based condition: `"Condition": {"DateLessThan": {"aws:CurrentTime": "2025-01-15T00:00:00Z"}}` in the Allow statement. After January 15, 2025: the Allow condition fails, access is implicitly denied. No manual revocation needed. Set a calendar reminder to delete the Access Point after expiry for hygiene.<br> *Alternative: IAM role in the company's account assumable by the auditor's account. Set maximum session duration to 3 months (max STS session is 12 hours, so this requires a role federation with longer validity or time-based bucket policy). The Access Point time condition is simpler for pure time-based expiration.<br> *Auditing access: CloudTrail data events on the audit prefix. Every GetObject by the auditor's IAM principal is logged. After the engagement: provide the CloudTrail logs to compliance team as proof of what the auditor accessed and when.<br>

976. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 Intelligent-Tiering but is getting charged unexpectedly for data retrieval. What could be the cause? ; Objects in IT's optional Archive Access or Deep Archive Access tiers incur retrieval fees when accessed (IT auto-moves them back to Frequent Access, but the retrieval incurs a fee). The Archive tiers are optional and must be explicitly enabled — if they were enabled (inadvertently or by previous admin), objects >90 or >180 days old are in Archive tiers and incur retrieval fees when accessed. <br><br> *Retrieval fee tiers: IT Frequent Access and Infrequent Access tiers have NO retrieval fee. IT Archive Instant Access: retrieval fee ($0.01/GB). IT Archive Access: retrieval fee (~$0.01/GB). IT Deep Archive Access: retrieval fee (~$0.02/GB). Only the optional archive tiers have retrieval fees.<br> *Fix: if Archive Access tiers were enabled and retrieval fees are unexpected: disable the Archive and Deep Archive Access tiers on the IT configuration. Objects currently in those tiers move back to Archive Instant Access or IA tier over time (when accessed). No immediate force-move available — objects stay in their tier until accessed or until tier-eligibility changes.<br> *Prevention: when enabling IT, carefully review whether the optional Archive and Deep Archive tiers should be enabled. Only enable if: (1) retrieval time of hours to days is acceptable, (2) retrieval fee cost is less than storage savings. For workloads that need instant access at any time: enable only up to Archive Instant Access tier (no retrieval fee).<br>

977. [ S3 ] A data engineering team needs to process only the first and last 100 lines of 10,000 CSV files stored in S3, each file is 1 GB. Downloading all 10,000 × 1 GB = 10 TB is too expensive. What are the options? ; Use S3 Select with LIMIT clause for first 100 lines: `SELECT * FROM S3Object LIMIT 100`. For last 100 lines: byte-range fetch of the last N bytes of the file. Or S3 Select with OFFSET (not supported directly — use application-level logic). Alternatively: byte-range fetch (first 10 KB for first 100 lines header, last 10 KB for last 100 lines). <br><br> *S3 Select cost: $0.002/1,000 requests + $0.002/GB returned + $0.002/GB scanned... Actually for LIMIT 100: S3 Select scans until it finds 100 rows, then stops. For the first 100 rows of a 1 GB CSV (rows are small): scans ~100 KB (first rows in file), returns ~5 KB. Cost: minimal. For 10,000 files: 10,000 × $0.002/1,000 = $0.02 for requests + tiny scanned/returned costs.<br> *Byte-range fetch for last 100 lines: `Range: bytes=-10240` (last 10 KB). Assumes last 100 lines fit in 10 KB (true for typical CSV rows). Retrieve last 10 KB only — not 1 GB. 10,000 files × 10 KB = 100 MB downloaded (vs 10 TB without range). Dramatic bandwidth reduction.<br> *S3 Select limitation: no native "last N rows" SQL. S3 Select starts from beginning. For last rows: byte-range fetch is the correct tool. Combine: S3 Select for first 100 rows, byte-range fetch for last 100 rows. Total data transferred: ~100 KB per file × 10,000 = 1 GB vs 10 TB. 10,000× reduction.<br>

978. [ S3 ] A company needs to move 5 PB of data from on-premises tape storage to S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Internet upload would take years. What is the fastest solution? ; AWS Snowball Edge (Storage Optimized): each device holds 80 TB. Order 63 Snowball Edge devices (63 × 80 TB = 5,040 TB ≈ 5 PB). Restore data from tape to Snowball Edge on-premises. Ship devices to AWS. AWS imports data to S3. Specify `DEEP_ARCHIVE` storage class in the Snowball Edge import job. Transfer time: days to weeks of on-premises loading + shipping, vs years over internet. <br><br> *AWS Snow Family decision: <10 TB → Snowcone (8 TB). 10 TB – 80 TB → Snowball Edge (80 TB each). 80 TB – multiple PB → Snowball Edge fleet. >10 PB → Snowmobile (truck-based, 100 PB capacity). 5 PB = ~63 Snowball Edge devices or fewer Snowmobile runs.<br> *Snowball Edge import to Glacier: specify target storage class at import time. Alternatively: import to S3 Standard, then apply lifecycle rule or Batch Operations to transition to Glacier Deep Archive. Note: Snowball Edge import job supports specifying storage class directly.<br> *DataSync complement: after the initial bulk Snowball import, use AWS DataSync to sync ongoing tape additions to S3 automatically (via DataSync on-premises agent → S3). Snowball for the initial 5 PB bulk, DataSync for the incremental ongoing additions. Combined migration strategy.<br>

979. [ S3 ] A company runs an Athena data lake on S3. Analysts complain that some queries take 30+ minutes and cost $50+ per query. How do you optimize? ; Convert data from CSV/JSON to Parquet (columnar, compressed). Add Hive-style partitioning (`year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/`). Use Athena partition projection for dynamic partition pruning. Add Glue bookmarks to prevent reprocessing. Run Glue ETL jobs daily to convert new data. Expected improvement: 100× less data scanned = 100× cost reduction and much faster queries. <br><br> *Parquet: columnar format stores each column separately. `SELECT status, count(*) FROM events WHERE status='error'` only reads the `status` column (not all 50 columns). 10:1 compression typical for logs. Combined: 50 columns × 10:1 compression = 500× less data read for single-column queries.<br> *Partition pruning: `WHERE year='2024' AND month='10'` reads only October 2024 data (one directory). Without partitioning: reads all data to filter by date. For a 2-year dataset: partition pruning reduces scan from 2 years to 1 month = 24× improvement. Combined with Parquet: 24 × 500 = 12,000× scan reduction.<br> *Athena data catalog optimization: enable Glue statistics collection (column-level statistics help Athena's query planner). Use Athena's CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) to create optimized Parquet tables from CSV sources. Workgroup data usage controls: set per-query data scan limit to $10 max — queries exceeding limit automatically fail, protecting budget.<br>

980. [ S3 ] A company's application uploads thousands of small files (1-50 KB) per second to S3. After one month, S3 costs are much higher than expected. Storage class analysis shows all objects are in Standard and accessed once on upload then never again. What is the most cost-effective design change? ; Add lifecycle rule: `Expiration: 30 days` (or appropriate retention period) for the small file prefix. If files must be retained: (1) Combine small files into larger Parquet/ORC batches before uploading (use Kinesis Firehose with buffering → S3 to automatically batch). (2) After batching, expire individual small files. Retaining billions of 1-50 KB individual files in any S3 storage class incurs minimum billable size charges. <br><br> *Root cause: thousands of small files × S3 Standard request rate ($0.005/1,000 PUTs) = significant request cost. 1 billion PUTs/month = $5,000 just in request costs. Storage cost adds up even for small files (no minimum size in Standard, but sheer volume).<br> *Kinesis Data Firehose batching: Firehose buffers records (configurable: 1–128 MB buffer size, 60–900 second buffer interval) and writes to S3 as one larger file per batch. Convert small files to columnar: Firehose can convert JSON → Parquet/ORC directly using Glue schema. One 100 MB Parquet file per minute instead of 60,000 × 1 KB JSON files per minute.<br> *Cost comparison: 1 billion × 1 KB = 1 TB/month in Standard = $23/month storage + $5,000/month PUT requests = $5,023/month. After Firehose batching: 1 TB Parquet (compressed to 200 GB) = $4.60/month + ~100 PUT requests = $0.0005/month. ~99.9% cost reduction. The PUT request cost was the hidden driver, not storage.<br>

990. [ S3 ] A company's auditors are asking for proof that all data in S3 has been encrypted and they want to see the encryption status for every object across all 200 buckets with billions of objects total. How do you provide this evidence? ; Enable S3 Inventory on all 200 buckets with the `Encryption` field enabled. Daily inventory reports delivered to a central audit S3 bucket. Query with Athena: `SELECT bucket, encryption_status, COUNT(*), SUM(size) FROM inventory_table GROUP BY bucket, encryption_status`. This provides object-level encryption status across all buckets. Store query results as audit evidence. <br><br> *Inventory encryption field values: `SSE-S3`, `SSE-KMS`, `SSE-C`, `DSSE-KMS`, or `NONE`. Query for `encryption_status = 'NONE'` identifies unencrypted objects requiring remediation before audit submission.<br> *S3 Storage Lens: provides aggregate percentage of encrypted objects per bucket and account. Good for dashboard/trend reporting. For auditor-grade object-level evidence: Inventory + Athena is required. Auditors typically need per-object proof, not just aggregate percentages.<br> *Remediation pipeline: Inventory (find unencrypted) → Athena query (extract object list) → S3 Batch Operations (CopyObject with SSE-KMS) → new Inventory report (verify all encrypted) → Athena proof query → export to PDF/Excel for auditors. Complete automated compliance remediation workflow.<br>


991. [ S3 ] A financial services firm must store transaction records for 7 years with strict regulatory requirements: records cannot be modified or deleted, must be encrypted, must have audit trail of all access, and must be accessible within 24 hours. Design the S3 architecture. ; S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (24-hour access SLA met with millisecond retrieval) + Object Lock in Compliance mode (7-year retention period, root cannot delete) + SSE-KMS encryption + S3 Inventory weekly for compliance reporting + CloudTrail data events for access audit trail. Central dedicated bucket in security account with SCPs preventing deletion. <br><br> *Storage class choice: Glacier Flexible Retrieval retrieval takes 3–5 hours (Standard) or up to 12 hours. Glacier Instant Retrieval: millisecond retrieval — far exceeds 24-hour requirement and provides instant access for eDiscovery. Cost: $0.004/GB/month vs Standard $0.023/GB. For 7 years of transaction records: 73% cost reduction while exceeding access SLA.<br> *Object Lock Compliance: `RetainUntilDate` = transaction date + 7 years. No IAM policy, bucket policy, or even root account can delete objects before expiry. `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission doesn't apply to Compliance mode. Regulator-grade tamper protection.<br> *CloudTrail data events cost: $0.10 per 100,000 data events. For high-frequency transaction access: significant cost. Evaluate: enable data events only on the transaction archive bucket (not all S3 operations). Combined with S3 access logs (free) for per-object access detail.<br>

992. [ S3 ] A company is migrating a 500 TB on-premises NAS to S3. The NAS has 50 million files of various sizes (1 KB to 10 GB). The migration must complete within 2 weeks. They have a 1 Gbps Direct Connect connection. How do you execute this migration? ; AWS DataSync over Direct Connect: DataSync agent deployed on-premises, connects to NAS, transfers to S3. 1 Gbps DX = 10.8 TB/day max theoretical. 500 TB ÷ 10.8 TB/day = ~46 days. Too slow. Add Snowball Edge: copy data to 7 Snowball Edge devices (7 × 80 TB = 560 TB) in parallel with DataSync for the remaining incremental changes. <br><br> *Timeline math: 1 Gbps sustained (80% efficiency) = 8.64 TB/day. 500 TB ÷ 8.64 = 58 days. Even with 100% efficiency: 46 days. 2-week deadline: internet/DX alone is impossible. Snowball Edge physical transfer: each device at 80 GB, loading from NAS tape-to-disk at 1 Gbps DX speeds takes 7 × 7 days = available in parallel while DX handles incremental.<br> *Combined strategy: Week 1: Load 7 Snowball Edge devices with the largest 560 TB files. Ship to AWS (2-3 day transit). Week 2: DataSync over DX handles incremental changes (new/modified files since Snowball cutover point). Final sync delta = small (only files changed in the past 2 weeks).<br> *DataSync preserves metadata: file timestamps, permissions, ownership — important for NAS migration (applications may depend on file modification times). 993. [ S3 ] A company suspects an insider threat may have exfiltrated data from an S3 bucket. The security team needs to investigate what data was accessed in the last 30 days. What logs and tools are needed? ; AWS CloudTrail data events on the affected S3 bucket provides per-object GET/PUT/DELETE logs with requester IAM identity, source IP, timestamp, object key, and request size. Query CloudTrail logs via Athena. S3 server access logs provide complementary HTTP-level detail. Amazon Macie can scan for PII/sensitive data exposure patterns. GuardDuty S3 protection detects anomalous API call patterns. <br><br> *CloudTrail data events: must have been enabled BEFORE the incident (retroactive enablement shows only future activity). If not enabled: no object-level audit trail exists. Only bucket-level management events (CreateBucket, DeleteBucket, PutBucketPolicy) are in CloudTrail by default. Lesson: enable data events proactively on sensitive buckets.<br> *Athena investigation query: `SELECT eventTime, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.key, errorCode FROM cloudtrail_table WHERE eventName = 'GetObject' AND requestParameters.bucketName = 'sensitive-bucket' AND eventTime > '2024-09-15' ORDER BY eventTime`. Identifies who downloaded what objects, from where, and when.<br> *GuardDuty S3 findings: `S3/BucketPublicAccessGranted`, `S3/SensitiveDataRead`, `Exfiltration:S3/ObjectRead` — these fire in near-real-time. For the incident investigation: check GuardDuty findings for the 30-day window. Even without data events enabled: GuardDuty monitors S3 data plane events independently and may have recorded anomalous access patterns.<br>

994. [ S3 ] A company hosts a static website on S3 with global users. Page load times are slow for users in Asia-Pacific. What is the most effective solution? ; Enable CloudFront distribution in front of S3 static website. CloudFront has 600+ PoPs globally including APAC (Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Mumbai, Seoul, etc.). Static content cached at PoP nearest to user. First request: APAC PoP fetches from S3 origin (US-East or wherever bucket is). Subsequent requests: served from APAC PoP cache (milliseconds vs 200-400 ms round-trip to US). <br><br> *S3 Transfer Acceleration: speeds up UPLOADS to S3 (client → S3). Does not help with static website DOWNLOADS. Common distractor on exam. CloudFront is the correct answer for download/content delivery to global users.<br> *S3 MRAP: Multi-Region Access Point with buckets in multiple regions including APAC. Routes to nearest replica. But MRAP does not cache — every request goes to S3 (just the nearest S3 bucket). CloudFront adds a cache layer: truly static content (HTML, CSS, JS, images) served from edge cache. MRAP is for dynamic content that cannot be cached (user-specific data, real-time inventory). For static website: CloudFront always wins.<br> *CloudFront cache settings for static site: `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` for versioned assets (bundle.abc123.js). `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` for HTML pages. CloudFront OAC (Origin Access Control) restricts S3 bucket to CloudFront only (block direct S3 website URL access). Use S3 as origin (not website endpoint) with OAC for presigned URL support and HTTPS.<br>

995. [ S3 ] A company needs to enforce that all S3 buckets in all AWS accounts in their AWS Organization have server-side encryption enabled. They cannot rely on developers to enable it individually. How do you enforce organization-wide? ; AWS Config managed rule `s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled` + AWS Config Remediation Action (auto-remediate by calling SSM Automation to enable default bucket encryption). Or: SCP preventing `s3:CreateBucket` unless encryption is specified (SCPs cannot directly check CreateBucket params for encryption — use Config instead). Better: S3 default encryption (enabled via bucket property) must be set — Config detects buckets without it and auto-remediates. <br><br> *Config + Auto-remediation: Config rule evaluates all S3 buckets. Non-compliant (no default encryption): Config triggers remediation (Lambda or SSM document calls `aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket NAME --server-side-encryption-configuration ...`). Fully automated, runs across all accounts in the organization via AWS Config Aggregator + delegated admin.<br> *SCP approach: `"Deny", "s3:PutObject", "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": ["aws:kms", "AES256"]}}`. This denies PutObject without SSE header — prevents unencrypted object uploads at the SCP level, organization-wide. Combined with S3 default encryption (auto-adds SSE to all objects): belt-and-suspenders. SCP catches apps that don't set SSE header, default encryption catches them at the server side.<br> *Defense-in-depth: (1) SCP denies unencrypted PutObject. (2) S3 default bucket encryption encrypts all objects. (3) Config rule monitors and auto-remediates buckets without default encryption. (4) AWS Security Hub aggregates compliance posture. This covers new buckets (SCP blocks), existing buckets (Config remediates), and individual object uploads (SCP + default encryption).<br>

996. [ S3 ] A data lake on S3 serves multiple business units. Each unit must only see their own data. The data is organized as `s3://datalake/unit-a/`, `s3://datalake/unit-b/`, etc. There are 50 business units. How do you manage access without creating and maintaining 50 separate bucket policies or IAM policies? ; Create one S3 Access Point per business unit (50 Access Points). Each Access Point policy grants access only to its unit's prefix. Business unit users/roles access data through their Access Point ARN (not the bucket ARN). Bucket policy grants `s3:*` to all Access Points (delegated access control). Adding a new unit = create one new Access Point with appropriate policy. <br><br> *Access Point benefit: 50 separate policies maintained independently. Bucket policy is simple: `"Allow": "arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:123456789012:accesspoint/*"` (allows all Access Points). Each AP has its own policy — scoped to prefix, granular to specific actions. Isolates policy management: Unit-A admin can manage Unit-A's AP policy without touching the central bucket policy.<br> *Lake Formation alternative: define data lake permissions in Lake Formation (table-level, column-level, row-level security). Analysts from business units get Lake Formation permissions on their tables only. Lake Formation enforces through Athena, Glue, EMR. No S3 object-level permissions needed — Lake Formation catalog-layer controls access to S3-backed tables. More granular than Access Points (column-level) but requires Glue catalog registration.<br> *ABAC scaling: use IAM attribute-based access control with `s3:prefix` condition and user attribute tags. IAM policy: `"Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": "${aws:PrincipalTag/BusinessUnit}/*"}}`. Users tagged `BusinessUnit=unit-a` → access `unit-a/*` prefix only. New business unit = new tag value, no policy changes. Best scaling for large numbers of units.<br>

997. [ S3 ] A startup is running out of money and needs to cut AWS costs immediately. Their main cost is S3. They have 100 TB of data: 20 TB accessed daily, 30 TB accessed monthly, 50 TB never accessed in 12+ months. What changes would you make? ; 20 TB daily access: keep in Standard. 30 TB monthly: move to Standard-IA immediately (40% cost reduction). 50 TB never accessed in 12+ months: move to Glacier Deep Archive immediately (95% cost reduction). Set up lifecycle policies for ongoing automated tiering. Expected savings: $2,300/month → ~$700/month. <br><br> *Cost breakdown before: 20 TB Standard = $460/month. 30 TB Standard = $690/month. 50 TB Standard = $1,150/month. Total = $2,300/month.<br> *Cost after: 20 TB Standard = $460/month. 30 TB Standard-IA = $332/month (30 TB × $0.0125 - $125 retrieval buffer). 50 TB Glacier DA = $50/month (50 TB × $0.00099/GB ≈ $50). Total = ~$842/month. 63% reduction. Standard-IA minimum storage: 30 days. If monthly data is accessed unpredictably, calculate retrieval costs vs storage savings.<br> *Lifecycle policy: `aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration` with rules: (1) Transition to Standard-IA after 30 days of no access. (2) Transition to Glacier IR after 90 days. (3) Transition to Glacier DA after 365 days. S3 Analytics or S3 Storage Lens: identify actual access patterns before making changes (don't guess).
