998. [ S3 ] A machine learning team trains models using a 10 TB training dataset stored in S3. Training jobs run on EC2 GPU instances. Training is slow — instances spend 40% of time waiting for data from S3. What are the solutions? ; Use Amazon FSx for Lustre with S3 integration: Lustre is a high-performance parallel filesystem. S3 data linked to Lustre (lazy load on first access). EC2 GPU instances mount Lustre NFS endpoint. Lustre delivers 100s of GB/s throughput vs S3's per-prefix limits. Training data loads in seconds instead of minutes. <br><br> *S3 throughput limit: 3,500 PUT/5,500 GET per prefix per second. With many small files (common in ML datasets — millions of images): per-prefix limits become a bottleneck. Solutions: (1) Distribute files across many prefixes (hash sharding). (2) Mount FSx for Lustre — bypasses S3 per-prefix limits entirely by caching data on the Lustre filesystem.<br> *FSx for Lustre: creates a linked S3 data repository. First access to any file: loaded from S3 into Lustre (lazy import). Subsequent accesses: served from Lustre cache at full bandwidth. After training: export results back to S3. Lustre scratch (temporary): ~$0.14/GB/month. For a 10 TB dataset during a 1-week training run: ~$14 cost. Compare to engineer time wasted waiting for slow S3 reads during training.<br> *Alternative: copy entire dataset to EC2 instance NVMe storage before training. 10 TB on i3en.24xlarge: 60 TB NVMe, 100 Gbps network. Copy from S3 once (minutes at 100 Gbps), then train from NVMe. Simple but requires pre-copy step. Best for fixed training runs. Lustre is better for iterative training (data changes frequently).<br>

999. [ S3 ] A company uploads 10 million small JSON files per day to S3 for analytics. After 6 months, they have 1.8 billion files. Athena queries are taking 20+ minutes and timing out. What is the root cause and fix? ; Root cause: too many small files. Athena opens one file per mapper, overhead per file is high, 1.8 billion files = massive overhead. Fix: compact small JSON files into larger Parquet files using AWS Glue. Glue job groups JSON files by date partition, writes one large Parquet file per partition. After compaction: queries scan fewer, larger files. Performance improvement: 100x+ typical. <br><br> *Small file problem in distributed analytics: every file requires metadata lookup, DFS open, deserialization overhead. Athena/Presto is optimized for large sequential reads. 1,000 files × 1 MB vs 1 file × 1 GB: same data, very different performance. Target: Parquet files 128 MB – 1 GB each for optimal Athena performance.<br> *Glue compaction job: reads all JSON files in a partition, unions them, writes one Parquet file. Schedule daily: yesterday's JSON files → one Parquet file. Apply lifecycle to delete original JSON files after compaction (retention: 30 days for safety, then expire). S3 Inventory + Athena can verify compaction coverage.<br> *S3 prefix performance: 1.8 billion files across well-designed prefix hierarchy avoids S3 LIST throttling. But Athena's issue is file count overhead, not LIST throttling. Parquet compaction is the fix. Result: 10 million files/day → 1 Parquet file/day per partition → 180 files per partition per year. Athena query time: 20 minutes → 30 seconds typical.<br>

1000. [ S3 ] A company stores customer-uploaded profile images in S3. An attacker has discovered the bucket name and is attempting a PII enumeration attack by guessing object key names (UUIDs). How do you detect and stop this? ; Detection: GuardDuty S3 protection detects anomalous LIST and GET patterns (high-frequency, systematically incrementing keys). Blocking: WAF (if accessed through CloudFront/API GW) rate limits. S3 bucket policy: remove any public access. All access through presigned URLs with short expiration (5 minutes). AWS Shield Advanced for DDoS. CloudWatch metric alarms on `s3:ListObjects` and `s3:GetObject` error rates. <br><br> *Access control design: UUID key names + no public bucket access = attacker can't enumerate (403 Forbidden on any GET without presigned URL). Presigned URL generated server-side and delivered to authenticated user only. Without presigned URL: every request returns 403. UUID key names provide obscurity (but obscurity is not security — proper access control is the foundation).<br> *GuardDuty S3 finding types: `S3/BucketEnumeration`, `S3/AnomalousBehavior:GetObject`. These alert when API call rates, source IPs, or patterns deviate from baseline. Response: automatically add attacker IP to WAF IP set (Lambda remediation triggered by GuardDuty finding via EventBridge rule).<br> *Rate limiting: CloudFront in front of S3 + WAF rate-based rule: block IPs making >1000 GET requests/5 minutes to the /profiles/* path. Lambda@Edge validates presigned URL and requester identity before allowing CloudFront to fetch from S3. Defense in depth: IAM access control → presigned URLs → CloudFront + WAF rate limiting → GuardDuty detection → automated remediation.<br>


1001. [ S3 ] A media company stores 500 TB of raw video footage in S3 Standard. After analysis, 80% of files have not been accessed in 6+ months. The company wants to reduce costs but needs any file accessible within 12 hours. Design the lifecycle policy. ; S3 Lifecycle: Transition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 180 days. GFR Standard retrieval: 3–5 hours (well within 12-hour SLA). GFR Bulk retrieval: 5–12 hours (still within SLA for non-urgent). Storage cost reduction: $0.023/GB (Standard) → $0.0036/GB (GFR) = 84% reduction. For 400 TB cold data: $9,400/month → $1,475/month. <br><br> *12-hour SLA match: Glacier Flexible Retrieval Standard tier: 3–5 hours. Well within 12 hours. Bulk tier: up to 12 hours exactly — risky for the 12-hour SLA edge case. Use Standard tier for retrieval (not Bulk) to comfortably meet the 12-hour window. Retrieval cost: $0.01/GB Standard, $0.0025/GB Bulk. For infrequent access: Standard retrieval cost is acceptable vs missing 12-hour SLA.<br> *Alternative: Glacier Instant Retrieval (millisecond retrieval, $0.004/GB). Overkill if 12 hours is acceptable. For video footage that might be needed in editorial emergencies: GIR is better UX but 10x more expensive storage than GFR. Business decision: how often is the 12-hour window vs millisecond urgency triggered?<br> *Policy JSON: `{"Transitions": [{"Days": 180, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}], "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Prefix": "footage/"}}`. S3 Analytics recommendation (enable 30 days prior): S3 will confirm actual access pattern data before committing to lifecycle policy. Avoids premature transition of actually-active data.<br>

1002. [ S3 ] A company is building a document management system. Users must be able to upload documents directly from the browser (no backend proxy) to reduce server load. The backend must validate that only PDF files up to 10 MB are uploaded. How do you design the S3 upload? ; Presigned POST (not presigned PUT). Presigned POST allows server-side conditions: `["content-length-range", 1, 10485760]` (max 10 MB) and `["starts-with", "$Content-Type", "application/pdf"]`. Backend generates the presigned POST policy (expires in 5 minutes). Browser submits multipart form POST directly to S3. S3 validates conditions before accepting upload. Invalid files rejected by S3, never touch backend. <br><br> *Presigned POST vs PUT: Presigned PUT = single URL, no conditions. Any content-type, any size up to 5 GB. Presigned POST = form POST with policy document, supports conditions (content-length, content-type, key prefix, metadata). For server-enforced upload validation: Presigned POST is the correct choice.<br> *Presigned POST policy conditions: `{"expiration": "2025-01-15T12:00:00Z", "conditions": [{"bucket": "my-bucket"}, {"key": "uploads/USER_ID/DOCUMENT_ID.pdf"}, {"Content-Type": "application/pdf"}, ["content-length-range", 1, 10485760], ["starts-with", "$x-amz-meta-user-id", ""]]}`. If browser submits 11 MB file: S3 returns 400 EntityTooLarge. No server processing needed — S3 enforces conditions.<br> *Post-upload processing: S3 event notification → Lambda (PDF validation: check actual PDF magic bytes, not just Content-Type header). Lambda uses Amazon Textract for text extraction or PDF validation library. Malicious files with PDF content-type but executable content: rejected by Lambda post-upload. Two-stage validation: S3 policy (size/type) + Lambda (content verification).<br>

1003. [ S3 ] A company replicates S3 data from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 for DR. A developer accidentally deleted 10,000 objects in us-east-1. Replication propagated the deletes to eu-west-1. How do you recover the objects? ; If versioning is enabled (required for replication): deleted objects have a delete marker, not actual deletion. Recover by removing the delete markers: `aws s3api delete-object --bucket SOURCE-BUCKET --key KEY --version-id DELETE_MARKER_ID`. Or use S3 Batch Operations to bulk-remove delete markers across all 10,000 affected objects. Query deleted objects from S3 Inventory or CloudTrail. <br><br> *Versioning protects against accidental delete: `aws s3 rm s3://bucket/key` creates delete marker, does not destroy data. Previous versions intact. Delete marker removal restores the latest previous version. Without versioning: data is permanently gone (no recovery without backup).<br> *Replication and deletes: by default, CRR does NOT replicate delete markers (to protect destination from accidental source deletes). If Delete Marker Replication was explicitly enabled: both source and destination have delete markers. Recovery: remove markers in both regions (or just source if delete marker replication is off).<br> *S3 Batch Operations delete marker removal: create inventory → filter for `IsDeleteMarker=true` AND `LastModified > incident_time` → Batch Operations job → `DeleteObject` action targeting the delete marker versions → all 10,000 objects restored. Entire recovery: 30-60 minutes with Batch Operations vs days of manual recovery.<br>

1004. [ S3 ] A company's S3 bucket receives data from IoT devices worldwide. The devices are behind corporate firewalls and cannot use CloudFront. Devices upload 5 MB readings every hour. Uploads from Asia-Pacific devices are unreliable and frequently fail with timeout errors. How do you improve upload reliability from APAC? ; Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket. APAC devices upload to the nearest CloudFront edge PoP (instead of directly to S3 in us-east-1). Edge PoP → S3 via AWS backbone (low-latency, reliable). Device changes only the S3 endpoint: `bucket.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com`. No CloudFront configuration needed — Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront infrastructure transparently. <br><br> *Transfer Acceleration: optimizes uploads, not downloads (unlike CloudFront content delivery). Uses CloudFront edge network for the upload path. Device connects to nearest edge (e.g., Singapore PoP for APAC devices). Edge → S3 origin: AWS backbone with optimized routing, not public internet. Eliminates the long-haul public internet segment (APAC → US-East via Pacific undersea cables) which is the source of timeout failures.<br> *Cost: $0.04/GB additional charge over S3 standard transfer rates. For 5 MB × hourly from thousands of IoT devices: calculate ROI vs lost data value from failed uploads. For critical IoT telemetry: the cost is justified. AWS provides a speed comparison tool (s3-accelerate-speedtest.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com) to verify improvement before committing.<br> *IoT-specific design: IoT devices with intermittent connectivity benefit from multipart upload (retry failed parts only). Divide 5 MB reading into 5 × 1 MB parts. If timeout on part 3: retry only part 3. With Transfer Acceleration + multipart: robust upload pipeline for unreliable connections. SQS + Lambda for failed upload notifications (IoT device → SQS on failure → Lambda triggers re-upload).<br>

1005. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 for a healthcare application storing HIPAA-regulated patient records. They have bucket versioning enabled. A ransomware attack encrypted the bucket's objects (attacker had legitimate S3 credentials). How do you recover and prevent recurrence? ; Recovery: use S3 versioning to roll back to pre-attack versions (delete the ransomware-encrypted versions using specific version IDs). Use S3 Batch Operations to bulk-delete all post-attack versions. Prevention: S3 Object Lock (WORM mode) prevents overwriting existing objects. MFA Delete prevents version deletion. AWS Macie detects unusual mass-encryption patterns. IAM least privilege removes unnecessary s3:PutObject permissions. <br><br> *Ransomware on S3: attacker with s3:PutObject credentials uploads encrypted versions of all objects (creating new versions). Objects appear corrupted. With versioning: previous versions intact — ransomware-encrypted versions are just new versions. Recovery: list all versions modified after attack timestamp, delete those version IDs. Original data preserved in previous versions.<br> *Object Lock for ransomware prevention: WORM locks prevent overwriting. But ransomware can't create new versions either if Compliance mode is set — it blocks PutObject to existing keys. Governance mode: ransomware could use bypassGovernanceRetention. Use Compliance mode for healthcare records.<br> *Credential security: rotate compromised credentials immediately (IAM user/role), audit CloudTrail for all actions in attack window, enable GuardDuty (detects compromised credentials patterns like unusual S3 access), use IAM roles (not long-lived access keys), enable SCP to prevent root account from generating access keys. Post-incident: AWS Config rule `iam-no-console-access` and `access-keys-rotated` to prevent future credential compromise.<br>

1006. [ S3 ] A company wants to analyze their S3 access patterns and costs across 500 accounts in their AWS Organization to find optimization opportunities. How do you get a unified view? ; Enable S3 Storage Lens with organization-level configuration (requires delegated admin account in AWS Organizations). Storage Lens provides organization-wide aggregated metrics: total storage by class, access frequency, cost efficiency score, activity metrics per bucket. Identify: buckets with no access in 30+ days (lifecycle candidates), buckets with large numbers of noncurrent versions (lifecycle expiration needed), cost optimization recommendations built-in. <br><br> *Storage Lens vs CloudWatch: Storage Lens is purpose-built for S3 cost/access analytics. CloudWatch has S3 bucket-level metrics (storage, requests) but not the cross-account, cross-region aggregation and optimization recommendations that Storage Lens provides. For 500-account org: Storage Lens is the correct tool — scales automatically to organization level.<br> *Storage Lens free tier: 15 metrics free per account. Advanced metrics (detailed cost optimization, data protection, event activities): additional cost (~$0.20/1M objects/month). For 500 accounts with billions of objects: the advanced metrics cost is small vs the optimization savings identified.<br> *Storage Lens export: configure Storage Lens to export daily metrics to an S3 bucket as CSV or Apache Parquet. Query with Athena for custom analysis: custom threshold alerts, trend analysis over time, per-OU aggregation. Example: `SELECT account_id, bucket_name, storage_bytes, last_accessed_days FROM lens_export WHERE last_accessed_days > 90 AND storage_class = 'STANDARD'` — identify Standard-class buckets unused for 90 days (lifecycle opportunity).<br>

1007. [ S3 ] A SaaS company provides file storage to enterprise customers. Each enterprise customer has their own S3 bucket in the SaaS company's AWS account. A security audit found that the SaaS company's own employees can access customer data via IAM permissions. How do you isolate customer data from SaaS employees? ; Resource Control Policies (RCPs) in AWS Organizations + customer-managed KMS keys: RCP denies SaaS employees access to customer buckets. Customer controls KMS key (separate AWS account) — SaaS company cannot decrypt even if they access the S3 bytes. Alternatively: move each customer to their own AWS account (account-level isolation). <br><br> *RCPs (Resource Control Policies): organization-level SCPs applied to resources, not identities. RCP: `"Deny", Principal: "arn:aws:iam::SAAS_ACCOUNT:role/SaaSEmployees", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::customer-*"`. Even SaaS employees with broad IAM permissions cannot access customer-prefixed buckets. RCPs override IAM identity policies — the Deny is evaluated before Allow in the combined authorization logic.<br> *Customer-managed KMS in customer account: SaaS service role assumes cross-account role in customer account to use KMS key for encryption/decryption. SaaS employees don't have access to customer's KMS key (different account, customer controls the key policy). Data at rest: encrypted with customer key. SaaS employees can't decrypt even if they read the S3 bytes.<br> *AWS account isolation: most secure. Each customer gets a dedicated AWS account. SaaS employees have no IAM role in customer accounts. Cross-account access: customer grants SaaS service role a specific cross-account role (limited permissions, customer-controlled). This is the enterprise SaaS pattern for maximum isolation. Tradeoff: operational overhead of managing hundreds/thousands of accounts — use AWS Control Tower for account vending.<br>

1008. [ S3 ] A company's compliance team requires that no S3 object is ever stored without a specific metadata tag `data-classification` set to one of `public`, `internal`, `confidential`, or `restricted`. How do you enforce this at the time of upload? ; Bucket policy Deny condition: `"Deny": "s3:PutObject"` unless `"StringLike": {"s3:RequestObjectTagKey/data-classification": ["public", "internal", "confidential", "restricted"]}`. This bucket policy denies any PutObject request that doesn't include the correct tag. Applied to all prefixes in the bucket. Enforce via SCP across organization. <br><br> *Bucket policy tag condition: `{"Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*", "Condition": {"ForAllValues:StringNotEquals": {"s3:RequestObjectTagKey": ["data-classification"]}}}`. Combined with: `{"Effect": "Deny", "Condition": {"StringNotEqualsIfExists": {"s3:RequestObjectTag/data-classification": ["public", "internal", "confidential", "restricted"]}}}`. Two conditions: (1) tag key must be present, (2) tag value must be one of the allowed values.<br> *Object Tagging vs metadata: S3 object tags are queryable (S3 Inventory, S3 Batch Operations can filter by tag). Object user-defined metadata (x-amz-meta-*) is stored with the object but less queryable at scale. For compliance classification: object tags are the right mechanism (Macie integrates with tag-based classification, IAM conditions support tag values).<br> *Lambda validation alternative: S3 event notification (ObjectCreated:*) → Lambda → check tags → if non-compliant: delete object + notify. But this is async (object already stored momentarily). Bucket policy is synchronous — upload rejected before storage. Use bucket policy for enforcement, Lambda for audit/alerting.<br>

1009. [ S3 ] A company runs batch jobs that process 1 million S3 objects every night. The jobs need to list all objects, filter by metadata, and call a Lambda for each object. The current implementation uses a recursive S3 ListObjects loop with Lambda invocations in a loop — it's slow and sometimes fails partway through. How do you redesign? ; Use S3 Batch Operations: create inventory manifest (S3 Inventory daily manifest) → Batch Operations job with Lambda function invocation. Batch Operations parallelizes Lambda invocations across millions of objects, handles retries, provides progress tracking, generates completion report. Much faster and resilient than custom loop. <br><br> *S3 Batch Operations vs custom loop: custom loop → sequential or limited parallel invocations, single point of failure, no built-in retry. Batch Operations → massively parallel, automatic retry (up to 3 attempts), CloudWatch metrics for progress, completion report (per-object success/failure), runs to completion even if Lambda throttles (Batch Operations respects Lambda concurrency limits automatically).<br> *Batch Operations job creation: `aws s3control create-job --account-id 123456789012 --operation '{"LambdaInvoke": {"FunctionArn": "arn:aws:lambda:..."}}' --manifest '{"Spec": {"Format": "S3BatchOperations_CSV_20180820", "Fields": ["Bucket","Key"]}, "Location": {"ObjectArn": "arn:aws:s3:::manifest-bucket/manifest.csv", "ETag": "..."}}' --report '{"Bucket": "arn:aws:s3:::report-bucket", "Format": "Report_CSV_20180820", "Enabled": true, "ReportScope": "FailedTasksOnly"}'`. Completion report only for failures (saves storage).<br> *S3 Inventory for manifest: instead of ListObjects (which can take hours for 1 billion objects), use S3 Inventory (pre-computed daily manifest). Batch Operations can use Inventory CSV directly. Zero ListObjects overhead. Metadata filtering: include all metadata fields in Inventory, Lambda filters per-object on metadata. Total redesign time: 1 million objects with custom loop might take hours, Batch Operations: minutes (parallel Lambda invocations).<br>

1010. [ S3 ] A developer accidentally ran `aws s3 rb s3://critical-prod-bucket --force` which deleted the bucket AND all its contents. The bucket had versioning enabled but no Object Lock. How do you attempt data recovery? ; Versioning does not protect against bucket deletion — `rb --force` deletes all objects (all versions) then deletes the bucket. Once deleted: data is gone. Recovery options: (1) Check if Replication to another bucket existed — CRR/SRR destination bucket may have copies. (2) Check AWS Backup if bucket was protected (S3 Backup Policy). (3) Check if any snapshots or exports exist. If none: contact AWS Support — possible only within a very short window and not guaranteed. <br><br> *Versioning misconception: versioning protects against object-level deletes (creates delete markers). It does NOT protect against `DeleteBucket` API — which requires all objects and versions to be deleted first. `rb --force` in CLI: iterates all versions, deletes all, then deletes bucket. Irreversible without backup.<br> *Object Lock protection: Object Lock prevents object deletion/modification. A bucket with Object Lock + Compliance mode: `rb --force` will FAIL on every locked object (can't delete during retention period). Bucket cannot be deleted until all objects' retention periods expire. Object Lock is the correct protection for critical data — not just versioning alone.<br> *Prevention: (1) SCP: `"Deny": "s3:DeleteBucket"` for production accounts. (2) Tag-based: `"Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:ResourceTag/Environment": "prod"}}` prevents deleting prod-tagged buckets. (3) Object Lock on all objects. (4) CRR to separate account (cross-account delete of destination is separate action). (5) AWS Backup S3 policy with vault lock. Lesson: bucket-level deletion requires belt-and-suspenders protection — versioning alone is insufficient.<br>


1011. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 cross-region replication from us-east-1 to eu-central-1. A compliance requirement mandates that data written in the EU region must never leave the EU. Some of their applications write to the us-east-1 bucket. How do you redesign the architecture? ; Stop bidirectional replication (or never enable SRR to send EU-written data back to US). Separate EU data: write directly to eu-central-1 bucket (no US replication of EU-origin data). Use S3 Multi-Region Access Point (MRAP) with failover routing: MRAP routes EU-origin writes to eu-central-1, US-origin writes to us-east-1. Data stays in originating region unless explicitly replicated. <br><br> *MRAP routing: MRAP uses AWS Anycast IP to route requests to the nearest bucket. EU applications connecting to MRAP endpoint: requests routed to eu-central-1 bucket. US applications: routed to us-east-1. No cross-region data movement for writes (MRAP routes, not replicates). Set up MRAP with eu-central-1 and us-east-1 buckets, but configure replication ONLY as us-east-1 → eu-central-1 (not the reverse).<br> *Data residency enforcement: S3 bucket policy condition `"aws:RequestedRegion": "eu-central-1"` ensures only requests to the EU bucket endpoint are allowed. But applications must specifically target the EU endpoint — MRAP automatic routing is more foolproof for data residency enforcement. SCP: `"Deny": "s3:PutObject"` on eu-central-1 bucket from non-EU IAM principals (using IP or VPC endpoint conditions).<br> *GDPR data residency: AWS guarantees data stored in an S3 bucket stays in that region (AWS data residency commitment). Cross-region replication is always explicit opt-in — enabling CRR from EU → US is a deliberate act. With MRAP: architects control replication direction. Compliance evidence: CRR configuration shows one-way replication only (US → EU), no reverse replication enabled.<br>

1012. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 to store application logs. Logs are written every second by thousands of instances. After 1 year, they have 500 billion log objects. Simple queries (find all ERROR logs in the last hour) take 10+ minutes via Athena. The data is in JSON format with 50 fields per log entry. How do you optimize for fast log queries? ; Convert JSON to Parquet (columnar + compressed) with partitioning by `year/month/day/hour`. Compact log files: use Kinesis Data Firehose (buffers 128 MB or 5 minutes) to write one Parquet file per hour per instance group instead of individual per-second JSON files. Query `WHERE year=2025 AND month=01 AND day=15 AND hour=14 AND level='ERROR'` scans only the last hour's Parquet files (2 fields out of 50). <br><br> *File count problem: 1 per second × 1,000 instances × 31,536,000 seconds/year = 31.5 trillion files! Even 1 per minute = 525 billion files. List/open overhead makes Athena unusable. Firehose batching: 1 file per buffer period per shard. 1,000 instances → 1,000 Firehose streams → 1 file per 5 minutes per stream = 12 files/hour/stream × 1,000 = 12,000 files/hour. Then Glue compaction: 12,000 → 1 Parquet file per hour. Query: list 1 file, not 31 billion.<br> *Parquet columnar benefit: `level` field is the 3rd of 50 fields. Parquet reads only the `level` column (2% of data). Snappy compression: 10:1 typical for logs. Combined: 50 columns × 10 compression × partitioning (only last hour) = 500× scan reduction for this query pattern.<br> *OpenSearch Service alternative: stream logs to Amazon OpenSearch via Kinesis → OpenSearch ingestion. OpenSearch inverted index: `level:ERROR` queries in milliseconds regardless of volume. Full-text search, time-series dashboards (Kibana/OpenSearch Dashboards). Tradeoff: OpenSearch costs more than S3+Athena but provides real-time indexing and sub-second queries. For operational log search (last hour): OpenSearch. For historical batch analytics (last year trend): S3+Athena+Parquet.<br>

1013. [ S3 ] A company stores sensitive customer PII in S3. They want to allow data scientists to run queries on the data without ever seeing the raw PII values. The data scientists use Athena. How do you implement this? ; S3 Object Lambda: data scientists' Athena queries go through Object Lambda Access Point. Lambda function intercepts the GetObject, applies PII masking (tokenize SSNs, hash emails, mask credit cards) before returning the response. Data scientist sees `XXX-XX-XXXX` for SSN, `a3b9c2...` for email. Original S3 data unchanged. Or: Lake Formation column-level security (mask specific columns) + row-level security (data scientists see only their region's data). <br><br> *Object Lambda architecture: Standard S3 bucket (raw PII) → Object Lambda Access Point (with Lambda function) → Data Scientist's Athena table points to OL Access Point ARN (not bucket ARN directly). Lambda function code: reads original bytes, applies regex masking (`re.sub(r'\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}', 'XXX-XX-XXXX', text)`), returns masked bytes. Completely transparent to Athena — it just gets masked data.<br> *Lake Formation approach: register S3 location with Glue catalog. Define column security: SSN column masked for `data_scientists` group (shows as `null` or tokenized). Row-level filter: `region = current_user_region`. Grant SELECT on masked view to data scientists. Lake Formation enforces on every Athena query — can't bypass by querying S3 directly (data scientists don't have direct S3 GetObject permission, only Athena + Lake Formation execution role).<br> *Amazon Macie integration: Macie scans S3 for PII (SSNs, credit cards, email addresses), reports findings. Combined with Object Lambda: Macie identifies which columns have PII → inform Object Lambda masking rules → data scientists query safely. Audit: CloudTrail records every Athena query (who queried, when, what).<br>

1014. [ S3 ] A gaming company serves downloadable game assets (500 MB – 5 GB files) globally. They need to minimize infrastructure and maximize download speed. Bandwidth costs are significant. How do you design the distribution architecture? ; CloudFront with S3 origin + CloudFront's optimized pricing for large file downloads. Use CloudFront Origin Shield to reduce S3 origin load. Enable compression where applicable (text assets). Price Class 200 or All to serve APAC/EU. For massive files: BitTorrent protocol support (S3 supports S3 BitTorrent URLs for objects up to 5 GB — distribute load to peers). <br><br> *S3 BitTorrent: unique S3 feature. Add `?torrent` to any public S3 object URL to get a .torrent file. Clients download via BitTorrent protocol — distribute bandwidth across peers. Reduces S3+CloudFront bandwidth costs for viral/popular files (peers serve each other). Not widely used but exam-relevant. Only for public objects. Objects must be < 5 GB for BitTorrent (S3 limitation).<br> *CloudFront for gaming: Origin Shield in the region closest to the S3 bucket reduces origin fetches. Cache key: game version + region (different cache per game patch). S3 Transfer Acceleration is for UPLOADS, not downloads — do not use TA for asset distribution. CloudFront presigned URLs: game launcher generates presigned CloudFront URL (not S3 directly) for authenticated downloads (purchased DLC, etc.).<br> *Cost optimization: CloudFront DTO: $0.0085/GB (US/EU) vs S3 direct DTO: $0.09/GB. 10× cheaper through CloudFront for repeated access. For viral game launches (same asset downloaded millions of times): CloudFront caches at edge → most downloads served from edge, not S3 origin. S3 origin bandwidth (transfer to CloudFront): $0.02/GB within AWS (much cheaper than public DTO). CloudFront + S3 origin Shield = minimal S3 reads (cached at origin shield) + cheap CloudFront DTO.<br>

1015. [ S3 ] A fintech company wants to ensure that all API calls and object operations against their S3 buckets are logged with 100% fidelity — no lost log entries. Standard CloudTrail logging could have slight delays or delivery gaps. How do they achieve complete audit trail coverage? ; Enable CloudTrail with S3 data events on all buckets. Enable S3 server access logging as a secondary audit source (S3 SAL is best-effort but covers S3-side HTTP logs). Deliver CloudTrail to a separate dedicated logging account (prevents deletion from source account). Enable CloudTrail log file validation (SHA-256 hash chain). CloudWatch Logs real-time stream for alerting. No single mechanism is 100% guaranteed but CloudTrail with log file validation + dedicated account is the regulatory standard. <br><br> *CloudTrail log file validation: each log file has an SHA-256 hash. CloudTrail creates a digest file every hour with hashes of all log files delivered in that hour. Digest files are signed with a public/private key pair. `aws cloudtrail validate-logs --trail-arn ARN --start-time DATETIME` verifies chain of custody — any tampered or deleted log file fails validation. This is the "100% fidelity" evidence for auditors.<br> *S3 server access logs complement: SAL is HTTP-level logging on S3 infrastructure. Some operations visible in SAL may not be in CloudTrail (very rare). Combined: CloudTrail (API-level, signed) + SAL (HTTP-level, best-effort) = comprehensive coverage. SAL latency: delivered within a few hours. SAL not guaranteed (possible gaps under load). For legal/compliance: CloudTrail with validation is the primary record.<br> *Dedicated logging account: CloudTrail logs written to S3 bucket in logging account. Source account has `s3:PutObject` only (no ListBucket, GetObject, DeleteObject). Even if source account is compromised: attacker can't delete existing log files. Cross-account CloudTrail delivery is the security-conscious standard for regulated industries (PCI DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP all require this pattern).<br>

1016. [ S3 ] A company's S3 bucket policy previously had `s3:PutBucketPolicy` granted to a team. That team accidentally created a policy that blocks all access including the bucket owner's admin account. How do you fix this? ; Use the AWS account root user (not an IAM role or user) to call `aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket NAME --policy FILE` or `aws s3api delete-bucket-policy`. The root user bypasses all resource-based policies — bucket policies cannot block root account actions. Root credentials exist in every AWS account and cannot be restricted by bucket policies or SCPs (only by the root account itself). <br><br> *Root user exception: an S3 bucket policy `"Deny": "*"` blocks all IAM principals, but NOT the root user of the bucket-owner account (they are the same entity — the account itself). This is a special S3 exception: the bucket owner (account root) always retains the ability to modify the bucket policy. This prevents permanent self-lockout scenarios.<br> *SCP consideration: SCPs CAN restrict root user IAM actions. But for S3 bucket policy management: SCPs apply to IAM actions via AWS Organizations. The root account's S3 bucket management is not blocked by SCPs in the same account (SCPs restrict the account's principals' interactions with management APIs, but the account's root user is the account itself). This is a subtle distinction.<br> *Prevention: (1) Never grant `s3:PutBucketPolicy` without restrictive permission boundaries. (2) Enable AWS Config rule `s3-bucket-policy-not-more-permissive`. (3) Use IAM policy conditions to prevent policies that include Deny for the admin role. (4) Test bucket policy changes in a separate bucket before applying to production. (5) MFA Delete + Object Lock do NOT protect bucket policies — only the root user exception prevents permanent lockout.<br>

1017. [ S3 ] A company processes genomic research data. Each genomic sequencing file is 500 GB. They need to find 50-byte gene sequences within these files without downloading the entire 500 GB files. How do you design this query pattern? ; S3 Select with byte-range targeting is not applicable for searching arbitrary patterns within binary files. For genomic FASTQ/BAM files: AWS HealthLake or custom indexing. Alternative: S3 Select on CSV/JSON representations if data is converted. For exact byte-range known positions: byte-range fetch. For genomic search: build an index (Bloom filter or position index) stored in a separate S3 object, download the small index, identify byte ranges, fetch specific ranges. <br><br> *Byte-range fetch for genomic: BAM files (binary alignment format) are block-compressed with index files (BAI). The BAI index maps genomic coordinates → byte ranges in the BAM file. Workflow: (1) Download the 10 KB BAI index file. (2) Query index for target gene coordinate → returns byte range [offset, offset+N]. (3) Byte-range fetch only that range from 500 GB BAM. (4) Parse the returned bytes for the gene sequence. This is how GATK/IGV access genomic data from S3.<br> *S3 Select limitation: works on CSV, JSON, and Parquet formats only. Not for binary genomic formats (FASTQ, BAM, VCF). For structured genomic data (VCF variant calls in compressed CSV format): S3 Select can filter by chromosome, position, variant type. For raw FASTQ reads: no S3 Select support — need specialized tools.<br> *AWS HealthOmics: purpose-built genomic data service. Import FASTQ/BAM/VCF. Query at scale across thousands of sequencing runs. S3-compatible API but with genomic-aware query optimization. For production genomic workloads: HealthOmics rather than raw S3. For the exam: byte-range fetch + index pattern is the S3-native approach.<br>

1018. [ S3 ] A company wants to allow contractors to upload files to a specific S3 prefix but prevent them from listing or downloading files (write-only access). How do you configure this? ; Bucket policy: Allow `s3:PutObject` for contractor IAM role on `arn:aws:s3:::bucket/contractor-uploads/*`. Explicitly Deny `s3:GetObject`, `s3:ListBucket`, `s3:DeleteObject`, `s3:GetObjectVersion`. Deny ALL other S3 actions (allowlist approach). Result: contractors can upload files to their prefix but cannot see what else is in the bucket or download anything. <br><br> *Write-only bucket policy: `{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/Contractor"}, "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::bucket/contractor-uploads/*"}` + `{"Effect": "Deny", "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/Contractor"}, "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*"]}`. The Deny is broader than Allow — belt-and-suspenders approach.<br> *S3 write-only use case: security camera feeds (cameras can upload footage but can't access other cameras' footage), contractor file submission (submit invoices but not see others' invoices), IoT sensor data (device can PUT telemetry but not read historical data). Common pattern for data collection where submitters shouldn't see other submissions.<br> *Presigned URL for write-only: generate PutObject presigned URL on server side (5 min expiry). Contractor gets a URL to PUT their specific file. No AWS credentials required. No ability to list (presigned URL is for one specific key only). Better for external contractors without AWS accounts. But: new presigned URL needed for each upload. Automate with an API Gateway endpoint that generates presigned URLs after authentication.<br>

1019. [ S3 ] A company stores customer video files. Customers pay for different service tiers: Basic (360p), Premium (1080p), Enterprise (4K). The same original 4K video is stored once in S3. How do you serve different resolutions to different customer tiers without storing multiple copies? ; S3 Object Lambda: one Lambda function intercepts the GetObject request. Lambda reads the customer's tier from a JWT token in the request context. If Basic: Lambda calls MediaConvert or ffmpeg layer to transcode to 360p on-the-fly, returns 360p bytes. Or: pre-transcode to 3 resolutions stored in separate prefixes (360p/, 1080p/, 4k/). Object Lambda is better for on-demand access-tier control without pre-generating all formats. <br><br> *Object Lambda + tier control: Lambda function code checks `x-amz-meta-tier` header or JWT claims (passed via Lambda URL or API Gateway). Determines which resolution transformation to apply. Returns appropriate video quality. The customer cannot directly GET the 4K S3 object — they only have access to the Object Lambda Access Point ARN. Object Lambda Access Point has Lambda-enforced tier logic.<br> *Pre-transcoded approach (more practical for video at scale): MediaConvert job triggered on upload (EventBridge → Lambda → MediaConvert). Generates 360p, 1080p, 4K versions. Stored in tier-prefixed paths. Access Point per tier: Basic tier Access Point has GetObject only on `360p/` prefix. Object Lambda adds flexibility but video transcoding is expensive per-request — pre-transcoding is more cost-efficient for video.<br> *CloudFront Lambda@Edge for tier enforcement: CloudFront distribution with Lambda@Edge on viewer request. Lambda@Edge checks JWT tier claim → modifies origin path to point to tier-appropriate S3 prefix. CloudFront caches each version at edge. Premium customers get 1080p cached response, Basic get 360p cached response. Cache hit rate maximized per tier. Production video streaming architecture.<br>

1020. [ S3 ] A company migrated its data warehouse to a data lake on S3 with Athena. They had 200 ETL jobs that used JDBC to connect to the old database. Now they need to run the same SQL queries against S3 data. The queries use window functions, CTEs, and complex JOINs — will Athena support this? ; Athena supports ANSI SQL including window functions (OVER/PARTITION BY/ROW_NUMBER), CTEs (WITH clause), and complex JOINs (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, CROSS JOIN). Athena is powered by Trino (formerly PrestoSQL). Most standard SQL from relational databases works in Athena. Exceptions: stored procedures, triggers, DDL mutations (UPDATE/DELETE on Parquet — use Iceberg tables for DML), and some database-specific functions. <br><br> *Athena DML limitations: Athena is primarily read-only for non-Iceberg tables. No UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT INTO (existing tables). Use Athena Apache Iceberg tables for ACID transactions, UPDATE/DELETE operations. For the migrated ETL jobs that were INSERT-based (writing results): CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) or INSERT INTO Iceberg tables.<br> *JDBC to Athena: AWS provides Athena JDBC/ODBC drivers. Replace old DB JDBC connection string with Athena JDBC: `jdbc:awsathena://athena.REGION.amazonaws.com:443?s3_staging_dir=s3://BUCKET/staging&user=ACCESS_KEY&password=SECRET_KEY`. For 200 ETL jobs: just update the connection string and credentials — SQL queries work as-is (if ANSI-standard).<br> *Performance vs RDBMS: for complex JOINs on large datasets: Athena is faster than most relational DBs (massively parallel). But for small datasets with many JOINs: per-query startup cost ($0.005/query minimum + ~2 sec cold start). 200 ETL jobs × $0.005 = $1/day if each runs once daily. Athena is cost-effective vs traditional ETL database licensing.<br>

1021. [ S3 ] A company is building a data marketplace where sellers list datasets and buyers purchase access. When a buyer purchases a dataset, they get read access for 30 days. There are 10,000 sellers and 100,000 buyers. How do you manage access at this scale? ; S3 Access Grants: designed for vending temporary S3 access at scale. Register S3 locations (seller datasets) in Access Grants. When buyer purchases: call Access Grants API to create a grant (`CreateAccessGrant`) for the buyer's IAM/SSO identity on the specific location. Grant expires in 30 days. Buyer calls `GetDataAccess` to get temporary credentials scoped to their purchased dataset. Revoke via `DeleteAccessGrant`. <br><br> *Access Grants vs Access Points: Access Points: static, long-lived policies. Need one Access Point per buyer-seller combination: 10,000 × 100,000 = 1 billion Access Points. Not scalable. Access Grants: dynamic grants created/deleted programmatically via API. One S3 location registration per seller dataset. Grants created per purchase event. Designed for exactly this data marketplace pattern.<br> *Access Grants API workflow: (1) Seller registers dataset location: `CreateAccessGrantsLocation` for `s3://marketplace-bucket/sellers/SELLER_ID/`. (2) Buyer purchases: backend calls `CreateAccessGrant` with `grantee=BuyerIdentity, permissions=READ, accessGrantsLocationId=SELLER_LOCATION_ID, accessGrantsLocationConfiguration.s3SubPrefix=/DATASET_ID/`. (3) Buyer calls `GetDataAccess` with their identity → receives temporary STS credentials scoped to the exact purchased dataset. (4) After 30 days: grant expiry auto-revokes (or backend calls `DeleteAccessGrant`).<br> *Integration with IAM Identity Center: Access Grants natively integrates with IAM Identity Center (SSO). Buyers authenticated via SSO → Access Grants maps SSO identity to grant → `GetDataAccess` returns credentials. No IAM user management needed for 100,000 buyers. Enterprise SSO (Okta, Azure AD) → IAM Identity Center → S3 Access Grants. Production-scale identity-driven S3 access control.<br>

1022. [ S3 ] A company's application uploads files to S3 and immediately calls GetObject to process them. Sometimes the GetObject returns a 404 error immediately after a successful PutObject. How is this possible and how do you fix it? ; This should NOT happen with modern S3 (since December 2020: strong read-after-write consistency). If this is happening: the application is using a stale cached response from an old ListObjects result that showed the key not existing. Or: the GetObject is against a DIFFERENT bucket/region endpoint. Or: there is a conditional read (If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since) that returns 304/404 based on cache state. Application logic error, not an S3 consistency issue. <br><br> *S3 consistency history: before Dec 2020, S3 had eventual consistency for: (1) new object PutObject → immediate GetObject (rare 404). (2) ListObjects after PutObject (new key might not appear). (3) GetObject after PutObject → might serve old version. Since Dec 2020: all operations are strongly consistent. No more eventual consistency. No eventual consistency workarounds (sleep, retry loops, polling for object existence) are needed for code written after 2020.<br> *Possible causes for 404 after PUT in modern S3: (1) Client-side caching: HTTP client caches a 404 from a previous GET and returns cached 404 without hitting S3. Clear HTTP cache. (2) Wrong bucket: application writes to prod-bucket but reads from staging-bucket (config bug). (3) Pre-signed URL expiry: pre-signed GET URL for an object that doesn't exist yet (URL generated before upload completes). (4) Cross-account: PutObject succeeds in account A bucket, GetObject tries account B (same bucket name, different account — both exist). <br> *Fix: enable debug logging in the S3 SDK client to see actual HTTP requests. Verify bucket name and region in both PutObject and GetObject calls. Remove any sleep/retry workarounds written for pre-2020 eventual consistency — they're unnecessary noise. Add assertion: after PutObject, verify response contains `ETag` (not empty) before calling GetObject.<br>

1023. [ S3 ] A large company has hundreds of S3 buckets. A security audit requires them to block public access organization-wide without modifying each bucket individually. How? ; AWS Organizations + Account-level S3 Block Public Access (BPA): enable BPA at the account level (not bucket level). Account-level BPA setting applies to ALL buckets in that account. Use S3 Block Public Access console, AWS Config, or Terraform to set account-level BPA in all accounts. For Organizations: use AWS Config with `s3-account-level-public-access-blocks-periodic` managed rule + auto-remediation. Or use SCP to deny `s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock` with `BlockPublicAcls=false`. <br><br> *Account-level BPA: `aws s3control put-public-access-block --account-id ACCOUNT_ID --public-access-block-configuration "BlockPublicAcls=true, IgnorePublicAcls=true, BlockPublicPolicy=true, RestrictPublicBuckets=true"`. Applies to ALL current and future buckets in the account. Individual bucket BPA settings can still be stricter (enable) but not more permissive (cannot disable account-level BPA at bucket level).<br> *AWS Config auto-remediation: Config rule `s3-account-level-public-access-blocks-periodic` evaluates account-level BPA. Non-compliant: remediation action calls `s3control:PutPublicAccessBlock` to enable BPA. Deploy via CloudFormation StackSet to all accounts in the organization. Full coverage in one deployment.<br> *SCP prevention: `"Deny": "s3:PutPublicAccessBlock"` if block settings would be false. Prevents admins from disabling BPA across accounts. Combine with Config remediation: even if someone disables BPA manually (SCP may not cover all scenarios), Config auto-remediates within minutes. Defense in depth for public access prevention.<br>

1024. [ S3 ] A company stores sensitive financial data in S3 encrypted with SSE-KMS. They use a single KMS key (aws/s3 default key) for all buckets. The security team says this violates their key management policy which requires separate keys per data classification level. How do you migrate? ; Create new CMKs: one per classification level (Confidential, Internal, Public). Use S3 Batch Operations CopyObject with new SSE-KMS key ARN: copies each object to same bucket with new encryption key. Original object replaced with re-encrypted copy. Apply bucket default encryption policy (new CMK). Add bucket policy enforcement: Deny PutObject unless SSE-KMS with specific CMK ARN. <br><br> *Batch Operations re-encryption: `CopyObject` action with `SSE-KMS` server-side encryption using new CMK ARN. Copies object in-place (same bucket, same key name). In S3: a copy to the same bucket with new encryption = re-encryption. Old encrypted bytes replaced. The copy operation reads with old key, writes with new key atomically from S3's perspective. IAM requires both: `kms:Decrypt` on old key + `kms:GenerateDataKey` on new key.<br> *aws/s3 default key risk: AWS-managed key, rotated automatically by AWS, shared across all S3 operations in the account. No ability to set key policy (AWS controls). Cannot disable without affecting all objects using it. No KMS CloudTrail visibility per-object. Cannot share key with cross-account principals. Customer-managed CMK: full key policy control, cross-account sharing, independent disable/rotation, dedicated CloudTrail.<br> *Enforce post-migration: bucket policy `"Deny": "s3:PutObject" unless "aws:kms" AND "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:ACCOUNT:key/SPECIFIC-KEY-ID"`. Ensures no future objects accidentally use the wrong key. Separate policies per bucket (different CMK per classification bucket).<br>

1025. [ S3 ] A company is using AWS Lake Formation to manage a data lake on S3. A data scientist complains they can see tables in Glue catalog but Athena queries fail with access denied. What are the likely causes? ; Lake Formation decouples Glue catalog visibility from data access. Users with Glue:GetTable can see tables but need explicit Lake Formation `SELECT` permission on the table to query. Grant Lake Formation `SELECT` on the specific table (or column subset) to the data scientist's IAM principal. Also: the data scientist's IAM execution role needs S3 GetObject on the underlying S3 location (or Lake Formation uses its own service role that the data scientist assumes). <br><br> *Lake Formation permission model: two layers. (1) IAM permissions: `glue:GetTable` (see table metadata), `lakeformation:GetDataAccess` (execute query). (2) Lake Formation grants: `SELECT` on table/columns for the specific principal. BOTH required. Seeing the table in Glue (via Glue:GetTable) is separate from querying data in S3 (via Lake Formation SELECT grant). Many engineers confuse Glue catalog visibility with data access.<br> *Athena execution with Lake Formation: Athena queries use the user's IAM role (or an Athena workgroup service role). That role needs: IAM `s3:GetObject` on S3 location → Lake Formation overrides this if Lake Formation is managing the location (Lake Formation registered the S3 path). With Lake Formation: the user needs Lake Formation SELECT grant + IAM `lakeformation:GetDataAccess`. S3 permissions are delegated to the Lake Formation service role.<br> *Troubleshooting: `aws lakeformation list-permissions --resource '{"Table": {"DatabaseName": "mydb", "Name": "mytable"}}'` → check if data scientist's principal has SELECT. `aws lakeformation get-data-lake-settings` → verify the account is using Lake Formation (vs not). Check Athena workgroup IAM role: does it have `lakeformation:GetDataAccess`? Common mistake: configure Lake Formation but forget to add the Athena workgroup role to Lake Formation admin or grant it permissions.<br>

1026. [ S3 ] A company runs batch analytics jobs overnight that read from S3. During peak business hours (9am-6pm), S3 API costs spike because of analytics workflows accidentally running during business hours, conflicting with production workloads. How do you limit S3 API access to certain time windows? ; IAM policy with time-based condition: `"Condition": {"DateGreaterThan": {"aws:CurrentTime": "T18:00:00Z"}, "DateLessThan": {"aws:CurrentTime": "T06:00:00Z"}}` on the analytics IAM role. Role can only call S3 APIs between 6pm and 6am UTC. SCP at organization level for the analytics account. Or: EventBridge Scheduler disables the analytics service role during business hours (attach/detach deny policy). <br><br> *Time-based IAM condition: `aws:CurrentTime` condition key. `"Deny": "s3:*"` condition: `{"DateGreaterThanEquals": {"aws:CurrentTime": "2025-01-01T09:00:00Z"}, "DateLessThanEquals": {"aws:CurrentTime": "2025-01-01T18:00:00Z"}}` — blocks 9-6pm on a specific date. For recurring daily: use `aws:CurrentTime` with ISO 8601 time-of-day (not supported directly). Use Lambda-attached inline policy modification or Service Control Policy at account level.<br> *Lambda policy attach/detach: EventBridge rule fires at 9 AM → Lambda attaches DenyS3 policy to analytics role. EventBridge fires at 6 PM → Lambda detaches DenyS3 policy. Simple, reliable. Uses `iam:AttachRolePolicy` and `iam:DetachRolePolicy`. Analytics jobs launched outside window will fail as expected.<br> *Better architecture: don't let analytics jobs run during business hours. Use AWS Batch or Step Functions with schedule: `cron(0 18 * * ? *)` (6pm UTC start). Analytics job queue: SQS FIFO. Business hours: processing paused. 6pm: consume from queue. Production isolation via scheduling, not IAM restriction. IAM restriction is belt-and-suspenders.<br>

1027. [ S3 ] A healthcare company needs to build a data sharing platform where partner hospitals can submit patient records but each hospital must only see their own submissions. Hospitals use their own AWS accounts. There are 500 partner hospitals. Design the S3 architecture. ; One S3 bucket per hospital (prefix: `hospital-ID/`) or one bucket with per-hospital prefixes + S3 Access Points. Each hospital gets an Access Point scoped to only their prefix. Hospital's IAM role (cross-account) can only access their Access Point. S3 Access Grants for dynamic access management. Bucket policy: delegate all access decisions to Access Points. <br><br> *Cross-account Access Point: bucket in healthcare company account. Access Point created for Hospital-A with policy: `{"Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::HOSPITAL_A_ACCOUNT:root"}, "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:HEALTHCARE_ACCOUNT:accesspoint/hospital-a-ap/object/*"}`. Hospital A's AWS account's principals get access to hospital-a-ap Access Point only. <br> *HIPAA compliance requirements: SSE-KMS encryption (customer-managed key per hospital: if hospital A's data should be inaccessible to others even if S3 access control fails). KMS key per hospital in healthcare account → hospital A's cross-account role has `kms:Decrypt` permission on hospital-A-key only. BAA (Business Associate Agreement) with AWS required. VPC Endpoints: hospitals access S3 via Direct Connect + VPC Endpoint (no data over public internet). CloudTrail data events: log all PutObject/GetObject for HIPAA audit trail.<br> *Scale to 500 hospitals: Access Points (one per hospital): 500 Access Points. Well within S3 limits (1,000 Access Points per bucket). Or S3 Access Grants: register one S3 location per hospital prefix. Create grants dynamically per hospital account. Scales to thousands with same pattern. Access Grants is better for large scale — doesn't hit Access Point limits.<br>

1028. [ S3 ] A company has a multi-account AWS Organizations setup. The security team in the master account wants to ensure that all S3 buckets across all member accounts write access logs to a centralized logging bucket in the security account. How do you enforce this? ; SCP: Deny `s3:PutBucketLogging` unless target bucket is the central logging bucket ARN. But SCP cannot check the content of PutBucketLogging request parameters in standard SCPs. Instead: AWS Config managed rule `s3-bucket-logging-enabled` + custom Config rule that checks the logging target bucket = central logging bucket ARN. Auto-remediate: Lambda calls PutBucketLogging on non-compliant buckets, redirecting logs to the central bucket. <br><br> *Challenge: SCPs control which API calls are allowed but not the specific parameters within the call (parameter-level conditions are limited to resource tags, some specific condition keys). `s3:PutBucketLogging` doesn't have a condition key for the target bucket. Config with custom Lambda is the practical solution.<br> *Config custom rule (Lambda): `def evaluate_compliance(configuration_item): target = configuration_item['configuration']['loggingEnabled']['targetBucket'], return 'COMPLIANT' if target == 'CENTRAL-LOG-BUCKET-ARN' else 'NON_COMPLIANT'`. Auto-remediation: SSM Automation document calls `aws s3api put-bucket-logging` for non-compliant buckets.<br> *CloudFormation StackSets alternative: deploy a CloudFormation stack to all accounts that creates a Config rule + remediation Lambda. StackSet operates automatically when new accounts are added to the OU. Ensures new accounts get the Config rule automatically via StackSet auto-deployment. Ongoing compliance: Config evaluates every time a bucket's logging config changes.<br>

1029. [ S3 ] A company uses Terraform to manage S3 bucket configurations. During a deployment, Terraform reported "Error: error modifying S3 Bucket policy: MalformedPolicy: Principal in a policy cannot be a wildcard." This error occurred when trying to update a resource policy. What does this mean and how do you fix? ; The error means the bucket policy contains `"Principal": "*"` in an Allow statement without a proper condition. S3 resource-based policy allows wildcard principal with an Allow, but the policy is malformed in some other way. Actually, the exact error `MalformedPolicy: Principal in a policy cannot be a wildcard` occurs in IAM policies (not S3 bucket policies) — S3 bucket policies allow `"Principal": "*"`. Check if the policy is being applied to an IAM entity rather than an S3 bucket. <br><br> *IAM vs S3 policy distinction: IAM identity policies CANNOT have Principal element. IAM resource-based policies (trust policies for roles) CAN have Principal but cannot use `"*"` in some contexts. S3 bucket policies CAN have `"Principal": "*"` (public access). If Terraform is applying a bucket-policy-style JSON to an IAM policy resource: this error appears. Verify the Terraform resource type: `aws_s3_bucket_policy` vs `aws_iam_policy`.<br> *Common Terraform mistakes: using `aws_iam_policy` instead of `aws_s3_bucket_policy`. JSON template with Principal element applied to `aws_iam_role_policy`. Fix: use `aws_s3_bucket_policy` resource, not `aws_iam_policy`. Or: if this is a trust policy (role), the Principal must be a specific ARN, not `"*"` (trust policies restrict `"*"` Principal — highly insecure).<br> *S3 bucket policy validation: `aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket NAME --output text` to see current policy. `aws iam simulate-resource-policy` to test policy evaluation before applying. Terraform: use `jsonencode()` or heredoc for policy JSON — avoid escaping issues that create malformed JSON. Run `terraform plan` and inspect policy output before `apply`.<br>

1030. [ S3 ] A company's application generates user-specific reports stored in S3 as `reports/USER_ID/REPORT_ID.pdf`. There are 10 million users. Users should only access their own reports. Each user authenticates via Cognito. What is the most scalable approach? ; Cognito Identity Pool with IAM role mapping: user authenticates with Cognito User Pool → Cognito Identity Pool vends temporary IAM credentials with a role that has an IAM policy using `${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}` variable. Policy: `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/reports/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/*"`. User gets credentials that only allow access to their own prefix — no infrastructure changes needed per user. <br><br> *IAM policy variable: `${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}` is replaced at runtime with the authenticated user's Cognito Identity ID. For user `us-east-1:abc123`: resource becomes `reports-bucket/reports/us-east-1:abc123/*`. This user's IAM session can only access their prefix. GetObject on another user's prefix returns AccessDenied. Zero per-user configuration — policy variable is the magic.<br> *Cognito Identity Pool role mapping: authenticated users assume "authenticated" role. IAM role trust policy: `"Principal": {"Federated": "cognito-identity.amazonaws.com"}, "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud": "IDENTITY_POOL_ID"}}`. All 10 million users share ONE IAM role — but each session is scoped to their prefix via the policy variable. Massively scalable — no per-user IAM resources needed.<br> *Alternative for complex auth: API Gateway + Lambda + presigned URL. Cognito auth at API Gateway. Lambda validates user's Cognito token → generates presigned GetObject URL for the user's specific report → returns presigned URL. User downloads report via presigned URL directly from S3. Lambda-based: more code but allows additional authorization logic (check payment status, report access expiry) before vending the presigned URL.<br>

1031. [ S3 ] A company stores build artifacts in S3. Artifacts are referenced by Jenkins CI pipelines by their S3 URL. A developer accidentally deleted 3 months of artifacts that other pipelines depend on. Versioning was enabled. How do you restore them and how do you prevent this from happening again? ; Restore: S3 versioning preserves deleted objects as delete markers. List all delete markers added in the deletion window: `aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket artifacts --prefix builds/ --query 'DeleteMarkers[?LastModified>="2024-10-01"]'`. Delete those delete markers to restore previous versions. Batch Operations for scale. Prevention: SCP Deny `s3:DeleteObject` + `s3:DeleteObjects` for the artifacts bucket ARN (except via a specific break-glass role). Object Lock Governance mode on artifact objects. <br><br> *Bulk delete marker removal: S3 Batch Operations with `DeleteObject` action targeting the delete marker versions. Manifest: S3 Inventory filtered for `IsDeleteMarker=true` from the deletion date. Job runs in minutes for thousands of objects. Manual aws CLI for small batches: `aws s3api delete-object --version-id DELETE_MARKER_VERSION_ID`.<br> *Immutable artifact pattern: build artifacts once, never modify or delete. Object Lock Governance mode: `--object-lock-mode GOVERNANCE --object-lock-retain-until-date 2026-01-01`. Governance mode allows admin bypass (with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention`) for legitimate deletions (cost management, security). Compliance mode for strict WORM. Artifacts are typically well-suited for Governance mode.<br> *Jenkins artifact management: configure Jenkins to use artifact promotion (copy from `builds/staging/` to `builds/stable/` when tests pass). Never delete from stable. Separate lifecycle: builds/staging: expire after 30 days. builds/stable: Object Lock Governance for 1 year. Auto-generated deletion using Jenkins would require the break-glass role, preventing accidental `aws s3 rm --recursive` from a developer's credentials.<br>

1032. [ S3 ] An organization uses multiple AWS accounts. Development teams in each account frequently need to share datasets for collaboration. Currently they manually copy files between buckets, leading to data inconsistency. How do you design a scalable data sharing solution? ; S3 Access Grants (centralized data catalog account) or AWS Data Exchange (for formal data sharing). Practical approach: central data sharing account with S3 buckets. Teams register their datasets as S3 locations. Consumer teams get access grants. No copying — consumer reads directly from producer's bucket via cross-account access grant. Or: S3 Replication rules with event notifications. <br><br> *No-copy data sharing: cross-account bucket policy + IAM role allows consumer account to read producer's S3 bucket directly. Producer bucket policy: `"Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::CONSUMER_ACCOUNT:root"}, "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"]`. Consumer IAM role: `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::producer-bucket/*"`. Consumer reads directly from source — always up-to-date, no sync lag, no storage duplication cost.<br> *AWS Lake Formation cross-account sharing: for Glue catalog tables (data lake pattern). Producer account shares table via Lake Formation. Consumer account accepts share. Consumer's Athena can query producer's data directly. Lake Formation handles permissions — no manual bucket policy management. Column-level security: consumer sees only specific columns. Best for structured data lake sharing.<br> *AWS Data Exchange: formal catalog of AWS-hosted datasets. For teams that want to share data as a product (with versioning, data quality metadata, usage analytics). Producers publish datasets. Consumers subscribe. EventBridge integration: consumer gets notified of new data. Best for formalized data marketplace patterns within org.<br>

1033. [ S3 ] A company's security team detected that S3 objects with `Content-Type: text/html` are being served from their S3 static website, allowing XSS attacks when objects are directly accessed. How do you mitigate? ; Switch from S3 static website hosting to CloudFront + S3 (OAC). Configure CloudFront to add security headers: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000`. Use CloudFront Response Headers Policy for these security headers. Add CSP that prevents inline script execution. Disable S3 static website hosting endpoint (block direct access). <br><br> *S3 static website limitation: S3 static website serves files with their original Content-Type. Cannot add custom HTTP security headers. If an attacker uploads an HTML file with malicious script: S3 serves it with `Content-Type: text/html`, browser executes the script. No ability to override Content-Type at S3 level (only per-object at upload time).<br> *CloudFront Response Headers Policy: managed policies available (AWS-managed SecurityHeaders policy covers HSTS, X-Content-Type, X-Frame-Options). Custom policy adds CSP: `"Content-Security-Policy": "default-src 'self', script-src 'self' https://trusted-cdn.com, object-src 'none'"`. Headers added to all CloudFront responses regardless of origin Content-Type. CloudFront serves the HTML but with security headers that prevent XSS execution.<br> *Bucket upload control: even with CloudFront security headers, prevent malicious HTML upload: S3 Object Lambda validates Content-Type on upload, rejects HTML files if not expected. Lambda + EventBridge: scan uploaded objects for malicious content (Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 scans uploaded files). Delete malicious uploads before they're served.<br>

1034. [ S3 ] A company's S3 bucket stores CSV files that are updated frequently. Downstream Athena queries must always return the most recent version of the data. Sometimes queries return stale data. How do you fix this? ; S3 has strong read-after-write consistency since Dec 2020. Stale data in Athena is due to Athena's metadata cache or Glue catalog not reflecting new partition data. Fix: run `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` after new CSV files are added to add new partitions to the Glue catalog. Or use Athena partition projection (auto-detects new partitions without MSCK). If using Hive-style partitioning: ensure new file paths follow partition format. <br><br> *Athena stale partition problem: CSV at `data/year=2025/month=10/day=15/file.csv` is a new partition. Athena doesn't know about it until the Glue catalog is updated. `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` scans S3, adds new partitions to Glue. Alternative: Lambda trigger on S3 ObjectCreated event → Lambda calls `aws glue create-partition` for the new partition path → Athena immediately sees new data.<br> *Partition projection: define partition schema in table properties: `"projection.year.type" = "integer", "projection.year.range" = "2020,2030"`. Athena calculates all possible partitions without querying Glue catalog. New S3 files in partition paths are automatically queryable without any catalog update. Eliminates stale partition problem entirely. Tradeoff: more complex table configuration.<br> *Athena result cache: Athena caches query results for 24 hours. If the same query runs twice within 24 hours: second run returns cached result (even if S3 data changed). Disable result caching for queries on frequently updated data: `"resultConfiguration": {"removeOutputOnExpiry": true}` or use Athena's "reuse results" off option per query. Workgroup setting: disable result reuse.<br>

1035. [ S3 ] A company stores 100 TB of data in S3 Standard. They notice that their S3 Data Transfer Out costs are $9,000/month (100 TB × $0.09/GB). Most of this traffic is EC2 in the same region accessing S3. How do you eliminate this cost? ; EC2 in the same region accessing S3 via the internet incurs DTO charges. Fix: use VPC endpoint (Gateway Endpoint for S3) — data transfers between EC2 (in VPC) and S3 through the Gateway Endpoint are FREE. No DTO charges. No data leaves the AWS network. Replace internet route with VPC Endpoint route. $9,000/month → $0. <br><br> *S3 Gateway Endpoint: free service endpoint. Adds a route to the VPC route table: S3 service prefix list (com.amazonaws.REGION.s3) → Gateway Endpoint. EC2 HTTP requests to S3 (same region) automatically route through Gateway Endpoint (not internet GW). Zero cost for S3 access from EC2 in same region/VPC. Must update route table: private subnet route tables need the gateway endpoint route.<br> *Cross-region EC2 → S3: if EC2 in us-east-1 accesses S3 in us-west-2: there are data transfer costs (inter-region). No free tier. Options: (1) Move data to same region as EC2. (2) Use S3 CRR to replicate to EC2's region. (3) Accept the cost (inter-region transfer is $0.02/GB).<br> *CloudFront for public DTO: if the $9,000/month is public DTO (internet users accessing S3 content), CloudFront reduces cost: CloudFront DTO is $0.085/GB (us-east-1) vs S3 direct DTO $0.09/GB. Minor difference. But CloudFront edge caching reduces total DTO volume (cache hits don't reach S3). High cache hit rate: most downloads served from edge at edge price, reducing total DTO significantly.<br>

1036. [ S3 ] A company uses AWS Lambda functions triggered by S3 events. When large files (>1 GB) are uploaded, Lambda is triggered but times out before processing completes. (3) Store result to S3. (4) Lambda sends completion notification. Fargate tasks have no execution time limit. <br><br> *Lambda timeout limit: hard 15-minute maximum. Cannot be extended. For long-running processing: Lambda is wrong. Use Fargate (minutes to hours), EC2 Spot (hours to days), AWS Batch (job queues with no time limit). Lambda good for: trigger handling, job submission, small file processing (<100 MB in 15 minutes).<br> *Step Functions + Fargate pattern: S3 event → Lambda (submits Fargate task via Step Functions) → Step Functions monitors Fargate task → Fargate processes file → writes output to S3 → Step Functions receives task completion → Lambda sends SNS notification. Step Functions state machine handles retries, error handling, branching (different processing paths per file type).<br> *ECS Fargate S3 access: Fargate task IAM role needs `s3:GetObject` (source bucket) and `s3:PutObject` (output bucket). Pass S3 bucket/key via Fargate task environment variables or Step Functions input. Fargate task downloads file to ephemeral storage (up to 200 GB of ephemeral storage on Fargate): `COPY_TO_EFS_OR_FARGATE_STORAGE`. Process locally. Upload result. For files >200 GB: use EFS (Elastic File System) mounted to Fargate, or stream processing without full download.<br>

1037. [ S3 ] A company's compliance team requires that all objects deleted from S3 must generate an audit event. Currently they use versioning with delete markers. 1040. [ S3 ] A company processes healthcare imaging data (DICOM files, each 500 MB – 5 GB). The processing pipeline is: upload → validate → store → process → archive. 1041. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 for CI/CD artifact storage. Build times are slow because downloading a 2 GB Docker base layer from S3 to EC2 build agents takes 5 minutes. All build agents are in the same region. How do you optimize? ; First: ensure VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3 is configured (eliminates internet routing, maximizes bandwidth). Second: EC2 enhanced networking + S3 parallel multipart download (8+ parallel threads, 128 MB parts). Third: cache base layer on build agents (EBS snapshot or shared EFS). Fourth: use Amazon ECR with layer caching instead of raw S3 (ECR is optimized for container layers with layer deduplication). <br><br> *Bandwidth math: EC2 instance to S3 in same region via VPC endpoint: up to the instance's network bandwidth. c5.2xlarge: 10 Gbps network. 2 GB ÷ (10 Gbps / 8 bits/byte) = 1.6 seconds theoretical max. If taking 5 minutes: bottleneck is either (1) no parallel download (single-threaded), (2) routing through internet (no VPC endpoint), or (3) instance's CPU is the bottleneck (decompression).<br> *Parallel S3 download: AWS CLI `--multipart-chunksize 128MB` + `--multipart-threshold 64MB`. Python S3 Transfer manager: `TransferConfig(max_concurrency=20, multipart_threshold=64*1024*1024)`. 20 parallel threads × 10 Gbps = effectively limited by per-request bandwidth, but parallelism overcomes per-request latency. For 2 GB file: 16 × 128 MB parts downloaded in parallel. Time: 2 GB / (10 Gbps × 0.8 efficiency / 8) ≈ 2 seconds vs 5 minutes (single-threaded).<br> *ECR layer caching: Amazon ECR stores Docker layers. ECR pull in same region: free (no DTO charges), optimized for container pull patterns, layer deduplication (if base layer is the same across images: stored once, referenced many times). Build agents pull base layer from ECR in same region → cached at EC2 instance level by Docker daemon (layer already present: 0 download time). Best long-term solution for Docker build speed.<br>

1043. [ S3 ] An analytics team uses S3 + Athena for a 50 TB data lake. Data growth is 5 TB/month. After 12 months, queries are getting slower even though partitioning and Parquet conversion are already in place. What might be causing the slowdown as data grows? ; Too many small Parquet files accumulating per partition (S3 file proliferation). Athena performance degrades with large numbers of small files — each file = one mapper task = overhead. Solution: run periodic Glue compaction jobs to merge small Parquet files into larger ones (128 MB – 1 GB target). Also: partition strategy may create too many partitions (over-partitioning): e.g., partitioning by hour on low-cardinality data creates millions of tiny partitions. Rebalance partition granularity. <br><br> *Small file accumulation: daily 5 TB ingestion split across 1,000 hourly partitions = 5 GB/partition/day... but if each partition has 50 × 100 MB files (from 50 streaming jobs): Athena opens 50 files per partition scan. Over 12 months: 50 × 365 = 18,250 files per partition. Athena mapper overhead at 18,250 files is significant. Target: 1-2 large Parquet files per partition (compacted).<br> *Glue compaction job: `spark.read.parquet(partition_path).repartition(1).write.mode('overwrite').parquet(partition_path)`. Reads all small files, writes one large file. Run daily on previous day's partitions. Schedule in Glue workflow (EventBridge trigger). After compaction: delete original small files (Glue overwrite handles this).<br> *Apache Iceberg migration: Iceberg format tracks all files in a metadata layer. Iceberg automatic compaction: background compaction merges small data files. Iceberg time travel: query historical snapshots. Iceberg schema evolution: add/rename columns without rewriting data. Migrating from plain Parquet → Iceberg: one-time CTAS operation. Future growth managed by Iceberg's built-in optimization. Best long-term solution for growing data lakes.<br>

1044. [ S3 ] A company's S3 bucket stores customer uploaded files. They want to automatically scan for malware before files become accessible. 1045. [ S3 ] A manufacturing company stores sensor data from 100,000 machines in S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Monthly storage cost is $50,000. 1046. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 event notifications to trigger Lambda for file processing. An operations engineer accidentally deleted the SNS topic that was the target for S3 event notifications. 1047. [ S3 ] A company has a machine learning pipeline where data scientists submit model training requests. Each request includes a dataset reference (S3 URI) and training parameters. 1050. [ S3 ] A company's website uses S3 static website hosting. The site went viral and they're experiencing 1 million requests/minute. S3 is throttling requests with 503 SlowDown errors.
