1051. [ S3 ] A company uses Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream data to S3. They need the data organized by event timestamp (not Firehose delivery time) for accurate Athena partitioning. But Firehose uses delivery time for prefix. How do you fix the partition alignment? ; Enable Kinesis Data Firehose Dynamic Partitioning with a custom prefix using JQ expression on the record's event timestamp field. Example: `.event_timestamp | strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")` extracts the event time from the record body. Firehose writes to prefix `year=!{partitionKeyFromQuery:year}/month=!{partitionKeyFromQuery:month}/` using the event-embedded timestamp, not delivery time. <br><br> *Firehose Dynamic Partitioning: enables JQ expressions (or Glue metadata) to extract partition keys from record content. JQ expression: `.event_time` (or nested: `.metadata.timestamp`). Partition key expressions: `!{partitionKeyFromQuery:year}` uses the extracted year. Delivery prefix: `data/year=!{partitionKeyFromQuery:year}/month=!{partitionKeyFromQuery:month}/day=!{partitionKeyFromQuery:day}/`. Records from yesterday that arrive today go to yesterday's partition (event time), not today's (delivery time). Correct temporal partitioning.<br> *Without Dynamic Partitioning: Firehose uses `!{timestamp:yyyy/MM/dd}` which is delivery time. A record with event_time=2025-01-14T23:59:59 that arrives at 2025-01-15T00:00:01 would land in January 15 partition. Athena query for January 14 data misses this record. Breaks incremental processing (Lambda reading "new" data for Jan 15 won't see records from late Jan 14 delivery).<br> *Lambda transformation: Firehose supports Lambda inline transformation (before dynamic partitioning). Lambda can reformat records, add partition key fields, filter/enrich. Combine with dynamic partitioning: Lambda adds `partitionKey` field from event timestamp → Firehose uses that field for prefix. More control than JQ alone. Adds latency (Lambda invocation per batch). For simple timestamp extraction: JQ is simpler and lower latency.<br>

1052. [ S3 ] A company's security team wants to detect when any S3 bucket in their organization becomes publicly accessible. They need to be notified within 5 minutes of a bucket being made public. How do you implement this real-time alerting? ; AWS Config rule `s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited` + `s3-bucket-public-write-prohibited` with notification → but Config evaluation is near-real-time (minutes). OR: CloudTrail → EventBridge rule matching `PutBucketAcl` OR `PutBucketPolicy` events on S3 buckets → Lambda checks resulting public access status → SNS alert. CloudTrail + EventBridge: sub-1-minute detection. <br><br> *EventBridge rule for S3 public access: `{"source": ["aws.s3"], "detail-type": ["AWS API Call via CloudTrail"], "detail": {"eventName": ["PutBucketAcl", "PutBucketPolicy", "PutBucketPublicAccessBlock", "DeletePublicAccessBlock"]}}`. These are the API calls that can make a bucket public. Lambda triggered by EventBridge: calls `GetBucketPolicyStatus` + `GetBucketAcl` + `GetPublicAccessBlock` → checks if bucket is now public → SNS alert if yes.<br> *AWS Security Hub integration: Security Hub has built-in S3 checks including `s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited`. Security Hub receives findings from Config. Can set up EventBridge rule on Security Hub findings with severity = HIGH to trigger SNS alert. But Security Hub + Config: may take 5-15 minutes for finding to appear. CloudTrail → EventBridge → Lambda is faster (under 1 minute typically).<br> *GuardDuty S3 Protection: `S3/BucketPublicAccessGranted` finding when a bucket's ACL or policy grants public access. GuardDuty findings appear in minutes. EventBridge rule on GuardDuty findings (`GuardDuty Finding` event) → SNS alert. GuardDuty is contextual (correlates with threat intel) vs Config/CloudTrail which are purely policy-based. Both complement each other for complete coverage.<br>

1053. [ S3 ] A company generates millions of presigned URLs per day for customers to download their files from S3. Security team says presigned URLs can be shared with unauthorized users (URL sharing vulnerability). How do you prevent URL sharing? ; Add CloudFront signed cookies instead of presigned S3 URLs. CloudFront signed cookie binds to client IP and/or a token tied to the authenticated session. Alternatively: API Gateway + Lambda generates short-lived presigned URLs (5 minutes) tied to authenticated session. Add server-side token validation: presigned URL includes custom metadata header that Lambda verifies. Bind to device fingerprint or session token. <br><br> *Presigned URL sharing problem: presigned URL is just a URL — shareable by nature. If copied and pasted: works for anyone until expiry. No way to bind presigned URL to a specific client within S3's model. CloudFront signed URL/cookie: can bind to IP range (`IpAddress` condition), making URL useless from a different IP. But mobile users change IPs — balance between security and UX.<br> *CloudFront signed cookies: more flexible than signed URLs (applies to all resources matching a URL pattern). `CloudFront-Policy` cookie: encoded access policy with IP condition + expiry. `CloudFront-Signature` cookie: HMAC signature. Browser sends cookies on every request to CloudFront domain. Shared URL without the cookies: CloudFront rejects request. Cookie theft: still possible, but harder than URL sharing.<br> *Very short expiry presigned URLs: 5-minute expiry significantly reduces sharing risk. Practical for "share the download link with a friend" attack — friend must use the link within 5 minutes. For streaming video: 5 minutes is insufficient. Combine: 5-minute expiry + CORS policy restricting allowed origins + Referer check. Multiple layers make sharing difficult without preventing legitimate access.<br>

1054. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 Intelligent-Tiering but a review shows that objects < 128 KB make up 60% of their total objects by count but only 2% of storage by size. These small objects are incurring IT monitoring overhead costs. How do you optimize? ; Objects < 128 KB in Intelligent-Tiering are not automatically moved to lower tiers (IT minimum eligible object size is 128 KB). But there IS a per-object monitoring fee ($0.0025/1,000 objects/month) regardless of size. For very small objects: monitoring fee may exceed storage savings. Solution: use lifecycle rule to move small objects (<128 KB) to a different storage class or consolidate small objects (use Kinesis Firehose or Lambda to batch small files into larger ones before storing). <br><br> *IT monitoring fee: $0.0025 per 1,000 objects monitored/month. For 1 billion objects: $2,500/month in monitoring fees alone. If those objects are tiny: the monitoring fee exceeds the storage cost benefit. Identify via S3 Storage Lens: `ObjectsSmallThanIntelligentTieringMinSize` metric shows count of small objects in IT.<br> *Solutions: (1) Move small objects to S3 Standard (no monitoring fee, similar cost for tiny objects). (2) Consolidate: batch small files into larger archives (ZIP, Parquet) → larger object benefits from IT tiering. (3) Lifecycle: `ObjectSizeGreaterThan=131072` for IT tier, objects below that threshold stay in Standard. S3 lifecycle supports size-based filters: `"Filter": {"ObjectSizeGreaterThan": 131072}`. <br> *Cost comparison: 1 million × 50 KB objects in S3 Standard: 50 GB × $0.023 = $1.15/month storage, $0 monitoring. Same in IT: $1.15/month storage + $2.50/month monitoring = $3.65/month. Standard is 3× cheaper for small objects. IT is designed for large objects (>128 KB) where storage tier savings exceed monitoring cost.<br>

1055. [ S3 ] A data lake on S3 serves a team of 200 analysts. Some analysts run very expensive queries (100 GB scanned, $0.50 per query). Other analysts run cheap queries. Management wants to allocate a $500/month Athena budget per analyst team. How do you enforce this? ; Athena Workgroups with per-workgroup query data scan limits. Create workgroups per team: `Engineering`, `Marketing`, etc. Set workgroup-level: (1) `DataScannedPerQueryLimit` = 10 GB (prevent single expensive queries). (2) `BytesScannedCutoffPerQuery` = error if exceeded. (3) Set up CloudWatch billing alarms per workgroup. Tag Athena workgroup queries with team tag. AWS Cost Allocation Tags + budgets alert when team budget approaches $500. <br><br> *Athena Workgroup features: enforce query scan limits, separate query result S3 locations per team, publish metrics to CloudWatch (BiteesScannedByWorkGroup metric). Per-team accountability: each team uses their assigned workgroup → query costs attributable to team. Workgroup setting: `ResultConfiguration` → separate team bucket for results.<br> *AWS Budgets action: create Budget per team tag: `athena:workgroup = Engineering`. Set budget threshold $500/month. Budget action: apply SCP to restrict Athena operations when 80% budget reached ($400 spent). At 100% ($500): SCP Deny `athena:StartQueryExecution`. Automatically enforces hard budget cap. Reset monthly.<br> *Data scan reduction education: teach analysts to use partition pruning (`WHERE year='2025' AND month='10'`), column pruning (SELECT only needed columns from Parquet), preview with LIMIT 100 before full scan, use Athena query results cache (repeat same query: $0 cost for second run within 24 hours). Combined technical + education approach for budget management.<br>

1056. [ S3 ] A company runs a fleet of 10,000 IoT sensors. Each sensor uploads a 1 KB reading every minute to S3. After 6 months: 10,000 sensors × 43,800 minutes/month × 6 months = 2.6 billion objects. List operations are slow, Athena queries take 30 min, S3 costs $50,000+/month. What architectural changes would cut costs by 80%? ; Eliminate individual small object uploads. Use Kinesis Data Streams or Kinesis Firehose to aggregate sensor readings. Firehose buffers 100,000 readings → writes one 100 MB JSON/Parquet file. Result: 2.6 billion objects → ~26,000 Parquet files. Storage cost: $50K → <$5K (90% reduction). Athena query time: 30 min → 30 seconds (fewer, larger files). <br><br> *Kinesis Firehose architecture: IoT sensors → Kinesis Data Streams → Kinesis Firehose (buffer: 128 MB or 5 min) → S3 (JSON or Parquet with Glue schema). Firehose writes one file per buffer period: ~24 files/day. 6 months × 24 = 4,380 files total (vs 2.6 billion). Each file: 100 MB of compressed sensor data. S3 storage cost: 4,380 × 100 MB × 10:1 Parquet compression = 43.8 GB × $0.023 = $1.01/month. Compared to $50K+: 99.998% reduction.<br> *AWS IoT Core integration: AWS IoT Core native S3 Action: routes IoT messages to S3 directly (per-message upload = same small file problem). Better: IoT Core → Kinesis Data Streams → Firehose → S3. IoT Core rule SQL filter: `SELECT * FROM 'sensors/+/readings'` → Kinesis stream. All 10,000 sensors fan in to one Kinesis stream (10,000 sensors × 1 KB/min = 166 KB/sec — well within Kinesis shard capacity of 1 MB/sec).<br> *S3 request cost elimination: 2.6 billion PutObject × $0.005/1,000 = $13,000/month in PUT requests alone. 26,000 PutObjects/year × $0.005/1,000 = $0.13/year. One architectural change eliminates $13,000/month in PUT request costs before even considering storage.<br>

1057. [ S3 ] A company runs S3 Batch Operations to process 500 million objects. The job fails after processing 200 million objects due to a Lambda timeout on a specific object type. How do you recover without reprocessing the already-completed 200 million? ; S3 Batch Operations generates a completion report showing which objects succeeded and which failed. Filter the completion report for failed objects only. Create a new Batch Operations job using the failure report as the manifest (instead of the original inventory). The new job processes only failed objects. Fix the Lambda function first (handle the problematic object type). Rerun only the delta. <br><br> *Completion report: S3 Batch Operations generates CSV report per job. Report fields: TaskAttemptStatus (succeeded/failed), ErrorCode, ErrorMessage, ObjectKey. `--report '{"ReportScope": "FailedTasksOnly"}'` generates report with only failed objects (smaller file). Use this report directly as the manifest for the retry job.<br> *Idempotent Lambda: Lambda function should be idempotent (processing the same object twice = same result, no error). If the Lambda processes objects in-place (e.g., adds a tag, copies to another bucket): duplicate processing is safe. If Lambda is not idempotent: build idempotency check (DynamoDB item per object, skip if already processed). For Batch Operations retry: check for already-processed objects before applying transformation.<br> *Lambda fix: the specific object type causing timeout was likely an unusually large or malformed object. Lambda fix: check object size before processing (HeadObject), skip objects >500 MB (or handle differently), set error handler for malformed objects (catch exception, mark as skipped). Update Lambda code, then create the retry Batch Operations job. Total recovery: process only the failed 300 million objects (and fix) without touching the successful 200 million.<br>

1058. [ S3 ] A startup needs to store user-generated content (photos, videos, documents) from a mobile app. They expect to grow from 1,000 users to 10 million users within 2 years. They need a storage solution that scales without re-architecture. How do S3's scaling characteristics make it the right choice? ; S3 is infinitely scalable with no pre-provisioning: no capacity planning, no storage limits per bucket, automatically handles any request rate by distributing load internally. Multi-prefix architecture provides virtually unlimited throughput (5,500 GET/3,500 PUT per prefix per second — distribute across user ID-based prefixes). No database-like shard splits or cluster sizing required. Pay-as-you-grow: costs scale linearly with usage. <br><br> *S3 scaling proof: from 1,000 users: 1,000 uploads/day, a few GB storage. To 10 million users: 10 million uploads/day, potentially PBs storage. S3 handles both without any infrastructure changes. No "resize instance" or "add nodes" operations. Compare to self-hosted object storage (Ceph, MinIO): requires capacity planning, hardware procurement, cluster expansion as data grows. S3: zero ops for scaling.<br> *Prefix-based throughput distribution: with user-ID-based key paths (`users/USER_ID/photos/`), 10 million users create 10 million prefixes. S3 distributes load across all prefixes automatically. 10 million users × 1 upload/day = ~116 uploads/second total. Well within S3 throughput. Even if the same user uploads 1,000 times/day: their prefix gets 1,000 PUTs/day (< 1/second — nowhere near 3,500/second prefix limit).<br> *No-architecture-change growth: the same S3 bucket architecture (bucket + prefix-per-user) works from day 1 (1,000 users) to year 2 (10 million users). Unlike relational DBs (need sharding), DynamoDB (need capacity planning/DAX), or self-hosted systems (need node addition). S3 is the canonical "serverless storage" for startups expecting viral growth.<br>

1059. [ S3 ] A company migrates from S3 ACLs (Access Control Lists) to bucket policies. After migration, all ACL-based permissions are removed. Some objects were previously shared publicly via ACLs. After migration, customers report 403 errors on previously public objects. Why? ; ACL removal removes the ACL-based public access grant. Bucket policy must explicitly grant public access to replace ACLs. If bucket's S3 Block Public Access (BPA) is enabled: even a bucket policy allowing `"Principal": "*"` is blocked. Check: BPA settings on the bucket. S3 BPA `RestrictPublicBuckets=true` overrides any bucket policy allowing public access. Must disable BPA to allow public access via bucket policy. <br><br> *ACL to bucket policy migration: step 1: add bucket policy granting equivalent permissions. Step 2: enable `BucketOwnerEnforced` ACL setting (disables all ACLs). Step 3: test access before fully removing ACLs. If S3 Block Public Access was never configured: bucket policy `"Principal": "*"` grants public access after ACL removal. If BPA is enabled (recommended AWS default): `"Principal": "*"` is blocked. Need to determine: should these objects be publicly accessible? If yes: disable BPA for this bucket. If no: investigate why customers were accessing them publicly before (improper ACL-based public sharing).<br> *AWS recommendation: move all access control to bucket policies + IAM, disable ACLs with `BucketOwnerEnforced`. For public content (truly intended to be public, like static website assets): disable BPA for the specific bucket + add bucket policy Allow Principal: "*". For private content mistakenly made public via ACLs: correct behavior → fix the customer applications to use presigned URLs or authenticated access instead of public URLs.<br> *`BucketOwnerEnforced` mode: when set, all ACL-based grants are ignored (but existing ACLs remain as metadata — they just don't apply). New uploads cannot have ACL other than `private`. All new objects auto-owned by bucket owner. Simplifies access control to IAM + bucket policy only. Recommended setting for all new and migrated buckets.<br>

1060. [ S3 ] An enterprise has 5,000 S3 buckets across 100 AWS accounts. A new compliance policy requires that all buckets must use SSE-KMS with customer-managed keys (not the default AWS-managed aws/s3 key). The security team needs to identify which buckets are already compliant and which are using SSE-S3 or the default KMS key. How do you inventory the current state? ; Deploy AWS Config managed rule `s3-default-encryption-kms` across all accounts (via StackSet). Config identifies buckets NOT using customer-managed KMS key. Or: S3 Storage Lens Advanced metrics include encryption information. Or: AWS Config Aggregator with cross-account/cross-region view. Run `aws configservice list-discovered-resources --resource-type AWS::S3::Bucket` per account and check configuration details. <br><br> *Config rule `s3-default-encryption-kms`: evaluates each bucket. Compliant: default encryption is aws:kms with a customer-managed CMK (not `aws/s3`). Non-compliant: SSE-S3 (AES256) or aws:kms with `aws/s3` key. Config aggregator: view all non-compliant buckets across 100 accounts in one dashboard. Export as CSV: compliance status per bucket per account.<br> *CLI bulk check: `aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket NAME --query 'ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration.Rules[0].ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault'`. Returns: `{Algorithm: aws:kms, KMSMasterKeyID: <key-arn-or-null>}`. If KMSMasterKeyID is null: using `aws/s3` (not CMK). Script this across all 5,000 buckets. For each non-compliant bucket: (1) Create CMK for that account/region. (2) `aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket NAME --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules": [{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault": {"SSEAlgorithm": "aws:kms", "KMSMasterKeyID": "CMK_ARN"}}]}'`. (3) S3 Batch Operations to re-encrypt existing objects with new CMK. Config auto-marks as compliant after each remediation. Use Batch Operations in parallel across accounts to complete within the compliance deadline.<br>

1061. [ S3 ] A company's data engineering team needs to process files uploaded by external partners (different AWS account). Partners upload to the company's S3 bucket via cross-account access. After processing, the company stores derived data. Partners claim their uploads are being modified after arrival. How do you provide cryptographic proof of upload integrity? ; Enable S3 Versioning + CloudTrail data events for the bucket. After partner upload: run `aws s3api head-object --bucket NAME --key KEY` to get the ETag (MD5 hash for non-multipart uploads). Provide the ETag + version ID to the partner as the upload receipt. Any modification creates a new version with a different ETag. Partners can verify: `head-object` of the specific version ID still returns the original ETag = unmodified. <br><br> *ETag as integrity proof: ETag for simple PutObject (non-multipart) = MD5 of object content. If the object bytes change: ETag changes. Partner records ETag at upload time → company processing pipeline reads same ETag → both parties verify the same bytes. For multipart uploads: ETag format is different (MD5 of part ETags concatenated + `-N` where N is part count). Still usable as identity proof if both parties agree on the format.<br> *Version ID + timestamp in CloudTrail: CloudTrail records the original PutObject with requester ARN (partner's IAM role), timestamp, object key, version ID. Immutable log (with log file validation). If dispute arises: retrieve CloudTrail event for the specific version ID. Shows: partner uploaded at time T, version V, ETag E. Any subsequent modification shows as a new event with new version V2. Cryptographic timeline evidence.<br> *Hash-based verification workflow: partner computes SHA-256 of file before upload, transmits hash separately (email, API). After upload: company's Lambda computes SHA-256 of received object → compares to partner-provided hash → stores comparison result in DynamoDB with timestamp. SHA-256 match confirms unmodified receipt. This is independent of AWS ETag (which uses MD5 and doesn't apply to multipart). More robust for formal integrity chain.<br>

1062. [ S3 ] A company wants to implement data lifecycle governance: data moves from hot → warm → cold → archive → deletion over 5 years. Different data types have different retention rules. The governance team wants a centralized system to manage all lifecycle policies. How do you architect this? ; AWS Config + S3 Lifecycle Policies as code (Terraform/CDK). Define lifecycle policy templates per data type. Centralize in a Config-managed catalog. Or: S3 Storage Lens provides insights → EventBridge triggers lifecycle policy updates. Better: treat lifecycle policies as Infrastructure as Code — store in Git, deploy via CI/CD pipeline, enforce via Config rules that validate bucket lifecycle configurations match approved templates. <br><br> *IaC lifecycle management: Terraform modules with data-type-specific lifecycle variables. `lifecycle_hot_days = 30`, `lifecycle_warm_days = 90`, `lifecycle_cold_days = 365`, `lifecycle_archive_days = 1825 (5 years)`, `lifecycle_expire_days = 1826`. Module generates the lifecycle policy JSON. All 5,000 buckets use the same module with appropriate variable overrides. Changes: PR to Terraform → CI runs `terraform plan` → team review → merge → `terraform apply`. Version-controlled, auditable, consistent.<br> *AWS Config for compliance: custom Config rule validates each bucket's lifecycle policy matches the approved template for its data-type tag. Non-compliant (missing required lifecycle rule or wrong day counts): Config finding → notification → auto-remediation applies the approved policy. Buckets cannot deviate from approved lifecycle without triggering Config alert.<br> *S3 Object Tagging for lifecycle selection: tag each object at upload with `data-type=financial`, `data-type=logs`, `data-type=media`. Lifecycle rules use tag filters: `{"Filter": {"Tag": {"Key": "data-type", "Value": "logs"}}}, "Transition": {"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}`. Different retention for different data types within the same bucket. Tag-based lifecycle enables fine-grained control without managing thousands of separate buckets.<br>

1063. [ S3 ] A company has a real-time analytics pipeline. Events flow through Kinesis → Lambda → S3. They need to query data within 30 seconds of it landing in S3. Athena's startup time (~2 seconds) + query execution time makes some queries take 20+ seconds. How do you reduce latency? ; For sub-30-second S3 data availability: S3 strong consistency means newly written objects are immediately queryable. For true real-time: OpenSearch Service for streaming indexing, not Athena. Athena is for batch/interactive, not real-time. <br><br> *Athena limitations for real-time: Athena scans S3 files. For real-time dashboards: use Amazon OpenSearch (data arrives in seconds via Kinesis → OpenSearch ingestion, queries in milliseconds) or Kinesis Data Analytics (real-time SQL on the stream itself, before hitting S3).<br> *Kinesis Data Analytics (Managed Service for Apache Flink): process data in-stream. Real-time SQL on Kinesis stream. Results available in milliseconds (0 seconds after event arrival). Output: to S3, DynamoDB, OpenSearch. For the real-time analytics use case: KDA is correct architecture, not Athena. Real-time dashboards: query KDA. Historical analysis: query Athena. Data stitching: both systems process the same events from Kinesis stream. KDA results age out (in-memory or DynamoDB TTL). S3 + Athena has full history. Together: real-time + historical without gaps.<br>

1064. [ S3 ] A company stores clickstream data in S3. The data arrives as individual JSON files (one per click event). After 3 months: 10 billion files. For immediate listing of new objects: S3 Event Notifications (ObjectCreated) to SQS/Lambda for real-time awareness. Don't use ListObjects for at-scale operations — use Inventory. Fix root cause: batch small files (reduce to millions, not billions). <br><br> *S3 ListObjects scale: ListObjects can return up to 1,000 objects per page. 10 billion objects: 10 million pages of 1,000 each. Each page request: 5-20 ms. 10 million requests × 10 ms = 100,000 seconds (~28 hours) to list all objects. AWS may throttle at this rate. Incomplete results: ListObjects pagination is eventually consistent for listing (though objects are strongly consistent — listing can miss items added concurrently). For 10 billion objects: ListObjects is architecturally wrong.<br> *S3 Inventory: runs daily (or weekly). Result: complete CSV/Parquet manifest delivered to a target bucket. Processing 10 billion objects in inventory: 1-few hours (background process, managed by AWS). Manifest available as a Parquet file. Query with Athena: full metadata scan in minutes. For bulk operations: Batch Operations uses Inventory as manifest directly. Zero ListObjects API calls needed.<br> *Real-time awareness alternative: S3 Event Notifications → SQS → Lambda processes each new object as it arrives. No need to ever list the bucket — Lambda is notified of every new file. For downstream processing: SQS queue acts as the object registry. Query the SQS queue or a DynamoDB table maintained by Lambda. 1065. [ S3 ] A financial trading firm stores market data feeds in S3. The data is critical for trading decisions. The firm needs the data replicated to a second region for DR, with a maximum data loss of 15 minutes (RPO = 15 minutes). How do you ensure RPO compliance? ; Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication with Replication Time Control (RTC). RTC SLA: 99.99% of new objects replicated within 15 minutes. CloudWatch metrics: `ReplicationLatency` monitors actual replication time. Alert if replication latency exceeds 10 minutes (buffer before 15-minute RPO breach). RTC cost: $0.015/GB additional charge over standard replication. <br><br> *RTC SLA: S3 RTC guarantees 99.99% of objects replicated within 15 minutes. This is the only S3 replication SLA — standard CRR has no time commitment. For RPO = 15 minutes: RTC is the required feature. Without RTC: standard CRR may take hours for some objects. Trading firm regulatory requirement for RPO: RTC is mandatory.<br> *CloudWatch RTC metrics: `ReplicationLatency` (time from source PUT to destination replication). `BytesPendingReplication` (total bytes not yet replicated). Alert: `BytesPendingReplication > threshold` → page on-call team → investigate replication stall. SNS alarm action: send to PagerDuty for immediate response. SLA verification: periodically test replication time with synthetic objects (write a test object, measure time until it appears in destination).<br> *Failover testing: DR for trading data requires tested failover. Regular drill: (1) Primary region failure simulation. (2) Route traffic to secondary region (Route 53 health check failover). (3) Trading system uses secondary S3 bucket. (4) Data complete within RTC SLA. (5) Primary restored → sync any new secondary-region writes back (bidirectional CRR with SRR). Regular testing ensures RPO/RTO are achievable, not just theoretically designed.<br>

1066. [ S3 ] A company's legal team needs to place a litigation hold on all S3 objects related to a specific project. The hold must prevent any deletion or modification. It may last an indefinite amount of time (months to years, unknown duration). How do you implement an indefinite legal hold? ; Use S3 Object Lock Legal Hold (separate from retention periods). `put-object-legal-hold --legal-hold-status ON`. Legal hold has NO expiration date — remains until explicitly removed with `put-object-legal-hold --legal-hold-status OFF`. IAM permission required to remove: `s3:PutObjectLegalHold`. Existing buckets: enable Object Lock on the bucket, then apply legal holds to specific objects via S3 Batch Operations. <br><br> *Legal Hold vs Retention Period: Retention Period = set duration (days/date). Legal Hold = indefinite until removed. For litigation (unknown duration): use Legal Hold, not Retention Period. Legal holds can be applied alongside a retention period or standalone. Object is protected by EITHER a legal hold OR an active retention period (whichever is longer). <br> *Applying to existing objects: S3 Batch Operations with `PutObjectLegalHold` action. Manifest: S3 Inventory filtered by project tag (objects tagged `project=LAWSUIT-2025-001`). Batch Operations applies legal hold to all matching objects. To remove: same Batch Operations job with `LegalHoldStatus=OFF`. Legal team controls the IAM role with `s3:PutObjectLegalHold` permission — only legal team can remove holds.<br> *Audit trail: every `PutObjectLegalHold` (apply or remove) is logged in CloudTrail. For litigation: preserve CloudTrail logs for the legal hold period (use Object Lock on CloudTrail logs too). `aws s3api get-object-legal-hold --bucket NAME --key KEY` verifies hold status at any time. eDiscovery: S3 Inventory shows `ObjectLockLegalHoldStatus` field for each object — use to generate list of all objects under legal hold for attorneys.<br>

1067. [ S3 ] A company's application reads objects from S3 using presigned URLs generated by a backend API. The URLs expire after 1 hour. Customers complain that they get "Request has expired" errors even when the URL is fresh (generated seconds ago). What could cause this? ; Clock skew: the device clock is not synchronized with NTP (Network Time Protocol). AWS validates presigned URL signature against the current time. If the device clock is behind by >1 minute: the AWS server may see the request timestamp as expired or in the future. Fix: synchronize the backend server generating URLs to NTP. If mobile client clocks are off: URL must be generated closer to use, or extend expiry to accommodate clock drift. <br><br> *Clock skew root cause: `SignatureDoesNotMatch` or `RequestExpired` errors from S3. AWS SDK automatically adjusts for small clock skew (~15 minutes max adjustment). But if server clock is off by >15 minutes: requests fail. Check server clock: `date` command, compare to `time.nist.gov`. EC2 instances use Amazon Time Sync Service (169.254.169.123) — ensure NTP daemon is running (`timedatectl status`). On-premises servers: configure NTP to AWS Time Sync Service or public NTP pool.<br> *Other causes: (1) Presigned URL contains the generation time. If URL generated at 12:00 PM with 1-hour expiry: expires at 1:00 PM. But if the server generating the URL is in a different timezone offset than expected, and the URL is cached (CDN or client cache), the cached URL may be served after its actual expiry. (2) Long redirect chains: URL generated → 302 redirect → another redirect → request arrives late → expired. (3) DNS resolution time: unlikely to cause >1 minute delay but possible in extreme cases.<br> *Best practice: always use EC2 instances with Amazon Time Sync Service. For on-premises or other cloud servers: configure NTP. AWS SDK handles up to ±15 minutes clock skew automatically. For presigned URLs specifically: use credential-based expiry (short-lived STS credentials) rather than URL-embedded expiry, as credential expiry is server-side and not vulnerable to client clock issues.<br>

1068. [ S3 ] A company is building a backup solution for on-premises servers. They need: automated backup, versioned backups, point-in-time recovery for any time in the last 30 days, encrypted backups, and cost-effective long-term storage. How do you design this with S3? ; AWS Backup with S3 integration: configure S3 backup policy (lifecycle to Glacier after 30 days, retain 7 years). On-premises servers: use AWS DataSync or AWS Storage Gateway to sync to S3. S3 versioning for point-in-time recovery (last 30 days = 30 versions). S3 Lifecycle: noncurrent version expiration after 30 days (auto-delete older versions). SSE-KMS for encryption. <br><br> *DataSync for on-premises backup: DataSync agent on-premises, syncs file changes to S3 on schedule (hourly/daily). Incremental: only changed files synced each run. Transfer over Direct Connect or VPN (encrypted in transit). DataSync creates new S3 versions for changed files. Versioning: `GetObject --version-id` to restore any file at any point in last 30 days.<br> *Point-in-time recovery: S3 versioning + lifecycle `NoncurrentVersionExpiration: 30 days`. At any time: list versions of a file, select the version from the desired restore point (30 days of history). Restore: copy the old version ID to a recovery location. For thousands of files: S3 Batch Operations to restore all files from a specific timestamp (Batch Operations supports version-ID-based operations via Inventory). <br> *AWS Backup integration: AWS Backup creates recovery points from S3 bucket contents at scheduled intervals. Recovery points: versioned snapshots of the entire bucket state. Point-in-time restore: select a recovery point timestamp → AWS Backup restores the bucket to that state. Simpler than manual version management for the recovery team. Combine: DataSync (gets data to S3) + versioning (change history) + AWS Backup (recovery points management + retention policy) + lifecycle (cost management).<br>

1069. [ S3 ] A company ingests data from multiple sources into a single S3 bucket. Each source writes to a different prefix. Some prefixes are written by partners (external accounts). Some by internal teams. The data engineering team periodically runs ETL jobs that must read from all prefixes. How do you structure IAM permissions for this? ; Create one IAM role per data source (partner or internal): each role has PutObject only to their specific prefix. ETL IAM role: GetObject + ListBucket on all prefixes (with ListBucket scoped via condition on prefix). Use bucket policy to centralize access control. Bucket policy grants: source roles → write access to their prefix, ETL role → read access to all prefixes. <br><br> *Least privilege per source: PartnerA IAM role (cross-account) → PutObject on `s3://bucket/partnerA/*` only. InternalTeamB IAM role → PutObject on `s3://bucket/teamB/*` only. ETL role → GetObject on `s3://bucket/*` (all prefixes) + ListBucket with `Condition: StringLike: s3:prefix: ["partnerA/*", "teamB/*", ...]`. No source can read another source's data or write to another's prefix.<br> *ListBucket scope: `"Action": "s3:ListBucket", "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": "partnerA/*"}}`. This restricts ListBucket responses to only show objects under the `partnerA/` prefix. Without this condition: ListBucket returns ALL object keys (metadata leak between partitioned sources). Scoped ListBucket is important for multi-tenant bucket security.<br> *Cross-account bucket policy: `"Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::PARTNER_A_ACCOUNT:role/UploadRole"}, "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::bucket/partnerA/*"`. Partners authenticate with their own AWS account credentials, assume their upload role, and access the bucket via bucket policy (no cross-account IAM trust needed on the company side — bucket policy handles cross-account authorization directly).<br>

1070. [ S3 ] A company has enabled S3 server access logging but the audit team can't find logs older than 7 days. They expected logs going back 90 days. What happened? ; The target logging bucket likely has a lifecycle policy that expires logs after 7 days. Check: `aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket LOG-BUCKET`. Also: verify that server access logging was enabled 90 days ago (if recently enabled: only logs since enablement exist). Check: `aws s3api get-bucket-logging --bucket SOURCE-BUCKET` to confirm logging target and when it was enabled (CloudTrail: look for `PutBucketLogging` API call history). <br><br> *S3 server access log lifecycle: logging bucket often has short retention lifecycle (to control log storage costs). Common misconfiguration: someone adds a 7-day expiration lifecycle to the logging bucket to reduce costs, inadvertently violating the 90-day log retention requirement. Fix: update logging bucket lifecycle to 90+ day retention. Immediately loses logs already expired (no recovery).<br> *S3 access logging limitations: delivery is best-effort (may have gaps, no guarantee of 100% delivery). For compliance: CloudTrail data events are authoritative (guaranteed delivery, signed, validated). Server access logs are supplemental. If 90-day logs are required for compliance: CloudTrail should be the primary system (not SAL). SAL is good for operational HTTP-level debugging.<br> *Log retention best practices: separate logging bucket with versioning enabled. Lifecycle rule: expire noncurrent versions after 30 days (space management). Current version expires after 365 days (compliance retention). Object Lock on compliance log buckets (prevent deletion). CloudTrail logs: separate bucket in security account, no lifecycle expiration (keep indefinitely for compliance). Cost: CloudTrail logs compress well (Parquet/gzip), 365 days of logs ≈ manageable cost for most companies.<br>

1071. [ S3 ] A company wants to migrate their 100 TB data warehouse to an S3 data lake. The current DW runs complex SQL with JOINs across 50+ tables. After migration to S3+Athena, queries are 10x slower despite using Parquet format. Query performance is comparable to before migration only for simple queries. What is wrong? ; Athena has no query optimizer statistics (histograms, cardinality estimates) like enterprise databases. JOIN order matters significantly. Complex queries with 50+ table JOINs without statistics = suboptimal join order → full table scans. Fix: enable Glue statistics (run `ANALYZE TABLE` equivalent in Athena to generate column statistics). Or: migrate to Redshift Spectrum or Amazon Redshift (better JOIN optimization, zone maps, sort keys). For complex OLAP: Redshift is architecturally superior to Athena+S3. <br><br> *Athena vs DW for complex JOINs: Athena (Trino/Presto) lacks: (1) Zone maps (Redshift has them for fast range scans on sorted data). (2) Materialized views (Redshift Materialized Views dramatically speed up aggregations). (3) Sort keys/distribution keys (Redshift co-locates JOIN data). (4) Column-level statistics collected from data (Athena stats from Glue are limited). For 50-table JOIN queries: Redshift is the right tool.<br> *Glue statistics fix: in Athena: `ANALYZE table_name COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS col1, col2`. Or Glue crawler with statistics option enabled. Column statistics help Athena's query planner choose better JOIN order. `aws glue update-table --table-input '{"Parameters": {"STATS_REQ_COLUMN_COUNT": "50"}}'`. Even with statistics: Athena doesn't match Redshift for complex multi-table JOINs.<br> *Correct architecture: use Redshift as the query engine, S3 as the data lake storage. Redshift Spectrum reads directly from S3 Parquet. Redshift uses its optimizer for complex JOINs (statistics, sort keys, distribution keys). Results: enterprise DW query performance on S3 data. Best of both worlds: S3 storage cost + Redshift compute optimization. Simpler queries: continue using Athena (cheaper). Complex OLAP: Redshift Spectrum.<br>

1072. [ S3 ] A company stores highly sensitive research data in S3. The security team wants to ensure the data cannot be exfiltrated even if AWS account credentials are stolen. What is the strongest additional layer of defense? ; S3 Access Points + VPC-only restriction: all access must be from within a specific VPC (where the research applications run). Even stolen AWS credentials cannot access data from outside the VPC. Bucket policy condition: `"aws:SourceVpc": "vpc-research-xxx"`. Additional: SSE-KMS with customer-managed key stored in CloudHSM (HSM-backed, keys never leave HSM). Credential theft outside the VPC = useless. <br><br> *VPC restriction + stolen credentials: attacker steals IAM credentials, tries to call `aws s3 get-object` from their laptop. Request comes from public internet IP, not from the research VPC. S3 bucket policy: `"Deny": "s3:*" if not aws:SourceVpc = vpc-research-xxx"`. GetObject returns 403 Access Denied. Credentials are technically valid but useless from outside the VPC. This defeats credential theft as an attack vector for data exfiltration.<br> *CloudHSM key protection: if KMS key is stolen/compromised, attacker can decrypt S3 data. CloudHSM-backed KMS key: key material never leaves the HSM hardware. To use the key: must be in a VPC with connectivity to CloudHSM. Credential theft + CloudHSM key access: attacker must be inside the AWS VPC with HSM connectivity (much harder than stealing credentials alone).<br> *Defense depth layers: (1) VPC endpoint + source VPC restriction (access from internet = 403). (2) CloudHSM-backed KMS key (key never leaves HSM hardware). (3) VPC network ACL restricting outbound traffic from research instances (no outbound internet from research VPC — prevents data exfiltration even from inside the VPC). (4) GuardDuty + Macie for anomaly detection. (5) CloudTrail immutable logging. Each layer independently defeats common attack patterns.<br>

1073. [ S3 ] A company uses S3 Static Website hosting for their corporate website. The website needs to support HTTPS and a custom domain (www.company.com). Currently the S3 website endpoint only supports HTTP. How do you add HTTPS? ; S3 static website hosting does NOT support HTTPS directly. Add CloudFront in front of S3 (REST endpoint, not website endpoint). CloudFront terminates HTTPS with an ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) certificate for www.company.com. CloudFront forwards to S3 origin over HTTPS or HTTP (internal to AWS network, acceptable). Route 53: alias record → CloudFront distribution domain name. Cost: ACM cert is free, CloudFront pricing by request/data. <br><br> *S3 website endpoint limitations: (1) HTTP only — no TLS/HTTPS. (2) No custom SSL/TLS certificate. (3) S3 website URL format (bucket-name.s3-website-region.amazonaws.com). CloudFront solves all three: HTTPS termination, ACM free SSL cert, custom domain (CNAME or Route 53 alias). This is the standard static website architecture on AWS.<br> *CloudFront origin access: use S3 REST endpoint (not S3 website endpoint) with CloudFront OAC (Origin Access Control). OAC: CloudFront signs all requests to S3. S3 bucket policy allows only CloudFront OAC ARN. Direct S3 access blocked. Users must access through CloudFront (which enforces HTTPS via redirect HTTP→HTTPS). `aws cloudfront create-cloud-front-origin-access-control`.<br> *ACM certificate: must be in us-east-1 (for CloudFront, regardless of where bucket/distribution is). `aws acm request-certificate --domain-name www.company.com --validation-method DNS --region us-east-1`. DNS validation: Route 53 auto-validates (CNAME record added automatically). Certificate issued within minutes. CloudFront distribution: select ACM cert in us-east-1. Viewer protocol: `redirect-http-to-https`. Static website now fully HTTPS with custom domain.<br>

1074. [ S3 ] A company's CloudTrail logs are stored in S3. A security analyst needs to search for all `AssumeRole` events in the past 12 months — over 5 billion events total. Using the AWS Console is too slow. How do you efficiently query 12 months of CloudTrail logs? ; Athena + CloudTrail integration: create an Athena table over the CloudTrail S3 bucket (partitioned by region/year/month/day). Query: `SELECT eventTime, userIdentity.arn, requestParameters.roleArn FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventName = 'AssumeRole' AND year = '2025'`. Athena scans only `AssumeRole` events in the relevant partitions. Parquet conversion (via Glue) makes this even faster. <br><br> *Athena CloudTrail table: AWS provides a standard CREATE TABLE DDL for CloudTrail logs. Apply it to the CloudTrail S3 bucket. Partition projection (Athena): auto-compute partition paths `s3://bucket/AWSLogs/ACCOUNT/CloudTrail/REGION/YEAR/MONTH/DAY/`. Query scans only specified date range partitions — skips 11 months of data when querying 1-month window. 5 billion events across 12 months: well-partitioned Athena query runs in 30-60 seconds for a month's worth of data.<br> *CloudTrail Lake alternative: AWS CloudTrail Lake is a managed event data store. Automatically indexes and stores CloudTrail events. Query with Athena-compatible SQL via CloudTrail Lake API. Retention up to 7 years. No need to manage Athena tables or Glue catalog. CloudTrail Lake is the simpler option for organizations that want managed CloudTrail querying without S3/Athena DIY setup.<br> *Security Lake: Amazon Security Lake (based on OCSF Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework) centralizes security logs (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53, Lambda) in a normalized format. Query all security logs with one Athena query. For the use case: Security Lake provides cross-service correlation (AssumeRole + subsequent S3 access by the assumed role) in one query. More powerful than plain CloudTrail Athena queries for security investigation.<br>

1075. [ S3 ] A company's ETL pipeline reads from S3 using Spark on EMR. After a recent data quality issue, they need to implement schema validation — ensure incoming data matches the expected schema before loading into the data warehouse. Where in the pipeline should this validation occur? ; Validate at landing zone before transformation: S3 event notification (ObjectCreated in raw/ prefix) → Lambda → read first 100 rows → validate against schema registry (AWS Glue Schema Registry). Valid: proceed to ETL. Invalid: move to quarantine/ prefix + SNS alert to data engineering team. Use Glue Schema Registry to define expected schema, versioned and managed centrally. <br><br> *AWS Glue Schema Registry: central repository for data schemas (Avro, JSON Schema, Protobuf). Schemas versioned (v1, v2, ...). Schema compatibility modes (NONE, BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL). Lambda validation: `boto3.client('glue').get_schema_version(SchemaId={'SchemaName': 'events', 'RegistryName': 'default'}, SchemaVersionNumber={'VersionNumber': 1})`. Validate incoming data against the registered schema. Schema mismatch → quarantine.<br> *Glue Data Quality: AWS Glue has built-in data quality rules (`CheckCount`, `Completeness`, `Uniqueness`, `Referential Integrity`). Define ruleset: `Rules = [Completeness "user_id" >= 0.99, ColumnValues "status" in ["active", "inactive", "pending"]]`. Glue evaluates rules against each dataset. Rules pass/fail. Glue Data Quality results stored in S3 for tracking. Integrate into ETL job as validation step.<br> *Fail-fast pipeline: if invalid schema is detected at landing zone (Lambda check): ETL job is never triggered. EMR Spark cluster is not spun up for invalid data. Cost saved: EMR cluster startup ($0.05/instance-hour × 20 nodes × 10 minutes = $0.17) × 1,000 bad-data events/month = $170/month saved by early validation. Better: fix data at the source (producer) so schema violations never reach S3.<br>

1076. [ S3 ] A company's compliance team requires evidence that no S3 data has left the company's AWS environment (no data exfiltration to external accounts or internet). How do you provide this evidence? ; VPC endpoint policy restricting S3 access to company-owned buckets: `"Deny": "s3:*" if "s3:DataAccessPointAccount" != COMPANY_ACCOUNT_ID`. Combined with: VPC security groups (no outbound internet from data-processing instances) + CloudTrail S3 data events (shows all bucket access with destination) + S3 Inventory to verify all buckets are company-owned + GuardDuty findings (`Exfiltration:S3`) + no CRR to external accounts (Config rule). <br><br> *VPC endpoint policy for egress control: `{"Effect": "Deny", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"s3:ResourceAccount": ["COMPANY_ACCOUNT_1", "COMPANY_ACCOUNT_2", "COMPANY_ACCOUNT_3"]}}}`. Any S3 request from within the company VPC to buckets in other accounts is denied at the VPC endpoint. Data cannot be copied to an attacker's S3 bucket. Attacker who compromises EC2 instance: can't `aws s3 cp` to their personal bucket — VPC endpoint policy blocks it.<br> *CRR external check: Config rule: evaluate all S3 CRR configurations. Flag any rule that replicates to an external account (not in the company account list). Alert on any new cross-account CRR setup. Provides evidence: replication only to company-controlled accounts.<br> *Evidence package for compliance: (1) VPC endpoint policy document (blocks external S3). (2) CloudTrail log query: no S3 GetObject/CopyObject to external accounts. (3) Config findings: no non-compliant CRR rules. (4) GuardDuty report: no exfiltration findings. (5) Network flow logs: no outbound internet from data-processing VPCs. Together: multi-layer evidence that data cannot leave the environment.<br>

1077. [ S3 ] A company runs batch ML training on S3 datasets. After training completes, they want to notify downstream teams and automatically delete intermediate training data to save costs. The training runs in SageMaker. How do you automate this cleanup? ; SageMaker Training Job → EventBridge rule (training job completed/failed) → Lambda → (1) List and delete intermediate data from S3 (objects in `training-intermediate/JOB_ID/` prefix). (2) Copy model artifacts from SageMaker to S3 model registry. (3) Send SNS notification to downstream teams. All automated via EventBridge + Lambda post-training workflow. <br><br> *EventBridge SageMaker events: `{"source": ["aws.sagemaker"], "detail-type": ["SageMaker Training Job State Change"], "detail": {"TrainingJobStatus": ["Completed", "Failed", "Stopped"]}}`. Lambda triggered on any terminal state. For Completed: run cleanup. For Failed: preserve intermediate data for debugging (don't delete). EventBridge filter by status allows different actions per outcome.<br> *Lambda cleanup code: `s3_client.delete_objects(Bucket='training-data', Delete={'Objects': [{'Key': key} for key in intermediate_keys]})`. For large numbers of intermediate files: S3 Batch Operations (instead of Lambda list-and-delete, which may timeout for millions of objects). Lambda submits Batch Operations job, polls for completion, then sends SNS notification.<br> *Automated cost governance: SageMaker Training Job metadata includes: `InputDataConfig` (source S3 paths), `OutputDataConfig` (output S3 path), `TrainingJobArn`. Lambda uses job ARN to identify which S3 prefix to clean up. Tag intermediate data at creation with `TrainingJobArn` tag → Lambda deletes all objects with that tag (S3 Batch Operations tag-based filtering). Idempotent cleanup: even if Lambda runs twice, S3 delete is idempotent (deleting non-existent objects returns success).<br>

1078. [ S3 ] A company has a regulatory requirement: all S3 buckets must have MFA Delete enabled. When they try to enable it via the AWS CLI (`aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled,MFADelete=Enabled`), they get an error. What is the issue? ; MFA Delete can only be enabled by the root account user (not IAM users or roles), and requires an MFA token as part of the request. CLI command requires `--mfa` parameter: `aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket NAME --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled,MFADelete=Enabled --mfa "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:mfa/root-account-mfa-device MFA_CODE"`. Must use root credentials + MFA device. <br><br> *MFA Delete root-only requirement: only the bucket owner's root account can enable/disable MFA Delete. IAM users and roles (even AdministratorAccess) cannot enable MFA Delete — 403 error. Reason: MFA Delete is a safeguard against compromised admin credentials — if an admin account is taken over, attacker still can't delete versioned objects without root MFA. Root account + MFA device = highest trust level required for this action.<br> *Practical implementation: (1) Enable MFA on the root account (virtual or hardware MFA device). (2) Log in as root user (not federated, not IAM). (3) Generate MFA code from root MFA device. (4) Run CLI command with `--mfa` parameter. (5) Verify: `aws s3api get-bucket-versioning` shows `MFADelete: Enabled`. (6) Log out of root immediately (security best practice: root should not be used for daily operations).<br> *Compliance note: MFA Delete enables requirement for MFA token on every delete request for versioned objects and version management operations. Even if attacker steals IAM admin credentials: cannot delete versions without MFA. Combined with Object Lock: belt-and-suspenders. Some organizations prefer Object Lock Compliance mode (simpler, no MFA device dependency) over MFA Delete. Both provide deletion protection but via different mechanisms.<br>

1079. [ S3 ] A media company uploads raw video files to S3, and a video transcoding pipeline processes them. They want to trigger the pipeline automatically but only when the upload is complete (not during multipart upload). How do you ensure the event fires only after the complete file is available? ; S3 ObjectCreated:CompleteMultipartUpload event notification (not ObjectCreated:* which also fires on PutObject of individual parts). For multipart uploads: only `CompleteMultipartUpload` signals the final assembled file. Use event filter: `{"Filter": {"Key": {"FilterRules": [{"Name": "suffix", "Value": ".mp4"}]}}}` + event type `s3:ObjectCreated:CompleteMultipartUpload`. For PutObject (small files): use `s3:ObjectCreated:Put`. For all creates: `s3:ObjectCreated:*` fires only once per complete object (PutObject and CompleteMultipartUpload are both "complete" events — intermediate part uploads don't trigger ObjectCreated). <br><br> *S3 event types: `s3:ObjectCreated:Put` (single PutObject), `s3:ObjectCreated:Post` (browser POST), `s3:ObjectCreated:Copy` (CopyObject), `s3:ObjectCreated:CompleteMultipartUpload` (final multipart assembly). `s3:ObjectCreated:*` = all of the above. There's NO event for individual part uploads (`UploadPart` API) — S3 events only fire on complete, addressable objects. Misconception: developers sometimes think multipart uploads fire events for each part. They don't — only CompleteMultipartUpload fires.<br> *Lambda timeout for large video: 15-minute Lambda limit. For a 100 GB raw video file: Lambda cannot transcode (too large). Lambda role: validate upload, extract metadata, submit transcoding job to MediaConvert or Step Functions (Fargate). Lambda doesn't do the transcoding — it orchestrates the pipeline. Lambda triggered by S3 event → submits MediaConvert job → MediaConvert transcodes asynchronously → writes output to S3 → EventBridge notifies on MediaConvert job completion.<br> *File size validation in Lambda: Lambda reads S3 object metadata (HeadObject or event's `size` field). `event.Records[0].s3.object.size`. Filter: if size < 1 MB (probably corrupt/test): skip processing. If size > 50 GB: route to high-capacity Fargate task. If size 1-50 GB: standard MediaConvert job. Lambda event routing based on file size metadata.<br>

1080. [ S3 ] A company's S3 bucket has multiple prefixes with different access patterns. The team wants different storage classes for different prefixes but a single lifecycle policy is getting complex and hard to maintain. How do you simplify per-prefix lifecycle management? ; Use Object Tags for lifecycle rule targeting (instead of prefix-based rules). Tag objects at upload time with `storage-tier=hot`, `storage-tier=warm`, `storage-tier=cold`. Lifecycle rules use tag filters: `{"Filter": {"Tag": {"Key": "storage-tier", "Value": "warm"}}}`. Changing an object's lifecycle behavior: update its tag (no lifecycle rule changes needed). Simplifies: one lifecycle rule per tag value, applicable to any prefix. <br><br> *Tag-based lifecycle benefits: prefix changes don't break lifecycle rules. Objects from any prefix with `storage-tier=cold` follow the cold lifecycle (365-day transition). New prefixes automatically participate if tagged correctly. Lifecycle management: change the tag on an object to change its lifecycle. No IAM required for lifecycle changes — just tag updates (lower-privilege operation).<br> *Tag-based lifecycle example: `[{"ID": "warm-data", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Tag": {"Key": "storage-tier", "Value": "warm"}}, "Transitions": [{"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA"}]}, {"ID": "archive-data", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Tag": {"Key": "storage-tier", "Value": "cold"}}, "Transitions": [{"Days": 0, "StorageClass": "GLACIER_IR"}]}]`. Day 0 transition: immediately move to the specified storage class on creation (for objects already tagged as cold at upload time).<br> *Combining prefix + tag filters: lifecycle rules support `And` filter combining prefix + tag: `{"And": {"Prefix": "logs/", "Tags": [{"Key": "env", "Value": "prod"}]}}`. For complex multi-dimensional filtering: combine prefix (for namespace) + tag (for data classification). Reduces the number of lifecycle rules vs purely prefix-based (many prefixes × many rules = complexity).<br>

1081. [ S3 ] A company needs to provide temporary access to S3 objects to external partners without using AWS credentials. Partners use a variety of programming languages and platforms. What is the most universal access mechanism? ; Presigned URLs: standard HTTPS URL that includes the AWS authentication information embedded in query parameters. Partners use any HTTP client (curl, wget, browser, any language's HTTP library) to access the URL. No AWS SDK required. No AWS credentials required. Works from any platform. Expires after configured duration. <br><br> *Presigned URL universality: just an HTTPS GET request with query parameters. `curl "https://BUCKET.s3.REGION.amazonaws.com/KEY?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Credential=...&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Signature=..."`. Python, Java, Go, JavaScript, Bash, PHP, Ruby — any HTTP client works. No AWS SDK installation on partner machines. Browser download link works directly.<br> *Presigned URL generation best practices: generate on server side (backend), not client side. Expiry: 5 minutes for sensitive data, 1 hour for typical use, 7 days maximum. Use IAM role credentials (not long-lived access keys) for signing. Store generation timestamp in DynamoDB for audit. `aws s3 presign s3://BUCKET/KEY --expires-in 3600` (1 hour). Python: `s3_client.generate_presigned_url('get_object', Params={'Bucket': BUCKET, 'Key': KEY}, ExpiresIn=3600)`.<br> *Security considerations: presigned URLs are bearer tokens — anyone with the URL can access the object during the expiry window. Don't log presigned URLs in application logs (they contain authentication info). Use short expiry + HTTPS only. If compromised: revoke by deleting the object or rotating the signing credentials (all previous presigned URLs become invalid if the underlying IAM credentials are rotated).<br>

1082. [ S3 ] A company runs Apache Spark jobs on EMR that process hundreds of TB of data stored in S3. Jobs are slow because Spark tasks wait on S3 API calls. Network bandwidth from EMR to S3 is not the bottleneck — API call latency is. How do you optimize? ; S3 request rate optimization: distribute objects across many prefixes (hash sharding of object keys). Use EMRFS (EMR File System) with S3 access optimization settings. Enable EMR's S3 Select pushdown (filter data at S3, not Spark). Use Parquet format with predicate pushdown. EMRFS `fs.s3.maxConnections=200` (increase connection pool). Use S3 Express One Zone (Directory Buckets) for ultra-low latency scratch data. <br><br> *EMRFS S3 API optimization: `fs.s3.maxConnections` (default 50): increase to 200-500 for high-parallelism Spark. `fs.s3.maxRetries`: set higher for transient throttling. Enable EMRFS consistent view (uses DynamoDB to track S3 metadata — eliminates eventual consistency issues for Spark checkpointing). EMR instance types: m5.4xlarge has 10 Gbps network. For S3-intensive workloads: ensure network bandwidth matches expected S3 throughput (25 Gbps with c5n instances for very high throughput).<br> *S3 Express One Zone for hot data: 10× lower latency than S3 Standard for API calls. For Spark shuffle or intermediate results: use S3 Express One Zone scratch bucket instead of standard S3. Shuffle data read/written thousands of times during Spark job: latency reduction from S3 Express improves job completion significantly. Cost: $0.16/GB/month (vs $0.023 Standard) — justified for temporary scratch data (delete after job).<br> *Columnar + predicate pushdown: Parquet with `snappy` compression + Spark's Parquet reader pushes `WHERE` clause filters to the column file level. `spark.read.parquet().filter("status = 'error'")` reads only the status column from storage, not all 50 columns. S3 Select: Spark can optionally push CSV/JSON filter to S3 Select (server-side filtering before data reaches Spark). For Parquet: Spark's native predicate pushdown is more efficient than S3 Select.<br>

1083. [ S3 ] A company stores business documents in S3. Some documents contain personally identifiable information (PII). The company needs to identify all documents containing PII before a compliance audit in 30 days. There are 50 million documents. How do you complete this in time? ; Amazon Macie: create a discovery job on the S3 buckets. Macie uses ML + managed data identifiers to detect PII (SSNs, credit cards, emails, driver's licenses, passport numbers, custom identifiers). 50 million documents: Macie processes in parallel. Estimated time: 50 million × average processing time per document (depends on size). Enable sampling to prioritize high-risk prefixes. Export findings to Security Hub + EventBridge for dashboard visibility. <br><br> *Macie capacity: processes up to 5 GB/minute per account (managed by AWS, scales automatically). For 50 million small documents (avg 10 KB): 500 GB total. At 5 GB/min: ~100 minutes for all documents. Well within 30-day deadline. For large documents: assess total GB volume, not just document count.<br> *Macie findings: `SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal`, `SensitiveData:S3Object/Financial`, etc. For each finding: object ARN, sensitive data type, locations within the object (byte offsets), count of instances. Export to S3 as JSON for further analysis. Athena query on Macie findings: `SELECT bucket, key, category, COUNT(sensitiveData) FROM macie_findings GROUP BY bucket, key, category ORDER BY count DESC`.<br> *Remediation after discovery: Macie identifies → Lambda triggered by finding → apply object tag `pii-classification=contains-pii` → bucket policy restricts access to objects with PII tag (only authorized roles can read PII-tagged objects) → S3 Object Lambda masks PII for other readers. Macie custom identifiers: add company-specific patterns (employee IDs, internal codes) beyond Macie's managed identifiers. 30-day timeline: Macie discovery (week 1) → findings review (week 2) → remediation (weeks 3-4).<br>

1084. [ S3 ] A company wants to replicate an S3 bucket to another region but only objects with a specific tag (`replicate=true`). 70% of objects should NOT be replicated. How do you configure this? ; S3 Replication rule with tag filter: `"Filter": {"Tag": {"Key": "replicate", "Value": "true"}}`. Only objects with `replicate=true` tag are replicated to the destination bucket. Objects without the tag (70%): stay in source only. Tag objects at upload time via application code or Lambda. S3 Replication automatically applies the filter per-object at replication decision time. <br><br> *Tag-based replication filter: `{"Rules": [{"Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Tag": {"Key": "replicate", "Value": "true"}}, "Destination": {"Bucket": "arn:aws:s3:::destination-bucket"}}]}`. Only objects created/modified after rule creation with matching tag are replicated. Existing objects without the tag: not replicated. New objects without the tag: not replicated. Simple, no additional components needed.<br> *Combined prefix + tag filter: `{"And": {"Prefix": "critical/", "Tags": [{"Key": "replicate", "Value": "true"}]}}`. Only objects in `critical/` prefix AND tagged for replication. Two-dimensional filter for precise control. Prefix scopes the replication namespace, tag controls per-object replication opt-in.<br> *Retroactive tagging for existing objects: existing objects don't have the tag. S3 Batch Operations: add `replicate=true` tag to selected existing objects → triggers replication (Batch Replication) for those objects. Or: S3 Batch Operations with `ReplicateObject` action directly (bypasses tag filter — replicates explicitly selected objects regardless of tags). Two paths: ongoing replication (tag filter) and one-time historical backfill (Batch Replication).<br>

1085. [ S3 ] A startup's application architecture uses S3 as both object storage AND for simple key-value lookups. The team is calling `GetObject` for tiny (<1 KB) JSON blobs millions of times per day. Latency is critical. Is S3 the right tool for this, and if not, what should they use? ; S3 is NOT optimized for high-frequency tiny object lookup. S3 GetObject latency: 10-100ms per request. For millions of lookups/day with latency requirements: use DynamoDB (single-digit millisecond latency) or ElastiCache Redis/Memcached (sub-millisecond latency) for key-value lookups. S3 is wrong for this access pattern — it's optimized for large object storage, not KV lookup. <br><br> *S3 latency characteristics: first-byte latency 10-100ms per object. Very different from DynamoDB: 1-10ms, or ElastiCache: <1ms. For 1 million lookups/day at 100ms each: 100,000 seconds of aggregate wait time per day. At $0.0004/1,000 GET requests: $0.40/day in costs (moderate). Latency: the primary concern.<br> *DynamoDB for KV: same key-value schema as S3 object. DynamoDB table: PK = object key, attribute = JSON blob. GetItem: 1-5ms, consistent performance, auto-scaling. For <400 KB items: perfect DynamoDB use case. If blobs are <400 KB: DynamoDB is a drop-in replacement for the "key → tiny JSON blob" pattern. No separate storage service needed.<br> *Hybrid pattern: store infrequently changed configuration/metadata blobs in S3 (correct tool for persistence, durability, audit trail). Cache in ElastiCache/DAX: application reads from cache first. Cache miss: reads from S3, populates cache. Cache TTL: 5 minutes. Effectively: S3 latency = only on cache misses (rare). DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator): in-memory cache for DynamoDB. If already using DynamoDB: DAX reduces read latency to microseconds. Application sees <1ms for cached items.<br>

1086. [ S3 ] A company stores audit logs in S3 for 7 years (regulatory requirement). Each year generates 50 TB of logs. After year 3 (150 TB stored), S3 costs are $3,450/month (Standard storage). How do you achieve 90% cost reduction while maintaining 7-year retention and monthly access for audits? ; Transition to Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days (regulatory access: monthly = acceptable 12-hour retrieval time). `DEEP_ARCHIVE` at $0.00099/GB/month. 150 TB × $0.00099 × 1,024 = $152/month (vs $3,450/month). 95.6% reduction. S3 Lifecycle: `Transition: Days 30, StorageClass: DEEP_ARCHIVE`. Monthly audit retrieval: submit restoration request at beginning of month (Standard: 12 hours). <br><br> *Glacier Deep Archive retrieval for audits: Bulk retrieval: $0.0025/GB. Monthly audit download (say 1 TB of logs per audit): $2.56/month in retrieval costs. Total: $152/month storage + $2.56/month retrieval = $154.56/month vs $3,450/month. 95.5% cost reduction. One lifecycle rule change achieves this.<br> *Retrieval workflow for audits: first day of month → submit batch restore: `aws s3api restore-object --bucket logs-bucket --key PREFIX --restore-request '{"Days": 7, "GlacierJobParameters": {"Tier": "Standard"}}'`. Standard retrieval: 12 hours. Objects restored to temporary S3 for 7 days. Audit team queries with Athena during the 7-day window. After 7 days: objects return to Deep Archive (cost minimized). Lifecycle: expire objects after exactly 7 years (no indefinite retention).<br> *Cost growth projection: 50 TB/year, all in Deep Archive after 30 days. Year 7: 350 TB stored. Cost: 350 × 1,024 GB × $0.00099 = $355/month. Plus 50 TB of current-year data in Standard for first 30 days: minimal. Full 7-year retention at ~$355/month max. Without optimization: $8,050/month at year 7 (350 TB Standard). 95.6% cost difference maintained throughout retention period.<br>

1087. [ S3 ] A company receives daily CSV files from 50 partner companies via SFTP. Currently managed by an on-premises SFTP server that uploads to S3. The on-premises server is expensive to maintain. How do you migrate to a fully managed AWS solution? ; AWS Transfer Family with S3 backend: managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoint. Partners connect to Transfer Family SFTP endpoint (same SFTP protocol, no partner changes). Transfer Family authenticates via SSH key or Lambda custom authorizer. Files delivered directly to S3 (no intermediate server). Serverless, no maintenance. <br><br> *AWS Transfer Family: managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 service. Partners use standard SFTP clients (FileZilla, WinSCP, command-line sftp). Transfer Family server endpoint replaces the on-premises SFTP server. Authentication: SSH public keys (stored in Transfer Family user configuration) or custom Lambda authorizer (for enterprise SSO integration). Each partner's SFTP user maps to a specific S3 prefix: `s3://bucket/partner-name/`.<br> *S3 event integration: Transfer Family delivers files to S3. S3 ObjectCreated event → Lambda → process partner file. Same S3-event-based processing pipeline works regardless of how the file arrived (SFTP, direct S3 upload, API Gateway). Transfer Family is transparent — just an SFTP-compatible frontend for S3.<br> *Cost comparison: on-premises SFTP server: hardware, software licensing, maintenance, SLA overhead. Transfer Family: $0.30/hour per enabled endpoint ($216/month for 1 server) + $0.04/GB transferred. For 50 partners × 1 GB/day = 50 GB/day × $0.04 = $2/day + $7.20/day endpoint = $9.20/day = $278/month. Compare to on-premises server total cost of ownership (usually $10,000-50,000+/year). Transfer Family wins on cost and eliminates maintenance burden.<br>

1088. [ S3 ] After enabling S3 Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) on a bucket, a web browser still shows CORS errors when making JavaScript fetch requests. What are the most common misconfigurations? ; Most common CORS issues: (1) Origin mismatch: `AllowedOrigins` has `https://example.com` but browser sends `http://example.com` (HTTP vs HTTPS). (2) Wildcard with credentials: `AllowedOrigins: ["*"]` + `AllowCredentials: true` — browsers reject this combination. (3) Missing `AllowedHeaders` for custom headers. (4) Missing preflight (OPTIONS) support: `AllowedMethods` missing `GET` or `OPTIONS`. (5) Multiple CORS rules conflict. <br><br> *CORS rule anatomy: `AllowedOrigins` (exact match, no wildcard in path), `AllowedMethods`, `AllowedHeaders`, `MaxAgeSeconds` (preflight cache), `ExposeHeaders` (headers accessible to JS). Preflight: browser sends OPTIONS first. S3 must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods. `AllowedMethods` must include `GET` and any other method used by JS. Missing `ExposeHeaders`: JS can't read custom response headers (like ETag or custom metadata headers).<br> *Debugging CORS: (1) Check S3 CORS configuration: `aws s3api get-bucket-cors --bucket NAME`. (2) Test with curl: `curl -H "Origin: https://example.com" -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: GET" -X OPTIONS https://BUCKET.s3.REGION.amazonaws.com/KEY -v`. Check response headers for CORS headers. (3) Browser DevTools → Network tab → failed preflight OPTIONS request → check response headers.<br> *Complete CORS config example: `[{"AllowedHeaders": ["*"], "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD"], "AllowedOrigins": ["https://myapp.example.com"], "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag", "x-amz-request-id"], "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000}]`. Minimal for a web app serving S3 content to a specific origin. Avoid `"*"` for AllowedOrigins if dealing with credentials or sensitive data. Use specific origins for production.<br>

1089. [ S3 ] A company wants to store objects in S3 with immutable metadata that tracks who approved the object and when. Objects should be searchable by approval status and approver. Standard S3 metadata is mutable (can be overwritten via CopyObject). How do you store immutable approval metadata? ; Store approval metadata in a separate DynamoDB table (not in S3 metadata). When an object is approved: Lambda writes to DynamoDB: `{ObjectKey: "key", ApprovedBy: "user@company.com", ApprovedAt: "2025-01-15T10:00:00Z", ApprovalStatus: "approved"}`. Query DynamoDB for objects by approval status. DynamoDB is append-only (don't overwrite — add new approval records). S3 Object Lock ensures the objects themselves can't be modified. <br><br> *S3 metadata immutability problem: `CopyObject` can update metadata by copying to the same key with new metadata. Even with versioning: a new version has different metadata than the old version (metadata is per-version). Cannot prevent metadata modification via S3 mechanisms. External metadata store (DynamoDB) is mutable-proof: IAM controls who can write to DynamoDB, CloudTrail logs all DynamoDB changes, DynamoDB Streams create audit trail.<br> *DynamoDB for S3 metadata: common pattern for S3 workloads requiring rich metadata and search. S3 object tags (limited to 10 tags, simple KV) vs DynamoDB (unlimited attributes, complex queries, GSI for secondary indexes). DynamoDB GSI on `ApprovalStatus` field: query all approved objects efficiently. On `ApprovedBy` field: get all objects approved by a specific person. Neither query is possible natively in S3.<br> *Linking DynamoDB to S3: use S3 object's ETag or VersionId as part of the DynamoDB item. Approval record includes `ETag: "abc123"` → proves the approval was for the specific content hash. If object is modified (new version): ETag changes → old approval record has old ETag → approval is for specific content, not just key name. Cryptographic content binding in the approval record.<br>

1090. [ S3 ] A company is designing a data lake for a global financial services firm. Requirements: (1) data must reside in specific geographic regions (data sovereignty), (2) sub-100ms query latency for recent data (last 7 days), (3) cost-efficient storage for historical data (5+ years), (4) ACID transactions for concurrent writers, (5) compliance: all access audited, encryption at rest and in transit, 7-year retention with immutability. Design the complete S3 architecture. ; Multi-region S3 buckets with data residency constraints + Apache Iceberg for ACID + tiered storage + Object Lock. Architecture: Regional S3 buckets (EU: eu-central-1, US: us-east-1, APAC: ap-southeast-1). S3 MRAP (data stays in origin region). Iceberg tables (ACID transactions, schema evolution). Hot tier (last 7 days) in Standard + ElastiCache or Athena with Iceberg caching. Cold tier lifecycle to Glacier. Object Lock Compliance (7-year). CloudTrail + Macie + KMS. <br><br> *Data sovereignty enforcement: S3 bucket in each regulated region. SCP preventing CreateBucket or CopyObject across geographic boundaries (`aws:RequestedRegion` condition). MRAP for global application access (routes to nearest bucket without copying data). Replication: only within allowed regions (EU → EU: allowed. EU → US: SCP Deny). AWS Config: validate no cross-boundary replication rules exist. Evidence: Config compliance report shows all replication rules stay within approved regions.<br> *Apache Iceberg for ACID: Iceberg metadata (manifests, manifest lists) stored in S3. Iceberg transactions: optimistic concurrency control. Multiple writers: each writer commits a new Iceberg snapshot. Conflicts: detected via snapshot comparison. Athena + Iceberg: ACID insert, update, delete. `INSERT INTO orders VALUES (...)` with full transaction guarantees. No more partial write corruption in S3 data lake (classic S3 eventual consistency issue pre-Iceberg).<br> *Sub-100ms for recent data: Athena with Iceberg partition pruning (`WHERE event_date >= current_date - 7`). Last 7 days: small Iceberg partitions, quickly scanned. Athena provisioned capacity: eliminates cold start. For true <100ms: cache Iceberg metadata in ElastiCache. Or: DynamoDB Hot Tier for recent objects (copy latest 7 days to DynamoDB via Lambda, query DynamoDB at 5ms, Iceberg for historical). Business decision: 100ms acceptable = Athena + Iceberg. 5ms required = DynamoDB hybrid.<br> *Object Lock + Lifecycle: Iceberg data files: `RetainUntilDate = creation + 7 years` (Compliance mode). Iceberg metadata files: lifecycle expiration after Iceberg garbage collection (Iceberg `expire_snapshots` procedure manages metadata lifecycle). S3 Glacier Deep Archive for data > 90 days old (lifecycle transition). Object Lock prevents Glacier Deep Archive objects from being deleted before 7 years. Complete: data sovereignty + ACID + performance + cost optimization + compliance.<br>

1091. [ IAM ] A company has Account A (dev) and Account B (prod). A developer in Account A needs to read objects from an S3 bucket in Account B. What is the minimum configuration required? ; Two-sided authorization: (1) Account A: developer's IAM role needs `sts:AssumeRole` permission for the Account B role ARN. (2) Account B: IAM role trust policy must allow `sts:AssumeRole` from Account A principal. THEN: Account B role permission policy grants `s3:GetObject`. Without BOTH sides: access denied. <br><br> *Why both sides: AWS cross-account evaluation requires identity-based policy (Account A side) AND trust relationship (Account B side). Account A's SCP must also not deny sts:AssumeRole. Account B's SCP must not deny s3:GetObject. If Account B instead used a bucket policy granting Account A directly: Account A identity-based policy must also allow s3:GetObject — again both sides needed. There is no single-sided cross-account access in AWS.*<br> *Trust policy in Account B role: `{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_A:role/DevRole"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}`. Permission policy on Account B role: `{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::prod-bucket/*"}`. Account A DevRole policy: `{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"sts:AssumeRole","Resource":"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_B:role/CrossAccountRole"}`.*<br>

1092. [ IAM ] A solutions architect is told: "Developers can create IAM roles for their services, but they must not be able to create roles with more permissions than they themselves have." What IAM feature enforces this? ; Permission Boundaries. When a developer creates a role, they must attach a specific permission boundary policy (enforced via an IAM condition: `iam:PermissionsBoundary = arn:aws:iam::123:policy/DevBoundary`). The created role's effective permissions = intersection of its attached policies AND the boundary — cannot exceed the boundary.
