Developer cannot grant a role permissions they don't have themselves. <br><br> *Without permission boundaries: a developer with `iam:CreateRole` + `iam:AttachRolePolicy` can create a role with AdministratorAccess — a privilege escalation attack. With permission boundaries: `{"Effect":"Deny","Action":"iam:CreateRole","Resource":"*","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"iam:PermissionsBoundary":"arn:aws:iam::123:policy/DevBoundary"}}}` — deny role creation unless boundary is attached. Developer self-service with guardrails.*<br> *Permission boundary = ceiling, not grant. If boundary allows S3 but role policy allows EC2: effective = neither (no intersection). If boundary allows S3 and EC2, role policy allows S3: effective = S3. Boundary never adds permissions — only caps them. Used by AWS Control Tower to govern account factory roles.*<br>

1093. [ IAM ] A company's S3 bucket has this bucket policy: `"Effect":"Deny","Principal":"*","Action":"s3:*","Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:SecureTransport":"false"}}`. An IAM user with `s3:GetObject` permission gets a 403 when using HTTP. When switching to HTTPS, they still get 403. What else is wrong? ; The user's identity-based policy must still explicitly allow `s3:GetObject`. The bucket policy deny (for HTTP) blocks HTTP — correct. But switching to HTTPS removes the explicit deny. Then falls back to default deny — no explicit allow from any policy. The user needs BOTH: HTTPS (to pass the bucket policy condition) AND an explicit allow in identity-based policy OR bucket policy. <br><br> *Evaluation order: Explicit deny (HTTP condition) → triggers deny. HTTPS: condition false → deny does NOT apply → falls to explicit allow check → identity policy must allow s3:GetObject. If identity policy has the allow → access granted. If identity policy is missing the allow → implicit deny (default). The `SecureTransport` deny policy is a negative control only — it doesn't grant anything. Fix: ensure identity-based policy explicitly allows s3:GetObject.*<br> *Common mistake: administrators add the SecureTransport deny to "secure" the bucket but forget that it only blocks HTTP — it doesn't replace the need for explicit allows. Same bucket policy must include an Allow statement OR rely on identity policies for grants.*<br>

1094. [ IAM ] A Lambda function in Account A needs to invoke another Lambda function in Account B. What are the two approaches, and which is preferred? ; Approach 1 (resource-based): add a resource-based policy to Account B Lambda allowing Account A Lambda's execution role to invoke it — no role assumption needed, simpler. Approach 2 (role assumption): Account A Lambda assumes a cross-account role in Account B, then calls Lambda. Preferred: Approach 1 (resource-based policy) for Lambda-to-Lambda — no AssumeRole latency overhead, simpler configuration. <br><br> *Resource-based approach: `aws lambda add-permission --function-name AccountBFunction --principal arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_A:role/LambdaExecRole --action lambda:InvokeFunction --statement-id cross-account-invoke`. Account A Lambda's execution role needs `lambda:InvokeFunction` on the Account B function ARN in its identity policy. Both sides covered: resource policy (Account B) + identity policy (Account A).*<br> *Role assumption adds latency: sts:AssumeRole call = extra API call before the Lambda invoke. For synchronous invocations where latency matters: avoid role assumption. For async invocations or complex cross-account workflows with multiple services: role assumption may be cleaner (one assume → use credentials for multiple service calls). Lambda resource-based policy supports cross-account via Principal = specific role ARN (not the whole account).*<br>

1095. [ IAM ] An EC2 instance has an IAM instance profile attached with S3 read access. A developer SSH'd into the instance runs `aws s3 cp s3://bucket/file.txt .` and gets Access Denied. The IAM role clearly has s3:GetObject. What could cause this? ; Multiple possible causes: (1) IMDSv2 required but application/CLI not using it — credentials not retrieved. (2) An explicit deny in an SCP or bucket policy overrides the allow. (3) The S3 bucket is in a different account and has no bucket policy allowing this account. (4) VPC endpoint policy on the S3 gateway endpoint is restricting access. (5) Object is encrypted with a KMS key the role has no `kms:Decrypt` permission for. <br><br> *IMDSv2 check: `curl -X PUT "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token" -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600"` returns token. If IMDSv2 is enforced and old metadata retrieval fails: CLI can't get credentials → uses no credentials → access denied. Fix: `aws configure` with explicit keys (workaround) or fix IMDS configuration.*<br> *VPC endpoint policy: if VPC has an S3 gateway endpoint with a restrictive policy (e.g., allows only specific buckets), access to other buckets fails. Check: `aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints` and review endpoint policy. The endpoint policy AND IAM role AND bucket policy all participate in evaluation. S3 gateway endpoint = free, but endpoint policy is an additional authorization layer.*<br>

1096. [ IAM ] What is the difference between `aws:SourceIp` and `aws:VpcSourceIp` condition keys? ; `aws:SourceIp`: the public IP of the request origin. Does NOT work for requests through VPC endpoints (those arrive without a public IP). `aws:VpcSourceIp`: the private IP within the VPC — only applies when request comes through a VPC endpoint. For S3 bucket policies restricting VPC-only access: use `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:VpcSourceIp` (not `aws:SourceIp` which would deny all VPC traffic). <br><br> *Critical exam distinction: a bucket policy with `"Deny if aws:SourceIp not in [corporate_IPs]"` accidentally blocks ALL VPC endpoint traffic (VPC traffic has no source IP matching corporate range). Fix: `"Deny if aws:SourceIp not in [corporate_IPs] AND aws:SourceVpc != vpc-xxxx"` — allow either corporate IP OR VPC source. Or better: separate the conditions — one deny for non-corporate internet, one allow for VPC.*<br> *aws:VpcSourceIp use case: restrict S3 access to specific private IP ranges within VPC (e.g., only allow access from 10.0.1.0/24 subnet — the data processing subnet). aws:SourceVpc: coarser — allows any private IP within the VPC. aws:VpcSourceIp: finer — specific private IP ranges. For endpoint-only access: `Condition: StringEquals: aws:SourceVpc: vpc-xxxxx` is the most common approach.*<br>

1097. [ IAM ] A company uses AWS Organizations with 50 accounts. They want to prevent any account from disabling CloudTrail. What is the correct approach? ; Attach an SCP to the Root OU (or all OUs) denying `cloudtrail:DeleteTrail`, `cloudtrail:StopLogging`, `cloudtrail:UpdateTrail`. SCPs apply to all accounts and all principals (including account root users) in member accounts. Even an account administrator cannot override an SCP. Combined with CloudTrail organization trail (managed from management account): audit trail is protected across the entire org. <br><br> *SCP: `{"Effect":"Deny","Action":["cloudtrail:DeleteTrail","cloudtrail:StopLogging","cloudtrail:UpdateTrail","cloudtrail:PutEventSelectors"],"Resource":"*"}`. Attach to Root OU — applies to all 50 accounts. Even if a developer has AdministratorAccess in their account: cannot stop CloudTrail. SCP overrides all identity-based policies in member accounts.*<br> *Organization trail: management account creates a trail that applies to ALL accounts in the org. Logs delivered to a centralized S3 bucket in the security account. Member accounts cannot modify or delete the org trail (only management account can). Combination: org trail (collection) + SCP (protection) = comprehensive, tamper-resistant audit logging. AWS Config also monitors: `cloud-trail-enabled` managed rule detects any account where CloudTrail is disabled.*<br>

1098. [ IAM ] What is the confused deputy problem in IAM, and how is ExternalId used to prevent it? ; Confused deputy: a trusted third-party service (deputy) is tricked into acting on behalf of an attacker. Example: Company grants ThirdPartyService a role. Attacker also uses ThirdPartyService, sends company's role ARN → ThirdPartyService assumes company's role on attacker's behalf. ExternalId: a secret token the company shares only with their specific ThirdPartyService account. Trust policy condition: `sts:ExternalId = secret-token`. Attacker doesn't know the ExternalId → AssumeRole fails. <br><br> *Concrete example without ExternalId: Attacker has account 999. They know your role ARN: arn:aws:iam::111:role/ThirdPartyAccess. Attacker tells ThirdPartyService: "assume arn:aws:iam::111:role/ThirdPartyAccess and extract my data from account 999." ThirdPartyService (trusted by you) assumes YOUR role and returns data to the attacker. Your trust policy trusted the ThirdPartyService principal without additional verification.*<br> *ExternalId fix: your trust policy: `{"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"sts:ExternalId":"UNIQUE-SECRET-TOKEN-FOR-YOUR-ACCOUNT"}}}`. ThirdPartyService must pass this token when assuming your role. Attacker doesn't know your ExternalId — their request fails. ExternalId must be unique per customer (not reused across customers) and treated like a secret. Never put ExternalId in code or logs.*<br>

1099. [ IAM ] A company wants to enforce that all IAM roles created in their accounts can only be assumed from within the AWS organization. How do you implement this at scale? ; Use an SCP that denies `iam:CreateRole` unless the trust policy contains `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition for their organization. OR: use a permission boundary on all created roles that includes a deny for `sts:AssumeRole` from outside the org. Better: use AWS Control Tower + Customizations for Control Tower (CfCT) to automatically attach an organization-based trust policy template to all new roles. <br><br> *SCP approach limitation: SCPs can't inspect the content of a trust policy being created (SCP conditions don't read the role's trust policy document). Alternative: AWS Config rule + Lambda auto-remediation — detect roles with trusts outside the org and modify/alert. AWS Config custom rule: evaluate all IAM roles, flag any with Principal not constrained to `aws:PrincipalOrgID`. Lambda remediation: add deny condition to trust policy of non-compliant roles.*<br> *IAM Identity Center approach: if all role assumptions go through IAM Identity Center (permission sets), the underlying roles created by Identity Center automatically trust only the Identity Center SAML provider (org-internal). External assumption of these roles is prevented by design. For workload roles (not human access): enforce via code review + SCPs + Config rules as defense-in-depth.*<br>

1100. [ IAM ] A developer needs temporary elevated access to production for a hotfix. The company wants to implement just-in-time (JIT) access with approval workflow. What AWS-native architecture supports this? ; IAM Identity Center with approval workflow: define a permission set for elevated prod access. Use IAM Identity Center's temporary elevated access feature (TEAM) or build custom: Step Functions approval workflow → Lambda assumes a role with time-limited session → CloudWatch Events auto-revokes after N hours. Or: AWS Service Catalog self-service portal + Lambda + IAM. CloudTrail captures all elevated actions for audit. <br><br> *Custom JIT architecture: (1) Developer requests access via internal ticketing (Jira/ServiceNow). (2) Step Functions workflow: notify approver via SNS/Slack. (3) Approver clicks approve link (API Gateway → Lambda). (4) Lambda calls `sts:AssumeRole` with elevated role + short session duration (1-4 hours) + session name = ticket ID. (5) Lambda delivers temporary credentials via Secrets Manager (developer retrieves). (6) CloudWatch Events: after session TTL → Lambda rotates/invalidates credentials. (7) CloudTrail: all actions during elevated session tagged with ticket ID.*<br> *IAM Identity Center TEAM: AWS published a Temporary Elevated Access Management solution (open source on GitHub). Integrates with Identity Center. Manager approves → temporary account assignment → auto-revoked after expiry. Audit: CloudTrail shows assignment/revocation events. This is the preferred AWS-native JIT approach for human access to production environments.*<br>

1101. [ IAM ] An application running on EC2 assumes a cross-account role to access DynamoDB in another account. The application gets an error: "The security token included in the request is expired." The application is long-running (24+ hours). What is the issue? ; STS temporary credentials from AssumeRole expire (max 12 hours, often 1 hour default). Long-running applications must refresh credentials before expiry. Fix: use the AWS SDK's built-in credential refresh (SDK auto-refreshes if using instance profile credentials). If manually calling AssumeRole: implement a background thread that calls AssumeRole again when credentials are within 5 minutes of expiry (`Credentials.Expiration` field in AssumeRole response). <br><br> *SDK credential refresh: AWS SDK for Java/Python/Node automatically refreshes instance profile credentials. But if application calls `sts:AssumeRole` directly and caches the credentials: automatic refresh doesn't apply — application must implement refresh logic. Best practice: use SDK's credential provider chain which handles refresh. For cross-account: use `STSAssumeRoleSessionCredentialsProvider` (Java) or `botocore.credentials.AssumeRoleCredentialFetcher` (Python) — these auto-refresh.*<br> *Session duration: `AssumeRole` default = 1 hour. Maximum = role's `MaxSessionDuration` (1-12 hours). For long-running tasks: increase `MaxSessionDuration` to 12 hours AND implement refresh logic. Or: instead of a single AssumeRole call at startup, call AssumeRole per operation batch (fresh credentials each time). Refresh strategy: check `Credentials.Expiration` before each API call — if < 5 minutes away, refresh. This is the standard pattern for long-lived applications.*<br>

1102. [ IAM ] What is the difference between an IAM role's trust policy and a permission policy? Can you have a role with a trust policy but no permission policy? ; Trust policy: resource-based policy ON the role — defines WHO can assume it (Principal + Action=sts:AssumeRole). Permission policy: identity-based policy ATTACHED to the role — defines WHAT the assumed role can do. Yes — a role with a trust policy but no permission policy is valid. When assumed, the session has zero permissions (can't do anything). Useful: roles for cross-account trust that gain permissions from resource-based policies (e.g., role is trusted by a KMS key policy — key policy grants the permissions, role needs no attached policy). <br><br> *Exam scenario: a role has no attached permission policies. An S3 bucket policy says: `"Principal":"arn:aws:iam::123:role/MinimalRole","Action":"s3:GetObject"`. Developer assumes MinimalRole → can do ONLY s3:GetObject on that bucket (permission comes from the bucket policy, not role's attached policies). In same-account: resource-based policy allow is sufficient without identity-based policy allow. This is a valid architecture.*<br> *KMS key policy special case: KMS key policy alone can grant full key access to a role — no IAM identity policy needed. This is unique to KMS: `"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::123:role/KMSUser"},"Action":["kms:Decrypt","kms:GenerateDataKey"]` in the key policy is sufficient. For most other services: you need identity-based policy on the caller to start using the resource.*<br>

1103. [ IAM ] A company enforces MFA for all AWS Console access. A developer's MFA device is lost. What is the process to recover access, and what IAM operations are involved? ; Recovery process: (1) Another IAM admin (or root account) calls `iam:DeactivateMFADevice` for the lost device. (2) Admin calls `iam:DeleteVirtualMFADevice` to remove the virtual device. (3) Developer registers a new MFA device via `iam:CreateVirtualMFADevice` + `iam:EnableMFADevice`. (4) If no admins available: use root account to access IAM and perform deactivation. Root account itself needs MFA — if root MFA is lost: AWS Support account recovery process. <br><br> *IAM API calls involved: `iam:DeactivateMFADevice` (admin removes current device), `iam:ListMFADevices` (verify devices), `iam:CreateVirtualMFADevice` (create new virtual device — generates QR code), `iam:EnableMFADevice` (user completes enrollment with two consecutive codes). User cannot self-service deactivate their lost MFA (catch-22: MFA required to make changes but device is gone). Requires admin intervention.*<br> *Root account MFA loss: most serious scenario. AWS has an account recovery process requiring: (1) Phone number registered on account. (2) Email address registered on account. (3) Verification process via AWS Support. Takes 24-72 hours. Recommendation: have 2+ hardware MFA tokens for root account stored in separate secure locations. Never rely on virtual MFA only for root. IAM Identity Center: MFA reset can be done by administrators without requiring the root account.*<br>

1104. [ IAM ] A company's security team wants to receive alerts whenever anyone creates a new IAM role with a trust policy allowing external accounts (outside the organization). How do you implement this? ; CloudTrail → EventBridge rule for `CreateRole` API call → Lambda → parse `assumeRolePolicyDocument` from event → check if any Principal is outside the organization's account list → SNS alert. Or: AWS Config custom rule that evaluates all IAM roles and flags external trust relationships → Config notifications → SNS. IAM Access Analyzer also finds external trust relationships automatically. <br><br> *EventBridge rule: `{"source":["aws.iam"],"detail-type":["AWS API Call via CloudTrail"],"detail":{"eventName":["CreateRole","UpdateAssumeRolePolicy"]}}`. Lambda receives event, extracts `requestParameters.assumeRolePolicyDocument`, parses JSON, checks each Statement's Principal for external account IDs or `*`. If external found: `sns:Publish` alert with role ARN, creator ARN, trust policy.*<br> *IAM Access Analyzer: automatically analyzes all role trust policies. External trust = finding with `resourceType: AWS::IAM::Role`. Access Analyzer → EventBridge → Lambda → SNS for real-time alerting on new findings. Advantage over custom Lambda: AWS maintains the analysis logic, handles edge cases, no custom code to maintain. Access Analyzer finding: `{"analyzerArn":"...","resourceType":"AWS::IAM::Role","condition":{},"isPublic":false,"principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::EXTERNAL:root"}}` — clearly identifies the external principal.*<br>

1105. [ IAM ] What happens when an SCP denies an action that a service-linked role needs to perform? ; SCPs do NOT affect service-linked roles. Service-linked roles are explicitly excluded from SCP evaluation. This is by design — AWS needs service-linked roles to function correctly regardless of organization policies. Even `"Effect":"Deny","Action":"*","Principal":"*"` SCP does not block service-linked roles. Only IAM roles, users, and groups are affected by SCPs. <br><br> *Why service-linked roles are exempt: they are pre-defined by AWS with minimum required permissions for the service to function. If SCPs blocked service-linked roles, enabling an SCP could break core AWS services (ELB couldn't create ENIs, Auto Scaling couldn't terminate instances, etc.). AWS guarantees that service-linked role permissions cannot be misused: you cannot modify the permission policy, and the role can only be used by the specific service.*<br> *Practical implication: if your SCP denies `ec2:CreateNetworkInterface` (e.g., region restriction), ELB's service-linked role can still create ENIs for load balancers. But YOUR Lambda function or EC2 instance cannot create ENIs in the denied region. SCP = ceiling for human and application identities, not for service-linked roles. This is tested on the exam: "SCP denies ec2:* — can ELB still function?" Answer: yes, service-linked role is exempt.*<br>

1106. [ IAM ] A company's policy requires that no IAM user should have both AdministratorAccess and access to billing. How do you enforce this across all accounts in an AWS Organization? ; SCP on the root OU: deny attaching AdministratorAccess AND any billing policies simultaneously to the same user. More practical: deny `aws-portal:*` and `budgets:*` billing actions for any principal that has `AdministratorAccess` attached — BUT SCPs cannot condition on which OTHER policies are attached. Better approach: use AWS Config rule + Lambda to detect users with both policy combinations and send alerts. Architectural fix: separate identity (admin) from billing access — use separate IAM users or roles. <br><br> *SCP limitation: SCPs cannot inspect the full set of policies attached to an identity (no condition key for "attached policies"). You can deny specific billing actions globally and create a separate billing role, but you cannot dynamically check "this user also has AdminAccess." Config rule: `iam-user-no-policies-check` + custom rule that evaluates each user's attached policies. If user has both AdministratorAccess and billing policy: alert.*<br> *Architectural solution: activate IAM billing access for the root account. Create a separate `BillingAdmin` role with ONLY billing permissions. No user gets both AdministratorAccess and BillingAdmin role simultaneously — enforce via separation of duties (SoD) — different people hold each role. SCP: `{"Deny":"aws-portal:*","Condition":{"ArnLike":{"aws:PrincipalArn":"arn:aws:iam::*:user/*"}}}` — no IAM user can access billing at all, only via a designated billing role with limited access.*<br>

1107. [ IAM ] What is the difference between `iam:PassRole` and `sts:AssumeRole`? When is each needed? ; `sts:AssumeRole`: a principal calls STS to BECOME a different identity (get temporary credentials). Needed when your code explicitly calls `sts:AssumeRole` to switch identities. `iam:PassRole`: permission to hand a role to an AWS SERVICE so that service can use it. Not a credentials operation — you don't get credentials, the service does. Required whenever you specify a role ARN for a service to use (e.g., launch EC2 with instance profile, create Lambda with execution role, run Glue job with service role). <br><br> *PassRole examples: `aws ec2 run-instances --iam-instance-profile Name=MyProfile` — requires `iam:PassRole` on MyProfile role. `aws lambda create-function --role arn:aws:iam::123:role/LambdaRole` — requires `iam:PassRole` on LambdaRole. `aws glue create-job --role arn:aws:iam::123:role/GlueRole` — requires PassRole on GlueRole. Without PassRole: operation fails with "not authorized to perform iam:PassRole."*<br> *Privilege escalation via unscoped PassRole: if a developer has unscoped `iam:PassRole` (`Resource: "*"`) + `ec2:RunInstances`: they can launch an EC2 instance with an admin role attached, SSH in, and use the admin credentials. PassRole should always be scoped: `"Resource":"arn:aws:iam::123:role/specific-role"` + `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"iam:PassedToService":"ec2.amazonaws.com"}}`. This is a critical exam topic — PassRole is a privilege escalation vector if misconfigured.*<br>

1108. [ IAM ] A company uses SAML federation with their on-premises Active Directory. The AD group "AWS-Admins" should map to AdministratorAccess in a specific AWS account. How does the SAML attribute mapping work? ; SAML assertion from AD must include the `https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/Role` attribute with value = comma-separated RoleArn and SAMLProviderArn: `arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/AdminRole,arn:aws:iam::123456789:saml-provider/MyAD`. AWS ADFS/IdP maps the AD group membership to this SAML attribute. `AssumeRoleWithSAML` uses the assertion to determine which role to assume. Multiple roles possible in one assertion (user can choose). <br><br> *AD → SAML attribute mapping: in ADFS (AD Federation Services) or Okta: create a claim rule that maps AD group membership to the Role SAML attribute. Example ADFS claim rule: `c:[Type == "http://schemas.microsoft.com/ws/2008/06/identity/claims/groupsid", Value == "S-1-5-21-xxx-AdminGroupSID"] => issue(Type = "https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/Role", Value = "arn:aws:iam::123:role/AdminRole,arn:aws:iam::123:saml-provider/ADFS")`. One claim per role per account.*<br> *Session duration: SAML attribute `https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/SessionDuration` controls session length (900-43200 seconds). Set per-group: admins get 1-hour sessions, read-only users get 8-hour sessions. Without this attribute: default 1 hour. The IAM role's MaxSessionDuration is still the hard ceiling — SessionDuration attribute cannot exceed it.*<br>

1109. [ IAM ] What is IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) in EKS, and why is it better than giving EC2 node roles broad permissions? ; IRSA: each Kubernetes pod gets its own IAM role via an OIDC token. Pod A can access S3, Pod B can access DynamoDB — different roles, different permissions. Without IRSA: all pods on the same EC2 node share the node's IAM role. If the node role has S3 + DynamoDB access: every pod (including compromised ones) has full access. IRSA = pod-level least privilege instead of node-level broad access. <br><br> *IRSA mechanism: EKS creates an OIDC provider URL per cluster. IAM role trust policy: `{"Principal":{"Federated":"arn:aws:iam::123:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.region.amazonaws.com/id/XXXX"},"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"oidc.eks.../id/XXXX:sub":"system:serviceaccount:namespace:service-account-name"}}}`. Kubernetes ServiceAccount annotated with role ARN: `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123:role/PodRole`. EKS injects web identity token into pod. AWS SDK in pod automatically exchanges token for temporary credentials.*<br> *Security benefit: compromised pod can only use its assigned role permissions (e.g., read one S3 bucket). Node role: only needs minimal permissions (EKS node bootstrap, ECR pull). Blast radius of pod compromise: limited to that pod's IAM role. Without IRSA: compromised pod has all node permissions — could access production databases, secrets, exfiltrate from all buckets the node can access. IRSA is the mandatory pattern for production EKS security.*<br>

1110. [ IAM ] A company's audit team requires that all API calls made to production AWS accounts be traceable to individual human identities (not a shared service account). Currently, all automation uses a single IAM user "automation-user" with access keys. How do you fix this? ; Replace the shared IAM user with IAM roles: (1) Each automation system/pipeline gets its own role (e.g., `jenkins-deploy-role`, `terraform-apply-role`). (2) CI/CD systems assume their specific role. (3) For CI/CD in GitHub Actions: use OIDC federation — each repo/branch maps to a specific role. (4) For human operations: IAM Identity Center — each person has their own federated identity. CloudTrail then shows the specific role ARN and session name per action. <br><br> *CloudTrail with shared user: `userIdentity.userName = "automation-user"` — no way to distinguish which team, pipeline, or person made the call. CloudTrail with roles: `userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.arn = "arn:aws:iam::123:role/jenkins-deploy-role"` + `userIdentity.sessionContext.attributes.principalId = "jenkins-deploy-role:BuildID-12345"`. Role session name = build ID. Exact pipeline and run is traceable.*<br> *Access key rotation problem: shared access keys are never rotated because multiple systems depend on them. Single point of compromise: any system that has the shared key can impersonate all automation. Roles: automatic credential rotation (STS tokens expire). No long-lived secrets to manage. Each role has separate CloudTrail trail. Each role can be revoked independently (no impact on other automation). Migration: identify all systems using shared key (grep configs/secrets), create per-system roles, update each system, then delete the shared IAM user.*<br>

1111. [ IAM ] What is the maximum session duration for an assumed role, and what factors limit it? ; Hard maximum: 12 hours for most roles. Minimum: 15 minutes. The actual limit is the LOWER of: (1) Role's `MaxSessionDuration` setting (1-12 hours, default 1 hour). (2) Value passed in `--duration-seconds` to AssumeRole call. For roles assumed via console federation (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity/SAML): max 12 hours. Exception: if a role is assumed by another role (role chaining), the maximum is 1 hour — no way to extend. <br><br> *Role chaining limit: RoleA assumes RoleB — maximum session = 1 hour even if both roles have MaxSessionDuration=12hr. Role chaining is discouraged for long-running tasks specifically because of this 1-hour limit. Use direct role assumption instead (application assumes the target role directly, not via an intermediate role).*<br> *Changing MaxSessionDuration: `aws iam update-role --role-name MyRole --max-session-duration 28800` (8 hours). Then caller must also request the longer duration: `aws sts assume-role --duration-seconds 28800 ...`. If MaxSessionDuration=3600 and caller requests 28800: error. If MaxSessionDuration=28800 and caller requests 3600: gets 3600 (caller can always request less). Common exam question: role has MaxSessionDuration=1hr, caller requests 4hr → error (request exceeds role's maximum).*<br>

1112. [ IAM ] A DevOps engineer creates an IAM policy with `"Resource":"*"` and `"Action":"ec2:*"`. Later, a specific EC2 instance tag-based deny is added for production instances. The engineer can still start/stop prod instances. Why? ; Tag-based conditions in Deny statements require the condition to evaluate correctly. If the EC2 instance doesn't have the expected tag, or the tag condition syntax is wrong (`ec2:ResourceTag` requires the instance to already be tagged at launch — tags set after launch may not be reflected in the condition evaluation at the time of the API call). Or: the deny statement's condition is false → deny does not apply → original allow applies. <br><br> *Common tag condition mistake: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"ec2:ResourceTag/env":"prod"}}` in a Deny. If instance has tag `env=prod`: deny applies — correct. If instance has tag `env=production` (typo): condition false → deny does not apply → allow from original policy → engineer can manage "prod" instances with wrong tag value. Solution: use `StringLike` with wildcard or standardize tags via AWS Config + tag policies.*<br> *Tag policies (AWS Organizations): enforce tag key/value standards across the org. `"TagKey":"env","AllowedValues":["prod","staging","dev"]`. Non-compliant tags (e.g., "production") are flagged. Tag policies don't prevent actions — they enforce tag standardization. Combined with SCP or IAM condition: tag-based access control only works if tags are consistent. Enforce tags at resource creation with SCP: deny resource creation without required tags.*<br>

1113. [ IAM ] A company has an on-premises application that needs to call AWS APIs. The application cannot be modified to use IAM roles. What is the most secure credential approach? ; Create a dedicated IAM user for the application with minimum required permissions. Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager (not in config files or code). Application retrieves credentials from Secrets Manager via the API (still needs initial credentials — chicken-and-egg). Better hybrid: use AWS IAM Roles Anywhere. Presents an X.509 certificate from the on-premises CA → AWS STS issues temporary credentials. No static access keys needed. Most secure for on-premises workloads. <br><br> *IAM Roles Anywhere: create an IAM Roles Anywhere Trust Anchor (registers your CA certificate or AWS ACM Private CA). Create a Profile (which roles can be obtained). On-premises server presents X.509 cert → Roles Anywhere validates against the CA → issues temporary STS credentials. `aws_signing_helper` (open source tool) manages the certificate presentation and credential refresh. Same as EC2 instance profile but for on-premises machines.*<br> *If Roles Anywhere not feasible: IAM user + access keys + Secrets Manager. App calls Secrets Manager to get current credentials. Secrets Manager rotates credentials automatically (Lambda rotation function). App always gets fresh credentials. Problem: initial bootstrap (how does app get Secrets Manager credentials?). Solution: use a long-lived "bootstrap" credential with ONLY `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` permission for one specific secret. Rotate the bootstrap credential separately on a schedule. This limits blast radius: compromise of bootstrap credential = only access to retrieve (not use) the actual API credentials.*<br>

1114. [ IAM ] What AWS service provides continuous compliance monitoring for IAM configurations (unused roles, overly permissive policies, missing MFA)? ; AWS Config with IAM managed rules: `iam-user-mfa-enabled`, `iam-root-access-key-check`, `iam-user-no-policies-check`, `iam-policy-no-statements-with-admin-access`, `access-keys-rotated`, `iam-password-policy`. IAM Access Analyzer: `unused-access` analyzer finds unused roles/permissions (90+ days). AWS Security Hub aggregates findings from both Config and Access Analyzer with a compliance score. <br><br> *Key Config rules for IAM: `iam-user-mfa-enabled` (every user has MFA), `iam-root-access-key-check` (root has no access keys), `iam-user-no-policies-check` (users have no directly attached policies — use groups), `iam-policy-no-statements-with-admin-access` (no customer policies with star/star), `access-keys-rotated` (keys rotated within N days), `iam-no-inline-policy-check` (no inline policies). All are periodic rules evaluated on schedule.*<br> *Unused access analyzer (Access Analyzer): identifies IAM roles, users, access keys unused in last 90 days. Specific unused actions per role: "This role was granted s3:PutObject but never used it in 90 days — remove that permission." Enables least-privilege right-sizing automatically. Combined with Config (structural compliance) + Access Analyzer (behavioral compliance): comprehensive IAM hygiene program. Security Hub: compliance score across all IAM findings across all accounts in the org.*<br>

1115. [ IAM ] An IAM role has the `AmazonS3FullAccess` managed policy attached. A new SCP is applied to the account: `Deny s3:DeleteObject on *`. A user assumes this role and tries to delete an S3 object. What happens, and what can the user still do with S3? ; The `s3:DeleteObject` action is denied by the SCP. SCP overrides the role's identity-based policy allow. User gets 403 on DeleteObject. All other S3 actions allowed by `AmazonS3FullAccess` (GetObject, PutObject, ListBucket, etc.) are still available — SCP only denies the specific `s3:DeleteObject` action. Effective permissions = S3 Full Access minus DeleteObject. <br><br> *This demonstrates SCP as a selective restriction: SCPs don't have to deny everything. This SCP is a targeted control — prevent accidental or malicious deletion while allowing full read/write. Common use case: production environment SCP denying delete operations (S3, DynamoDB, RDS). Data can be written but not deleted (protection against ransomware or accidental bulk deletes).*<br> *SCP and all identities: the SCP applies to ALL principals in the account — EC2 instance roles, Lambda execution roles, IAM users, cross-account assumed roles. No identity in this account can call s3:DeleteObject. Exception: service-linked roles (as discussed). Exception 2: management account of the organization — SCPs don't apply to it. This is why the management account should have minimal workloads — it's ungoverned by SCPs.*<br>

1116. [ IAM ] A company wants to implement separation of duties: the person who deploys code cannot also approve deployments. How do you implement this in AWS IAM for a CodePipeline deployment workflow? ; Create two separate IAM roles: `ApproverRole` (can only `codepipeline:PutApprovalResult`) and `DeployerRole` (can trigger pipeline execution but NOT approve). The same person cannot hold both roles simultaneously. Enforce via IAM Identity Center: assign approver group to ApproverRole, deployer group to DeployerRole. Separate AD/IdP groups. Manager ensures no person is in both groups. CodePipeline manual approval step: only ApproverRole can approve. <br><br> *CodePipeline SoD: pipeline stage has a manual approval action. Only identities with `codepipeline:PutApprovalResult` on that specific pipeline/stage can approve. Deployer role has `codepipeline:StartPipelineExecution` but NOT `PutApprovalResult`. Approver role has `PutApprovalResult` but NOT `StartPipelineExecution`. Same person cannot deploy AND approve: they'd need to be in both IAM Identity Center groups — controlled by manager/HR.*<br> *Audit trail: CloudTrail records who called `StartPipelineExecution` (deployer identity) and who called `PutApprovalResult` (approver identity) with session names showing actual human identities via IAM Identity Center federation. Regulatory compliance: SOX, PCI-DSS require SoD for production deployments. IAM + Identity Center + CloudTrail provides the audit evidence. Automated SoD verification: Lambda function that parses CloudTrail → alerts if same person approved and deployed within the same pipeline run.*<br>

1117. [ IAM ] What is the difference between `aws:PrincipalArn` and `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys? ; `aws:PrincipalArn`: the full ARN of the principal making the request (e.g., `arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/MyRole`). Supports wildcards. `aws:PrincipalAccount`: just the account ID of the principal. Use `aws:PrincipalAccount` when you want to allow any identity from a specific account (regardless of role/user). Use `aws:PrincipalArn` when you need to allow/deny a specific identity. <br><br> *Use cases: `aws:PrincipalAccount` = "allow any principal from account 123456789" — useful for S3 bucket policies allowing all internal account access. `aws:PrincipalArn` = "allow only the specific role arn:aws:iam::123:role/AuditRole" — precise control. For `aws:PrincipalArn` with roles: the ARN is the assumed-role ARN format: `arn:aws:sts::123:assumed-role/MyRole/SessionName`. Use wildcard: `arn:aws:sts::123:assumed-role/MyRole/*` to match any session of that role.*<br> *vs aws:userid: `aws:userid` for assumed roles = `ROLEUNIQUEID:SessionName`. Can be used to match on session name (e.g., JobID embedded in session name). `aws:PrincipalArn` for assumed roles matches the role ARN pattern, not session. For service principals: `aws:PrincipalServiceName` = `ec2.amazonaws.com`. Different keys for different principal types — know which to use for each scenario.*<br>

1118. [ IAM ] A company wants to allow its Data Science team to launch SageMaker training jobs but prevent them from using instance types larger than ml.m5.4xlarge (to control costs). How do you implement this? ; IAM condition on `sagemaker:CreateTrainingJob`: `"Condition":{"ForAllValues:StringNotEquals":{"sagemaker:InstanceTypes":["ml.m5.xlarge","ml.m5.2xlarge","ml.m5.4xlarge","ml.c5.xlarge","ml.c5.2xlarge"]}}` → deny if instance type not in the allowed list. Or positive approach: Allow only specific instance types. Combined with AWS Budgets alert for SageMaker spend. <br><br> *SageMaker condition keys: `sagemaker:InstanceTypes` (list of instance types in the request), `sagemaker:VolumeKmsKey` (require KMS encryption), `sagemaker:RootAccess` (deny root access in notebooks), `sagemaker:InterContainerTrafficEncryption`. Use `ForAllValues:StringEquals` to require instance type from allowed set: `"Condition":{"ForAllValues:StringEquals":{"sagemaker:InstanceTypes":["ml.m5.xlarge","ml.m5.2xlarge","ml.m5.4xlarge"]}}`. ForAllValues: ALL values in the request must match the set.*<br> *Cost governance pattern: IAM restricts which instance types can be launched. Service Quotas: request quota decrease for expensive instance types (ml.p4d.24xlarge) in the Data Science account. AWS Budgets: alert when SageMaker spend exceeds threshold. Combined: IAM prevents large instances at the API level (hard limit), Budgets provides spend visibility and alerting. For very strict control: SCP at the account level: deny SageMaker instance types above a certain size (prevents any user from circumventing the IAM policy).*<br>

1119. [ IAM ] An organization has 200 AWS accounts. Each account has a security auditor who needs read-only access to all resources. How do you efficiently manage this access without creating 200 × N IAM users? ; AWS IAM Identity Center: create a permission set `SecurityAudit` with `SecurityAudit` managed policy (or custom read-only policy). Assign the permission set to the security auditor group in Identity Center. Assign to all 200 accounts (or the root OU). Identity Center automatically creates the corresponding IAM role in each account. Auditors authenticate once via corporate SSO → access any assigned account. <br><br> *Without Identity Center: 200 accounts × IAM users = 200 users to manage, 200 password policies, 200 MFA devices, 200 sets of access keys. With Identity Center: one user in IdP (AD/Okta), one group assignment in Identity Center, auto-provisioned roles in all 200 accounts. New account joins org: auto-assigned the SecurityAudit permission set (if assigned to root OU). Auditor leaves company: deprovisioned in IdP → SCIM syncs to Identity Center → access revoked from all 200 accounts simultaneously.*<br> *Permission set = IAM role template: define once, deployed everywhere. `SecurityAudit` AWS managed policy: read-only across most services + `cloudtrail:Get*`, `config:Get*`, `guardduty:Get*`. If custom policy needed: create custom managed policy in Identity Center, it's deployed to each account as an inline policy on the generated IAM role. Audit trail: CloudTrail in each account shows the Identity Center role ARN. CloudTrail org trail: all 200 accounts' CloudTrail forwarded to central bucket in security account — auditors query from one place.*<br>

1120. [ IAM ] A company's application uses `aws:SourceIp` to restrict API access from known office IP ranges. Employees working from home cannot access. What is the correct approach to allow home access without removing the IP restriction? ; Options: (1) VPN — employees connect VPN → traffic appears to come from corporate IP → no IAM changes needed. Best for security. (2) Add home IPs dynamically — complex, not scalable. (3) Require MFA instead of (or in addition to) IP restriction: `"Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}}` — employees with MFA can access from anywhere. (4) AWS Client VPN with Mutual TLS: assigns corporate IP range to VPN clients. <br><br> *MFA-based access is more secure than IP-based: stolen credentials from office IP = access. Stolen credentials with MFA = no access without the physical MFA token. Replace `aws:SourceIp` restriction with MFA requirement for home workers. IAM policy: `"Effect":"Allow","Action":"*","Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}}` — any location, but MFA required. For high-security actions: combine both — MFA required AND source IP restriction (MFA from non-office IP still denied).*<br> *aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: number of seconds since MFA was last verified in the current session. `{"NumericLessThan":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthAge":"3600"}}` — MFA must have been used within the last hour. For sensitive production access: combine with `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` to ensure MFA was actually used (not just enabled). Short age limit (300 seconds) for most sensitive operations (deleting production databases).*<br>

1121. [ IAM ] A company wants to give a third-party security vendor read-only access to their AWS environment for a penetration test lasting 2 weeks. What is the most secure approach? ; Create a time-limited cross-account IAM role with: (1) Trust policy: vendor's AWS account ARN + ExternalId. (2) Permission policy: SecurityAudit managed policy (read-only). (3) IAM condition: `"DateLessThan":{"aws:CurrentTime":"2026-11-15T00:00:00Z"}` to auto-expire the trust. (4) MaxSessionDuration: 4 hours. CloudTrail: all vendor actions logged. Delete role after engagement. <br><br> *Time-limited trust: DateLessThan condition in trust policy means AssumeRole fails after the date even if role still exists. After 2 weeks: vendor loses access automatically without manual intervention. Belt-and-suspenders: set a calendar reminder to delete the role after the engagement (don't rely solely on condition). CloudTrail: vendor's session name = their analyst name (require them to pass their name as session name via their trust agreement).*<br> *ExternalId for penetration test: prevents the vendor from accidentally or maliciously using your role ARN for other clients' tests. Vendor's tool must pass the ExternalId you shared. ExternalId = unique engagement ID (e.g., "PenTest-2026-November-COMPANY"). After engagement: revoke ExternalId (delete role). SecurityAudit policy: excludes write actions and sensitive operations. Explicitly deny: `kms:Decrypt` (don't let them decrypt actual data), `s3:GetObject` on sensitive buckets, `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` (no actual secrets). Read config/metadata only.*<br>

1122. [ IAM ] What is the difference between an IAM policy `Version` field value "2012-10-17" vs "2008-10-17"? ; "2012-10-17": current policy language version. Supports policy variables like `${aws:username}`, `${aws:userid}`. Required for condition keys, variables, and modern features. "2008-10-17": legacy version. No policy variables. Limited condition support. Always use "2012-10-17". If Version is omitted: defaults to 2008-10-17 (no variables). Missing Version with policy variables = variables treated as literal strings. <br><br> *Common mistake: write a policy with `${aws:username}` in the Resource ARN but forget to set Version to "2012-10-17". Policy evaluates but `${aws:username}` is treated as a literal string "aws:username" — no match to actual resource — all requests denied. Always include `"Version":"2012-10-17"` at the top of every policy. Every AWS documentation example includes it — follow the examples.*<br> *Policy variables: enable ABAC and per-user personalization. `"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::company-bucket/home/${aws:username}/*"` — each user can only access their home folder without creating per-user policies. `${aws:userid}` for role assumptions. `${aws:PrincipalTag/department}` — use the caller's tag value in the resource ARN. Variables only work with Version 2012-10-17 and only in certain policy elements (Resource, Condition values, not in Action or Effect).*<br>

1123. [ IAM ] A company has an SCP that denies all actions except a specific whitelist. New developers are unable to use services not on the whitelist. Who needs to approve whitelist additions and what is the process? ; SCP changes require access to AWS Organizations in the management account (or a delegated administrator account). Process: (1) Developer team submits request to Cloud Operations team with justification. (2) Cloud Operations reviews the service — verify it meets security requirements. (3) Management account admin adds the service's `Allow` statement to the SCP (or removes a specific `Deny`). (4) Change tested in a non-production OU first. (5) Promoted to production OU. Change takes effect immediately (no restart needed). <br><br> *SCP whitelist (allow-list) vs blacklist (deny-list): allow-list SCP: `"Effect":"Allow","Action":["whitelisted actions"]` — everything else implicitly denied by "no explicit allow." More restrictive, harder to manage, causes issues when new services are needed. Deny-list SCP: `"Effect":"Deny","Action":["denied actions"]` — only specific things blocked, everything else allowed via identity policies. AWS recommends deny-list (more flexible, FullAWSAccess SCP provides baseline allows). Allow-list SCPs are used in high-security environments where the risk of accidental access to new services outweighs operational friction.*<br> *Delegated administrator for Organizations: management account can delegate SCPs management to a specific member account (security team account). Security team can manage SCPs without needing management account access for everything. Separation: management account = billing + organization structure. Security account = SCPs + CloudTrail + Config. Operational teams = member accounts.*<br>

1124. [ IAM ] What is the IAM policy evaluation for a Lambda function with an execution role that has S3 read access, when the function tries to write to an S3 bucket that has a bucket policy denying all writes from Lambda? ; Access Denied. Bucket policy explicit deny overrides the Lambda role's identity-based allow. Explicit deny from resource-based policy takes precedence over identity-based allow. The evaluation order: explicit deny anywhere → denied. Lambda role allows PutObject, but bucket policy denies PutObject from Lambda → bucket policy wins. Lambda cannot write to this bucket. <br><br> *Resource-based policy explicit deny: same power as identity-based explicit deny. Either side can deny — both are equal in the denial hierarchy. A bucket policy `"Effect":"Deny","Principal":"*","Action":"s3:PutObject","Condition":{"ArnLike":{"aws:PrincipalArn":"arn:aws:lambda:*:*:function:*"}}` denies ALL Lambda function write attempts to that bucket. Even admin-level Lambda role cannot write. Only removing or modifying the bucket policy allows writes.*<br> *Why this matters: defense-in-depth. A bucket containing reference data (only for reads) can have a bucket policy denying all writes. Even if a Lambda function has broad S3 permissions (S3FullAccess), it cannot corrupt the reference data. Bucket policy acts as an independent control layer from IAM policies. Useful for protecting configuration buckets, audit logs, immutable reference data from accidental writes by overly permissive roles.*<br>

1125. [ IAM ] What is the difference between inline policies and customer managed policies? When should each be used? ; Customer managed policies: standalone policy objects. Can be attached to multiple identities. Version history (5 versions). Can be updated without re-attaching. Visible in policy list. Recommended for most cases. Inline policies: embedded directly in one specific user/group/role. Deleted when the identity is deleted. Not reusable. No version history. No separate existence. Use inline ONLY when a policy must be strictly unique to one identity and must not accidentally be attached to others. In practice: prefer managed. <br><br> *Managed policy benefits: one policy update applies to all attached identities simultaneously. Example: update `S3DataAccess` managed policy → all 50 roles with this policy get updated. Inline: must update 50 individual inline policies separately. Versioning: managed policies keep 5 versions (rollback available). Inline: no rollback. Audit: managed policies listed in IAM console, searchable. Inline: must look at each identity to find inline policies.*<br> *When inline is legitimate: a highly specific permission that is logically tied to one role and should NOT be reused. If the role is deleted, the permission disappears with it (no orphaned policy). Example: a very sensitive permission (like `sts:AssumeRole` with a specific ExternalId) that is unique to one service and should never be accidentally attached to another role. AWS Config `iam-no-inline-policy-check` flags inline policies as non-compliant — shows AWS recommends managed policies by default.*<br>

1126. [ IAM ] A company has a requirement: "No IAM access keys should be older than 90 days." How do you detect violations and auto-remediate? ; Detection: AWS Config rule `access-keys-rotated` with `maxAccessKeyAge = 90` days. Auto-remediation: Config → SSM Automation document → Lambda → `iam:UpdateAccessKey` (deactivate) + `iam:CreateAccessKey` (create new) + notify key owner via SNS. CloudTrail: log all key rotation actions. Alternatively: Security Hub aggregates Config findings for centralized visibility. <br><br> *Config auto-remediation: AWS Config supports auto-remediation via SSM Automation. When `access-keys-rotated` finds a non-compliant key: trigger `AWS-RotateIAMAccessKey` SSM Automation document (or custom Lambda). Automation: (1) Create new access key. (2) Store in Secrets Manager (tagged with IAM user name). (3) Deactivate old key (not delete — application might still use it). (4) Wait 7 days. (5) Delete old key. (6) Notify application owner.*<br> *Notification workflow: before deactivating: SNS email to key owner (from IAM user tags: `email = owner@company.com`) — give 7-day warning. After 90 days + 7 days grace: deactivate. After 97 days: delete. Lambda checks key last used date before deactivating: if used within last 24 hours — delay rotation + escalate to manager (key in active use, needs careful migration). If unused for 90+ days: deactivate immediately (potentially abandoned key). Unused + old = highest risk.*<br>

1127. [ IAM ] What is the difference between `aws:PrincipalOrgID` and `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths` condition keys? ; `aws:PrincipalOrgID`: matches any principal in the entire organization (`o-exampleorgid`). `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`: matches principals in specific OUs (Organizational Units) or the management account — uses path format: `o-orgid/r-root/ou-XXXX-parentou/ou-XXXX-childou/`. More granular — allow access only to principals in the Production OU, not the Development OU. <br><br> *PrincipalOrgPaths example: Production OU path = `o-abc123/r-root1/ou-prod-111/`. S3 bucket policy: `"Condition":{"ForAnyValue:StringLike":{"aws:PrincipalOrgPaths":["o-abc123/r-root1/ou-prod-111/*"]}}` — only prod-OU accounts' principals can access. Dev-OU accounts: denied. Management account: also denied (not in prod OU path).*<br> *Use case: data lake S3 bucket should only be accessible by data-processing accounts (in DataProcessing OU), not by developer accounts (in Dev OU). Both are in the same org — PrincipalOrgID would allow all of them. PrincipalOrgPaths allows only the DataProcessing OU. As accounts are added to the OU: they automatically gain access. Accounts moved to different OU: automatically lose access. OU-based access control that scales with org structure.*<br>

1128. [ IAM ] A company wants to prevent their AWS accounts from being able to disable AWS Security Hub findings. How do you enforce this? ; SCP denying `securityhub:DeleteInsight`, `securityhub:BatchUpdateFindings` (to change finding severity/status), `securityhub:DisassociateFromMasterAccount`, `securityhub:DisableSecurityHub`. Attach SCP to all member account OUs. Security Hub delegated administrator (security account): manages hub for all accounts. Member accounts cannot opt out or disable. <br><br> *SCP for security services protection: common pattern — deny disabling GuardDuty, Security Hub, CloudTrail, Config, Macie. Single SCP: `{"Effect":"Deny","Action":["guardduty:DeleteDetector","guardduty:DisassociateFromMasterAccount","securityhub:DisableSecurityHub","config:DeleteConfigurationRecorder","cloudtrail:DeleteTrail","macie2:DisableMacie"]}`. Protects all core security services. Attach to root OU.*<br> *Security Hub delegated administrator: management account designates the security account as delegated admin. Security account can enable/configure Security Hub for all org accounts (even new accounts auto-enrolled). Member accounts lose ability to modify their Security Hub configuration — only the delegated admin can. SCP prevents members from disabling. Delegated admin pattern: security tooling controlled by security team, not individual account owners.*<br>

1129. [ IAM ] Explain the IAM policy element `NotAction` and when it should be used versus `Action`. ; `NotAction`: matches everything EXCEPT the listed actions. `"Effect":"Allow","NotAction":"iam:*"` = allow all actions EXCEPT IAM. Use `NotAction` with `Allow` for "allow everything except this service." Dangerous with `Effect:Allow` + `Resource:*` — can accidentally allow unintended services. Safer: `NotAction` with `Effect:Deny`. Common use case: "Deny all actions EXCEPT sts:AssumeRole" for a policy that allows only role assumption. <br><br> *NotAction with Deny: `{"Effect":"Deny","NotAction":["s3:GetObject","s3:ListBucket"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket*"}` — deny all S3 actions on this bucket EXCEPT GetObject and ListBucket. Safer than NotAction with Allow because deny is explicit. With Allow + NotAction: if a new AWS service action is added that you didn't intend to allow, it's automatically allowed. With Deny + NotAction: only the explicitly listed exceptions are allowed.*<br> *NotResource: similar concept for resources. `"Effect":"Deny","Action":"s3:*","NotResource":["arn:aws:s3:::allowed-bucket","arn:aws:s3:::allowed-bucket/*"]` — deny S3 actions on all buckets EXCEPT allowed-bucket. Used for policies that should only allow access to specific buckets and deny all others. NotAction and NotResource should be used carefully and always with explicit intent — they match broadly and can surprise if the exception list grows.*<br>

1130. [ IAM ] What are the IAM policy condition operators and when do you use `StringEquals` vs `StringLike`? ; `StringEquals`: exact case-sensitive match. `StringLike`: case-sensitive with wildcards (`*` = any chars, `?` = one char). `StringEqualsIgnoreCase`: case-insensitive exact. `StringLikeIfExists`: `StringLike` but if key is missing (key doesn't exist in request), condition evaluates to true. Key distinction for exams: `StringEquals` on tags requires EXACT match. `StringLike` allows wildcard patterns. <br><br> *Operator families: String (String*), Numeric (Numeric*), Date (Date*), Bool (Bool), Binary (BinaryEquals), Arn (Arn*, ArnLike, ArnEquals), IpAddress, Null (checks if key is absent/present). `Null` operator: `{"Null":{"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption":"true"}}` — condition is true if the encryption header is NOT present. Used to deny unencrypted uploads: `{"Effect":"Deny","Action":"s3:PutObject","Condition":{"Null":{"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption":"true"}}}` — deny PutObject if encryption header absent.*<br> *ForAllValues vs ForAnyValue: for multi-valued condition keys. `ForAllValues:StringEquals`: EVERY value in the request must match the condition. `ForAnyValue:StringEquals`: AT LEAST ONE value in the request must match. Example with s3:RequestObjectTagKeys: `ForAllValues:StringEquals` ensures ALL tag keys are in the allowed set. `ForAnyValue:StringEquals` requires at least one tag key to be in the set. ForAllValues on empty set: evaluates to true (vacuously true) — potential security gap. Use Null operator alongside for defense.*<br>

1131. [ IAM ] A Lambda function needs to write to an SQS queue and an S3 bucket, but only during business hours (8am-6pm UTC). How do you implement this time-based restriction? ; IAM condition on the Lambda execution role's policy: `"Condition":{"DateGreaterThan":{"aws:CurrentTime":"2000-01-01T08:00:00Z"},"DateLessThan":{"aws:CurrentTime":"2000-01-01T18:00:00Z"}}` — but this uses date, not time-of-day. For time-of-day: use EventBridge schedule to enable/disable the Lambda trigger, not IAM conditions (IAM CurrentTime is absolute date, not recurring daily time). Better: EventBridge cron to enable SQS trigger at 8am, disable at 6pm. <br><br> *IAM CurrentTime limitation for recurring business hours: `aws:CurrentTime` is a full timestamp (date + time). You can't express "between 8am-6pm EVERY day" in IAM. Workarounds: (1) EventBridge schedule: cron(0 8 * * ? *) = enable trigger, cron(0 18 * * ? *) = disable trigger. (2) Lambda itself checks time at invocation start and rejects outside hours. (3) API Gateway resource policy with CurrentTime for one-time access windows (not recurring). IAM CurrentTime is useful for one-time windows (access during a maintenance window: Jan 15 8am-10am).*<br> *Production approach: EventBridge Scheduler (newer, more precise than cron) creates/deletes SQS event source mapping on the Lambda function. 8:00am UTC: `CreateEventSourceMapping`. 6:00pm UTC: `DeleteEventSourceMapping`. Lambda receives no messages outside business hours. For strict compliance: combine with Lambda code check (defense-in-depth) — if message arrives outside hours (processing backlog), Lambda rejects and puts message back in queue with delay.*<br>

1132. [ IAM ] What is the IAM policy simulator, and how does it differ from running actual IAM API calls for testing? ; IAM Policy Simulator: evaluates policies against hypothetical API calls WITHOUT actually executing them. Tests what a specific user/role can or cannot do. Tests policy changes before applying. Simulates SCPs, permission boundaries, resource-based policies. Accessible via console (iam.amazonaws.com/home#/policysimulator) or CLI: `aws iam simulate-principal-policy`. Unlike actual API calls: no resources created, no CloudTrail events for the simulated actions. <br><br> *Policy Simulator vs dry-run: simulator tests IAM authorization only. Does not test: resource-level conditions requiring actual resources (e.g., `ec2:ResourceTag` — simulator doesn't know the actual tag on the instance unless you specify it). Actual dry-run (`ec2:RunInstances --dry-run`): tests IAM + resource availability + quotas. Use both: simulator first (fast, no cost) then dry-run in test environment (confirms with real resource state).*<br> *CLI example: `aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::123:role/DevRole --action-names s3:PutObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/test.txt`. Response: `{"EvalDecision":"allowed"}` or `{"EvalDecision":"explicitDeny","MatchedStatements":[...]}`. `MatchedStatements` shows which specific policy statement caused the allow/deny — valuable for debugging complex policy interactions. Include resource-based policies: `--resource-policy` parameter.*<br>

1133. [ IAM ] A company discovers that an IAM user's access keys were leaked on GitHub. What is the immediate response process? ; Immediate: (1) `aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id LEAKEDKEY --status Inactive` — disable immediately (don't delete yet — need for audit). (2) Check CloudTrail for all API calls made with this key (last 24-48 hours). (3) Revoke any sessions that were initiated with this key: `aws iam delete-access-key --access-key-id LEAKEDKEY` after investigation. (4) `aws iam create-access-key --user-name affected-user` — issue new key. (5) Rotate any secrets the key had access to. <br><br> *CloudTrail investigation: `aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=Username,AttributeValue=affected-user --start-time 2026-10-25 --end-time 2026-11-01`. Review all events: any IAM changes (new users, new policies), any data exfiltration (S3 GetObject on sensitive buckets), any infrastructure changes (EC2 launches), any cross-account access. Determine blast radius before rotating credentials.*<br> *GuardDuty findings: leaked key used from unusual IP (outside corporate range) → GuardDuty generates `UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/AnomalousBehavior` finding. Check GuardDuty: `aws guardduty list-findings --detector-id DETECTOR_ID --finding-criteria '{"Criterion":{"resource.accessKeyDetails.accessKeyId":{"Equals":["LEAKEDKEY"]}}}'`. GuardDuty may have already detected unauthorized use. Incident timeline: GitHub exposure time → first unauthorized use → detection → response. Shorter detection-to-response = less damage.*<br>

1134. [ IAM ] What is the difference between IAM Identity Center (SSO) and federation directly via IAM SAML? Which should new organizations use? ; Direct IAM SAML federation: configure per-account, per-role. Each account needs its own IAM SAML provider + roles. No centralized management. Works for single account. IAM Identity Center: centralized across all org accounts. Single IdP connection. Permission sets applied to multiple accounts. Automatic role provisioning. Application SSO. SCIM provisioning. New orgs: always use Identity Center. Direct SAML federation: legacy pattern, avoid for new deployments. <br><br> *Migration from direct SAML to Identity Center: create Identity Center instance → connect same IdP (AD/Okta) → create permission sets matching existing IAM roles → assign to accounts → test parallel access → retire old SAML providers and roles. Blue-green migration: keep old SAML roles working while migrating groups to Identity Center. CloudTrail shows which identities still use old SAML roles (session issuer type = SAMLUser vs IdentityCenter) — migrate until old SAML roles have zero activity.*<br> *Identity Center advantages at scale: 50 accounts with 10 roles each = 500 IAM roles to manage manually (SAML). Identity Center: 10 permission sets → assigned to 50 accounts automatically = 500 roles auto-created and managed. New account joined org: permission sets applied automatically (no manual role creation). Employee joins: add to IdP group → access appears across all accounts. Employee leaves: remove from IdP → SCIM revokes across all accounts. 10x operational efficiency at scale.*<br>

1135. [ IAM ] A company wants to implement AWS IAM best practices. List the top 10 IAM security best practices and their implementation methods. ; (1) Enable MFA for root: `iam:EnableMFADevice` on root account — hardware key preferred. (2) Delete root access keys: `iam:DeleteAccessKey` for root. (3) Use groups, not direct user policies: attach policies to groups, add users to groups. (4) Roles over users for workloads: `iam:CreateRole` for every service. (5) Least privilege: start with minimum, use Access Analyzer to identify unused. (6) Rotate credentials: Config rule `access-keys-rotated` + automation. (7) Use Config + Security Hub for compliance monitoring. (8) Enable CloudTrail org trail for all accounts. (9) Use permission boundaries for delegated admin. (10) Regular access review with IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings. <br><br> *Implementation priority: root MFA + delete root keys (5 minutes, immediate risk reduction). Then CloudTrail org trail (audit baseline). Then Config + Security Hub (compliance visibility). Then IAM roles for all workloads (eliminate static keys). Then Access Analyzer (continuous monitoring). Then least privilege campaign (ongoing). Root account checklist: enable MFA, delete access keys, don't use email as root for daily operations, set up recovery phone and email, test root access once per quarter.*<br> *AWS Security Hub IAM standard: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard includes IAM controls. Score out of 100. Common failing controls: root MFA not enabled (critical), IAM users with console access have MFA enabled (high), access keys rotated within 90 days (medium). Security Hub integrates with AWS Config — findings from Config IAM rules appear in Security Hub. Remediation guidance in Security Hub for each failing control.*<br>

1136. [ IAM ] What is the difference between an IAM role's `MaxSessionDuration` and the `DurationSeconds` parameter in AssumeRole? ; `MaxSessionDuration`: the MAXIMUM duration that can be requested when assuming the role. Set on the role itself (default: 1 hour, range: 900-43200 seconds). `DurationSeconds`: what the CALLER requests for a specific AssumeRole call (must be ≤ MaxSessionDuration). If DurationSeconds > MaxSessionDuration: error. If DurationSeconds omitted: defaults to 1 hour or MaxSessionDuration (whichever is less). Role controls the ceiling, caller controls the actual duration within that ceiling. <br><br> *Example: MaxSessionDuration=28800 (8hr). Caller requests DurationSeconds=3600 (1hr) → gets 1hr session. Caller requests DurationSeconds=7200 (2hr) → gets 2hr session. Caller requests DurationSeconds=28801 → error: "DurationSeconds exceeds maximum value 28800." Caller omits DurationSeconds → gets 3600 (1hr default). To get an 8hr session: caller must explicitly request DurationSeconds=28800.*<br> *Practical scenario: a batch job needs 8-hour sessions. MaxSessionDuration=28800 on the role. Job calls AssumeRole with DurationSeconds=28800. Gets 8-hour credentials. Background refresh (optional): if job tracks Credentials.Expiration, refreshes when 5min remain. If job doesn't refresh: after 8hr, API calls fail with expired token. Design decision: request maximum session OR implement refresh. Both valid — depends on job complexity and duration predictability.*<br>

1137. [ IAM ] A company's SCP accidentally denied `ec2:DescribeInstances` to all accounts. All monitoring and management tools failed. How do you recover, and what is the rollback process? ; SCP changes: go to management account (or delegated Organizations admin account) → AWS Organizations → Policies → find the SCP → edit or detach from the OU. SCP changes are immediate (no propagation delay). Remove the deny statement or detach the SCP from the affected OU. Test in one account before reattaching. Monitoring tools recover immediately after SCP fix — no EC2 restart needed. <br><br> *Rollback process: (1) Log into management account (SCPs only manageable there or from delegated admin). (2) `aws organizations list-policies --filter SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY` — find the SCP. (3) `aws organizations detach-policy --policy-id SCP_ID --target-id OU_ID` — immediate detach. (4) Tools recover. (5) Edit SCP to fix the error. (6) Re-attach to OU. (7) Verify tools work. Total recovery time: 2-5 minutes if you have management account access.*<br> *Prevention: test SCP changes in a dedicated "SCP-test" OU with non-production accounts before applying to production OUs. Use SCP change management process: (1) Draft change. (2) Test in SCP-test OU. (3) Verify no breakage in test account. (4) Apply to dev OU. (5) Verify. (6) Apply to prod OU. SCP policy simulator: AWS Organizations doesn't have a built-in SCP simulator — use IAM Policy Simulator with SCP as input. Break-glass: management account credentials in a vault — never use for daily operations but available for SCP emergencies.*<br>

1138. [ IAM ] What is the `aws:CalledVia` condition key and when is it used? ; `aws:CalledVia`: identifies which AWS services made the API call on behalf of the principal. When CloudFormation calls EC2 on your behalf: `aws:CalledVia = ["cloudformation.amazonaws.com"]`. Use case: allow a user to only call DynamoDB via CloudFormation (not directly). `"Condition":{"ForAnyValue:StringEquals":{"aws:CalledVia":["cloudformation.amazonaws.com"]}}` — allows DynamoDB access only when called via CloudFormation (infrastructure-as-code enforcement). <br><br> *aws:CalledVia vs aws:PrincipalServiceName: `aws:CalledVia` = the chain of services that called on the principal's behalf. `aws:PrincipalServiceName` = if the principal itself IS a service. CalledVia supports: `["cloudformation.amazonaws.com","athena.amazonaws.com","glue.amazonaws.com"]` etc. Example: `athena.amazonaws.com` calls S3 on behalf of a user running a query. CalledVia allows you to require Athena as the intermediary.*<br> *Practical use: prevent direct S3 access from application code while allowing S3 access via Athena queries (analytics-only access pattern). `"Deny","s3:GetObject","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:CalledVia":"athena.amazonaws.com"}}` — only Athena can read from this analytics bucket, not direct SDK calls. Enforces the data access architecture (query layer, not raw access). aws:CalledViaFirst / aws:CalledViaLast: first/last service in the call chain for more precise control.*<br>

1139. [ IAM ] A company wants to implement a "break-glass" procedure for emergency access to production AWS accounts. Design the complete IAM architecture. ; Break-glass role in each prod account: `EmergencyAdminRole` with AdministratorAccess. Trust policy: management account + `aws:PrincipalArn` condition (specific break-glass user ARNs only). AssumeRole requires MFA: `"Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}}`. CloudTrail alerts on any AssumeRole for this role: EventBridge → SNS → PagerDuty/Slack (immediate notification to security team). Credentials stored in password vault (CyberArk/1Password) with access requiring manager approval. <br><br> *Break-glass design principles: (1) Available but highly visible — any use immediately alerts the security team. (2) MFA required — physical hardware token, not virtual. (3) Time-limited — session recorded, expected to last < 4 hours. (4) Fully audited — CloudTrail captures every action during break-glass session. (5) Post-incident review — every break-glass use triggers an incident ticket and post-mortem. (6) Tested regularly — quarterly drill to verify break-glass access works.*<br> *EventBridge alert rule: `{"source":["aws.sts"],"detail-type":["AWS API Call via CloudTrail"],"detail":{"eventName":["AssumeRole"],"requestParameters":{"roleArn":["arn:aws:iam::PROD_ACCOUNT:role/EmergencyAdminRole"]}}}` → SNS → on-call engineer + CISO + security team. Alert includes: who assumed the role, from where (IP), session name, time. Break-glass session naming: `EmergencyAdmin-JIRA-INCIDENT-12345-2026-11-01-johndoe` — embeds incident ticket ID and engineer name in session name (visible in CloudTrail). Zero ambiguity about purpose and actor.*<br>

1140. [ IAM ] Explain the trust relationship between AWS accounts in an AWS Organization. How does account membership affect IAM policy evaluation? ; AWS Organization = logical container for multiple AWS accounts. Accounts trust each other ONLY when explicitly configured (via cross-account roles or resource-based policies) — not automatically. Organization membership enables: `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition (verify caller is in org), SCPs (governance from management account), AWS services that use org (CloudTrail org trail, Config aggregator, Security Hub). Accounts are isolated by default — no implicit trust. <br><br> *Organization vs account: Organization = management structure (OUs, SCPs, billing consolidation). Account = independent security and resource boundary. Being in the same org does NOT mean account A can access account B's resources. Cross-account access still requires explicit trust (role trust policy + identity policy, or resource-based policy). Organization adds: (1) SCPs for governance. (2) Conditions using org membership. (3) Centralized services across accounts. But does NOT create implicit trust between accounts.*<br> *Trust relationship scenarios: Account A (dev) wants to read from Account B (prod) S3: needs explicit cross-account role OR bucket policy. Being in same org doesn't help unless bucket policy uses `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition. Management account trusts: implicitly trusted by org (SCPs don't apply to it). Service-linked role: trusted by the specific AWS service (not by the org structure). Federated identity (SAML): trusted by the IAM SAML provider in each account — not org-wide unless Identity Center is used.*<br>

1141. [ IAM ] A company runs a multi-tier app: frontend (EC2), API (Lambda), database (RDS). Each tier should only communicate with adjacent tiers. Frontend should NOT be able to call RDS directly. How do you enforce this with IAM? ; Each tier gets a specific IAM role. Frontend role: permission to invoke Lambda API (`lambda:InvokeFunction`) only. Lambda execution role: permission to access RDS IAM authentication (`rds-db:connect`) only — not the frontend's Lambda. Frontend role has no `rds-db:connect` at all. Even if frontend code calls RDS directly: access denied (no permission). Layers are IAM-separated. <br><br> *RDS IAM authentication: instead of RDS master password, Lambda authenticates via IAM. `rds-db:connect` permission on the DB resource ARN. Only Lambda execution role has this permission. Frontend EC2 role: has Lambda invoke, explicitly no `rds-db:connect`. Defense-in-depth: (1) Security groups (network layer — frontend SG cannot reach RDS port). (2) IAM (identity layer — frontend role has no RDS IAM auth permission). Two independent controls.*<br> *Lambda resource policy: restrict which identities can invoke the Lambda. `aws lambda add-permission --principal arn:aws:iam::123:role/FrontendRole --action lambda:InvokeFunction`. Only FrontendRole can invoke this Lambda (not other Lambdas, not other EC2 roles). Combined with IAM execution role permissions: tight, auditable tier separation. CloudTrail: if frontend ever directly calls RDS → access denied → CloudTrail logs the denied attempt → alert via CloudWatch Metric Filter → investigate.*<br>

1142. [ IAM ] A company creates 20 IAM roles for different services. All roles share 5 common permissions (CloudWatch logging, X-Ray tracing, SSM parameter read). How do you avoid duplicating these 5 permissions across all 20 role policies? ; Create one managed policy `CommonServicePermissions` with the 5 shared permissions. Attach it to all 20 roles alongside their service-specific managed policies. Each role has 2 policies: `CommonServicePermissions` + `ServiceSpecificPermissions`. When the 5 common permissions change (e.g., new X-Ray API added): update ONE policy → all 20 roles automatically updated. <br><br> *Managed policy reuse: 20 roles × 5 permissions inline = 100 permission entries to maintain. 1 shared managed policy + 20 service-specific policies = 21 policies to maintain. When a new CloudWatch API needs to be added: update 1 vs update 20. IAM managed policy limit: 10 policies per identity (can request increase to 20). For most services: 2-3 policies is fine (common + specific + boundary).*<br> *AWS managed policies as base: AWS provides `CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy` (CloudWatch agent permissions), `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` (SSM permissions), `AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess` (X-Ray). Attach these AWS managed policies instead of creating custom common policies. AWS manages updates to these policies as services evolve. Risk: AWS occasionally adds new permissions to managed policies — could over-grant. Review AWS managed policy release notes. For strict environments: copy the managed policy into a customer managed policy (control over additions).*<br>

1143. [ IAM ] What is the `aws:PrincipalTag` condition key and how does it differ from `aws:ResourceTag`? ; `aws:PrincipalTag`: the tags on the IAM principal (user, role, or federated user) making the request. `aws:ResourceTag`: the tags on the resource being accessed. `aws:PrincipalTag` = who is asking. `aws:ResourceTag` = what they're asking about. ABAC combines both: allow access when principal's team tag matches resource's team tag. `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"aws:ResourceTag/team":"${aws:PrincipalTag/team}"}}` — policy variable references principal's tag value. <br><br> *PrincipalTag use cases: (1) Environment access — principal tagged `env=prod` can access resources tagged `env=prod`. (2) Department data isolation — principal tagged `dept=finance` can only access `dept=finance` S3 prefixes. (3) Seniority-based access — principal tagged `clearance=top` can access `classification=top-secret` resources. Tags on IAM principals can be set by administrators (not self-service), making them trustworthy for policy conditions.*<br> *Federated identity tag injection: for SAML federation: SAML assertion can include `https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/PrincipalTag:department` = "Engineering". STS session tag set from SAML assertion. Principal tag available in IAM conditions immediately. For IAM Identity Center: attribute mappings → assign AD attributes to principal tags. User's AD department automatically becomes their PrincipalTag in AWS. One policy handles all departments via PrincipalTag/department matching.*<br>

1144. [ IAM ] A company wants to prevent any IAM user or role from modifying their CloudTrail configuration or deleting CloudTrail logs from S3.
