Design both preventive and detective controls. ; Preventive: (1) SCP denying `cloudtrail:*Delete*`, `cloudtrail:StopLogging`, `cloudtrail:UpdateTrail`. (2) S3 bucket policy on CloudTrail bucket: deny `s3:DeleteObject` to all except the CloudTrail service. (3) S3 Object Lock on CloudTrail bucket (Governance mode, 1-year retention). Detective: (1) CloudTrail → CloudWatch Logs → Metric Filter for CloudTrail API calls → alarm. (2) AWS Config: `cloud-trail-enabled` rule. (3) GuardDuty: `Stealth:IAMUser/CloudTrailLoggingDisabled`. <br><br> *S3 bucket policy for CloudTrail logs: `{"Effect":"Deny","Principal":"*","Action":["s3:DeleteObject","s3:DeleteBucket","s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::cloudtrail-bucket*","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:PrincipalServiceName":"cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"}}}`. Only the CloudTrail service can write to this bucket. Even account administrators cannot delete logs. CloudTrail service writes logs, nobody deletes them.*<br> *Defense depth: SCP (IAM level) → CloudTrail API calls blocked. S3 bucket policy (resource level) → even if SCP bypassed, S3 denies deletes. Object Lock (storage level) → even if S3 policy removed, objects locked until retention expires. MFA Delete on bucket (authentication level) → deletion requires root account + MFA. Four independent layers — attacker must defeat all four to destroy logs. Immutable audit trail is the foundation of cloud security forensics.*<br>

1145. [ IAM ] What is the `sts:SetSourceIdentity` action and `aws:SourceIdentity` condition, and how do they support audit traceability? ; `sts:SetSourceIdentity`: allows a caller to set a persistent identity string when assuming a role. Once set, cannot be changed in the session or in further role assumptions. `aws:SourceIdentity`: condition key containing the set identity. Use: a CI/CD system assumes a role, sets SourceIdentity to the pipeline/user name. All actions taken with that role session in CloudTrail show the SourceIdentity. Even if the role chains further (assumes another role), SourceIdentity persists — always traceable to the original human/pipeline. <br><br> *SourceIdentity vs session name (RoleSessionName): RoleSessionName is set at AssumeRole time and visible in CloudTrail as the session identifier. But RoleSessionName changes with each new AssumeRole call (role chaining = new session name). SourceIdentity: set once, persists through the ENTIRE chain. 3-hop role chain: SourceIdentity remains constant across all 3 hops in CloudTrail. Each hop has a different RoleSessionName but the same SourceIdentity.*<br> *Implementation: `aws sts assume-role --role-arn ARN --role-session-name SESSION --source-identity "jenkins-pipeline-deploy-12345"`. Trust policy must allow `sts:SetSourceIdentity` for the caller. Once set: cannot unset or change. CloudTrail field: `userIdentity.sessionContext.sourceIdentity = "jenkins-pipeline-deploy-12345"`. Correlation: search CloudTrail for all actions with `sourceIdentity = "jenkins-pipeline-deploy-12345"` across ALL roles in the chain — complete audit trail for one pipeline run.*<br>

1146. [ IAM ] A company receives a compliance requirement: "No AWS account should have more than 2 active IAM access keys per user." How do you detect and remediate this automatically? ; AWS Config custom rule evaluating `iam:ListAccessKeys` for each user. Flag users with > 2 active keys (Status=Active). Config auto-remediation: Lambda deactivates the oldest active key (based on `CreateDate`). SNS notification to user. CloudTrail logs the deactivation. Scheduled: run weekly. Or: CloudWatch Events + Lambda periodic audit. <br><br> *IAM limits: maximum 2 access keys per IAM user (hard limit, cannot be increased). No user can ever have more than 2 keys — compliance requirement matches AWS hard limit. The real requirement: "no more than 1 ACTIVE key at a time" (the 2nd key exists for rotation purposes only). Config rule: `{"Parameters":{"MaxActiveKeys":"1"}}`. Flag any user with 2 active keys (should deactivate old after rotation).*<br> *Rotation process: user has Key1 (active). Create Key2 (active — now 2 active keys). Update application to use Key2. Deactivate Key1 (now 1 active key). After 7 days → delete Key1. Config rule tolerates 2 active keys for up to 7 days (rotation window). After 7 days: flag as non-compliant. Lambda remediation: if 2 active keys AND older key > 7 days old AND older key last used date > 30 days ago → deactivate older key. If older key was recently used: send alert instead of auto-deactivating (active use = needs manual migration).*<br>

1147. [ IAM ] Explain IAM Credential Reports. What information do they provide and how are they used for security audits? ; IAM Credential Report: CSV file of all IAM users in the account with: user creation date, password last used, password last changed, access key IDs, last used dates, MFA status (virtual/hardware/none), access key active status. Generated on demand (up to once per 4 hours). Used for: identifying unused accounts, keys older than 90 days, users without MFA, dormant accounts (no activity > 90 days). <br><br> *Generate and retrieve: `aws iam generate-credential-report` (triggers generation). `aws iam get-credential-report` (returns base64 CSV). Decode: `aws iam get-credential-report --query Content --output text | base64 -d`. CSV columns: user, arn, user_creation_time, password_enabled, password_last_used, password_last_changed, password_next_rotation, mfa_active, access_key_1_active, access_key_1_last_rotated, access_key_1_last_used_date, access_key_1_last_used_region, access_key_1_last_used_service, access_key_2_active (same fields for key 2).*<br> *Security audit workflow: (1) Generate report. (2) Filter users where mfa_active=false AND password_enabled=true → require MFA immediately. (3) Filter users where access_key_1_last_used_date > 90 days → deactivate. (4) Filter users where password_last_used > 90 days AND access keys last used > 90 days → dormant accounts → disable login profile. (5) Root user: check `password_last_used` (should be rare), verify no access keys. Monthly scheduled Lambda: generate report → analyze → SNS alerts for violations. Automates what would otherwise be a manual audit.*<br>

1148. [ IAM ] What are IAM service control policies (SCPs) vs resource control policies (RCPs), and how do they differ? ; SCPs (Service Control Policies): limit what IAM PRINCIPALS (users/roles) in member accounts can do. Applied to accounts/OUs — restrict the caller's permissions. RCPs (Resource Control Policies): limit what can be DONE TO RESOURCES regardless of who calls. Applied to resources across the org — restrict permissions from the resource side. New in 2024: RCPs prevent external access to org resources even if resource-based policies allow it. <br><br> *SCP vs RCP: SCP = gates on the caller (identity side). RCP = gates on the resource (resource side). Example: SCP denying `s3:PutBucketPolicy` prevents account admins from setting permissive bucket policies. RCP `"Deny if caller not in org"` on S3 prevents buckets from being accessed externally — even if an admin sets a public bucket policy, RCP blocks the actual external access. RCP is newer and more powerful for data perimeter enforcement.*<br> *Data perimeter with RCPs: AWS Organizations now supports RCPs on S3 (and expanding to other services). RCP example: `{"Effect":"Deny","Principal":"*","Action":"s3:*","Resource":"*","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:PrincipalOrgID":"o-orgid"}}}`. Applied at org level → ALL S3 buckets in ALL member accounts deny access from outside the org — regardless of individual bucket policies. Complements SCP (controls what identities in org can do) with RCP (controls who can access org resources). Together: complete data perimeter.*<br>

1149. [ IAM ] A company is migrating from a monolith application with a single admin IAM role to microservices. Each microservice needs different permissions. How do you approach the IAM redesign? ; Per-service least-privilege roles: (1) Identify each microservice and its AWS service calls (analyze code or use Access Analyzer policy generation from CloudTrail). (2) Create one IAM role per microservice (naming: `service-name-role`). (3) Generate minimum-privilege policy from actual CloudTrail usage (Access Analyzer). (4) Attach service-specific policy + common logging policy. (5) Use ABAC (service tags) for resource access where applicable. <br><br> *Policy generation from CloudTrail: `aws accessanalyzer start-policy-generation --policy-generation-details principalArn=arn:aws:iam::123:role/MonolithRole --cloud-trail-details trails=[{cloudTrailArn:ARN,allRegions:true}],startTime:2026-09-01,endTime:2026-11-01`. Access Analyzer analyzes 2 months of CloudTrail → generates minimum-privilege policy showing only what was actually called. Use as starting point for each microservice (which subset of the monolith's calls does this service make?).*<br> *Migration path: (1) Monolith runs on monolith-role (broad permissions). (2) New microservices deployed with specific roles (least privilege). (3) Monolith gradually decomposed — each extracted service gets its own role. (4) Final state: monolith-role deleted. (5) Access Analyzer unused access findings: identify remaining over-provisioned permissions in microservice roles after 90 days of operation. Right-size periodically. Container-level IAM: EKS IRSA means each pod/deployment gets its own role — even microservices composed of multiple pods can have per-deployment IAM isolation.*<br>

1150. [ IAM ] What are the IAM limits you must know for the SAP-C02 exam, and which ones are hard limits that cannot be changed? ; Hard limits (cannot increase): inline policy document size = 2,048 characters. Managed policy document size = 6,144 characters. Policy versions per managed policy = 5. Groups a user can belong to = 10. Role session duration maximum = 43,200 seconds (12 hours). Role chaining max session = 3,600 seconds (1 hour). STS GetFederationToken session max = 129,600 seconds (36 hours). Soft limits (can increase): IAM users/account = 5,000. Groups/account = 300. Roles/account = 1,000. <br><br> *Why hard limits matter for design: policy size 6,144 chars can be reached for complex microservice policies (especially with many resource ARNs). Solution: use `Resource: "*"` with condition keys instead of enumerating ARNs. Or split into multiple managed policies and attach all (max 10, increaseable to 20). Policy version limit = 5: when you have 5 versions and save a new one, oldest is deleted. Version history = rollback capability — limited to last 4 changes.*<br> *Role chaining 1-hour limit exam trap: question describes a system where Lambda assumes Role A, then Role A's code assumes Role B. Session duration request for Role B = 8 hours → error (role chaining = max 1 hour). Fix: Lambda directly assumes Role B (no chaining) → gets full MaxSessionDuration. Role chaining should be avoided for long-running tasks. Service catalog, CloudFormation, and some AWS services do role chaining internally — if you see unexpected 1-hour session limits, check for hidden chaining.*<br>

1151. [ IAM ] Trust policy conditions — compare StringEquals, ArnEquals, ArnLike, and explain AND/OR logic in trust policies. How do multiple Condition blocks or multiple values in one block evaluate? ; Within one `Condition` block: multiple keys = AND (all must be true). Multiple values under one key = OR (any value matches = condition true). Two separate `Condition` blocks in one Statement: not valid (second overrides first) — AND multiple keys inside the same `Condition` block. For OR across different condition keys: use separate `Statement` entries (two Allow statements with different conditions). ArnEquals = exact ARN match. ArnLike = ARN with wildcards (`*`,`?`). StringEquals ≠ ArnEquals for ARNs (StringEquals has no ARN-aware parsing). <br><br> *AND logic: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"aws:RequestedRegion":"eu-central-1"},"Bool":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}}` — BOTH must be true: region must be eu-central-1 AND MFA must be present. If either false → condition false → deny (in Deny statement). Multiple condition keys in one block = AND.*<br> *OR logic across statements: Statement 1: Allow with Condition X. Statement 2: Allow with Condition Y. Effective: allow if X OR if Y. Within one condition key, multiple values = OR: `"aws:RequestedRegion":["eu-central-1","eu-west-1"]` = region must be eu-central-1 OR eu-west-1. Combining: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"aws:RequestedRegion":["eu-central-1","eu-west-1"],"s3:prefix":["uploads/","downloads/"]}}` = region in [eu-central-1 OR eu-west-1] AND prefix in [uploads/ OR downloads/].*<br> *ArnLike use in trust policies: `"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::*:root"}` — but Principal doesn't support wildcards. Solution: use ArnLike in Condition: `"Condition":{"ArnLike":{"aws:PrincipalArn":"arn:aws:iam::*:role/DevRole*"}}` — allows any account's DevRole* to assume the role. ArnEquals = exact ARN match (same as StringEquals for well-formed ARNs but semantically cleaner). Use ArnEquals for exact role ARNs, ArnLike when wildcard matching on ARN components.*<br>

1152. [ IAM ] A trust policy has these two condition operators: `"Null":{"aws:TokenIssueTime":"false"}` and `"BoolIfExists":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}`. Explain what each means and the combined logic. ; `"Null":{"aws:TokenIssueTime":"false"}` — condition is true when `aws:TokenIssueTime` IS NOT NULL (false means "key is not null/absent"). Evaluates to true for temporary credentials (STS sessions have a token issue time) and false for long-term credentials (no token issue time). Combined with MFA: `"BoolIfExists":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}` — if the key exists, it must be true, if key doesn't exist (some contexts), condition passes. Combined: require temp credentials AND MFA if MFA key is present. <br><br> *Null operator reference: `"Null":{"key":"true"}` = condition is true when the key IS absent. `"Null":{"key":"false"}` = condition is true when the key IS present (not null). Confusing naming: "Null":"true" means "the key is null/missing." Null:"false" means "the key is NOT null (it exists)." Common exam trap: `"Null":{"aws:TokenIssueTime":"true"}` = requires NO token issue time = only long-term credentials allowed (deny for STS sessions). The OPPOSITE of what you'd want for MFA enforcement.*<br> *BoolIfExists vs Bool: `Bool` = condition false if key is absent. `BoolIfExists` = condition true if key is absent (skips check when key doesn't exist). For `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent`: when using IAM access keys directly (not console), this key may not be present. `Bool:MultiFactorAuthPresent:true` = denies all access key usage (key absent = false). `BoolIfExists:MultiFactorAuthPresent:true` = allows access key usage (key absent = condition passes). For console MFA requirement: use Bool. For "require MFA when using console, allow access keys without MFA": use BoolIfExists.*<br>

1154. [ IAM ] Explain the `NotPrincipal` element in IAM policies. What is the danger and when is it legitimately used? ; `NotPrincipal`: matches any principal EXCEPT the listed ones. Used with Effect:Deny. Example: deny all actions to everyone EXCEPT the break-glass admin role. Danger: if combined with Effect:Allow: allows all principals EXCEPT the listed one — typically unintended (allows the world except one). Always use NotPrincipal with Effect:Deny. Even with Deny: if your list is wrong or missing, you deny legitimate principals. Rarely used — usually there's a safer alternative. <br><br> *Legitimate use case: S3 bucket policy that prevents ANY principal from deleting objects, except one authorized admin. `{"Effect":"Deny","NotPrincipal":{"AWS":["arn:aws:iam::123:role/BucketAdmin","arn:aws:iam::123:root"]},"Action":["s3:DeleteObject","s3:DeleteBucket"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::protected-bucket*"}`. Only BucketAdmin role and root can delete. Every other principal (any user, any role, any service) is denied.*<br> *Critical: always include root account in NotPrincipal for deny policies. Without root: even the account owner is locked out permanently (cannot modify the bucket policy to fix it — policy evaluation includes root). `NotPrincipal` without root account = potential permanent lockout. Also include the policy admin's role. Test thoroughly before applying: IAM Policy Simulator with a non-listed principal to verify the deny applies, and with the listed principals to verify they're exempt.*<br>

1156. [ IAM ] A company wants to allow cross-account access but ONLY when the calling account is in a specific OU (not just the org). Two accounts in the same org but different OUs. How do you restrict by OU? ; Use `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths` condition key: `"Condition":{"ForAnyValue:StringLike":{"aws:PrincipalOrgPaths":["o-orgid/r-rootid/ou-prod-1111/*"]}}`. Only principals in the prod OU (and any sub-OUs) can assume this role. Dev OU accounts: PrincipalOrgPaths doesn't match → denied. Same org, different OU = different access. <br><br> *OU path format: `o-ORGID/r-ROOTID/ou-FIRST-LEVEL/ou-SECOND-LEVEL/.../`. Each OU level adds a segment. Use `StringLike` with `*` wildcard to match all accounts in an OU and its sub-OUs. `ForAnyValue` because a principal might be in multiple OUs (nested org structure). Example: account in nested OU → path: `o-abc/r-root/ou-parent/ou-child/ACCOUNT_ID`. StringLike pattern `o-abc/r-root/ou-parent/*` matches (parent OU includes all nested).*<br> *Account-level path: each AWS account also appears in the path as a terminal element. `"ForAnyValue:StringLike":{"aws:PrincipalOrgPaths":["*/123456789012/*"]}` — any principal from account 123456789012 (regardless of OU). Combining org path with ExternalId + MFA = very granular, difficult-to-spoof trust control. Add to trust policies for production roles that should only be accessible from approved-OU production accounts.*<br>

1158. [ IAM ] Explain the `ForAllValues` and `ForAnyValue` set operators for multi-valued condition keys. What is the security gap with ForAllValues on empty sets? ; `ForAllValues:StringEquals`: EVERY value in the request set must match. Empty set → vacuously true (0 items checked → 0 violations → true). Security gap: if no values present, condition passes. `ForAnyValue:StringEquals`: AT LEAST ONE value in the request set must match one value in the condition. Empty set → false (nothing to match). For security conditions (denies): use `ForAnyValue` to avoid empty-set bypass. <br><br> *ForAllValues security gap exploit: `"Condition":{"ForAllValues:StringEquals":{"s3:RequestObjectTagKeys":["env","team"]}}` — intended to restrict tagging to only allowed keys. Attacker sends request with NO tags: ForAllValues on empty set = true (vacuously). Condition evaluates to true → allow applies. Attacker bypasses the restriction by sending no tags at all. Fix: add `Null` operator: `"Null":{"s3:RequestObjectTagKeys":"false"}` — requires at least one tag key to be present. Combined: at least one tag present AND all tags in allowed set.*<br> *ForAnyValue use: checking if at least one requested tag key is in the allowed set. `"ForAnyValue:StringEquals":{"aws:TagKeys":["CostCenter","Project"]}` — at least one of the applied tags must be CostCenter or Project. Useful for "you must include at least one of these tags." ForAllValues: "everything you include must be from this set." Different semantic purposes: ForAllValues = whitelist enforcement on all values. ForAnyValue = at least one match required.*<br>

1159. [ IAM ] A company has three accounts: Management (111), Security (222), and Production (333). Design the IAM trust architecture for a security auditor to access Production read-only through a cross-account role chain via the Security account. ; Chain: Auditor (IAM Identity Center in Management) → assumes SecurityAuditRole in Security account → SecurityAuditRole assumes ProductionReadRole in Production account. Management account deploys Identity Center. Security account has SecurityAuditRole trusted by Identity Center SAML provider. Production account has ProductionReadRole trusted by SecurityAuditRole ARN in Security account. Auditor's session: Identity Center → Security → Production. <br><br> *Warning: role chaining = max 1-hour sessions regardless of individual role MaxSessionDuration settings. For an auditor needing 4+ hours: avoid the chain. Alternative: direct Identity Center permission set → deployed as role in BOTH Security and Production accounts. Auditor switches between accounts in Identity Center portal. No chaining. Each session independent with its own duration.*<br> *Role chain configuration: Security account SecurityAuditRole trust: `"Principal":{"Federated":"arn:aws:iam::111:saml-provider/IdentityCenterSAML"}`. Production account ProductionReadRole trust: `"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::222:role/SecurityAuditRole"}`. Security account SecurityAuditRole permission: `sts:AssumeRole` on `arn:aws:iam::333:role/ProductionReadRole`. SecurityAuditRole needs no direct production permissions — only the ability to assume the production role. Production role has the actual read permissions (SecurityAudit AWS managed policy).*<br>

1160. [ IAM ] Explain NotAction with Deny vs NotAction with Allow, with concrete examples of when each creates security problems. ; `NotAction` with `Allow` — ALLOW everything except listed = dangerous over-grant. `NotAction` with `Deny` — DENY everything except listed = restrictive (safer). Problem with Allow+NotAction: if you write `"Allow","NotAction":"iam:*"` with `Resource:*` — user can access ALL of AWS except IAM. If a new AWS service is launched that you didn't intend to allow, it's automatically allowed. Policy creep via new services. Problem with Deny+NotAction: if your exception list is incomplete, you accidentally deny legitimate services. <br><br> *Allow+NotAction real exploit: `{"Effect":"Allow","NotAction":["iam:*","sts:AssumeRole"],"Resource":"*"}`. Intended to allow everything except IAM and STS. But allows: ec2:RunInstances, s3:GetObject, lambda:InvokeFunction, secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, ssm:GetParameter — and every other AWS service action. If secrets are stored in Secrets Manager: this policy allows reading them. Not IAM, but still sensitive. Always enumerate WHAT you want to allow, not what you don't.*<br> *Deny+NotAction for boundary enforcement: `{"Effect":"Deny","NotAction":["s3:GetObject","s3:ListBucket","s3:HeadObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::analytics-bucket*"}`. Effectively: on analytics-bucket, ONLY allow read operations — deny everything else (write, delete, policy changes). Cleaner than enumerating every S3 write action. Exception list (read actions) is small and stable, deny catches all current and future write actions automatically. Safer pattern: Deny+NotAction vs Allow+NotAction.*<br>

1161. [ IAM ] What is the order of IAM policy evaluation for a request involving: (1) SCP, (2) resource-based policy, (3) identity-based policy, (4) permission boundary, (5) session policy? Write the complete decision flowchart. ; Evaluation order: (1) Explicit DENY in any policy type → DENY immediately. (2) SCP: is action within SCP ceiling? No → DENY. (3) Resource-based policy: does it have a Allow with cross-account? → check if identity also allows. Same account: resource-based allow → ALLOW (identity not required). Cross-account: need BOTH. (4) Identity-based + permission boundary: both must allow (intersection). (5) Session policy: further restricts. Final: must pass ALL applicable gates. <br><br> *Simplified decision tree: Explicit Deny anywhere? → DENY. → SCPs allow? → No → DENY. → Permission boundary allows? → No → DENY. → Session policy allows? → No → DENY. → Is it same account? Yes → resource-based OR identity-based allow → ALLOW. No (cross-account) → BOTH resource-based AND identity-based allow → ALLOW. All others → implicit DENY.*<br> *Common exam trap — same account shortcut: lambda.amazonaws.com assumes a role in the SAME account. Lambda's resource policy (function policy) is a resource-based policy. Lambda execution role is identity-based policy. For SAME account: if Lambda resource policy allows `lambda:InvokeFunction` for a specific caller → allowed WITHOUT identity-based policy allowing it. Cross-account: caller's identity-based policy MUST also allow the invocation. Same account = OR logic. Cross-account = AND logic. This is the most tested IAM evaluation rule.*<br>

1162. [ IAM ] What are the differences between AWS managed policies, customer managed policies, and inline policies in terms of versioning, shareability, and lifecycle? Which policy type should be used for each scenario? ; AWS managed policies: versioned by AWS (not user-controllable), shared/reused across accounts, not deletable, updated by AWS. Customer managed policies: 5 user-controlled versions (rollback available), shareable within account, survives identity deletion. Inline policies: no versioning, not shareable (1:1 with identity), deleted with identity. Use AWS managed for standard access patterns, customer managed for custom reusable policies, inline only for strictly identity-unique permissions. <br><br> *Version management: customer managed policy has version 1 through 5 (max). Save a new version: oldest deleted if at 5. `aws iam create-policy-version --set-as-default`. Rollback: `aws iam set-default-policy-version --version-id v3`. Default version = active version used for evaluation. Non-default versions: stored but not applied until set as default. CloudTrail: tracks which version is default — version rollback is auditable.*<br> *Scenario mapping: EC2 needs S3 read → attach `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess` (AWS managed — no maintenance). Custom data science policy with specific SageMaker + S3 permissions → customer managed (reuse across 50 data scientist roles). Specific one-time permission for a deployment pipeline role that must not be reused → inline (intentionally non-reusable, clearest intent). Permission boundary for delegated admin → customer managed (must be specific and controlled). Security Hub SCP → customer managed (org-specific, needs versioning).*<br>

1163. [ IAM ] Which AWS services support resource-based policies? For each, what is the policy called and what are the key differences in how they work? ; Key services with resource-based policies: S3 (Bucket Policy — both cross-account and public access). KMS (Key Policy — REQUIRED, without it nobody can use the key). SQS (Queue Policy). SNS (Topic Policy). Lambda (Function Policy — controls invoke). API Gateway (Resource Policy). ECR (Repository Policy). Secrets Manager (Resource Policy). IAM Role (Trust Policy — technically a resource-based policy). EventBridge (Event Bus Policy). Glacier (Vault Access Policy). CloudWatch Logs (Resource Policy). Glue (Resource Policy). <br><br> *KMS key policy uniqueness: only service where resource-based policy is REQUIRED and identity-based policy alone is NOT sufficient. `"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::123:root"}` in the key policy gives the account full key access (then identity policies control specific access). Without ANY key policy: nobody can use the key (not even root). This is tested heavily. New KMS keys: automatically get a default key policy allowing the account root. Rotating this: update key policy carefully.*<br> *Lambda function policy (resource-based) vs execution role (identity-based): function policy = who can invoke the function (source). Execution role = what the function can do (destination). Both policies apply. Resource-based = someone else's IAM triggers (EventBridge, S3, ALB) or cross-account invocation. Execution role = the Lambda's own permissions for calling other AWS services. `aws lambda add-permission` adds a statement to the function policy. `aws iam attach-role-policy` modifies the execution role.*<br>

1164. [ IAM ] When does a resource-based policy alone (without identity-based policy) grant access? What is the "same-account shortcut"? ; Same account: if a resource-based policy grants permission to a principal in the SAME account, that principal can access the resource WITHOUT needing an identity-based policy allow. The resource-based policy is sufficient for same-account access. Exception: KMS — identity-based policy ALWAYS needed even same-account (unless the key policy explicitly grants all actions to root). Cross-account: resource-based policy AND identity-based policy BOTH needed. <br><br> *Same-account shortcut examples: S3 bucket policy `"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::SAME_ACCOUNT:role/MyRole"},"Action":"s3:GetObject"` → MyRole can GetObject without explicit S3 permission in its identity policy. Lambda function policy `"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::SAME_ACCOUNT:user/alice"}` → Alice can invoke without explicit `lambda:InvokeFunction` in her identity policy. SQS queue policy granting same-account role SendMessage → role can send without identity policy.*<br> *Why this matters for design: simplify permission management for same-account services by using resource policies centrally. Instead of updating 20 Lambda execution roles to allow SQS SendMessage: add one SQS queue policy allowing those 20 roles. Single management point. Cross-account: cannot use this shortcut — both sides always required. Audit: check resource policies for accidental broad same-account grants (`"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:root"}` = all principals in account → any IAM identity can access the resource if their identity policy allows any S3 action).*<br>

1165. [ IAM ] What is the difference between S3 bucket policy and S3 ACL? When should each be used? Can both be used simultaneously? ; S3 Bucket Policy: IAM JSON policy attached to the bucket. Supports complex conditions, cross-account access, public access control, VPC endpoint restrictions. S3 ACL: legacy XML-based access control at bucket or object level. Cannot use conditions. Limited grant types (READ, WRITE, READ_ACP, WRITE_ACP, FULL_CONTROL). Grantees: AWS account canonical ID or predefined groups (AllUsers=public, AuthenticatedUsers=any AWS account). AWS recommends disabling ACLs (S3 Object Ownership: BucketOwnerEnforced). <br><br> *When ACLs still apply: cross-account object ownership. If Account B puts an object in Account A's bucket: by default, Account B owns the object (even though it's in A's bucket). Account A cannot access or delete B's object without ACL grant. Solution: enable S3 Object Ownership = `BucketOwnerPreferred` → uploading account must set `bucket-owner-full-control` ACL on upload → A gets ownership. Or `BucketOwnerEnforced` → ACLs disabled, bucket owner always owns all objects → no ACL needed, bucket policy controls access.*<br> *Can both be used: yes, both are evaluated. An object can have an ACL AND the bucket has a policy. If EITHER denies → denied (explicit deny wins). If ACL allows but bucket policy denies → denied. If bucket policy allows but ACL denies (e.g., cross-account upload without proper ACL) → denied. Modern practice: disable ACLs (BucketOwnerEnforced), use only bucket policies. ACLs are pre-IAM technology and should be phased out. S3 Access Analyzer: flags both ACL and policy-based external access.*<br>

1166. [ IAM ] A company has 5 AWS accounts for different environments (dev, test, staging, prod, security). Design the cross-account IAM architecture so the security account can audit all others, and prod cannot be directly accessed by dev engineers. ; Hub-and-spoke IAM design: Security account = hub. Each environment account has `SecurityAuditRole` trusted by security account. Security team assumes `SecurityAuditRole` in any account for auditing. Dev engineers: Identity Center permission set for dev account only (no prod assignment). Prod account: separate Identity Center permission set, assigned only to senior engineers + SRE. SCP on prod OU: deny `sts:AssumeRole` from dev account (PrincipalAccount condition). <br><br> *Security account trust: each member account's `SecurityAuditRole` trust policy: `"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::SECURITY_ACCOUNT:role/SecurityAuditorRole"}`. Security account `SecurityAuditorRole`: has `sts:AssumeRole` on all environment account audit roles. Security team: assumes SecurityAuditorRole in security account → then assumes target account's SecurityAuditRole. Two-hop (role chaining — 1hr limit, acceptable for audit sessions).*<br> *Preventing dev → prod: (1) Identity Center: no dev engineer has permission set assigned to prod account. (2) SCP on prod OU: `"Deny","sts:AssumeRole","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"aws:PrincipalAccount":"DEV_ACCOUNT_ID"}}` — no identity from dev account can assume roles in prod. (3) Prod IAM roles: trust policies don't include dev account ARNs. Three independent controls. If a dev engineer gets a prod role ARN: (1) they have no identity policy allowing AssumeRole of that role, (2) SCP denies it, (3) trust policy doesn't include them. Belt-suspenders-superglue.*<br>

1167. [ IAM ] What is the AWS STS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` action and how does it differ from `AssumeRole`? Provide a complete OIDC federation flow. ; `AssumeRole`: caller presents AWS IAM credentials (user/role). `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`: caller presents an OIDC JWT token from an external identity provider (Google, GitHub, Cognito, EKS OIDC). No AWS credentials needed for the initial call. IAM role's trust policy must reference the OIDC provider. AWS validates the JWT signature against the provider's public key → issues temporary AWS credentials. <br><br> *Complete OIDC flow for GitHub Actions: (1) GitHub Actions runner receives a JWT from GitHub's OIDC endpoint. (2) Runner calls `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` with the JWT. (3) IAM validates JWT: checks signature (GitHub's public key registered in IAM OIDC provider), checks `aud` claim = `sts.amazonaws.com`, checks `sub` claim matches trust policy condition (`repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main`). (4) All valid → IAM issues STS credentials. (5) GitHub Actions runner uses credentials for AWS API calls. No static AWS credentials ever stored in GitHub.*<br> *Difference summary: AssumeRole = AWS-to-AWS identity handoff. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity = external identity system to AWS handoff. AssumeRoleWithSAML = enterprise SSO (SAML 2.0) to AWS handoff. GetFederationToken = old federation method (avoid — creates user-bound credentials, not recommended). AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is the modern standard for applications, mobile apps, CI/CD systems, and Kubernetes pod identity.*<br>

1168. [ IAM ] What is AWS IAM Roles Anywhere and what problem does it solve? Compare it to EC2 instance profiles. ; IAM Roles Anywhere: allows on-premises servers, VMs, or any non-AWS compute to obtain temporary IAM credentials by presenting X.509 certificates signed by a trusted CA. No static AWS access keys needed for on-premises workloads. EC2 instance profile: same concept but for EC2 instances (uses IMDS endpoint). Roles Anywhere: the X.509 cert is the proof of identity, IMDS is replaced by the Roles Anywhere signing helper. <br><br> *Roles Anywhere components: (1) Trust Anchor: register your CA certificate or AWS ACM Private CA in IAM Roles Anywhere. (2) Profile: defines which IAM roles can be obtained and for how long. (3) `aws_signing_helper` tool (open source): presents the X.509 cert to Roles Anywhere → gets temporary credentials → refreshes automatically. On-premises server: install cert + configure aws_signing_helper → SDK uses standard credential chain → picks up Roles Anywhere credentials. Application unchanged.*<br> *vs EC2 instance profile: both provide auto-rotating temporary credentials to compute. EC2: IMDS endpoint (169.254.169.254), automatic. Roles Anywhere: `aws_signing_helper serve` process (local HTTP endpoint), configured. EC2 is simpler (zero configuration). Roles Anywhere requires: PKI infrastructure (CA + cert issuance + rotation), aws_signing_helper installed and running. For on-premises: Roles Anywhere is the best option. For EC2: instance profiles (no change needed). For EKS: IRSA. For Lambda: execution role. Each compute type has its native IAM credential mechanism.*<br>

1170. [ IAM ] What is the IAM Access Analyzer "policy generation" feature? How does it work and what are its limitations? ; Policy generation: analyzes CloudTrail logs for a principal (user/role) over a period (up to 90 days) → produces a generated least-privilege policy showing ONLY the actions the principal actually used. Limitations: (1) Only captures what happened — doesn't predict future needs. (2) CloudTrail must be enabled and have data. (3) 90-day lookback maximum. (4) Some services not fully supported (CloudTrail events missing for some operations). (5) Generated policy may need manual review for accuracy. <br><br> *How it works: `StartPolicyGeneration` → Access Analyzer queries CloudTrail for `IDENTITY_ARN`'s API calls → correlates events to IAM actions → generates JSON policy with only the actions/resources observed. Result: `GetGeneratedPolicy` returns the policy document. Generated policy is a starting point — review and adjust before applying. Some CloudTrail events don't map 1:1 to IAM actions (especially newer services).*<br> *Limitations in practice: if a principal makes a broad action monthly (not in 90-day window): not captured → generated policy missing that action → role breaks after applying. Solution: run policy generation over the longest observation period available. Test generated policy in non-production before replacing existing policy. Also: generated policy may list individual resource ARNs (from CloudTrail) — may be too specific (hardcodes specific S3 object keys). Clean up: replace specific ARNs with prefix patterns. Policy generation is a TOOL to assist, not a replacement for human review of permissions.*<br>

1171. [ IAM ] What are IAM service last accessed information and how does it help achieve least privilege? ; Service last accessed: for each IAM user, group, role, or policy → shows the last time each AWS service was accessed, what actions were taken, from which region. Access via `GetServiceLastAccessedDetails` API or IAM console. Use: identify services a role claims permission to but never actually uses → remove those permissions. Granular action-level data (not just service-level) for most services. <br><br> *Access: `aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details --arn arn:aws:iam::123:role/MyRole` → async job → `aws iam get-service-last-accessed-details --job-id JOB_ID`. Response includes each service, last authenticated time, total authenticated entities (how many principals used it). Null lastAuthenticated = never used. Confidence interval: data available for last 365 days only (older access not shown).*<br> *Right-sizing process: (1) Generate service last accessed for the role. (2) List all services with `lastAuthenticated == null` (never used in last 365 days). (3) List services last used > 90 days ago (rarely used). (4) Remove permissions for null services (safe). (5) For rarely-used: review with the team → confirm no upcoming need → remove. Repeat quarterly. IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings automate this: findings for roles with permissions unused > 90 days. Access Analyzer + service last accessed = comprehensive least-privilege management.*<br>

1172. [ IAM ] A SaaS company needs to give each customer a separate, isolated AWS role that can only access that customer's data in a shared S3 bucket. The bucket has customer data in prefixes (customer-id/). How do you implement this with one IAM role (not one per customer)? ; Use session tags + ABAC: one IAM role `CustomerRole`. When customer authenticates (Cognito → `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`): pass session tag `customerId = CUSTOMER_ID`. IAM policy on `CustomerRole`: `"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::shared-bucket/${aws:PrincipalTag/customerId}/*"`. Each customer's session can only access their prefix. One role, N customers, isolated access. <br><br> *Session tags mechanism: `aws sts assume-role --role-arn ARN --session-tags '[{"Key":"customerId","Value":"CUST-12345"}]'`. PrincipalTag in the session = `customerId = CUST-12345`. IAM policy resource: `arn:aws:s3:::shared-bucket/CUST-12345/*` (resolved from policy variable). No other customer's prefix accessible. One policy handles all customers.*<br> *Transitive tag enforcement: mark `customerId` as transitive: `--transitive-tag-keys customerId`. If this customer session further assumes another role: `customerId` tag persists. Cannot be removed or changed by the customer (trust policy enforces who can set session tags). Security property: customer can never spoof another customer's ID in the tag — they authenticate via Cognito which sets the tag from the JWT. Cognito JWT sub → customerId mapping → session tag. Immutable from the customer's perspective.*<br>

1173. [ IAM ] What is the difference between IAM Identity Center's `ACCOUNT_ASSIGNMENT` and `PERMISSION_SET`? How are they related? ; Permission Set: a template defining what access to grant (IAM policies, managed policies, inline policies, permission boundary). Like a "role definition template." Account Assignment: binds a Permission Set + a User/Group + a specific AWS Account. Creates an IAM role in the target account populated with the Permission Set's policies. Permission Set defines WHAT. Account Assignment defines WHO gets WHAT in WHICH account. <br><br> *Lifecycle: create Permission Set once → it has no effect until assigned. Create Account Assignment: IdentityCenter deploys an IAM role in the target account (role name: `AWSReservedSSO_PermissionSetName_RandomSuffix`). Role trust policy trusts the Identity Center SAML provider. Role policies = permission set's policies. User/group can now access that account. Delete assignment: role removed from account. Modify permission set: all deployed roles in all assigned accounts auto-updated.*<br> *Scale example: `DevReadOnly` permission set = ReadOnlyAccess + developer-specific custom policy. Assign to: Dev-Engineers group + [dev-account-1, dev-account-2, dev-account-3]. Result: IAM role `AWSReservedSSO_DevReadOnly_abc123` created in each of 3 accounts, each trusting Identity Center. 10 developers in the group: all get access to all 3 dev accounts via this one assignment. New dev added to group in IdP → SCIM sync → gets all 3 account accesses automatically.*<br>

1174. [ IAM ] What is the difference between the root account and the management account in AWS Organizations? ; Root account (before Organizations): the AWS account's primary owner account — the one created with the email. Has the root user (superuser with unconstrained access). Every account has one. Management account (Organizations): the account that creates and manages the AWS Organization. Is ALSO the root account of itself. NOT subject to SCPs. Pays for all member accounts in consolidated billing. Has org-level administrative powers. Before orgs: every account was just "the root account." After orgs: one account becomes the "management account" for the org. <br><br> *Why management account is ungoverned: SCPs apply to all member accounts but NOT the management account. This is why: (1) No workloads in management account (only billing, org management, Identity Center). (2) Management account compromise = org-wide blast radius. (3) Keep the management account empty — minimal IAM users, MFA on root, no EC2/Lambda/S3 workloads. AWS Well-Architected: "use management account only for billing and organization management." All workloads in member accounts (governed by SCPs).*<br> *Root user in management account: can create/delete org, create/delete member accounts, manage consolidated billing, can override any SCP (SCPs don't apply to management account). Root user in member account: CAN be restricted by SCPs (member account root IS subject to SCPs). This surprises people: member account root user is not omnipotent — SCPs limit even them. Only management account root is truly unrestricted within the organization.*<br>

1175. [ IAM ] Summarize ALL AWS IAM concepts relevant to SAP-C02 in a structured table format covering: identities, policies, evaluation, federation, and advanced features. ; Full IAM concept map for SAP-C02: **Identities**: Users (permanent creds), Groups (collection of users, max 10 per user), Roles (temp creds, trust + permission policy), Service-linked roles (AWS-managed, SCP-exempt). **Credentials**: Password, Access Keys (rotate < 90 days), STS tokens (15min-12hr, role chaining=1hr max), IMDS (EC2), IRSA (EKS pods). **Policy types**: Identity-based (inline/managed/AWS-managed), Resource-based (Principal field, cross-account), SCP (org ceiling, no grants), Permission boundary (identity ceiling), Session policy (further restrict). **Evaluation**: Explicit deny wins. SCP → Boundary → Session → Identity or Resource-based (same account: OR, cross-account: AND). **Federation**: SAML 2.0 (enterprise SSO), OIDC (GitHub/Cognito), IAM Identity Center (recommended for multi-account), Roles Anywhere (on-prem). <br><br> *Advanced features: ABAC (PrincipalTag + ResourceTag + RequestTag = scalable policy). Policy variables (${}). Condition operators (String*, Numeric*, Date*, Bool, Null, Arn*, IpAddress, ForAllValues/ForAnyValue). PassRole (required to delegate role to a service, privilege escalation risk). SourceIdentity (persistent cross-chain identity label). ExternalId (confused deputy prevention). IAM Access Analyzer (external access findings, unused access, policy generation). Credential Report (CSV audit of all users/keys). Service last accessed (least privilege enforcement). Permission boundaries (delegation with guardrails). Organizations + SCPs + RCPs (data perimeter).*<br> *Key exam numbers: users/account=5000, groups/account=300, roles/account=1000, policies attached to identity=10 (soft), policy size=6144 chars, policy versions=5, max session=12hr, role chain max=1hr, access key max per user=2, inline policy=2048 chars, groups per user=10. Know these — calculation scenarios appear in exam questions.*<br>

1191. [ Network Security ] A company needs to allow private EC2 instances in a VPC to download OS patches from the internet without exposing them to inbound connections. What is the recommended solution? ; Deploy a managed NAT Gateway in a public subnet. Configure the private subnet route table with `0.0.0.0/0 → nat-gateway-id`. The NAT Gateway has an Elastic IP and routes through the IGW. Private instances can initiate outbound connections, no inbound connections are possible because NAT doesn't create forwarding rules for unsolicited inbound traffic. <br><br> *NAT Gateway is the managed replacement for NAT Instances. AWS manages availability, patching, and scaling (5 Gbps to 100 Gbps auto-scaling). NAT Instance (legacy EC2 with source/dest check disabled) is not recommended for production: requires manual HA setup, manual patching, limited bandwidth by instance type.* <br> *For HA: deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ. Private subnet in AZ-A routes to NAT GW in AZ-A. Private subnet in AZ-B routes to NAT GW in AZ-B. Cross-AZ NAT: works but incurs $0.01/GB cross-AZ charge and creates AZ-level single point of failure. Rule: route table per AZ, NAT GW per AZ.* <br>

1192. [ Network Security ] A private EC2 instance in a VPC needs to communicate outbound to the internet using IPv6. The instance must NOT be reachable from the internet. What do you use? ; Egress-Only Internet Gateway (EIGW). Add route `::/0 → eigw-id` to the private subnet route table. EIGW allows IPv6 egress while blocking unsolicited inbound IPv6 connections. NAT Gateway does not support IPv6. IGW supports IPv6 bidirectionally (allows inbound). EIGW is the only option for IPv6 egress-only. <br><br> *IPv6 does not use NAT — all IPv6 addresses are globally routable. This means a regular IGW with IPv6 route would expose the instance to inbound connections from anywhere on the internet. EIGW solves this by maintaining connection state: only responses to connections initiated by the EC2 are allowed inbound.* <br> *EIGW is free (no hourly charge, no data processing fee). One EIGW per VPC. It is a VPC-level resource that spans all AZs. Configuration: VPC → Enable IPv6 CIDR → Assign IPv6 to subnet → Create EIGW → Add ::/0 → eigw-id to private subnet route table → EC2 gets IPv6 auto-assigned.* <br>

1193. [ Network Security ] A NACL has the following inbound rules: Rule 100 ALLOW TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, Rule 110 DENY TCP port 443 from 10.0.5.0/24. Traffic from 10.0.5.10 on port 443 is being allowed. What is the problem and how do you fix it? ; NACLs evaluate rules in ascending order by rule number, the first match wins. Rule 100 (ALLOW all 443) is evaluated before Rule 110 (DENY 10.0.5.0/24). 10.0.5.10 matches Rule 100 first → ALLOWED. Fix: renumber the DENY rule below 100 (e.g., Rule 90: DENY TCP 443 from 10.0.5.0/24). Now 10.0.5.10 hits Rule 90 first → DENIED. <br><br> *NACL vs Security Group rule evaluation: Security Groups evaluate ALL rules simultaneously — most permissive wins, no ordering. NACLs evaluate rules numerically ascending — first match wins, rest ignored. This is the critical behavioral difference for the exam.* <br> *NACL rule numbering best practice: leave gaps between rules (100, 200, 300) so you can insert rules between existing ones without renumbering. AWS recommends increments of 10 or 100. Default NACL: ALLOW ALL (rules 100: allow all, *: implicit deny). Custom NACL: no rules except implicit DENY * → blocks everything until you add ALLOW rules.* <br>

1194. [ Network Security ] A Security Group allows all outbound traffic (default). An EC2 instance initiates an HTTPS connection to 8.8.8.8:443. The NACL has an inbound ALLOW for TCP 443 but NO rule for ephemeral ports (1024-65535). Will the connection succeed? ; No. The NACL is stateless. The EC2 sends a packet to 8.8.8.8:443 (outbound — this is allowed by SG outbound rule and NACL outbound if configured). The response comes back from 8.8.8.8 to the EC2 on a random ephemeral port (e.g., 52341). The NACL inbound rule only allows port 443 — the response on port 52341 is DENIED by the NACL. Connection fails. Fix: add NACL inbound rule ALLOW TCP 1024-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0. <br><br> *Ephemeral port range: Linux kernels use 32768-60999. Windows: 49152-65535. AWS recommends allowing 1024-65535 to cover all OS variations. This is the most common NACL misconfiguration: engineers add rules for destination ports but forget response ports.* <br> *Security Group is stateful: the SG tracks the connection and automatically allows the response on port 52341 without an explicit inbound rule. This is why Security Groups are easier to work with for application traffic. NACLs require both directions explicitly. Use NACLs for broad subnet-level controls (block a /24), use SGs for fine-grained instance-level controls.* <br>

1195. [ Network Security ] A company wants to block all traffic from a known malicious IP range (198.51.100.0/24) to all instances in a subnet. What is the most efficient method? ; Add a DENY rule in the subnet's NACL: Rule number (lower than any existing ALLOW): DENY ALL from 198.51.100.0/24. This blocks all traffic from the range at the subnet boundary before it reaches any instance. Security Groups cannot create deny rules (allow-only). NACL is the correct layer for subnet-wide IP blocking. <br><br> *Why not Security Group: Security Groups are allow-only. You cannot add a DENY rule. You would have to ensure NO security group allows traffic from 198.51.100.0/24 — across all instances in the subnet — which is error-prone and doesn't scale. NACL deny covers all current and future instances in the subnet automatically.* <br> *NACL approach for threat response: known attacker IP detected in VPC Flow Logs → automated Lambda → adds DENY rule to NACL → attacker blocked subnet-wide. This is a common automated incident response pattern. Remove the rule after threat mitigated. For persistent blocks, maintain a deny list in a centralized firewall (Network Firewall or WAF) rather than managing individual NACL rules.* <br>

1196. [ Network Security ] What does VPC Flow Logs capture and what does it NOT capture? ; CAPTURES: Source/destination IP, source/destination port, protocol number, packet count, byte count, start/end time, ACCEPT or REJECT action, log status. Does NOT capture: packet payloads/content, DNS queries to Route 53 Resolver, DHCP traffic, metadata service traffic (169.254.169.254), Windows license activation traffic (169.254.169.250), instance metadata traffic. <br><br> *Flow logs are metadata-only — you see WHO communicated with WHOM on WHICH PORT but not WHAT was said. For payload inspection: AWS Network Firewall (inspects inline), or mirror traffic with VPC Traffic Mirroring to a security appliance. Traffic mirroring copies actual packets to an inspection instance/NLB — this has cost and performance implications.* <br> *Practical use: REJECT entries in flow logs = security group or NACL blocking. If you see many REJECT entries from the same source IP → potential port scan or brute force. GuardDuty analyzes flow logs automatically using ML — it detects these patterns without you having to query flow logs manually. Flow logs are the raw data, GuardDuty is the intelligence layer on top.* <br>

1197. [ Network Security ] A company enables VPC Flow Logs but notices that the `action` field shows ACCEPT for traffic they believe should be blocked by a Security Group. What are the possible explanations? ; Possible explanations: (1) Security Group was recently changed and old connections still active (SGs are stateful — existing connections not immediately terminated). (2) Different ENI than expected — traffic going through a different network interface with different SG. (3) Traffic is internal to the same Security Group (SG allows inbound from same SG by default in some configurations). (4) Flow logs capture some AWS internal traffic as ACCEPT even if SG would block it. Investigate: check which ENI the flow log entry references, verify the SG attached to that ENI. <br><br> *Flow log `interface-id` field identifies the exact ENI. Use this to find the EC2 instance and its attached SGs: `aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --network-interface-ids eni-xxx`. Check inbound rules of each attached SG. If SG looks correct, check NACL (NACLs are checked before SGs — wait, actually SGs are checked first... correction: for inbound traffic, NACLs are evaluated at subnet ingress BEFORE the packet reaches the SG. So ACCEPT in flow logs means BOTH NACL and SG allowed it.* <br> *Flow log timing: aggregation interval is 1 or 10 minutes. A REJECT at 10:00:01 and ACCEPT at 10:00:02 (after rule fix) may appear in the same aggregation window. Review timestamps carefully. Custom flow log format with `flow-direction` field helps distinguish ingress vs egress. `pkt-srcaddr` vs `srcaddr` helps when NAT is in the path.* <br>

1198. [ Network Security ] A company wants to implement IDS/IPS for all traffic entering and leaving their VPC. They use AWS-native services only. What is the architecture? ; AWS Network Firewall in inspection subnets (one per AZ). Configure stateful rule groups with IDS rules (ALERT) or IPS rules (DROP). Route all internet-bound and internet-incoming traffic through the firewall endpoints. Ingress: IGW Ingress Routing → Firewall Endpoint → ALB/EC2. Egress: Private subnet → Firewall Endpoint → NAT GW → IGW. <br><br> *AWS Network Firewall uses Suricata-compatible rule syntax. AWS provides managed rule groups (threat intelligence feeds, malware signatures, bot control) that auto-update — no manual signature management. For IDS mode (monitoring only): set stateful rule group default action to ALERT. For IPS mode (active blocking): set to DROP. Start with ALERT, analyze logs, tune rules, switch to DROP when confident to avoid false-positive business impact.* <br> *Route table design for inspection: (1) IGW Ingress Route Table: attach to IGW, route `10.0.0.0/16 → firewall-endpoint-az-a` (AZ-specific). (2) Firewall Subnet Route Table: `0.0.0.0/0 → IGW` for egress. (3) Private Subnet Route Table: `0.0.0.0/0 → NAT GW` (traffic goes NAT GW → Firewall Endpoint → IGW). Alternatively: private → firewall → NAT GW → IGW (firewall before NAT). Order matters for source IP visibility.* <br>

1199. [ Network Security ] A company is migrating from on-premises Palo Alto firewalls to AWS. They require SSL/TLS inspection, User-ID (firewall rules based on AD user), and WildFire zero-day analysis. Which AWS architecture satisfies these requirements? ; GWLB + Palo Alto VM-Series on EC2. Deploy Palo Alto VM-Series instances in an inspection VPC as GWLB target group (UDP 6081 Geneve). Configure GWLB Endpoints in spoke VPCs. Bootstrap VM-Series with S3 bootstrap bucket (init-cfg.txt points to Panorama). Panorama pushes SSL decryption profiles, User-ID agents, and WildFire policy. AWS Network Firewall cannot satisfy these requirements (no SSL decryption, no User-ID, no WildFire). <br><br> *SSL decryption requirement: to inspect HTTPS traffic content (not just metadata), the firewall must perform SSL forward proxy. This requires: (1) Firewall with SSL decryption capability (Palo Alto, Fortinet, Check Point). (2) Corporate root CA certificate deployed to client browsers/OS. (3) Firewall generates a re-signed certificate for each HTTPS session. AWS Network Firewall has no SSL decryption capability — it can only inspect cleartext protocols and TLS metadata (SNI, certificate subject).* <br> *GWLB flow stickiness: 5-tuple hash ensures all packets of a TLS session go to the same Palo Alto instance. Critical for stateful TLS inspection — if packets of the same session went to different appliances, SSL handshake state would be lost. GWLB health checks (HTTP, TCP, or custom) automatically remove failed Palo Alto instances from rotation. Auto Scaling Group for Palo Alto instances: scale out on CPU > 70%, scale in on CPU < 30%.* <br>

1200. [ Network Security ] What is the Geneve protocol and why does GWLB use it instead of simply routing packets? ; Geneve (Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation, RFC 8926, UDP port 6081) encapsulates the original packet inside a Geneve tunnel while preserving original source/destination IP headers. GWLB uses Geneve so the firewall appliance sees the real client and server IPs (not GWLB IPs). Without Geneve: GWLB would modify the packet, losing source IP — firewall rules based on real IPs would be impossible. With Geneve: appliance decapsulates Geneve wrapper, inspects original packet, makes policy decision, re-encapsulates, returns to GWLB. <br><br> *Geneve vs VXLAN: VXLAN (UDP 4789) uses a fixed 24-bit VNI for tenant identification. Geneve has extensible TLV (Type-Length-Value) headers allowing arbitrary metadata. GWLB uses Geneve TLV headers to pass AWS-specific metadata (VPC ID, flow ID) to the appliance. This metadata allows the appliance to apply per-VPC policies even in a shared inspection infrastructure.* <br> *Linux Geneve support: `ip link add geneve0 type geneve id 100 remote 10.0.0.1` — creates a Geneve tunnel interface. Open vSwitch (OVS) uses Geneve for overlay networking in OpenStack and KVM environments. If you've used OpenStack Neutron with OVS, you've used Geneve/VXLAN. Azure Gateway Load Balancer also uses Geneve for the same reason — preserving original packet headers for appliance inspection.* <br>

1201. [ Network Security ] A multi-account AWS organization wants to centralize all outbound internet traffic from 20 spoke VPCs through a single egress VPC with Network Firewall inspection. What is the architecture? ; Egress VPC with: (1) Network Firewall endpoints per AZ. (2) NAT Gateways in public subnets. (3) IGW. Transit Gateway connecting all spoke VPCs to Egress VPC. TGW route table for spokes: `0.0.0.0/0 → Egress VPC attachment`. Egress VPC TGW attachment subnet route table: `0.0.0.0/0 → Firewall Endpoint (AZ-specific)`. Firewall subnet route table: `0.0.0.0/0 → NAT GW`. Return traffic: NAT GW → IGW → internet → IGW → Firewall → TGW → spoke. <br><br> *Benefits of centralized egress: (1) Single set of Elastic IPs — external partners allowlist one IP range, not 20 separate VPC NAT GW IPs. (2) Centralized security policy — one Network Firewall, one set of rules, one logs destination. (3) Cost — 1 NAT GW per AZ in Egress VPC instead of 1 per AZ per spoke VPC (20 VPCs × 3 AZs × $32/month = $1,920/month saved). (4) Governance — traffic through inspection VPC, logged, audited.* <br> *AZ affinity is critical: spoke traffic arriving at TGW in AZ-B must route to Firewall Endpoint in AZ-B. If it routes to Firewall Endpoint in AZ-A: cross-AZ fees ($0.01/GB both ways) AND asymmetric routing if the return path uses AZ-B. TGW with Appliance Mode enabled ensures symmetric routing for stateful appliances. Enable Appliance Mode on the TGW attachment to the Egress VPC.* <br>

1202. [ Network Security ] What is "Appliance Mode" on a Transit Gateway attachment and when is it required? ; Appliance Mode on a TGW attachment ensures that traffic flows to/from a VPC are consistently routed through the same AZ's ENI on the attachment, regardless of which AZ the source instance is in. Required when: stateful network appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS) are deployed in the target VPC and require seeing both directions of a flow through the same appliance instance. Without Appliance Mode: TGW may route request and response through different AZs → different appliance instances → stateful inspection fails → connections dropped. <br><br> *Default TGW routing: TGW routes to the attachment ENI in the same AZ as the source. For a VPC with appliances in multiple AZs, this means: EC2 in AZ-A sends traffic → TGW → attachment in AZ-A → appliance in AZ-A. Response: server in AZ-B → TGW → attachment in AZ-B → appliance in AZ-B. Two different appliances see each direction — stateful firewall drops the asymmetric flow.* <br> *Appliance Mode fix: TGW with Appliance Mode enabled on the inspection VPC attachment: routes all traffic for a given flow to the same AZ's attachment (based on flow hash). Both request and response go through AZ-A's appliance. Enabled per attachment: `aws ec2 modify-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment --transit-gateway-attachment-id tgw-attach-xxx --options ApplianceModeSupport=enable`. Cost: no additional TGW charge for Appliance Mode, but cross-AZ data transfer may apply.* <br>

1203. [ Network Security ] A company needs to filter outbound DNS queries from EC2 instances to block queries for known malicious domains. What is the recommended AWS solution? ; Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall. Create a domain list with known malicious domains. Associate the domain list with a rule group set to BLOCK action. Associate the rule group with the VPC. DNS queries from EC2 instances to Route 53 Resolver (169.254.169.253) are inspected — queries for blocked domains return NXDOMAIN or custom response. <br><br> *Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall is specifically designed for DNS-level filtering. It integrates with AWS-managed domain lists (AWS Route 53 Resolver Managed Domain Lists include malware domains, botnet C2, threat intelligence feeds). Custom domain lists can be uploaded via CSV or manually added.* <br> *Why not Network Firewall for DNS: Network Firewall can filter DNS (it has domain list rules), but if EC2s use Route 53 Resolver (the default), they query 169.254.169.253 which is local — traffic never passes through Network Firewall endpoints. DNS Firewall intercepts at the resolver level. Use both: DNS Firewall for DNS-level blocking, Network Firewall for non-DNS traffic inspection. They are complementary.* <br>

1204. [ Network Security ] Explain the difference between AWS WAF, AWS Network Firewall, and AWS Shield. When should each be used? ; WAF: Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS only). Protects web applications against OWASP Top 10 (SQL injection, XSS, etc.). Deployed on CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync. Rule-based HTTP inspection. Network Firewall: Layer 3-7 (any protocol). VPC-level stateful inspection, IDS/IPS, domain filtering. Requires routing traffic through firewall endpoints. Shield: DDoS protection. Shield Standard (free, automatic, L3/L4). Shield Advanced (paid, L3-L7, 24/7 DRT, cost protection). Use all three together for defense in depth. <br><br> *WAF cannot inspect non-HTTP protocols (SSH brute force, SMTP relay abuse, non-standard port attacks). Network Firewall handles these. WAF is "closer to the application" — deployed at the edge (CloudFront) or load balancer layer. Network Firewall is "at the VPC perimeter" — all VPC traffic passes through it if correctly routed.* <br> *Shield Standard is automatic and free for all AWS customers — always active. Shield Advanced adds: advanced attack attribution, real-time attack visibility, 24/7 AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT), automatic WAF rule creation during attacks, cost protection (refund of scaling costs caused by DDoS). Shield Advanced is worth it when: public-facing application with high DDoS risk, or when application downtime cost exceeds ~$3,000/month (Shield Advanced cost). Required for: financial services, gaming, media streaming with high attack surface.* <br>

1205. [ Network Security ] A company needs to implement centralized firewall management across 50 AWS accounts in an Organization. They want to enforce Network Firewall policies on all accounts. What service enables this? ; AWS Firewall Manager. Firewall Manager centrally manages: AWS Network Firewall policies, AWS WAF rules, Security Group policies, Shield Advanced protection, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall. With Organizations integration: define a Firewall Manager policy → automatically applied to all accounts/OUs. New accounts added to OU: policy automatically deployed. Non-compliant accounts: Firewall Manager alerts and can auto-remediate. <br><br> *Firewall Manager prerequisites: (1) Organization with all features enabled. (2) Firewall Manager administrator account designated (usually security account). (3) AWS Config enabled in all member accounts (Firewall Manager uses Config for compliance tracking). (4) AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) enabled for sharing resources across accounts.* <br> *Firewall Manager Network Firewall policy: defines firewall rule groups and their priority. Firewall Manager creates a Network Firewall in each account/VPC that matches the scope. OR: Centralized model — Firewall Manager deploys firewall in a designated inspection VPC, routes all spoke VPC traffic through it (requires TGW configuration). Distributed model: firewall in each VPC (more endpoints = higher cost, but no inter-VPC routing needed).* <br>

1206. [ Network Security ] What is the difference between a NAT Gateway and an Internet Gateway? Can a private subnet use an IGW directly? ; IGW: enables bidirectional communication between VPC and internet for instances with public IPs. One per VPC. NAT Gateway: enables outbound-only internet access for private instances (no public IP required). One per AZ (for HA). Private subnet CANNOT use IGW directly — the route `0.0.0.0/0 → igw-id` in a private subnet route table routes packets to IGW, but IGW performs 1:1 NAT only for public/Elastic IPs — private instances have no public IP to NAT to, so IGW drops the packet. Private subnet needs: `0.0.0.0/0 → nat-gateway-id`. <br><br> *Common misconception: "just add IGW route to private subnet for internet." This fails because IGW NAT requires a public IP on the instance. Without Elastic IP or auto-assigned public IP: IGW receives the packet, looks up NAT table, finds no public IP for the private IP → drops packet. The private subnet is "private" by definition — no public IP → IGW routing doesn't work.* <br> *Private subnet internet flow: EC2 (10.0.2.5) → Route: 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-gw → NAT GW translates src=10.0.2.5 to src=52.x.x.x (NAT GW's EIP) → IGW → internet. Return: internet → IGW → NAT GW (dst=52.x.x.x:port → 10.0.2.5:original-port) → EC2. The NAT GW maintains the port mapping state. This is classic NAPT (Network Address and Port Translation).* <br>

1207. [ Network Security ] A company uses AWS Network Firewall and wants to block all outbound traffic except to specific approved domains (whitelist approach). How do you implement this? ; Create a stateful rule group with domain list rules. Add approved domains (e.g., amazonaws.com, example.com). Set the rule group default action to DENY. Traffic to listed domains: ALLOW. Traffic to all other domains: DENY. Associate rule group with Network Firewall policy. Configure firewall in egress path. <br><br> *Domain list rules in Network Firewall operate at the SNI (Server Name Indication) level for HTTPS and the Host header for HTTP. They do not require SSL decryption. Trade-off: if a malicious site uses a trusted CDN (cloudfront.net), domain-based allow of cloudfront.net allows ALL CloudFront content including malicious. For stricter control: Network Firewall IPS rules checking specific URLs, or Palo Alto with URL categories.* <br> *Whitelist vs blacklist approach: whitelist (allow-list) — deny all, allow known good. More secure but higher operational overhead (must add every new legitimate destination). Blacklist (deny-list) — allow all, deny known bad. Easier to operate but zero-day domains not in blacklist. Production recommendation: blacklist for general web access, whitelist for highly sensitive systems (payment processing, data exfiltration prevention).* <br>

1208. [ Network Security ] A security engineer needs to inspect ALL traffic between VPCs in a Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke model, including east-west (VPC-to-VPC) traffic. What architecture do you design? ; East-west inspection with TGW: (1) Create separate TGW route tables — one for spokes, one for inspection VPC. (2) Spoke route table: all destinations (including other VPC CIDRs) → inspection VPC attachment. (3) Inspection route table: VPC CIDRs → respective spoke attachments. (4) Enable Appliance Mode on TGW inspection VPC attachment. Traffic path: Spoke A → TGW (spoke route table) → Inspection VPC → Network Firewall/GWLB → TGW (inspection route table) → Spoke B. <br><br> *This is called the "hair-pin" or "tromboning" model — traffic from Spoke A to Spoke B goes Spoke A → Inspection VPC → back through TGW → Spoke B, rather than directly A → B. The inspection VPC is the mandatory transit point for all inter-VPC traffic. This requires static routes in TGW route tables pointing ALL spoke CIDR ranges to the inspection VPC attachment.* <br> *Without this architecture: TGW by default routes traffic directly between spokes (Spoke A attachment → Spoke B attachment), bypassing the inspection VPC entirely. The inspection VPC only sees traffic explicitly routed to it. For east-west inspection: you MUST route spoke-to-spoke traffic through the inspection VPC via separate TGW route tables. This is the most common gap in enterprise AWS network security architectures.* <br>

1209. [ Network Security ] What are the limitations of Security Groups that make NACLs necessary? List specific scenarios where only NACLs work. ; Security Groups limitations: (1) Allow-only — cannot create DENY rules. (2) Applied per-instance — must be manually applied to every new instance. (3) Cannot reference IP ranges for blocking. (4) No ordering — all rules evaluated simultaneously (most permissive wins). NACLs needed for: (1) Block specific malicious IP/CIDR (SG cannot deny). (2) Subnet-wide policy (SG requires per-instance config). (3) Emergency IP block response (NACL covers all subnet instances immediately). (4) Regulatory compliance requiring subnet-level controls. <br><br> *Scenario: attacker scanning from 198.51.100.5. With SG alone: you can remove the allow rule for port X, but if SG has allow-all-inbound (0.0.0.0/0), you cannot create a deny for 198.51.100.5 specifically. NACL: add Rule 50: DENY ALL from 198.51.100.5/32. Immediate effect across all instances in the subnet. This is why both layers are needed.* <br> *Scenario 2: compliance requirement — "database subnet must not accept connections from anything outside the application subnet (10.0.1.0/24)." SG: add rule allowing only 10.0.1.0/24 on port 5432. NACL: add rule denying everything except 10.0.1.0/24 on port 5432. Defense in depth: both controls independently enforce the policy. An SG misconfiguration (accidentally adding 0.0.0.0/0) is caught by the NACL. An NACL misconfiguration (adding overly broad allow) is caught by the SG.* <br>

1210. [ Network Security ] A company has EC2 instances generating 100GB/day of VPC Flow Logs. They need to query these logs for security investigations. What is the most cost-effective architecture? ; Send VPC Flow Logs to S3 in Parquet format with Hive-compatible prefixes (partitioned by account, region, year, month, day). Use Athena with partition projection for zero-overhead partition management. Create Athena table with partition projection on `year`, `month`, `day`, `region`, `account`. Queries scan only the partitions matching the date/account filter. Cost: S3 (~$2.30/day for 100GB) + Athena ($5/TB scanned, use partition pruning to minimize scan). <br><br> *Parquet format: columnar storage. Athena can skip columns it doesn't need (e.g., query only srcaddr, dstaddr, action without reading all other fields). Compression: Parquet with Snappy compression reduces 100GB/day JSON to ~15-20GB/day. Athena cost reduction: from $0.50/query (scan all JSON) to ~$0.08/query (scan compressed Parquet with partition pruning). For 100 queries/day security investigations: $50/day → $8/day.* <br> *CloudWatch Logs alternative: $0.50/GB ingestion = $50/day for 100GB. Too expensive for this volume. Appropriate for: small VPCs (<10GB/day), real-time metric filters and alarms (S3 has 5-15 min delay). Kinesis Data Firehose → S3: lower cost than CloudWatch Logs, supports Parquet conversion via Lambda transform. For SIEM integration (Splunk, OpenSearch): Firehose delivers flow logs directly to the SIEM in near-real-time.* <br>

1211. [ Network Security ] An EC2 instance in a private subnet cannot reach S3. The route table has `0.0.0.0/0 → nat-gateway-id`. NAT Gateway is running. What else could prevent S3 access? ; Check in order: (1) Security Group outbound rules — does the SG allow TCP 443 outbound to S3 CIDR ranges (or 0.0.0.0/0)? Default SG outbound is allow-all — but custom SGs may restrict. (2) NACL outbound rules — does NACL allow TCP 443 and ephemeral port returns? (3) S3 Bucket Policy — does the bucket policy deny requests from private IP CIDRs? (4) VPC Endpoint — is there a VPC Endpoint for S3 that has a more specific route (`pl-xxxxx → vpce-id`) overriding the NAT route? (5) IAM Role — does the EC2 instance role have `s3:GetObject` permission? <br><br> *VPC Endpoint override is a common trap: if a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 exists and the route table has `pl-xxxxx (S3 prefix list) → vpce-id`, ALL S3 traffic uses the endpoint, not the NAT GW. If the endpoint policy is restrictive, or the bucket is in a different region, endpoint routing may fail. Check: `aws ec2 describe-route-tables` — look for prefix list routes.* <br> *S3 Bucket Policy restriction: `"Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:SourceVpc":"vpc-xxx"}}` blocks access from outside the VPC — but via NAT GW, the source appears as the NAT GW's public IP, not the VPC. Use VPC Endpoint + bucket policy `aws:SourceVpce` condition for private access without internet. Or use `aws:SourceIp` with NAT GW EIP in the bucket policy for NAT GW access.* <br>

1212. [ Network Security ] What is the purpose of IDS vs IPS in AWS Network Firewall? How do you implement each and when do you use each mode? ; IDS (Intrusion Detection System): ALERT action — traffic passes, match generates a log/alert. Use during initial deployment to understand traffic patterns without blocking legitimate traffic. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): DROP action — matching traffic is blocked. Use when confident rules don't produce false positives. AWS Network Firewall rule group actions: `ALERT` = IDS, `DROP` = IPS, `PASS` = explicit allow (overrides deny rules). Recommended approach: start with ALERT for 2-4 weeks, analyze CloudWatch/S3 logs, identify false positives, tune rules, switch to DROP. <br><br> *False positive risk: a rule matching legitimate business traffic in DROP mode = outage. Example: rule blocks HTTP User-Agent strings containing "Python" (common for bots). Your monitoring agent also uses Python urllib. IPS mode: monitoring breaks, alerts stop, on-call gets paged. IDS mode: alert fires, engineer reviews, discovers false positive, adds exception before enabling IPS. Process: IDS discovery → tune → IPS enforcement.* <br> *AWS managed rule groups have a recommended default action. Some are IDS-only (ALERT) by design because they have high false positive rates. Custom Suricata rules: `alert` keyword = IDS, `drop` keyword = IPS. Mixed mode: some rules on ALERT (discovering new attack patterns), others on DROP (confirmed attack signatures with no false positives). Layered: rule group 1 (managed, DROP for known malware C2), rule group 2 (custom, ALERT for anomalous patterns under investigation).* <br>

1213. [ Network Security ] A company uses GWLB with third-party firewall appliances. An appliance becomes unhealthy. How does GWLB handle this and what happens to existing connections? ; GWLB performs health checks (configurable: TCP, HTTP, or HTTPS) at configurable intervals. Unhealthy appliance: GWLB stops sending new connections to it. Existing connections: depends on 5-tuple stickiness. New flows: redistributed to healthy appliances. Existing flows in progress: if the unhealthy appliance is the sticky target, GWLB may need to redirect existing flows to a new appliance — this may break stateful inspection for those flows (sessions may be dropped and need to re-establish). <br><br> *Health check configuration: `HealthyThresholdCount: 3` (default) — appliance must pass 3 consecutive health checks to be marked healthy. `UnhealthyThresholdCount: 3` — must fail 3 consecutive checks to be marked unhealthy. At 30s interval: 90 seconds to detect failure. During this 90 seconds: GWLB still sends traffic to the failing appliance → some traffic may be dropped. Reduce interval to 10s for faster detection at higher health check cost.* <br> *Mitigation: Blue-green appliance deployment. Use AWS Auto Scaling with lifecycle hooks: before instance termination, drain connections (deregister from GWLB target group → wait for connection drain → terminate). Connection draining allows existing connections to complete before the appliance is removed. For zero-downtime appliance upgrades: launch new appliances → register with target group → deregister old appliances → connection drain → terminate old.* <br>

1214. [ Network Security ] Describe the defense-in-depth network security model for a three-tier web application in AWS. ; Layer 1 (Edge): CloudFront + AWS WAF (SQL injection, XSS, geo-blocking, rate limiting). Shield Standard (automatic DDoS, free). Layer 2 (Perimeter): IGW (single internet entry point). Network Firewall (stateful inspection, IPS rules, domain filtering) in dedicated firewall subnets. Layer 3 (Subnet): NACLs on each tier subnet (explicit deny for known bad CIDRs, allow only required ports). Layer 4 (Instance): Security Groups per tier (web-SG allows 443/80 from CloudFront prefix list only, app-SG allows app port from web-SG only, db-SG allows DB port from app-SG only). Layer 5 (Application): IAM roles, KMS encryption, Secrets Manager, application-level authorization. <br><br> *Each layer provides independent protection.
