Attack scenario: attacker bypasses WAF (zero-day technique) → Network Firewall IPS catches the exploit signature → traffic blocked before reaching EC2. Attack scenario 2: attacker exploits app vulnerability and tries lateral movement → app-SG only allows DB port from app-SG → attacker cannot directly scan DB from web tier → movement blocked.* <br> *CloudFront + WAF positioning: deploy WAF on CloudFront (not ALB) when possible. Traffic never reaches your VPC for WAF-blocked requests — lower load on ALB and Network Firewall. Origin protection: ALB configured to accept traffic only from CloudFront managed prefix list. Direct IP access to ALB blocked. This prevents WAF bypass by targeting ALB IP directly.* <br>

1215. [ Network Security ] A company has internet-facing EC2 instances with public IPs in a public subnet. They want to move them to private subnets for security. What changes are required? ; (1) Remove public/Elastic IPs from EC2 instances. (2) Move instances to private subnets (or change subnet configuration: remove auto-assign public IP, remove IGW route). (3) Add NAT Gateway in public subnet for outbound internet access. (4) Add ALB (or NLB) in public subnet as the internet-facing entry point. (5) Update security groups: instances allow inbound only from ALB security group (not 0.0.0.0/0). (6) Update DNS (Route 53) to point to ALB DNS name. <br><br> *Moving EC2 to private subnet is not just about subnet — it's about removing direct internet reachability. Even in a private subnet with a route table pointing to IGW, an instance with a public IP IS reachable from the internet (if SG allows). Private subnet truly private = no public IP + route to NAT GW (not IGW). Defense: no public IP = no inbound attack surface, regardless of firewall misconfiguration.* <br> *ALB as the public-facing entry point: ALB provides: SSL termination, WAF integration, sticky sessions, health checks. Application EC2s behind ALB: no public IP, not directly reachable. ALB security group: allow 443/80 from 0.0.0.0/0. EC2 security group: allow port 8080 from ALB security group only. This is the standard AWS 3-tier architecture for public web applications. Any direct port scan of EC2 IPs fails — no public IP to scan.* <br>

1216. [ Network Security ] A company's security team notices VPC Flow Logs showing many REJECT entries from external IPs to port 22 (SSH) on all EC2 instances. What is the likely cause and what are the remediation options? ; Likely cause: internet-wide SSH scanning/brute-force bots scanning port 22 on public IPs. These are REJECT because SG correctly blocks SSH from unknown IPs. Remediation options: (1) Change SSH to non-standard port (security through obscurity — minimal protection). (2) Restrict SSH SG inbound to known corporate IPs only (best practice). (3) Use Systems Manager Session Manager instead of SSH — no port 22 needed (most secure). (4) Deploy a bastion host with SG allowing SSH only from known IPs, application instances' SG allows SSH only from bastion-SG. <br><br> *Systems Manager Session Manager (recommended): eliminates SSH entirely. No port 22 open. No key management. Session audit trail in CloudTrail. Connection over HTTPS to SSM endpoints (or PrivateLink). For private instances: no internet required if SSM VPC endpoint exists. Session Manager = zero attack surface for SSH brute force. Cannot detect SSH scanning if port 22 is not open — no entries in flow logs.* <br> *REJECT entries in flow logs for port 22: not a security incident if SG is correctly configured — attacker is being blocked. But useful for GuardDuty: GuardDuty analyzes flow logs and identifies `UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce` finding when a source IP generates many SSH REJECT entries. Automated response: EventBridge rule on GuardDuty finding → Lambda → add NACL DENY for the attacker IP. Feedback loop: flow logs → GuardDuty → automated blocking.* <br>

1217. [ Network Security ] What is AWS Firewall Manager and how does it differ from deploying Network Firewall manually in each account? ; Firewall Manager: centralized policy management service for Organizations. Define a security policy once → automatically deployed to all accounts/VPCs matching the scope (OU, account tags). Detects policy drift (VPC without firewall, or firewall with wrong rules) → alerts or auto-remediates. Manual per-account deployment: engineer deploys Network Firewall in each account → no central visibility → policy drift undetected → new accounts not automatically protected. Firewall Manager ensures consistency and compliance across 50, 100, 500 accounts. <br><br> *Firewall Manager policy types: (1) AWS WAF — deploy WAF rules to all ALBs/CloudFront distributions. (2) Shield Advanced — enroll resources across accounts. (3) Network Firewall — deploy and manage Network Firewall policies. (4) Security Group — enforce common SG rules or detect overly permissive SGs. (5) DNS Firewall — deploy Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rules. One policy → all matching resources across all accounts.* <br> *Firewall Manager compliance reporting: for each policy, shows compliant vs non-compliant accounts/resources. Non-compliant = VPC exists matching policy scope but has no firewall (or firewall doesn't match policy). Remediation: automatic (Firewall Manager creates firewall) or manual (alert engineer). Audit: CloudTrail logs all Firewall Manager actions. Config rule linked to policy: continuous compliance monitoring.* <br>

1218. [ Network Security ] A developer accidentally opens Security Group inbound port 0-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0. How do you detect and prevent this in real-time? ; Detection: AWS Config rule `restricted-ssh` / `vpc-sg-open-only-to-authorized-ports` — fires on non-compliant SG changes. EventBridge rule matching CloudTrail `AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress` event → Lambda checks if rule adds 0.0.0.0/0 with wide port range → SNS alert + automatic SG rule removal. Prevention: SCP denying `ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress` for non-admin IAM roles (or requiring condition key `ec2:Cidr` to not equal 0.0.0.0/0). IAM permission boundary limiting SG modification. <br><br> *EventBridge + Lambda auto-remediation pattern: Lambda receives CloudTrail event, extracts SG rule details, checks if CIDR is 0.0.0.0/0 AND port range is > 1000 ports, calls `revoke_security_group_ingress` to remove the rule, sends SNS alert to security team. Response time: < 1 minute. For compliance: log the violation, alert, revoke, require manual review before re-opening.* <br> *AWS Config custom rule (proactive mode): before SG rule is applied, Config checks compliance. If non-compliant → blocks the API call (Config proactive compliance in Organizations). More powerful than reactive: prevents the misconfiguration instead of detecting and remediating after. Proactive mode requires Organizations Config delegated admin. Better for preventing accidental opens, reactive is fine for detecting intentional but policy-violating changes.* <br>

1219. [ Network Security ] Compare NAT Gateway, NAT Instance, and NAT with VPC Endpoint. When should you use each? ; NAT Gateway: managed, highly available per-AZ, auto-scales to 100Gbps, $0.045/hr + $0.045/GB. Use for general outbound internet access. NAT Instance: EC2 with source/dest check disabled, manual HA, limited bandwidth by instance type, cheaper for low-volume traffic. Use only for cost optimization with very low (<5GB/day) internet traffic. VPC Endpoint (Gateway): free, no internet routing, private connectivity to S3 and DynamoDB only. Use to REPLACE NAT GW for S3/DynamoDB traffic — eliminates NAT GW data charges. VPC Endpoint (Interface/PrivateLink): $0.01/hr + $0.01/GB, private connectivity to 100+ AWS services. Use to replace NAT GW for AWS service access (SSM, SQS, SNS, etc.). <br><br> *Cost optimization hierarchy: (1) First: replace all S3 and DynamoDB access with Gateway VPC Endpoints (free). (2) Second: evaluate Interface VPC Endpoints for high-volume services (SSM, SQS, KMS, etc.) — compare endpoint cost vs NAT GW data charge. Rule: if > 10GB/day through NAT GW to an AWS service, Interface Endpoint is cheaper ($0.01/GB endpoint < $0.045/GB NAT GW).* <br> *NAT Instance last resort: t3.nano NAT Instance (~$3.50/month) vs NAT Gateway (~$32/month). For sandbox/dev VPCs with minimal traffic: NAT Instance saves $28.50/month. Not for production (no managed HA, no auto-scaling, requires manual maintenance). Only acceptable with: automated replacement via Auto Scaling Group, careful bandwidth monitoring, tolerance for brief outages during maintenance.* <br>

1220. [ Network Security ] A company uses AWS Network Firewall with Suricata rules. They want to detect and block traffic to Tor exit nodes and known botnet C2 servers. What is the most efficient approach? ; Use AWS-managed Network Firewall rule groups: `AWSManagedRulesThreatIntelligence` rule group. This includes AWS-maintained threat intelligence feeds covering Tor exit nodes, known C2 servers, malicious IPs. AWS updates the list automatically. Set action to DROP (IPS mode). Optionally add custom Suricata rules for organization-specific threat intelligence (internal threat intel feeds). <br><br> *AWS-managed rule groups are updated by AWS Threat Intelligence team using data from multiple sources. You don't need to maintain the IP/domain lists. Managed rule group versions: AWS may release new versions automatically (auto-update) or require manual approval. For critical production environments: set to manual update to control when new rule versions deploy (prevents unexpected blocking of legitimate traffic from new rules).* <br> *Custom threat intelligence: many enterprises subscribe to commercial threat intel feeds (Recorded Future, Mandiant, CrowdStrike). Export IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) → Lambda → update Network Firewall custom rule group → automated blocking within minutes of new IOC publication. This extends Network Firewall with commercial threat intel without deploying Palo Alto WildFire (expensive) for basic IOC blocking.* <br>

1221. [ Network Security ] What are the network-level implications of enabling VPC Flow Logs? Does it affect network performance? ; VPC Flow Logs do NOT affect network performance or latency. Flow logs are captured asynchronously at the hypervisor level — packets are not held waiting for log capture. The capture process is completely transparent to the network path. Implications: (1) Cost: CloudWatch Logs ingestion or S3 storage depending on destination. (2) Delay: flow log records appear 1-15 minutes after the actual flow, not real-time. (3) Aggregation: traffic during the interval (1 or 10 minutes) is aggregated into one record. Multiple flows between same src/dst/port/protocol = one record per interval. <br><br> *Flow log capture is a AWS-infrastructure-level feature — it operates at the Nitro hypervisor/ENA driver level, capturing packet metadata without inserting into the packet path. Compare to VPC Traffic Mirroring (does affect bandwidth — copies entire packets to a mirror target, consuming instance network bandwidth).* <br> *What to enable at what level: VPC-level flow logs: catch all traffic in the VPC with one configuration. Subnet-level: useful for specific subnet monitoring without VPC-wide overhead. ENI-level: most granular, for specific instance troubleshooting. Recommendation: VPC-level to S3 with 10-minute aggregation for ongoing compliance logging. ENI-level to CloudWatch with 1-minute aggregation for active incident investigation. Disable ENI-level after investigation (high cost, not needed ongoing).* <br>

1222. [ Network Security ] A company's compliance team requires all network traffic between VPCs to be encrypted in transit. They use Transit Gateway. How do you satisfy this requirement? ; For TGW inter-VPC traffic: traffic travels on the AWS backbone (never leaves AWS physical infrastructure) and is encrypted by default using AES-256 encryption at the hardware layer (AWS Nitro and fiber links). For additional application-layer encryption: use TLS between services (ALB with HTTPS, mTLS for microservices). For VPN over TGW (on-premises): use IPSec VPN attachments. For regulatory compliance stating explicit encryption: document that AWS backbone encryption satisfies the requirement, or add TLS at application layer. <br><br> *AWS backbone encryption: since 2021, all inter-AZ and inter-region traffic is encrypted at the physical layer. This satisfies most compliance requirements. However, some auditors require explicit documentation or additional application-layer encryption. Check the specific compliance standard: PCI-DSS requires encryption of cardholder data in transit (TLS at application layer satisfies this). HIPAA requires encryption of PHI in transit — AWS backbone + TLS satisfies this.* <br> *Application-layer TLS for inter-service communication: ALB with HTTPS listeners, EC2 to ALB TLS, EC2 to RDS TLS, Lambda to RDS TLS. Certificate management: AWS Certificate Manager (free certs for ALB/CloudFront), ACM Private CA for internal mTLS. mTLS: both client and server present certificates — used for zero-trust service-to-service auth. AWS App Mesh with mTLS enforces zero-trust networking between microservices.* <br>



1223. [ Athena ] A company stores 10 TB of CloudTrail logs in S3 as JSON files with no partitioning. Athena queries take 5 minutes and cost $50 per query. What is the most cost-effective optimization? ; Convert to Parquet format using CTAS and add Hive-compatible partitioning by year/month/day. New cost per daily query: ~$0.025 (5GB Parquet with partition pruning vs 10TB JSON). Steps: (1) CTAS to convert JSON to Parquet with partitions. (2) Enable Partition Projection on new table. (3) Redirect queries to new table. Result: 99% cost reduction. <br><br> *CTAS conversion: `CREATE TABLE cloudtrail_parquet WITH (format='PARQUET', parquet_compression='SNAPPY', partitioned_by=ARRAY['year','month','day'], external_location='s3://bucket/ct-parquet/') AS SELECT *, year(from_iso8601_timestamp(eventtime)) AS year, month(from_iso8601_timestamp(eventtime)) AS month, day(from_iso8601_timestamp(eventtime)) AS day FROM cloudtrail_json`. After CTAS: drop old table, point analysts to new table.* <br> *Why Parquet beats JSON: (1) Columnar — query only needed columns (SELECT useridentity, eventname scans 2 columns instead of all 30+). (2) Compressed — Snappy reduces 10TB to ~1.5TB. (3) Partitioned — WHERE year=2024 AND month=10 scans only October data. Combined: scan 50MB instead of 10TB = $0.00025 vs $50. Partition Projection means no MSCK REPAIR TABLE needed for new daily data.* <br>

1224. [ Athena ] What is MSCK REPAIR TABLE in Athena and why is it problematic at scale? ; MSCK REPAIR TABLE scans all S3 prefixes under the table location to discover new Hive-compatible partitions and registers them in the Glue Data Catalog. Problem at scale: for a table with 3 years of daily data (1,095 partitions), MSCK scans all 1,095 S3 prefixes every time it runs. Slow (minutes), consumes Athena resources, blocking if run in ETL pipeline. Solution: Partition Projection (no MSCK needed), or manual ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION for each new partition. <br><br> *Alternative to MSCK: AWS Glue Crawler. Crawler scans S3, detects new partitions, updates Glue catalog. More efficient than MSCK (incremental crawl), but still slower than Partition Projection. Crawlers run on schedule (every 15min, hourly, daily) and have their own cost ($0.44/DPU-hour).* <br> *Partition Projection eliminates both MSCK and Crawlers: Athena computes partition paths mathematically. New day of data lands in `s3://bucket/logs/year=2024/month=11/day=01/` — immediately queryable without any catalog update. Zero administrative overhead. Only limitation: partition structure must be predictable (time-series, enums, integer ranges). For irregular partitions (customer IDs, random strings): must use catalog-based partitions.* <br>

1225. [ Athena ] A company wants to query both their RDS PostgreSQL operational database and S3 data lake in a single SQL query from Athena. How? ; Use Athena Federated Query. Deploy the Amazon Athena PostgreSQL connector (Lambda function in the VPC containing RDS). Register the connector as a data source in Athena. Query using the connector catalog name: `SELECT s.user_id, r.customer_name, s.total_sales FROM "s3catalog"."sales"."transactions" s JOIN "lambda:postgres-connector"."public"."customers" r ON s.user_id = r.user_id`. <br><br> *Federated Query architecture: Athena orchestrates the query. For each referenced data source, Athena invokes the Lambda connector. Lambda connector executes the relevant sub-query against RDS (SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE user_id IN (...)) and returns results. Athena performs the JOIN on the results. Runs in your VPC if connector Lambda is VPC-configured.* <br> *Performance consideration: Federated Query is not a full pushdown optimizer. Large JOINs between S3 and RDS may transfer significant data through Lambda. Best practice: filter aggressively in the federated source (push predicates down), retrieve small result sets, join in Athena. Not suitable for joining 100M RDS rows with 1B S3 rows — use proper ETL (Glue) for that scale.* <br>

1226. [ Athena ] What file format should you use for Athena if you need schema evolution (adding/removing columns over time) without breaking existing queries? ; Apache Parquet with schema evolution support, or Apache Avro. Parquet handles column addition: new columns appear as NULL for old files (readers use schema from Glue catalog, not file). Column removal: old files still have data for removed columns — Athena ignores them. ORC has similar capabilities. Avro: schema stored in file header, excellent schema evolution with Avro schema registry. JSON: implicit schema evolution (just add fields) but expensive to query. <br><br> *Parquet schema evolution best practices: (1) Only ADD columns, never remove or rename (breaking change for old files). (2) Update Glue catalog schema via `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS`. (3) New queries get NULL for new columns on old files (before the column was added) — handle in SQL with COALESCE. (4) Avoid reordering columns — Parquet stores columns by name, not position (safe). (5) Changing data types: generally unsafe — may cause query errors.* <br> *Glue catalog schema enforcement: Glue Crawler can auto-detect schema changes and update the catalog. Configure crawler to merge schemas (safe: adds new columns) vs replace (dangerous: overwrites schema). For production: disable auto-update, manage schema changes manually or via Terraform/CDK to prevent accidental schema corruption.* <br>

1227. [ Athena ] A team of 50 analysts uses Athena. The data engineering team wants to prevent analysts from accidentally scanning more than 1GB per query. How? ; Create a dedicated Athena Workgroup for analysts. In the workgroup settings, enable "Override client-side settings" and set "Data usage controls: Per query limit = 1 GB". When any analyst query would scan > 1GB, Athena cancels it before execution and returns an error: "Query exhausted resources at this scale factor". Analysts must refine their query (add partition filters, use LIMIT) before re-running. <br><br> *Workgroup per-query scan limit: enforced by Athena before query execution. The query planner estimates data to be scanned, if it exceeds the limit, query is rejected. Important: this is an estimate — actual scanned data may differ slightly. The limit prevents obviously bad queries (SELECT * FROM 10TB_table WHERE 1=1) but may occasionally reject borderline legitimate queries.* <br> *Additional workgroup controls: (1) Separate result bucket per team (`s3://athena-results/team-name/`). (2) KMS encryption per workgroup. (3) CloudWatch metrics per workgroup for cost chargeback. (4) IAM policy: `athena:StartQueryExecution` only allowed for specific workgroups — analysts cannot switch to unrestricted workgroup. Full cost governance: IAM restricts workgroup access + workgroup limits scan size.* <br>

1228. [ Athena ] Explain the difference between Glue Data Catalog and an External Hive Metastore in the context of Athena. When would you use each? ; Glue Data Catalog: AWS-managed, serverless, fully integrated with Athena, Glue ETL, EMR, Lake Formation. No server to manage. Supports Glue Crawlers, Schema Registry, Lake Formation permissions. Use for all new AWS-native data lake workloads. External Hive Metastore: existing Hive/EMR cluster with large metadata repository. Connect via Athena Hive Metastore connector (Lambda). Use when: migrating from on-premises Hive, maintaining consistency between EMR Hive jobs and Athena queries, or avoiding Glue catalog migration effort. <br><br> *External metastore limitations: requires Lambda function deployment and maintenance. Lambda timeout limits complex metadata operations. Latency higher than Glue (Lambda cold start). No Glue Crawler support (cannot auto-discover partitions). No Lake Formation fine-grained access control. Use as temporary bridge during migration, not permanent architecture.* <br> *Migration path: (1) Deploy Athena Hive Metastore connector pointing to existing EMR Hive Metastore. (2) Validate Athena queries against existing Hive tables. (3) Export Hive DDL (`SHOW CREATE TABLE`). (4) Recreate tables in Glue Data Catalog. (5) Validate again. (6) Switch Athena to use Glue catalog. (7) Decommission Hive Metastore connector. This avoids a big-bang migration while allowing gradual validation.* <br>

1229. [ Athena ] What is Athena for Apache Spark and when should it be used instead of standard Athena SQL? ; Athena for Spark: serverless Spark environment accessed via Athena console or API. Runs Python/PySpark notebooks or batch Spark jobs without managing EMR clusters. Use when: complex data transformations requiring procedural logic (loops, ML training, custom UDFs), Python ecosystem needed (pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib), iterative notebook-style exploration. Standard Athena SQL: use for SQL-based analytics, BI tool integration, simple to moderately complex queries. <br><br> *Athena Spark vs EMR: Athena Spark is serverless (no cluster management), auto-scales, pay-per-use. EMR: cluster-based, more control, broader Spark configuration, better for long-running jobs and complex dependencies. For occasional Spark jobs on a data lake: Athena Spark (no cluster startup wait). For continuous ETL pipelines or jobs >1hr: EMR (cost efficiency at scale, persistent cluster).* <br> *Pricing model difference: Athena SQL = $5/TB scanned. Athena Spark = $0.30/DPU-hour (Spark processing capacity). A complex Spark job may cost more or less than equivalent SQL depending on data volume and processing complexity. For pure analytics (GROUP BY, JOIN, aggregations): SQL is almost always cheaper. For ML feature engineering or complex Python logic: Spark may be necessary regardless of cost.* <br>

1230. [ Athena ] A query on an Athena table with thousands of small files (10KB each) in S3 is very slow despite Parquet format and partitioning. What is the cause and fix? ; Small file problem: Athena Presto workers have overhead per file (open S3 file, read Parquet footer, read row groups). With 100,000 × 10KB files vs 10 × 1GB files: same data, but 100,000 S3 API calls + 100,000 file header reads vs 10. Fix: compact small files. Options: (1) S3 Object Lambda or Glue ETL to merge small Parquet files into larger ones (target: 128MB-1GB per file). (2) CTAS to rewrite partition with optimized file sizes. (3) For streaming data: Kinesis Firehose buffer (128MB or 15min) before writing to S3. <br><br> *Small file problem is common with streaming pipelines: Kafka → Lambda → S3 writes one file per event. Result: millions of 1KB files. Athena query on this = extremely slow. Fix at source: Kinesis Firehose with buffer of 128MB or 15 minutes (whichever comes first) writes one 128MB file instead of thousands of 1KB files. Alternatively: Glue streaming ETL compaction job runs hourly to merge small files.* <br> *Apache Iceberg on Athena: Iceberg table format supports MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE, and automatic compaction. `OPTIMIZE table REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK` merges small files. Iceberg also supports time travel queries and schema evolution. For new data lake workloads with frequent updates or streaming: Iceberg is the modern choice over raw Parquet with Hive partitioning.* <br>

1231. [ Athena ] What SerDe should be used for querying Apache web server access logs stored in S3? ; RegexSerDe (org.apache.hadoop.hive.serde2.RegexSerDe). Apache access logs have a non-standard format that cannot be parsed by CSV or JSON SerDes. RegexSerDe uses a Java regex pattern to extract fields. Example pattern: `(\\S+) \\S+ \\S+ \\[([^]]+)\\] "(\\S+) (\\S+) \\S+" (\\d+) (\\d+) "([^"]*)" "([^"]*)"` extracts IP, datetime, method, URI, status, bytes, referer, user-agent. <br><br> *RegexSerDe DDL example: `ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.apache.hadoop.hive.serde2.RegexSerDe' WITH SERDEPROPERTIES ('input.regex' = '(\\S+)...')`. Each capture group maps to a column in the CREATE TABLE definition. Non-matching lines: all columns return NULL (RegexSerDe does not fail on non-matching lines, it silently returns NULL).* <br> *Alternative: use Glue ETL to preprocess logs into Parquet before querying with Athena. Pre-processing: parse regex in Glue (Python Glue script), validate/clean data, write Parquet. Benefits: faster Athena queries (Parquet columnar), no regex overhead per query, handle malformed log lines gracefully. For very high log volumes (>100GB/day): Glue preprocessing + Parquet is significantly cheaper than RegexSerDe JSON scanning.* <br>

1232. [ Athena ] Athena is used to query VPC Flow Logs stored in S3. The logs are in the default format (space-separated text). How do you set up the table and optimize for cost? ; Create table with LazySimpleSerDe (space-delimited) or use the AWS-provided flow log DDL. Optimize: (1) Enable custom flow log format with Parquet output directly from VPC Flow Logs (available since 2022). (2) If using default text format: convert with CTAS to Parquet + add partitioned_by account, region, year, month, day. (3) Enable Partition Projection on the new table. Parquet + partitioning = 95%+ cost reduction over raw text. <br><br> *VPC Flow Logs native Parquet: in VPC Flow Log settings, select S3 destination, format=Parquet. AWS writes flow logs directly as Parquet files. Eliminates Glue ETL conversion step. Still need partitioning and Partition Projection for cost optimization. Custom fields (flow-direction, pkt-srcaddr, vpc-id) are available in custom format — include them for richer security analysis.* <br> *Athena flow log analysis examples: `SELECT srcaddr, COUNT(*) as connections FROM flow_logs WHERE action='REJECT' AND day='2024-11-01' GROUP BY srcaddr ORDER BY connections DESC LIMIT 20` — finds top sources of rejected traffic (potential scanners). `SELECT srcaddr, dstaddr, SUM(bytes) as total FROM flow_logs WHERE year='2024' AND month='11' GROUP BY srcaddr,dstaddr ORDER BY total DESC` — identifies top talkers (data exfiltration detection). With partition pruning: these queries cost cents, not dollars.* <br>

1233. [ Federation ] A company uses on-premises Active Directory (AD FS). Employees need to access the AWS Console and CLI across 30 AWS accounts without creating IAM users in each account. What is the recommended solution? ; AWS IAM Identity Center connected to on-premises AD via AD Connector (or AWS Managed Microsoft AD with trust). In Identity Center: configure AD as the identity source. Create permission sets (DevAccess, ReadOnly, AdminAccess). Assign groups (from AD) to permission sets + accounts. Employees: log in with AD credentials to Identity Center SSO portal → access any assigned account. CLI: `aws configure sso` + `aws sso login`. <br><br> *Architecture choice: AD Connector vs AWS Managed AD. AD Connector: proxy to on-premises AD, no user sync to AWS, no new directory. Risk: on-premises AD outage = AWS access broken. AWS Managed AD with trust: AWS-hosted AD, trusts on-premises AD, users authenticate to AWS Managed AD which proxies to on-premises AD for identity. More resilient: if on-premises AD is briefly unavailable, AWS Managed AD may have cached Kerberos tickets.* <br> *Identity Center benefit over direct SAML federation: with direct SAML + AD FS, you map AD groups to IAM roles IN EACH ACCOUNT manually (30 accounts = 30 configurations). Identity Center: configure once, manage centrally, new accounts automatically get permission sets via Organizations. SCIM not available with AD Connector (SCIM requires external IdP like Okta/Azure AD). With AD Connector: users/groups sync via AD protocol directly.* <br>

1234. [ Federation ] Explain SAML 2.0 federation for AWS Console access. What must be configured in both the IdP and AWS? ; IdP side: (1) Create a SAML 2.0 application pointing to `https://signin.aws.amazon.com/saml` as the ACS URL. (2) Configure attribute mappings: `https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/Role` = `role_arn,idp_arn` (comma-separated). (3) Configure `RoleSessionName` attribute = user email or username. (4) Export IdP SAML metadata XML. AWS side: (1) Create SAML Identity Provider in IAM (upload IdP metadata XML). (2) Create IAM role with trust policy: Principal=Federated:idp-arn, Action=sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML. (3) Attach permissions policies to the role. <br><br> *SAML assertion role attribute format: `arn:aws:iam::123:role/DevRole,arn:aws:iam::123:saml-provider/OktaIdP`. The comma-separated pair is mandatory — both the role ARN AND the IdP ARN must be present. Missing the IdP ARN: `InvalidIdentityToken` error. Multiple Role attribute values: user presented with role selection screen at AWS sign-in. Maximum 10 roles in one assertion.* <br> *SessionDuration attribute: `https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/SessionDuration` = number of seconds (e.g., 28800 for 8 hours). This overrides the role maximum session duration ONLY if it is LESS than or EQUAL to the role maximum. Role maximum session duration is the ceiling — SAML cannot extend beyond it. Default: 1 hour if not specified. For workday access without re-authentication: set to 28800 + increase role max session to 8hr.* <br>

1235. [ Federation ] What is the difference between SAML 2.0 and OIDC federation with AWS STS? When should you use each? ; SAML 2.0: XML-based, enterprise-focused, uses AssumeRoleWithSAML. Use for: workforce SSO from enterprise IdPs (Okta, Azure AD, AD FS, Ping). Good for: browser-based console access, established enterprise IdP integration. OIDC: JSON/JWT-based, modern, uses AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Use for: applications, CI/CD pipelines, mobile apps, Kubernetes pods (IRSA), cross-cloud federation. Good for: programmatic AWS access, GitHub Actions, modern web apps. <br><br> *SAML is designed for browser-based SSO flows (POST binding). The IdP generates an XML assertion, the browser POSTs it to the SP (AWS). Not ideal for API/programmatic flows. OIDC is designed for both browser and API flows. JWT tokens are compact, can be passed in HTTP headers, easy to validate. GitHub Actions, Lambda, containers: all use OIDC natively.* <br> *Coexistence: many organizations use BOTH. SAML for employee console access (Okta SAML → Identity Center → AWS Console). OIDC for CI/CD (GitHub Actions OIDC → STS → S3/ECR). These are complementary patterns. Identity Center internally uses SAML but abstracts it — you configure Okta SAML once in Identity Center, get both console SSO and CLI access. CI/CD pipelines should always use OIDC (no static credentials).* <br>

1236. [ Federation ] A mobile app allows users to sign in with Google. After signing in, users need to upload photos to their own S3 prefix. What AWS architecture handles this? ; Cognito Identity Pool with Google as external IdP. Flow: (1) User signs in to Google in the mobile app → receives Google ID token (JWT). (2) App passes Google ID token to Cognito Identity Pool. (3) Identity Pool calls STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, mapping Google identity to an IAM role. (4) App receives temporary AWS credentials. (5) App uploads to S3 using credentials, with key prefix enforced by IAM policy: `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::photos/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/*"`. <br><br> *IAM role policy for per-user S3 prefix enforcement: `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-photos/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/*"`. The `${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}` is a policy variable replaced at runtime with the authenticated user ID from the Cognito identity pool. User A can only write to `s3://my-photos/us-east-1:AAAA-BBB-CCC/`, user B cannot write there. This is attribute-based access control (ABAC) enforced via IAM policy variables.* <br> *Why Cognito Identity Pool instead of direct OIDC with STS: Cognito Identity Pool supports multiple IdPs simultaneously (Google, Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Cognito User Pool, SAML, OIDC custom). User can sign in with any provider and still get the same Cognito identity (identity pool links multiple provider identities to one Cognito identity). Also supports unauthenticated (guest) access with restricted IAM role. Direct STS OIDC: only one IdP per role trust policy.* <br>

1237. [ Federation ] What is the OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials grant type and where is it used in AWS? ; Client Credentials: machine-to-machine OAuth flow. No user involved. The application authenticates with its own client ID + client secret, receives an access token. Used in AWS: (1) Cognito User Pool machine clients — microservice calling another microservice, authenticates with Cognito, gets JWT, calls API Gateway. (2) API Gateway OAuth 2.0 authorizer — Lambda authorizer validates the JWT from Cognito. (3) ALB OIDC authentication — ALB validates OAuth tokens for incoming requests. <br><br> *Client Credentials vs Authorization Code: Authorization Code has a user who logs in and authorizes the app. Client Credentials: no user, the application IS the principal. Use Client Credentials for: background jobs, scheduled tasks, service-to-service calls, CLI tools. Use Authorization Code for: user-facing apps where a human delegates access.* <br> *AWS Cognito with Client Credentials: create a Cognito User Pool, add a Resource Server (the API), define scopes (e.g., `api.read`, `api.write`). Create an App Client with Client Credentials grant. The microservice calls `POST /oauth2/token` with `grant_type=client_credentials` → receives JWT access token → calls API Gateway with `Authorization: Bearer JWT` → API Gateway validates JWT with Cognito → allows request. This is zero-user OAuth 2.0 for microservices.* <br>

1238. [ Federation ] How does GitHub Actions OIDC federation with AWS work? What are the security benefits? ; GitHub Actions requests an OIDC token from GitHub for each workflow run. The token is a JWT signed by GitHub containing: repository, branch, workflow, environment claims. The workflow calls STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the JWT + IAM role ARN. STS validates the JWT signature against GitHub OIDC endpoint. If valid and trust policy conditions match: returns temporary credentials (1hr). Security benefits: (1) No static AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID stored in GitHub Secrets. (2) Credentials expire after 1hr. (3) Role trust policy can restrict to specific repo/branch. <br><br> *Trust policy repo+branch restriction: `"StringEquals": {"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:myorg/myrepo:ref:refs/heads/main"}`. This ensures ONLY the main branch of myorg/myrepo can assume the role. A fork cannot assume the role (different repo). A feature branch cannot deploy to production (wrong ref). This eliminates the most common CI/CD credential attack: leaked AWS keys in GitHub.* <br> *Comparison with static credentials: static `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in GitHub Secrets: key never expires, can be extracted from compromised workflow, applies to any branch/fork if not carefully scoped, requires manual rotation. OIDC: credentials last 1 hour, cannot be extracted (workflow gets credentials at runtime, not stored), automatically scoped by trust policy to specific repo/branch, no rotation needed. OIDC is strictly superior — migrate all GitHub Actions to OIDC.* <br>

1239. [ Federation ] What is Kubernetes IRSA and how does it use OIDC? ; IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) allows Kubernetes pods in EKS to assume IAM roles without node-level credentials. EKS cluster has an OIDC issuer (URL like `https://oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/CLUSTER_ID`). Register this as an OIDC provider in IAM. Create IAM role with trust policy trusting the OIDC provider with conditions matching the namespace and service account name. Annotate the Kubernetes ServiceAccount with the IAM role ARN. Pods using that ServiceAccount automatically get projected OIDC tokens → kubelet calls STS → gets temporary credentials → mounted at `/var/run/secrets/eks.amazonaws.com/serviceaccount/token`. <br><br> *Before IRSA: all pods on a node shared the node IAM role (EC2 instance profile). Node role had broad permissions (needed for any pod). Compromise one pod = access to all AWS resources the node role allows. IRSA: each pod gets its own IAM role with minimum permissions. Compromise a pod = only that pod role access. Blast radius reduction is the key benefit.* <br> *IAM trust policy for IRSA: `"Condition": {"StringEquals": {"oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/CLUSTER:sub": "system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:SERVICEACCOUNT"}}`. The `sub` claim contains the Kubernetes namespace and service account name. Different namespaces get different IAM roles. AWS SDKs in pod automatically use the token (EKS-injected env var `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` points to the projected token file). No code changes needed in the application.* <br>

1240. [ Federation ] Compare Okta, Azure AD, and Google Workspace as AWS federation IdPs. When would you choose each? ; Okta: IdP-agnostic, excellent AWS marketplace app, easiest SAML + SCIM setup with IAM Identity Center, supports all platforms. Best for: organizations not standardized on Microsoft/Google, or requiring complex federation logic. Azure AD: native for Microsoft shops (M365, Windows, Teams). Azure AD Connect syncs on-prem AD. Tighter Windows integration. Best for: Microsoft-centric organizations already paying for Azure AD P2. Google Workspace: best for Google-first organizations (G Suite). Simple SAML from Admin Console. Best for: startups/tech companies using Google productivity tools. <br><br> *Key difference Okta vs Azure AD: Azure AD is a directory service first (creates user objects), IdP second. Okta is pure IdP/directory (no Microsoft ecosystem dependencies). Azure AD requires Azure subscription, Okta is standalone. For AWS-only organizations on Google Workspace: Google Workspace SAML → Identity Center works well. For enterprises with Active Directory: AD Connector or AWS Managed AD + Identity Center, or Azure AD if already using M365.* <br> *SCIM support comparison: Okta SCIM to Identity Center: well-documented, official AWS-Okta integration guide, battle-tested. Azure AD SCIM to Identity Center: also officially supported, but configuration is in Azure AD Enterprise Apps (more steps). Google Workspace: SCIM to Identity Center also supported but less widely deployed. SCIM automates user/group provisioning — critical at 5,000+ employee scale. Without SCIM: manual user management in Identity Center = operational burden.* <br>

1241. [ Federation ] What is the difference between Cognito User Pools and Cognito Identity Pools? How do they work together? ; Cognito User Pool: user directory for authentication. Handles sign-up, sign-in, MFA, password reset, social login federation. Issues JWT tokens (ID token, access token). Does NOT issue AWS credentials. Cognito Identity Pool: exchanges identity tokens (from User Pool, Google, Facebook, etc.) for temporary AWS credentials via STS. Issues AWS access keys. Does NOT handle user sign-in directly. Together: User Pool authenticates user → issues JWT → Identity Pool exchanges JWT for AWS credentials → app accesses S3/DynamoDB. <br><br> *Use case without Identity Pool: web app uses Cognito User Pool for authentication, calls API Gateway secured with Cognito authorizer. App never directly calls AWS services. User Pool JWT is sufficient. Use case WITH Identity Pool: mobile app authenticates via User Pool, then needs to directly upload to S3 (not via API Gateway). Identity Pool converts the User Pool JWT to temporary AWS credentials. App uses credentials to call S3 directly.* <br> *Identity Pool unauthenticated role: allows guest users to access AWS resources without signing in. Common use: read-only S3 access for public content (CDN origin, public datasets). Unauthenticated role should have minimal permissions. Can be disabled if guest access not needed. Authenticated role: what signed-in users can do. Can use ABAC (policy variables based on Cognito claims) for per-user resource isolation.* <br>

1242. [ Federation ] A company federated with Okta via SAML directly to IAM roles (not Identity Center). They have 50 accounts. How should they modernize this? ; Migrate to IAM Identity Center with Okta as external IdP. Current state: Okta SAML → each of 50 accounts has Okta IdP trust + IAM roles (50 configurations). Future state: Okta SAML + SCIM → Identity Center (one configuration) → all 50 accounts managed centrally. Migration: (1) Enable IAM Identity Center. (2) Configure Okta as external IdP in Identity Center. (3) Enable SCIM provisioning. (4) Recreate IAM roles as permission sets. (5) Test with pilot users. (6) Migrate users. (7) Remove old per-account Okta IdP trusts. <br><br> *Why migrate: current per-account SAML is brittle. Adding account 51 requires: new Okta SAML config, new IAM IdP resource, new IAM roles — all manual. Identity Center: account 51 added to Organizations → permission sets automatically provisioned → zero manual work. Also: CLI access. Per-account SAML: no standard CLI flow (must use tools like saml2aws). Identity Center: `aws sso login` standard, supported by AWS CDK, Terraform, official AWS tools.* <br> *Migration risk mitigation: run both systems in parallel during migration. Users can use either the old SAML flow or the new Identity Center SSO. Monitor Identity Center usage. Once all users migrated and validated: disable old Okta SAML app → delete IAM IdP resources in member accounts (50 deletions). Rollback: re-enable Okta SAML app if issues found during migration. Timeline: 2-4 weeks for 50 accounts + 5,000 users with SCIM automation.* <br>

1243. [ Federation ] What is Auth0 and how does it integrate with AWS for customer-facing applications? ; Auth0 (Okta Customer Identity Cloud) is a cloud IdP focused on customer identity management (CIAM). It supports social login (Google, Facebook, Apple), passwordless, MFA, and custom databases. Integration with AWS: (1) Auth0 as OIDC provider in IAM — `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` with Auth0 JWT. (2) Auth0 → Cognito Identity Pool — configure Auth0 as custom OIDC developer provider, Identity Pool issues AWS credentials. (3) Auth0 JWT → API Gateway Lambda authorizer. (4) Auth0 JWT → ALB OIDC authentication. <br><br> *Auth0 vs Cognito User Pools: Auth0 is a full-featured CIAM platform with advanced features (Organizations for B2B, Actions for custom logic, Anomaly Detection). Cognito User Pools is simpler and tightly integrated with AWS but has limitations (no advanced B2B features, basic UI customization). Choose Auth0 when: complex B2B identity requirements, existing Auth0 investment, need advanced auth flows. Choose Cognito when: AWS-native integration priority, simpler requirements, cost sensitivity (Cognito free tier covers 50,000 MAU).* <br> *Auth0 → Cognito Identity Pool pattern: Auth0 issues OIDC ID token → Cognito Identity Pool configured with Auth0 domain as OIDC provider → Identity Pool calls STS → returns AWS credentials. App uses credentials for direct AWS API calls (S3, DynamoDB). The user identity from Auth0 (sub claim) is available in IAM policy variables: `${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}` for per-user S3 prefix enforcement.* <br>

1244. [ KMS ] What is the difference between AWS Owned Keys, AWS Managed Keys, and Customer Managed Keys? When should each be used? ; AWS Owned: managed entirely by AWS, no customer visibility or control, free, used by S3 SSE-S3/DynamoDB default. Use when: encryption at rest required but customer key control not needed. AWS Managed: created in customer account by AWS service, visible in console, free, automatic annual rotation, CloudTrail logs usage, cannot be shared cross-account. Use when: compliance requires encryption + CloudTrail key usage audit, but not customer-controlled rotation or cross-account sharing. CMK: customer-created, full control, $1/month, custom policy, cross-account, BYOK, multi-region. Use when: compliance requires customer key control, cross-account encryption, custom rotation, or key material import. <br><br> *The compliance progression: basic compliance → AWS Owned Keys (encryption exists). Better compliance → AWS Managed Keys (can audit who used the key via CloudTrail). Full compliance (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP) → CMK (customer controls key, custom rotation, can revoke access by disabling key). Revoking access with AWS Managed Key: cannot disable — the AWS service controls it. Revoking access with CMK: disable the key → all services using it immediately lose ability to decrypt → immediate data access revocation.* <br> *Cost consideration: 100 CMKs = $100/month in key fees. Plus API call costs. For large organizations with hundreds of services: evaluate whether per-service CMK vs shared CMK makes sense. Security vs cost: per-service CMK = blast radius limited (compromise one service does not expose other services data). Shared CMK: lower cost but broader impact if key is compromised or accidentally disabled.* <br>

1245. [ KMS ] Explain envelope encryption. Why does KMS use it for large data? ; Envelope encryption: KMS generates a Data Encryption Key (DEK). Application uses DEK to encrypt data locally (fast, no KMS call per byte). Application stores encrypted data + the KMS-encrypted DEK together. To decrypt: application calls KMS to decrypt the DEK, then decrypts data locally. Why: KMS Encrypt API is limited to 4KB — cannot directly encrypt a 1GB file. Also: KMS API calls have latency (HTTPS to AWS). Encrypting 1GB locally with DEK = 1 KMS call + fast local AES. Without envelope: 262,144 KMS API calls for 1GB in 4KB chunks. <br><br> *Envelope encryption is used by every AWS service that uses KMS: S3 (GenerateDataKey per object), EBS (GenerateDataKey per volume), RDS (GenerateDataKey for TDE). The DEK is stored alongside the data (in S3 object metadata, EBS volume metadata). The DEK can only be decrypted by someone with access to the CMK. Even if the S3 object is stolen: the attacker has encrypted data + encrypted DEK, but cannot decrypt the DEK without KMS access.* <br> *AWS Encryption SDK implements envelope encryption with data key caching: GenerateDataKey once, use the same DEK for N operations or T seconds (configurable), then rotate to a new DEK. Trade-off: multiple objects encrypted with same DEK (slightly weaker per-object isolation vs unique DEK per object). Benefit: N-1 fewer KMS API calls. For S3 with millions of small objects: data key caching reduces cost dramatically. S3 Bucket Key is essentially this: a single GenerateDataKey call per bucket every 5 minutes.* <br>

1246. [ KMS ] A customer managed KMS key has the following key policy: the root principal is NOT included. An IAM role in the same account tries to use the key. What happens? ; Access denied. Without the root principal in the key policy, IAM identity-based policies cannot grant access to the key. The key policy is the only access control that matters. Even if the IAM role has `kms:Decrypt *` in its identity policy: if the key policy does not allow the role (and does not have the root principal to delegate to IAM), the call is denied. Fix: add the root principal to the key policy: `"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:root"}`, `"Action":"kms:*"`. <br><br> *This is the most important KMS concept: KMS key policy is evaluated independently from IAM policies. For KMS specifically: BOTH must allow (key policy AND IAM policy), UNLESS the key policy explicitly grants access to a specific principal directly (then IAM policy is not needed for that principal). The root principal in the key policy is a delegation statement: "let the account use IAM policies to control this key." Without it: only principals explicitly listed in the key policy have access.* <br> *Lockout scenario: if you accidentally save a key policy that removes all principals (or remove the root principal), the key becomes inaccessible. AWS has a process to recover: contact AWS Support with proof of ownership. They can restore the default key policy as a break-glass procedure. This is why AWS console warns before saving a key policy that excludes the root principal. Best practice: always test key policy changes on a non-production key first, always keep root principal unless you explicitly want pure key-policy-only access control.* <br>

1247. [ KMS ] A company encrypts RDS instances with CMK key-id-A. They want to rotate the key. What is the impact on existing data and how do rotation works? ; Enabling automatic key rotation: KMS creates a new backing key (new key material). New data is encrypted with the new backing key. Old data (encrypted with old backing key) is STILL DECRYPTABLE — KMS retains all backing key versions. Key ID, ARN, alias unchanged. No re-encryption of existing data. No downtime. No impact on RDS. RDS continues to work transparently. <br><br> *Key rotation granularity: when KMS says "rotate the key," it means rotate the key MATERIAL (the actual AES-256 bytes). The key RESOURCE (ID, ARN, alias) stays the same. Applications referencing the key by ARN or alias do not need any changes. The old backing key is never deleted — it is retained for decryption of data encrypted with it. Mathematically: the new backing key handles new encryptions, all old encryptions are still handled by their original backing key version.* <br> *When to re-encrypt existing data: if you NEED to ensure old data is also encrypted with the new key material (e.g., compliance requirement that key rotation means ALL data uses new key), you must manually re-encrypt. For S3: use S3 Batch Operations with Lambda to re-encrypt objects. For EBS: create new volume, copy data. For RDS: create snapshot, restore to new instance with new key. This is an operational exercise, not automatic. In most compliance frameworks: key rotation = new data uses new key, old data retention under old key is acceptable.* <br>

1248. [ KMS ] How does cross-account KMS key sharing work? A Lambda in Account B needs to decrypt data encrypted with a CMK in Account A. ; Two-step process: (1) Account A key policy: add Account B role ARN (or Account B root) as a principal with `kms:Decrypt` permission. (2) Account B IAM policy: attach policy to Lambda execution role granting `kms:Decrypt` on the specific CMK ARN in Account A. Both must be configured. Key policy alone: Account B has the ceiling but no IAM permission. IAM policy alone: no effect without key policy granting Account B access. <br><br> *Key policy entry for cross-account: `{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_B:root"},"Action":["kms:Decrypt","kms:DescribeKey"],"Resource":"*"}`. Using Account B root (not a specific role): allows Account B to use its own IAM policies to control which of its roles can use the key. Using specific role ARN: only that exact role can use the key (more restrictive, less flexible).* <br> *Cross-account S3 with CMK: Account A has S3 bucket encrypted with CMK from Account A. Account B IAM role needs to read the objects. Account B role needs: (1) S3 GetObject on the bucket (via bucket policy in Account A). (2) KMS Decrypt on the CMK (via key policy in Account A + IAM policy in Account B). Both S3 and KMS must allow Account B. This is a common three-way setup: S3 bucket policy + KMS key policy (both in Account A) + IAM policy in Account B.* <br>

1249. [ KMS ] What is BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) in AWS KMS? When should it be used and what are the risks? ; BYOK: customer generates key material in their own HSM or key generator (never inside AWS), imports it into a KMS CMK (origin: EXTERNAL). Use for: compliance requiring that key material was generated outside AWS, audit requirements for key material provenance, migrating from on-premises HSM to AWS while keeping existing key material. Risk: if the imported key material is deleted from KMS AND the customer loses their local copy, all data encrypted with it is permanently unrecoverable. AWS cannot help. <br><br> *BYOK import process: (1) Create CMK with `Origin=EXTERNAL` in KMS. (2) Download import parameters: RSA public key (AWS KMS wrapping key) + import token. (3) Encrypt your 256-bit key material with the RSA public key (RSA-OAEP-SHA-256). (4) Upload encrypted key material + import token to KMS. (5) KMS decrypts key material with its private key, stores in HSM. The RSA wrapping key and import token expire after 24 hours — re-download if expired.* <br> *BYOK vs BYOHSM (CloudHSM): BYOK = you generate the key, import into AWS KMS (AWS HSMs now hold it). AWS manages the HSM hardware. BYOHSM = CloudHSM: you provision and manage HSM cluster, keys never leave customer-controlled HSM hardware. BYOK satisfies "we generated the key." CloudHSM satisfies "our team is the only one with physical/logical access to the key material at all times." Different compliance requirements.* <br>

1250. [ KMS ] What is the KMS key deletion process and why is there a mandatory waiting period? ; To delete a CMK: schedule key deletion with a waiting period of 7-30 days. During waiting period: key is disabled (cannot be used for new cryptographic operations). CloudTrail alert: every decrypt/encrypt attempt generates `KMSInvalidStateException` — allows you to discover applications that still use the key. After waiting period: key is permanently deleted — data encrypted with it is permanently inaccessible. Cancel deletion during waiting period: key restored to enabled state. <br><br> *Why waiting period: KMS keys are used by many AWS services and applications. A key may have been used years ago to encrypt a backup that is still in S3 Glacier. If you delete the key immediately: that backup is permanently unreadable. The waiting period forces discovery: any application/service that attempts to decrypt using the key during the waiting period will fail, generating CloudWatch alarms and CloudTrail events. You can discover all key usages before permanent deletion.* <br> *Best practice for key deletion: (1) Disable the key (not schedule deletion). (2) Monitor CloudWatch for `KMSInvalidStateException` events for 30 days. (3) If no alarms: schedule key deletion. (4) If alarms: re-enable key, migrate the application to a new key first, then retry. Disabling is reversible, deletion is not. For automated key management: AWS Config rule detecting disabled keys >60 days → trigger cleanup workflow.* <br>

1251. [ KMS ] What are Multi-Region KMS Keys and when should they be used? ; Multi-Region Keys: CMK with same key ID and key material replicated across multiple AWS regions. Primary key in one region (e.g., us-east-1), replica keys in others (eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1). Use cases: (1) DynamoDB Global Tables — data replicates across regions, encryption/decryption must work in each region. (2) Active-active multi-region apps — data written in us-east-1 must be readable in eu-west-1 without re-encryption. (3) Disaster recovery — if us-east-1 KMS is unavailable, use eu-west-1 replica to decrypt. <br><br> *Multi-Region Key behavior: encrypting in us-east-1 with mrk-key → ciphertext contains the key ID. Decrypting the same ciphertext in eu-west-1 with the REPLICA of mrk-key (same key ID) → works. The replica has the same key material, so decryption succeeds. Without Multi-Region Keys: us-east-1 CMK encrypts data → replicated to eu-west-1 → eu-west-1 cannot decrypt (wrong region, different key). Must re-encrypt in us-east-1 before sending to eu-west-1.* <br> *Each replica is an independent resource: has its own key policy (can be different from primary), separate CloudTrail, can be disabled independently, costs $1/month. Promotion: replica can be promoted to primary (useful for DR: failover primary to another region). After promotion: the old primary becomes a replica. This is an operational procedure, not automatic failover. For automated failover: use Route 53 health checks + Lambda to trigger promotion if primary region fails.* <br>

1252. [ KMS ] What is an S3 Bucket Key and how does it reduce KMS costs? ; S3 Bucket Key: when enabled on an S3 bucket, S3 generates a short-lived symmetric key (the "bucket key") from your CMK using a single GenerateDataKey call. This bucket key is used to encrypt individual object data keys for all objects in the bucket. The bucket key is cached for up to 5 minutes. Instead of one KMS API call per object (potentially millions/day), there is one KMS API call per 5-minute window. Cost reduction: up to 99% fewer KMS API calls. <br><br> *Without Bucket Key: PUT 1 million objects = 1 million GenerateDataKey KMS API calls = $3 (1M × $0.03/10,000 × 10 units = $3). With Bucket Key: 1 million objects in 5 minutes = 1 GenerateDataKey call = $0.000003. For S3-heavy workloads: Bucket Key is a mandatory optimization. Enable via: bucket properties → default encryption → enable Bucket Key. Or per-object header: `x-amz-server-side-encryption-bucket-key-enabled: true`.* <br> *Security trade-off: with Bucket Key, multiple objects share the same intermediate key. If the bucket key is somehow compromised during its 5-minute lifetime, all objects encrypted in that window use the same material. In practice: the bucket key never leaves S3's servers (S3 internal caching, not your application), so this is not a realistic attack vector. The security reduction is theoretical, the cost reduction is concrete and significant.* <br>

1253. [ KMS ] A Lambda function needs to decrypt a secret stored in Secrets Manager. The secret is encrypted with a CMK. What permissions does the Lambda execution role need? ; Lambda execution role needs: (1) `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on the specific secret ARN. (2) `kms:Decrypt` on the specific CMK ARN (or the KMS key ARN). Both are required. Secrets Manager calls KMS to decrypt the secret value, it does so on behalf of the caller using the caller identity. If the Lambda role lacks `kms:Decrypt`, Secrets Manager returns AccessDeniedException even if `GetSecretValue` is allowed. <br><br> *If using AWS Managed Key (`aws/secretsmanager`): Lambda execution role only needs `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`. The KMS permission is not required for AWS Managed Keys — Secrets Manager has implicit permission to use the `aws/secretsmanager` key on behalf of the account. CMK: explicit permission required. This is a common exam trap: CMK requires explicit KMS permission, AWS Managed Key does not.* <br> *Cross-account secret access: Account A Secrets Manager secret encrypted with Account A CMK. Account B Lambda needs access. Requirements: (1) Account A secret resource policy allows Account B role `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`. (2) Account A KMS key policy allows Account B role `kms:Decrypt`. (3) Account B Lambda execution role has `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` and `kms:Decrypt` on the cross-account ARNs. Three separate policy updates required.* <br>

1254. [ KMS ] What KMS key types are appropriate for: (a) a startup with no compliance requirements, (b) a healthcare company needing HIPAA compliance, (c) a bank requiring HSM with customer-exclusive key custody? ; (a) Startup: AWS Owned Keys or AWS Managed Keys. Free, no management overhead. Encryption at rest satisfied. Compliance not required = customer-controlled keys not needed. (b) HIPAA healthcare: Customer Managed Keys (CMK). HIPAA requires encryption of PHI + ability to audit key usage (CloudTrail) + ability to revoke access (disable key). AWS Managed Keys satisfy encryption but customer cannot disable them. CMK required for full HIPAA control. (c) Bank with exclusive custody: CloudHSM with KMS Custom Key Store. CloudHSM = customer provisions and manages HSM hardware, AWS never accesses key material. FIPS 140-2 Level 3 with exclusive customer custody. <br><br> *HIPAA compliance with KMS: the HIPAA Security Rule requires: (1) Encryption of PHI at rest. (2) Access controls on PHI. (3) Audit logs of PHI access. AWS Managed Key covers (1) and partially (3) (CloudTrail logs service calls but not key-level operations as granularly). CMK covers all three: encryption, key policy for access control, CloudTrail for every decrypt operation (who decrypted which key at what time). Also: CMK can be disabled to immediately revoke access to all PHI — critical for breach response.* <br> *CloudHSM cost reality: minimum 2 HSMs for HA = 2 × $1.05/hour = ~$1,512/month. Plus KMS custom key store overhead. For startups or small healthcare companies: CMK provides HIPAA-compliant controls at $1/month per key. CloudHSM is for: financial institutions with regulatory requirements specifying HSM custody, government contractors (FedRAMP High), or extremely large enterprises with dedicated security teams.* <br>

1255. [ KMS ] What happens to data encrypted with a KMS CMK when the key is disabled vs deleted? ; Disabled: key cannot be used for new cryptographic operations (Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey). Existing data: encrypted data is inaccessible while key is disabled (decrypt calls return KMSDisabledException). Re-enable key: data accessible again. Reversible. Deleted (after waiting period): key permanently destroyed. All data encrypted solely with this key is permanently and irrecoverably inaccessible. AWS cannot restore. Irreversible. <br><br> *Practical use of disable: temporary access revocation. Example: security incident — disable CMK immediately → all services using it (S3, RDS, EBS) lose ability to decrypt → effective data lockdown in seconds. Investigation complete, no breach found → re-enable key → services recover. This is a powerful incident response tool that does not require deleting data.* <br> *Why deletion cannot be immediate: if you could delete a key instantly, a confused employee or malicious insider could permanently destroy terabytes of encrypted data in seconds. The 7-30 day waiting period and the disable→monitor→delete workflow provide multiple safety nets. During waiting period: key is disabled (data inaccessible) but not gone. You can discover all usages, migrate data, and cancel deletion. After deletion: no recovery. AWS makes this hard by design.* <br>

1256. [ KMS ] A company uses KMS CMK to encrypt EBS volumes. They want to share an encrypted EBS snapshot with another AWS account. What is required? ; (1) Modify the EBS snapshot to share with Account B (snapshot must be in COMPLETED state). (2) Account A CMK key policy: add Account B as a principal with `kms:DescribeKey`, `kms:CreateGrant`, `kms:Decrypt`, `kms:ReEncryptFrom`, `kms:ReEncryptTo`, `kms:GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext`. (3) Account B: when copying the snapshot, re-encrypt with an Account B CMK (recommended) or use the Account A CMK (requires ongoing cross-account key access). Best practice: Account B copies snapshot and re-encrypts with its own CMK for full independence. <br><br> *Re-encrypting on copy is the recommended pattern: Account B copies shared snapshot, specifying its own CMK. KMS ReEncrypt: Account A CMK decrypts the data key, Account B CMK re-encrypts it. New snapshot in Account B is encrypted with Account B CMK. Account B is now fully independent — no ongoing dependency on Account A CMK. If Account A disables/deletes their CMK: Account B snapshot is unaffected.* <br> *Without re-encryption: Account B copies snapshot using Account A CMK. Account B EBS volume is encrypted with Account A CMK. Every time Account B starts an EC2 instance with this volume: requires `kms:Decrypt` on Account A CMK. Account A can revoke this access at any time by modifying their key policy. Operational risk: Account A change breaks Account B infrastructure. Always re-encrypt on cross-account snapshot copy.* <br>


1257. [ KMS ] What is KMS key tagging and why is it important for large organizations? ; CMKs support resource tags (key-value pairs). Use: (1) Cost allocation — tag by team/project, view KMS costs per team in Cost Explorer. (2) IAM tag-based access control (ABAC) — IAM policies with `aws:RequestedRegion` or custom condition keys based on key tags. (3) Config rules — detect CMKs without required tags (compliance). (4) Automation — Lambda scripts managing key lifecycle based on tags (auto-disable keys tagged `environment=dev` after 30 days). <br><br> *ABAC with KMS tags: tag CMK with `environment=prod`. IAM policy: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"aws:ResourceTag/environment":"prod"}}`. Only principals with this policy can use prod-tagged keys. Developers cannot access prod encryption keys, only dev-tagged keys. Environment-level key separation without maintaining separate key policies per role.* <br> *Tag enforcement via SCP: SCP denying `kms:CreateKey` unless `aws:RequestTag/CostCenter` is present. All new CMKs must have CostCenter tag at creation time. Existing untagged keys: Config rule `required-tags` on `AWS::KMS::Key` resource type — non-compliant keys flagged. Automated remediation: Lambda triggered by Config non-compliance → SNS notification to key owner → 7-day grace period → auto-disable if not tagged.* <br>

1258. [ KMS ] A company needs to audit who decrypted which S3 objects in the last 90 days. How? ; S3 SSE-KMS + CloudTrail data events for KMS. Enable CloudTrail management events (default) — this logs KMS API calls including `kms:Decrypt`. Each S3 GetObject call triggers a KMS Decrypt call on the underlying DEK. CloudTrail records: who (IAM principal), when (timestamp), which key (key ARN), source IP, request parameters. Query: Athena on CloudTrail S3 logs — filter `eventName=Decrypt AND resources.ARN=arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123:key/key-id AND eventTime>2024-08-01`. <br><br> *CloudTrail KMS events: every `kms:Decrypt`, `kms:GenerateDataKey`, `kms:Encrypt` call is logged as a management event. The CloudTrail record includes `requestParameters.keyId` (which key), `userIdentity` (who called), `sourceIPAddress`, `requestParameters.encryptionContext` (which contains S3 bucket/key if using SSE-KMS). For S3: the encryption context includes `aws:s3:arn:S3_OBJECT_ARN` — you can correlate which S3 object was decrypted.* <br> *Encryption context: key-value pairs passed to KMS with every encrypt/decrypt call. S3 automatically sets the encryption context to `{"aws:s3:arn":"arn:aws:s3:::bucket/key"}`. CloudTrail logs this. Query: find all decrypts of objects in bucket X by user Y. Also: key policy can enforce encryption context: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"kms:EncryptionContext:aws:s3:arn":"arn:aws:s3:::sensitive-bucket/*"}}`. This CMK can ONLY be used for this specific S3 bucket — cannot be accidentally used for another service.* <br>

1259. [ KMS ] What is the ReEncrypt API in KMS and when is it used? ; ReEncrypt: atomically decrypts ciphertext using the original CMK and re-encrypts it using a new CMK — without the plaintext ever leaving the HSM or being exposed to the caller. Use cases: (1) Migrating from one CMK to another (key rotation to new key resource, not just new material). (2) Cross-region migration (re-encrypt with Multi-Region Key replica for target region). (3) Changing from AWS Managed Key to CMK. (4) Key consolidation or separation. <br><br> *ReEncrypt vs manual re-encryption: manual = `Decrypt` (plaintext in your application) → `Encrypt` with new key. Plaintext briefly in application memory = security risk. ReEncrypt = single KMS call, plaintext inside HSM only, never in application memory. Use ReEncrypt whenever changing keys on existing ciphertext.* <br> *Large-scale re-encryption: ReEncrypt is for individual encrypted blobs. For S3 objects: use S3 Batch Operations with a Lambda function that calls ReEncrypt on each object data key. For EBS: create snapshot → copy with new CMK (uses ReEncrypt internally). For RDS: snapshot → restore with new CMK. All these use ReEncrypt under the hood — you do not call it directly for AWS-managed services, but understanding it helps when building custom encryption.* <br>

1260. [ Athena ] What is Athena Workgroup and how does it differ from a default workgroup? ; A workgroup is a named group of query settings, results location, permissions, and usage controls. Default workgroup (`primary`): used if no workgroup specified, no restrictions. Custom workgroup: (1) Dedicated S3 results location (isolation between teams). (2) Per-query data scan limit (cost control). (3) KMS encryption for results. (4) CloudWatch metrics scoped to workgroup (cost attribution). (5) IAM: restrict users to specific workgroup via `athena:workgroup` condition. Create: `aws athena create-work-group --name analytics-team --configuration ResultConfiguration={OutputLocation=s3://results/analytics/},EnforceWorkGroupConfiguration=true`. <br><br> *EnforceWorkGroupConfiguration=true: ignores any client-side result location settings — all queries go to the workgroup result bucket regardless of what the client specifies. Without this: client can override result location, defeating the isolation. Always set to true for production workgroups.* <br> *Workgroup-level access control: `iam:athena:StartQueryExecution` with condition `"StringEquals":{"athena:WorkGroup":"analytics-team"}` — analyst can only run queries in analytics-team workgroup, not in primary (which may have no scan limits). Combined with workgroup scan limit: full cost governance. Different workgroups for: production (high scan limit, KMS encrypted results), development (low scan limit, unencrypted results), batch ETL (no limit, service role only).* <br>

1261. [ Athena ] A company needs to query JSON logs where each line contains a nested JSON object. The logs have arrays within objects. How does Athena handle nested JSON? ; Athena supports nested JSON via `struct` and `array` types in the table schema with JsonSerDe. Arrays: `ARRAY<STRING>`, `ARRAY<STRUCT<field:type>>`. Structs: `STRUCT<field1:STRING, field2:INT>`. Access nested fields: `SELECT event.user.id, event.action.type FROM logs`. Access array elements: `SELECT arr[1] FROM logs` (1-indexed). Flatten arrays: `CROSS JOIN UNNEST(event.tags) AS t(tag)`. <br><br> *DDL example for nested JSON: `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE events (event_id STRING, user STRUCT<id:STRING, email:STRING, country:STRING>, actions ARRAY<STRUCT<type:STRING, timestamp:BIGINT>>, tags ARRAY<STRING>) ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.openx.data.jsonserde.JsonSerDe' LOCATION 's3://bucket/events/'`. Query: `SELECT event_id, user.country, action.type FROM events CROSS JOIN UNNEST(actions) AS t(action) WHERE user.country = 'DE'`.* <br> *Performance with nested JSON: even with JsonSerDe, Athena must read entire lines to parse nested structures (row-based). For frequently queried nested fields: convert to Parquet with flattened schema using Glue ETL (extract nested fields to top-level columns). This enables columnar scanning of specific fields without reading the entire nested JSON. Trade-off: Glue ETL cost vs repeated Athena query savings.* <br>

1262. [ KMS ] How does KMS integrate with S3 SSE-KMS? What is the difference between SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, and SSE-C? ; SSE-S3 (AES-256): AWS Owned Key, AWS manages all encryption. No customer key control, no CloudTrail, free. Default for all S3 objects. SSE-KMS: AWS Managed Key (aws/s3) or CMK. CloudTrail logs key usage. CMK = customer controls key, can disable/revoke. Bucket Key optimization available. SSE-C: Customer-Provided Key. Customer sends key with every request (never stored in S3). Customer manages key lifecycle entirely. Not recommended (key transmission risk, no key management features). <br><br> *SSE-KMS vs SSE-C: SSE-KMS keys stored in AWS KMS (AWS manages HSMs). SSE-C: key in customer hands only, sent over HTTPS with every API call, immediately discarded by S3. SSE-C use case: extreme compliance requirements where keys must never be stored by AWS in any form. Risk: if customer loses the key material, all objects encrypted with it are unrecoverable. No CloudTrail, no key management, no rotation support from AWS.* <br> *Enforce SSE-KMS via bucket policy: `"Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption":"aws:kms"}}` → deny any PUT object that does not use KMS encryption. Combined with: `"Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id":"arn:aws:kms:..."}}` → enforce specific CMK. Prevents: accidental SSE-S3 uploads, unencrypted uploads, uploads using the wrong key.* <br>

1263. [ Federation ] What is the STS AssumeRole API and how does it differ from AssumeRoleWithSAML and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity? ; AssumeRole: IAM principal (user, role, service) assumes another IAM role. Requires the caller to already have IAM credentials. Used for: cross-account access, privilege escalation within account, service role assumption. AssumeRoleWithSAML: external identity (user authenticated by SAML IdP) assumes IAM role. Caller has no IAM credentials — presents SAML assertion instead. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity: external identity (user with OIDC/OAuth token from Google, Cognito, GitHub) assumes IAM role. Presents JWT instead of SAML XML. <br><br> *Chain: Lambda → AssumeRole → cross-account role (Lambda has its own execution role, assumes a role in another account). GitHub Actions → AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity → deployment role (GitHub Actions has no IAM identity, uses OIDC JWT). Okta user → AssumeRoleWithSAML → developer role (Okta user has no IAM identity, uses SAML assertion from Okta). All three produce the same result: temporary credentials (AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, SessionToken, Expiration).* <br> *GetFederationToken (legacy): called by an IAM USER (not role) to generate credentials for a federated user. The generated credentials have the intersection of the user permissions and the specified policy. Limitations: cannot be called by IAM roles, credentials can last up to 36 hours, no MFA support, legacy authentication pattern. Replaced by AssumeRoleWithSAML and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. AWS documentation recommends against GetFederationToken for new implementations.* <br>

1264. [ Federation ] A company uses Ping Identity (PingFederate) on-premises for employee SSO. They want to federate with AWS. What are the options? ; Option 1 (recommended): PingFederate → SAML 2.0 → IAM Identity Center. Configure PingFederate as external IdP in Identity Center (upload PingFederate SAML metadata). Configure SCIM provisioning from PingFederate to Identity Center. Create permission sets. Option 2 (legacy): PingFederate → SAML 2.0 → STS AssumeRoleWithSAML directly. Requires per-account IAM role + IdP configuration. Option 3: Migrate to PingOne (cloud), connect PingOne → Identity Center (same SAML + SCIM flow). <br><br> *PingFederate on-premises considerations: PingFederate must be reachable from employee browsers (SAML POST binding). AWS console initiates SP-initiated flow: user goes to Identity Center SSO portal → redirected to PingFederate → authenticates → SAML assertion → Identity Center. PingFederate must be internet-accessible OR employees must be on VPN to reach it. Availability: if PingFederate is down, AWS access is down. HA deployment: PingFederate cluster with load balancer.* <br> *PingFederate SCIM to Identity Center: PingFederate 10.x supports SCIM 2.0 outbound provisioning. Identity Center generates a SCIM endpoint URL and token. PingFederate SCIM provisioner sends user/group creates/updates/deletes to Identity Center. Real-time sync: employee added to AWS-Dev group in PingFederate → SCIM push → Identity Center group updated → permission set assigned. Deprovisioning: employee terminated → removed from PingFederate → SCIM delete → Identity Center access revoked across all accounts.* <br>

1265. [ Athena ] What is the CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) statement in Athena and what are its use cases? ; CTAS creates a new table in Glue catalog and writes query results to S3 in the specified format. Use cases: (1) Format conversion: convert JSON to Parquet for cheaper future queries. (2) Partition rebalancing: rewrite a poorly partitioned table with optimal partitions. (3) Data sampling: `CTAS AS SELECT * FROM big_table LIMIT 1000000` — create development sample. (4) Materialized aggregations: pre-aggregate daily metrics into a summary table. (5) Data archival: write old data to Parquet in cold storage tier. <br><br> *CTAS syntax: `CREATE TABLE new_table WITH (format='"'"'PARQUET'"'"', parquet_compression='"'"'SNAPPY'"'"', partitioned_by=ARRAY['"'"'year'"'"','"'"'month'"'"'], external_location='"'"'s3://bucket/new/'"'"') AS SELECT *, year(ts) as year, month(ts) as month FROM old_table`. The WITH options control: format (PARQUET, ORC, AVRO, JSON, TEXTFILE), compression, partitioning, S3 destination.* <br> *INSERT INTO: companion to CTAS. After creating a table with CTAS, use INSERT INTO to add new data: `INSERT INTO new_table SELECT * FROM source WHERE date = '"'"'2024-11-01'"'"'`. Athena does not support traditional UPDATE/DELETE (except on Iceberg tables). For Iceberg tables: MERGE INTO, UPDATE, DELETE are supported. CTAS + INSERT INTO = immutable append pattern (standard data lake practice).* <br>

1266. [ KMS ] What is a KMS grant and how does it differ from a key policy? Provide a scenario where grants are the right choice. ; Key policy: JSON document defining all access for the CMK. Must be modified by a key administrator. Permanent until explicitly changed. Grant: programmatic, time-limited delegation of specific key operations to a grantee principal. Created via API, does not require key policy modification. Can be retired/revoked. Use grants when: (1) AWS service needs temporary access to your key (EBS creates a grant when attaching an encrypted volume). (2) Application needs to delegate key access to a sub-component without admin involvement. (3) Time-limited key access for an operation. <br><br> *EBS grant example: when you create an encrypted EBS volume, EC2 service automatically creates a KMS grant on your CMK: grantee=EC2 service, operations=Decrypt,GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext. This grant allows EC2 to decrypt the volume data key every time the instance boots. The grant has a constraint: can only be used with encryption context matching the volume ID. When you delete the volume: EC2 retires the grant. No key policy modification needed.* <br> *Retiring vs revoking grants: retire = grantee calls `RetireGrant` (self-service, used when operation complete). Revoke = key administrator calls `RevokeGrant` (forceful removal). Retired grants: cannot be re-activated. Create a new grant if access needed again. For temporary access patterns: create grant with `RetiringPrincipal` set to the grantee — grantee can retire their own grant when done, no admin involvement.* <br>

1267. [ Athena ] What compression format is best for Athena if you need to query individual parts of a large file (splittable compression)? ; For Parquet and ORC: compression is applied at the row group level (not the whole file). Any compression codec (Snappy, GZIP, ZSTD) is splittable within Parquet/ORC because multiple workers can each read different row groups.
