For raw text files (CSV, JSON): BZIP2 and LZO (with index file) are splittable. GZIP and Snappy are NOT splittable for text files — entire file must be read by one worker. Recommendation: use Parquet with Snappy (fast decompression, splittable at row group level). <br><br> *Splittability for text files: a 10GB GZIP-compressed CSV file can only be processed by one Athena worker (cannot decompress middle of GZIP stream). Query performance: sequential, not parallel. Same file as LZO with .lzo.index file: Athena can split at LZO block boundaries, assign different chunks to different workers. Parallel processing. But: LZO compression ratio worse than GZIP. The better solution: just use Parquet (splittable + columnar + good compression ratio).* <br> *Parquet row group size: default 128MB. Each row group is independently compressed and can be read by a separate worker. A 10GB Parquet file has ~80 row groups → 80 parallel workers. Each reads/decompresses one row group. Much faster than single-worker GZIP CSV. File size guideline for Parquet: 128MB-1GB per file. Too small: overhead per file. Too large: not enough parallelism if file count < worker count.* <br>

1268. [ KMS ] How does the encryption context work in KMS and why is it important? ; Encryption context: optional key-value pairs passed with every KMS encrypt/decrypt call. KMS binds the ciphertext to the context — decryption requires the SAME context. If you encrypt with `{"purpose":"s3-storage","bucket":"my-bucket"}` and try to decrypt with `{"purpose":"other"}`: decryption fails. Use: (1) Additional authentication data (AAD) — binds ciphertext to its intended use. (2) CloudTrail audit — context logged with every operation. (3) Key policy conditions — restrict key usage to specific contexts. <br><br> *S3 SSE-KMS encryption context example: S3 sets `{"aws:s3:arn":"arn:aws:s3:::bucket/prefix/object.txt"}`. Logged in CloudTrail: every decrypt shows which S3 object was accessed. If attacker intercepts the encrypted DEK from S3 and tries to decrypt it outside S3 context: different encryption context → decryption fails. The DEK is bound to its specific S3 object — cannot be reused elsewhere.* <br> *Key policy enforcement with encryption context condition: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"kms:EncryptionContext:classification":"confidential"}}`. This CMK can only be used when the caller provides `classification=confidential` in the encryption context. Any service not passing this context gets AccessDenied. Enforces: only applications that know the required context can use this key. Defense in depth: even if an unauthorized role somehow gets `kms:Decrypt` permission, the encryption context requirement still blocks it.* <br>

1269. [ Federation ] What is the difference between Identity Provider-initiated (IdP-initiated) and Service Provider-initiated (SP-initiated) SAML SSO? ; SP-initiated: user navigates to the SP (AWS console) first → SP redirects to IdP for authentication → IdP authenticates → sends SAML assertion back to SP. User starts at AWS. IdP-initiated: user navigates to IdP portal first (e.g., Okta dashboard) → selects AWS app → IdP sends SAML assertion to AWS → user lands in AWS. User starts at Okta. Both result in the same SAML assertion flow, they differ in where the user begins. IAM Identity Center supports both. Direct SAML federation to IAM supports both (via IdP-specific configuration). <br><br> *SP-initiated advantages: standard bookmark (users can bookmark the Identity Center URL), works with deep links (direct link to specific AWS service). IdP-initiated advantages: single Okta portal for ALL apps (AWS, Salesforce, Office 365, etc.) — user goes to one place. Enterprises prefer IdP-initiated for UX: one portal, all apps, SSO context maintained. Many organizations configure Okta as the IdP-initiated entry point with tiles for prod/dev/sandbox accounts.* <br> *Security consideration: IdP-initiated is slightly less secure because the SP (AWS) receives an unsolicited assertion without having issued a prior request. AWS validates the assertion signature but cannot validate it was issued in response to a specific request. Some security frameworks prefer SP-initiated for this reason. Modern implementation: RelayState parameter in IdP-initiated can pass context to AWS about where to redirect after authentication.* <br>

1270. [ KMS ] What is CloudHSM and when should it be used instead of KMS? ; CloudHSM: AWS-provisioned, customer-managed Hardware Security Modules in an AWS data center. Customer has exclusive logical control — AWS cannot access key material. FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated. Use instead of KMS when: (1) Regulatory requirement that keys are in customer-exclusive HSM (some financial, government regulations). (2) Custom cryptographic algorithms not supported by KMS. (3) Offloading SSL/TLS termination to HSM (SSL acceleration). (4) Oracle TDE with external HSM. Cost: ~$1.45/hour per HSM (~$1,050/month). Minimum 2 for HA. <br><br> *KMS vs CloudHSM: KMS is multi-tenant (shared HSMs managed by AWS). CloudHSM is single-tenant (dedicated HSM in customer VPC). KMS: simpler, integrated with 100+ AWS services, pay-per-API-call. CloudHSM: complex, manual integration, high fixed cost, no native AWS service integration (except via KMS custom key store). Most regulatory requirements satisfied by KMS CMK (AWS HSMs, FIPS 140-2 Level 3, but AWS manages them). Only use CloudHSM when regulation explicitly requires customer-exclusive HSM custody.* <br> *CloudHSM integration with KMS: KMS custom key store uses a CloudHSM cluster to store CMK key material. You get KMS API convenience (works with S3, EBS, RDS) + CloudHSM key custody. The combination: KMS handles API and service integration, CloudHSM stores the key material. More complex than standard KMS but simpler than raw CloudHSM API integration. Use when: need KMS service integration AND customer-exclusive HSM custody.* <br>

1271. [ Athena ] What is Athena Federated Query and how does the Lambda connector architecture work? ; Athena Federated Query uses AWS Lambda as the bridge to external data sources. Architecture: (1) Register a Lambda function as a data catalog connector in Athena (the Lambda implements the Athena Query Federation SDK). (2) Athena query engine identifies federated source tables, calls the Lambda for each predicate pushdown batch. (3) Lambda queries the target data source (RDS, DynamoDB, on-prem DB via VPC Lambda) and returns Arrow-format records. (4) Athena assembles results from all sources and executes joins/aggregations. <br><br> *Available connectors (AWS-maintained): Amazon Athena RDS/Aurora connector, DynamoDB connector, Redshift connector, OpenSearch connector, DocumentDB connector, HBase on EMR connector, JDBC connector (generic: MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Snowflake). Custom connector: implement the `RecordHandler` and `MetadataHandler` interfaces from the Athena Query Federation SDK, deploy as Lambda, register in Athena.* <br> *Spill to S3: Federated Query results that exceed Lambda memory limits are "spilled" to a temporary S3 location. Lambda writes partial results to S3, Athena reads from S3. Configure spill bucket in connector settings. For large joins: significant S3 I/O. Performance: federated queries are slower than native S3 queries due to Lambda overhead and potential network latency to external sources. Not suitable for interactive BI dashboards — better for batch analytics and scheduled reports.* <br>

1272. [ KMS ] A developer calls KMS Encrypt on data larger than 4KB. What error occurs and what is the correct pattern? ; Error: `InvalidCiphertextException` or `ValidationException` — plaintext exceeds 4096 bytes. KMS Encrypt is limited to 4KB. Correct pattern: envelope encryption. (1) Call `kms:GenerateDataKey` → receive 256-bit plaintext DEK + encrypted DEK. (2) Encrypt large data locally with plaintext DEK using AES-256-GCM (AWS Encryption SDK, Boto3 KMS client, or direct AES library). (3) Store encrypted data + encrypted DEK. (4) Discard plaintext DEK. <br><br> *AWS Encryption SDK: Python/Java/Go/C library implementing envelope encryption with best practices. `aws_encryption_sdk.encrypt(source=large_data, key_provider=kms_key_provider)` handles GenerateDataKey, local AES encryption, and message format automatically. `aws_encryption_sdk.decrypt(source=ciphertext, key_provider=kms_key_provider)` handles the reverse. The encrypted message format includes the encrypted DEK, algorithm ID, and initialization vectors.* <br> *When is direct Encrypt appropriate: small data (< 4KB): passwords, API keys, small config values, short tokens. For these: `kms:Encrypt` is fine (one API call, small plaintext). Large data (> 4KB): always envelope encryption. Rule of thumb: if the plaintext fits in a config file or environment variable, direct Encrypt is okay. If it is file content, object data, or database records, use GenerateDataKey.* <br>

1273. [ Federation ] A company has both workforce users (employees) and customer users (app end-users). What is the correct AWS identity architecture for each? ; Workforce (employees): IAM Identity Center + external IdP (Okta/Azure AD). Employees get SSO access to AWS accounts via permission sets. Centrally managed, multi-account, SCIM provisioning. Customer users (app end-users): Amazon Cognito User Pools for authentication (sign-up, sign-in, MFA, social login). Cognito Identity Pools (optional) to grant temporary AWS credentials for direct AWS resource access. Never mix: do not put customer users in Identity Center, do not put employees in Cognito User Pools. <br><br> *Why not Cognito for employees: Cognito User Pools is designed for millions of customer identities with self-service sign-up. It does not integrate with AWS Organizations multi-account access, does not have permission sets concept, and is not designed for corporate IdP integration at scale. Identity Center is designed for employees: integrates with AD/SAML IdPs, manages multi-account permissions, free service.* <br> *Why not Identity Center for customers: Identity Center is limited to workforce-scale (tens of thousands of users). No self-service sign-up, no social login (Google, Facebook, Apple), no customer-appropriate MFA options. Cognito User Pools supports millions of users, self-service sign-up, social login, hosted UI. Building a customer auth system on Identity Center would be using the wrong tool entirely.* <br>

1274. [ Athena ] Explain the Hive partition format and how Athena discovers partitions in S3. ; Hive partition format: S3 key prefixes in `column=value` format, e.g., `s3://bucket/table/year=2024/month=11/day=01/file.parquet`. Athena (and Glue Crawlers) automatically recognize this format as partitioned data. The column names in the prefix must match the `PARTITIONED BY` clause in the DDL. Discovery methods: (1) Glue Crawler: scans S3, detects partition format, registers partitions in Glue catalog. (2) MSCK REPAIR TABLE: Athena SQL command, scans S3, registers new Hive partitions. (3) ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION: manual explicit registration. (4) Partition Projection: no registration needed. <br><br> *Non-Hive format (custom prefix): `s3://bucket/table/2024/11/01/file.parquet` — no `key=value` format. MSCK REPAIR TABLE will NOT detect this. Must use: ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION (year='"'"'2024'"'"', month='"'"'11'"'"', day='"'"'01'"'"') LOCATION '"'"'s3://bucket/table/2024/11/01/'"'"'. Or use Partition Projection with `storage.location.template=s3://bucket/table/${year}/${month}/${day}/` and `projection.year.type=integer`. Partition Projection handles non-Hive format via the location template.* <br> *VPC Flow Logs partition format: AWS-generated flow logs use: `AWSLogs/ACCOUNT_ID/vpcflowlogs/REGION/YEAR/MONTH/DAY/file.log.gz`. Non-Hive format (no key=value). Must use Partition Projection with location template: `storage.location.template=s3://bucket/AWSLogs/${account}/vpcflowlogs/${region}/${year}/${month}/${day}/` with projection types: account (enum), region (enum), year/month/day (integer or date). This is the standard pattern for VPC Flow Log analysis with Athena.* <br>

1275. [ KMS ] What is the difference between enabling and disabling a KMS CMK? What are the operational implications? ; Enabling: key operational state, can be used for cryptographic operations (Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey). Default state after creation. Disabling: key not deleted, key metadata retained, but ALL cryptographic operations return `KMSDisabledException`. Data encrypted with the key becomes temporarily inaccessible. Re-enabling restores access. Operational implications of disabling: all S3 objects using the key return AccessDenied on GetObject. EBS volumes encrypted with the key cannot be attached. RDS instances using the key may fail to start. <br><br> *Use cases for disabling: (1) Security incident response — suspect a key is compromised, disable immediately to block access while investigating. (2) Planned decommission — disable for 30 days, monitor CloudWatch for `KMSDisabledException` alarms to discover all key usages, then schedule deletion. (3) Environment controls — disable keys for non-production environments after hours to reduce exposure window.* <br> *Cascading effects of disabling: EBS encrypted volume attached to running instance — instance continues to run (key used at attach time, not every read). If instance stops: cannot restart (EBS re-attach calls KMS). RDS encrypted instance running — continues to run (TDE key loaded at startup). If RDS restarts: cannot start. S3 SSE-KMS: GetObject calls KMS on every read — immediate impact when key disabled. Plan disable operations during maintenance windows for critical infrastructure.* <br>

1276. [ Athena ] What is the maximum query timeout in Athena and what happens when a query exceeds it? ; Default timeout: 30 minutes. Query exceeding 30 minutes: automatically cancelled with status FAILED, error "Query exhausted resources at this scale factor" or timeout error. Partial results: not saved (Athena returns complete results or nothing). Fix: optimize query (add partition filters, reduce data scanned, use Parquet), or use Athena for Spark for complex long-running transformations, or break query into smaller time-range queries and union results. <br><br> *Timeout increase: cannot increase beyond 30 minutes for standard Athena SQL. For longer-running analytics: (1) Break into multiple queries with date range partitioning. (2) Use Glue ETL (can run for hours). (3) Use EMR Spark (arbitrary runtime). (4) Use Athena for Spark (separate timeout limits). (5) Materialize intermediate results with CTAS, then run final aggregation.* <br> *Query optimization to prevent timeouts: (1) Always filter on partition columns first. (2) Use LIMIT 100 in exploratory queries. (3) Pre-aggregate data with Glue ETL before querying. (4) Check `data_scanned_in_bytes` in Athena query history — if > 100GB, optimization needed. (5) Use Athena explain (`EXPLAIN SELECT ...`) to see query plan and identify full table scans.* <br>

1277. [ KMS ] A company needs all S3 objects across 100 accounts to be encrypted with CMKs (not AWS Owned or AWS Managed keys). How do you enforce this across the organization? ; SCP at root OU level: deny `s3:PutObject` unless condition `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption = aws:kms` AND `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id` is set (ensuring CMK, not AWS Managed key). Additional: AWS Config rule `s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled` scoped to CMK requirement. Optionally: S3 bucket-level default encryption with CMK (new objects automatically encrypted without requiring clients to specify). <br><br> *SCP approach: forces all PutObject calls organization-wide to include SSE-KMS headers with a CMK ARN. Developers cannot accidentally upload unencrypted objects or objects encrypted with AWS Owned keys. Limitation: SCP condition keys for S3 encryption headers are available (`s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption`, `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id`) but the CMK ARN check requires knowing the CMK ARN in the SCP — use a pattern with account-specific CMKs or a condition matching CMK ARN pattern.* <br> *S3 default encryption + bucket policy: set bucket default encryption to SSE-KMS with specific CMK ARN. Objects without explicit encryption header inherit bucket default (SSE-KMS with CMK). Bucket policy: deny PutObject with wrong encryption header (override prevention). This is account-level control, SCP provides organization-level enforcement. Defense in depth: SCP prevents wrong encryption, bucket default ensures right CMK, bucket policy blocks override attempts.* <br>

1278. [ Federation ] How does Cognito Identity Pool handle unauthenticated (guest) access? When should it be enabled? ; Unauthenticated access: Cognito Identity Pool can issue temporary AWS credentials to users who have NOT authenticated with any IdP. The credentials map to a configurable unauthenticated IAM role. Use cases: (1) Read-only access to public S3 content (app loads without sign-in). (2) Offline capabilities (app works without network IdP call). (3) Analytics: track anonymous user behavior in DynamoDB before sign-in. Enable when: app has legitimate guest functionality requiring AWS resource access. <br><br> *Security for unauthenticated role: must be extremely restrictive. Example: allow GetObject on specific S3 prefix (`s3://app-assets/public/*`), GetItem from specific DynamoDB table for public product catalog. Never allow: PutObject (anonymous writes), database writes, any admin operations. The unauthenticated role is the most exposed IAM role in your architecture — any internet user can assume it.* <br> *Unauthenticated enhanced vs basic flow: enhanced (simplified) flow: Cognito calls STS on your behalf (two API calls behind the scenes). Basic (classic) flow: your app calls GetId → GetCredentialsForIdentity directly. Enhanced recommended for most use cases. Enhanced flow supports Cognito-specific policy variables (sub, aud, amr) for dynamic policy conditions. Basic flow more flexible for custom scenarios but more code.* <br>

1279. [ KMS ] What is the KMS request quota and how do you handle quota exhaustion in a high-throughput application? ; Default quotas: 30,000 symmetric cryptographic operations/second per account per region (varies by operation type and key). `kms:Decrypt`: 30,000/sec. `kms:GenerateDataKey`: 30,000/sec. If exceeded: `ThrottlingException` with HTTP 400. Handling: (1) Retry with exponential backoff. (2) Use data key caching (AWS Encryption SDK) — reuse the same DEK for N operations before requesting a new one. (3) S3 Bucket Key — reduces KMS calls per S3 operation by ~99%. (4) Request quota increase via Service Quotas. <br><br> *Data key caching with AWS Encryption SDK: configure `LocalCryptoMaterialsCache(max_age=300, max_messages_encrypted=1000)`. The SDK reuses the same plaintext DEK for up to 1000 encryptions or 5 minutes, whichever comes first. After limit: requests new DEK from KMS. Effect: 1,000 applications calls = 1 KMS call (instead of 1,000). Trade-off: all messages in the cache window share the same DEK — weaker per-message isolation. Acceptable for most use cases. Not appropriate for: high-security scenarios requiring unique DEK per message (e.g., individual message non-repudiation).* <br> *High-throughput architecture: microservice processing 1M events/second needs to encrypt each event. Without caching: 1M KMS calls/second — quota exhausted immediately. With data key caching (max 10,000 messages, 60 seconds): 1,000 KMS calls/second — well within quota. Architecture: cache manager generates new DEK every 60s, distributes to worker threads, each worker encrypts locally without additional KMS calls.* <br>

1280. [ Athena ] What are the differences between Athena, Redshift, and Redshift Spectrum for analytics use cases? ; Athena: serverless, no cluster, $5/TB scanned, best for ad-hoc queries on S3, no ETL required, slow cold start for first query (Presto coordination). Redshift: MPP data warehouse cluster, storage on Redshift nodes, fast for complex BI queries, requires ETL to load data, expensive ($0.25-$6.80/node-hour), best for regular complex analytics, ML integration. Redshift Spectrum: extends Redshift to query S3 external tables without loading data, charged separately ($5/TB scanned like Athena), best when you need S3 data + Redshift warehouse data in same query. <br><br> *When Redshift beats Athena: (1) Complex multi-table JOINs with aggregations on structured data loaded in Redshift. (2) Regular BI dashboard queries (consistent sub-second performance after warm-up). (3) Concurrent query workloads (Redshift workload management). (4) ML predictions via Redshift ML (Amazon SageMaker integration). Athena beats Redshift: (1) Irregular/ad-hoc queries on large S3 datasets. (2) No cluster management desired. (3) Variable or unpredictable query frequency (Athena has no idle cost). (4) Direct S3 data lake queries without ETL.* <br> *Redshift Spectrum use case: you have a Redshift data warehouse with 3 years of hot data. S3 has 10 years of cold archive data. Business requirement: query all 10 years together. Solution: Redshift Spectrum external tables in Glue catalog pointing to S3 archive. Single SQL query JOINs Redshift hot data + Spectrum S3 cold data. No data migration. Pay for Spectrum scans ($5/TB) only when querying cold data.* <br>

1281. [ KMS ] Explain the KMS key hierarchy: region, CMK, backing key, data key. How do they relate? ; Region: KMS keys exist in a specific region (except Multi-Region Keys which have replicas). CMK (Customer Master Key / KMS Key): the logical key resource in KMS — has an ARN, alias, metadata, key policy. The CMK is the container. Backing key: the actual cryptographic key material (AES-256 bytes) stored in the HSM. After rotation, a CMK can have multiple backing keys (old ones retained for decryption). Data key: generated by `GenerateDataKey` — a per-operation symmetric key used to encrypt actual data. Data key is itself encrypted by the CMK backing key. <br><br> *Hierarchy relationship: CMK (logical container) → backing key (actual AES-256 material, one per rotation cycle) → data key (per-object AES-256 key, encrypted by backing key). S3 object: data encrypted with data key. Data key encrypted with CMK backing key. CMK backing key in KMS HSM. To access data: need access to the CMK → KMS decrypts the data key using the backing key → you decrypt data with the plaintext data key.* <br> *After key rotation: CMK ARN unchanged. New backing key created (e.g., backing key v2). All new GenerateDataKey calls use backing key v2. Existing S3 objects: encrypted with data keys encrypted by backing key v1. KMS retains backing key v1 for decryption. Decrypt call: KMS checks which backing key version was used (embedded in the encrypted DEK), uses the correct version. Transparent to the application.* <br>

1282. [ Federation ] What is the JWT (JSON Web Token) structure and how does AWS validate it in OIDC federation? ; JWT structure: three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots. Header: `{"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT","kid":"key-id"}` (signing algorithm + key ID). Payload: `{"iss":"https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com","sub":"repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main","aud":"sts.amazonaws.com","exp":1700000000,"iat":1699996400}`. Signature: RS256 signature of header.payload using IdP private key. AWS STS validation: (1) Decode header, get `kid`. (2) Fetch IdP JWKS endpoint (`/.well-known/jwks.json`) to get public key matching `kid`. (3) Verify RS256 signature. (4) Check `iss`, `aud`, `exp` claims. (5) Apply trust policy conditions to `sub`, `aud`, and other claims. <br><br> *AWS STS caches the JWKS (public keys) from the IdP. Does not fetch on every call. Cache TTL: approximately 24 hours. If IdP rotates its signing key: there is a brief window where STS cache has old public key. JWT signed with new key fails validation until cache refreshes. IdPs handle this with `kid` (key ID) rotation — keep old key active in JWKS for overlap period.* <br> *Trust policy condition matching on JWT claims: `"StringEquals": {"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"}` validates the audience claim. `"StringLike": {"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:myorg/*"}` allows any repo in myorg. Custom claims: if your OIDC IdP includes custom claims (department, team, clearance_level), you can reference them in trust policy conditions: `"StringEquals": {"your-idp.com:custom_claim": "value"}`. Powerful ABAC at the federation boundary.* <br>

1283. [ Athena ] What is the difference between Glue Crawler and MSCK REPAIR TABLE for partition discovery? ; MSCK REPAIR TABLE: Athena SQL command, scans S3 prefixes for Hive-compatible `key=value` partitions, adds new partitions to Glue catalog. Runs synchronously in Athena query engine. Limitations: only discovers Hive-format partitions, does not update schema (no new column detection), slow for large partition counts, cannot delete removed partitions. Glue Crawler: AWS Glue managed service, scheduled or on-demand, scans S3, detects partition format AND schema, updates catalog, can handle schema changes (new columns), can delete stale partitions. More capable, separate cost. <br><br> *MSCK REPAIR TABLE limitations: does not delete partitions whose S3 data was deleted (stale partition metadata). Future queries on deleted partitions: succeed but return no results (empty partition scan). Glue Crawler with `Delete` configuration: removes stale partitions from catalog. For data with frequent deletes (GDPR erasure, data lifecycle): use Glue Crawler to keep catalog consistent.* <br> *Cost comparison: MSCK REPAIR TABLE: Athena query cost (min $0.005, data scanned is DDL so free). Glue Crawler: $0.44/DPU-hour. A crawler processing 1,000 partitions in 5 minutes = $0.022. For high-frequency partition addition (new partition every minute): MSCK every minute = 1,440 Athena queries/day (free DDL, but query slot usage). Glue Crawler every 15 minutes = 96 crawl runs/day. Partition Projection: zero cost, zero API calls. Always prefer Partition Projection for predictable partition structures.* <br>

1284. [ KMS ] How does KMS pricing work? Estimate the monthly cost for: 10 CMKs, 1 million S3 object uploads/day with SSE-KMS without Bucket Key, and same with Bucket Key. ; Key fees: 10 CMKs × $1/month = $10/month. API calls without Bucket Key: 1M S3 PutObject = 1M GenerateDataKey calls/day × 30 days = 30M calls/month. Cost: (30M / 10,000) × $0.03 = $90/month. Plus GetObject: assume 5M downloads/day = 5M Decrypt calls/day × 30 = 150M calls/month = $45/month. Total without Bucket Key: $10 + $90 + $45 = $145/month. With Bucket Key: 99% fewer API calls. API cost ≈ $1.35/month. Total: $10 + $1.35 = ~$11.35/month. Savings: $134/month. <br><br> *Bucket Key pricing impact scales dramatically at high volume. 100M S3 PutObject/day without Bucket Key: 3B API calls/month = $9,000/month KMS API cost. With Bucket Key: $90/month. Enabling Bucket Key is a one-checkbox optimization that saves thousands of dollars for high-S3-volume workloads. Always enable for production S3 buckets with SSE-KMS.* <br> *EBS/RDS API call costs: lower than S3. EBS: GenerateDataKey once per volume creation. Decrypt at instance start. For a fleet of 100 EC2 instances with daily restart: 100 KMS Decrypt calls/day × 30 = 3,000 calls/month = negligible ($0.009/month). EBS is much cheaper than S3 in KMS API terms because volumes are not recreated constantly.* <br>

1285. [ Federation ] A company wants to implement MFA for AWS Console access via SAML federation (Okta). Where is MFA enforced? ; MFA is enforced at the IdP level (Okta), not in AWS IAM or Identity Center. The IdP authenticates the user including MFA. The SAML assertion (issued after successful MFA) contains the authentication level. AWS trusts the assertion without re-prompting MFA. Identity Center: configure Okta as external IdP, enable MFA in Okta policy (adaptive MFA, always MFA for AWS app, or risk-based). Users who bypass MFA in Okta: Okta does not issue SAML assertion, no AWS access. <br><br> *IAM STS MFA condition (`aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent`): works for IAM users with MFA, not for SAML-federated users. Federated users via AssumeRoleWithSAML: the `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` context key is not set (federated authentication context). You cannot use IAM policies to enforce MFA for SAML-federated users — enforce at IdP level (Okta MFA policy, Azure AD Conditional Access).* <br> *Identity Center MFA settings: Identity Center has its own MFA configuration when using the built-in Identity Center directory (not external IdP). When using external IdP (Okta): MFA is fully delegated to Okta. Identity Center does not prompt for additional MFA. Okta Adaptive MFA: context-aware MFA — if user is on corporate network, no MFA prompt. From unknown location: MFA required. Risk-based: anomalous login patterns trigger step-up MFA. This is the enterprise-grade MFA approach: smart, frictionless for trusted contexts, strong for risky ones.* <br>

1286. [ KMS ] What is the GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext API and when is it preferable to GenerateDataKey? ; GenerateDataKey: returns BOTH plaintext DEK and encrypted DEK. Use when encrypting data immediately. GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext: returns ONLY the encrypted DEK. Use when: (1) Preparing encryption material in advance without immediate encryption need. (2) Key escrow: generate encrypted DEK, store alongside data slot, decrypt DEK only when actual encryption needed. (3) Distributed system: master service generates encrypted DEKs for worker services to use later (workers call Decrypt to get plaintext DEK when ready). (4) Reduce KMS calls: generate many encrypted DEKs in bulk, distribute to workers. <br><br> *Security advantage of WithoutPlaintext: plaintext DEK never exists in the caller process. The encrypted DEK is stored, plaintext DEK only appears in the worker process memory at encryption time (via a Decrypt call). Minimizes the window during which plaintext key material is in memory. For the master key management service that distributes DEKs: it handles only encrypted DEKs, never plaintext. Strict key material handling policy: plaintext DEK only in the process that actually encrypts data.* <br> *Example pattern: batch encryption service. Pre-generation phase (off-peak): call GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext 1000 times, store 1000 encrypted DEKs in queue. Encryption phase: worker dequeues encrypted DEK, calls KMS Decrypt (1 call → plaintext DEK), encrypts data, discards plaintext DEK. KMS calls (1000) happen during pre-generation phase at controlled rate, not during peak encryption. Smoothes KMS API call rate, avoids peak-hour throttling.* <br>

1287. [ Athena ] What are the Athena limits for concurrent queries and how do they affect production workloads? ; Default limits: 20 concurrent DML queries (SELECT, CTAS, INSERT INTO) per account per region. 20 concurrent DDL queries (CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, etc.) per account per region. When limit exceeded: additional queries queue but may time out after 30 minutes waiting. Impact: if 30 analysts run simultaneous queries: 10 wait. For high-concurrency workloads: (1) Request quota increase. (2) Use query result caching (identical queries within 7 days return cached results, no concurrency slot used). (3) Distribute workloads across multiple Athena workgroups in multiple regions. <br><br> *Result caching: Athena automatically caches query results for 7 days. Identical query (same SQL, same database, same partition filter) re-run within 7 days: returns cached S3 result instantly, no data scanning, no concurrency slot. For dashboards with frequent identical queries: caching dramatically reduces both cost and concurrency pressure. Cache key: exact SQL text (case-sensitive) + workgroup + database. Adding a LIMIT or changing whitespace: different cache key, re-executes.* <br> *BI tool integration (QuickSight, Tableau, PowerBI): BI tools generate SQL per dashboard refresh. If 50 users refresh simultaneously: 50 concurrent queries. With Athena result caching (and SPICE in QuickSight): QuickSight SPICE caches the Athena results in QuickSight memory, serves all 50 users from SPICE without 50 Athena queries. SPICE refresh: one Athena query per schedule (hourly, daily). Reduces Athena concurrency from 50 per refresh to 1 per schedule.* <br>

1288. [ KMS ] What is the difference between key policy and IAM policy for controlling KMS access, and how do they interact? ; KMS access requires: key policy ALLOWS the principal OR key policy has root principal (enabling IAM delegation) AND IAM policy ALLOWS the action. Key policy alone: if key policy explicitly allows a role, no IAM policy needed. IAM policy alone: insufficient without root principal in key policy — IAM policies cannot grant KMS access without key policy delegation. Both required: most common pattern — key policy allows root (delegation), IAM policy grants specific actions to specific roles. Neither alone provides full control without the other in the delegation pattern. <br><br> *Evaluation logic: (1) Is there an explicit DENY in key policy for the principal? → DENY. (2) Is there an explicit ALLOW in key policy for the principal? → ALLOW. (3) Does key policy have root principal? → check IAM policies. If IAM policy allows → ALLOW. If not → DENY. This three-step evaluation is unique to KMS — other services evaluate key/resource policy + IAM policy independently with "ALLOW in either = access" (for same-account access). KMS is stricter: key policy must explicitly permit access or delegate to IAM.* <br> *Cross-account difference: Account B access to Account A key. Account A key policy must explicitly list Account B principal (or Account B root). Account A key policy CANNOT delegate to Account B IAM (root delegation only works within the same account). So for cross-account: key policy explicitly lists Account B role/root + Account B IAM policy allows the action on the key ARN. Both explicit.* <br>

1289. [ Athena ] What is the difference between Athena SQL and Athena for Spark? When should each be used? ; Athena SQL: serverless Presto/Trino SQL engine. Query S3 data with standard SQL. Pay $5/TB scanned. Immediate results (seconds to minutes). No infrastructure. Best for: SQL analytics, BI tool integration, ad-hoc data exploration, scheduled SQL reports. Athena for Spark: serverless Apache Spark. Run PySpark notebooks or batch jobs. Pay $0.30/DPU-hour. Best for: complex data transformations requiring procedural logic, Python data science libraries (pandas, scikit-learn), ML feature engineering, iterative notebook exploration, operations not expressible in SQL. <br><br> *Athena Spark vs EMR: Athena Spark: fully serverless, no cluster to manage, auto-scales, start immediately (no cluster boot), limited Spark configuration. EMR: cluster-based, full Spark configurability (custom JARs, JDBC drivers, complex dependencies), persistent cluster for continuous workloads, better for >1hr jobs, can be cheaper at very high scale with spot instances. For data scientists doing exploratory analysis: Athena Spark (no cluster management overhead). For production ETL pipelines running hourly: EMR (cost efficiency, reliability, full control).* <br> *Athena SQL vs Athena Spark for the same task: GROUP BY aggregation on 1TB Parquet → Athena SQL: $5 query cost, 30 seconds. Complex feature engineering with Python pandas, ML model training → Athena Spark: $0.30/DPU-hour, 10 DPUs for 20 minutes = $1. Athena SQL wins for SQL-expressible tasks. Athena Spark wins for Python-required tasks. Never use Athena Spark just to avoid writing SQL — SQL is faster and cheaper for SQL tasks.* <br>

1290. [ Federation ] What is the SCIM protocol and how does it work with IAM Identity Center? ; SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management): REST API protocol for automating user/group provisioning between IdP (Okta, Azure AD) and service provider (IAM Identity Center). SCIM operations: Create user, Update user, Deactivate user, Create group, Add/remove group members. Identity Center generates a SCIM endpoint URL and bearer token. IdP sends HTTPS requests to the endpoint for every HR event: new hire → create user + group assignment → user gets AWS access. Termination → deactivate user → immediate access revocation across all accounts. <br><br> *SCIM vs manual provisioning: 5,000 employees, 200 AWS accounts. Manual: IT team creates Identity Center user, assigns permission sets — hours of work per hire/termination. SCIM: HR updates IdP → SCIM push in minutes → Identity Center updated automatically → zero IT action. SCIM is mandatory for Identity Center at scale. Without SCIM: orphaned accounts (terminated employees still have access), delayed provisioning (new hires wait days for access).* <br> *SCIM limitations with AD Connector: AD Connector in Identity Center does not support SCIM — it proxies authentication to on-premises AD but does not sync user objects to Identity Center. With AD Connector, Identity Center discovers users at authentication time (not pre-provisioned). Cannot pre-assign permission sets to users not yet authenticated. For SCIM-based automation: use an external IdP (Okta, Azure AD) with SCIM, not AD Connector. AWS Managed AD also does not support SCIM — for automated provisioning with AD, use Okta or Azure AD as the SCIM source.* <br>


1291. [ KMS ] A company needs to encrypt existing unencrypted EBS volumes. What is the process and are there any limitations? ; Existing unencrypted EBS volume cannot be directly encrypted (no in-place encryption). Process: (1) Create snapshot of unencrypted volume. (2) Copy snapshot and enable encryption with CMK: `aws ec2 copy-snapshot --source-snapshot-id snap-xxx --encrypted --kms-key-id arn:aws:kms:...`. (3) Create new volume from encrypted snapshot. (4) Stop EC2 instance. (5) Detach old unencrypted volume. (6) Attach new encrypted volume. (7) Start instance. Limitation: cannot encrypt a running volume in-place. Requires downtime for root volumes. <br><br> *Account-level encryption by default: enable "EBS encryption by default" in EC2 settings per region. All new EBS volumes created in the region are automatically encrypted with the specified CMK (or default key). This does NOT encrypt existing volumes — only new ones created after the setting is enabled. For existing volumes: still need the snapshot copy process.* <br> *Automation for large fleet: AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook `AWSSupport-CopyEC2Instance` can migrate an instance to encrypted volumes. For a fleet of 500 unencrypted EC2 instances: create SSM Automation document, run in batch (20 instances at a time to avoid disruption), verify application health after each batch. Terraform: `aws_ebs_default_kms_key_id` and `aws_ebs_encryption_by_default` resources enforce encryption for all future volumes.* <br>

1292. [ Athena ] What are Athena named queries and saved queries? How are they useful in enterprise environments? ; Named queries: SQL queries saved in Athena with a name and description. Stored in S3 (within Athena metadata). Can be shared within a workgroup. Use: standardize common queries (security investigations, compliance reports), prevent analysts from writing incorrect SQL for complex joins, version control via CloudFormation/CDK. Saved queries: same concept, different UI term. Access: `aws athena list-named-queries`, `aws athena get-named-query`. Execute: `aws athena start-query-execution --query-string "$(aws athena get-named-query --named-query-id xxx --query 'NamedQuery.QueryString' --output text)"`. <br><br> *Enterprise use case: security team creates named query "Find all failed logins from external IPs last 7 days" against CloudTrail logs. SOC analysts run this query with one click from Athena console (no SQL knowledge needed). Query is consistent (no typos, correct partition pruning), produces auditable results (same query each time). Named queries are workgroup-scoped (analysts in analytics-workgroup see their queries, security team in security-workgroup sees theirs).* <br> *Named queries in CloudFormation: `AWS::Athena::NamedQuery` resource. Define all standard queries as infrastructure code. Deploy via CI/CD pipeline. Version controlled in Git. New team members instantly have access to all standard queries on first deployment. Combine with workgroup configuration: production analytics environment deployed as code — workgroup + named queries + result bucket + encryption = complete analytics setup via CloudFormation.* <br>

1293. [ Federation ] What happens to AWS access when the SAML IdP (Okta) is unavailable? ; All new authentication attempts fail. Existing sessions: STS temporary credentials issued before the outage remain valid until expiration (up to 12 hours for SAML). Once expired: no renewal possible (cannot re-authenticate to get new credentials). Break-glass access: maintain a small number of direct IAM users with MFA in a break-glass vault (LastPass, 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager). These bypass federation. Scope: only management tasks, hardware MFA, audited access, used only during IdP outages. <br><br> *Identity Center with external IdP: same behavior. If Okta is down, Identity Center cannot issue new sessions. Users with active sessions (within session duration) continue to work. New login: fails. CLI with SSO: `aws sso login` fails (cannot authenticate to Okta). Active CLI sessions (cached credentials): work until credential expiration.* <br> *Best practices for IdP HA: (1) Okta/Azure AD are SaaS — high availability by design. (2) For on-premises IdP (AD FS, PingFederate): multi-server HA deployment with load balancer. (3) DNS failover: Route 53 health check on IdP endpoint → SNS alert when IdP unreachable. (4) Break-glass IAM users: 2-3 accounts per account, credentials in vault, never used in normal operations. (5) Test break-glass quarterly: verify credentials work, verify audit trail generated. (6) Cross-region IdP deployment if regulatory allows: IdP in two regions, Route 53 latency routing.* <br>

1294. [ KMS ] What is the KMS Decrypt API response structure and what do you do with the plaintext? ; KMS Decrypt response: `Plaintext` (Base64-encoded plaintext bytes), `KeyId` (ARN of the key that decrypted), `EncryptionAlgorithm` (SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT / RSAES_OAEP / etc.). The plaintext is the raw decrypted bytes — for envelope encryption, this is the DEK (32 bytes for AES-256). Use the DEK to decrypt your data locally with AES-256-GCM. Immediately zero/clear the plaintext bytes from memory after use — minimize the window the plaintext key is in memory. <br><br> *Memory handling best practices: in Python: `plaintext_key = response['"'"'Plaintext'"'"']`, use for decryption, then `del plaintext_key`, `gc.collect()`. In Java: use `Arrays.fill(plaintextKey, (byte)0)` after use. Python bytearrays can be zeroed: `ba = bytearray(plaintext_bytes), ... use ba ..., ba[:] = b'"'"'\x00'"'"' * len(ba)`. Not all languages/runtimes guarantee memory zeroing (Python garbage collection may not immediately free memory). For high-security: use dedicated security libraries (AWS Encryption SDK handles this internally).* <br> *EncryptionContext validation on Decrypt: pass the same EncryptionContext you used during Encrypt. If context does not match: `InvalidCiphertextException`. This validation happens inside the HSM — you cannot accidentally decrypt ciphertext intended for a different purpose. For envelope encryption: store the encryption context alongside the encrypted DEK. At decrypt time: read the stored context, pass to KMS Decrypt. This is additional authentication data (AAD) that binds the ciphertext to its original context.* <br>

1295. [ Athena ] Explain how Athena pricing works. A query scans 500GB of Parquet data but only 50GB of relevant columns are read due to columnar projection. What is the cost? ; Athena pricing: $5/TB of data scanned. Data scanned = bytes read from S3 (after columnar and partition pruning, before decompression). For Parquet with column projection: Athena reads only the columns referenced in the query (columnar storage). If 500GB Parquet has 20 columns but query only uses 3 columns: Athena reads ~3/20 × 500GB ≈ 75GB (rough estimate, depends on actual column sizes). Minimum charge: 10MB per query. Cost for 75GB: 75/1024 TB × $5 = $0.366. <br><br> *Billing unit: 10MB minimum per query, rounded up to nearest MB. A query scanning 1MB is billed as 10MB. A query scanning 5GB is billed as 5GB. Athena does not charge for: DDL queries (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE), failed queries (error before scan begins), cached queries (result reuse within 7 days).* <br> *Compression effect on cost: Athena charges on compressed bytes read from S3. 500GB uncompressed Parquet with Snappy compression = ~300GB on S3. Athena reads 300GB from S3 (compressed), decompresses to 500GB in memory. Billing: based on 300GB compressed bytes. Cost: 300/1024 × $5 = $1.46. Another reason compression reduces cost: both storage cost AND query cost. Parquet + Snappy + partition pruning + column projection = typically 95%+ cost reduction vs raw uncompressed JSON.* <br>

1296. [ KMS ] What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric KMS keys? ; Symmetric key (SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT): AES-256, single key material used for both encryption and decryption, same key must be used for both operations, only usable within AWS (key material never leaves HSM), used by all AWS services for SSE. Cost: standard CMK pricing. Asymmetric key: key pair (public key + private key). Types: RSA (2048, 3072, 4096) or ECC (P-256, P-384, SM2). Use cases: (1) Digital signing (sign/verify outside AWS using public key). (2) Public key encryption: encrypt with public key (downloadable), decrypt with private key (stays in KMS). <br><br> *Asymmetric key use cases: (1) JWT signing: use KMS private key to sign JWTs, distribute public key for verification. Verifiers can verify JWT without KMS access. (2) Code signing: sign software artifacts with KMS private key. CI/CD distributes public key for verification. (3) Cross-organization encryption: publish your KMS public key, partner encrypts data with it, only you can decrypt (private key in KMS). (4) TLS private key: store TLS private key in KMS, use for SSL termination (AWS Certificate Manager uses this internally).* <br> *Symmetric vs asymmetric for AWS services: all AWS service integration (S3 SSE-KMS, EBS, RDS, Secrets Manager) requires SYMMETRIC key — services call GenerateDataKey which requires symmetric AES key. Asymmetric keys cannot be used with AWS managed service encryption. Asymmetric = your application code calls KMS Sign/Verify or Encrypt/Decrypt directly. Never try to use an asymmetric CMK for S3 SSE-KMS — it fails.* <br>

1297. [ Athena ] How do you handle sensitive data in Athena query results? What security controls are available? ; Controls: (1) Workgroup with SSE-KMS on result bucket (encrypted results in S3). (2) S3 bucket policy on result bucket — only workgroup service role and authorized users can access results. (3) IAM policy limiting `athena:GetQueryResults` to specific workgroups. (4) Result expiry: S3 lifecycle policy to delete query results after 30/60/90 days. (5) Column-level security via Glue/Lake Formation: grant SELECT on specific columns only — Athena enforces column-level access. (6) Row-level security via Lake Formation: filter rows based on IAM principal tags. <br><br> *Lake Formation column-level security: grant user A access to columns [user_id, action, timestamp] but not [ssn, credit_card]. When user A queries the table in Athena: Lake Formation intercepts, rewrites the query to exclude restricted columns. User A gets NULL for columns they cannot access. Transparent to the user.* <br> *Lake Formation row-level security: data filter `department = '"'"'ENGINEERING'"'"'` applied to user A. User A queries employee table: Lake Formation adds WHERE clause `department='"'"'ENGINEERING'"'"'`. User A sees only engineering employees. Finance employees see only finance rows. Row-level security implemented at the catalog level — works with Athena, Glue ETL, and EMR Spark (all Lake Formation-integrated engines). Centralized security policy without modifying application queries.* <br>

1298. [ KMS ] A company uses multiple AWS services (S3, EBS, RDS, Secrets Manager) and wants to ensure a security incident can immediately revoke all data access. How do you design the key strategy? ; One CMK per service category (or per data classification). To revoke access: disable the relevant CMK(s). Immediate effect: all services using that CMK cannot decrypt data. S3: GetObject fails. EBS: cannot re-attach volumes (running instances continue until reboot). RDS: cannot restart (running instance continues until reboot). Secrets Manager: GetSecretValue fails. To restore access after incident cleared: re-enable CMK. <br><br> *Key design for incident response: CMK-per-data-classification approach: (1) `CMK-PUBLIC`: non-sensitive data (logs, metrics, configs). (2) `CMK-INTERNAL`: internal business data. (3) `CMK-CONFIDENTIAL`: PII, financial data. (4) `CMK-RESTRICTED`: credentials, keys, most sensitive. In incident: disable CMK-CONFIDENTIAL → all PII/financial data inaccessible. Other data continues functioning. Blast radius control: incidents affect only the relevant classification.* <br> *Alternative: CMK per environment. `CMK-PROD`, `CMK-STAGING`, `CMK-DEV`. Incident in production: disable CMK-PROD → only production data locked. Dev/staging continue. Never share CMKs across environments — incident response scope would be too broad. SCP: enforce CMK-per-environment via tagging conditions. Config rule: detect shared CMK usage across environments.* <br>

1299. [ Federation ] How does Cognito Identity Pool map authenticated users to IAM roles? What is the difference between basic and enhanced (simplified) authentication? ; Enhanced flow (recommended): app calls GetCredentialsForIdentity with OpenID token from IdP. Cognito internally calls STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. App receives final AWS credentials directly. Simpler (two steps instead of three). Role mapping in Identity Pool: (1) Default authenticated role (all authenticated users get this role). (2) Role mapping rules: match token claims to different roles. Example: if `custom:group = admin` in Cognito User Pool token → assume admin-role, if `custom:group = user` → assume user-role. (3) Token-based role mapping: embed IAM role ARN in Cognito User Pool custom attribute. Basic flow: app calls GetId → GetOpenIdToken → then calls STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity itself. More control, more code. <br><br> *Role selection rule priority: rules are evaluated in order. First match wins. If no rule matches: fall back to default role (or deny if no default). Rule example: `claim:cognito:groups CONTAINS "premium-users" → arn:aws:iam::123:role/PremiumUserRole`. Groups are set in Cognito User Pool group membership. User pool groups mapped to roles in Identity Pool.* <br> *Cross-account Identity Pool: Identity Pool in Account A, IAM roles in Account B. Identity Pool assumes role in Account B via cross-account role trust: trust policy allows `cognito-identity.amazonaws.com` as principal with condition `"cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud": "us-east-1:pool-id"`. User gets credentials for Account B role. Uncommon but possible for architectures where identity management and application resources are in different accounts.* <br>

1300. [ Athena ] What is Apache Iceberg on Athena and what problems does it solve compared to standard Hive tables? ; Apache Iceberg: open table format for large-scale analytics. Problems solved: (1) ACID transactions: Iceberg supports MERGE INTO, UPDATE, DELETE (standard Hive tables are immutable append-only). (2) Time travel: query historical versions of data (`SELECT * FROM table FOR TIMESTAMP AS OF 2024-01-01`). (3) Schema evolution: add/rename/drop columns without full table rewrite. (4) Partition evolution: change partitioning strategy without full table rewrite. (5) Automatic compaction: `OPTIMIZE table REWRITE DATA` merges small files. (6) Snapshot isolation: concurrent reads and writes without locking. <br><br> *Iceberg vs Delta Lake vs Hudi: Iceberg: Apache project, best multi-engine support (Athena, Spark, Flink, Trino). Delta Lake: Databricks-originated, excellent Spark integration, also supported in Athena. Hudi: Uber-originated, best for streaming upserts, excellent CDC (Change Data Capture) support. On Athena: all three are supported. Choice: Iceberg for general purpose, Hudi if primary use case is CDC/streaming upserts.* <br> *Iceberg compaction in Athena: `OPTIMIZE db.table REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK WHERE year=2024 AND month=10`. Merges small files in the specified partition into optimal size (128MB-1GB). Run after high-frequency streaming writes that create many small files. Schedule: daily compaction Glue job or Athena named query on schedule. Also: `VACUUM db.table` removes orphan files and expired snapshots to reduce S3 storage cost.* <br>

1301. [ KMS ] How do you implement key rotation for a CMK that was created with imported key material (BYOK)? ; Imported key material (origin=EXTERNAL) does NOT support automatic rotation. To rotate: (1) Generate new key material in your external HSM/key generator. (2) Call `ImportKeyMaterial` with the new key material to the SAME CMK (overwrite existing material). This changes the backing key while keeping the CMK ARN. Old material: gone (no automatic retention). OR: (3) Create a new CMK with new key material, re-encrypt all data keys from old CMK to new CMK using `ReEncrypt`. Delete old CMK after migration. <br><br> *Overwrite limitation: when overwriting imported key material, the old material is NOT retained. Unlike AWS-generated key rotation (old backing key kept for decryption), overwriting imported key material destroys the old material. Any ciphertext encrypted with the old material becomes permanently unreadable after overwrite. Must re-encrypt all existing ciphertext BEFORE overwriting key material.* <br> *Safe BYOK rotation process: (1) Create a NEW CMK with new imported key material. (2) Re-encrypt all DEKs from old CMK to new CMK using `ReEncrypt` API (batch operation for all S3 objects, EBS snapshots, etc.). (3) Update all services to use new CMK ARN. (4) Disable old CMK. (5) Verify no usage of old CMK (CloudWatch KMS metrics). (6) Schedule old CMK for deletion. This is the safe zero-data-loss rotation. Overwrite approach risks data loss if any ciphertext with old material is not migrated first.* <br>

1302. [ Federation ] A company wants to allow developers to access AWS resources from their laptops without storing AWS credentials in `~/.aws/credentials`. What are the options? ; Options: (1) IAM Identity Center + Okta SAML: `aws sso login` issues short-lived credentials, stored in `~/.aws/sso/cache/`. No permanent credentials in credentials file. (2) AWS IAM Identity Center alone (no external IdP): same `aws sso login` flow with built-in directory. (3) Roles Anywhere: x.509 certificates issued by corporate PKI, `aws_signing_helper` CLI tool exchanges certificate for STS credentials. For on-premises laptops not in cloud IdP. (4) OIDC with corporate IdP: custom CLI tool that authenticates via OIDC, calls STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. <br><br> *IAM Identity Center CLI workflow: `aws configure sso` → enter SSO start URL + region → browser opens for authentication → select account and role → CLI profile created. Daily use: `aws sso login --profile my-profile` (browser opens once) → all CLI commands use STS credentials from SSO session. Session duration: up to 12 hours (configurable in Identity Center). No permanent credentials stored, no rotation needed.* <br> *Roles Anywhere: for on-premises servers and laptops that cannot use EC2 instance profiles or Identity Center. Uses PKI certificates (issued by corporate CA). Certificate validity period = access period. Revoke certificate = revoke AWS access (no waiting for key rotation). AWS Roles Anywhere validator verifies certificate chain against a registered Trust Anchor (your corporate CA). STS returns temporary credentials valid 1hr-12hr. Useful for hybrid environments where some machines are outside AWS but need to call AWS APIs.* <br>

1303. [ Athena ] What is the Glue Data Catalog and how does it serve as the Hive Metastore for Athena? ; Glue Data Catalog: fully managed, serverless metadata repository storing: databases, tables (schema + location + SerDe + partition keys), partitions, column statistics, connections. Implements Hive Metastore API — tools compatible with Hive Metastore (EMR, Spark, Presto, Trino) can use Glue catalog directly. Athena queries Glue catalog to resolve table locations, schemas, and partitions before executing SQL. Schema updates: use `ALTER TABLE`, `CREATE TABLE`, Glue Crawlers, or Glue API. Cross-region: catalog is regional, tables reference S3 data which can be cross-region (but cross-region S3 access has latency and cost). <br><br> *Glue Data Catalog cross-account access: account A has Glue catalog with table pointing to S3 in account A. Account B Athena needs to query it. Configure: (1) S3 bucket policy allows Account B read access. (2) Glue catalog resource policy allows Account B `glue:GetDatabase`, `glue:GetTable`, `glue:GetPartitions`. (3) Account B Athena query specifies the cross-account catalog: `SELECT * FROM AwsDataCatalog_AccountA.database.table` (requires Athena Federated Query with Glue cross-account catalog configuration).* <br> *Lake Formation on top of Glue catalog: Lake Formation adds fine-grained access control on Glue catalog objects. Without Lake Formation: Athena user with `glue:GetTable` can see all tables. With Lake Formation: user only sees tables explicitly granted to them (table-level, column-level, row-level). Lake Formation replaces the IAM+S3 bucket policy model with centralized data lake permissions. Required for column-level and row-level security in Athena.* <br>

1304. [ KMS ] What is the difference between key deletion and key disabling in KMS? Can deleted keys be recovered? ; Disabled: key metadata retained, cryptographic operations blocked (KMSDisabledException), reversible (re-enable key → operations resume). All data encrypted with key becomes temporarily inaccessible. Key can be re-enabled at any time before deletion. Deleted: after the mandatory waiting period (7-30 days), the key is permanently destroyed. Key metadata, key material, all cryptographic capabilities permanently gone. Data encrypted solely with deleted key is permanently unrecoverable. AWS cannot recover deleted keys. No exceptions. <br><br> *Prevention of accidental deletion: (1) Disable first, monitor for 30 days, delete only if no alarms. (2) CloudWatch alarm on `kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion` API call → SNS alert → human review. (3) IAM policy: restrict `kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion` to key administrator role with MFA condition (`"Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}}`). (4) Require approval workflow (ServiceNow, Jira) before key deletion can be triggered. (5) Config rule: alert on CMK scheduled for deletion.* <br> *Waiting period configuration: `aws kms schedule-key-deletion --key-id arn:... --pending-window-in-days 30`. Maximum: 30 days (you cannot extend further). Minimum: 7 days (you cannot shorten). During waiting period: key is disabled. Cancellation: `aws kms cancel-key-deletion --key-id arn:...` → key returns to disabled state → manually re-enable. The waiting period is a safety net, not a time limit — you can cancel deletion any time before the period expires.* <br>

1305. [ Federation ] What is the STS regional endpoint and why should it be used instead of the global endpoint? ; Global endpoint `sts.amazonaws.com`: always routes to us-east-1. Single point of failure: if us-east-1 has an outage, all STS calls worldwide fail even if your workload is in eu-west-1. Regional endpoint `sts.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com`: routes to eu-west-1. Resilient: eu-west-1 outage does not affect us-east-1 STS. For CI/CD in Frankfurt: use `sts.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com`. Lower latency. AWS recommends regional endpoints for all new applications. <br><br> *Enabling regional endpoints: configure in IAM settings: `aws iam set-security-token-service-preferences --global-endpoint-token-version v2Token`. This enables STS v2 tokens (valid in all regions) instead of v1 tokens (global only). Once enabled, configure SDK to use regional endpoint: environment variable `AWS_STS_REGIONAL_ENDPOINTS=regional` or config file `sts_regional_endpoints = regional`. With this: AssumeRole calls go to the regional STS endpoint, not sts.amazonaws.com.* <br> *Token validation: STS v1 tokens (global endpoint) are only valid in the region where they were issued (actually valid everywhere but signed by global endpoint). STS v2 tokens (regional endpoint): valid in all regions. Migrating to regional STS: some older SDK versions do not support v2 tokens — upgrade SDKs first. AWS CLI v2: supports v2 tokens. Lambda: automatically uses regional STS (Lambda runtime configured appropriately). EC2 instance profiles: automatically regional.* <br>

1306. [ Athena ] How do you implement column-level security in Athena? ; Use AWS Lake Formation column-level permissions. In Lake Formation: grant SELECT on specific columns to specific IAM principals. Example: grant `user_id, timestamp, action` to analyst role, do not grant `ssn, credit_card_number`. When analyst queries the table in Athena: Lake Formation intercepts, modifies the query plan to exclude restricted columns. Analyst sees NULL (or column not visible) for restricted columns. Cannot bypass by using `SELECT *` — restricted columns return NULL. <br><br> *Lake Formation setup: (1) Register S3 data lake location with Lake Formation. (2) Create Lake Formation data permissions (replace S3 bucket policy model). (3) Grant TABLE permissions with specific columns listed. IAM principal must have both Lake Formation table-level permission and `glue:GetTable` (usually granted via Lake Formation). (4) Athena query: Lake Formation authorization middleware filters columns before Athena reads from S3.* <br> *Column masking (beyond column-level security): Lake Formation data filters can also implement column masking (show partial value, hash, or constant instead of actual value). Example: SSN column → show last 4 digits only. Credit card → mask to `****-****-****-1234`. Implemented via Lake Formation `DataFilter` with custom masking expression. Analysts see masked data (cannot reconstruct original), but data is still useful for analysis (last 4 digits for support tickets).* <br>

1307. [ KMS ] What is the purpose of the `kms:ViaService` condition key? Provide a usage example. ; `kms:ViaService` restricts CMK usage to specific AWS services. Value format: `service-name.region.amazonaws.com`. Example: allow KMS Decrypt only when called via S3 (`s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`). Key policy condition: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"kms:ViaService":"s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"}}`. Effect: the role can decrypt using this CMK ONLY when S3 is the calling service. Direct `kms:Decrypt` calls from the role (CLI, SDK) are denied. Prevents role from directly decrypting data outside the S3 context. <br><br> *Use case: application role needs to read S3 objects (S3 calls KMS Decrypt on behalf of the role). But you do not want the application to directly call KMS to decrypt arbitrary data. Key policy: `kms:ViaService = s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`. App role: (1) `s3:GetObject` on bucket → S3 calls KMS with ViaService=s3 → allowed. (2) Direct `kms:Decrypt` from app code → no ViaService (or ViaService != s3) → denied. The application can read S3 objects but cannot use the KMS key for anything else.* <br> *Combining ViaService with EncryptionContext: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"kms:ViaService":"s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com","kms:EncryptionContext:aws:s3:arn":"arn:aws:s3:::specific-bucket/*"}}`. This CMK can only be used by S3 (ViaService) AND only for objects in specific-bucket (EncryptionContext). Maximum restriction: even if the app role somehow compromises another bucket with the same CMK, the CMK cannot be used for that other bucket.* <br>

1308. [ Athena ] A company stores CloudTrail logs in S3 across 50 AWS accounts in an organization. How do you set up Athena to query all accounts centrally? ; Use Organization Trail (management account) delivering all logs to central S3 bucket. Create Athena table with partition projection including `account` as an enum partition: `projection.account.type=enum, projection.account.values=111111111111,222222222222,...`. Or: use `projection.account.type=injected` if querying specific accounts dynamically. Storage location template: `s3://central-bucket/AWSLogs/${account}/CloudTrail/${region}/${year}/${month}/${day}/`. Single Athena query scans selected accounts. <br><br> *Partition projection with enum for 50 accounts: list all 50 account IDs in `projection.account.values`. When querying with `WHERE account_id='"'"'111111111111'"'"'`: Athena scans only that account prefix. Without filter: scans all 50 account prefixes (all accounts). Combined partition filters: `WHERE account_id='"'"'111111111111'"'"' AND year='"'"'2024'"'"' AND month='"'"'11'"'"' AND region='"'"'eu-central-1'"'"'` → scans exactly one day of one account in one region. Extremely cost-effective for targeted investigations.* <br> *Cross-account read access: central S3 bucket (in security account) must allow Athena service role in analytics account to read. Bucket policy: allow `s3:GetObject` and `s3:ListBucket` to analytics account role. Alternative: deploy Athena in the security account itself (where bucket lives) — no cross-account S3 access needed. Lake Formation: register S3 bucket in Lake Formation in security account, share database via RAM (Resource Access Manager) to analytics account. Analytics account Athena can query the shared database without S3 policy management.* <br>

1309. [ KMS ] What is the maximum number of key versions (backing keys) KMS retains for an automatically-rotated CMK? ; AWS does not publish an explicit limit on retained backing key versions. AWS retains all prior backing key versions for the lifetime of the CMK — there is no expiry or deletion of old backing keys as long as the CMK exists. Even after 10+ years of annual rotation, all 10+ backing key versions are retained. Deleting the CMK deletes all backing key versions. This ensures any ciphertext ever created with the CMK can always be decrypted (within the CMK lifetime). <br><br> *Practical implication: even data encrypted with the very first key version (before any rotation) is still decryptable after 10 years of rotation. KMS determines which backing key version to use based on metadata in the ciphertext blob. The ciphertext contains a key ID and version identifier — KMS uses the correct backing key for decryption automatically.* <br> *Key version vs key alias: alias always points to the CMK ARN (not a specific backing key version). When you use an alias for encryption: uses the current (latest) backing key version. Decryption: uses whatever version is embedded in the ciphertext (automatically). No action needed from the application for key rotation — it is transparent.* <br>

1310. [ Athena ] What is the role of Snappy vs GZIP compression for Parquet files in Athena? ; Snappy: faster compression/decompression (CPU-efficient), lower compression ratio (~30-40% reduction), splittable within Parquet row groups. Default for Parquet. Use for: frequent query workloads (fast decompression reduces query latency). GZIP: slower compression/decompression, higher compression ratio (~60-70% reduction), more CPU at read time. Use for: cold data (rare queries, storage cost priority), or writing once and reading infrequently. ZSTD: best balance (GZIP-level ratio, near-Snappy speed). Recommended for Parquet v2+. <br><br> *Cost analysis: 1TB uncompressed JSON data. Parquet + Snappy: ~200-300GB on S3 ($5.50-8.25/month storage, $1-1.50/TB-scanned query cost). Parquet + GZIP: ~120-180GB on S3 ($3.30-4.95/month storage, $0.60-0.90/TB-scanned query cost). GZIP saves ~30-40% more storage but queries are 2x slower (decompression CPU). For a data lake queried hundreds of times/day: Snappy (lower latency, similar cost). For archive queried rarely: GZIP (lower storage cost dominates).* <br> *Parquet row group compression: Snappy and ZSTD are applied per row group (128MB default). Each row group is independently compressed. Athena workers decompress row groups in parallel. GZIP per row group: also splittable at row group boundaries (unlike GZIP on raw files). So for Parquet: any codec is effectively splittable at row group granularity. The "GZIP not splittable" limitation only applies to raw GZIP-compressed text files, not Parquet.* <br>

1311. [ KMS ] An EC2 instance profile role needs to use a KMS CMK in another account (cross-account). Walk through the complete setup. ; Account A (CMK account): (1) CMK key policy: add Account B instance role ARN as principal with `kms:Decrypt`, `kms:GenerateDataKey`, `kms:DescribeKey`. Account B (EC2 account): (2) EC2 instance profile IAM role: attach inline policy allowing `kms:Decrypt`, `kms:GenerateDataKey`, `kms:DescribeKey` on the Account A CMK ARN. Application: (3) Reference CMK by full ARN (`arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:ACCOUNT_A:key/key-id`) in SDK calls. Both the key policy (Account A) and IAM policy (Account B) must be configured. <br><br> *Testing cross-account KMS access: from EC2 in Account B: `aws kms describe-key --key-id arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:ACCOUNT_A:key/key-id`. If returns key metadata: DescribeKey works. Then: `aws kms generate-data-key --key-id arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:ACCOUNT_A:key/key-id --key-spec AES_256`. If returns encrypted DEK: full access working. If AccessDenied: check both key policy in Account A AND IAM policy in Account B.* <br> *Common issue: IAM policy uses `"Resource":"*"` for KMS (allowing all KMS keys) but the key policy in Account A does NOT include the Account B role. Result: IAM policy allows, key policy denies → AccessDenied. Both must explicitly allow. Conversely: key policy in Account A allows Account B root → Account B can now use IAM to control access, but if Account B IAM policy restricts KMS to specific keys and the ARN is wrong → AccessDenied. Verify ARN in both policies is identical.* <br>

1312. [ Athena ] What is the minimum recommended file size for Parquet files in Athena and why? ; Recommended: 128MB to 1GB per Parquet file. Too small (< 10MB): excessive S3 ListObjects API calls + per-file overhead (open S3 file, read Parquet footer metadata, process row groups). 1,000 × 1MB files vs 1 × 1GB file: same data but 1,000× more S3 API calls. Too large (> 1GB): insufficient parallelism if file count < available Presto workers. Also: re-processing a 10GB file for a small fix requires reading the entire file. Optimal: 128MB-1GB, enough row groups for parallel processing, manageable file count. <br><br> *Kinesis Firehose optimal configuration: buffer size = 128MB, buffer interval = 15 minutes (whichever comes first). At high volume: 128MB hits first → file written. At low volume: 15 minutes hits first → file written (smaller than 128MB, acceptable). Dynamic partitioning: Firehose can partition records by a field value (e.g., region, customer_id) into separate S3 prefixes. Combined with 128MB buffer: each partition gets its own Firehose stream, each target file is ~128MB.* <br> *Compaction strategy for existing small files: (1) Athena CTAS: `CREATE TABLE compacted_table WITH (external_location='"'"'s3://new/location/'"'"', format='"'"'PARQUET'"'"') AS SELECT * FROM fragmented_table WHERE year=2024 AND month=10`. This reads all small files in the partition and writes optimally-sized files to new location. (2) Glue ETL DynamicFrame repartition: `df.repartition(N)` then write to S3. (3) Apache Iceberg OPTIMIZE: `OPTIMIZE table REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK WHERE ...`. Choose based on: Iceberg = schema flexibility, CTAS = simplest for Hive tables, Glue = most control over output.* <br>

1313. [ KMS ] What are AWS KMS condition keys and how are they used in key policies? ; KMS condition keys are IAM condition keys specific to KMS operations. Key condition keys: `kms:ViaService` (restrict to specific AWS service), `kms:EncryptionContext:key` (enforce specific encryption context), `kms:EncryptionContextKeys` (enforce context key presence), `kms:CallerAccount` (restrict to specific account), `kms:KeyOrigin` (EXTERNAL/AWS_KMS/AWS_CLOUDHSM), `kms:KeySpec` (SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT/RSA_*), `kms:DataKeyPairSpec` (for GenerateDataKeyPair), `kms:GrantConstraintType`, `kms:RequestAlias`. <br><br> *Practical examples: (1) Only allow CMK usage from specific region: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"kms:ViaService":"s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com"}}` — prevents CMK from being used in other regions via S3. (2) Enforce specific application context: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"kms:EncryptionContext:AppName":"MyApp"}}` — only MyApp can use this CMK (other apps passing different context = denied). (3) Enforce caller account: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"kms:CallerAccount":"123456789012"}}` — CMK only usable from specific account (even if cross-account access granted, other accounts denied).* <br> *RequestAlias: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"kms:RequestAlias":"alias/production-cmk"}}`. IAM policy allows using the CMK only when referenced by this specific alias (not by key ID or other aliases). Use case: IAM policy allows encryption operations, condition enforces that production CMK is used (not dev CMK). The alias ensures the right key is used for the right environment.* <br>

1314. [ Athena ] What is Partition Projection with injected type? When is it used? ; Injected type: partition value is NOT pre-defined in the projection configuration — instead the value is injected at query time from the WHERE clause. The projection has no range or enum, just a template. Use case: partitions where the set of values is large/unknown (customer IDs, random UUIDs, account numbers). DDL: `'projection.customer_id.type' = 'injected'`. Query: `WHERE customer_id = '12345'` → Athena resolves the path from template: `s3://bucket/data/customer_id=12345/`. Without the filter on customer_id: query fails (injected partition requires explicit filter). <br><br> *Injected vs enum vs integer: enum = fixed list (`us-east-1,eu-west-1`) — list all values. Integer = range (`1 to 1000`). Injected = any value — filter required. Injected partition must always have a WHERE clause filter. Useful for: customer-partitioned data (millions of customer IDs), device-partitioned IoT data (thousands of device IDs), where you never want to scan all partitions (full scan = all customers = expensive).* <br> *Combining projection types: `year=integer(2020,2030)`, `month=integer(1,12)`, `customer_id=injected`. Query: `WHERE year=2024 AND month=10 AND customer_id='"'"'ABC123'"'"'`. Athena computes path: `s3://bucket/year=2024/month=10/customer_id=ABC123/`. Zero catalog lookups, zero MSCK calls, queries are always correct. Required filter enforced: if customer_id not specified → query error (prevents accidental full-customer-base scans).* <br>

1315. [ KMS ] What happens when you try to use a KMS CMK from a different region? ; Error: `InvalidKeyId` or `KMSInvalidStateException`. KMS keys are regional resources. A key in us-east-1 (`arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123:key/xxx`) cannot be used in eu-west-1. AWS SDK regional endpoint routing: if your application is in eu-west-1 and calls KMS with a us-east-1 key ARN, the SDK routes to eu-west-1 KMS endpoint which returns an error (key does not exist in eu-west-1). Solution: (1) Create separate CMK in each region. (2) Use Multi-Region Key (primary + replica, same key ID, usable in both regions). <br><br> *Cross-region replication scenario: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) with SSE-KMS. S3 objects in us-east-1 encrypted with us-east-1 CMK. CRR replicates to eu-west-1. S3 must re-encrypt the object in eu-west-1 (cannot use us-east-1 CMK). CRR configuration: specify a KMS key for the destination region (eu-west-1 CMK or Multi-Region Key replica). S3 CRR: decrypts with source CMK (us-east-1), re-encrypts with destination CMK (eu-west-1). The destination bucket uses the eu-west-1 CMK for ongoing reads.* <br> *Multi-Region Key for global S3: create Multi-Region Key in us-east-1 (primary), create replica in eu-west-1. S3 buckets in both regions use the Multi-Region Key (same key ID: `mrk-xxx`). CRR: S3 can use the same key ID in both regions — no separate destination key needed. Objects encrypted in us-east-1 with mrk-xxx, replicated to eu-west-1, readable with the eu-west-1 replica (same key material). Simplifies multi-region key management.* <br>

1316. [ Athena ] What is the Athena pricing model for CTAS and INSERT INTO operations? ; CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT): charged on data scanned from the SOURCE table (same as SELECT). Writing to S3 (the output): not charged by Athena. INSERT INTO: charged on data scanned from the source SELECT. Output writes: not charged. DDL operations (CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, ALTER TABLE): free, no charge. Minimum charge per query: 10MB. If CTAS source scans 1TB Parquet: $5. If CTAS source scans 0 bytes (inserting hardcoded values): charged minimum 10MB ($0.000048). <br><br> *Cost optimization for CTAS: use partition filters on the source query to minimize scanned data. Example: `CREATE TABLE monthly_parquet ... AS SELECT * FROM daily_json WHERE year='"'"'2024'"'"' AND month='"'"'10'"'"'` — scans only October data (if partitioned). Without filter: scans all historical data. For iterative format conversion: process one month at a time (multiple CTAS queries, each scanning only the target month). Cheaper than one massive CTAS and allows parallel processing.* <br> *S3 write cost for CTAS: Athena writes results to S3 standard storage (PUTs). For 1TB output: ~300GB compressed Parquet. S3 PUT cost: $0.005/1,000 requests × (300GB / 128MB per file) ≈ $0.012 for PUT requests. Storage: $0.023/GB × 300GB = $6.90/month. Query cost ($5) + write cost (negligible) + storage ($6.90/month ongoing). For one-time format migration: CTAS is cost-effective, ongoing storage is the primary cost.* <br>

1317. [ KMS ] Compare the security implications of using one shared CMK for all services vs one CMK per service. ; Shared CMK: (1) Cost: $1/month vs $N/month. (2) Blast radius: if CMK is disabled/deleted, ALL services lose access simultaneously. (3) Audit: CloudTrail mixes operations from all services in one key log. (4) Access control: key policy must allow all services → broader permissions. (5) Revocation: cannot selectively revoke access for one service without affecting others. Per-service CMK: opposite — higher cost, smaller blast radius, clean audit per service, minimal key policy, selective revocation. <br><br> *Recommended approach: at minimum, one CMK per data classification level (public, internal, confidential, restricted) rather than one per service. This balances cost vs blast radius. For high-value services (Secrets Manager, RDS with PII): dedicated CMK. For lower-value services (CloudWatch Logs, non-sensitive S3 buckets): shared CMK by classification.* <br> *Selective revocation use case: incident response — attacker compromised application EC2 instance. Application role has access to CMK used for S3, RDS, and Secrets Manager. With shared CMK: disabling it breaks ALL three services (S3 inaccessible, RDS cannot restart, Secrets Manager broken).
