With per-service CMKs: disable only the S3 and application-specific CMK → isolate the incident to the compromised service without breaking the RDS database used by other healthy services.* <br>

1318. [ Federation ] What is Azure AD External Identities and how does it compare to AWS Cognito User Pools for B2C scenarios? ; Azure AD External Identities (B2C): Microsoft identity platform for customer-facing apps. Supports social login (Google, Facebook, Apple), email/password, custom identity providers. Issues tokens (OIDC/OAuth). Customizable sign-in flows (user journeys/policies). Azure AD B2C tenant: separate from corporate Azure AD tenant. Compare to AWS Cognito User Pools: similar feature set (social login, sign-up flows, MFA, JWT tokens). Cognito: tighter AWS integration (ALB, API Gateway, Amplify), simpler for pure AWS workloads. Azure AD B2C: better for Microsoft-ecosystem apps (Power Apps, Azure API Management), familiar for organizations already using Microsoft identity. <br><br> *Integration with AWS: Azure AD B2C → OIDC → API Gateway Lambda authorizer (validate Azure AD B2C JWT). Azure AD B2C → Cognito Identity Pool (OIDC provider) → temporary AWS credentials → S3/DynamoDB. Same pattern as Auth0/Google — Azure AD B2C is just another OIDC provider. AWS-side configuration: create OIDC Identity Provider in IAM pointing to Azure AD B2C tenant OIDC discovery URL.* <br> *Choosing between providers: pure AWS stack, app deployed on ECS/Lambda → Cognito User Pools (native integration, Amplify support). Multi-cloud or existing Azure investment → Azure AD B2C. Best-of-breed CIAM features (advanced bot detection, multi-tenant B2B) → Auth0 (Okta CIC). Google-workspace enterprise → Google Identity Platform. All can integrate with AWS via OIDC or SAML. The choice is primarily driven by existing enterprise platforms and CIAM feature requirements, not AWS compatibility.* <br>

1319. [ Athena ] What is Athena query result reuse (caching) and what are its limitations? ; Result reuse: if an identical query was run within the last 7 days in the same workgroup, Athena returns the cached result without re-scanning data. Identical = same SQL text (case-sensitive, whitespace-sensitive), same database/workgroup. Cost: zero (no data scanning charge for cached results). Enable: workgroup setting "Enable result reuse" with max age (1 minute to 7 days). Limitations: (1) New data in S3 partitions is NOT reflected in cached results. (2) Cache is per-workgroup (not cross-workgroup). (3) Adding a space or changing case invalidates cache. (4) User-specific queries (WHERE user_id=? with parameterized value) have different cache entries per user. <br><br> *Cache staleness: if data is updated hourly and cache max-age is 24 hours, analysts see 24-hour-old results. For dashboards: accept staleness (set 15-minute cache for near-real-time experience). For real-time analytics: disable caching (every query re-scans). For daily reports (data does not change): 24-hour cache is perfect.* <br> *BI tool interaction with caching: QuickSight SPICE + Athena result reuse: SPICE refresh runs one Athena query per dataset per schedule. Caching does not help (SPICE refresh always wants fresh data). But: 50 QuickSight users drilling into the same SPICE dataset → no Athena calls (SPICE serves all queries in-memory). Athena caching helps when: direct Athena queries from multiple users (Jupyter notebooks, SQL clients) run the same analytics repeatedly.* <br>

1320. [ KMS ] How does AWS Secrets Manager use KMS? What is the difference between using AWS Managed Key vs CMK for secrets? ; Secrets Manager uses KMS to encrypt secret values at rest. AWS Managed Key (aws/secretsmanager): free, automatic, no configuration. CloudTrail logs `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` (Secrets Manager API calls) but not the individual KMS operations. CMK: customer-controlled, $1/month, CloudTrail logs BOTH the Secrets Manager API call AND the KMS Decrypt call (full audit trail). Cross-account secret access requires CMK (AWS Managed Key cannot be shared cross-account). <br><br> *Cross-account secrets: Account A has RDS password in Secrets Manager. Account B Lambda needs the password. With AWS Managed Key: cross-account access impossible (cannot share aws/secretsmanager key). Solution: create CMK in Account A, re-create secret using CMK. Key policy: allow Account B role. Secret resource policy: allow Account B role GetSecretValue. Account B Lambda: allow kms:Decrypt on Account A CMK ARN + allow secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on Account A secret ARN. Three policies required.* <br> *Secrets Manager rotation + KMS: when Secrets Manager rotates a secret (Lambda rotation function creates new password in RDS, updates secret value), the new secret value is encrypted with the same CMK (or AWS Managed Key). The rotation does not change the KMS key — only the secret content changes. If CMK is disabled: rotation FAILS (cannot encrypt the new secret value). Always ensure the CMK used by Secrets Manager is enabled and healthy, especially during rotation windows.* <br>

1321. [ Athena ] How does Athena Federated Query handle connectivity to on-premises databases? ; On-premises database connectivity: deploy the Athena JDBC Lambda connector (or custom connector) in a VPC with connectivity to on-premises (via Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN). Lambda function runs in the VPC, accesses on-premises database via the private network. Athena invokes the VPC Lambda → Lambda queries on-premises DB → returns results to Athena. Security: database credentials stored in Secrets Manager, referenced by Lambda connector. VPC security groups control Lambda access to on-premises IP ranges. <br><br> *Network requirements: Lambda in VPC → Security Group allows outbound on DB port (e.g., 1521 for Oracle, 5432 for PostgreSQL) to on-premises CIDR range. On-premises firewall: allows inbound on DB port from Lambda subnet CIDR. VPC: has Direct Connect or VPN attachment to on-premises network. Lambda in private subnet (no internet route needed — Direct Connect provides on-premises connectivity). VPC endpoints for Athena, Lambda, Secrets Manager: Lambda can call these AWS services without internet.* <br> *Performance considerations: each Athena query that hits the federated source invokes Lambda. Lambda cold start: ~500ms. Query latency: on-premises DB query time + Lambda invocation overhead + network round-trip (DX latency). For a query joining S3 (fast) with on-premises Oracle (slow): the on-premises side is the bottleneck. Push as much filtering as possible to the connector (predicate pushdown) to minimize the data transferred from Oracle to Lambda to Athena. Not suitable for interactive dashboards with 1-second latency requirements.* <br>

1322. [ KMS ] Summarize the most common KMS exam traps and their correct answers. ; (1) "Customer-generated key material" → CMK with BYOK (origin=EXTERNAL), NOT CloudHSM. (2) "Keys never accessible to AWS" → CloudHSM, NOT standard KMS. (3) "Cross-account S3 bucket with CMK" → key policy in source account + IAM policy in target account + S3 bucket policy. Three policies. (4) "Key rotation breaks existing data" → FALSE. Old backing key retained, existing data always decryptable. (5) "Delete CMK immediately" → impossible, 7-day minimum waiting period. (6) "AWS Managed Key can be shared cross-account" → FALSE, only CMK can be cross-account. <br><br> *(7) "Asymmetric CMK for S3 SSE-KMS" → fails, S3 SSE-KMS requires symmetric key. (8) "IAM policy alone grants KMS access" → insufficient without root principal in key policy. (9) "Key alias can be used in all IAM conditions" → almost everywhere, but ARN is more specific for cross-account. (10) "Rotation re-encrypts existing data" → FALSE, only new data uses new backing key. (11) "RDS CMK can be changed after creation" → FALSE, must set CMK at RDS creation, cannot change on existing instance (must use snapshot + restore with new CMK). (12) "AWS Owned Keys appear in KMS console" → FALSE, invisible to customer.* <br> *(13) "S3 Bucket Key works with AWS Owned Keys" → FALSE, Bucket Key requires SSE-KMS (AWS Managed or CMK). (14) "Multi-Region Key makes API calls cross-region" → FALSE, each replica is in its own region, API calls are regional. (15) "Disabling a CMK deletes key material" → FALSE, key material retained, just disabled. Re-enable restores access. (16) "KMS Encrypt can encrypt 1GB file" → FALSE, 4KB limit, use GenerateDataKey + local AES. (17) "Grant requires key policy modification" → FALSE, grants are independent of key policy.* <br>

1323. [ ACM ] A company has an ALB in eu-central-1 and a CloudFront distribution fronting it. They provision an ACM certificate in eu-central-1. When they attach it to CloudFront, the certificate is not available. Why? ; ACM certificates for CloudFront MUST be provisioned in us-east-1, not the region where the origin (ALB) is located. CloudFront is a global service and only looks for certificates in us-east-1. The eu-central-1 cert cannot be used with CloudFront regardless of where the origin is. Solution: provision a second ACM certificate in us-east-1 for CloudFront, keep the eu-central-1 cert for the ALB. <br><br> *This is the most common ACM exam trap. CloudFront is a globally distributed service — its certificate management is centralized in us-east-1. The ALB in eu-central-1 uses a regional cert correctly. CloudFront requires a separate cert in us-east-1. Result: two ACM certs for one application — one in us-east-1 (CloudFront), one in the ALB region.* <br> *The same rule applies to API Gateway Edge-Optimized type: Edge-Optimized API Gateway routes through CloudFront infrastructure internally, so its custom domain cert must also be in us-east-1. Regional API Gateway uses a cert in its own region. This is why API Gateway type selection impacts certificate placement requirements.* <br>

1324. [ ACM ] A company wants to install an ACM public certificate directly on an EC2 instance web server (nginx/Apache). Can they do this? ; No. ACM public certificates cannot be exported — the private key never leaves ACM. ACM public certs can only be used with integrated AWS services: ALB, NLB (TLS listener), CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync, Elastic Beanstalk. To install a cert directly on EC2, options are: (1) Import a third-party certificate (with private key) into ACM and use an ALB in front of EC2. (2) Use Let's Encrypt (certbot) directly on the EC2 instance. (3) Use ACM Private CA to issue a private cert (exportable) for the EC2. <br><br> *The non-exportable design is intentional security. AWS keeps the private key in its managed infrastructure so it cannot be stolen from an EC2 instance. For EC2-direct TLS: use an ALB in front (terminating TLS at ALB with ACM cert) rather than TLS on the EC2 itself. This is the recommended architecture anyway — ALB provides health checks, scaling, WAF integration.* <br> *ACM Private CA certs ARE exportable (you can download the cert and private key). This is why Private CA costs money ($400/CA/month) — it provides full PKI functionality including private key export. For IoT devices, on-premises servers, or applications that need the private key directly, ACM Private CA is the solution.* <br>

1325. [ ACM ] A security team requires that all internal microservices authenticate each other via mutual TLS (mTLS). What AWS services implement this? ; ACM Private CA issues client and server certificates. For ALB mTLS: configure the ALB HTTPS listener with mutual authentication, upload a trust store (CA bundle from ACM Private CA) to an S3 bucket, ALB validates client certificates on every connection. For API Gateway mTLS: upload truststore to S3, configure custom domain with mTLS. For application-level mTLS: export certs from ACM Private CA, install on application servers, configure TLS client authentication in application code or service mesh. <br><br> *ALB mTLS flow: client sends TLS ClientHello → ALB requests client certificate → client presents cert → ALB validates against trust store (ACM Private CA CA cert) → if valid: connection established, ALB passes X-Amzn-Mtls-Clientcert-Subject header to target. If invalid: ALB returns 400/403. Application can extract identity from the forwarded header.* <br> *AWS App Mesh with mTLS: automated mTLS for ECS/EKS microservices. Envoy sidecars handle TLS — application code does not need TLS configuration. ACM Private CA issues certs for each service. App Mesh Envoy automatically rotates certs. This is zero-code mTLS for service meshes. Much simpler than manual mTLS implementation.* <br>

1326. [ ACM ] What is DNS validation vs email validation in ACM? Which is recommended and why? ; DNS validation: ACM provides a CNAME record to add to your DNS zone. ACM verifies domain ownership by querying this CNAME. Persistent: ACM auto-renews by re-checking the CNAME — no action required from you. Recommended. Email validation: ACM sends email to WHOIS registrant contacts (admin@, hostmaster@, etc.) with a validation link. Must be clicked within 72 hours. Requires manual action on every renewal. Not recommended for production (renewal failure if email missed = cert expiry = outage). <br><br> *DNS validation requirement: you need control over the DNS zone. If using Route 53: ACM can automatically create the CNAME record (one-click validation in console). For external DNS providers (GoDaddy, Cloudflare): manually add the CNAME provided by ACM. Once added, it persists — no further action needed for any number of renewals.* <br> *Email validation use case: when you do not control the DNS zone (e.g., requesting cert for a domain managed by another team or department). But be warned: for production systems, cert expiry due to missed renewal email is a real operational risk. Always prefer DNS validation when DNS zone access is available.* <br>

1327. [ CloudHSM ] A financial institution must comply with a regulation stating that encryption keys must be stored exclusively in hardware under the customer's control, with no possibility of AWS accessing the keys. Which solution satisfies this requirement? ; AWS CloudHSM. CloudHSM provides dedicated HSM appliances in the customer's VPC. AWS provisions and maintains the hardware, but has NO access to key material — keys are managed exclusively by the customer using customer-managed HSM credentials. AWS cannot retrieve, export, or use the keys. KMS (even with BYOK/external key material) does NOT satisfy this requirement because KMS HSMs are shared infrastructure managed by AWS. <br><br> *KMS and customer trust: AWS KMS is FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated and has extensive access controls. However, from a regulatory/contractual standpoint, KMS HSMs are AWS-managed. For regulations that require "customer-exclusive control" or "key material never accessible to the cloud provider," only CloudHSM satisfies. This is common in: regulated financial services (certain OCC guidance), government (FedRAMP High), healthcare with specific BAA requirements.* <br> *CloudHSM is significantly more expensive (~$1,044/month minimum for 2 HSMs) and operationally complex (customer manages HSM user credentials, backup procedures, cluster management). CloudHSM as KMS custom key store: you can configure KMS to use CloudHSM as the backing key store, getting KMS API simplicity with CloudHSM key custody. Best of both worlds for services that integrate with KMS but need CloudHSM custody.* <br>

1328. [ CloudHSM ] What is the difference between CloudHSM as a standalone service vs CloudHSM as a KMS custom key store? ; Standalone CloudHSM: applications use CloudHSM directly via PKCS#11, JCE, or CNG APIs. No KMS API. Requires application code changes to use CloudHSM SDK. CloudHSM as KMS custom key store: CloudHSM cluster connected to KMS. KMS API calls (Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey) performed, but key material stored and crypto operations executed in CloudHSM. All AWS services that integrate with KMS (S3 SSE-KMS, EBS, RDS, Secrets Manager) work unchanged — they call KMS API, KMS delegates to CloudHSM. <br><br> *Custom key store benefit: AWS services (EBS, S3, RDS) do not natively support CloudHSM. They only support KMS. Custom key store bridges this gap: EBS volume encrypted "with KMS CMK" but the actual key is in CloudHSM. Compliance requirement: keys in CloudHSM. Operational requirement: EBS encryption. Solution: custom key store satisfies both.* <br> *Custom key store limitation: KMS operations are synchronous calls to CloudHSM — latency is higher than standard KMS (CloudHSM network round-trip added). Performance: standard KMS ~5ms, custom key store ~20-50ms per crypto operation. For high-throughput applications: test performance before committing. Also: if all CloudHSM cluster HSMs are unavailable, KMS custom key store operations fail — KMS cannot fall back to software HSMs.* <br>

1329. [ Config ] A company wants to automatically detect and remediate whenever an S3 bucket has "Block Public Access" disabled. What is the architecture? ; AWS Config managed rule `s3-bucket-level-public-access-prohibited`. When non-compliant: Config triggers remediation action using SSM Automation document `AWS-DisableS3BucketPublicReadWrite` (or custom SSM document to re-enable Block Public Access). Configure remediation: auto-remediation = true, retry on failure. Result: S3 bucket public access disabled → Config detects non-compliant within minutes → SSM Automation re-enables Block Public Access automatically. <br><br> *Config evaluation timing: resource change triggers evaluation immediately. Periodic evaluation (every 1/3/6/12/24 hours) catches resources that changed without triggering Config. For S3: Config evaluates on bucket creation and on any S3 bucket policy/ACL change. Auto-remediation maximum: 5 automatic retries per 24-hour period per resource.* <br> *SSM Automation remediation requires: (1) Config must have an IAM role with permission to invoke SSM Automation. (2) SSM Automation document must have an IAM role with permission to modify S3 (s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock). Least-privilege: Config IAM role allows only ssm:StartAutomationExecution. SSM Automation role allows only s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock. Two separate IAM roles.* <br>

1330. [ Config ] What is the difference between AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail? A company asks which service to use to answer: "What was the configuration of this security group last Tuesday?" ; AWS Config. Config records the configuration state of resources at specific points in time and shows the configuration timeline. For "what did this security group look like last Tuesday": Config console → security group resource → Configuration Timeline → select date → view inbound/outbound rules at that point in time. CloudTrail shows WHAT API calls were made (who called AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress), not what the resulting configuration state was. <br><br> *Config vs CloudTrail mental model: Config = "snapshot camera" — takes pictures of resource state at each change. CloudTrail = "security camera" — records every action (API call). To answer "what was the config": use Config timeline (snapshots). To answer "who changed it and when": use CloudTrail (API audit log). Both complement each other: Config shows WHAT the state was, CloudTrail shows WHO/WHEN/WHY it changed.* <br> *Config timeline can reconstruct the exact resource state at any past time. For compliance audits: "prove this security group only allowed port 443 during Q3 2026." Config timeline → export resource configuration history → show inbound rules for each time period. This is only possible if Config was enabled at the time. Enable Config at account creation — cannot reconstruct past history retroactively.* <br>

1331. [ Config ] A company has 200 AWS accounts in an organization. They want a centralized compliance dashboard showing which accounts violate the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. What is the architecture? ; Security Hub with CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark standard + Config aggregator. (1) Enable Config in all accounts (required for Security Hub standards). (2) Enable Security Hub with Organizations — delegated admin in Security account. (3) Enable CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark standard in Security Hub. (4) Security Hub runs Config-based compliance checks against CIS controls in all accounts. (5) Security account Security Hub dashboard shows compliance score and non-compliant resources per account. <br><br> *Why both Config and Security Hub: Security Hub security standards use Config rules to evaluate controls. Config must be enabled in each account for Security Hub to run these checks. Config records resource states → Security Hub evaluates them against CIS controls → compliance findings. Without Config: Security Hub cannot run configuration-based standards (it can still aggregate GuardDuty/Macie threat findings).* <br> *Config aggregator separately: Config aggregator in the security account provides raw config data for all accounts. This allows custom Athena queries on resource configuration across all accounts. Security Hub provides the compliance framework layer on top. Together: Config aggregator = raw data lake, Security Hub = compliance scoring and finding management.* <br>

1332. [ GuardDuty ] An EC2 instance starts generating DNS queries to domain names with high entropy (e.g., `a3f8k2mxp9z.malicious.com`). GuardDuty generates a finding. What type of finding and what is the likely cause? ; Finding: `Trojan:EC2/DNSDataExfiltration` or `CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS`. High-entropy subdomain queries are characteristic of Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) malware — malware generates random domain names to find C2 servers, or DNS tunneling (data exfiltration encoded in DNS queries). GuardDuty detects this via DNS log analysis using ML models trained on malicious domain patterns. <br><br> *DNS tunneling: attacker encodes data in DNS query labels (max 253 chars per DNS name). Data exfiltrated: `c2VjcmV0ZGF0YQ==.c2.evil.com` (base64 encoded in subdomain). DNS response carries data back. Bypasses many firewalls (DNS port 53 usually allowed). GuardDuty detects via: high query frequency, high entropy subdomains, query length distribution analysis.* <br> *Response: isolate the EC2 instance (modify SG to block all outbound except security team access). Capture memory and disk forensics. Analyze what process is generating the DNS queries. Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall: add the malicious domain pattern to a deny list. Network Firewall Suricata rule: block DNS queries matching high-entropy subdomain pattern. GuardDuty finding → EventBridge → Lambda → automatically isolate instance (SG modification) + snapshot EBS.* <br>

1333. [ GuardDuty ] GuardDuty is enabled in all 50 accounts of an organization. A developer in a member account disables GuardDuty in their account. What happens? ; When GuardDuty is managed by a delegated administrator (via Organizations), member accounts CANNOT disable GuardDuty. The delegated admin centrally controls GuardDuty enrollment. Member account: the GuardDuty console shows the service as managed by the administrator — no disable option. If the developer tries via CLI/API: `aws guardduty delete-detector --detector-id xxx` → Access Denied (Organizations service control prevents it). <br><br> *This is a key multi-account security architecture principle. Member accounts enrolled via Organizations delegated admin lose the ability to disable security monitoring services. GuardDuty, Security Hub, Config, Macie — all can be centrally locked via Organizations delegated admin. The security team in the security account maintains full control.* <br> *Complementary SCP: `"Effect":"Deny","Action":["guardduty:DeleteDetector","guardduty:DisassociateFromMasterAccount","guardduty:StopMonitoringMembers"]` in root OU SCP. Belt-and-suspenders: (1) GuardDuty delegated admin prevents disable via GuardDuty API. (2) SCP prevents disable via Organizations. Two independent controls. If the GuardDuty API enforcement fails for any reason, SCP still blocks.* <br>

1334. [ GuardDuty ] What is the difference between GuardDuty Malware Protection and Amazon Inspector? ; GuardDuty Malware Protection: scans EBS volumes of EC2 instances that have ALREADY triggered a GuardDuty finding (e.g., suspicious network activity). Reactive — triggered by behavioral threat detection. Scans for known malware (trojan files, ransomware, cryptocurrency miners). Amazon Inspector: proactive vulnerability scanning — continuously scans EC2 AMIs/instances, Lambda functions, and container images for known CVEs (software vulnerabilities). Does NOT detect behavioral threats. Not triggered by GuardDuty findings — runs on schedule. <br><br> *Combined workflow: Inspector finds CVE-2024-XXXX in a library on EC2 → alerts (not an active attack, just a vulnerability). Patch the library. GuardDuty detects EC2 connecting to C2 server → Malware Protection scan triggered → malware found on EBS → finding escalated. Two different detection patterns: Inspector = "you have a door that could be kicked in." GuardDuty = "someone is trying to kick your door in right now."* <br> *Inspector finding output: CVE ID, severity (CVSS score), affected package, fixed version, remediation guidance. Feeds to Security Hub. GuardDuty Malware Protection finding: malware family (e.g., Trojan:Script/Mimikatz), file path on EBS, hash, action (quarantine). Combined: Security Hub aggregates both finding types for holistic security posture.* <br>

1335. [ Macie ] A company discovers they have been storing customer PII (social security numbers) in S3 buckets without encryption or access controls. They need to identify ALL buckets with SSNs and classify their sensitivity. Which service and configuration? ; Amazon Macie with automated sensitive data discovery. Enable Macie in the account (or org-wide via Organizations). Enable automated sensitive data discovery — Macie continuously samples objects across ALL S3 buckets. Macie has a built-in managed data identifier for US Social Security Numbers (`USA_SOCIAL_SECURITY_NUMBER`). Sensitive data findings generated for each S3 object containing SSNs. Macie also generates policy findings for unencrypted or publicly accessible buckets. <br><br> *Automated sensitive data discovery vs on-demand jobs: automated discovery = continuous, samples across all buckets (cost-effective for discovery phase). On-demand job = targeted scan of specific buckets/prefixes (full scan, higher cost). For initial discovery across many buckets: automated discovery. For deep compliance scan of known sensitive buckets: on-demand job with 100% sampling.* <br> *Response workflow: Macie finding `SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal` → EventBridge rule → Lambda: (1) Tag the S3 object with `DataClassification=PII`. (2) Move object to encrypted bucket with restrictive access. (3) Alert compliance team. (4) Generate compliance report. Macie finding `Policy:IAMUser/S3BucketPubliclyAccessible` → separate Lambda: enable S3 Block Public Access, send alert to bucket owner.* <br>

1336. [ Control Tower ] A company sets up a new AWS environment using Control Tower. A developer then manually adds a custom SCP to the root OU in AWS Organizations. What problem does this cause? ; Control Tower drift. Control Tower manages specific SCPs and Config rules. Manually adding SCPs to the root OU outside Control Tower can conflict with Control Tower's managed guardrails and causes Control Tower to report drift. In worst case: the manually added SCP may conflict with existing Control Tower guardrails — breaking account vending or compliance monitoring. Solution: use Customizations for Control Tower (CfCT) to add custom SCPs through Control Tower's approved mechanism. <br><br> *Drift detection: Control Tower periodically checks that its managed SCPs, Config rules, and IAM roles match expected state. Drift = difference detected. Control Tower console shows drift status per OU/account. Remediation: "Repair" button in Control Tower re-applies its managed configuration, potentially overwriting conflicting manual changes.* <br> *CfCT (Customizations for Control Tower): CodePipeline-driven solution that applies custom SCPs and CloudFormation StackSets through Control Tower. Custom SCP defined in CfCT config → CodePipeline applies it → Control Tower aware of it → no drift. For organizations needing custom guardrails beyond Control Tower defaults: CfCT is the correct mechanism. Direct Organizations console changes = bypass Control Tower = drift.* <br>

1337. [ Control Tower ] A company wants to vend new AWS accounts automatically whenever a developer team requests one via a ServiceNow ticket. What architecture enables this? ; Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) + ServiceNow integration. ServiceNow ticket approved → webhook → API Gateway → Lambda → calls AFT Terraform pipeline (via CodePipeline in the AFT management account) → AFT vends new account with pre-configured settings (Control Tower enrolled, Identity Center access, Config enabled, baseline SCPs applied). Or: Service Catalog Account Factory (non-Terraform) with ServiceNow API integration for catalog item ordering. <br><br> *AFT account request: a Git commit to the AFT account-requests repository triggers the pipeline. The commit contains account definition (account name, email, OU, tags). Lambda (called from ServiceNow webhook) creates the Git commit programmatically. CodePipeline picks up the commit → Terraform creates the account → Control Tower enrolls it → customizations applied. End-to-end: ~30 minutes from ServiceNow approval to ready account.* <br> *Account customizations: AFT supports pre-hooks (run before account creation), post-hooks (run after account creation), and global customizations (apply to all accounts). Post-hook: install baseline Config rules, create default VPC resources, set up Identity Center assignment, create Cost Budget alerts. This ensures every account has identical baseline configuration regardless of who requested it.* <br>

1338. [ Security Hub ] A company has GuardDuty, Macie, and Inspector enabled across 100 accounts. Security analysts complain about too many alerts and cannot prioritize. What is the recommended architecture? ; AWS Security Hub as centralized aggregation + correlation layer. (1) Enable Security Hub with Organizations delegated admin in Security account. (2) All accounts auto-send findings to Security Hub. (3) Security Hub normalizes all findings to ASFF. (4) Create Security Hub insights (custom correlations) — e.g., "EC2 instances with both GuardDuty findings AND Inspector HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs" = immediate priority. (5) EventBridge rules on Security Hub findings with severity=CRITICAL → PagerDuty/SNS. (6) Suppression rules for known false positives/acceptable risks. <br><br> *Insights reduce noise: a Security Hub insight combining GuardDuty behavioral threat + Inspector known CVE on same resource = confirmed high-risk (actively exploited vulnerability). Single resource appearing in multiple findings = higher priority than a resource with one finding type. Insights: filter + group + sort across thousands of findings in seconds.* <br> *Finding workflow lifecycle: Security Hub finding `Workflow.Status`: NEW → analyst reviews → NOTIFIED (ticket created) → RESOLVED (fixed) or SUPPRESSED (accepted risk). This lifecycle management in Security Hub replaces manual spreadsheet tracking. Integration: Security Hub → Jira via EventBridge + Lambda: automatically creates Jira tickets for CRITICAL/HIGH findings with 24-hour SLA.* <br>

1339. [ Security Hub ] What is the difference between Security Hub security standards and GuardDuty findings? ; Security Hub security standards: compliance checks against frameworks (CIS, PCI-DSS, NIST) using Config rules. They evaluate resource configurations — "is this S3 bucket encrypted?" "Is MFA enabled for root?" Findings represent configuration drift from a compliance baseline. GuardDuty findings: real-time threat detection based on actual behavior — "this EC2 is communicating with a known C2 server right now." Findings represent active or recent threats. Both appear in Security Hub (aggregation), but serve different purposes: compliance vs threat detection. <br><br> *Timing difference: Security Hub standard checks run periodically (every 12 hours or on Config change) — compliance state may be hours old. GuardDuty findings are near-real-time (minutes from event to finding). For incident response: GuardDuty findings are more actionable (immediate threat). For compliance reporting: Security Hub standards provide the evidence trail.* <br> *Together they form a complete picture: Security Hub standards say "your EC2 has an unpatched vulnerability (Inspector finding) and is in a public subnet (Config non-compliant) and is receiving brute-force SSH (GuardDuty finding)." All three data points in one Security Hub console, correlated by resource ARN. This multi-dimensional view is the value of Security Hub over individual service consoles.* <br>

1340. [ Access Analyzer ] A company wants to find all S3 buckets in their AWS Organization that are accessible by external AWS accounts (outside the org). What is the quickest method? ; Create an IAM Access Analyzer with zone of trust set to "Organization." The organization-level analyzer evaluates all resource policies across the org and flags any S3 bucket accessible by principals outside the organization. In the IAM Access Analyzer console: Findings → filter Resource type = S3 Bucket → all external-access findings. This takes minutes to complete after enabling. <br><br> *Account-level analyzer would generate false positives: cross-account access within the org (e.g., Spoke VPC accessing Log Archive S3 bucket) would appear as "external" even though it is legitimate intra-org access. Organization-level analyzer correctly ignores intra-org access, only flagging truly external access. Use org-level for org-wide external exposure assessment.* <br> *Access Analyzer finding: each finding shows the resource ARN, the external principal, the access level (Read, Write, etc.), and when it was first/last observed. Mark finding as "Resolved" after fixing the bucket policy. Mark as "Archived" if external access is intentional (audit log). Regular review: schedule monthly Access Analyzer review — new buckets or policy changes may introduce new external exposure. Integrate with Security Hub: findings auto-forwarded for centralized tracking.* <br>

1341. [ Access Analyzer ] A company wants to implement least-privilege IAM for a Lambda function but is not sure what permissions it needs. How does IAM Access Analyzer help? ; IAM Access Analyzer policy generation. (1) Start a policy generation for the Lambda execution role. (2) Access Analyzer monitors CloudTrail events for API calls made by that role for 1-90 days. (3) After the observation period, Access Analyzer generates an IAM policy containing exactly the actions and resources the Lambda actually used. (4) Review and attach the generated policy. (5) Remove the original overly-permissive policy. <br><br> *Policy generation accuracy: based on ACTUAL usage from CloudTrail, not guessed permissions. If Lambda never called S3:DeleteObject, the generated policy will not include it. This is strictly least-privilege from observed behavior. Limitation: if the Lambda needs to handle edge-case scenarios not hit during the observation period, the generated policy may be too restrictive. Recommendation: test the generated policy in a staging environment before applying to production.* <br> *Complementary: IAM Access Advisor (legacy, simpler) shows which services a role has accessed in the last 90 days at the service level. Access Analyzer policy generation is more granular — action level and resource level. For new roles or after code changes: re-run policy generation to capture updated usage patterns. Combine: Access Analyzer (fine-grained generation) + Access Advisor (quick service-level unused check).* <br>

1342. [ Identity Center ] A company is using IAM Identity Center with built-in directory. They hire 500 new employees via a merger. Manually creating 500 users is too slow. What should they migrate to? ; Migrate from Identity Center built-in directory to an external IdP (Okta, Azure AD, or Google Workspace) with SCIM provisioning. SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) auto-syncs users from the IdP to Identity Center. HR onboards 500 employees in the IdP → SCIM pushes all 500 users to Identity Center automatically. AWS access appears for each user based on group-to-permission-set mappings. No manual user creation in Identity Center. <br><br> *Migration from built-in directory to external IdP: (1) Set up SAML integration with IdP. (2) Enable SCIM provisioning from IdP. (3) Create IdP groups matching existing Identity Center permission set assignments. (4) Assign IdP groups to permission sets in Identity Center. (5) Test with pilot users. (6) Migrate all users (they log in via IdP now). (7) Delete built-in directory users (or leave — both can coexist temporarily). (8) Keep 1-2 built-in break-glass users as emergency access.* <br> *SCIM at scale: Okta can sync 100,000+ users to Identity Center. When an employee leaves: HR deactivates in Okta → SCIM push → Identity Center deactivates user → all AWS account access revoked in minutes. Without SCIM: manual deprovisioning across 50 accounts takes hours/days = security risk window. SCIM closes the offboarding gap.* <br>

1343. [ Security Audit ] A company's external auditor needs read-only access to security configurations in all 50 AWS accounts. They should NOT be able to read business data (S3 object contents, RDS data, SQS messages). What is the architecture? ; IAM Identity Center permission set using the `SecurityAudit` AWS-managed policy. Create a permission set: assign `arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/SecurityAudit` policy. Assign this permission set to the auditor group in Identity Center. Apply assignment to all 50 accounts. Auditor logs into Identity Center portal → selects account → gets AWSReservedSSO_SecurityAuditAccess role → read-only access to security configurations, no data-plane access. <br><br> *SecurityAudit policy specifically: allows GetBucketPolicy, GetBucketAcl, ListBuckets — but NOT GetObject (no S3 data reading). Allows DescribeDBInstances — but NOT Connect or query access. Allows DescribeSecurityGroups, GetTrailStatus, DescribeConfigRules — all security configuration reads. This is exactly what an external auditor needs: verify controls exist without accessing protected data.* <br> *Additional hardening: add a session duration to the permission set (max 4 hours for auditor sessions). Enable MFA requirement for the auditor group in Identity Center. Log all auditor API calls to CloudTrail (SecurityAudit allows CloudTrail reads but CloudTrail itself logs all API calls including read-only). Audit the auditor: monthly review of what API calls the auditor group made via CloudTrail.* <br>

1344. [ ACM ] A company uses ALB with multiple domains (api.example.com, app.example.com, admin.example.com). Each domain has a separate ACM certificate. How many HTTPS listeners are needed on the ALB? ; One HTTPS listener. ALB supports multiple certificates on a single HTTPS listener using SNI (Server Name Indication). The client's TLS ClientHello includes the hostname → ALB selects the matching cert from the listener's certificate list. Maximum 25 certificates per HTTPS listener by default (can be increased). One listener, one port (443), multiple certs. The default certificate is returned if no SNI match found. <br><br> *SNI selection flow: client sends TLS ClientHello with SNI extension `server_name=api.example.com` → ALB listener has 3 certs: api.example.com, app.example.com, admin.example.com → ALB selects api.example.com cert → TLS handshake completes with correct cert. Without SNI (very old clients, pre-2014): ALB returns the default cert (first cert in list or explicitly set default).* <br> *Wildcard alternative: if all domains share the same parent (example.com), use one wildcard cert `*.example.com` — covers all three domains with a single cert on the listener. Simpler cert management, but cannot cover different base domains (api.example.com, api.company.org would need separate certs even with wildcard). Trade-off: wildcard = simpler management, SAN cert = flexibility for multiple base domains.* <br>

1345. [ Config ] What is the difference between a Config managed rule and a Config conformance pack? ; Managed rule: single individual Config rule evaluating one specific compliance check (e.g., `encrypted-volumes` checks if EBS volumes are encrypted). You enable and manage rules individually. Conformance pack: a collection of Config rules + optional remediation actions packaged together as a CloudFormation template and deployed as a unit. One conformance pack can contain 130 rules. Deploying one conformance pack deploys all included rules simultaneously. AWS provides pre-built conformance packs for CIS, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, NIST. <br><br> *Conformance pack deployment: `aws configservice put-conformance-pack --conformance-pack-name CIS-Benchmark --template-s3-uri s3://my-bucket/CIS-conformance-pack.yaml`. All rules in the pack deploy at once. Compliance dashboard shows per-rule and per-pack compliance across all accounts. Organizations conformance pack: deploy to all accounts in org simultaneously from management or delegated admin account.* <br> *Customizing conformance packs: AWS-provided packs are CloudFormation templates — download, modify (add/remove rules, adjust parameters), re-upload as your own custom pack. Example: CIS Level 1 pack has 41 rules — remove rules not applicable to your environment (e.g., remove CloudFront-specific rules if you do not use CloudFront), add your own custom rules. Result: organization-specific compliance pack combining industry standard + internal requirements.* <br>

1346. [ GuardDuty ] A GuardDuty finding of type CredentialAccess:IAMUser/AnomalousBehavior is generated. What does this indicate and what is the immediate response? ; This indicates ML-detected anomalous IAM API activity — the IAM user is making API calls that are unusual compared to their historical baseline (different time of day, different geolocation, different API call types or volumes). Could indicate: stolen credentials, insider threat, or compromised workstation. Immediate response: (1) Determine if the activity is legitimate (contact user). (2) If not legitimate: rotate/disable access keys immediately. (3) Review CloudTrail for all API calls made in the anomaly period. (4) Check for newly created IAM users/roles/access keys (privilege escalation indicators). (5) Revoke any unauthorized permissions granted. <br><br> *ML-based detection: GuardDuty builds a behavioral baseline for each IAM principal over time. Anomalous = statistical deviation from baseline. This catches zero-day credential compromises where the attacker is using real credentials (no malware signatures, no known-bad IPs). Traditional signature-based tools miss this — GuardDuty ML catches it.* <br> *Follow-up investigation: CloudTrail Lake query: `SELECT eventTime, eventName, requestParameters, sourceIPAddress FROM events WHERE userIdentity.arn='arn:aws:iam::123:user/compromised-user' AND eventTime > 'anomaly-start-time' ORDER BY eventTime`. Look for: CreateUser, AttachRolePolicy, PutUserPolicy, CreateAccessKey (privilege escalation). Look for: AssumeRole calls to other accounts (lateral movement). Look for: S3 GetObject on sensitive buckets (data exfiltration).* <br>

1347. [ Macie ] A company stores employee payroll data in S3 in Parquet format. Macie is enabled but generates no findings for these files. Why might this be, and what is the solution? ; Macie may not scan Parquet files in all cases — Macie supports specific file formats for sensitive data analysis. Check: is the Parquet detection enabled? Is the bucket included in Macie discovery scope? Is the file size within Macie scan limits (individual file max 20MB for Parquet)? Solution: (1) Verify Macie data discovery job includes the payroll bucket and all prefixes. (2) Check file format support in Macie documentation. (3) For large Parquet files: consider converting payroll data to smaller chunks. (4) If Macie still misses: use Athena to query the Parquet data + Macie custom data identifier for payroll-specific patterns. <br><br> *Macie file format support: JSON, JSONL, CSV, TSV, Parquet, Apache Avro, Excel (.xlsx), Word (.docx), PDF, plain text, and more. Compressed files (gzip, bzip2) are decompressed and scanned. File size limits: up to 20MB after decompression. Large Parquet files split across multiple S3 objects: each object scanned independently.* <br> *Macie sampling in automated discovery vs full scan: automated sensitive data discovery samples objects (not every object, representative sample). If payroll Parquet files are small in number, they might not be sampled. Run an on-demand Macie job targeting the specific bucket with 100% sampling: `aws macie2 create-classification-job --job-type ONE_TIME --s3-job-definition BucketDefinitions=[{...}] --sampling-percentage 100`. This scans every object.* <br>

1348. [ Control Tower ] What happens when a new AWS account is created via Control Tower Account Factory compared to creating it directly in AWS Organizations? ; Account Factory: (1) New account automatically enrolled in Control Tower. (2) Mandatory guardrails (SCPs) applied. (3) Config recorder and delivery channel configured. (4) CloudTrail organization trail covers it. (5) Identity Center permission sets assigned per Account Factory configuration. (6) Account appears in Control Tower dashboard. (7) Baseline CloudFormation StackSets applied. Direct Organizations creation: raw account — none of the above applied automatically. No guardrails, no Config, no CloudTrail, no Identity Center setup. Must manually enroll in Control Tower ("Enroll account") or it remains unmanaged. <br><br> *Unmanaged accounts in Organizations: a significant security risk. Account has no security guardrails, no Config recording, no CloudTrail. An attacker who gains access to the account can operate undetected (no logging). GuardDuty may still work if deployed org-wide, but Config-based compliance and Control Tower guardrails are absent. Best practice: immediately enroll all new accounts in Control Tower or prevent direct account creation via SCP (require account creation through Account Factory only).* <br> *Enrolling existing accounts in Control Tower: `aws controltower enroll-account` (or via console). Control Tower deploys its managed guardrails, Config recorder, IAM roles. Existing resources in the account are not modified. This is the remediation path for accounts created outside Account Factory. Enrollment takes 20-30 minutes per account. For 200 existing accounts: batch enrollment via automation (Lambda + Step Functions iterating account list).* <br>

1349. [ Access Analyzer ] A security policy states that no IAM role should have a trust policy allowing external AWS accounts outside the company org. How do you continuously enforce this? ; IAM Access Analyzer with organization zone of trust + EventBridge automation. (1) Create org-level IAM Access Analyzer. (2) Any IAM role with external trust relationship (outside org) generates an Access Analyzer finding. (3) EventBridge rule: `{"source":["aws.access-analyzer"],"detail-type":["Access Analyzer Finding"]}` → Lambda. (4) Lambda checks if the external principal is an expected exception (e.g., AWS service principal). (5) If unexpected external trust: alert security team + optionally update the trust policy to remove the external principal. <br><br> *Access Analyzer finding for IAM roles: `ResourceType: AWS::IAM::Role`, `FindingType: ExternalAccess`. The finding shows the exact external principal (account ID or * wildcard). Wildcard trust policy `"Principal":"*"` is critical severity — any AWS account can assume the role. Finding generated immediately when the role is created with external trust.* <br> *Complementary real-time detection: EventBridge rule on CloudTrail `CreateRole` and `UpdateAssumeRolePolicy` → Lambda parses trust policy → checks for non-org external accounts → immediate alert. Access Analyzer provides the authoritative finding (with context, remediation guidance) while CloudTrail EventBridge provides faster real-time detection (before Access Analyzer evaluates). Use both: CloudTrail for immediate alerting, Access Analyzer for authoritative finding management.* <br>

1350. [ ACM ] What is the difference between an ACM certificate renewal for a DNS-validated vs email-validated certificate? When does automatic renewal happen? ; DNS-validated: ACM renews automatically 60 days before expiry by re-checking the CNAME record. If the CNAME is still valid (unchanged in DNS zone), renewal completes without any action from the user. This is fully automatic. Email-validated: ACM sends renewal approval emails to WHOIS registrant contacts 60 days before expiry. A human must click the approval link. If no response within 72 hours, ACM sends reminder emails. If not approved before expiry, the certificate expires — causing service outage. <br><br> *Why DNS validation is strongly preferred: no human action required for renewal. CNAME records persist in DNS zones indefinitely (unlike email addresses which can change when admins leave). For production environments: email validation is an operational risk — cert expiry incidents are almost always caused by missed renewal emails. DNS validation eliminates this risk entirely.* <br> *Certificate in-use renewal: ACM only renews certificates that are actively associated with a supported AWS service (ALB, CloudFront, API GW). Imported certificates are NEVER automatically renewed — you manage renewal entirely. After renewal: ALB/CloudFront/API GW automatically pick up the new certificate without any configuration change or downtime. The ARN remains the same — services referencing the ARN do not need updating.* <br>

1351. [ CloudHSM ] A company needs Oracle database Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) with keys stored in a customer-controlled HSM on AWS. What is the solution? ; AWS CloudHSM. Oracle Database 12c+ supports TDE with an external key store using PKCS#11 interface. Deploy CloudHSM cluster in the same VPC as the Oracle RDS Custom or Oracle EC2 instance. Install CloudHSM PKCS#11 library on the Oracle host. Configure Oracle sqlnet.ora and wallet to use CloudHSM as the external key store. Oracle TDE master key generated and stored in CloudHSM — never leaves the HSM. All tablespace/column encryption operations use CloudHSM for key operations. <br><br> *Oracle RDS vs EC2: standard Amazon RDS Oracle supports KMS for TDE (not CloudHSM). For CloudHSM-backed TDE: must use RDS Custom for Oracle (customer-managed EC2 with Oracle license) or self-managed Oracle EC2. RDS managed Oracle does not support CloudHSM PKCS#11 integration. This is a key architectural constraint: CloudHSM Oracle TDE = RDS Custom or self-managed EC2, not standard RDS.* <br> *CloudHSM cluster for Oracle TDE HA: minimum 2 HSMs in 2 AZs. Oracle connects to all cluster HSMs for load balancing and HA. If one HSM fails, Oracle uses the other. Key synchronization: CloudHSM automatically synchronizes key material between cluster members. Backup: CloudHSM cluster backup to S3 (encrypted). Critical: if all CloudHSM HSMs are destroyed without a backup, the TDE master key is permanently lost and all encrypted data is unrecoverable. Backup policy is non-negotiable.* <br>

1352. [ Config ] A Config rule `encrypted-volumes` shows 15 non-compliant EBS volumes. The security team wants to automatically encrypt them without deleting data. What is the remediation process? ; EBS volumes cannot be encrypted in-place (cannot change encryption on existing unencrypted volume). Remediation: (1) Create snapshot of unencrypted volume. (2) Copy snapshot with encryption enabled (specify KMS CMK). (3) Create new encrypted EBS volume from encrypted snapshot. (4) Detach original volume from EC2. (5) Attach new encrypted volume to EC2. (6) Verify application works with new volume. (7) Delete original unencrypted volume. Config auto-remediation SSM Automation document can handle steps 1-5 automatically but step 6 (verify application) requires human validation for production. <br><br> *SSM Automation for EBS encryption: `AWS-EnableEbsEncryptionByDefault` enables account-level default encryption (all NEW volumes encrypted). For existing volumes: custom SSM Automation needed (snapshot → encrypted copy → volume swap). Account-level default encryption: `aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default`. After enabling: all new EBS volumes and snapshots encrypted with default KMS key automatically. Does not affect existing unencrypted volumes.* <br> *Config remediation timing: after non-compliant resource detected, auto-remediation starts within minutes. For EBS snapshot/copy: can take 15-60 minutes per volume depending on size. For 15 volumes: run remediations in parallel (Config can remediate multiple resources concurrently). Monitor: CloudWatch metric for SSM Automation execution success/failure. Alert if remediation fails.* <br>

1353. [ Security Hub ] A company receives 10,000 Security Hub findings per day. The security team can only action 20 per day. How do you reduce noise and prioritize? ; Multiple strategies: (1) Suppression rules: automatically suppress known false positives (e.g., specific resource in test environment, specific rule always false-positive). (2) Findings filter: show only severity=CRITICAL or HIGH. (3) Insights: "EC2 instances with both HIGH GuardDuty AND HIGH Inspector findings" = confirmed exploitable. (4) Workflow status automation: auto-set `NOTIFIED` for medium findings, ticket only CRITICAL/HIGH. (5) Suppression for accepted risks: `status=SUPPRESSED` for intentional deviations from compliance. <br><br> *Finding volume breakdown: most Security Hub volume comes from Config compliance checks (run every 12 hours on hundreds of resources). Strategy: tune Config rules to exclude dev accounts from strict production checks. Use separate Security Hub aggregation regions or accounts for dev vs prod. Dev findings: lower severity threshold. Prod findings: immediate escalation.* <br> *Automation pipeline for prioritization: Security Hub finding → EventBridge → Lambda → score finding (base severity × asset criticality × public exposure indicator) → enrich finding with asset owner from CMDB → create ticket only if enriched score > threshold → mark lower-scoring findings as NOTIFIED with 30-day SLA. This transforms 10,000 findings/day into 20 actionable tickets with appropriate SLA.* <br>

1354. [ Access Analyzer ] What is the difference between IAM Access Analyzer and AWS Trusted Advisor for IAM security? ; IAM Access Analyzer: precise resource policy analysis using automated reasoning (formal logic). Identifies exact external access paths to specific resources (S3 bucket ARN, specific SQS queue). Generates actionable findings with the specific principal and access level. Also: policy validation, policy generation. Trusted Advisor: broad best-practice checks (IAM password policy, MFA on root, unused access keys older than 90 days, overly permissive SG rules). Higher-level, account-wide health checks. Not resource-specific. <br><br> *Complementary: Trusted Advisor for broad hygiene (is MFA enabled? is root used?). Access Analyzer for precise external exposure (which exact S3 buckets are accessible by account 999999?). Together: Trusted Advisor catches systemic security hygiene issues, Access Analyzer catches specific resource misconfigurations. Both feed findings to Security Hub for centralized view.* <br> *Access Analyzer automated reasoning advantage: mathematical proof that a resource IS or IS NOT accessible by a given principal. Not heuristic or sample-based — exhaustive analysis of all possible policy combinations (condition keys, deny statements, permission boundaries). This is why Access Analyzer can definitively say "this S3 bucket is publicly accessible" even with complex policy conditions that would confuse a human reviewer.* <br>


1355. [ ACM ] A company wants to issue certificates for 10,000 IoT devices. Each device needs a unique client certificate for mTLS. What is the cost-effective AWS solution? ; ACM Private CA with bulk certificate issuance. Create a Private CA ($400/month). Issue individual certificates for each device ($0.75/cert × 10,000 = $7,500 one-time). Devices use client certificates for mTLS to an API Gateway or ALB. Certificates managed centrally — revoke any compromised device certificate via Private CA CRL (Certificate Revocation List) or OCSP. Monthly cost: $400/month (CA) regardless of number of active certs (no per-cert monthly fee after issuance). <br><br> *IoT certificate revocation: if a device is stolen or compromised, revoke its certificate in ACM Private CA. The CRL (or OCSP) must be checked by the TLS termination point (API Gateway, ALB). ALB mTLS with CRL: configure the truststore with CRL distribution point URL. API Gateway mTLS: truststore in S3, must manually update S3 file when certs revoked (API GW does not auto-check CRL). For IoT at scale: AWS IoT Core with its own certificate management (per-device certs, just-in-time registration) may be better than ACM Private CA.* <br> *CRL vs OCSP: CRL (Certificate Revocation List) = periodic published list of revoked serial numbers. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) = real-time check per cert. OCSP is more timely but requires OCSP responder availability. ACM Private CA supports both. For IoT: OCSP preferred (immediate revocation effect) but requires all devices to reach the OCSP endpoint — may not work for offline/intermittent devices.* <br>

1356. [ GuardDuty ] GuardDuty is enabled in an account. An EC2 instance performs a port scan on other EC2 instances in the same VPC. Does GuardDuty detect this? ; GuardDuty analyzes VPC Flow Logs. Internal port scanning (EC2-to-EC2 within VPC) IS visible in flow logs as traffic between private IPs. GuardDuty can generate `Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort` or `Recon:EC2/Portscan` findings for internal port scanning if the pattern matches known reconnaissance activity. However, GuardDuty is primarily optimized for detecting external threats — its ML models for port scanning are tuned for external sources. Internal port scans may or may not generate findings depending on volume and pattern. <br><br> *GuardDuty VPC flow log analysis: analyzes both ingress and egress flows. EC2 in subnet A scanning EC2 in subnet B: flow logs capture REJECT entries (SG blocking) + ACCEPT entries (open ports). GuardDuty correlates: many REJECT entries from one source EC2 to many destination ports = port scan pattern. For definitive internal threat detection: consider Amazon Inspector (network reachability analysis) or a dedicated IDS solution.* <br> *For guaranteed internal east-west threat detection: route all VPC traffic through AWS Network Firewall (requires route table changes). Network Firewall IDS rules detect port scan signatures regardless of source (internal or external). GuardDuty for external threats + Network Firewall IDS for internal threats = comprehensive coverage. Defense-in-depth for east-west traffic.* <br>

1357. [ Config ] A company uses Config with 50 rules. They notice Config is expensive. How do you reduce Config costs without eliminating compliance monitoring? ; Cost reduction strategies: (1) Scope recording: record only security-relevant resource types (SG, VPC, IAM, S3, KMS) instead of all resources. Reduces Config items recorded. (2) Periodic evaluation instead of on-change: change trigger rules to periodic (every 24 hours) for non-critical checks. Fewer evaluations = lower cost. (3) Consolidate to conformance packs: eliminates duplicate rule evaluations. (4) Exclude dev accounts from expensive rules. (5) Use AWS Security Hub security standards (which run Config rules) to avoid enabling the same rules separately. <br><br> *Config recording scope: `aws configservice put-configuration-recorder --recording-group AllSupported=false,ResourceTypes=[AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup,AWS::S3::Bucket,AWS::IAM::Role,AWS::KMS::Key,AWS::EC2::VPC]`. Records only 5 resource types instead of 200+. Cost reduction: typically 70-80% fewer Config items. Trade-off: cannot track configuration history for excluded resource types.* <br> *Periodic vs change-triggered rules: change-triggered = evaluate every time resource changes (can be many times per day for busy resources). Periodic = evaluate once per interval regardless of changes. For rules checking account-wide settings (e.g., `root-account-mfa-enabled`) — change-triggered makes no sense (root MFA does not change resource configs). Switch these to daily periodic. Cost: $0.001/evaluation × 1,000 resources × 24 evaluations/day = $24/day change-triggered vs $1/day daily periodic.* <br>

1358. [ Macie ] A company processes GDPR-regulated personal data. They need to prove to regulators that they know where all personal data is stored in AWS. What service provides this evidence? ; Amazon Macie. Enable Macie org-wide with automated sensitive data discovery. Macie scans S3 buckets and generates a sensitive data coverage report showing: which buckets contain personal data (PII), what types of personal data (names, emails, addresses, IDs), which buckets were not scanned (coverage gaps). Use Macie findings export to S3 → Athena queries → generate data inventory report for GDPR Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). <br><br> *GDPR Article 30 requirement: organizations must maintain records of processing activities. For data stored in S3: Macie provides automated inventory. Custom data identifiers: for GDPR-specific EU data types (EU passport numbers, IBAN bank accounts, national ID numbers), use custom identifiers with the appropriate regex patterns. Macie has built-in managed identifiers for common GDPR data types but custom identifiers extend coverage.* <br> *Macie sensitivity score per bucket: Macie scores S3 buckets 1-100 based on volume and type of sensitive data detected. High-scoring buckets = priority for encryption, access controls, and monitoring. Macie bucket inventory: CSV export of all analyzed buckets with sensitivity score, object count, encryption status, public access status. This inventory is evidence for regulators that a systematic data discovery process is in place.* <br>

1359. [ Control Tower ] A company has Control Tower deployed. They want to add a guardrail preventing any account from creating EC2 instances larger than c5.4xlarge (for cost governance). How do you implement this? ; Customizations for Control Tower (CfCT). Create a custom SCP: `"Effect":"Deny","Action":"ec2:RunInstances","Resource":"*","Condition":{"ForAnyValue:StringLike":{"ec2:InstanceType":["*.8xlarge","*.12xlarge","*.16xlarge","*.24xlarge","*metal","*.32xlarge"]}}`. Deploy via CfCT to the target OU. CfCT adds this SCP to the OU through Control Tower's managed process without causing drift. <br><br> *CfCT process: define SCP in a manifest.yaml file in the CfCT CodePipeline repository. CodePipeline applies the SCP to specified OUs when the pipeline runs. New accounts added to the OU automatically get the SCP (CfCT re-runs on account vending). This is how to extend Control Tower guardrails beyond the built-in set.* <br> *Instance type SCP condition: `ec2:InstanceType` is an IAM condition key. The SCP condition can use wildcards: `*.8xlarge` matches c5.8xlarge, m5.8xlarge, r5.8xlarge, etc. Test the SCP in a sandbox OU first — incorrect condition key usage may block more than intended or have no effect (SCP syntax errors are silently ignored in some cases). Use IAM policy simulator to validate SCP logic before deploying to production OUs.* <br>

1360. [ Security Hub ] A company is undergoing a PCI-DSS audit. The auditor asks for evidence that AWS security controls meet PCI-DSS requirements. What is the fastest way to generate this evidence? ; AWS Security Hub with PCI-DSS v3.2.1 standard enabled. (1) Enable the PCI-DSS standard in Security Hub. (2) Security Hub runs 100+ automated compliance checks against PCI-DSS controls. (3) Generate compliance report: Security Hub → PCI-DSS standard → export findings as CSV or via API. (4) Filter to PASSED controls (these are your compliance evidence). For FAILED controls: show remediation actions taken. AWS Artifact: provides AWS PCI-DSS Attestation of Compliance (AoC) — demonstrates AWS infrastructure meets PCI-DSS. Combined: AWS Artifact (AWS responsibility) + Security Hub report (customer responsibility) = complete PCI-DSS evidence package. <br><br> *PCI-DSS shared responsibility: AWS is responsible for the physical/infrastructure layer (documented in AWS PCI-DSS AoC from AWS Artifact). Customer is responsible for their configuration on AWS (documented by Security Hub compliance checks). Auditor needs both pieces. Security Hub PCI-DSS checks map to specific PCI-DSS requirements (e.g., Requirement 1: Network access controls → Security Hub checks for SG rules, NACL configuration).* <br> *Evidence export: Security Hub API `get-findings` with filter `ComplianceStatus=PASSED` and `ProductArn=SecurityHub-PCI-DSS-standard-ARN`. Export as JSON or CSV. For continuous compliance: schedule weekly Security Hub report generation → S3 → Athena query → automatically email to compliance team. Shows compliance trend over time (important for PCI-DSS audit demonstrating sustained compliance, not just point-in-time snapshot).* <br>

1361. [ Identity Center ] A company wants to enforce hardware MFA (YubiKey) for all users accessing production AWS accounts via Identity Center, while allowing TOTP for dev accounts. How do you implement different MFA policies? ; Identity Center MFA configuration is global (one MFA policy for all users) — you cannot natively set different MFA requirements per OU or account. Workaround: (1) Create two Identity Center instances (not supported — only one per org). (2) Use IAM condition in permission set policy: require `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent:true` AND MFA type via `sts:RoleSessionName` tricks (complex). Better: (3) Use Okta or Azure AD as IdP — configure Okta step-up MFA policies (YubiKey required for Production groups, TOTP allowed for Dev groups). Identity Center receives already-authenticated SAML assertion with MFA level from Okta. <br><br> *Okta Adaptive MFA: configure Okta sign-on policies per application or per group. Production-access Okta group → requires YubiKey (WebAuthn). Dev-access group → TOTP sufficient. Identity Center trusts the Okta assertion — does not re-challenge for MFA (trusts IdP authentication). This is how enterprise organizations implement tiered MFA requirements for AWS access.* <br> *IAM session condition `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent`: permission set inline policy can include `Condition:{"Bool":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}}` — requires MFA to use the permission set. But this checks if MFA was used at login, not the MFA type. For MFA type enforcement (hardware-only): IdP-level enforcement (Okta/Azure AD policy) is the only practical approach. Identity Center itself cannot differentiate TOTP from WebAuthn.* <br>

1362. [ ACM ] An ACM public certificate is about to expire in 5 days. The company uses DNS validation. Why has it not auto-renewed, and what should they do? ; Auto-renewal failure reasons: (1) CNAME validation record was deleted from DNS zone. (2) Domain no longer resolves (DNS zone changed or domain expired). (3) Certificate is not in use (not associated with an ALB/CloudFront/etc.) — ACM only auto-renews in-use certs. (4) S3 static website hosting changed to a different cert. Investigate: ACM console → certificate → check renewal status → "Pending validation" means CNAME check failing. Fix CNAME record → auto-renewal resumes. If cert already expired: ACM will issue a new cert (not renew) — update the association with ALB/CloudFront. <br><br> *ACM renewal timeline: ACM attempts renewal 60 days before expiry. Sends notification emails (to AWS account root email) at 45, 30, 15, 7, 3, 1 days before expiry if renewal is pending. CloudWatch metric: `aws/certificatemanager/DaysToCertExpiry` — set alarm at 30 days for early warning. Route 53 Health Check alternative: monitor the HTTPS endpoint, alert if TLS cert is within 30 days of expiry.* <br> *If cert expires: ALB continues serving the expired cert (ALB does not automatically drop expired certs). Browsers show security warning. Users may bypass or be blocked depending on browser/configuration. Resolution: request new ACM cert with DNS validation → validate CNAME → associate with ALB (replace expired cert) → ALB starts serving new cert within minutes. Zero downtime if done before complete expiry.* <br>

1363. [ Config ] How does AWS Config work with AWS Organizations? What is the difference between enabling Config in each account vs using an Organizations configuration recorder? ; Per-account Config: each account has its own Config recorder enabled separately. Data stays in each account's S3 bucket. Central view requires Config Aggregator. Organizations configuration recorder (delegated admin): Config delegated admin deploys a recorder configuration to all accounts in the org simultaneously. Ensures ALL accounts have Config enabled (including new accounts — auto-enrolled). Centralized delivery to audit account S3. No account can disable Config (SCP). <br><br> *Organizations Config delegated admin: `aws organizations register-delegated-administrator --account-id SECURITY_ACCOUNT --service-principal config.amazonaws.com`. Security account then manages Config recording across org. Key benefit: new account added to org → Config automatically enabled → no manual action. Without org Config: new accounts created via Account Factory must have Config enabled during vending.* <br> *Config aggregator: collects Config data from all accounts/regions into one view. Does NOT deploy or manage Config recorders — only aggregates existing Config data. Config aggregator + org Config recorder together: recorder ensures Config is running everywhere, aggregator brings all data to central account. Cost: aggregation is free, recording cost in each account applies. For 200 accounts × 1,000 resources each: significant Config item volume — tune recording scope to essential resources.* <br>

1364. [ Security Audit ] A new employee joins the security team and needs immediate read-only access to all 100 AWS accounts to perform an initial security assessment. They need to see IAM policies, security group rules, CloudTrail settings, and Config compliance. What is the fastest and safest architecture? ; Identity Center permission set with `SecurityAudit` AWS-managed policy. (1) Create permission set `SecurityAuditAccess` using `SecurityAudit` policy + short session duration (4 hours). (2) Create Identity Center group `Security-Assessors`. (3) Assign the group to the permission set across ALL 100 accounts. (4) Add new employee to the `Security-Assessors` group. Done. Employee can log into Identity Center portal and access all 100 accounts instantly with read-only security config access. No data exposure risk. <br><br> *Speed advantage: adding user to an IdP group (Okta/Azure AD/Identity Center directory) → SCIM sync → Identity Center access active within minutes. Without Identity Center: create IAM user in each of 100 accounts = 100 separate operations + credential management. Identity Center eliminates this operational burden for any future team changes.* <br> *Duration security: 4-hour session = even if session token is stolen, attacker has only 4 hours. After session expires, new MFA-authenticated login required. Set minimum session duration for security roles (1-4 hours) vs developer roles (8-12 hours) based on risk profile. Log all activities via CloudTrail — SecurityAudit policy allows read-only API calls that are all logged, providing a full audit trail of what the assessor examined.* <br>

1365. [ GuardDuty ] A Lambda function in an AWS account starts making outbound connections to a known cryptocurrency mining pool. GuardDuty is enabled. What finding is generated and what is the automated response? ; Finding: `CryptoCurrency:Lambda/BitcoinTool.B!DNS` or `UnauthorizedAccess:Lambda/MaliciousIPCaller` (Lambda network protection plan). Automated response via EventBridge: GuardDuty finding → EventBridge → Lambda: (1) Extract affected Lambda function name. (2) Disable Lambda concurrency (`aws lambda put-function-concurrency --reserved-concurrent-executions 0`) — stops all invocations. (3) Alert security team via SNS. (4) Preserve evidence: export Lambda environment variables, function code, and recent CloudWatch Logs. (5) Analyze function code for crypto miner injection. <br><br> *Lambda crypto mining: attacker injects malicious code into Lambda (via CI/CD pipeline compromise, dependency confusion, or vulnerable Lambda layer). Lambda has CPU/memory resources — crypto mining uses these. Cost: Lambda billed per ms × high CPU usage = unexpected Lambda bill spike. CloudWatch billing alarm on Lambda costs: early detection before GuardDuty finding.* <br> *Lambda network protection plan: analyzes Lambda function network activity (VPC and non-VPC). Detects: Lambda calling known malicious IPs/domains, unusual outbound ports (mining typically port 3333, 4444, 8333). Disable this protection plan if not using Lambda (avoid unnecessary GuardDuty cost). Enable it in accounts with Lambda workloads. Cost: per Lambda invocation analyzed.* <br>

1366. [ Macie ] What is the difference between Macie automated sensitive data discovery and a Macie classification job? When should each be used? ; Automated sensitive data discovery: continuous, AWS-managed, samples S3 objects across ALL buckets in the account. Runs daily. Low cost ($0.10/bucket/month). Purpose: coverage-wide discovery — find buckets containing sensitive data you were not aware of. Cannot guarantee 100% object coverage (sampling). Classification job: targeted, manually configured scan of specific buckets/prefixes. Configurable sampling percentage (up to 100%). One-time or scheduled. Higher cost ($1/GB scanned). Purpose: deep compliance scan of known sensitive buckets, full coverage audit. <br><br> *Use case for automated discovery: GDPR initial inventory — "find all S3 buckets in this org that contain any PII." Run automated discovery for 30 days → sensitivity score for each bucket → focus compliance efforts on high-scoring buckets. This is the discovery phase. Use case for classification job: "scan the customer-data bucket with 100% coverage for PCI-DSS audit evidence." Full scan, every object, exportable results for auditor. This is the evidence-generation phase.* <br> *Combined workflow: (1) Automated discovery identifies 20 buckets with PII sensitivity score > 70. (2) Run one-time 100% classification jobs on those 20 buckets. (3) Results: exact count of objects with credit card numbers, their prefixes, object keys. (4) Remediation: encrypt, restrict access, apply lifecycle policies to delete after retention period. (5) Re-run classification job after remediation to verify clean state.* <br>

1367. [ Control Tower ] A company using Control Tower wants to allow developers in the Sandbox OU to create any EC2 instance type, but restrict the Production OU to only t3, m5, c5 families. How do you implement this? ; Two SCPs via Customizations for Control Tower (CfCT): SCP-1 applied to Production OU: `"Effect":"Deny","Action":"ec2:RunInstances","Resource":"arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*","Condition":{"StringNotLike":{"ec2:InstanceType":["t3.*","m5.*","c5.*","t3a.*","m5a.*","c5a.*"]}}`. SCP-2 for Sandbox OU: no restriction (FullAWSAccess default). Different OUs get different guardrails. <br><br> *SCP NotLike logic: "Deny RunInstances unless the instance type matches these patterns." Any instance type NOT in the allow-list triggers the deny. Test: `c5.xlarge` matches `c5.*` → NOT denied → allowed. `p3.16xlarge` (GPU) does not match any pattern → DENIED. This allows the approved families while blocking everything else.* <br> *OU structure matters: Sandbox OU inherits no denial SCP for instance types (just FullAWSAccess from root). Production OU inherits the restrictive SCP. Developers in Sandbox can experiment with any instance type. Production workloads are cost-controlled by the SCP. This is the multi-OU governance model: each OU represents a different risk/cost profile, different guardrails.* <br>

1368. [ Access Analyzer ] A company enables IAM Access Analyzer and immediately gets hundreds of findings for S3 buckets. Most are legitimate cross-account sharing within their AWS organization. How do they reduce noise? ; Create an organization-level IAM Access Analyzer (zone of trust = organization). This treats all AWS accounts within the org as "internal" — cross-account access within the org does NOT generate findings. Only access from principals OUTSIDE the org generates findings. The hundreds of intra-org findings disappear. Account-level analyzer (zone of trust = account) treats any other AWS account as external — including other accounts in your own org. <br><br> *Org-level analyzer requirement: must be created from the Organizations management account or delegated admin account. Member accounts can create account-level analyzers but not org-level analyzers. For org-wide external access analysis: delegated admin account creates one org-level analyzer — covers all accounts in the org from one analyzer. Account-level analyzers in each member account are redundant if org-level analyzer exists.* <br> *Archiving legitimate findings: for intentional external sharing (e.g., S3 bucket shared with a partner account outside org), archive the finding in Access Analyzer with a justification note. Archived findings are not shown in active findings view. If the bucket policy changes to expose more than intended: new finding generated (archived finding for previous state does not suppress new findings). This maintains ongoing monitoring while reducing noise from known-good configurations.* <br>

1369. [ ACM ] What happens to services using an ACM certificate if the certificate is deleted? ; Deleting an ACM certificate that is currently associated with a service (ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway) is BLOCKED by ACM — you cannot delete a certificate in use. You must first disassociate the cert from all services (remove it from ALB listener, CloudFront distribution, API GW domain). After disassociation, the cert can be deleted. If deleted, the service falls back to its default behavior (may use a different cert or fail TLS). For ALB: the listener must have a replacement cert — cannot have an HTTPS listener with no certificate. <br><br> *Protection mechanism: ACM prevents deletion of in-use certificates. This is a safeguard against accidental deletion causing production outages. Even with full IAM permissions (`acm:DeleteCertificate`), the API call fails with an error if the cert is in use. This is different from KMS where you can schedule key deletion even if the key is associated with resources (though operations on those resources will fail after deletion).* <br> *Certificate replacement process: (1) Request/import new cert. (2) Validate new cert. (3) Update ALB/CloudFront/API GW to use new cert. (4) Verify services working with new cert. (5) Now old cert can be deleted (no longer in use). This is also the process for cert migration (e.g., moving from imported cert to ACM-managed cert for auto-renewal benefit).* <br>
