1370. [ Config ] An organization deploys a conformance pack for HIPAA compliance across all 100 accounts. 40 accounts show non-compliant status for the `rds-storage-encrypted` rule. What does this mean and what is the remediation? ; 40 accounts have RDS instances with storage encryption disabled. HIPAA requires encryption of PHI at rest. `rds-storage-encrypted` checks if RDS instances have `StorageEncrypted=true`. Remediation: RDS storage encryption cannot be enabled on existing instances. Process: (1) Take snapshot of unencrypted RDS instance. (2) Copy snapshot with encryption enabled (specify KMS CMK). (3) Restore new RDS instance from encrypted snapshot. (4) Update application connection string. (5) Verify application. (6) Delete original unencrypted instance. Per-account, per-instance. <br><br> *RDS encryption restriction: unlike EBS (snapshot copy with encryption), RDS has no in-place encryption. Must snapshot → encrypted copy → restore. This is a data migration, not a configuration change. For large RDS databases: snapshot copy can take hours. Plan: (1) Schedule maintenance window. (2) Take snapshot. (3) Restore encrypted instance (parallel, while original still running). (4) Test encrypted instance with application. (5) Promote encrypted instance (brief downtime for connection string change). (6) Confirm encryption. Minimizes downtime.* <br> *Preventive control: enable account-level RDS encryption default: `aws rds modify-db-cluster --storage-encrypted`. Also: SCP denying `rds:CreateDBInstance` without `StorageEncrypted: true` condition. Config rule becomes redundant when preventive controls exist — but keep as detective backup. Defense in depth: prevent (SCP) + detect (Config) + remediate (SSM Automation snapshot/restore).* <br>

1371. [ Security Hub ] What is the Amazon Security Finding Format (ASFF)? Why is it important for Security Hub? ; ASFF is a standardized JSON schema that ALL Security Hub findings must conform to, regardless of source (GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, 3rd-party). Every finding has: SchemaVersion, Id, ProductArn (source), GeneratorId, AwsAccountId, Severity (label + normalized 0-100), Title, Description, Resources (affected resources with ARNs), Workflow.Status (NEW/NOTIFIED/SUPPRESSED/RESOLVED), RecordState (ACTIVE/ARCHIVED), FindingProviderFields, Remediation. Importance: normalization enables cross-source querying, filtering, and automated response without source-specific parsing. <br><br> *ASFF Severity normalization: GuardDuty severity scale (1-10) mapped to ASFF (0-100). Palo Alto Cortex XDR severity (Low/Medium/High/Critical) mapped to ASFF. All sources normalized to the same scale enables unified prioritization. Without ASFF: writing an EventBridge rule for "any HIGH finding from any source" requires separate rules for each source with source-specific field names. With ASFF: one rule on `detail.findings[0].Severity.Label=HIGH` covers all sources.* <br> *Custom product integration: 3rd-party security tools (Splunk, CrowdStrike, Tenable) can send findings to Security Hub in ASFF format via the Security Hub `BatchImportFindings` API. This makes Security Hub the single pane of glass for all security findings — AWS native + 3rd party. For organizations with existing Splunk SIEM: Security Hub → EventBridge → Firehose → Splunk (Security Hub pushes to Splunk) OR Splunk → Security Hub (Splunk sends findings to Security Hub via ASFF API).* <br>

1372. [ Identity Center ] A company uses AWS Identity Center with Okta as the external IdP. An employee leaves and is immediately deactivated in Okta. When will the employee lose AWS access? ; SCIM deprovisioning is near-immediate (minutes). When HR deactivates the employee in Okta: Okta SCIM push → Identity Center deactivates user → all active SSO sessions revoked (existing tokens invalidated) → all future login attempts denied. Any unexpired AWS temporary credentials (STS tokens issued before deactivation) remain valid until their expiry (1-12 hours). To revoke active sessions completely: also revoke all active Identity Center sessions (Identity Center console → Active Sessions) and rotate any long-lived access keys if the user had any. <br><br> *STS credential lifetime: even after user deactivation in Identity Center, any STS credentials already issued continue to work until their natural expiry (session duration set on permission set, max 12 hours). For privileged roles (AdminAccess): set short session duration (1 hour) to minimize this window. For read-only roles: 12 hours is acceptable (lower operational burden vs marginally increased risk window).* <br> *This is the key advantage of Identity Center over per-account IAM users: deactivating one Okta user = immediate loss of all AWS account access across all 200 accounts simultaneously. Without Identity Center: IT team must manually delete IAM user in each of 200 accounts = hours of work = security risk window. SCIM deprovisioning eliminates this gap. Critical for compliance: HIPAA/PCI-DSS require timely access revocation upon employment termination.* <br>

1373. [ CloudHSM ] A company needs to sign code (software releases) using an HSM-backed signing key. The signing key must never leave the HSM. What AWS service enables this? ; AWS CloudHSM. Store RSA or ECDSA private signing key in CloudHSM. Application uses CloudHSM PKCS#11 or JCE library to perform signing operation — the key material never leaves the HSM, only the signature is returned. OR: AWS Signer (managed code signing service) for Lambda functions, IoT devices, and containers — Signer uses ACM Private CA-backed signing certificates. For custom PKI-based code signing with HSM custody: CloudHSM + custom signing workflow. For AWS-native code signing: AWS Signer. <br><br> *CloudHSM signing workflow: (1) Generate RSA-4096 or ECDSA P-256 key in CloudHSM (key_class=PRIVATE). (2) Export corresponding public key (public key CAN be exported, private key cannot). (3) Create self-signed or CA-signed certificate for the public key. (4) Distribute certificate to verifiers (embedded in build system, OS trust store). (5) Sign each release: application calls CloudHSM PKCS#11 C_Sign() with private key handle → CloudHSM returns signature → bundle signature with release artifact.* <br> *AWS Signer: managed code signing for Lambda (deployment packages), IoT Greengrass components, container images. Signer uses signing profiles with validity periods. Signer stores signing certificate in ACM (not CloudHSM). Not suitable for custom code signing with customer-controlled HSM key. Use case: "lambda functions must be signed and verified" → AWS Signer. "Internal software releases must be signed with our corporate PKI HSM key" → CloudHSM + custom signing workflow.* <br>

1374. [ Config ] A company wants to ensure that all new EC2 instances are launched with an IAM instance profile (no EC2 without IAM role). How do you implement detection and prevention? ; Detection (Config): create custom Config rule (Lambda-based). Lambda checks `aws ec2 describe-instances` — for each instance checks if `IamInstanceProfile` is present. If absent → non-compliant finding. Schedule: on EC2 instance change. Prevention (SCP/IAM): SCP condition `"Condition":{"Null":{"ec2:InstanceProfile":"true"}}` with Deny — blocks `RunInstances` if no instance profile specified. Combined: SCP prevents launch without profile, Config detects any that slip through (e.g., instances launched before SCP). <br><br> *SCP instance profile condition: `"Effect":"Deny","Action":"ec2:RunInstances","Resource":"arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*","Condition":{"Null":{"ec2:InstanceProfile":"true"}}`. This denies EC2 launch unless an IAM instance profile is specified. Forces developers to always attach a role (even a minimal one) to every EC2 instance. Prevents anonymous EC2 instances that cannot be identified via IAM.* <br> *Why require instance profiles: EC2 without IAM role cannot use AWS APIs securely (must hard-code credentials in app = security anti-pattern). All EC2 instances should have a role, even if minimal (e.g., SSM access for Session Manager, CloudWatch Logs agent). Instance profile requirement also ensures every EC2 can be managed via SSM without hard-coded SSH keys. Security benefit: instance has known IAM identity, all its API calls are attributed to its role in CloudTrail.* <br>

1375. [ GuardDuty ] A GuardDuty finding shows an EC2 instance communicating on port 25 (SMTP) outbound. The company does not run any mail servers. What does this indicate and how do you respond? ; Finding: `Backdoor:EC2/Spambot`. The EC2 instance is likely compromised and being used to send spam/phishing emails. Immediate response: (1) Isolate the instance — modify security group to deny all outbound traffic except from the security team. (2) Capture memory forensics (snapshot, netstat, process list). (3) Check VPC Flow Logs for all outbound connections from this instance in the past 24-48 hours (data exfiltration indicators). (4) Analyze what process is listening on port 25 (installed malware). (5) Check if other instances in same VPC/SG are also affected (lateral movement). <br><br> *Port 25 in AWS: AWS by default blocks outbound port 25 on EC2 instances in VPCs (to prevent spam abuse). However, companies can request removal of this restriction for legitimate mail servers. If port 25 was never unblocked: this finding may be a false positive (GuardDuty analyzing DNS queries about SMTP, not actual SMTP connections). Verify: VPC Flow Logs for actual port 25 traffic ACCEPT entries. If no ACCEPT entries: GuardDuty detected DNS query patterns, not actual SMTP.* <br> *Containment playbook: (1) Document timeline: when did C2 communication start? (GuardDuty finding timestamp is when first detected, may not be when compromise occurred — flow logs show earlier.) (2) Scope: which instances/accounts are affected? (3) Contain: isolate affected instances. (4) Eradicate: terminate compromised instances, launch clean replacements from known-good AMIs. (5) Recover: restore service. (6) Post-incident: root cause analysis, patch vulnerability, update security controls.* <br>

1376. [ Macie ] A company uses a third-party data lake that stores Parquet files in S3 from multiple sources. Some sources include data from EU customers (GDPR). The data lake bucket policy allows access from multiple IAM roles across accounts. Macie is enabled. What findings might Macie generate? ; Two finding categories: (1) Sensitive data findings: Macie scans Parquet files → detects EU PII (names, addresses, email addresses, EU VAT IDs) → `SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal`. (2) Policy findings: bucket accessible by multiple IAM roles across accounts → `Policy:IAMUser/S3BucketSharedExternally` (if any cross-account access outside org). Macie shows bucket sensitivity score combining both finding types. <br><br> *GDPR cross-border concern: Macie detects EU PII. Policy finding shows cross-account access. Combination: EU PII accessible by accounts in non-EU regions. This is a potential GDPR Chapter V (cross-border transfer) compliance issue. Macie findings feed to Security Hub → compliance team alerted → investigate: are the cross-account roles in EU-based accounts or US-based? Are standard contractual clauses in place?* <br> *Data lake security architecture: bucket policy should use `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` conditions to restrict access to specific VPC endpoints. IAM roles should be scoped to specific prefixes (`s3:prefix` condition). Macie custom data identifier for GDPR: create identifiers for EU-specific data (French INSEE codes, German Ausweis numbers, Dutch BSN). Combine with automated quarantine: Macie finding on EU PII → Lambda → tag S3 prefix with GDPR classification → enforce object lock (retention) → restrict access to EU-region IAM roles only.* <br>


1377. [ Config ] What is the difference between Config rules with `CHANGE` trigger vs `PERIODIC` trigger? Give an example of when to use each. ; CHANGE trigger: Config evaluates the rule every time a relevant AWS resource changes (create, update, delete). Detects non-compliance immediately after a change. Good for: security groups (detect when 0.0.0.0/0 rule added immediately), S3 bucket policies, IAM policy changes. PERIODIC trigger: Config evaluates on a fixed schedule (every 1, 3, 6, 12, or 24 hours). Good for: account-wide checks that are not driven by resource changes (root MFA status, IAM password policy, checking third-party API status). <br><br> *Example CHANGE trigger: `restricted-ssh` on SecurityGroup resource type. When someone adds port 22 inbound from 0.0.0.0/0 to a SG → Config item recorded → rule evaluated immediately → non-compliant finding within seconds. Auto-remediation triggered. Without CHANGE trigger: would only detect at next periodic interval — attacker has hours to exploit the open port.* <br> *Example PERIODIC trigger: `root-account-mfa-enabled`. Root MFA is an account-wide setting, not tied to a specific resource creation/modification event. Config uses periodic evaluation (daily) to check the IAM service for root MFA status. Similarly: `iam-user-mfa-enabled` — checks all IAM users for MFA. Not triggered by a specific change event. Runs on schedule. Cost optimization: periodic rules cost less than change-triggered rules for high-frequency-changing resources (reduces evaluation count).* <br>

1378. [ GuardDuty ] What is GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring and how does it differ from VPC Flow Log analysis? ; Runtime Monitoring deploys a lightweight agent (eBPF-based) on EC2 instances, ECS containers, and EKS pods. The agent monitors: process activity (which processes are running), file system access, network connections at the process level, system calls. VPC Flow Log analysis: network metadata only (src/dst IP, port, bytes) — no information about which process or user generated the traffic. Runtime Monitoring provides context: "process `/usr/bin/wget` on EC2 instance made outbound connection to 203.0.113.5:443 at 14:32:05 by user `www-data`." <br><br> *Runtime Monitoring finding example: `Execution:EC2/NewBinaryExecuted` — a new binary was executed on EC2 that was not part of the original AMI. Could indicate malware dropping a new executable. Flow logs cannot detect this — they only see the resulting network traffic. Runtime Monitoring detects it at the execution level, even before network activity starts.* <br> *Agent deployment: ECS — add GuardDuty agent as a sidecar container (managed by GuardDuty, no manual install). EKS — DaemonSet deployed by GuardDuty. EC2 — SSM agent must be installed, GuardDuty deploys its agent via SSM. Performance overhead: lightweight eBPF agent, ~2-5% CPU overhead. For performance-sensitive workloads: test overhead before enabling. Cost: Runtime Monitoring billed per vCPU-hour monitored.* <br>

1379. [ Macie ] Can Macie scan EFS (Elastic File System), DynamoDB, or RDS for sensitive data? ; No. Macie is S3-only. It scans only Amazon S3 object storage. For other data stores: EFS — no native AWS managed scanning service, use third-party DLP tools or custom Lambda + regex scanning. DynamoDB — no native scanning, custom Lambda exporting to S3 + Macie, or custom regex scanning. RDS — no native scanning, use Glue/Lambda to export data to S3 + Macie, or database-native tools. For comprehensive data discovery across all data stores: Macie (S3) + custom tooling for other services. <br><br> *Why S3 only: Macie was originally designed for S3 and the team has not expanded it. S3 is the most common destination for data lakes and bulk storage where PII most frequently lands accidentally. Other services (DynamoDB, RDS) have structured schemas that make it easier to classify data at design time.* <br> *Workaround for DynamoDB/RDS: (1) AWS Glue job exports DynamoDB/RDS data to S3 (parquet/JSON). (2) Macie scans the S3 export. (3) Findings reference S3 object, not original data source. (4) Correlate back to source. This approach works for periodic compliance audits but not continuous monitoring. Amazon Comprehend (AI/NLP service) can detect PII in text data from any source — another option for RDS text columns.* <br>

1380. [ Control Tower ] A company sets up Control Tower. What accounts are created automatically by Control Tower in the Security OU? What is each account used for? ; Control Tower creates two accounts in the Security OU: (1) Log Archive Account: dedicated S3 bucket receiving ALL CloudTrail logs and Config snapshots from all org accounts. Read-only access for most users — only security/audit team can access. S3 Object Lock ensures logs cannot be deleted or modified. (2) Audit Account (also called Security Tooling account): runs security services centrally. Cross-account read-only roles in every member account (auditors use these). GuardDuty delegated admin, Security Hub delegated admin, Config aggregator typically deployed here. <br><br> *Log Archive account isolation: this account has minimal IAM access — only the AWS services (CloudTrail, Config) can write to it. No developers have access. SCPs prevent deletion of the S3 bucket or objects. Even the management account cannot delete Log Archive data (SCP blocks it). This ensures audit logs are available for investigation even after a security incident affecting the management account.* <br> *Audit account cross-account roles: Control Tower creates `AWSControlTowerExecution` role in every member account. This role trusts the Audit account — allows audit account to assume the role and perform security investigations in any member account. SecurityAudit permission set in Identity Center maps to this role. Without this role: auditors cannot access member accounts without separate per-account IAM user setup.* <br>

1381. [ Security Hub ] A company wants Security Hub findings to automatically create ServiceNow incidents for CRITICAL findings and Jira tickets for HIGH findings, with different assignment rules. What is the architecture? ; EventBridge rules on Security Hub findings: Rule 1: `detail.findings[0].Severity.Label = CRITICAL` → Lambda → ServiceNow API: create Priority 1 incident, assign to security-oncall team. Rule 2: `detail.findings[0].Severity.Label = HIGH` → Lambda → Jira API: create issue in SEC project, assign based on `detail.findings[0].Resources[0].Type` (EC2 → infra team, S3 → data team). Lambda enrichment: add asset owner (from AWS Organizations account tags), affected service name, remediation guidance. <br><br> *Lambda enrichment value: raw Security Hub finding has resource ARN but no business context. Lambda lookups: (1) Get account ID from finding → call Organizations API → get account name and tags (team owner). (2) Get EC2 instance ID → call EC2 API → get instance tags (application, environment). (3) Look up remediation playbook URL from internal wiki API. Enriched ticket: "EC2 i-xxx (Application: PaymentService, Owner: payments-team@company.com) has CRITICAL GuardDuty finding: cryptocurrency miner detected. Runbook: wiki.company.com/security/crypto-miner-response."* <br> *Deduplication: Lambda checks Jira/ServiceNow for existing open ticket for same finding ID before creating duplicate. Security Hub finding ID is persistent — same configuration issue generates the same finding ID. Lambda: query Jira for `labels IN [finding-id]` → if exists: add comment + update severity. If not: create new ticket. Prevents multiple tickets for the same ongoing issue.* <br>

1382. [ Access Analyzer ] An IAM role has a trust policy with `"Principal":"*"` (wildcard — any AWS principal can assume it). What is the risk and how does IAM Access Analyzer handle this? ; Risk: ANY AWS account in the world can call `sts:AssumeRole` on this role. If the role has any permissions, an attacker can assume it and use those permissions. This is effectively a public IAM role — critical severity misconfiguration. IAM Access Analyzer generates a finding: `ExternalAccess`, resource=IAM Role, principal=`*` (Public), action=`sts:AssumeRole`. Finding severity: CRITICAL (public principal). Immediate remediation required: restrict the trust policy to specific account IDs or remove the wildcard. <br><br> *How wildcard trust happens: developers sometimes copy a Lambda execution role trust policy and accidentally leave `"Principal":"*"` instead of `"Principal":{"Service":"lambda.amazonaws.com"}`. Or testing trust and forgetting to restrict before deploying to production. IAM Access Analyzer catches this immediately upon role creation.* <br> *IAM Access Analyzer automated response for wildcard trust: EventBridge rule on Access Analyzer finding with `principal.type = Public` → Lambda → `aws iam update-assume-role-policy` to remove the wildcard → alert security team. The role is neutered immediately before any attacker can discover and abuse it. Also: CloudTrail alert on `iam:CreateRole` or `iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy` where the role policy contains `"Principal":"*"` — catches it at creation time, even before Access Analyzer evaluates.* <br>

1383. [ ACM ] A company migrates from a self-managed Apache web server with Let's Encrypt certificates to an AWS ALB + EC2 architecture. What certificate strategy do they use with ACM? ; Use ACM-managed public certificate for the ALB HTTPS listener. (1) Request ACM public certificate for the domain (DNS validation with Route 53 — automatic CNAME creation). (2) Associate ACM cert with ALB HTTPS listener. (3) Route 53 Alias record → ALB. (4) EC2 instances behind ALB: no TLS needed (HTTP only between ALB and EC2, or use ACM Private CA for internal TLS if required). Benefits gained: free cert, automatic renewal (no certbot cronjob), no private key on EC2 instances, no cert expiry incidents. <br><br> *Let's Encrypt migration path: existing Let's Encrypt cert expires → ACM cert takes over at ALB level. Or: immediately switch to ACM cert, point DNS to ALB, configure ALB HTTPS listener with ACM cert, terminate Let's Encrypt at server → Apache on EC2 no longer handles TLS. ALB handles all TLS. EC2 runs HTTP internally (ALB to EC2). Security of internal HTTP: in same VPC, no internet exposure, ALB enforces HTTPS externally.* <br> *For internal EC2 TLS (EC2 to EC2, or ALB to EC2 with encrypted internal traffic): ACM Private CA issues private certs (exportable, installable on EC2). This provides end-to-end encryption: client → ALB (ACM public cert) → EC2 (ACM Private CA cert). More complex but satisfies "encrypt everything" requirements. Cost: $400/CA/month + $0.75/cert. Worth it for regulated environments (financial, healthcare).* <br>

1384. [ Config ] What is AWS Config Proactive Compliance? How is it different from reactive Config rules? ; Proactive compliance evaluates resources BEFORE they are created (at CloudFormation template authoring time or pre-deployment). Uses AWS CloudFormation Guard or Config proactive rules with CloudFormation hooks. If the resource configuration would be non-compliant → deployment blocked. Reactive compliance (standard Config rules): evaluates AFTER the resource is created/changed. Resource exists in non-compliant state until Config detects and remediation runs. Proactive: "prevent the misconfiguration." Reactive: "detect and fix the misconfiguration." <br><br> *CloudFormation Guard: declarative rule language for validating CloudFormation templates. Write rules like: `rule s3_bucket_encrypted { aws_s3_bucket.properties.BucketEncryption exists }`. Run in CI/CD pipeline: `cfn-guard validate --data template.yaml --rules s3-rules.guard`. Fails pipeline if template violates rules. Never deploys the non-compliant resource. Config proactive rules integrate with CloudFormation natively.* <br> *Combined prevention strategy: proactive (CloudFormation Guard in CI/CD, Config proactive rules) + reactive (Config rules + remediation) + preventive (SCPs). Three layers: (1) At code time: Guard rejects bad templates in CI/CD. (2) At deployment time: Config proactive rule blocks CloudFormation deployment. (3) At runtime: Config reactive rule detects resources created via console/CLI (not CloudFormation). SCP: prevents console/CLI resource creation that bypasses CloudFormation. Full coverage: no non-compliant resource should exist.* <br>

1385. [ Identity Center ] What are the MFA options in IAM Identity Center? Which is most phishing-resistant and why? ; MFA options in Identity Center: (1) TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password): Google Authenticator, Authy, Microsoft Authenticator. 6-digit code changes every 30 seconds. Not phishing-resistant — MITM attacker can relay TOTP in real-time (real-time phishing). (2) WebAuthn/FIDO2: hardware security keys (YubiKey, Titan Key), biometric (Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello), passkeys. Cryptographically bound to the origin URL — cannot be used on fake login pages. Most phishing-resistant. (3) Email OTP: fallback. Lowest security. <br><br> *WebAuthn phishing resistance: the WebAuthn credential is cryptographically bound to the specific domain (e.g., d-xxx.awsapps.com). When the authenticator signs the challenge, it includes the origin (domain). If a phishing site at d-xxx.awsapps.com.evil.com tries to relay the WebAuthn authentication: the authenticator detects origin mismatch and refuses to sign. The phishing attack fails even if the user enters their password on the fake site.* <br> *TOTP real-time phishing: attacker creates a convincing fake Identity Center login page. User enters username/password/TOTP → attacker immediately uses these credentials on the real Identity Center → session established. User sees an error on fake page. Attacker has active AWS session. This attack takes < 30 seconds (within TOTP validity window). For privileged access (AdminAccess permission sets, SecurityAudit, finance roles): mandate WebAuthn/FIDO2. For general access: TOTP acceptable as minimum.* <br>

1386. [ GuardDuty ] A company has GuardDuty enabled but wants to ensure their internal penetration testing does not generate false-positive findings. How do they configure this? ; Two approaches: (1) Trusted IP List: add the IP addresses of the pentest team or pentest tool to a GuardDuty trusted IP list. GuardDuty will not generate findings for traffic from/to these IPs. Limitation: only works for network-based findings, IAM-based findings (anomalous behavior) may still fire. (2) Suppression Rules: create suppression rules that automatically archive findings from specific IPs, instances, or accounts during the pentest window. (3) Notify GuardDuty team: during pentest, create suppression rule for pentest scope, remove after pentest ends. <br><br> *Trusted IP list vs threat intelligence list: trusted IP list = whitelist (never generate findings for these IPs). Threat intelligence list = blacklist (always generate findings for these IPs, in addition to built-in intelligence). Trusted IP list is ideal for: pentest vendors, internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys), monitoring systems. Limit: max 2,000 IPs per trusted IP list file, one list per GuardDuty detector.* <br> *Alternative: GuardDuty suppression rules (preferred for temporary scenarios). Suppression rule: automatically archive findings matching specific criteria (source IP, resource ID, finding type). Create suppression rule before pentest: `FindingType = Recon:EC2/* AND SourceDetails.IpAddressV4 = pentest-IP-range`. Remove suppression rule after pentest. Advantage over trusted IP: time-limited, audit-trailed, does not permanently whitelist the pentest IP.* <br>

1387. [ Macie ] A company wants to implement automated data lifecycle for S3 objects detected as containing PII. Objects older than 90 days with PII should be automatically deleted. How do you implement this? ; Macie finding → EventBridge → Lambda: (1) Lambda receives Macie `SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal` finding. (2) Lambda adds object tag: `DataClassification=PII`, `MACIEDetectedDate=2026-11-01`. (3) S3 Lifecycle Policy on bucket: `Filter: Tag = DataClassification: PII, Transition/Expiration: after 90 days`. S3 lifecycle automatically deletes tagged objects 90 days after detection. Alternatively: Lambda immediately tags the BUCKET (not object) and the lifecycle rule applies to all current and future PII-tagged objects. <br><br> *Object-level tagging limitation: S3 lifecycle rules can filter by object tags. Lambda tags each individual PII-containing object → lifecycle rule expires tagged objects after 90 days from tagging date. This requires Lambda execution permission: `s3:PutObjectTagging`. Consider: if the object is in a versioned bucket, lifecycle deletes current version → adds delete marker → older versions remain. Add lifecycle rule for noncurrent versions expiration too.* <br> *Compliance consideration: before implementing automatic deletion, verify it complies with data retention requirements. GDPR requires deletion of personal data when no longer needed — supports this automation. But: some regulations require minimum retention (e.g., financial records 7 years, healthcare 7+ years). PII deletion policy must balance GDPR erasure right against retention legal requirements. Tag objects with both data type AND applicable regulation — different lifecycle rules per regulation.* <br>

1388. [ Control Tower ] Can Control Tower manage accounts in multiple AWS regions simultaneously? What is the Control Tower home region? ; Control Tower has a home region (selected at setup) where its management infrastructure runs. Account Factory and the Control Tower console operate from the home region. Control Tower CAN manage accounts across all regions via: (1) SCPs applying org-wide regardless of region. (2) Config rules deployed to all opted-in regions. (3) CloudTrail organization trail covering all regions. Control Tower does NOT have multi-home-region support — there is exactly one home region. But the governance it enforces (SCPs, Config) operates in all enabled regions. <br><br> *Governed regions: Control Tower allows you to select which regions are "governed" (have Config recording, Control Tower guardrails applied). New regions can be added as governed regions after initial setup. Ungoverned regions: Config may not record, guardrails may not apply — security gap if workloads exist there.* <br> *Exam point: "Control Tower home region is us-east-1. Company also runs workloads in eu-central-1. Are workloads in eu-central-1 governed?" Yes — if eu-central-1 is added as a governed region in Control Tower. Control Tower deploys Config recorders and guardrails to eu-central-1 across all accounts. The home region being us-east-1 does not mean eu-central-1 is ungoverned — region governance is a separate configuration.* <br>

1389. [ Access Analyzer ] A company generates IAM policies using IAM Access Analyzer policy generation. After applying the generated policy, some Lambda functions break with AccessDenied errors. What is the most likely cause? ; The Lambda functions use code paths or features not exercised during the policy generation observation period. Policy generation is based on ACTUAL CloudTrail-observed API calls. If the Lambda has error-handling code paths (called only when errors occur), seasonal features (called only during month-end processing), or rarely-executed branches — these API calls were never observed → not in the generated policy → AccessDenied when these paths execute for the first time after policy application. <br><br> *Mitigation: extend the observation period to cover at least one full business cycle (month-end, quarter-end, peak season, error conditions). Alternatively: run the Lambda with injected errors and edge cases in a staging environment during the observation period. After applying the generated policy: monitor CloudTrail for AccessDenied events on the Lambda role — add missing permissions incrementally.* <br> *Best practice for policy generation: (1) Generate policy after extended observation (30-90 days minimum for complex Lambdas). (2) Apply in staging first. (3) Run full integration test suite. (4) Monitor for AccessDenied errors for 30 days. (5) Add missing permissions via additive changes. (6) Apply to production. Never apply generated policies directly to production Lambda without staging validation. The generated policy is a starting point, not a guaranteed complete policy.* <br>

1390. [ Security Hub ] A company receives Security Hub findings about `S3.2: S3 buckets should prohibit public read access`. They know some buckets are intentionally public (static website hosting). How do they prevent these findings from cluttering their dashboard? ; Create Security Hub suppression rules for the specific bucket ARNs that are intentionally public. Suppression: filter `ProductName=Security Hub`, `ComplianceStatus=FAILED`, `ResourceId=arn:aws:s3:::my-public-website-bucket`, `Title CONTAINS S3.2`. Suppressed findings: status=SUPPRESSED, hidden from default view. Document the justification in the suppression rule description. Alternative: add resource-level exception to Config rule `s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited` (scope the rule to exclude specific bucket names). <br><br> *Suppression vs archiving: Security Hub suppression = rule-based, automatic, ongoing. New findings for the suppressed resource automatically get status=SUPPRESSED. Manual archiving = one-time, finding-specific. Use suppression rules for known exceptions (public website bucket will always be non-compliant — suppress automatically). Use manual archive for transient exceptions (will be fixed in 30 days — archive now, resolve later).* <br> *Security Hub exceptions management: maintain an exceptions register (spreadsheet or ticketing system) with: bucket ARN, business justification, risk acceptance sign-off (CISO), review date (annual). Security Hub suppression rule references the exception ID in description. Annual review: verify the exception still applies — website bucket still intentional? If decommissioned: remove suppression rule. This is formal risk acceptance documentation required for compliance audits.* <br>

1391. [ ACM ] What is ACM Private CA and when should it be used instead of ACM public certificates? ; ACM Private CA: private PKI service for issuing certificates to internal resources. Use when: (1) Need exportable certificates (for EC2, on-premises, IoT devices). (2) mTLS requiring client certificates. (3) Internal services not reachable from internet (cannot have public CA validate). (4) Short-lived certificates (hours/days) for zero-trust or rotation. (5) Non-standard SAN types (IP SANs, custom OIDs). ACM public certs: for internet-facing services (ALB, CloudFront, API GW), free, no management overhead, cannot be exported. <br><br> *Short-lived certs use case: zero-trust architectures issue certificates valid for 24 hours. Even if compromised, the cert expires within 24 hours. No need for certificate revocation (CRL/OCSP) — short validity makes revocation moot. ACM Private CA supports issuing certs with 1-day or 1-hour validity. High issuance rate requires: Private CA with higher throughput mode ($200/month extra) for > 25 certs/second.* <br> *IP SAN certificates: ACM public certificates support domain names only (no IP address as SAN). ACM Private CA can issue certificates with IP SANs (e.g., cert for 10.0.1.5 internal service). Required for services accessed directly by IP (not DNS) within VPCs. Also: custom OIDs in certificates for specialized applications (healthcare HL7, SCADA systems) — only possible with Private CA.* <br>

1392. [ Config ] A company deploys a conformance pack for CIS AWS Benchmark Level 1 to their 100-account organization. The deployment fails in 15 accounts. What are the most common causes? ; Common failure causes: (1) Config not enabled in those 15 accounts — conformance pack requires Config recorder. (2) S3 delivery bucket for Config not configured or missing bucket policy allowing Config to write. (3) IAM role for Config recorder missing required permissions. (4) Account does not have required services enabled (e.g., some CIS controls check CloudTrail — if CloudTrail disabled, rule cannot evaluate). (5) Service Quotas: too many Config rules already in the account (default limit: 150 rules per account). <br><br> *Troubleshooting deployment failure: `aws configservice describe-organization-conformance-pack-statuses --organization-conformance-pack-names CIS-Benchmark` → shows status per account: CREATE_FAILED with error message. Common error: `InsufficientPermissionsException` — Config role lacks permission for the rule evaluation. Fix: update Config recorder IAM role with required permissions.* <br> *Config recorder prerequisite automation: when deploying org conformance pack from delegated admin, ensure all accounts have Config recorder enabled. Use AWS Systems Manager State Manager with document `AWSQuickSetup-ConfigurationRecorder` to ensure Config recorder is enabled in all accounts. Or: Organizations Config recorder deployment (auto-enables Config in all accounts). Without this: conformance pack deployment to accounts without Config recorder fails predictably.* <br>

1393. [ GuardDuty ] What is the difference between GuardDuty threat intelligence lists and trusted IP lists? ; Threat intelligence list: list of known malicious IP addresses. GuardDuty generates findings for ANY communication with IPs on this list, even if the traffic would not otherwise trigger a finding. Extends GuardDuty with organization-specific or commercial threat intel. Trusted IP list: list of IP addresses to NEVER generate findings for. Traffic from/to these IPs is ignored. Used for: pentest IPs, internal security scanners, known partner IPs generating high traffic. Maximum 2,000 IPs per list. One list active per detector. <br><br> *Threat intelligence list use case: subscribe to a commercial threat intel feed (Recorded Future, Mandiant). Export malicious IPs as a text file (one IP per line). Upload to S3. Configure GuardDuty to use this list: `aws guardduty create-threat-intel-set --detector-id xxx --format TXT --location s3://bucket/malicious-ips.txt --activate true`. GuardDuty generates findings for any communication with these IPs immediately. Update the S3 file regularly as new malicious IPs are added to the feed.* <br> *Trusted IP list operational use: company runs monthly Nessus vulnerability scans from a dedicated IP range (10.50.0.0/24). Without trusted IP list: every scan triggers GuardDuty Recon findings. Security team spends hours suppressing them. With trusted IP list: scan IPs added → no findings for scanner IPs. But: if the scanner is compromised and starts real attacks from those IPs, GuardDuty will NOT generate findings (trusted list blindspot). Review trusted IP list regularly — remove IPs no longer in use.* <br>

1394. [ Macie ] How does Macie integration with AWS Organizations work? Who manages Macie across the org? ; Designate an AWS account as Macie delegated administrator (usually Security or Audit account). From management account: `aws macie2 enable-organization-admin-account --admin-account-id SECURITY_ACCOUNT`. From delegated admin account: `aws macie2 enable-organization-admin-account` or via Macie console → auto-enable Macie in all current and future member accounts. Delegated admin: configures discovery settings, classification jobs, custom identifiers for all accounts. Member accounts: cannot disable Macie or change org-wide settings. All findings flow to delegated admin account. <br><br> *Auto-enable for new accounts: when a new account joins the organization, Macie is automatically enabled in it (if configured in delegated admin). No manual action per account. This ensures every new account is immediately protected. Configuration: delegated admin → Auto-enable settings → enable for new accounts with selected protection plan.* <br> *Cross-account data sensitivity: Macie in member accounts scans S3 buckets in those accounts. Findings go to the delegated admin. The actual S3 data stays in the member account — Macie findings contain snippets/samples but not full object contents. Delegated admin can see: which S3 objects contain PII, bucket sensitivity scores, policy violations — without having access to the actual S3 data. Privacy-preserving central visibility.* <br>

1395. [ Security Hub ] A company uses Splunk as their primary SIEM. They want Security Hub findings to flow into Splunk automatically. What are the two integration approaches? ; Approach 1 (Security Hub → Splunk): Security Hub → EventBridge → Kinesis Data Firehose → Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC). All findings pushed to Splunk in near-real-time. Firehose handles batching, retry, and delivery. Approach 2 (Splunk AWS Add-on): Splunk AWS Add-on pulls Security Hub findings via API polling. `aws securityhub get-findings` → Splunk ingests on schedule (every 1 minute). Push (Approach 1) is preferred for low-latency near-real-time. Pull (Approach 2) is simpler to configure. <br><br> *Firehose → Splunk HEC: Firehose has native Splunk destination support. Configure: Splunk HEC endpoint URL + HEC token. Firehose handles: batching (buffer 5MB or 5 minutes), retry (on HTTP 429/500), S3 backup for failed events. ASFF finding is the event — parse in Splunk using AWS Security Hub add-on for Splunk (field extractions pre-built). Results: Security Hub findings in Splunk within 2-3 minutes of generation.* <br> *Bidirectional integration: Splunk can also SEND findings to Security Hub (via `BatchImportFindings` API). If Splunk detects something from its own log analysis (not AWS-native): create a finding in Security Hub → centralized tracking → EventBridge automation. This makes Security Hub the authoritative finding store even for non-AWS security tools. Useful for organizations that want Security Hub as their security-tool-of-record regardless of original detection source.* <br>

1396. [ Access Analyzer ] What is the difference between IAM Access Analyzer external access analysis and unused access analysis? ; External access analysis: examines resource-based policies (S3 bucket policies, IAM role trust policies, KMS key policies, etc.) to find resources accessible by principals OUTSIDE the zone of trust (account or org). Proactive — runs continuously. Unused access analysis: examines IAM identity-based policies to find IAM entities (users, roles) with permissions they have never used, or have not used recently (last 90 days). Helps right-size over-permissive IAM. Reactive — based on historical CloudTrail data. External access: "who can reach in." Unused access: "who has more permission than they use." <br><br> *Unused access finding types: `UNUSED_PERMISSION` — IAM entity has granted actions never called in CloudTrail. `UNUSED_ROLE` — IAM role has not been assumed in 90 days. `UNUSED_IAM_USER_ACCESS_KEY` — access key not used in 90 days. `UNUSED_IAM_USER_PASSWORD` — console password not used in 90 days. Each finding includes the specific unused permissions and resources, enabling surgical permission removal.* <br> *Cost: external access analysis via IAM Access Analyzer is FREE (basic analyzer). Unused access analyzer has a cost per IAM resource analyzed per month (~$0.20/IAM entity/month as of 2025). For large organizations with many IAM roles: costs can add up. Prioritize: enable unused access analyzer for accounts with sensitive data or privileged roles first. Free external access analysis: always enable (no cost, high security value).* <br>

1397. [ ACM ] A company needs to verify that ACM auto-renewal will work before their current certificate expires in 30 days. How do they test this? ; Cannot force ACM renewal (no manual trigger). Verification options: (1) Confirm DNS CNAME record exists and resolves correctly: `nslookup _abc123.example.com` should return the ACM validation value. (2) Check ACM console: certificate status → "Renewal status" → should show "Pending" (if 60-day window not yet reached) or "Success." (3) AWS CLI: `aws acm describe-certificate --certificate-arn xxx` → check `RenewalSummary.RenewalStatus`. If status `PENDING_VALIDATION` with reason `DNS_NOT_VALIDATED` → CNAME record missing → fix immediately. If `SUCCEEDED` → auto-renewal will complete. <br><br> *Renewal status states: `PENDING_AUTO_RENEWAL` (in renewal window, not yet attempted), `PENDING_VALIDATION` (attempted but CNAME check failed — action required), `SUCCESS` (renewed), `FAILED` (renewal failed, manual intervention required). CloudWatch alarm on ACM certificate expiry: `aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --metric-name DaysToExpiry --alarm-threshold 30` → alerts 30 days out.* <br> *Proactive renewal test: request a NEW ACM cert for the same domain using DNS validation. If the validation CNAME resolves correctly and the new cert issues successfully within minutes → DNS validation infrastructure works → auto-renewal will work. Delete the test cert after validation confirmed. This tests the full validation flow without impacting the production cert. Useful for post-migration validation (DNS zone migration, Route 53 hosted zone transfer, etc.).* <br>

1398. [ Config ] A company wants to use AWS Config to track configuration changes to their RDS instances over 90 days for a compliance audit. Config was enabled 60 days ago. How do they handle the 30-day gap? ; Gap in Config history: Config can only show configuration history from the date it was enabled. The 30-day gap (before Config was enabled) has no Config records — no retroactive history. Options: (1) Accept the limitation: document that Config was enabled 60 days ago and history is available from that date. (2) Supplement with CloudTrail: CloudTrail has RDS API call history (ModifyDBInstance, CreateDBSnapshot, etc.) for the full retention period (default 90 days for event history, longer if trail to S3). CloudTrail shows WHO changed WHAT, though not full config snapshots. <br><br> *Best practice: enable Config at account creation via Control Tower Account Factory / Organizations Config recorder. Never face a gap in Config history. For new compliance requirements: enable Config immediately, not retroactively. The 90-day history starts accumulating from enablement.* <br> *CloudTrail as partial substitute for Config gaps: CloudTrail ModifyDBInstance events show parameter changes (engine version, instance class, multi-AZ). Not as comprehensive as Config snapshots (Config captures full configuration state including parameter groups, subnet groups, security groups, etc.). For audit: combine Config history (from enablement) with CloudTrail history (full period) to give the most complete picture. Explicitly document the gap and its coverage in the audit report.* <br>

1399. [ Identity Center ] A company has IAM Identity Center with Azure AD as external IdP. A user logs in successfully but cannot see any AWS accounts in the portal. What is the most likely cause? ; User is not a member of any group that has Identity Center account assignments. Login works (Azure AD authentication succeeded via SAML). But without a group assignment to a permission set and account, the user has zero account access — empty portal. Solution: (1) Verify user is in Azure AD groups that are synced to Identity Center via SCIM. (2) In Identity Center: check if those groups have account assignments (group → permission set → account). (3) If group is in Identity Center but has no assignment: add assignment. (4) Provision the assignment (wait for sync). <br><br> *SCIM sync required: user in Azure AD must be in a group that is in scope for SCIM provisioning to Identity Center. If the group is not in the SCIM provisioning scope (not added to the Identity Center Enterprise Application in Azure AD): group does not exist in Identity Center → no assignments → user sees empty portal. Fix: add group to the Azure AD Enterprise Application for AWS Identity Center.* <br> *Troubleshooting steps: Identity Center console → Users → find user → check "Group memberships" tab. If groups are missing: SCIM is not syncing them. Azure AD → Enterprise App → IAM Identity Center → Provisioning → check which groups are in scope. Identity Center console → Groups: if the group exists but has no assignments → create assignment. Permission set provisioning: after assignment is created, it must be provisioned to the account — status shows "Provisioned" when complete.* <br>

1400. [ Security Hub ] What is the difference between Security Hub and AWS Config in terms of compliance checking? When does Security Hub use Config? ; Security Hub security standards use Config rules to perform compliance checks. When you enable a Security Hub standard (e.g., CIS Benchmark): Security Hub creates Config rules in the account (visible in Config console). These Config rules evaluate resources and report compliance. Security Hub aggregates the Config rule findings and presents them as Security Hub findings under the applicable standard. Config must be enabled for Security Hub standards to work. Without Config: Security Hub can still aggregate GuardDuty/Macie/Inspector findings, but cannot run configuration-based compliance standards. <br><br> *Config rules created by Security Hub: named `securityhub-CONTROL-ID-xxxx` (e.g., `securityhub-s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited-abc123`). They appear in Config console alongside your own Config rules. Do not delete these — they are managed by Security Hub. If you delete them: Security Hub re-creates them. They count toward your Config rule quota (150 rules/account default).* <br> *Duplication: if you already have Config rule `s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited` AND Security Hub enables `securityhub-s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited-xxx`: same check runs twice, costs double Config rule evaluations. Optimization: if using Security Hub standards, disable duplicate standalone Config rules. Or: do not enable standalone Config rules for controls covered by Security Hub standards. Cost optimization at scale: 100 accounts × 50 duplicate rule evaluations/day = significant cost savings from deduplication.* <br>


1401. [ CloudHSM ] A company asks whether CloudHSM is a regional or global service. What are the HA implications? ; CloudHSM is a regional service. HSM instances are deployed in a VPC within a specific region. A CloudHSM cluster contains HSMs in multiple AZs within the same region — but all in one region. For multi-region HA: deploy separate CloudHSM clusters in each region with separate key material. Key synchronization across regions is NOT automatic — must implement manual synchronization or cross-region key backup procedures. Global HA requires: CloudHSM cluster in each active region, application-level key management for cross-region operations. <br><br> *CloudHSM within-region HA: 2+ HSMs in 2+ AZs. CloudHSM client load-balances across all cluster HSMs. HSM failure: client automatically routes to remaining HSMs. Single AZ failure: remaining AZ HSM handles all traffic. For within-region: 2 HSMs is minimum HA. Recommended: 3 HSMs (1 per AZ in 3-AZ region) for tolerance of any single HSM failure with continued HA.* <br> *Cross-region DR: if primary region fails, application fails over to DR region. DR region must have its own CloudHSM cluster with the same or equivalent key material. Key synchronization: CloudHSM backup/restore (CloudHSM backup to S3 → restore in DR region cluster). Backup is encrypted with CloudHSM hardware, HSM-specific — not portable to KMS or other HSM vendors. Test restore regularly. RPO: time since last backup. RTO: time to restore cluster + deploy from backup.* <br>

1402. [ ACM ] An API Gateway uses a custom domain name. The company changes their certificate from an imported self-signed cert to an ACM-managed cert. What steps are required and is there any downtime? ; Steps: (1) Request ACM cert for the custom domain (DNS validation). (2) Wait for ACM cert to be issued (minutes with DNS validation). (3) In API Gateway: update the custom domain name to use the new ACM cert ARN instead of the imported cert. (4) API Gateway updates immediately — clients receive the new cert on the next TLS handshake. No deployment needed. No downtime: TLS connections in progress complete with old cert, new connections use new cert. Old imported cert can be deleted from ACM after transition confirmed. <br><br> *API Gateway custom domain update: `aws apigateway update-domain-name --domain-name api.example.com --patch-operations op=replace,path=/certificateArn,value=arn:aws:acm:...`. For Regional API Gateway: the cert must be in the same region. For Edge-Optimized: cert must be in us-east-1. Zero-downtime cert swap is possible because API Gateway handles the transition gracefully.* <br> *Certificate deprecation: imported cert in ACM can be deleted after the custom domain points to the ACM-managed cert. Verify: `aws apigateway get-domain-name --domain-name api.example.com` shows new cert ARN. CloudWatch: no TLS error rate increase after switch. Wait 24 hours before deleting old imported cert (cached connections, CDN edge caches may still use old cert for a brief period). After 24 hours: imported cert deletion is safe.* <br>

1403. [ Config ] A company wants to use AWS Config to verify that all Lambda functions use the latest runtime version. AWS Config does not have a managed rule for this. How do they implement it? ; Create a custom AWS Config rule using Lambda: (1) Write Lambda function that calls `lambda:ListFunctions`, checks each function runtime against the latest supported versions. (2) Deploy Lambda function. (3) Create Config custom rule: trigger on Lambda function configuration changes, evaluate using the Lambda function. (4) Non-compliant finding: Lambda function using deprecated runtime (e.g., Python 3.7 when 3.11+ is available). Auto-remediation: SSM Automation calls `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` to change runtime. <br><br> *Custom Config rule Lambda: receives event with `invokingEvent` (Config item for the evaluated resource). For Lambda runtime check: Config evaluates AWS::Lambda::Function resource type. Lambda function extracts `runtime` field from Config item → compares to list of supported runtimes → returns compliance status (COMPLIANT/NON_COMPLIANT). Maintain supported runtime list in a Lambda environment variable or SSM Parameter Store (update when AWS deprecates runtimes).* <br> *Runtime update complexity: changing Lambda runtime requires testing (runtime behavior differences between Python 3.7 and 3.11). SSM Automation can update the runtime configuration, but cannot test the function. Better auto-remediation: create a notification (SNS/Slack) for non-compliant functions rather than auto-updating. Human reviews and updates Lambda code + runtime together. Config rule = detection + notification. Human = update with testing. Full auto-remediation for runtime is risky — could break Lambda functions without testing.* <br>

1404. [ GuardDuty ] A company enables GuardDuty EKS Audit Log Monitoring. What threats can it detect that VPC Flow Log analysis cannot? ; EKS Audit Log Monitoring detects Kubernetes-specific attacks: (1) `Execution:EKS/ExecInKubernetes` — kubectl exec command run against a container (potential shell access). (2) `PrivilegeEscalation:EKS/PrivilegedContainer` — pod deployed with `securityContext.privileged: true`. (3) `Impact:EKS/SuccessfulAnonymousAccess` — Kubernetes API accessed without authentication. (4) `Persistence:EKS/ContainerWithSensitiveMount` — container with sensitive host path mounted. These are Kubernetes control-plane events invisible to VPC Flow Logs (which only see L3/L4 network traffic). <br><br> *EKS Audit Log source: Kubernetes API server audit logs (kube-apiserver). Every kubectl command, every pod creation, every RBAC binding creates an audit log entry. GuardDuty reads these from EKS directly (no CloudWatch Logs setup needed). Flow logs see: pod-to-pod traffic, pod-to-internet traffic. EKS Audit Logs see: who created which pod, what commands were run, which secrets were accessed, RBAC changes.* <br> *Combined EKS threat detection: GuardDuty EKS Audit (control plane) + GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring (data plane) + VPC Flow Logs (network). Audit: detects privilege escalation at scheduling/RBAC level. Runtime: detects malicious process execution inside containers. Flow Logs: detects C2 communication from containers. Full stack coverage. For EKS workloads: enable all three. Cost: EKS Audit Log monitoring ($per EKS node) + Runtime Monitoring ($per vCPU) + Flow Logs (S3 storage).* <br>

1405. [ Security Hub ] A company needs their Security Hub cross-region aggregation configured. They want all findings from eu-central-1, eu-west-1, us-east-1, and ap-southeast-1 to appear in a single Security Hub view in eu-central-1. How do they configure this? ; In Security Hub console in eu-central-1 (aggregation region): Configuration → Regions → Link regions → select eu-west-1, us-east-1, ap-southeast-1. Security Hub in eu-central-1 becomes the aggregation region. Linked regions send all findings to eu-central-1. All regions must have Security Hub enabled. Findings visible in eu-central-1 include the originating region in the finding metadata. <br><br> *Cross-region aggregation limitations: findings from linked regions replicated to aggregation region. Finding updates (workflow status changes) made in aggregation region propagate back to source regions. Billing: Security Hub charges in each region independently — findings counted in originating region AND in aggregation region (double billing for replicated findings). Aggregation region findings: combination of local + replicated from linked regions.* <br> *Best practice: designate aggregation region = same region as Security Hub delegated admin account. All findings flow to one place: cross-account (via delegated admin) AND cross-region (via aggregation). Security operations team works from one Security Hub view covering all accounts and all regions. EventBridge rules for automated response: deploy in aggregation region — single set of rules handles findings from all regions and accounts.* <br>

1406. [ Access Analyzer ] When Access Analyzer performs policy validation, what categories of issues does it identify? Give an example of each. ; Four categories: (1) Error: policy syntax is incorrect and would be rejected by IAM. Example: missing closing bracket in JSON, invalid action name `s3:GetObjectt` (typo). (2) Security Warning: policy is more permissive than necessary, creating security risk. Example: `"Action":"*","Resource":"*"` wildcard — overly broad. (3) Warning: policy has issues that are not security risks but deviate from best practices. Example: using a deprecated condition key. (4) Suggestion: improvement recommendations. Example: using `s3:GetObject` when `s3:GetObject*` is specified (redundant wildcard). <br><br> *Policy validation API: `aws accessanalyzer validate-policy --policy-document file://policy.json --policy-type IDENTITY_POLICY`. Returns findings list with: `findingType` (ERROR/SECURITY_WARNING/WARNING/SUGGESTION), `findingDetails` (human-readable explanation), `locations` (line/column in JSON), `learnMoreLink` (AWS docs).* <br> *Integrate in CI/CD: IAM policy changes → pull request → CI pipeline runs `validate-policy` → any ERROR or SECURITY_WARNING fails the pipeline (blocks merge). WARNING and SUGGESTION: report but do not block. This prevents deploying syntactically wrong or overly permissive policies. Combined with: `cfn-guard` for CloudFormation templates, OPA for Terraform plans. Policy-as-code: IAM policies reviewed as code, not manually.* <br>

1407. [ Macie ] A company discovers that a developer has accidentally committed AWS access keys to a public GitHub repository. The keys were also accidentally backed up to S3. How does Macie help? ; Macie detects AWS access keys in S3: managed data identifier `AWS_CREDENTIALS` matches AWS access key IDs (AKIA...) and secret access key patterns. When Macie scans the S3 backup bucket: finding `SensitiveData:S3Object/Credentials` → alerts security team → immediate action. EventBridge rule on Macie finding → Lambda: (1) Identify the AWS access key from the finding (Macie shows a sample). (2) Immediately revoke/delete the exposed key: `aws iam delete-access-key`. (3) Audit CloudTrail for any API calls made with this key SINCE the S3 object was created. (4) Rotate any resources the key had access to. <br><br> *GitHub exposure vs S3 exposure: GitHub exposure is more critical (public internet). S3 exposure is internal (assuming private bucket). AWS has an automated partner notification for GitHub — AWS scans public GitHub repos and automatically quarantines (adds deny policy to) detected AWS keys within minutes. Macie catches the S3 copy. Both detections should trigger the same key revocation response.* <br> *Key revocation timeline matters: check CloudTrail for API calls using the compromised key from the S3 object creation timestamp. If the key was in S3 for 30 days: 30 days of potential attacker usage. If CloudTrail data events not enabled: may not see S3 GetObject calls that exposed the key to an attacker. GuardDuty: may have generated `CredentialAccess:IAMUser/AnomalousBehavior` if attacker used the key from an unusual IP/location.* <br>

1408. [ Control Tower ] What is the difference between Control Tower Mandatory, Strongly Recommended, and Elective guardrails? Can Mandatory guardrails be disabled? ; Mandatory guardrails: always enforced by Control Tower, cannot be disabled. Example: "Disallow changes to CloudTrail set up by Control Tower," "Disallow deletion of log archive." These protect Control Tower integrity. Strongly Recommended: enabled by default, can be disabled (not recommended). Based on AWS best practices. Example: "Detect whether MFA for the root user is enabled." Elective: disabled by default, can be enabled per OU. For specific compliance requirements. Example: "Detect whether Amazon EBS volumes are encrypted." <br><br> *Mandatory guardrail enforcement: implemented as SCPs or AWS Lambda-backed Config rules that Control Tower re-applies if drift is detected. If someone manually removes a mandatory guardrail SCP: Control Tower detects drift → when you click "Repair" in Control Tower → re-applies the SCP. Mandatory = always present, always enforced. Cannot be disabled via Organizations console, API, or Control Tower console.* <br> *Guardrail scope: guardrails apply to specific OUs (not individual accounts). Enable/disable on OU level. Child OUs inherit parent OU guardrails. Production OU: enable many elective guardrails (EBS encryption, RDS encryption, CloudTrail enabled, VPC Flow Logs). Sandbox OU: fewer guardrails (developers need freedom to experiment). The OU hierarchy enables applying different governance levels to different environments.* <br>

1409. [ Security Audit ] A company creates a custom Identity Center permission set for database administrators. The DBAs need full RDS management but should not be able to access data (no ability to create DB instances that bypass encryption, no ability to read Secrets Manager secrets). How do you construct this? ; Custom permission set with: (1) AWS managed policy `AmazonRDSFullAccess` as baseline. (2) Inline policy with DENY for specific high-risk actions: `"Effect":"Deny","Action":["rds:CreateDBInstance","rds:RestoreDBInstanceFromDBSnapshot"],"Resource":"*","Condition":{"Bool":{"rds:StorageEncrypted":"false"}}` — prevents creating unencrypted RDS. (3) Deny `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` — cannot read credentials. (4) Deny `rds:CreateDBClusterEndpoint` for writer (prevents creating new writer endpoints, data modification path). <br><br> *Permission set inline policies: in addition to managed policies, each permission set can have inline session policies. These inline policies function as permission boundaries — further restrict what the managed policy allows. The DBA role gets RDSFullAccess (broad management) scoped down by inline denies (no unencrypted instances, no secret reading).* <br> *Fine-grained DBA access: `rds:ModifyDBInstance` (change instance class, multi-AZ) = DBA task. `rds:CreateDBInstance` = deployment task (perhaps DevOps, not DBA). `rds:DescribeDBInstances` = read metadata = DBA. `rds:Connect` (via IAM database auth) = data access = NOT DBA (handled by application credentials). Separation of duties: DBAs manage the RDS infrastructure, application teams manage data access. Never give DBAs application credentials or ability to read Secrets Manager (application database passwords).* <br>

1410. [ Config ] A company uses AWS Organizations with 200 accounts. They want to see which specific EC2 instances across ALL accounts are using deprecated AMIs. How do they query this with Config? ; Config Aggregator query using the advanced query feature (SQL-based). From the aggregator account: `SELECT accountId, awsRegion, resourceId, configuration.imageId, configuration.state.name FROM aws_ec2_instance WHERE configuration.imageId IN ('ami-xxx','ami-yyy','ami-zzz')`. This returns all EC2 instances across all 200 accounts and all regions in the aggregator using the deprecated AMI IDs. <br><br> *Config aggregator advanced query: uses SQL-like syntax against all aggregated Config items. Supports: filtering, grouping, joining (limited). Resource schema per resource type: `aws_ec2_instance`, `aws_s3_bucket`, `aws_iam_role`, etc. Check Config supported resource types documentation for schema. Query across accounts and regions simultaneously — no need to iterate each account.* <br> *Proactive AMI deprecation management: create Config rule checking for deprecated AMI IDs. When an EC2 instance uses a deprecated AMI → Config non-compliant finding → auto-create ticket for the account owner to update. EventBridge rule on Config finding → Lambda → look up account owner tag from Organizations → create Jira ticket assigned to that team. This workflow scales to 200 accounts without manual effort.* <br>

1411. [ GuardDuty ] What happens to GuardDuty findings after they are generated? How long are they retained, and how should they be archived? ; GuardDuty findings are retained for 90 days in the GuardDuty service (visible in console/API). After 90 days: automatically deleted from GuardDuty. For long-term retention: export findings to S3 via GuardDuty findings export feature (JSON format). Or: EventBridge → Firehose → S3 (real-time export). For compliance requiring 1+ year retention: S3 with Object Lock + lifecycle policies. Security Hub: ingests GuardDuty findings and retains them per Security Hub retention settings (90 days by default, configurable). CloudTrail: logs who generated/updated findings (meta-audit). <br><br> *Findings export configuration: `aws guardduty create-publishing-destination --detector-id xxx --destination-type S3 --destination-properties DestinationArn=arn:aws:s3:::guardduty-findings,KmsKeyArn=arn:aws:kms:...`. KMS CMK required for S3 export encryption. Findings exported as JSONL (one finding per line) in an S3 prefix organized by account/region/date. Athena table on this S3 data enables SQL investigation of historical findings.* <br> *Finding suppression vs archival: suppression = finding generated but immediately archived by rule (still exported to S3 and Security Hub). Archive = manually archive a specific finding after review. Suppressed findings still appear in GuardDuty export (with archived status). For compliance: all findings (including suppressed) should be exported to S3. Suppressed = policy decision, not "did not happen." Auditors may ask about suppressed findings — having them in S3 with archive reason documented satisfies audit requirements.* <br>

1412. [ ACM ] What is the difference between RSA and ECDSA certificates in ACM? When should each be used? ; RSA (2048 or 4096-bit): widely supported, computationally heavier for handshake. More CPU on server for large key sizes. RSA-2048: fast, minimum acceptable. RSA-4096: slower handshake, higher security margin. ECDSA (P-256 or P-384): mathematically based on elliptic curves. Same security at smaller key sizes (P-256 = equivalent to RSA-3072). Faster TLS handshakes, lower CPU usage. Preferred for performance-sensitive high-traffic ALBs. Downside: slightly less widely supported (very old clients may not support ECDSA). ACM supports both types for new certificate requests. <br><br> *Performance comparison: RSA-2048 TLS 1.2 handshake: ~2ms server CPU. ECDSA P-256 TLS 1.2 handshake: ~0.5ms server CPU. For ALB handling 10,000 TLS handshakes/second: RSA-2048: 20 CPU seconds/second. ECDSA P-256: 5 CPU seconds/second. ECDSA reduces TLS handshake CPU by 75%. For CloudFront and ALB (which handle massive handshake volumes): ECDSA P-256 is recommended.* <br> *Modern recommendation: ECDSA P-256 for new certificates. RSA-2048 for backward compatibility (if you have very old clients: pre-2014 Android, IE 6, very old embedded devices). Check your client fingerprints in ALB access logs to identify RSA-only clients before switching. For internal services (microservices, APIs): all modern clients support ECDSA — use P-256. For public internet-facing services with unknown client base: RSA-2048 for maximum compatibility.* <br>

1413. [ Config ] What are the costs of AWS Config and how can they be controlled in a large organization? ; Config costs: (1) $0.003 per configuration item recorded. (2) $0.001 per rule evaluation. (3) $0.0012 per conformance pack evaluation. (4) $0 for Config aggregator itself (data aggregation free). Cost control: (1) Scope recording to essential resource types only (SG, IAM, S3, KMS, EC2, VPC) — eliminates 70-80% of items. (2) Use periodic rules instead of change-triggered for infrequently-changing checks. (3) Avoid duplicate Config rules (manage via Security Hub standards to reduce duplication). (4) Exclude dev accounts from expensive conformance packs. <br><br> *Large org cost example: 200 accounts × 500 resource changes/day × $0.003 = $300/day for config items. 200 accounts × 100 rules × 100 evaluations/day × $0.001 = $2,000/day for rule evaluations. Total: ~$2,300/day = ~$69,000/month. With scope reduction (recording only 10 resource types instead of 100): $6,900/month. Significant savings from targeted recording.* <br> *Organizational Config vs per-account: Organizations Config recorder ensures all accounts have Config enabled (compliance requirement). But cannot limit recording scope per-account from org level — each account sets its own recording scope. Implement via CloudFormation StackSet: deploy Config recorder with limited ResourceTypes via StackSet to all accounts. Ensures consistent recording scope + limited cost across the org.* <br>

1414. [ Identity Center ] What is the maximum session duration for an IAM Identity Center permission set? What are the security implications of different session durations? ; Maximum session duration for Identity Center permission sets: 12 hours. Minimum: 1 hour. Default: 1 hour. Security implications: longer sessions = more convenient (fewer re-authentication prompts) but longer window if credentials are compromised. Short sessions (1-2 hours) for privileged access (AdminAccess, SecurityAudit): compromise window limited. Long sessions (8-12 hours) for read-only developer access: acceptable risk. STS temporary credential window: if stolen after login, valid until expiry. <br><br> *Session duration vs STS credential duration: Identity Center session is the portal session (how long the user stays logged into the portal). STS credential duration (per permission set) is how long the CLI/SDK temporary credentials are valid. Set BOTH in the permission set configuration. Portal session: 1-12 hours. STS credentials: 1-12 hours. Set STS credential duration shorter than portal session for privileged permission sets.* <br> *Continuous re-authentication: for critical production operations (AdminAccess, database admin, finance roles): configure short permission set duration (1 hour). User must log back into Identity Center portal to get fresh credentials. MFA re-challenge at each new session (configurable in Identity Center → MFA settings). This ensures every privileged operation is preceded by recent MFA authentication. Trade-off: operational friction vs security.* <br>

1415. [ CloudHSM ] A company wants to use CloudHSM to protect the private key of their internal Root Certificate Authority. What are the design considerations? ; Root CA key in CloudHSM: generate RSA-4096 or ECDSA P-384 key pair in CloudHSM cluster. Export public key only. Root CA key never leaves HSM. Sign Intermediate CA certificates using HSM PKCS#11 API. Root CA: kept offline (air-gapped) in some high-security designs — CloudHSM is always online (requires network access). Compromise: if CloudHSM cluster is compromised, root CA key could theoretically be used to sign malicious certs. Mitigation: M-of-N quorum authentication for root CA signing operations. <br><br> *M-of-N quorum authentication: CloudHSM supports requiring M out of N HSM users to approve high-value operations. For root CA signing: require 2-of-3 security officers to authenticate before the HSM performs the signing operation. This means an attacker with access to only one security officer credential cannot sign malicious root CA certificates. HSM quorum is a true multi-party authorization (not just IAM policy).* <br> *ACM Private CA with CloudHSM backing: create ACM Private CA and configure it to use a CloudHSM custom key store. ACM Private CA manages the PKI operations (issuance, revocation, CRL) while the key material remains in CloudHSM. This combines: ACM Private CA ease of use (managed PKI) + CloudHSM key custody (key never leaves HSM). Best of both worlds for organizations requiring managed PKI with HSM key custody.* <br>

1416. [ Security Hub ] What is a Security Hub insight and how does it differ from a finding? Give an example of a useful custom insight. ; Finding: individual security event or compliance check result (one resource, one issue, one point in time). Insight: aggregated view of related findings — grouped and sorted to surface patterns or high-risk combinations. Example custom insight: "EC2 instances with both CRITICAL GuardDuty findings AND PUBLIC exposure (security group allows 0.0.0.0/0)." This combines two finding types to identify the highest-risk instances: actively under attack AND publicly accessible. Without the insight: thousands of individual findings, no prioritization. <br><br> *Insight definition: `aws securityhub create-insight --name "Public EC2 with Critical GuardDuty" --filters FilterKey=ResourceType,Value=AwsEc2Instance,Comparison=EQUALS FilterKey=ProductName,Value=GuardDuty,Comparison=EQUALS FilterKey=Severity,Value=CRITICAL,Comparison=EQUALS --group-by-attribute ResourceId`. Insight result: EC2 instances grouped by ResourceId, showing how many CRITICAL GuardDuty findings each has. Security team focuses on instances with the most critical findings.* <br> *Built-in insights from AWS: Security Hub includes pre-built insights like "AWS resources with the most findings," "EC2 instances involved in known tactics," "S3 buckets with sensitive data and public access." These cover common prioritization needs out of the box. Custom insights fill gaps specific to your environment. Review built-in insights before creating custom ones — many needs are already covered.* <br>

1417. [ Access Analyzer ] A company uses IAM roles extensively for EC2 instance profiles. Some roles have not been used in over 180 days. How does IAM Access Analyzer identify and help clean these up? ; IAM Access Analyzer unused access analysis. Enable unused access analyzer: creates findings for IAM roles not assumed in the configured look-back period (up to 90 days). For 180-day requirement: set unused access analyzer to 90 days (maximum), accept that roles unused 91-180 days were not flagged before the analyzer was enabled — run for 90 days then re-evaluate. Findings: `UNUSED_ROLE` for each role not assumed in 90+ days. Review each finding: archive if role is intentionally idle (disaster recovery role), remove if truly unused. <br><br> *Role cleanup process: Unused role finding → Lambda: (1) Check CloudTrail for any role usage beyond 90-day Access Analyzer window. (2) Check EC2 instances using this role as instance profile: `aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=iam-instance-profile.arn,Values=arn:aws:iam::xxx:instance-profile/role-name`. If instances exist: role is in use (instance profile associated, even if no API calls made recently). (3) If no instances and no recent usage: create change request to remove role. Never auto-delete roles without human review.* <br> *Access Advisor complement: IAM Access Advisor (simpler, free) shows last-accessed service data per IAM entity. Combined: Access Analyzer (which roles unused) + Access Advisor (which services within the used roles are actually being accessed). Right-sizing: remove entire unused roles (Access Analyzer) + remove unused service permissions from used roles (Access Advisor).* <br>

1418. [ Config ] A new AWS Config rule is added to an account. When does it evaluate existing resources for the first time? ; When a new Config rule is created: Config evaluates ALL in-scope resources immediately (initial evaluation) as soon as the rule is created. For periodic rules: evaluates at the next scheduled interval. For change-triggered rules: evaluates immediately on creation (scope = all current resources), then on each resource change thereafter. Initial evaluation may show many non-compliant resources (baseline state). <br><br> *Initial evaluation use case: company has 1,000 EC2 instances. Creates Config rule `encrypted-volumes`. Config immediately evaluates all 1,000 EBS volumes — shows 350 non-compliant. Security team now has the full current non-compliance scope. From this point: new non-compliant resources (new unencrypted volumes) trigger finding immediately. Existing 350: schedule for remediation.* <br> *Resource deletion: when an EC2 instance is deleted, Config records the deletion as a Config item. Config rules evaluate the deletion event. Rules that check for resource EXISTENCE (e.g., "this critical EC2 instance must exist") generate non-compliant when the resource is deleted. Most rules focus on resource configuration, not existence — deletion does not change compliance for those rules (resource no longer exists to be evaluated).* <br>

1419. [ GuardDuty ] A GuardDuty finding is generated for account A. The affected resource is in account B (assumed via cross-account role). Which account receives the finding? ; The finding is generated in account A (the account where GuardDuty is running and observed the activity). The finding references the resource ARN in account B but appears in account A's GuardDuty findings. In a multi-account setup with delegated admin: all findings (including account A's) flow to the delegated admin (Security account). Security Hub in the Security account: shows finding associated with account A. <br><br> *Cross-account activity in GuardDuty: EC2 in account A assumes role in account B → makes API calls in account B → CloudTrail in account B records the activity → GuardDuty in account B sees the activity. If GuardDuty is in both accounts: finding could appear in BOTH accounts (account A for the outbound activity, account B for the inbound activity of the role). With org delegated admin: both findings flow to Security account, correlated by the IAM role ARN.* <br> *Forensics implication: if account A is compromised and the attacker laterally moved to account B: GuardDuty findings appear in account A (attacker origin) AND account B (where damage occurred). Investigation in Security Hub: filter by both account IDs, correlate timeline. CloudTrail in account B: shows what the attacker did via the cross-account role.
