CloudTrail in account A: shows how the attacker got the cross-account credentials (compromised role assumption event).* <br>

1420. [ Macie ] A company runs Macie on 500 S3 buckets. After one year, they realize they have not reviewed any Macie findings. The finding backlog is enormous. How do they prioritize? ; Prioritize by: (1) Severity: Critical findings first (exposed credentials: AWS keys, passwords). High: PII (SSNs, credit cards). Medium: general PII (email, names). (2) Bucket public access status: sensitive data in PUBLIC buckets = immediate critical action (data already exposed). (3) Bucket encryption status: sensitive data in unencrypted buckets = compliance gap. (4) Finding age: older unresolved findings in active buckets are higher priority (ongoing exposure). Strategy: Security Hub insight "S3 buckets with Macie critical findings AND public access" → immediate list. <br><br> *Bulk archiving: for findings older than 90 days on buckets that have since been secured (encrypted, access restricted): bulk archive these findings (they represent historical state, now remediated). Use Macie `BatchUpdateFindings` API: archive findings matching criteria (bucket ARN, finding type, created-before date). Reduces backlog to current active findings only.* <br> *Prevent future backlog: configure EventBridge rule on ALL new Macie findings → SNS notification to bucket owner (tagged in S3 bucket tags). Bucket owner gets immediate alert when PII detected in their bucket → responsibility to remediate within SLA. Security Hub for oversight: escalate unresolved findings after 7 days. This creates a self-service model where bucket owners handle their own findings, security team handles only escalations.* <br>

1421. [ Identity Center ] A company has separate AWS Organizations for production and non-production. They want employees to use the same Okta login for both. Is this possible? ; AWS Organizations supports only ONE IAM Identity Center per organization. Two separate AWS Organizations = two separate Identity Center instances. Both can connect to the same Okta IdP: (1) Create two Enterprise Applications in Okta: one for Production org Identity Center, one for Non-Production org Identity Center. (2) Configure SAML + SCIM for each. (3) Users see both applications in Okta portal — "AWS Production" and "AWS Non-Production." Single Okta login → access to both org Identity Centers. From employee perspective: one Okta login, two separate Identity Center portals. <br><br> *Management overhead: two Identity Center instances = two separate sets of permission sets to manage. Best practice: use the same naming convention and structure for permission sets in both (DevAccess, AdminAccess, ReadOnly). Groups in Okta mapped to both Identity Centers: `AWS-PROD-DevAccess` group → prod Identity Center → Dev permission set. `AWS-NONPROD-DevAccess` group → nonprod Identity Center → Dev permission set. Or use one Okta group `AWS-DevAccess` mapped to both Identity Centers.* <br> *Alternative architecture: merge the two Organizations into one using AWS Organizations account migration (complex but possible). Single Organizations = single Identity Center = single set of permission sets to manage. OUs separate production from non-production workloads. SCPs enforce environment-specific controls. This is the recommended enterprise architecture for new environments — avoid separate Organizations when possible.* <br>

1422. [ Security Hub ] A company wants to measure their security posture improvement over time using Security Hub. What metrics do they track? ; Track: (1) Security score per standard (CIS, PCI-DSS) as percentage of passing controls — trend over weeks/months. (2) Number of critical/high findings open > 7 days — measures remediation velocity. (3) Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) per finding type — identify slow-moving finding categories. (4) New findings per day — measures new security debt introduced. (5) Suppressed finding ratio — measures false positive rate of security tools. (6) Accounts reaching 100% compliance score — measures org-wide security maturity. <br><br> *Security Hub score: available per standard, per account, per region. Export via API: `aws securityhub describe-standards-controls --standards-subscription-arn xxx`. Automate weekly snapshot to DynamoDB or S3 → QuickSight dashboard showing security score trend. Targets: Q1 baseline 60%, Q2 target 75%, Q4 target 90%. Executive reporting: monthly security posture report generated automatically from Security Hub data.* <br> *MTTR calculation: Security Hub finding created timestamp vs Workflow.Status changed to RESOLVED timestamp. Lambda function: daily batch, queries Security Hub for resolved findings from last 30 days, calculates average days-to-resolve per finding type per account. High MTTR for specific finding type: investigate root cause (no remediation runbook? Complex fix? Wrong team assignment?). Low MTTR: evidence of effective security operations process.* <br>

1423. [ SQS ] A company processes financial transactions using SQS. They need guaranteed exactly-once processing and strict ordering. Which SQS configuration should they use? ; FIFO queue with Message Group ID set to the account ID. FIFO provides exactly-once processing via deduplication ID (5-minute window) and strict ordering within each Message Group ID. Standard queue cannot provide either guarantee — duplicates and out-of-order delivery are possible. <br><br> *FIFO queue name must end in `.fifo`. Throughput limit: 300 TPS without batching, 3,000 TPS with batching (10 messages per SendMessageBatch call), 70,000 TPS with High Throughput Mode enabled. For financial transactions where ordering matters per account: set Message Group ID to the account/customer ID — all transactions for the same account are strictly ordered while different accounts process in parallel.* <br> *Deduplication ID: producer generates a unique ID per transaction attempt. If the same ID is sent within 5 minutes (retry scenario), SQS silently drops the duplicate. Content-based deduplication: SQS computes SHA-256 of message body as dedup ID — useful when message body is naturally unique (transaction ID in body). Standard queue with idempotent consumer is an alternative but does NOT guarantee ordering.* <br>

1424. [ SQS ] A Lambda function processes SQS messages. The function occasionally times out after 30 seconds. Messages keep reappearing in the queue and are processed multiple times. What is the fix? ; Increase the SQS visibility timeout to at least 6x the Lambda function timeout. If Lambda times out at 30 seconds, set visibility timeout to at minimum 3 minutes (180 seconds). When Lambda times out, the message remains in the queue after the visibility timeout expires (30 seconds) and gets re-delivered before Lambda has fully cleaned up. Increasing visibility timeout gives processing time to complete or expire before re-delivery. <br><br> *Visibility timeout mechanics: when Lambda receives a message, SQS hides it for the visibility timeout duration. If Lambda does NOT delete the message within that window (due to timeout/failure), SQS makes the message visible again. With visibility timeout = 30s and Lambda timeout = 30s: Lambda times out exactly as visibility expires — race condition guarantees duplicate delivery.* <br> *Best practice: set visibility timeout = 6 * Lambda timeout. Also fix the root cause: Lambda should not time out — optimize the processing logic, use async patterns, or increase Lambda timeout. Enable `ReportBatchItemFailures` to only retry failed messages in a batch rather than the entire batch. Monitor `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage` metric — high values indicate consumer lag.* <br>

1425. [ SQS ] Messages in an SQS queue are not being processed. The queue depth is growing. The consumer EC2 fleet is healthy and running. What are the possible causes? ; Check in order: (1) All messages are in-flight (invisible) — consumer received messages but not deleting them (processing hanging, visibility timeout too long). Check `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible` metric. (2) Consumer is not calling ReceiveMessage (application bug, wrong queue URL, IAM permission issue). (3) Messages are in the DLQ, not the source queue — consumer is processing DLQ separately. (4) Queue is encrypted with KMS and consumer IAM role lacks `kms:Decrypt` permission. (5) VPC endpoint issue — consumer cannot reach SQS endpoint. <br><br> *CloudWatch metrics to diagnose: `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` (unprocessed), `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible` (in-flight/invisible), `NumberOfMessagesSent` (producer activity), `NumberOfMessagesDeleted` (consumer success). If NotVisible is high and Visible is low: messages are received but not deleted — processing is stuck. If both are low and queue depth is growing: producer is sending but receiver metrics show nothing — networking or permission issue.* <br> *Common cause: long-running processing with visibility timeout shorter than processing time. Messages become visible, other consumers receive them, duplicates processed. Meanwhile original consumer finishes and tries to delete — gets `ReceiptHandle expired` error. Fix: use `ChangeMessageVisibility` to extend timeout mid-processing, or increase queue visibility timeout.* <br>

1426. [ SQS ] A company needs to send 1MB payloads through SQS. What is the recommended approach? ; Use the SQS Extended Client Library (available for Java, Python, and other SDKs). The library automatically stores payloads exceeding the threshold (default 256KB) in S3, then sends a pointer message to SQS. The consumer uses the same library to transparently retrieve the S3 object. Alternatively: manually store the large object in S3 before sending, include the S3 bucket and key in the SQS message body, consumer retrieves from S3. <br><br> *SQS hard limit: 256KB per message including message body + attributes. This cannot be increased. Extended Client Library handles the S3 storage transparently — producer and consumer code changes are minimal (just use the library instead of standard SQS client). Library adds `software.amazon.payloadoffloading` attribute to indicate S3-backed message.* <br> *Security considerations: the S3 bucket storing large payloads must be accessible by both producer and consumer. Use a shared S3 bucket with IAM policies granting both roles access. Encrypt S3 objects with SSE-KMS matching the SQS queue encryption key. After message processing, consumer should delete the S3 object to avoid accumulation (Extended Client Library can do this automatically with `deleteMessageAlways` option).* <br>

1427. [ SQS ] A company has a FIFO queue processing orders. They have 500 consumers processing in parallel, but orders for the same customer must be processed in sequence. How do you achieve this? ; Set the Message Group ID to the customer ID. FIFO queue processes messages within each group strictly in order. Messages with different group IDs (different customers) are processed in parallel — up to 20,000 in-flight simultaneously. One customer sequential + all customers parallel = Message Group ID per customer. <br><br> *Message Group ID is the key to FIFO parallelism. Without it (all messages in one group): completely serial processing — one message at a time, no parallelism. With per-customer group IDs: 500 customers with orders simultaneously → 500 independent ordered streams, all parallel. Lambda + FIFO: Lambda creates one concurrent invocation per active Message Group ID — natural parallelism matching the group structure.* <br> *FIFO throughput with groups: with 500 active Message Group IDs and batching: 500 * 10 messages/batch = 5,000 messages potentially in flight per poll cycle. At 3,000 TPS with batching (standard FIFO): this comfortably handles most order volumes. For higher throughput: enable High Throughput Mode (70,000 TPS). Group ID cardinality: more groups = more parallelism = higher throughput.* <br>

1428. [ SQS ] An application sends messages to SQS but the consumer keeps receiving duplicate messages even with a FIFO queue. What could cause this? ; Possible causes: (1) Producer is sending messages without a Deduplication ID, and content-based deduplication is not enabled. Without dedup ID, FIFO cannot deduplicate. (2) Producer is sending the same logical message with DIFFERENT dedup IDs (e.g., using a random UUID per send attempt instead of a stable transaction ID). (3) Dedup window (5 minutes) expired between retries — sending same message 6 minutes apart = both accepted. (4) Message Group ID mismatch — messages for the same logical entity are using different group IDs. <br><br> *Fix: enable content-based deduplication (SHA-256 of message body used as dedup ID) if message body is naturally unique and identical retries send identical bodies. Or: generate stable, deterministic dedup IDs in producer code based on transaction/operation ID (not random UUID). Dedup ID should be: same value for retries of the same logical operation, different value for new distinct operations.* <br> *5-minute deduplication window: if the consumer is slow and processing takes >5 minutes, producer may retry thinking the message was lost — sends same dedup ID again → beyond window → accepted → duplicate. Solution: increase producer retry timeout beyond 5 minutes for slow-processing scenarios. Or process confirmation via separate channel (DynamoDB item set by consumer) rather than relying on SQS deduplication for end-to-end exactly-once.* <br>

1429. [ SQS ] A company wants to implement a fan-out pattern where one order event is processed by three independent systems: inventory, billing, and notifications. They currently use SQS. How do you redesign? ; Add Amazon SNS as the fan-out layer. Replace direct SQS publishing with: producer → SNS topic → three separate SQS queues (inventory-queue, billing-queue, notification-queue). Each system subscribes its SQS queue to the SNS topic. Each queue has its own DLQ. Benefits: each system scales independently, one system failure does not affect others, adding a new consumer = add SNS subscription without changing producer. <br><br> *Current design limitation with SQS only: one consumer per message. You cannot have three consumers each receive the same message from a single SQS queue — the first consumer to receive it makes it invisible to others. You would need the producer to send to three queues directly — tight coupling (producer must know all consumers, adding a new consumer requires producer code change).* <br> *SNS topic policy: allow producer application role `sns:Publish`. SQS queue policy for each queue: allow `sns.amazonaws.com` `sqs:SendMessage` with `ArnEquals aws:SourceArn` = SNS topic ARN. This prevents other SNS topics from sending to your queues. Encryption: if SNS topic uses SSE-KMS, each SQS queue must use the same KMS CMK (or an AWS-managed key — note: SSE-SQS and SSE-SNS use different key materials, ensure compatible configuration).* <br>

1430. [ SQS ] What is the difference between SQS and Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for message processing? When should you use each? ; SQS: pull-based queue, at-least-once (Standard) or exactly-once (FIFO), no ordering in Standard, consumer deletes message after processing, 14-day max retention, no replay of deleted messages. Kinesis: pull-based stream, at-least-once, per-shard ordering, data stays for 24hr-365 days (replay possible), multiple independent consumers can read same data, suited for streaming analytics. Use SQS for: task queues, decoupling services, worker patterns. Use Kinesis for: real-time analytics, log aggregation, event sourcing with replay. <br><br> *Key difference: SQS is a queue — message consumed = deleted. Multiple consumers compete for messages (one gets each message). Kinesis is a stream — data persists regardless of consumption. Multiple consumer applications each read all the data independently (each has its own shard iterator position). Multiple teams reading the same stream = Kinesis. One worker pool processing each job once = SQS.* <br> *Replay capability: Kinesis Extended Retention (up to 365 days) allows replaying from any point. SQS: deleted messages are gone. For event sourcing (rebuild state by replaying events) → Kinesis or EventBridge Archive. For simple decoupled worker queue → SQS. Cost comparison: Kinesis charges per shard-hour ($0.015/shard/hour minimum). SQS charges per request. Low-volume fanout to many consumers → SNS+SQS cheaper. High-volume ordered streaming → Kinesis.* <br>

1431. [ SQS ] A company needs to delay the processing of messages by 10 minutes after they are sent. How do you implement this? ; Use SQS Delivery Delay. Set `DelaySeconds=600` (10 minutes) on the queue or per-message. Messages become invisible to consumers for 600 seconds after being sent. After 10 minutes, messages appear in the queue and consumers can receive them. For Standard queues: apply at queue level (default delay) or per message. For FIFO queues: queue-level delay only (no per-message delay override). <br><br> *Delivery delay use cases: (1) Scheduled processing — order confirmation email 10 minutes after order (gives customer time to cancel). (2) Retry delay — send failed webhook back to queue with 60-second delay before retry. (3) Deferred processing — batch jobs triggered by delayed messages instead of cron. Delivery delay max is 900 seconds (15 minutes). For longer delays: use EventBridge Scheduler (schedule a Lambda that sends to SQS at the right time) or Step Functions Wait state.* <br> *Delivery delay vs visibility timeout: delivery delay applies at send time (message not visible at all until delay expires). Visibility timeout applies after receive (message hidden while being processed). Both make messages temporarily invisible but for different purposes. A message with both a delivery delay AND a visibility timeout: first waits the delivery delay, then becomes visible, then when consumed enters visibility timeout.* <br>

1432. [ SQS ] A Lambda function processes SQS messages in batches of 10. One message in the batch causes an exception. Without `ReportBatchItemFailures`, what happens? What changes when you enable it? ; Without ReportBatchItemFailures: Lambda returns an error → ALL 10 messages in the batch return to the queue → ALL 10 messages are reprocessed (even the 9 that succeeded). This causes unnecessary duplicate processing and can push all 10 messages toward DLQ. With ReportBatchItemFailures: Lambda returns `{"batchItemFailures": [{"itemIdentifier": "failed-msg-id"}]}` → only the 1 failed message returns to queue → the 9 successful messages are deleted. <br><br> *Implementation: enable `ReportBatchItemFailures` on the event source mapping. Lambda function must: (1) wrap each message in try/catch, (2) collect failed message IDs, (3) return the batch item failures structure. If Lambda throws an uncaught exception (crashes): ALL messages return regardless (partial batch failure only works when Lambda exits normally with the failure list).* <br> *Partial batch failure is critical for poison-pill prevention: without it, one consistently failing message causes the entire batch to retry repeatedly until all messages hit maxReceiveCount and go to DLQ — even the healthy messages. With it: the 9 healthy messages are deleted immediately, only the poison pill retries. The poison pill eventually hits maxReceiveCount and goes to DLQ for investigation without dragging healthy messages with it.* <br>

1433. [ SNS ] A company uses SNS to send order events to multiple downstream systems. They want only the fraud detection Lambda to receive orders over $10,000. How do you implement this? ; Add a message filter policy to the Lambda subscription. Filter policy on the Lambda subscription: `{"orderAmount": [{"numeric": [">=", 10000]}]}`. Other subscriptions have different or no filter policies. Lambda only receives messages where the `orderAmount` attribute is >= 10000. All other messages pass Lambda by silently. <br><br> *Filter policy is per-subscription, not per-topic. Each subscriber independently filters. The filter works on message attributes (key-value pairs set by the publisher) or on the message body (if body filtering is enabled on the topic). Publisher must include `orderAmount` as a message attribute (Number type) for the numeric filter to work.* <br> *Cost benefit: without filtering, Lambda is invoked for every order (most are < $10,000). With filtering: Lambda only invoked for high-value orders (e.g., 1% of orders). 99% reduction in Lambda invocations = 99% cost reduction for that Lambda. Filter policy is evaluated by SNS — messages that do not match are not delivered at all (no Lambda invocation, no SQS message). This is more efficient than Lambda inspecting every message and returning early.* <br>

1434. [ SNS ] An HTTP endpoint subscribed to an SNS topic is not receiving messages. The subscription shows as pending. What is the problem and how do you fix it? ; SNS requires HTTP/HTTPS subscribers to confirm their subscription. When you create the subscription, SNS sends a GET request to the endpoint URL containing a `SubscribeURL` with a confirmation token. The endpoint must make an HTTP GET request to the `SubscribeURL` to confirm. Until confirmed, the subscription is in `PendingConfirmation` status and receives no messages. Fix: implement a subscription confirmation handler in the endpoint that processes SNS subscription confirmation requests. <br><br> *Confirmation request format: SNS sends a POST (not GET) to the endpoint with `Type: SubscriptionConfirmation` in the JSON body. The endpoint must extract the `SubscribeURL` and make an HTTP GET to it (or call SNS `ConfirmSubscription` API with the token). After confirmation, subscription becomes `Confirmed` and messages start flowing. Confirmation link expires after 3 days — after that, delete and recreate the subscription.* <br> *Why confirmation exists: prevents unauthorized subscriptions. Without confirmation, anyone could subscribe any HTTP endpoint to receive your SNS messages — a privacy and security issue. Confirmation proves the endpoint owner wants the subscription. For Lambda and SQS subscriptions: no confirmation needed (AWS handles it automatically). For Email: recipient receives a confirmation email and must click a link. For HTTPS: automate confirmation handling in application code.* <br>

1435. [ SNS ] A company wants to send mobile push notifications to iOS and Android users. Describe the complete SNS mobile push architecture. ; Architecture: (1) Register Platform Applications in SNS: one for APNs (iOS, using APNs certificate or key) and one for FCM (Android, using FCM server key). (2) On app first launch: mobile app requests device token from Apple/Google. (3) App sends token to your backend. (4) Backend calls SNS `CreatePlatformEndpoint` to register device → gets an SNS Platform Endpoint ARN. (5) Store endpoint ARN in database linked to user. (6) To send notification: call SNS `Publish` to endpoint ARN (single device) or SNS topic with mobile push subscriptions (broadcast). <br><br> *Platform Application per platform: `aws sns create-platform-application --platform APNS --name MyiOSApp --attributes PlatformCredential=key.p8,PlatformPrincipal=keyId`. Each device has a unique Platform Endpoint ARN. Tokens can become stale (user uninstalls app, OS reset) — SNS returns `EndpointDisabled` exception → remove or update the endpoint. Implement token refresh: when app launches, check if stored token matches, update endpoint if changed.* <br> *Message structure for mobile: raw delivery vs JSON message structure. JSON structure: `{"default": "fallback", "APNS": "{\"aps\":{\"alert\":\"Hello\",\"badge\":1}}", "GCM": "{\"notification\":{\"title\":\"Hello\"}}"}`. SNS delivers platform-specific payload to each platform. Enable `RawMessageDelivery` for SQS/HTTP subscribers to receive raw message without SNS wrapper.* <br>

1436. [ SNS ] A company uses SNS Standard topic to broadcast order events. A new requirement: if the downstream SQS consumer goes down, no order events should be lost. How do you ensure this? ; SNS Standard topics do not retain messages — if a subscriber is unavailable when the message is published, it is lost. Solution: (1) Add a subscription DLQ to the SQS subscription — SNS retries delivery and failed deliveries go to the DLQ. But if SQS itself is down (very rare — SQS is regional/AZ-redundant), messages could still be lost. (2) Better: also subscribe to EventBridge Pipes or S3 via Firehose as a backup subscriber for archiving. (3) Best: use the SNS-to-SQS fan-out correctly — SQS is almost never down. The real concern is consumer application processing, not SQS availability. <br><br> *SNS retry policy for SQS subscribers: SNS retries failed deliveries to SQS with exponential backoff (up to 100,000 retries over 23 days for HTTP, for SQS, retries are faster). SQS failures are extremely rare given AZ-redundant storage. The real failure scenario is: consumer application crashes. In this case: messages are in SQS (durable), consumer restarts and processes them. SQS provides the durability, not SNS.* <br> *If SNS itself needs replay capability: add an S3 subscriber via Kinesis Firehose. SNS → Firehose → S3 archives all published events. If SQS consumer misses events, replay from S3 archive (Lambda reading S3, sending to SQS, or using EventBridge). This is more complex but provides true event sourcing capability. For simpler replay: SNS FIFO with archiving enabled.* <br>

1437. [ SNS ] What is the difference between SNS message filtering on message attributes vs message body? When should you use each? ; Message attribute filtering: producer attaches key-value metadata attributes to the message. Filter policy matches on these attributes. Fast, AWS handles at SNS layer before message body is read. Works with both Standard and FIFO topics. Message body filtering: filter policy evaluates the JSON message body itself. Requires enabling `FilterPolicyScope: MessageBody` on the subscription. Useful when producer cannot add attributes (third-party, legacy). Slightly more compute, same SNS-layer filtering efficiency. <br><br> *Message attribute filtering is preferred when you control the producer: add meaningful attributes like `{"eventType": "OrderPlaced", "region": "EU", "tier": "premium"}`. These are lightweight, do not require JSON parsing. Message body filtering is useful for legacy integrations or when the event schema is already defined in the body (e.g., CloudWatch Events routed through SNS — the event JSON is the body).* <br> *Filter policy scope is per-subscription. One subscription can use attribute filtering, another body filtering, on the same topic. Body filtering can access nested JSON fields: `{"detail": {"state": ["terminated"]}}`. Attribute filtering can only access top-level attributes (key-value pairs). Complex nested JSON routing: EventBridge (full event pattern matching) is more powerful than SNS body filtering for complex scenarios.* <br>

1438. [ SNS ] A company wants to send transactional SMS OTP codes to users in 50 countries. What SNS configuration is critical? ; Set SMS type to Transactional (not Promotional). Transactional SMS has higher delivery priority and is not subject to time-of-day restrictions that apply to promotional messages in some countries. Set a reasonable monthly SMS spending limit (default $1 is too low — request increase via AWS Support). Configure origination numbers or Sender IDs per country (requirements vary). Enable SMS sandbox for testing. <br><br> *Transactional vs Promotional: Transactional = OTP, security codes, delivery confirmations. Promotional = marketing, offers. Different delivery routes, different regulations per country. Some countries (India, for example) require registration of SMS templates for transactional messages. GDPR countries: ensure user has opted in for promotional but transactional (OTP) generally does not require opt-in.* <br> *Origination: long code (10-digit phone number), short code (5-6 digits, high deliverability but requires registration), Sender ID (alphanumeric name like "MyBank" — not supported in all countries, notably US and Canada). For global OTP at scale: consider using AWS End User Messaging (formerly Pinpoint) which provides more granular control over origination, delivery receipts, and analytics than raw SNS SMS.* <br>

1439. [ EventBridge ] A company wants to automatically stop EC2 instances tagged with `Environment=dev` every day at 7 PM to reduce costs. What EventBridge configuration achieves this? ; EventBridge Scheduler: create a recurring schedule with cron `cron(0 19 * * ? *)` (7 PM UTC) or use timezone support for local time. Target: EC2 `StopInstances` API directly (EventBridge Scheduler supports 270+ AWS APIs). Use a resource-based filter or pass instance IDs via the schedule input. Alternatively: EventBridge rule on a schedule → Lambda → describe instances with tag `Environment=dev` → stop them all. <br><br> *EventBridge Scheduler can call EC2 `StopInstances` directly without Lambda — pass a static list of instance IDs as the schedule input (JSON). But if the dev fleet changes frequently, Lambda approach is better: Lambda queries EC2 with tag filter `Environment=dev` → stops all matching instances dynamically.* <br> *Timezone support: EventBridge Scheduler supports any IANA timezone. `cron(0 19 * * ? *)` in `Europe/Warsaw` timezone stops instances at 7 PM Warsaw time (CET/CEST). CloudWatch Events (legacy) only supports UTC — you would need to calculate UTC offset manually and update twice a year for DST. Scheduler is the exam-correct answer for time-zone-aware scheduling.* <br>

1440. [ EventBridge ] How does EventBridge cross-account event routing work? A security account needs to receive all GuardDuty findings from all 50 member accounts in an Organization. ; In each member account: create EventBridge rule matching `source: aws.guardduty`, `detail-type: GuardDuty Finding`. Target: event bus ARN in the security account. In the security account: add resource policy to the custom event bus allowing all org accounts to `events:PutEvents`. Security account event bus receives all findings → local rules route to Lambda, SQS, or SIEM. <br><br> *Resource policy on security account event bus:* <code>{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":"*","Action":"events:PutEvents","Resource":"arn:aws:events:us-east-1:SECURITY_ACCT:event-bus/security-hub","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"aws:PrincipalOrgID":"o-xxxxx"}}}</code> <br> *Using `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition restricts to only accounts in your org — prevents external accounts from sending events to your security bus.* <br> *Alternative with AWS Security Hub: GuardDuty integrates with Security Hub natively. Security Hub supports org-wide aggregation from a delegated admin account. For EventBridge-based routing specifically: the cross-account bus approach gives more flexibility (custom routing rules, API Destinations to SIEM, etc.). Use Security Hub for consolidated findings view, EventBridge for automated response workflows.* <br>

1441. [ EventBridge ] A developer wants to invoke a Lambda function whenever an S3 object is uploaded to a specific bucket with prefix `uploads/` and suffix `.pdf`. What is the most efficient approach? ; Use S3 Event Notifications directly to Lambda (not EventBridge). S3 event notifications: configure on the S3 bucket, filter by prefix `uploads/` and suffix `.pdf`, target Lambda function ARN. This is free and lower latency than routing through EventBridge. EventBridge approach: S3 sends events to EventBridge default bus (must enable EventBridge notifications on the bucket) → rule matching `source: aws.s3`, `detail.object.key` with prefix/suffix filter → Lambda. <br><br> *When to prefer S3 event notifications over EventBridge: simple one-to-one trigger (S3 → one Lambda or SQS). Free. Minimal latency. When to prefer EventBridge: need to route to multiple targets, need content-based filtering beyond prefix/suffix, need to combine with other event sources, need cross-account routing. EventBridge adds ~1 second latency vs S3 direct notifications.* <br> *S3 EventBridge integration (when used): enable on bucket with `aws s3api put-bucket-notification-configuration --notification-configuration EventBridgeConfiguration={}`. All S3 events flow to EventBridge default bus. EventBridge rule: `{"source":["aws.s3"],"detail":{"bucket":{"name":["my-bucket"]},"object":{"key":[{"prefix":"uploads/"},{"suffix":".pdf"}]}}}`. This gives full EventBridge power: archive, replay, cross-account, multiple targets.* <br>

1442. [ EventBridge ] A company needs to send events from their AWS account to a third-party Splunk instance whenever a GuardDuty High severity finding occurs. What is the recommended approach without writing Lambda code? ; EventBridge API Destinations. Create a Connection with Splunk HEC (HTTP Event Collector) URL and API key authentication. Create an API Destination pointing to `https://splunk-instance:8088/services/collector` using the Connection. Create EventBridge rule matching `source: aws.guardduty` + `detail.severity >= 7.0` → API Destination target. EventBridge handles retry with exponential backoff if Splunk is temporarily unavailable. <br><br> *API Destination components: (1) Connection — stores auth credentials (API key stored in Secrets Manager behind the scenes). (2) API Destination — endpoint URL + HTTP method + rate limit. (3) EventBridge rule — matches events, targets the API Destination. Rate limit: set max invocations per second to avoid overwhelming Splunk (Splunk recommends 100-1000 events/second for HEC).* <br> *Input transformation for Splunk: Splunk HEC expects `{"event": {your_data}, "sourcetype": "_json"}`. Use EventBridge Input Transformation to wrap the GuardDuty finding in Splunk format before sending. No Lambda code needed. Retry policy: configure retries (default 24 hours with exponential backoff) — failed deliveries can go to an SQS DLQ for manual replay. Alternative without API Destinations: GuardDuty → Security Hub → Splunk Security Hub integration (Splunk app in AWS Marketplace).* <br>

1443. [ EventBridge ] What is EventBridge Pipes and when should you use it instead of a Lambda polling function? ; EventBridge Pipes: managed point-to-point integration with source → optional filter → optional enrichment → target. Sources include SQS, DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis Data Streams, MSK, Amazon MQ. Pipes manages polling, batching, retry, and scaling. Use instead of Lambda polling when: (1) you have a source that requires polling (DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis) and want to avoid writing/maintaining polling Lambda code. (2) You need enrichment (call another API to add data to event) before delivering to target. (3) You want to filter events at the pipe level before enrichment/target (cost savings). <br><br> *Lambda polling pattern (before Pipes): Lambda event source mapping polls SQS/Kinesis/DDB Streams, invokes Lambda function. Works well but Lambda IS the processing logic. Pipes use case: when the processing is more of routing/transformation than business logic. Example: DynamoDB Stream events → Pipe filter (only INSERT events) → enrichment (call API GW to get additional data) → SQS target → separate consumer. Lambda is used only for enrichment, not for polling/routing.* <br> *Cost comparison: Lambda event source mapping: Lambda invocation per batch (even empty batches cost Lambda memory*time). Pipes: charged per event processed ($0.40/million). For DynamoDB Streams with low write volume: Pipes may be more cost-effective (no Lambda invocation cost for empty batches). For high-volume streams: Lambda event source mapping with batch sizes is more efficient. Pipes also support more target types than Lambda event source mapping.* <br>

1444. [ EventBridge ] A company accidentally deployed a bug in their event consumer Lambda. Events were processed incorrectly for the last 2 hours. They have fixed the Lambda. How do they reprocess the affected events? ; Use EventBridge Archive + Replay. Prerequisite: archive was enabled on the event bus before the incident. Steps: (1) Navigate to EventBridge Archives, select the bus archive. (2) Start a replay specifying the time range (2 hours ago to now). (3) Select the destination event bus (same bus). (4) Existing rules on the bus will re-match the replayed events and invoke the fixed Lambda again. Events are replayed as if they were published originally, with original timestamps preserved in `replay-name` metadata. <br><br> *Archive must be enabled before the incident — you cannot retroactively archive events. Best practice: always enable archive on critical custom event buses with at least 7-day retention (longer for compliance). Archive storage cost: S3-equivalent pricing. The replay injects events back into the event bus as new events — all matching rules fire. If you only want the fixed Lambda to process them (not other downstream systems), temporarily disable other rules or use a separate replay bus.* <br> *Replay filtering: you can filter which event types to replay using an event pattern filter on the replay. Example: replay only `detail-type: OrderProcessed` events from the 2-hour window, not all event types. This prevents unintended side effects from replaying irrelevant events. After replay completes, verify event counts match expected (CloudWatch metrics: `MatchedEvents` per rule during replay window).* <br>

1445. [ SQS ] A company has an SQS Standard queue. Processing errors are causing messages to cycle through the queue indefinitely, consuming compute resources. How do you prevent this? ; Configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) with a `maxReceiveCount`. Set `maxReceiveCount=3` (or appropriate for your retry tolerance). After 3 failed processing attempts, the message is moved to the DLQ automatically. Monitor DLQ depth with CloudWatch alarm → SNS → engineer alert. After fixing the bug, use DLQ redrive to replay messages back to the source queue. <br><br> *Without DLQ: a poison-pill message (one that always causes an exception) stays in the queue forever, consuming compute on every visibility timeout expiry. With high concurrent consumers, this one message gets processed hundreds of times per hour — wasting Lambda invocations or EC2 CPU and potentially obscuring real processing failures in logs.* <br> *DLQ retention: set DLQ retention longer than source queue. If source queue retention is 4 days, set DLQ retention to 14 days — gives you 14 days to investigate and fix the issue before the message expires. DLQ redrive (2021 feature): select all or specific messages in DLQ → redrive to source queue → automatic reprocessing after bug fix. Before redrive: ensure the bug is fixed, test with one message, then redrive the full DLQ.* <br>

1446. [ SNS ] A company uses SNS to notify multiple teams when an AWS Config rule compliance violation occurs. The security team needs JSON format, the ops team needs plain text email. How do you configure this? ; Create two subscriptions to the same SNS topic: (1) Security team: Email-JSON subscription → receives structured JSON including all event metadata. (2) Ops team: Email subscription → receives human-readable plain text formatted from the SNS notification. Alternatively for greater control: route both through SQS or Lambda and format per audience. The native Email vs Email-JSON subscription types provide the simplest solution. <br><br> *Email-JSON: delivers the raw SNS message envelope as JSON including Subject, Message, Timestamp, TopicArn, Type, MessageId. Security team can parse this programmatically. Plain Email: delivers only the Message body as human-readable text (subject line from SNS subject attribute). For richer formatting (HTML email, custom templates): SNS → Lambda → SES (Simple Email Service). SES allows full HTML email templates, tracking, bounce handling — far more powerful than SNS Email subscription.* <br> *Subscription confirmation: both Email and Email-JSON subscriptions require manual confirmation. Each email address receives a confirmation email with a link. Until clicked, the subscription is in PendingConfirmation. In enterprise environments: use distribution list email addresses (teams@company.com) rather than individual emails — team members join/leave the list without changing SNS configuration.* <br>

1447. [ EventBridge ] What is the difference between EventBridge rules with schedules and EventBridge Scheduler? When should you use each? ; EventBridge rules with schedules: part of EventBridge, UTC only, ~5 target types, no time zone, no one-time schedules, no flexible window. Free (included in EventBridge). EventBridge Scheduler: standalone service, 270+ time zones, 270+ AWS API targets, one-time schedules, flexible time window, millions of schedules. Cost: $1/million after 14 million free. Use rules: simple UTC-based recurring triggers for Lambda/SQS/SNS. Use Scheduler: time-zone-aware schedules, one-time future events, targeting any AWS API directly, large-scale scheduling (millions of schedules). <br><br> *EventBridge Scheduler advantage: directly invokes 270+ AWS API operations without Lambda. Example: schedule EC2 `StartInstances` at 8 AM London time every Monday — no Lambda wrapper needed. EventBridge rule targeting Lambda: Lambda must then call EC2 API — extra hop, extra cost, extra latency. Scheduler eliminates the Lambda middleman for AWS service calls.* <br> *Migration: AWS recommends migrating CloudWatch Events scheduled rules to EventBridge Scheduler for new features. Existing rules continue to work but lack timezone support and one-time schedule capability. For SAP-C02: if question mentions timezone-aware scheduling or one-time scheduled events → EventBridge Scheduler is the answer, not CloudWatch Events or Lambda cron.* <br>

1448. [ EventBridge ] A company has 50 AWS accounts in an Organization. They want a single EventBridge rule to detect when ANY account creates an unencrypted S3 bucket. How do you architect this? ; Option 1: EventBridge rule in each account (automated via CloudFormation StackSets deployed by Control Tower or Organizations StackSets) → cross-account event bus in security account. Security account EventBridge rule matches S3 bucket creation events + checks encryption configuration. Option 2: Use AWS Config with `s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled` managed rule org-wide via Config aggregator → Config findings to Security Hub → EventBridge rule in security account on Security Hub findings. <br><br> *Option 1 detail: each member account needs EventBridge rule matching `source: aws.s3`, `detail-type: AWS API Call via CloudTrail`, `detail.eventName: CreateBucket`. Target: security account event bus (cross-account). Security account receives events from all 50 accounts and evaluates encryption. CloudFormation StackSets deployed via Organizations automatically applies the rule to new accounts (auto-deployment option).* <br> *Option 2 detail (simpler, recommended): AWS Config `s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled` managed rule detects unencrypted buckets continuously. Config aggregator in security account collects compliance data from all member accounts. Non-compliant buckets generate Config findings → Security Hub → EventBridge rule in security account → Lambda → SNS alert + auto-remediation (put bucket encryption). This covers both new buckets AND existing buckets that have encryption removed later.* <br>

1449. [ SQS ] A company processes SQS messages with a Lambda function. They want to ensure that if Lambda is throttled or at concurrency limits, messages are not lost and will be retried. How does SQS handle this? ; SQS messages are not lost during Lambda throttling. When Lambda is throttled (concurrency limit reached), the SQS message remains in the queue (visibility timeout expires → message reappears). SQS event source mapping automatically backs off polling when Lambda is throttled. Messages stay safely in the queue for up to 14 days (retention period) waiting to be processed when Lambda capacity is available. <br><br> *Lambda throttling + SQS: Lambda event source mapping uses 5 simultaneous polling threads per queue by default. When all Lambda concurrency is consumed, new SQS messages pile up in the queue. As Lambda concurrency frees up, event source mapping automatically resumes. The key is: visibility timeout > Lambda function timeout > backoff time. If visibility timeout is too short (30s default vs Lambda throttle recovery which may take minutes), messages can be received, Lambda throttled, message returns to queue and is immediately tried again — retry storm.* <br> *Mitigation: set visibility timeout to accommodate throttle recovery time (e.g., 5 minutes). Set Lambda reserved concurrency to ensure the SQS consumer has guaranteed capacity (prevents other Lambda functions consuming all account concurrency). Use SQS as the buffer — it scales to absorb bursts that Lambda cannot immediately process. CloudWatch alarm on `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage` alerts when queue is backing up faster than Lambda can process.* <br>

1450. [ EventBridge ] Explain EventBridge Global Endpoints and when you would use them for a mission-critical event processing system. ; EventBridge Global Endpoints provide active-active multi-region event routing with automatic failover. Two event buses in two regions (primary + secondary). Route 53 health check monitors primary region endpoint. Normal operation: events routed to primary region. Failover: if primary region health check fails → Route 53 + EventBridge automatically route new events to secondary region. Event replication: events sent to primary are automatically replicated to secondary for recovery. Use when: event processing system must survive a full AWS region outage. <br><br> *Architecture: primary event bus in us-east-1 + secondary in eu-west-1. Global endpoint ARN spans both. Publisher uses the global endpoint ARN for PutEvents — EventBridge routes to healthy region. Each regional bus has identical rules and Lambda targets. If Lambda in us-east-1 has a bug: fix and redeploy independently in each region. Events during failover: replicated to secondary, so events are not lost.* <br> *When NOT to use: most applications do not need global endpoint complexity. Single-region EventBridge with multi-AZ redundancy (already built-in) is sufficient for 99.99% uptime. Global endpoint is for compliance requirements (RPO/RTO near zero) or applications that cannot tolerate a region outage (critical financial infrastructure, real-time safety systems). Cost: event replication doubles event volume (cross-region data transfer charges apply).* <br>

1451. [ SNS ] A company wants to route order events to different SQS queues based on order region (EU vs US). They currently have one SNS topic with all subscribers receiving all events. What is the most cost-effective solution? ; Add message filter policies to each SQS subscription. EU queue subscription: filter `{"orderRegion": ["EU", "eu-west-1", "eu-central-1"]}`. US queue subscription: filter `{"orderRegion": ["US", "us-east-1", "us-west-2"]}`. Publishers must add `orderRegion` as a message attribute. No additional services, no Lambda, no schema changes — just filter policies on existing subscriptions. <br><br> *This is pure SNS feature usage — no cost for filter policies themselves. Without filters: EU queue and US queue both receive all events, consumer code inspects and discards irrelevant events. With filters: SNS discards irrelevant events before delivery — 50% fewer SQS messages, 50% fewer Lambda invocations. Cost scales linearly with filter effectiveness.* <br> *Alternative with EventBridge: if filtering logic is complex (nested JSON, numeric ranges, multiple conditions) or you need to route to more than just SQS (Lambda, Step Functions, etc.), migrate to EventBridge with custom event bus and content-based routing rules. EventBridge pattern matching is more powerful than SNS filter policies. But for simple attribute-based routing, SNS filters are simpler and cheaper.* <br>

1452. [ EventBridge ] What happens when an EventBridge rule fails to invoke its target (Lambda throws error, SQS unavailable)? How do you configure fault tolerance? ; EventBridge retries failed target invocations based on the retry policy: maximum event age (1 minute to 24 hours, default 24 hours) and maximum retry attempts (0-185, default 185). Retries use exponential backoff. If all retries exhausted: event is sent to a dead-letter SQS queue (if configured) or dropped. Configure DLQ: on the rule target, set `DeadLetterConfig: {Arn: "arn:aws:sqs:..."}`. Monitor: CloudWatch metric `FailedInvocations` per rule. <br><br> *Retry behavior per target type: Lambda synchronous invocations are retried by EventBridge (not Lambda itself). For Lambda async invocations from EventBridge: EventBridge handles retry, not Lambda destination. SQS target: if SQS is unavailable (extremely rare), EventBridge retries. DLQ for EventBridge rule target stores the original event JSON — engineer can inspect and manually reprocess. DLQ message includes the original event plus an `ErrorCode` and `ErrorMessage`.* <br> *Best practice: always configure a DLQ on EventBridge rule targets for critical workflows. Set maximum event age based on business requirements (financial events: 24 hours. operational events: 1 hour). Set CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth → SNS → PagerDuty. This creates a complete audit trail of every event that failed processing — no silent failures. EventBridge Archive + Replay as complementary recovery mechanism.* <br>

1453. [ SQS ] A company uses SQS FIFO with Lambda. They observe that processing throughput is lower than expected — only 10 messages/second. The queue has High Throughput Mode enabled. What is the bottleneck? ; With FIFO + Lambda: Lambda creates one concurrent invocation per active Message Group ID. If all messages share the same Message Group ID (e.g., all using `"group-1"`), only ONE Lambda runs at a time — serial processing. Throughput = Lambda processing time / 1. Fix: use more Message Group IDs (one per order, customer, or partition key). With 100 active Message Group IDs: 100 concurrent Lambda invocations = 100x throughput increase. <br><br> *High Throughput Mode increases FIFO queue API throughput (up to 70,000 TPS) but does NOT increase Lambda parallelism — that is governed by Message Group IDs. High Throughput Mode helps when the bottleneck is SQS API calls, not Lambda concurrency. The exam question distinguishes: "queue throughput" (SQS API limit) vs "processing throughput" (Lambda concurrency).* <br> *Optimal Message Group ID strategy: granularity = desired parallelism. Too coarse (one global group): serial. Too fine (one group per message UUID): maximum parallelism but no ordering guarantee across messages (each group has one message = no ordering benefit). Right balance: group by logical entity requiring ordering (customer ID, order ID). If no ordering needed: use Standard queue — no group ID concept, unlimited Lambda concurrency.* <br>

1454. [ SNS ] A company migrates from a publish-subscribe pattern where each consumer reads all messages independently (like Kafka) to SNS + SQS. A new consumer team joins and wants to start receiving all historical messages from the past 7 days. How do you provide this? ; SNS Standard topics have no message retention — historical messages are unavailable. Options: (1) Use Kinesis Data Streams instead of SNS (retention up to 365 days, new consumer reads from any position). (2) Add an S3 archive subscriber to SNS via Kinesis Firehose (SNS → Firehose → S3) — new consumer reads from S3 archive. (3) If using SNS FIFO: enable archiving with 7-day retention → new SQS FIFO subscription can replay archived messages. <br><br> *This is a fundamental difference between SNS (push, no retention) and Kafka/Kinesis (pull stream, retention). SNS is designed for real-time notification — not for consumer catch-up on historical events. Migrating to SNS from Kafka without considering this breaks the "late consumer" use case.* <br> *Recommended architecture for "multiple consumers, independent positions, historical replay": Kinesis Data Streams or EventBridge Archive. Kinesis: each consumer group tracks its own shard iterator position independently. New consumer starts at sequence position TRIM_HORIZON (oldest available). EventBridge custom bus with Archive: archive all events, new subscriber replays from archive. If SNS is required: supplement with Firehose → S3 archival for historical access, new consumers bootstrap from S3 before going live on SNS.* <br>

1455. [ EventBridge ] A company has CloudTrail enabled. They want to detect and alert in near-real-time whenever any IAM user is created outside of their standard provisioning pipeline. What EventBridge configuration achieves this? ; EventBridge rule on default event bus: event pattern matching CloudTrail management event `CreateUser`. Pattern: `{"source":["aws.iam"],"detail-type":["AWS API Call via CloudTrail"],"detail":{"eventName":["CreateUser"]}}`. Target: Lambda (checks if creation was via approved pipeline — e.g., checks if the caller ARN matches the provisioning service role) → SNS alert. Or simpler: any `CreateUser` call → SNS alert, security team reviews. <br><br> *CloudTrail events flow to EventBridge default bus automatically (no extra config needed beyond CloudTrail being enabled). CloudTrail management events appear in EventBridge typically within 15 minutes. For near-real-time (< 5 minutes): enable CloudTrail Insights or use EventBridge with CloudTrail data events — but standard management events already appear within minutes in most regions.* <br> *Lambda enrichment: Lambda receives the EventBridge event containing the CloudTrail `CreateUser` API call details including caller identity (`userIdentity.arn`), time, source IP. Lambda compares caller ARN against allowed list (provisioning service role ARNs stored in Parameter Store). If caller is not in allowed list → send SNS alert with details. This pattern (EventBridge + Lambda + SNS) is the standard AWS real-time compliance alerting architecture.* <br>


1456. [ SQS ] What is the maximum number of in-flight messages for Standard and FIFO SQS queues, and what happens when this limit is reached? ; Standard queue: 120,000 in-flight messages maximum. FIFO queue: 20,000 in-flight messages. When the limit is reached: `OverLimit` error returned on ReceiveMessage. New messages are not lost — they remain visible in the queue — but consumers cannot receive additional messages until they delete currently in-flight messages. This indicates consumers are not processing fast enough (slow processing, not deleting after completion, or not enough consumers). <br><br> *In-flight messages = received but not yet deleted (within visibility timeout). High in-flight count = consumers are slow or visibility timeout is very long. Diagnosis: `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible` metric = in-flight count. If this approaches 120,000 (Standard): add more consumers or reduce visibility timeout. If consumers are processing but not deleting: check consumer code for delete logic.* <br> *FIFO in-flight limit (20,000) is much lower due to the ordering guarantees requiring state tracking per message group. For high-throughput FIFO workloads: ensure consumers process and delete quickly. High Throughput Mode helps with API TPS but does not increase the in-flight limit. Design: if in-flight limit is a concern, consider Standard queue + idempotent consumer instead of FIFO.* <br>

1457. [ SNS ] A company receives CloudWatch Alarm notifications through SNS to their on-call system (HTTP endpoint). During a major incident, SNS floods the on-call system with 1,000 alarms/second, causing it to become overwhelmed. How do you solve this? ; Add SQS between SNS and the on-call system. Change the subscription: SNS → SQS queue (instead of SNS → HTTP). On-call system polls SQS at its own sustainable rate (e.g., 10 messages/second). SQS buffers the burst. Alternatively: use SNS → Lambda → rate-limited delivery to on-call API. Or: use the on-call system SNS integration with built-in rate limiting (PagerDuty, Opsgenie). <br><br> *This is the classic SQS buffering pattern. SNS pushes instantly to all subscribers — no rate limiting. HTTP endpoint gets overwhelmed. SQS absorbs the burst (unlimited messages, persists for 14 days). On-call system polls at sustainable rate. During incident flood: messages queue up in SQS, processed over minutes instead of all at once. Trade-off: slight latency increase (polling interval). For emergency alerts: acceptable (1-minute polling is fine for human response).* <br> *EventBridge API Destinations alternative: configure max invocation rate in the API Destination (e.g., 10/second). EventBridge automatically throttles delivery to the configured rate. Failed deliveries retry with backoff and go to DLQ. This is cleaner than SQS for on-call webhook delivery as it handles retry and rate limiting natively. Both approaches valid — SQS is simpler if you already have the on-call system polling infrastructure.* <br>

1458. [ SQS ] Describe the SQS access control model. What is the difference between IAM policies and queue policies (resource-based policies) for SQS access? ; IAM policies: identity-based, attached to IAM users/roles/groups. Control which AWS principals can call SQS APIs (sqs:SendMessage, sqs:ReceiveMessage, etc.). Effective within the same account. Queue policies (resource-based): JSON policy attached to the queue resource. Controls who can access the queue from any account. Required for: cross-account access (other account IAM roles), AWS services publishing to queue (SNS, S3, EventBridge). Both can grant access — IAM union with resource policy. <br><br> *When you need BOTH: cross-account Lambda in Account B accessing queue in Account A: Account A queue policy must allow Account B principal. Account B Lambda role IAM policy must allow sqs:SendMessage. Both conditions must be satisfied. If either is missing: Access Denied. For same-account access: IAM policy alone is sufficient (no queue policy needed). For AWS service access (SNS publishing to SQS): queue policy with `Principal: {"Service": "sns.amazonaws.com"}` + SourceArn condition.* <br> *Deny in queue policy: explicit Deny in queue policy overrides Allow in IAM policy (standard AWS IAM evaluation logic). Use case: enforce HTTPS-only by denying requests where `aws:SecureTransport` is false. Enforce encryption at rest by denying queues without SSE. Enforce VPC origin: deny requests where `aws:SourceVpc` is not your VPC ID — all access must come from VPC (not internet).* <br>

1459. [ SNS ] A company wants to implement a notification system where infrastructure events (EC2, RDS, etc.) trigger notifications via SNS. Some events should page the on-call engineer (PagerDuty) and some should just log to a ticketing system. How do you design this? ; SNS fan-out with message filtering: (1) EventBridge rule per event type → SNS topic with `severity` message attribute. (2) PagerDuty subscription: filter `{"severity": ["CRITICAL", "HIGH"]}`. (3) Ticketing subscription: no filter (receives all). Or: separate SNS topics per severity (CRITICAL-topic → PagerDuty, INFO-topic → ticketing). Or: EventBridge API Destinations routing directly to each system without SNS. <br><br> *SNS message attribute approach: publisher adds `{"severity": {"DataType": "String", "StringValue": "CRITICAL"}}`. PagerDuty HTTPS endpoint subscription with filter `{"severity":["CRITICAL","HIGH"]}` only receives pages. Ticketing SQS subscription with no filter receives everything. Clean, no Lambda, no additional services. Best for < 5 downstream systems with attribute-based routing.* <br> *EventBridge alternative for more complex routing: CloudWatch Alarm → EventBridge rule with pattern matching on alarm state (`ALARM` vs `OK`) and alarm name (prefix matching `prod-*` for production alerts). EventBridge API Destination to PagerDuty (CRITICAL) and to Jira (all). More powerful pattern matching, more target types, archive+replay capability. For enterprises with 10+ notification destinations and complex routing: EventBridge.* <br>

1460. [ EventBridge ] What is the relationship between CloudWatch Events and EventBridge? Are they the same service? ; Yes, they are the same service. EventBridge is the evolution of CloudWatch Events. In 2019, AWS renamed and extended CloudWatch Events to Amazon EventBridge, adding: custom and partner event buses, schema registry, API Destinations, Pipes, Scheduler, Archive + Replay. All CloudWatch Events rules, scheduled events, and targets still work without changes. The CloudWatch Events console is deprecated but API/CLI commands still function. New features (Pipes, Scheduler, Global Endpoints) are EventBridge-only. <br><br> *Migration: existing CloudWatch Events scheduled rules automatically appear in EventBridge console. No migration needed — they work as-is. For new features: create new resources in EventBridge. Exam context: if a question says "CloudWatch Events rule" — treat it as EventBridge rule. If question mentions features only in EventBridge (Schema Registry, API Destinations, Pipes, Scheduler time zones) — answer is EventBridge.* <br> *Practical difference for architects: always use EventBridge console/APIs for new work. CloudWatch Events API works but is the legacy path. Terraform users: `aws_cloudwatch_event_rule` still works but `aws_scheduler_schedule` (Scheduler) and `aws_pipes_pipe` (Pipes) are EventBridge-specific resources. AWS documentation now refers to everything as EventBridge.* <br>

1461. [ SQS ] A company wants to implement request-response pattern over SQS. A web server sends a job request to a worker via SQS and needs to get the result back. How do you implement this? ; Temporary response queue pattern: (1) Web server creates a temporary SQS queue (or uses a per-request `MessageGroupId` on a shared FIFO queue). (2) Web server sends request with `ReplyTo` attribute pointing to the temp queue ARN. (3) Worker processes the request, sends result to the queue specified in `ReplyTo`. (4) Web server polls the temp queue for response with matching correlation ID. (5) Web server deletes temp queue after response received. Better alternative: use Step Functions (orchestrate worker invocation synchronously) or Lambda with SQS (async) + WebSocket/polling for result. <br><br> *Temporary queue creation overhead: ~1 second per queue creation. For high-volume request-response: create a shared response queue with one queue per web server instance (not per request). Each request includes a `correlationId`. Worker sends response with matching `correlationId`. Web server polls and filters by `correlationId`. Amazon SQS does not natively filter by message attributes on receive — consumer must receive and check `correlationId` (or use FIFO with Message Group ID = correlationId for approximate filtering).* <br> *Better patterns: (1) AWS Step Functions Express Workflows — synchronous, request/response, handles retry and state. (2) API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB — Lambda processes async, result stored in DynamoDB, client polls. (3) WebSocket API Gateway + SQS + Lambda — client opens WebSocket, server processes async via SQS + Lambda, pushes result back via WebSocket connection ID. The SQS temporary queue pattern is a valid but dated pattern from before Step Functions existed.* <br>

1462. [ EventBridge ] A company uses EventBridge to trigger Lambda when an RDS instance is stopped. They want to prevent accidental stops in the production environment. How do you implement this? ; Two complementary approaches: (1) EventBridge rule: detect RDS stop event → Lambda → check if instance is tagged `Environment=prod` → if yes, restart instance immediately + send alert. (2) Prevention: SCP or IAM condition denying `rds:StopDBInstance` for production account or for instances tagged `Environment=prod`. EventBridge provides detection and correction. IAM/SCP provides prevention. Defense in depth: use both. <br><br> *EventBridge event pattern for RDS stop: `{"source":["aws.rds"],"detail-type":["RDS DB Instance Event"],"detail":{"EventID":["RDS-EVENT-0087"]}}` (RDS-EVENT-0087 = DB instance stopped). Lambda receives event, calls `describe_db_instances` to check tags. If `Environment=prod`: calls `start_db_instance` to restart it + sends SNS alert "Production RDS was stopped and auto-restarted."* <br> *IAM condition for prevention: `"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"rds:db-tag/Environment":"prod"}}` with Deny in IAM policy or SCP. Prevents the stop from happening at all (better than detecting and reverting — revert = brief outage). Combine: SCP Deny `rds:StopDBInstance` for production OU accounts + EventBridge detection as defense-in-depth (catch if someone bypasses SCP via management account or breaks glass procedure).* <br>

1463. [ SNS ] Explain the SNS message delivery retry policy. What happens to a message that cannot be delivered to an HTTP/HTTPS endpoint? ; SNS retry policy for HTTP/HTTPS subscribers: Phase 1 (no delay retries, up to 3 attempts). Phase 2 (pre-backoff phase, up to 2 attempts, 20s apart). Phase 3 (backoff phase, up to 10 attempts, exponential backoff from 20s to 20 minutes). Phase 4 (post-backoff phase, up to 100,000 attempts, 20 minutes apart). Total: ~23 days of retries by default. If all retries fail and a DLQ is configured: message sent to DLQ. Without DLQ: message is silently dropped. <br><br> *Total retry duration for HTTP endpoints: 100,015 attempts over approximately 23 days. This is extremely generous — most transient endpoint outages resolve within minutes. For persistent outages (endpoint decommissioned): the DLQ becomes critical. Without DLQ: 23 days of silent retries then permanent loss. With DLQ: engineer is alerted, can fix endpoint and redrive messages.* <br> *SQS subscriber retry policy: different from HTTP. SQS delivery failures are rare (SQS is highly available). SNS retries SQS delivery with shorter retry windows. Lambda subscriber: synchronous invocation — if Lambda returns error, SNS retries per the configured retry policy (shorter than HTTP, typically minutes). The HTTP retry policy is the most generous because HTTP endpoints are the most fragile (can be down for hours due to deployment, network issues, etc.).* <br>

1464. [ SQS ] A company needs SQS messages to be accessible only from within their VPC. External internet access to the queue should be denied. How do you implement this? ; Two layers: (1) Create Interface VPC Endpoint for SQS in the VPC. This provides private access from within VPC. (2) Add a queue policy condition denying access from outside the VPC: `"Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:SourceVpc":"vpc-12345"}}` with `Effect: Deny`. All SQS API calls from outside the VPC are denied, including over the internet. Applications in the VPC use the VPC endpoint DNS name (or private DNS automatically resolves `sqs.region.amazonaws.com` to VPC endpoint). <br><br> *VPC endpoint policy: additionally restrict which queues are accessible via the endpoint. Endpoint policy: allow `sqs:SendMessage` only to specific queue ARNs. This prevents using the VPC endpoint to access queues in other accounts or other queues in the same account. Defense-in-depth: VPC endpoint (routing) + queue policy (access control) + VPC endpoint policy (endpoint-level restriction).* <br> *Private DNS resolution: Interface VPC Endpoint with `PrivateDnsEnabled=true` means `sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` resolves to the private endpoint IP within the VPC. No code changes needed — existing applications using the public DNS name automatically use the private endpoint. Without private DNS: applications must update to use the endpoint-specific DNS name (`vpce-xxx.sqs.us-east-1.vpce.amazonaws.com`).* <br>

1465. [ EventBridge ] A company uses EventBridge Pipes to route DynamoDB Stream events to Lambda. Some events should be skipped (DELETE events). How do you filter these? ; Add a filter to the EventBridge Pipe. Filter expression for Pipe: `{"eventName": [{"anything-but": "REMOVE"}]}` (DynamoDB Streams uses REMOVE for DELETE operations, INSERT for new items, MODIFY for updates). Configure on the Pipe source filter. Events not matching the filter are discarded before enrichment and target — no Lambda invocation for DELETE events, no cost. <br><br> *DynamoDB Stream event names: INSERT (new item created), MODIFY (existing item updated), REMOVE (item deleted). Pipe filter syntax matches EventBridge pattern syntax. `{"anything-but": "REMOVE"}` passes INSERT and MODIFY events. Or use explicit list: `{"eventName": ["INSERT","MODIFY"]}` to be explicit about allowed events.* <br> *Cost benefit of filtering at Pipe level: Lambda invocations not consumed for filtered events. DynamoDB Streams charges per shard-hour (already paying). Pipe charges $0.40/million events processed — but filtered events are NOT counted as processed. Only events that pass the filter and reach the target are charged. This makes Pipes more cost-effective than Lambda polling (which invokes Lambda for every batch including DELETE events that must be filtered in code).* <br>

1466. [ SNS ] What is SNS Data Protection Policy and what sensitive data patterns can it detect? ; SNS Data Protection Policy allows you to audit, mask, or block sensitive data in SNS message bodies before delivery to subscribers. Built-in managed data identifiers detect: credit card numbers (Visa, Mastercard, Amex), SSNs, passport numbers, driver license numbers, bank account numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, IP addresses, AWS credentials (access key patterns), and more. Custom data identifiers: your own regex patterns. Actions: Audit (log to CloudWatch, no blocking), Deny (block message delivery), Deidentify (mask data, e.g., replace SSN with ****). <br><br> *Use case: multi-tenant SaaS where customer data flows through SNS. Data protection policy ensures PII is never inadvertently sent to subscribers. Example: order events include customer email → policy detects email pattern → masks before delivery to analytics SQS subscriber (which does not need PII). Audit action: logs to CloudWatch Logs with the detected type and position in message — does not block delivery. Useful for compliance reporting.* <br> *Comparison with Macie: Macie scans S3 objects for PII. SNS Data Protection Policy scans messages in transit. Both complement each other. For end-to-end PII control: Macie (S3 at rest) + SNS Data Protection (in transit through SNS). For real-time PII scrubbing before delivery (not just detection): use Deny action (blocks message if PII detected) + require producer to fix the source data.* <br>

1467. [ SQS ] A company has 10 EC2 consumers polling an SQS queue. They use short polling. How can they reduce costs without changing the consumer count? ; Switch from short polling to long polling. Set `WaitTimeSeconds=20` in ReceiveMessage calls. With short polling: consumer polls, gets empty response, polls again immediately — thousands of empty API calls per hour. With long polling: consumer waits up to 20 seconds for messages — if no messages after 20 seconds, returns empty (one API call per 20 seconds instead of one per second). 20x reduction in empty API calls = significant cost reduction for queues with intermittent traffic. <br><br> *Long polling configuration: queue-level default `ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds=20` (all receive calls use 20s wait). Or per-call: `ReceiveMessage --wait-time-seconds 20`. Both achieve same result. Queue-level setting is simpler (no code change needed). AWS recommends long polling as best practice for all SQS consumers — only use short polling when you need the absolute minimum receive latency (rare).* <br> *Cost calculation: 10 consumers × short poll 1/second = 600 polls/minute × 60 = 36,000 polls/hour. At $0.40/million = $0.0144/hour. With long polling (1 poll/20s): 10 × 3/minute × 60 = 1,800 polls/hour. $0.00072/hour. 20x reduction. For a busy queue (messages always available): short vs long polling makes little difference (messages found immediately). Long polling matters most for sparsely used queues — dev/staging queues, overnight batch, seasonal traffic.* <br>

1468. [ EventBridge ] A company publishes custom application events to EventBridge. They want to automatically generate type-safe Python classes for these events that their Lambda developers can use. What EventBridge feature enables this? ; EventBridge Schema Registry with code bindings. Enable schema discovery on the custom event bus — EventBridge automatically infers JSON schemas from observed events. Or manually upload schemas. Then generate code bindings: download auto-generated Python code (dataclasses) for the event schema. Lambda developers import the generated classes — type-safe event handling with IDE autocomplete. No manual schema maintenance. <br><br> *Schema discovery process: enable discovery on event bus → EventBridge monitors PutEvents calls → infers OpenAPI 3.0 schema from JSON structure → stores in registry. Schema is updated as new event shapes are observed. Code binding generation: EventBridge console → Schema Registry → select schema → Get code bindings → Python/Java/TypeScript → download zip. Classes include typed fields matching the event JSON.* <br> *Practical benefit: without schema registry, Lambda developer receives `event['detail']['orderId']` (string key, runtime error if typo). With generated Python dataclass: `event.detail.order_id` (typed attribute, IDE catches typos at development time). Schema versioning: EventBridge maintains schema versions — if event structure changes, new schema version is added. Developers can regenerate code bindings for the new version. Cost: $0.10/million events scanned for discovery. Schema storage and code bindings: free.* <br>

1469. [ SQS ] What are the SQS queue limits a solutions architect must know for SAP-C02? ; Key limits: (1) Message size: 256 KB max (Extended Client Library for larger). (2) Message retention: 1 minute – 14 days (default 4 days). (3) Visibility timeout: 0 seconds – 12 hours (default 30 seconds). (4) Delivery delay: 0 – 900 seconds (15 minutes). (5) In-flight messages: 120,000 (Standard) / 20,000 (FIFO). (6) Batch size: 10 messages per batch operation. (7) Message attributes: 10 per message. (8) FIFO TPS: 300 without batching, 3,000 with batching, 70,000 High Throughput Mode. (9) Queue name: 80 characters (FIFO must end in .fifo). (10) Long polling wait: 0–20 seconds. <br><br> *Exam traps involving limits: (1) Payload > 256KB → Extended Client Library (cannot increase limit). (2) Visibility timeout = 0 → message immediately re-visible after receive (use for inspection without delay). (3) Retention > 14 days → not possible with SQS (use Kinesis with 365-day retention for longer retention). (4) FIFO throughput > 3,000 TPS → need High Throughput Mode. (5) In-flight limit hit → consumers not deleting fast enough (not a queue capacity issue).* <br> *Additional operational limits: 1 million queues per account (soft limit). 1 million requests per API call (10 messages × 256KB = 2.5MB max payload per batch). Polling threads: Lambda event source mapping uses 5 polling threads per queue. To process faster: increase Lambda concurrency or batch size, not polling threads (managed by AWS).* <br>

1470. [ SNS ] A company wants to send push notifications to 10 million mobile app users. The SNS platform application is set up. How does the push architecture scale and what are failure modes to handle? ; SNS handles scale automatically — publish to SNS topic → SNS delivers to all 10 million Platform Endpoints. Failure modes: (1) Stale device tokens (user uninstalled app, OS reset) → APNs/FCM returns `DeviceTokenNotForTopic` or `RegistrationId` invalid → SNS marks Platform Endpoint as disabled. (2) Delivery failures stored if endpoint disabled. Handle: implement token refresh flow — on app launch check token, update endpoint if changed. Periodically query and delete disabled endpoints. <br><br> *Platform Endpoint lifecycle: device registers → `CreatePlatformEndpoint` → endpoint ARN stored in your database. App updated (new token from APNs) → `SetEndpointAttributes` to update token. User uninstalls → APNs/FCM reports token invalid → SNS marks endpoint disabled → publish to disabled endpoint returns exception. Your backend: catch `EndpointDisabled` exception → delete endpoint ARN from database + call `DeleteEndpoint` in SNS.* <br> *Scaling: SNS fan-out to 10 million endpoints is handled by SNS internally — no architecture changes needed. SNS batches deliveries to APNs/FCM using their APIs. APNs HTTP/2 API supports multiplexing (many simultaneous requests per connection). FCM supports batch sends. For time-sensitive broadcasts (breaking news, emergency): no throttle on SNS side. For marketing campaigns: consider time-of-day targeting via segmented sends to avoid peak APNs/FCM rate limits.* <br>

1471. [ EventBridge ] How do you implement an idempotent consumer pattern when EventBridge delivers events at-least-once? ; EventBridge delivers events at-least-once. To handle duplicates: implement idempotency in the Lambda function. Approach: (1) Extract `id` field from EventBridge event (unique per event). (2) Before processing: check DynamoDB (or ElastiCache) for `id`. (3) If exists: event already processed → return success without re-processing. (4) If not exists: process the event, then write `id` to DynamoDB with TTL = event retention + buffer. <br><br> *EventBridge event ID: each event has a unique `id` field (UUID) generated by EventBridge. Same event delivered twice has the same `id`. Use this as idempotency key. DynamoDB conditional write: `PutItem` with `ConditionExpression: "attribute_not_exists(id)"`. If condition fails (item exists): event already processed → idempotent no-op. If condition succeeds: first time seen → process and write.* <br> *TTL strategy: set DynamoDB TTL = event maximum age + 24 hours. If EventBridge retries for up to 24 hours: keep idempotency record for 48 hours (24h retry window + 24h buffer). After TTL expires: DynamoDB auto-deletes record. This bounds idempotency table size. For high-volume events: ElastiCache Redis SET NX (set if not exists) with TTL is faster and cheaper than DynamoDB for hot idempotency checks.* <br>

1472. [ SQS ] A company's Lambda function processes SQS messages that call an external API. The external API rate-limits to 10 calls/second. Lambda scales to 100 concurrent invocations. How do you prevent exceeding the rate limit? ; Options: (1) Reserve Lambda concurrency at 10 for the SQS consumer function — limits concurrency to 10 (one call per Lambda invocation = 10 API calls/second). (2) Set SQS batch size to 1 and Lambda reserved concurrency to 10. (3) Use EventBridge API Destinations as intermediary with rate limit set to 10/second (if applicable). (4) Implement token bucket in Lambda using ElastiCache for distributed rate limiting across concurrent invocations. <br><br> *Reserved concurrency approach is simplest: set `ReservedConcurrentExecutions=10` on the Lambda function. SQS event source mapping scales Lambda up to the reserved concurrency limit. At 10 concurrent = 10 API calls/second (assuming <1s per call). Trade-off: other Lambda functions in account may not use this concurrency (reserved = dedicated). Also reduces processing throughput — if each Lambda invocation takes 500ms, you get 20 API calls/second maximum.* <br> *For sub-second rate limiting across concurrent functions: Redis INCR with expiry (token bucket).
