Consumer: poll HIGH first (long poll 1 second), if message: process. If no message: poll MEDIUM, then LOW. This prioritizes high-priority messages. Approximate — if consumer is busy with MEDIUM message: HIGH messages wait. For strict priority: consume only from HIGH until empty → then MEDIUM. Consumer complexity increases.* <br> *Amazon MQ alternative: if migration complexity is high, Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ) provides native RabbitMQ API compatibility. Drop-in replacement — no code changes. Downside: requires running instance (not serverless), higher cost than SQS. Migration path: RabbitMQ → Amazon MQ (immediate, no code change) → SQS (eventual, requires code refactoring for full serverless benefits). Exam: Amazon MQ = for lift-and-shift from RabbitMQ/ActiveMQ, SQS = cloud-native messaging.* <br>

1526. [ SNS ] A company sends large batches of messages (millions) to SNS at once. What SNS limits must they consider for message publishing rate? ; SNS publish API: 300 transactions per second (TPS) for Standard topics (soft limit, can be increased). Hard limit: varies by region, typically 3,000 TPS after limit increase. Publish in batch: SNS `PublishBatch` API — up to 10 messages per request. Effective TPS with batching: 300 TPS × 10 messages = 3,000 messages/second. For millions of messages: may take hours at 3,000 msg/sec rate. Use parallel publishers (multiple threads/processes) each publishing batches. <br><br> *Request Service Quotas increase for high-volume: submit AWS Support request for SNS TPS limit increase. Specify: messages/day, burst rate (peak messages/second), use case. Service quota increases: typically available for qualified workloads (marketing, notifications). SNS FIFO: lower limit (300 TPS with batching = 3,000 messages/sec max). Standard topic: higher limits available.* <br> *Alternative for bulk publish: Kinesis Data Streams → Lambda → SNS (process Kinesis records, publish to SNS). Kinesis: 1,000 records/second per shard. With 10 shards: 10,000 records/second into Lambda. Lambda publishes batches to SNS. Adds complexity but handles very high burst rates. For millions of messages in a few minutes: this architecture scales better than direct SNS publish.* <br>

1527. [ EventBridge ] How does EventBridge ensure event durability? What happens if a target service is temporarily unavailable? ; EventBridge retries failed deliveries: retries with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours. Retry window: configurable per rule target (1 minute to 24 hours). Default: 24 hours. If target unavailable for 24 hours: EventBridge drops the event (unless DLQ configured). With DLQ: events surviving retry window go to DLQ. EventBridge stores events in transit — not just fire-and-forget for synchronous delivery. At-least-once delivery guarantee within the retry window. <br><br> *Retry behavior: exponential backoff starting at 1 second, doubling until max retry window. For Lambda target: Lambda throttles trigger retry. For SQS target: SQS is almost always available (very rare to need retries for SQS). HTTP target: most common case for retries — HTTP endpoint down. EventBridge → API Destinations: uses API Destination's own retry config (separate from rule target retry). Combined retries: API Destination retry policy + rule target retry.* <br> *DLQ configuration for rule target: `DeadLetterConfig: {"Arn": "arn:aws:sqs:..."}`. EventBridge requires permission to send to DLQ: SQS queue policy allowing `events.amazonaws.com` to `sqs:SendMessage`. Events in DLQ: manual investigation and replay. For automated replay: Lambda triggered by DLQ → reprocesses events → re-publishes to EventBridge.* <br>

1528. [ SQS ] Describe the SQS Extended Client Library architecture. How does it handle large messages? ; Extended Client Library: Java/Python/Node.js library that transparently handles messages > 256KB. Architecture: (1) Producer: checks message size. If ≤ 256KB: send directly to SQS. If > 256KB: upload payload to S3, store S3 pointer (bucket + key) in SQS message body with metadata flag `["software.amazon.payloadoffloading.PayloadS3Pointer"]`. SQS message = small pointer, not actual payload. (2) Consumer: receives SQS message, detects S3 pointer flag, downloads payload from S3, processes full message. (3) After processing: deletes SQS message + deletes S3 object. <br><br> *S3 bucket configuration: Extended Client Library requires an S3 bucket. Library uses: `new ExtendedClientConfiguration().withPayloadSupportEnabled(s3Client, "my-bucket")`. Key naming: UUID-based keys. IAM: Lambda/EC2 role needs S3 read/write on the specified bucket. `deleteMessagePayloadFromS3` flag: controls whether to delete S3 object on message deletion (should be true to avoid S3 orphaned objects).* <br> *Failure handling: if S3 object deleted before message processed: consumer receives pointer, tries to download → S3 404 → error. DLQ receives the pointer message (not the payload). DLQ investigation: download S3 object if still available. S3 lifecycle policy: if S3 objects expire (lifecycle rule) before DLQ retention: permanent data loss. Set S3 lifecycle expiry = SQS message retention (14 days) + DLQ retention (14 days) + buffer. Best: no S3 lifecycle on Extended Client Library bucket except to delete objects tagged as processed.* <br>

1529. [ SNS ] What are the supported AWS Lambda destinations for SNS in terms of Lambda async invocation DLQs and the difference with SNS subscription DLQs? ; Lambda async invocation from SNS: SNS invokes Lambda synchronously. If Lambda returns error → SNS retries (its own retry policy, not Lambda's). SNS → Lambda does NOT use Lambda's async invocation model — it's a synchronous invoke. Therefore: Lambda's own `DestinationConfig` DLQ does NOT capture SNS failures. SNS subscription DLQ (configured on the subscription): captures messages where SNS exhausted its delivery retries. For SNS → Lambda failures: configure DLQ on the SNS subscription, not on Lambda. <br><br> *Lambda DLQ (async invocations): applies to Lambda invoked asynchronously (S3 events, SQS DLQ delivery to Lambda, EventBridge direct invocation). EventBridge → Lambda: Lambda is invoked asynchronously → Lambda's DLQ applies. SNS → Lambda: synchronous invocation → Lambda's DLQ does NOT apply → SNS subscription DLQ applies.* <br> *Configuration: SNS subscription DLQ: `aws sns set-subscription-attributes --subscription-arn arn:... --attribute-name RedrivePolicy --attribute-value '{"deadLetterTargetArn":"arn:aws:sqs:..."}'`. Queue policy: allow SNS to send to DLQ. Lambda invocation destination (for async): `aws lambda put-function-event-invoke-config --function-name ... --destination-config '{"OnFailure":{"Destination":"arn:aws:sqs:..."}}'`. These are completely separate mechanisms.* <br>

1530. [ EventBridge ] A company uses EventBridge to trigger CodePipeline when code is pushed to CodeCommit. CodePipeline builds and deploys. How do you prevent multiple simultaneous pipeline runs when a developer pushes multiple commits in quick succession? ; EventBridge delivers each CodeCommit push as a separate event. Each triggers CodePipeline, which starts a new execution. To prevent multiple simultaneous runs: (1) CodePipeline pipeline execution mode: `QUEUED` mode — new executions queue behind the current running one. (2) `SUPERSEDED` mode (default): new execution supersedes the queued one (only one queued at a time, most recent commit wins). (3) `PARALLEL` mode: all run simultaneously (not what you want). Use `SUPERSEDED` for CD pipelines: last push = most recent code = should deploy. <br><br> *SUPERSEDED behavior: developer pushes commit A → pipeline runs. Developer immediately pushes commit B → pipeline queues B. Developer pushes commit C → C supersedes B (B is dropped). Result: only A (running) and C (queued) — the intermediate B is skipped. This is ideal for feature branches where only the latest state matters. QUEUED: every push runs eventually. Better for audit (complete history) but slower (queue can back up during active development).* <br> *EventBridge throttling alternative: not recommended (EventBridge doesn't have native event deduplication or rate limiting in event delivery). Better to configure at CodePipeline level. Or: EventBridge → SQS (dedup window) → Lambda → StartPipeline (lambda checks if pipeline already running, skips if so). Most elegant: just use CodePipeline's built-in execution mode.* <br>


1531. [ SQS ] Compare SQS, Kinesis Data Streams, and Kinesis Data Firehose for message streaming. When do you choose each? ; SQS: message queue for work distribution. At-least-once delivery. Consumer deletes message. Multiple consumers get different messages. Retention: 14 days. No ordering (Standard) / per-group ordering (FIFO). Best for: task distribution, decoupling, workload leveling. Kinesis Data Streams: real-time data streaming. Consumer reads without deleting. Multiple consumer groups read same data (fan-out). Retention: 1-365 days. Ordering per shard. Best for: real-time analytics, event sourcing, multiple consumers of same data. Kinesis Firehose: fully managed ETL delivery to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch. No consumer code. Best for: data lake ingestion, near-real-time (60s minimum latency). <br><br> *Decision tree: (1) Task queue (work to distribute to workers) → SQS. (2) Same event consumed by multiple services independently → Kinesis or SNS. (3) Real-time analytics/ML inference → Kinesis Data Streams (millisecond latency). (4) Log/event ingestion to S3/data lake → Kinesis Firehose. (5) Ordering with fan-out → Kinesis (shard ordering + multiple consumer groups). (6) Retention > 14 days → Kinesis (365 days).* <br> *Kinesis vs SQS cost: Kinesis Data Streams charged per shard-hour ($0.015/shard-hour) + per-million records. For 1 million records/day: 1 shard = $0.015 × 24 × 30 = $10.80/month. SQS: 1 million messages × $0.40 = $0.40/month. SQS cheaper for low-volume. Kinesis: better at scale with multiple consumers (you're not paying per consumer). For 10 consumers reading same data: SQS cost × 10 (each message stored 10 times or 10 queues), Kinesis cost × 1.* <br>

1532. [ SNS ] What is the SNS message filtering feature called "filter policy scope" and how does it affect filtering? ; Filter policy scope: two options — `MessageAttributes` (default) and `MessageBody`. `MessageAttributes` (default): filter policy applies to message attributes. Message body content irrelevant for filtering. Subscribe with `FilterPolicyScope=MessageAttributes` + `FilterPolicy={"color":["red"]}` → receives only messages where `color` attribute = "red". `MessageBody` scope: filter policy applies to the JSON message body content directly. No attributes needed. Subscribe with `FilterPolicyScope=MessageBody` + `FilterPolicy={"event":{"type":["order.created"]}}` → receives messages where body JSON has `event.type = "order.created"`. <br><br> *When to use MessageBody filtering: (1) Publisher cannot add message attributes (legacy system, third-party). (2) Routing logic based on complex nested body fields. (3) Shopify/partner event bus events (body-based). MessageBody filtering requires message body to be valid JSON. Non-JSON body messages: not matched by body filter policy (delivered if filter policy is empty, dropped if filter policy exists).* <br> *MessageAttributes filtering remains preferred: simpler, faster (no body parsing), works with any content type. Design principle: put routing metadata in attributes, business data in body. MessageBody filtering: use only when attribute-based filtering is not possible. Cost: filter evaluation is free (no charge for filtered-out messages). Subscribe with both scope options simultaneously: not possible — one scope per subscription.* <br>

1533. [ EventBridge ] How do you implement a circuit breaker pattern using EventBridge and Step Functions? ; Circuit breaker with Step Functions + EventBridge: (1) Normal state: EventBridge → Lambda (direct). (2) Failure detection: Lambda returns errors → CloudWatch Alarm → EventBridge. (3) EventBridge triggers Step Functions: `CircuitBreaker` state machine. (4) State machine: sets DynamoDB item `circuit_state = OPEN`. (5) Open state: Lambda reads DynamoDB, sees OPEN → returns fallback response without calling downstream. (6) Recovery: Step Functions Wait state (5 minutes) → try half-open → if success → DynamoDB `circuit_state = CLOSED`. <br><br> *DynamoDB circuit state: partition key = service name. Attributes: state (CLOSED/OPEN/HALF_OPEN), failure_count, last_failure_time. Lambda reads at start of each invocation: `get_item(Key={"service_name": "downstream_api"})`. If state=OPEN: return cached/fallback response. If state=CLOSED: proceed normally, on error: increment failure_count, if > threshold: update state to OPEN.* <br> *EventBridge for state transitions: CloudWatch Alarm (failure rate > X%) → EventBridge → Lambda → update DynamoDB to OPEN. After recovery wait: EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedule → Lambda → set HALF_OPEN, test single request. Success → CLOSED. Failure → reset OPEN timer. Full pattern: resilient distributed system with visibility into circuit state via CloudWatch dashboard + EventBridge events for each state transition.* <br>

1534. [ SQS ] A company wants to send messages to SQS from an EC2 instance without using AWS access keys (no static credentials). What is the correct approach? ; Attach an IAM Role to the EC2 instance (Instance Profile). IAM Role Policy: `{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["sqs:SendMessage","sqs:GetQueueAttributes"],"Resource":"arn:aws:sqs:region:account:queue-name"}`. EC2 instance metadata service provides temporary credentials via the role. AWS SDK on EC2 automatically uses instance metadata credentials (no access key configuration needed). SDK credential chain: 1. Environment variables → 2. Java system properties → 3. AWS credentials file → 4. Container/ECS credentials → 5. Instance metadata (EC2 role) → uses role credentials. <br><br> *Instance Profile = IAM Role assigned to EC2 at launch. Console: EC2 → Launch Instance → Advanced Details → IAM Instance Profile. Or attach to existing: `aws ec2 associate-iam-instance-profile --instance-id i-xxx --iam-instance-profile Name=MyRole`. Credentials rotation: automatic (rotated ~hourly by AWS). No manual rotation needed. Never better than a role with temp creds.* <br> *Least privilege for SQS: producer role → only `sqs:SendMessage` on specific queue ARN. Consumer role → `sqs:ReceiveMessage` + `sqs:DeleteMessage` + `sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility` + `sqs:GetQueueAttributes`. No `sqs:*` wildcard. Separate roles for producer and consumer EC2 instances (principle of least privilege). Add `sqs:GetQueueUrl` if application uses queue name (not URL).* <br>

1535. [ SNS ] What is the difference between SNS A2A (Application-to-Application) and SNS A2P (Application-to-Person) messaging? ; A2A (Application-to-Application): SNS core functionality. Applications communicate via topics. Subscribers: SQS, Lambda, Kinesis Firehose, HTTP/HTTPS endpoints. Use: microservices, event-driven architecture, fan-out. No human recipient. A2P (Application-to-Person): SNS SMS and push notifications. Subscribers: phone numbers (SMS), mobile device tokens (APNs/FCM). Use: user notifications, OTPs, alerts to humans. Different pricing, compliance requirements, and regulatory considerations (SMS carrier regulations, TCPA). <br><br> *Regulatory: A2P SMS in US: Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA) compliance. Must have opt-in consent before sending marketing messages. AWS SNS SMS: you are responsible for TCPA compliance (opt-in management). DND registry: some countries (India) require checking Do Not Disturb registry before sending. AWS provides tools (opt-out management) but responsibility is on the customer.* <br> *Cost comparison: A2A (SQS subscriber): $0.50/million messages. A2P (SMS): $0.00645/message (US standard). A2P (mobile push): $0.50/million push (cheap). A2P SMS is 13,000x more expensive per message than SQS. Design principle: use push notifications instead of SMS where possible (cheaper, richer UX). SMS: for time-sensitive alerts where user may not have app installed (OTP, emergency).* <br>

1536. [ EventBridge ] How does EventBridge handle schema versioning when event structure changes? Describe best practices for managing breaking schema changes. ; EventBridge Schema Registry: new version auto-discovered when event structure changes (Schema Discovery enabled). Each version is separate schema entry (v1, v2, etc.). Generated code bindings per version. Breaking change handling: (1) Publish both old and new event format during transition period. (2) Consumers: generate code for v2, update to handle v2 first while accepting v1 as fallback. (3) After all consumers upgraded: stop publishing v1 format. (4) Use `version` field in event detail: consumers route based on version. <br><br> *Forward compatibility: add optional fields to existing events (consumers that don't know about new fields ignore them). Backward compatible: old consumers still work. Breaking change: rename/remove required field, change data type → breaks old consumers. Additive-only changes: preferred for event schemas. Versioned event type: `detail-type: "OrderPlaced.v2"` — consumers subscribe only to their supported version. Old consumers: still subscribed to `"OrderPlaced.v1"`. Publish to both types during transition.* <br> *Schema Registry governance: for team-wide schema management, register schemas manually (don't rely only on auto-discovery). Schema naming convention: `com.company.service/event-type`. Review new schema versions in CI/CD: use `aws schemas get-schema` in deployment pipeline to check for incompatible schema changes. Alert if new schema version auto-created (may indicate unintended schema change).* <br>

1537. [ SQS ] A Lambda function that processes SQS messages needs to call an RDS database. RDS is in a private subnet. Lambda is not in VPC. How do you configure this correctly? ; Put Lambda in VPC (same VPC as RDS). VPC configuration for Lambda: specify VPC ID, subnets (private subnets with route to NAT if Lambda needs internet), security group. Lambda security group: allow outbound to RDS security group on port 3306 (MySQL) or 5432 (PostgreSQL). RDS security group: allow inbound from Lambda security group on DB port. Lambda VPC networking: Lambda ENI in VPC allows private routing to RDS. No internet needed for Lambda→RDS communication. <br><br> *Lambda VPC trade-offs: VPC Lambda: can access RDS but cold starts slightly higher (ENI provisioning — this was true pre-2020, now mitigated by ENI reuse). Without VPC: Lambda cannot reach private RDS (VPC-only resource). Only way to access private RDS: Lambda in VPC or RDS Proxy (which also requires Lambda in VPC for private access) or RDS with public endpoint (not recommended for production).* <br> *SQS VPC endpoint for VPC Lambda: Lambda in VPC needs to communicate with SQS. Options: (1) NAT Gateway in VPC (Lambda in private subnet → NAT → SQS public endpoint). (2) VPC Interface Endpoint for SQS (Lambda → SQS via private endpoint, no NAT needed). Interface VPC Endpoint is preferred: no data transfer through NAT (saves cost), private routing. Configure: SQS VPC endpoint in Lambda's VPC subnets.* <br>

1538. [ SNS ] What are the SNS best practices for high-throughput applications sending 10,000+ messages/second? ; Best practices: (1) Parallel publishing: multiple threads/processes each publishing to SNS (not single-threaded sequential). (2) SNS PublishBatch: 10 messages per API call. (3) Connection pooling: reuse HTTPS connections (SDK handles this). (4) Retry with backoff: SDK handles ThrottlingException retries. (5) Multiple SNS topics (fan-out): if one topic has many subscribers with complex filters, consider sharding across topics. (6) SQS subscriber queues: ensure SQS can handle delivery rate (SQS: near-unlimited ingest). (7) Request TPS limit increase if needed. <br><br> *Thread pool sizing: 10,000 msg/sec ÷ 10 msg/batch = 1,000 API calls/sec needed. Default SNS TPS: 300 TPS. 1,000 TPS: request limit increase. Or: 10 parallel publishers × 100 TPS each = 1,000 effective TPS. Java: `ExecutorService` with fixed thread pool. Python: asyncio + aiohttp for async SNS calls. AWS SDK: not async natively (use threads or aiobotocore for Python async).* <br> *Subscriber scaling: 10,000 msg/sec to SNS topic → each subscriber gets 10,000 deliveries/sec. Lambda subscribers: Lambda scales automatically. SQS subscribers: SQS ingest is unlimited. HTTP subscribers: must handle 10,000 req/sec (may need load balancer + multiple instances). Mobile push: APNs/FCM rate limits may apply. Firehose subscriber: 1,000 records/sec per PUT (shard equivalent) — request limit increase for 10,000/sec.* <br>

1539. [ EventBridge ] A company wants to implement event sourcing for their order management system using EventBridge and DynamoDB. Describe the architecture. ; Event sourcing with EventBridge + DynamoDB: (1) OrderService publishes domain events to EventBridge: `order.created`, `order.updated`, `order.cancelled`. (2) EventBridge rule → Lambda (EventStore function) → writes event to DynamoDB `Events` table (PK=orderId, SK=timestamp#eventType, payload=full event). (3) EventBridge rule → Lambda (Projection function) → updates read model in DynamoDB `Orders` table (current state). (4) Replay: EventBridge Archive → enable replay → replay all historical events → rebuild projection. <br><br> *DynamoDB Events table design: partition key = `orderId`, sort key = `version` (incrementing number) or `timestamp`. Stores immutable event log. GSI: `type-timestamp-index` for querying events by type and time range. Stream all events to Kinesis Firehose → S3 for long-term archive.* <br> *Projection rebuild (CQRS read model): when projection logic changes (new field, bug fix): delete read model table → replay all events via EventBridge → Projection Lambda recreates read model. This is the power of event sourcing. EventBridge Archive retention = retention of event history needed for rebuild. Indefinite retention: no rebuild limit. 30-day retention: can only rebuild from last 30 days. Cost: $0.10/GB/month for EventBridge archive.* <br>

1540. [ SQS ] Explain how Lambda scales with SQS event source mapping in detail, including the scaling algorithm. ; Lambda ESM scaling for SQS: initial: 5 polling threads. Each poll: `ReceiveMessage(MaxNumberOfMessages=batchSize)`. If messages available: Lambda invokes 1 function per 5 messages (rate scales). After 1 minute: if queue has messages and functions are processing: adds 60 more concurrent functions. Continues adding 60/minute until: (a) no messages remain, (b) concurrent limit reached, (c) scaling limit reached. Maximum: 1,000 concurrent (Standard queues), 1 per Message Group (FIFO). Scaling down: gradual as queue drains. <br><br> *Key scaling parameters: `batchSize` (1-10,000 for Standard, 1-10 for FIFO). `maximumBatchingWindow` (0-300s): wait before invoking Lambda to accumulate messages into larger batches. `startingPosition`: TRIM_HORIZON or AT_TIMESTAMP or LATEST (Kinesis only — for SQS: always oldest unprocessed message). `functionResponseTypes`: ["ReportBatchItemFailures"] for partial batch failure.* <br> *FIFO scaling: 1 Lambda invocation per active Message Group ID (per group = sequential). N concurrent groups = N concurrent Lambda invocations. Max FIFO concurrency = number of active message groups × 1. 1,000 active FIFO message groups → 1,000 concurrent Lambda. For FIFO: concurrency limited by groups, not by Lambda limits. Scaling rate: as fast as new groups become active. Unlike Standard (60/minute scale-up): FIFO scales with message group activity.* <br>

1541. [ EventBridge ] What is EventBridge content filtering and what operators are supported? How do these reduce Lambda costs? ; EventBridge content filtering operators: (1) `prefix` — string starts with value: `{"prefix":"order-"}`. (2) `suffix` — string ends with value (newer feature). (3) `anything-but` — value is NOT in list: `[{"anything-but":"deleted"}]`. (4) `numeric` — range: `[{"numeric":[">",0,"<",100]}]`. (5) `cidr` — IP in CIDR range: `[{"cidr":"10.0.0.0/8"}]`. (6) `exists` — field present/absent: `[{"exists":true}]`. (7) Exact match: `["value"]`. Combine with AND (multiple fields) and OR (multiple values in array). <br><br> *Cost reduction: each filtered event costs $0/Lambda invocation. EventBridge evaluates pattern match for free (up to 5M/month free tier). Without filtering: Lambda invoked for ALL events, must filter in code. 1M events/month, 90% filtered in Lambda: 1M Lambda invocations. With EventBridge filtering: 100K Lambda invocations. Lambda cost reduction: 90%. For 128MB Lambda with 100ms avg duration: 1M invocations = $2/month. Filtered to 100K: $0.20/month. Meaningful for high-volume event buses.* <br> *Numeric filtering use case: order amount routing. Filter: `{"detail":{"order":{"amount":[{"numeric":[">",1000]}]}}}` → trigger Lambda for orders > $1000. Filter: `{"detail":{"error_code":[{"numeric":[">=",400,"<",500]}]}}` → trigger Lambda for 4xx HTTP errors. Cidr filtering: security events from specific IP ranges. Prefix filtering: S3 key prefixes (`{"prefix":"uploads/images/"}`) — route image uploads differently from document uploads.* <br>

1542. [ SQS ] How do you implement SQS-based job scheduling where jobs need to run at specific future times (up to 24 hours in advance)? ; Option 1: EventBridge Scheduler — create one-time schedule per job, fires at specified time → Lambda → process job. Up to 1 million schedules, exact time. Best for jobs hours/days in future. Option 2: SQS with delivery delay — max 15 minutes. Not suitable for hours in advance. Option 3: DynamoDB + EventBridge Scheduled Rule — store future jobs in DynamoDB with scheduled_at timestamp. EventBridge rule runs every minute → Lambda → query DynamoDB `scheduled_at ≤ now` → process due jobs. Simple, scalable, any time in future. <br><br> *EventBridge Scheduler for SQS: EventBridge Scheduler → SQS target. Scheduler invokes SQS `SendMessage` at specified time. Lambda consumes from SQS when message arrives. This combines Scheduler's exact timing with SQS's durability. Best for: high-value jobs where timing matters + durability needed.* <br> *DynamoDB approach at scale: GSI on `scheduled_at` attribute. Lambda scans records with `scheduled_at` between previous execution and now (using `scheduled_at BETWEEN last_run AND now`). 1-minute poll interval: jobs run within 1 minute of scheduled time. For 1 million scheduled jobs: DynamoDB handles the query efficiently via GSI. Delete job record after processing. Benefit: any future time (no 15-minute SQS delay limit, no 1-million-schedule Scheduler limit).* <br>

1543. [ SNS ] A company wants to implement pub/sub where subscribers can specify complex routing rules based on nested JSON message body fields. What are the options? ; Option 1: SNS with MessageBody filter scope. Filter policy on subscription targeting nested JSON fields: `{"order":{"type":["premium"],"amount":[{"numeric":[">",500]}]}}`. Matches messages where `order.type = "premium"` AND `order.amount > 500`. JSON body must be valid JSON. Option 2: EventBridge — native support for complex content filtering on any event detail field, more operators, better tooling. Option 3: Lambda fan-out — SNS → Lambda → evaluate complex conditions → publish to target queues/functions. <br><br> *SNS MessageBody filter limitations: filter only works on first-level JSON properties in `Message` body (flat filter). Nested objects (like `order.amount`): supported in newer versions. String, number, exists operators supported. Cannot: compare two fields to each other, use computed values, regex matching. For complex routing beyond what SNS filters support: EventBridge provides more operators (prefix, suffix, anything-but, numeric ranges, cidr, exists) and handles nested paths natively.* <br> *Decision: SNS: if already using SNS, 1-2 routing dimensions (e.g., event type + priority). EventBridge: if routing logic is complex, needs event transformation, or requires many event sources/targets. Lambda fan-out: when routing logic requires business logic (database lookup, complex calculations). Cost: SNS filter = free. EventBridge = $1/million custom events. Lambda fan-out = Lambda cost. For most routing: SNS + EventBridge are preferred over Lambda fan-out.* <br>

1544. [ EventBridge ] What are the EventBridge service limits (quotas) a solutions architect must know? ; Key quotas: (1) Event buses: 100 per account per region. (2) Rules per event bus: 300 (default, increasable). (3) Targets per rule: 5 (default, increasable up to 15). (4) Invocation rate: 400 concurrent rule invocations per region (soft limit). (5) PutEvents: 400 entries per request, 256KB max per entry, 256KB max total request payload. (6) Event retention on bus: no storage (events not persisted unless archived). (7) Archive: 1 per event bus. (8) API Destinations: 3,000 per account. (9) EventBridge Scheduler: 1 million schedules per account. (10) Global Endpoints: 5 per account. <br><br> *Targets per rule: 5 default, 15 maximum. If you need more than 15 targets: use fan-out (rule → SNS topic → multiple SNS subscribers) or rule → Lambda → multiple targets. Multiple rules for same event pattern: each rule invoked separately, each with up to 15 targets. Event pattern limit: 4KB per pattern JSON. PutEvents: max 10 entries per call in SDK (not 400 — that's the limit, but SDK default batch = 10). Use parallel calls for high throughput.* <br> *Schema Registry: 1,500 schemas per registry, 100 registries per account. Schema versions: 100 per schema. Schema discovery: requires enabling per bus. Scheduler TPS: 5,000 API calls per second (CreateSchedule, GetSchedule, etc.). Schedule groups: 500 per account. Flexible time window: 0-1440 minutes. Scheduler min interval: 1 minute (cannot sub-minute). For sub-minute: CloudWatch Events with Lambda is not supported either — use Lambda triggered by SQS or Step Functions.* <br>

1545. [ SQS ] A Lambda function must process SQS messages exactly once, even if the Lambda is retried due to throttling or provisioned concurrency. Describe the complete solution. ; Complete exactly-once processing: (1) Use SQS FIFO (5-minute dedup window). (2) Lambda ESM with `ReportBatchItemFailures`. (3) DynamoDB conditional write as idempotency key. (4) Lambda processing: `a` — receive SQS event. `b` — for each message: extract idempotency key (MessageId). `c` — DynamoDB PutItem conditional (`attribute_not_exists(id)`). `d` — if conditional fails: already processed, delete from SQS (return success for that message). `e` — if conditional succeeds: process business logic. `f` — if business logic succeeds: DynamoDB update complete marker. `g` — if business logic fails: DynamoDB delete item (rollback idempotency), return failure for that message ID in batchItemFailures. <br><br> *Why step g (rollback): if Lambda writes DynamoDB idempotency record but business logic fails: message goes to DLQ (failed) but idempotency record remains (marking as processed). DLQ redrive: Lambda sees idempotency record → skips → permanent data loss. Fix: either don't write idempotency until after successful processing OR rollback on failure. Rollback approach: write idempotency with `status: in_progress` → process → update `status: completed`. On failure: delete `in_progress` record. On retry: no record found → retry processing.* <br> *FIFO dedup + DynamoDB: two-layer defense. FIFO catches duplicates within 5-minute window (common case: Lambda retry due to transient error). DynamoDB catches: duplicates from DLQ redrive (days later), message visible again after visibility timeout, rare SQS dedup window expiry. Together: very strong exactly-once guarantee.* <br>

1546. [ SNS ] What is the SNS cross-account delivery scenario and what permissions are required? ; Cross-account SNS → SQS: Account A has SNS topic. Account B has SQS queue. SNS → SQS cross-account. Required: (1) Account B SQS queue policy: allow SNS ARN from Account A. `{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"sns.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sqs:SendMessage","Condition":{"ArnEquals":{"aws:SourceArn":"arn:aws:sns:region:ACCOUNT_A:topic-name"}}}`. (2) Account B IAM user/role subscribing: must have `sns:Subscribe` permission on Topic ARN from Account A. (3) Account A SNS topic policy (optional but best practice): allow `sns:Subscribe` from Account B. <br><br> *Cross-account SNS publish (Account A Lambda → Account B SNS): (1) Account B SNS topic policy must allow `sns:Publish` from Account A principal. (2) Account A Lambda role must have `sns:Publish` on Account B topic ARN. SNS topic policy: `{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_A:role/LambdaRole"},"Action":"sns:Publish","Resource":"arn:aws:sns:region:ACCOUNT_B:topic"}`. Lambda IAM role: `{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"sns:Publish","Resource":"arn:aws:sns:region:ACCOUNT_B:topic"}`.* <br> *Cross-account mobile push: not possible to publish to another account's Platform Application endpoint directly. Platform Applications are account-specific. Architecture for multi-account mobile push: centralize push in one account (PushAccount), all other accounts publish to PushAccount's SNS topic, PushAccount delivers to APNs/FCM. Cross-account event topic → PushAccount via resource policy.* <br>

1547. [ EventBridge ] Describe how EventBridge Pipes can be used to implement an event-driven ETL pipeline from DynamoDB to OpenSearch. ; EventBridge Pipes: DynamoDB Stream → Filter → Enrichment → OpenSearch. (1) Source: DynamoDB Stream (INSERT/MODIFY events). (2) Filter: `{"eventName": ["INSERT","MODIFY"]}` (skip REMOVE). (3) Enrichment: Lambda function transforms DynamoDB JSON format (attribute value types like `{"S":"value"}`) to plain JSON (`{"field":"value"}`). (4) Target: EventBridge API Destination to OpenSearch `_bulk` API endpoint. Or target: OpenSearch Service's HTTP endpoint via Lambda. <br><br> *DynamoDB → OpenSearch via Pipes: Source: DynamoDB Stream. Enrichment Lambda: converts DynamoDB AttributeValue format to standard JSON. Example: `{"userId":{"S":"123"},"name":{"S":"Alice"}}` → `{"userId":"123","name":"Alice"}`. Target: OpenSearch Serverless or domain via API Destination (HTTPS). Authentication: OAuth or API key for OpenSearch fine-grained access control.* <br> *Alternative (traditional): DynamoDB Streams → Lambda (direct ESM) → OpenSearch. Same result but Lambda is the consumer and must manage scaling, DLQ, etc. Pipes advantage: managed fan-out, built-in filter, visual flow in console, no consumer code for source/target. Lambda advantage: more complex transformations, custom error handling. For simple ETL: Pipes. For complex transformation or conditional routing: Lambda.* <br>

1548. [ SQS ] What is the SQS `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage` metric and how does it help with SLA monitoring? ; `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage`: CloudWatch metric showing age (in seconds) of the oldest message currently in the queue that has NOT been deleted. Increases when consumers fall behind or stop. Decreases when consumers catch up. Zero: queue is empty or all messages are being processed quickly. Key SLA metric: if SLA = process all messages within 5 minutes, alarm when `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage > 300`. Triggers scale-out or alerting before SLA breach. <br><br> *Auto Scaling trigger: create CloudWatch alarm on `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage > SLA_threshold`. Alarm → SNS → Auto Scaling policy (scale out EC2 instances or ECS tasks). More precise than `ApproximateNumberOfMessages` for SLA: a queue with 0 messages but one 10-minute-old message in flight (stuck consumer) → age metric catches this, count metric doesn't.* <br> *Monitoring pattern: (1) `ApproximateNumberOfMessages`: backlog (how many waiting). (2) `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible`: in-flight count. (3) `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage`: SLA health. (4) `NumberOfMessagesSent`: incoming rate. (5) `NumberOfMessagesDeleted`: processing rate. If `MessagesSent > MessagesDeleted` consistently: backlog growing → scale consumers. If `Age > SLA`: consumers too slow → optimize processing or scale.* <br>

1549. [ SNS ] What AWS services can directly subscribe to SNS topics? List all supported protocols. ; SNS subscription protocols: (1) `sqs` — Amazon SQS queue (ARN). (2) `lambda` — AWS Lambda function (ARN). (3) `http` — HTTP URL (endpoint confirms subscription). (4) `https` — HTTPS URL (endpoint confirms subscription). (5) `email` — email address (human confirms via link). (6) `email-json` — email with JSON body (human confirms). (7) `sms` — phone number (immediate, no confirmation). (8) `application` — mobile platform endpoint ARN (APNs, FCM, ADM, Baidu push). (9) `firehose` — Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose stream ARN (for S3/Redshift/OpenSearch delivery). <br><br> *Firehose subscriber (added 2020): SNS → Kinesis Data Firehose → S3/Redshift/OpenSearch/HTTP. No custom Lambda needed for event archival. Set up: subscribe Firehose delivery stream to SNS topic. Message format: SNS envelope (or raw with RawMessageDelivery). Firehose batches events, delivers to S3 every 60 seconds or 128MB. S3 prefix: can include timestamp partitioning for Athena querying.* <br> *Cross-account subscriptions: SQS, Lambda, HTTP/HTTPS, Firehose — all support cross-account (with appropriate resource policies). SMS and email: account-specific (phone numbers/emails can be in any account, but delivery is to external systems). Application (mobile push): cross-account not directly supported (platform application is account-specific).* <br>

1550. [ EventBridge ] A company uses EventBridge + Lambda for fraud detection. Lambda analyzes each transaction event in real-time. Peak transaction volume: 5,000 events/second. What design considerations are needed? ; Design for 5,000 events/second: (1) EventBridge PutEvents: 400 concurrent invocations per region default — request increase or use multiple event buses. (2) Lambda concurrency: 5,000 concurrent invocations needed if processing is <1s each. Request concurrency limit increase (default 1,000/region). (3) Provisioned Concurrency: eliminates cold starts at peak (important for real-time fraud detection). (4) Lambda timeout: set to minimum viable (fraud detection should be < 1s). (5) Connection pooling: reuse database connections (Aurora Serverless, RDS Proxy). <br><br> *Alternative: Kinesis Data Streams instead of EventBridge for 5,000 events/sec. Kinesis: designed for high-throughput streaming. 5 shards × 1,000 records/sec = 5,000 records/sec. Lambda ESM on Kinesis: scales automatically. Kinesis cost < EventBridge at 5,000/sec (EventBridge $1/million = $0.005/second = $432/month, Kinesis 5 shards = $0.015 × 24 × 30 × 5 = $54/month + data cost). Kinesis cheaper at high volume.* <br> *Fraud detection latency: EventBridge → Lambda: ~100ms delivery. Lambda cold start: 200-500ms. With Provisioned Concurrency: <100ms. Total: ~100-200ms per event. For real-time fraud (prevent transaction): synchronous path needed (not EventBridge async). EventBridge is async — payment API has already returned. Pattern: sync path (payment API → synchronous Lambda → fraud score → allow/deny) + async EventBridge (for post-transaction analysis, ML model updates, alerting).* <br>

1551. [ SQS ] What is an SQS message attribute vs a SQS system attribute? Give examples of each. ; Message attributes (user-defined): metadata set by producer. Up to 10 attributes. Data types: String, Number, Binary, String.Array. Used for routing, filtering, business metadata. Example: `{"OrderType":{"DataType":"String","StringValue":"PRIORITY"},"Amount":{"DataType":"Number","StringValue":"150.00"}}`. Not part of message body. System attributes (AWS-managed): automatically set by SQS. Examples: `ApproximateFirstReceiveTimestamp` (epoch ms, first time received), `ApproximateReceiveCount` (how many times received), `MessageDeduplicationId` (FIFO), `MessageGroupId` (FIFO), `SentTimestamp` (epoch ms, when sent), `SequenceNumber` (FIFO ordering number). <br><br> *Requesting system attributes in ReceiveMessage: `--attribute-names All` or specific: `--attribute-names SentTimestamp ApproximateReceiveCount`. Without requesting: these are not returned. Message attributes: `--message-attribute-names All` or specific names. Lambda event: system attributes in `Attributes` map, message attributes in `messageAttributes` map.* <br> *Use case for system attributes: `ApproximateReceiveCount` in Lambda: if receive count approaching MaxReceiveCount (before DLQ), send pre-DLQ alert with full message details. `SentTimestamp`: calculate processing latency (current time - sent time). `SequenceNumber` (FIFO): debug message ordering issues. `ApproximateFirstReceiveTimestamp`: measure how long message waited in queue before first processing.* <br>

1552. [ SNS ] How do you implement cross-region SNS delivery? Is it natively supported? ; SNS does not natively replicate topics across regions. Cross-region delivery requires explicit configuration. Options: (1) Publisher publishes to SNS topics in multiple regions directly (simplest). (2) SNS → Lambda → publishes to SNS topic in another region (`boto3.client('sns', region_name='us-west-2').publish(...)`). (3) EventBridge → cross-region event routing → Lambda in target region → SNS publish. (4) For mobile push: publish to Platform Application in the region where app users are registered. <br><br> *Global mobile push: users in EU and US. SNS Platform Applications created in both us-east-1 and eu-west-1. User registration: register device token to nearest region's Platform Application (CloudFront geolocation or Route53 latency routing → appropriate regional API). Publisher: knows which region each user's endpoint is in (store with user record). Cross-region publish from Lambda: Lambda in us-east-1 can publish to SNS in eu-west-1 (STS credentials are regional but IAM is global — same role works across regions).* <br> *Fan-out with global reach: EventBridge Global Endpoints → single PutEvents call → events in both regions → each region's SNS topic delivers locally. Elegant solution: one API call, both regions receive event, each region processes locally. For disaster recovery: same events in both regions, each region processes independently.* <br>

1553. [ EventBridge ] What is the EventBridge partner integration and how does it differ from a custom event bus? ; Partner event bus: a dedicated event bus created by an AWS partner (Salesforce, Shopify, Zendesk, Datadog, etc.) in the customer's AWS account. Partner pushes events directly to the partner event bus. Customer creates EventBridge rules on the partner bus to route events. No API Gateway, no Lambda bridge needed. Customer cannot publish to the partner bus (read-only from customer perspective). Custom event bus: created by the customer, customer publishes events to it. Customer controls everything. Partners use officially registered EventBridge Integrations (PutPartnerEvents API). <br><br> *Partner setup process: (1) Customer subscribes to partner integration in EventBridge console (or marketplace). (2) EventBridge creates a partner event bus in the customer account. (3) Customer configures integration in the partner's system (e.g., Shopify admin: AWS EventBridge settings → AWS account ID + region). (4) Partner starts delivering events to customer's partner event bus. (5) Customer creates EventBridge rules on the partner bus to route events to Lambda/SQS/Step Functions.* <br> *Partner vs webhook: partner integration is more reliable (direct AWS service-to-service), no public endpoint to secure/manage, partner handles retry on failure, built-in authentication (partner authenticates with AWS). Webhook: HTTP endpoint (you manage security, availability, retry). EventBridge partners: native integration preferred over webhook for supported partners.* <br>

1554. [ SQS ] How does SQS handle server-side encryption and what are the options? ; SQS SSE (Server-Side Encryption): at-rest encryption of messages in SQS storage. Two options: (1) SSE-SQS: managed key (free, AWS-managed SQS key, AES-256). Enable: queue attribute `SqsManagedSseEnabled=true`. Simplest option. (2) SSE-KMS: customer KMS key. Enable: `KmsMasterKeyId=your-key-id`. Full KMS control (CMK, key rotation, cross-account, CloudTrail audit of key usage). Default: no encryption (messages in plaintext at rest). <br><br> *In-transit encryption: SQS API calls always over HTTPS (TLS). No additional configuration needed for in-transit. At-rest: choose SSE-SQS (free, simple) or SSE-KMS (auditable, cross-account, CMK). SSE-KMS cost: each SendMessage, ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage = KMS API call ($0.03/10,000 calls). High-volume queues: consider cost. SSE-SQS: no KMS calls, no per-call cost.* <br> *Cross-account scenario: Queue in Account A, SSE-KMS with CMK. Lambda in Account B wants to receive messages. Lambda role in Account B needs: (1) sqs:ReceiveMessage on the queue (via queue policy). (2) kms:Decrypt on the CMK (via key policy). Key policy must allow Account B's Lambda role to decrypt. Without KMS permission: Lambda receives encrypted blob, cannot decrypt. SSE-SQS: no cross-account KMS complexity.* <br>

1555. [ SNS ] What is the maximum message size for SNS, what happens to large messages, and how does SNS Extended Client Library help? ; SNS maximum message size: 256KB (262,144 bytes) including message attributes. If message exceeds 256KB: PublishBatch API returns `MessageTooLarge` error. Solution: SNS Extended Client Library (Java/Python/Node) — similar to SQS Extended Client Library. Payload > 256KB → library stores in S3, publishes SNS message with S3 pointer. Subscriber receives S3 pointer → library downloads from S3 transparently. Applications don't see S3 complexity. <br><br> *Configuration: `snsClient = SNSExtendedClient(boto3.client('sns'), S3BucketName="my-bucket", AlwaysS3=False, MessageSizeThreshold=256*1024)`. `AlwaysS3=False`: only use S3 when needed (> threshold). `AlwaysS3=True`: always store in S3 regardless of size.* <br> *SNS + SQS Extended Client: if SNS uses Extended Client (stores in S3) and SQS consumer uses Extended Client (reads from S3): works together transparently. If SQS consumer does NOT use Extended Client: receives JSON pointer (not payload). Consumer code must handle both cases or always use Extended Client. Consistency requirement: if producer uses Extended Client → all consumers must also use Extended Client. Standard SNS publish → SQS → consumer without Extended Client: works fine for < 256KB.* <br>

1556. [ EventBridge ] How does EventBridge API Destinations work with OAuth 2.0 authentication? Describe the flow. ; EventBridge API Destinations with OAuth 2.0: (1) Create Connection (credential store): specify OAuth endpoint URL, client_id, client_secret, OAuth scopes. EventBridge manages token lifecycle (requests/refreshes token). (2) Create API Destination: specify endpoint URL, connection, HTTP method, rate limit (max invocations/second). (3) Create EventBridge Rule: target = API Destination. When rule fires: EventBridge retrieves current OAuth access token from Connection → makes HTTP request to endpoint with `Authorization: Bearer {token}`. Token refresh: EventBridge handles automatically before expiry. <br><br> *Connection credential security: client_secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager (managed by EventBridge). Customer does not manage secret — EventBridge handles rotation/storage. Connection can be reused across multiple API Destinations (same IdP, different APIs). EventBridge never exposes the raw token to the customer — it's used internally.* <br> *Rate limiting: `InvocationRateLimitPerSecond` on API Destination: EventBridge throttles delivery to the configured rate. Events exceeding rate: buffered by EventBridge (up to retry window), then delivered. DLQ: events that cannot be delivered within retry window → DLQ SQS queue. Monitor: `Throttles` metric on API Destination → if high: increase rate limit (request increase from target API) or add SQS buffer.* <br>

1557. [ SQS ] A company runs 1,000 EC2 worker instances polling 50 different SQS queues (20 per instance). How should they optimize the polling architecture? ; Problems with 1,000 instances × 20 queues = 20,000 concurrent polling threads: high CPU for polling, many empty responses, high SQS API costs. Solutions: (1) Long polling: `WaitTimeSeconds=20` on all queues — reduces empty responses by 20x. (2) Consolidate queues: fewer queues, use message attributes for routing within queue. (3) Lambda-based workers: replace EC2 + SQS polling with Lambda ESM (AWS manages polling, no cost for empty polls). (4) SQS → SNS fan-out → Lambda: no polling at all. (5) Connection pooling: reuse SQS client across queue polls (not one client per queue). <br><br> *Lambda ESM advantage: AWS manages polling threads (you don't pay for empty ReceiveMessage calls). Lambda scales automatically with queue depth. 50 queues × Lambda ESM: 50 event source mappings, Lambda scales per queue. No EC2 instances needed for pure SQS workers. Cost: Lambda invocations only when messages present. EC2 polling: constant compute cost even when queues empty.* <br> *If EC2 workers must be used: Batch ReceiveMessage on each queue poll (10 messages per call). Long polling (20s). Adaptive polling: if queue was empty last N polls → reduce frequency (sleep 10s before next poll). Monitor: SQS `NumberOfEmptyReceives` metric — if high, increase long polling window or reduce polling frequency.* <br>

1558. [ SNS ] Explain SNS topic-based fan-out vs queue-based fan-out and when to use each. ; SNS topic fan-out: one publish → multiple subscribers simultaneously. Parallel, immediate delivery. Use: when multiple consumers need the same event independently. Pattern: OrderPlaced → SNS → [InventoryService SQS, BillingService SQS, EmailService Lambda]. Queue-based fan-out (without SNS): separate queues, producer sends to each separately. Sequential publish. Tighter coupling (producer knows all consumers). SNS fan-out: producer decoupled from consumers. Consumers subscribe/unsubscribe without producer changes. <br><br> *Queue-only fan-out problems: (1) Producer must know all consumer queues and publish to each. (2) Adding new consumer: requires producer code change and deployment. (3) Sequential publish: if one SQS SendMessage fails → inconsistency (some queues got message, some didn't). (4) Higher code complexity. SNS fan-out: producer publishes once to SNS → SNS delivers to all subscribers atomically (all or none attempt). New consumer: just subscribe to SNS (producer unaware).* <br> *Hybrid patterns: SNS → SQS (fan-out + durability). SNS → Lambda (fan-out + real-time processing). SNS → Firehose (fan-out + data lake). One SNS topic, multiple subscriber types. Example: UserRegistered SNS topic → [SQS (email worker), Lambda (real-time analytics), Firehose → S3 (data lake)]. Three different consumers, each gets the same event, each processes in its own way.* <br>

1559. [ EventBridge ] How would you use EventBridge to implement an SLA monitoring system that alerts when a multi-step process takes too long? ; Architecture: (1) Step 1 completion: service publishes `step1.completed` event to EventBridge with `processId`. (2) EventBridge rule: on `step1.completed` → Lambda → creates EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedule N minutes later (SLA time limit) for `processId`. (3) Scheduler fires if process not completed: `sla.breach` event published. (4) `step2.completed` event: Lambda cancels the Scheduler schedule (process completed on time). (5) `sla.breach` rule → SNS alert. <br><br> *Alternative: Step Functions Wait state with heartbeat. Step Functions starts on `step1.completed`. Wait for `step2.completed` event (using `.waitForTaskToken`). If `step2.completed` arrives: success. If heartbeat timeout (= SLA): state machine transitions to SLA Breach state → notify.* <br> *EventBridge Scheduler cancel on success: `aws scheduler delete-schedule --name sla-{processId}`. Lambda on `step2.completed` extracts `processId` → deletes Scheduler schedule with that name. If Scheduler fires before `step2.completed` → SLA breach alert. Race condition: both `step2.completed` and Scheduler could fire simultaneously. Handle: SLA breach Lambda checks DynamoDB for `processId` completion status before alerting (idempotent check).* <br>

1560. [ SQS ] Describe the complete flow of a Lambda function processing SQS FIFO messages, including ordering, error handling, and partial batch failures. ; Flow: (1) SQS FIFO queue: messages in groups (MessageGroupId). (2) Lambda ESM: polls queue, receives batch per active message group. (3) Lambda receives event with `Records` array. (4) Lambda processes each record sequentially (FIFO within group). (5) Partial failure: return `batchItemFailures: [{itemIdentifier: messageId}]` for failed messages. SQS: failed messages remain in queue (or DLQ after MaxReceiveCount), successful messages deleted. (6) Failed messages: block their Message Group until resolved (FIFO ordering maintained). (7) Success: all messages deleted, group unblocked. <br><br> *Lambda FIFO batch: Lambda can receive multiple messages from SAME group (up to batch size). Or multiple groups simultaneously (different Lambda invocations). FIFO guarantee: within one Lambda invocation, messages are in order. Across invocations of same group: Lambda ESM ensures sequential processing (next batch of a group only after previous batch completes).* <br> *Error handling: option 1 — `batchItemFailures` for granular failure. Failed messages stay in queue, succeed messages deleted. Option 2 — throw exception: entire batch fails, all messages return to queue (simple but wastes successful processing). Option 3 — DLQ routing: after MaxReceiveCount failures, message goes to DLQ. Lambda + FIFO + DLQ: when message goes to DLQ, the message group is unblocked (DLQ message = no longer in main queue). DLQ inspection: analyze failed message, fix bug, redrive from DLQ to main queue.* <br>

1562. [ SQS ] What is the SQS FIFO queue `ContentBasedDeduplication` feature and when is it appropriate to use? ; Content-based deduplication: SQS computes SHA-256 hash of message body as the deduplication ID (no need for producer to set `MessageDeduplicationId`). Two messages with identical body sent within 5 minutes: second is deduplicated (not delivered). Enable: queue attribute `ContentBasedDeduplication=true`. OR: producer specifies `MessageDeduplicationId` per message (overrides content-based if both configured). Appropriate: when message body uniquely identifies the event AND duplicate body always means duplicate event. <br><br> *When NOT to use: (1) Same event body represents different intents at different times: "deposit $100" sent twice = two legitimate transactions → content dedup would drop second transaction → data loss. (2) High-volume systems where multiple identical events are expected (sensor readings with same value). (3) Any scenario where same body = different events.* <br> *Best practice: explicit `MessageDeduplicationId` is safer. Use UUID from upstream transaction ID, order ID, or event UUID. Content-based: only for immutable events where exact same content = definite duplicate (idempotent by nature). If unsure: use explicit `MessageDeduplicationId`. Content-based saves the overhead of generating/tracking dedup IDs on the producer side.* <br>

1563. [ SNS ] What is the relationship between SNS and SES (Simple Email Service) for email delivery? When should you use each? ; SNS email: subscription-based notification delivery. Subscribers confirm subscription (click link). SNS sends email when topic receives message. Limited formatting (plain text). No email templates. No delivery statistics. Use for: operational alerts to internal teams. SES: full email service. Custom email templates (HTML, text). Delivery analytics (open rates, bounces, complaints). Bounce/complaint handling. Domain verification, DKIM, DMARC. Dedicated IPs. Use for: transactional emails (order confirmation, receipts), marketing emails, application-generated emails with HTML. <br><br> *Cost comparison: SNS email: $2/100,000 notifications. SES: $0.10/1,000 emails (10x cheaper). For high-volume emails: SES is significantly cheaper. For low-volume internal alerts: SNS email is simpler (no setup needed). SES requires: verified email/domain, sandbox exit for production.* <br> *Integration: SNS → SQS → Lambda → SES (processing SNS events, sending formatted HTML emails via SES). EventBridge → Lambda → SES (application event triggers SES email). SNS email subscription is the quick-and-dirty solution for "notify this email when alarm fires." SES is the proper solution for any user-facing email communication.* <br>

1564. [ EventBridge ] What EventBridge features support multi-account, multi-region architectures? Describe each briefly. ; (1) Cross-account event bus delivery: rule target = event bus ARN in another account. Resource policy on target bus allows PutEvents. (2) Cross-region event bus: rule target = event bus ARN in another region (same or different account). (3) Global Endpoints: active-active or active-passive multi-region with automatic DNS failover. (4) EventBridge Archive: per-region, can replay events to any account's event bus. (5) EventBridge Replication (Pipes cross-region): Pipe from SQS in region A to SQS in region B. (6) Organization-wide rules: EventBridge rule with Organization resource policy (all accounts in org). <br><br> *Hub-and-spoke security pattern: Central Security Account = hub. All member accounts = spokes. Each member account default bus → rule → Central Security Account bus → rules for SIEM/GuardDuty/Config. Organization resource policy on central bus: allow `PutEvents` where `aws:PrincipalOrgID = o-xxxxx`. New accounts joining org: automatically can route to central bus.* <br> *Multi-region disaster recovery: EventBridge Global Endpoint with Archive. Events published to global endpoint → primary region. If primary fails: DNS failover → secondary region. Secondary region has identical rules + targets + Lambda functions. Archive in primary region: enables replay if secondary region needs to catch up on missed events during switchover.* <br>

1565. [ SQS ] Explain the concept of SQS "poison messages" and strategies to handle them. ; Poison message: a message that consistently fails processing, causing it to be re-queued repeatedly until it consumes consumer resources and blocks processing of other messages (in FIFO). Causes: malformed data that crashes consumer, business logic exception for specific data, external dependency failure. Strategies: (1) DLQ with MaxReceiveCount: poison messages moved to DLQ after N failures (prevents infinite retry). (2) Exponential backoff: change visibility timeout exponentially on each failure. (3) Dead letter analysis: inspect DLQ messages, fix bug, redrive. (4) Pre-processing validation: validate message before processing (discard invalid early). <br><br> *Visibility timeout exponential backoff in Lambda: `receive_count = int(record['attributes']['ApproximateReceiveCount'])`. `backoff = min(2 ** receive_count, 900)` (seconds, max 15 min). `sqs.change_message_visibility(QueueUrl=..., ReceiptHandle=receipt_handle, VisibilityTimeout=backoff)`. Let message reprocess after increasing delay. After MaxReceiveCount: moves to DLQ automatically.* <br> *FIFO poison message: more severe. Poison message in FIFO group blocks ALL subsequent messages in that group (FIFO ordering: cannot skip). Strategy: lower MaxReceiveCount (2-3 attempts), quick DLQ routing. DLQ receives message → group unblocked → subsequent messages process. Investigation and fix in DLQ. Critical: never set MaxReceiveCount too high for FIFO queues with critical ordering (10+ attempts = 10x delay for all downstream messages in group).* <br>

1567. [ EventBridge ] How do you use EventBridge to automatically deregister unhealthy ECS tasks from a target group? ; Architecture: (1) ECS task state change event: `{"source":["aws.ecs"],"detail-type":["ECS Task State Change"],"detail":{"lastStatus":["STOPPED"]}}`. (2) EventBridge rule → Lambda. (3) Lambda: extract `taskArn`, check which target group the task was registered in (via ECS service description or stored task metadata), call `elbv2.deregister_targets(TargetGroupArn=..., Targets=[{"Id":container_ip,"Port":container_port}])`. (4) Ensures stopped containers are removed from target group immediately. <br><br> *Normal ECS operation: ECS service controller handles registration/deregistration with ALB target groups automatically. This EventBridge pattern is for non-service tasks (standalone tasks) or for custom logic when deregistration needs additional steps.* <br> *Enhanced pattern: EventBridge catches task stop → Lambda → (1) deregister from target group (2) log incident to DynamoDB (3) notify ops team if task stopped due to OOMKilled (`stopCode = EssentialContainerExited`, `containers[].reason = OOMKilled`). Lambda code extracts `detail.containers[].reason` to determine stop cause. OOMKilled: alert to increase task memory. Normal exit (code 0): expected → no alert needed.* <br>

1569. [ SNS ] A company needs to implement a notification system for 50 million users with both email and SMS preferences per user. Describe the architecture. ; Architecture: (1) User preference store: DynamoDB table — `userId` → `{email, phone, preferred_channel, notification_types: [...]}`. (2) Event trigger: application publishes `notification.requested` event with `userId`, `templateId`, `variables`. (3) Lambda (Notification Router): queries DynamoDB for user preferences. Builds message from template. Routes to email (SES) or SMS (SNS SMS) or push (SNS Platform Endpoint) based on preference. (4) Batch: for bulk notifications, Step Functions with DynamoDB read + Lambda fan-out. <br><br> *SNS role: SNS handles SMS (A2P SMS) and push notification delivery. SES handles email. SNS SNS topic fan-out not ideal for 50M users with different preferences — individual routing logic in Lambda is cleaner. SNS for individual SMS: `sns.publish(PhoneNumber="+1555...", Message="...")` or via Platform Endpoint (APNs/FCM).* <br> *Scale: 50M users × 1 notification = 50M Lambda invocations. Lambda concurrency limit: default 1,000/region. Batch Lambda: each invocation processes 100 users (from DynamoDB batch get). 50M ÷ 100 = 500,000 Lambda invocations. At 1,000 concurrent: 500 seconds (8 minutes) for full broadcast. For faster: increase Lambda concurrency limit. Kinesis: parallel processing. Multiple regions: partition users by region for parallel processing.* <br>

1570. [ EventBridge ] What is the difference between an EventBridge rule and an EventBridge Pipe? When would you use a Pipe instead of a rule? ; Rule: event pattern matching → multiple targets. One-to-many. Event sourced from any event bus. No built-in filtering beyond pattern. Targets invoked in parallel (all matching targets get the event). Pipes: single source → single target. Source: SQS, DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis, Kafka, ActiveMQ, RabbitMQ. Optional filter → optional enrichment (Lambda/Step Functions/API GW) → single target. Sequential pipeline, not broadcast. Use Pipe when: consuming from stream/queue source (not event bus), need enrichment before target, simpler point-to-point integration. <br><br> *Pipe vs Rule comparison: Rule: `Event Bus → Rule (pattern match) → Targets (1-15 in parallel)`. Pipe: `Source (SQS/Kinesis/DDB) → Filter → Enrichment → Target (1)`. Rules don't consume from SQS/Kinesis/DDB directly. Pipes don't source from event buses. Complementary, not competing.* <br> *When Pipe is better: (1) DynamoDB → OpenSearch: Pipe is cleaner than Lambda ESM (no consumer code, built-in filter, enrichment stage). (2) SQS → target with enrichment: Pipe filters + enriches before target, no Lambda polling code. (3) Point-to-point integration with one source, one target, optional transformation. Rule is better: (1) Event bus routing to multiple targets. (2) CloudWatch Events / AWS service events (only event bus sources work with rules). (3) Fan-out patterns (one event → many consumers).* <br>


1571. [ SQS ] A company wants to implement retry logic with exponential backoff for failed SQS message processing. Lambda is the consumer. Describe the complete implementation. ; Implementation with SQS: (1) Lambda processes message. On failure: DO NOT let Lambda throw exception. Instead: (2) Lambda changes visibility timeout with backoff: `backoff = min(30 * (2 ** receive_count), 900)`. `sqs.change_message_visibility(ReceiptHandle=..., VisibilityTimeout=backoff)`. (3) Lambda returns success (batchItemFailures empty for this message). (4) Message reappears after backoff. (5) After MaxReceiveCount failures: DLQ. Alternative: throw exception and rely on SQS natural visibility timeout (less control). <br><br> *Why manual visibility change is better: SQS natural retry = immediate re-visibility after visibility timeout. Multiple consumers might immediately pick up the failed message → thundering herd. Manual backoff: 30s, 60s, 120s, 240s, 900s (max) per failure. Receives are counted even during backoff. After MaxReceiveCount (say 5): DLQ. Total attempts: 5 × increasing delays. Time in queue before DLQ: 30+60+120+240+900 = ~23 minutes. Reasonable for transient failures.* <br> *batchItemFailures strategy: for messages you explicitly backoff (manually changed visibility): do NOT include in batchItemFailures. Mark as success in Lambda (you manually extended timeout). SQS won't re-deliver during backoff window. For messages that should retry immediately (transient Lambda error): include in batchItemFailures. This mix allows: manual backoff for known-transient errors, immediate retry for others.* <br>

1572. [ EventBridge ] A company needs a complete observability solution for their EventBridge-based microservices. What should the monitoring architecture include? ; Complete EventBridge observability: (1) CloudWatch Metrics: `Invocations`, `FailedInvocations`, `ThrottledRules` per rule per bus. Dashboard with all rules. (2) DLQ depth alarms: `ApproximateNumberOfMessages > 0` on each rule's DLQ. (3) EventBridge Archive: all events archived (compliance + replay). (4) Lambda logs: structured JSON logging with `eventId`, `ruleArn`, `processingTime` in CloudWatch Logs. (5) X-Ray: trace end-to-end event processing. Lambda X-Ray → downstream service X-Ray → correlate with EventBridge event ID. (6) Custom metrics: business metrics published by Lambda (`orderProcessed`, `fraudDetected`) to CloudWatch. (7) CloudWatch Insights: query Lambda logs for event ID to reconstruct full event journey. <br><br> *EventBridge correlation ID: EventBridge event `id` field is unique per event. Pass this ID through the entire processing chain. Lambda: log `{"event_id": event["id"], "action": "started"}`. DynamoDB: store `event_id`. SQS: pass as message attribute. CloudWatch Logs Insights query: `filter event_id = "uuid" | sort @timestamp` → full trace of event processing across all Lambda functions.* <br> *Distributed tracing: X-Ray service map shows EventBridge → Lambda connections. EventBridge → SQS → Lambda: X-Ray shows the full chain. Use Lambda Power Tools (Python/Node.js): structured logging, metrics, X-Ray tracing with minimal code. `tracer.capture_lambda_handler()` decorator automatically traces Lambda invocations. Alarm → runbook: each DLQ alarm should link to a runbook (wiki page) in the alarm description explaining how to investigate and redrive DLQ messages.* <br>
